In the year of Jihai of the Wanli era, when I was eighteen years old—the twenty-seventh year of our Emperor Shenzong Xianhuang—I was ordered by my late Palace Protector (Gongbao) to read the Śūraṅgama Sūtra during my leisure time from official examinations.
On the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, while reading the chapter on "The Karmic Results of Sentient Beings," I suddenly experienced a profound awakening. It was desolate...
It was as if a cool breeze were stirring a flute, or the morning bell striking against a pillow;

I dreamed at night that I had entered an empty hall where the World-Honored One stood facing south, his brow-mark of white hair radiating brilliant light from his countenance, and the robes and sleeves of his body shimmering.
All emerged within a white light. Beside me, someone called out, "Prostrate to the Buddha! I hurried forward and, having completed my prostrations, held a scripture case in my hands.
Inside were stored the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, as well as a copy of the *Da Xue*.

The World-Honored One took the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* with his own hand and placed it atop the *Vajracchedikā*, then personally instructed me, saying: "While worldly people know that reciting the *Vajracchedikā* brings merit..."
He knew that maintaining the recitation of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* brings especially great merit.

He knelt again to receive the scripture case, rose with solemn prostrations, and upon waking, the golden voice and perfect sounds of the Buddha fell clearly into his ears. From this, he recalled events from a previous life and reflected upon his former dream;

it permeated his spirit and reached his very bones, so that he believed it with absolute certainty and without doubt. While serving as an official in the literary garden (the Hanlin Academy), he researched historical precedents and heard that during the Jiajing era...
Zhao Dazhou of Neijiang served as a tutor for the Shuji (Imperial Academicians).

While supervising their studies of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he said to them, "You gentlemen are forty years old at most, or at least thirty. If you do not read this scripture now, when will you? He repeated these words three times.
The shadow of the whip has entered my heart; unaware of it, my mouth gapes and my teeth clash, as if struck by a sudden blow to the chest.

I have collapsed upon the path of officialdom and wandered through national calamities. I have endured ten thousand deaths, with scarcely anything remaining of my single body. Waves of rebuke fill my ears, and axes and spears crowd my frame.
The blood-path returns to the *p'o*, and the soul returns from the mountain of knives. The nightmare suddenly ceases, and the solitary clarity of the *ālaya-vijñāna* shines forth.
The accumulated causes of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* manifest as shadows within the mind and eyes. As the Sūtra says:

"Just as when you saw a wondrous object in years past, and after many years had passed, you suddenly beheld it again and remembered it vividly, without the slightest loss—truly true are these words. In the winter of the Gengyin year...

He set fire to the scriptures. Five chariots of ten thousand scrolls were reduced to the ashes of a kalpa; yet the Buddha images and the library kitchens, as the flames licked them, suddenly turned back.
The golden countenances and the Buddhist sutras seemed as if protected by divine spirits; for a long while they remained motionless, until he was struck with sudden alarm and awakened to realization.

This is truly due to the profound kindness and great compassion of our Buddha, the World-Honored One, who takes pity on me for wandering through the ocean of worldly texts throughout many births and vast eons.
I have sunk into a deep abyss and am unable to emerge on my own; therefore, I dispatch the Fire-Head Vajra to deliver this urgent warning so that you may pull me out and rescue me.

May you bear this affliction in mind and earnestly seek its remedy. With a hollowed heart, I make this vow to devote the remainder of my life to turning worldly letters and conditions toward Prajñāpāramitā, memorizing, reciting, and practicing it until the conditions for this sutra ripen. Even as I gaze upon the world, I have not yet...

I forgot it. Yet, when I opened the text, it was as if it were still there; I stroked these remaining embers from after the kalpa as if I were a person awakened from sleep recounting the events of a dream.
Opening the sutra-casket from within that dream was like a person who has woken up taking an object from a dream. This is the primary circumstantial origin of the *Foding mengchao*.
I have privately reflected upon the causes, and there are three: the habitual tendencies of names and words, the literary style of a scholar, and [the act of] plundering...

In contemplating the profound meaning of the "River" (the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*), I have modeled my work after the flowing stream; in gathering the remaining fragments of the "Perfect Penetration" (*Śūraṅgama Sūtra*), I have brought forth the principle of "hearing with compliance.
I have plucked the essence and spread out the painted colors, yet I have added water to the milk and mixed it with the clarified butter (*sarpis*);

I have gathered the mud left behind and smeared it upon this site. This bartering is no different from exchanging millet seeds, and this play is likewise like piling up grains of sand. The cause is one and the same.

Furthermore, my former companion from Shangdang once left behind the *Zhengmai* (The Correct Pulse). [This was obtained by my friend Cheng Mengyang of Youzhe while traveling through Ze and Lu. My fellow practitioner from Wumen—

First, I present the *Yuantong* (Complete Penetration). (When the first edition of the *Youxi Yuantong Shu* was published, my elder brother sent it to me, saying: "From now on, this shall serve as the standard for reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Eventually, three volumes were recovered from the ashes of oblivion, yet two copies still remained in their old covers. Only this initial volume serves as my primary resource.

Although it is not a perfect pearl from the ocean of enlightenment, it is nonetheless a bundle of torches for the path of darkness. This is the second cause. Regarding the inquiry into the mind at the Eastern Sea, [it was] brief...

Relying upon the lecture hall (referring to Master Guan Dongming), Mount Lao hangs its mirror; attending long at his robe and flask (referring to Great Master Haiyin Hanzhao), the established precedents grow ever more distant.

I am ashamed of my own lack of realization regarding the transmission of the Dharma. To depart from the circumstances of the Master, the diverging paths stretch vast and boundless; I trouble the wise with my reproaches.
I have inquired about various aspects of the bridge [to enlightenment], yet my turning of the mind has been slow and my years advanced. I now look up to you, Master, as my teacher;

the Great Dharma of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is clearly manifest, and the words that awaken the deluded are fully present. To enter your chamber, I dare to consider myself a true son; to cross the sea, I must ultimately rely upon a guide. This is the third reason.

The chapters and sections of this sutra are vast and extensive, and their indications vary. The three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) are divided horizontally, and the three samādhis intersect one another.

Since the old interpretations have already failed to clarify the provisional nature of the teachings, and the new chapters merely follow the defeated like those fleeing together, I humbly desire to distinguish between the general and the specific, to examine the similarities and differences, and to excavate the fundamental roots.
I shall weed out the tares and weeds so that the essential keys may be opened and cleansed, ensuring that the teachings and contemplations are clearly distinguished.
Thus, one may enter the gate of *samādhi*, illuminate the sun of *nirvāṇa*, and demonstrate the path for returning home with clarity, practicing the three...
The untainted study washes away with the waters of *śamatha*, severing the root of saṃsāric birth and death.

Only then can one repay the Buddha’s kindness above and fulfill one’s vows below; this is the fundamental intent. Having compiled this scripture over three years of diligent research, I have produced ten volumes of abridged excerpts. These are merely the "traps" for capturing meaning; they are not the fish themselves.
In the ten chapters of consultation and resolution, I dare to call this a preliminary introduction. My wisdom is as meager as that of a small bird in the sky, yet I laugh at my own dullness.
I, Ren Niu, hold this brush with a sense of shame and sigh deeply as I face these texts.
In the past, the Song Dynasty scholar Jìnglǎn once remarked that the Great Being of Qingliang followed the Bequeathed Teachings of the Tathāgata, taking no teacher as fixed in his studies:

he inquired about the Vinaya from Master Lǐ and received the *Nanshan xingshì* (Practices of the Southern Mountain) from Dànyī, before returning to transmit the *Nirvāṇa*, *Qǐxìn*, and *Fajie guān* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm).

Yuan recorded [his studies] at Waguan; he consulted Da Xun regarding the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; he studied the commentaries on the *Tiantai Zhiguan*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* under Jingxi;
and he sought resolution regarding the Chan teachings of the Southern School from Niu-tou Zhong and Jing-shan Qin.

He encompassed all capacities for enlightenment and harmonized all myriad principles, standing preeminent as a teacher of his era. As the distance from the Sage grew ever greater, the learning of the later generations became fragmented.

I have divided [this work] with the desire to gather the various schools together, to provide a definitive synthesis and comprehensive integration. I regret that there are few who can speak meaningfully on this matter.

Living in this present age, when the Dharma of the Final Age flows in reverse, the teachings of the times have declined, and demonic and heterodox forces arise like sharp blades; if one truly wishes to synthesize both the nature (xìng) and characteristics (xiàng) [of reality], [one must do so now].

Reconciling the teachings of Tiantai and Xuanzang, he plucks out the blindness of the born-blind and provides a supporting pillar against evil perceptions; therefore, one should propagate and expound this sutra to lead them along the foremost path.
This is the lamp of wisdom that illuminates the myriad dharmas and the mirror of the mind that exposes all manner of heterodoxy, rescuing and gathering in those of the final age.
This ferry and raft are for those who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). I place this statement at the beginning of the scripture, hoping it may serve as a text for making vows.

I look up and strike upon the Three Honored Ones, seeking their secret empowerment. May the World’s Dharma General, the Wise Awakening Wheel-Turner, one who bears the burden with profound resolve such as this scholar, bestow upon me the eye of wisdom;
may he examine and assist me. In the year of *Ātong Dunsang* (the Year of the Wood Sheep).

On the third day of the month, Qian Qianyi, the disciple of Haiyin from Mount Yu, the Elder of Meng, burned incense and prostrated himself with reverence, writing this in the right chamber of the surviving embers of the Jiyun Pavilion.
Qian Qianyi says: My transcription of this sutra began in the first month of the year of Xinmao.

It was not until the Mid-Autumn Festival of this year that I first began to draft the work. Over the course of seven years, the text has been revised seven times, and the manuscript has undergone five changes.
During these seven years, I have been gradually overcome by chronic illness and pressed by calamities; my lodgings have been cramped and frequent, and travelers have clamored around me.

Yet there was not a single day that I did not keep the scripture with me—whether in the fine rain on a solitary boat, amidst the cold wind by a short lamp, at dawn when the rooster crows by the window, or at the autumn door.
Insects chirp; by the dim light of a lamp, I gather my brush. Dregs of oil soak the paper as I write in minute characters, following the rules of calligraphy.
Marginal notes crowd the lines until my eyes feel like bursting with sparks and my shoulders and thighs feel as if weighed down by stones, my breaths coming in short, gasping intervals.

Only then do I retire to bed. Such is the hardship of composition for an old man with failing sight. That I have now been able to bring this work to completion is truly fortunate. The draft has been roughly finalized.
The arrangement was roughly completed; I set down my pen upon the bookshelf and sighed three times with deep emotion. What did I sigh for?
It was because I deeply lamented the true difficulty of exegesis and how difficult it is for one of our time to even approach the level of the ancients.

When I first unraveled this commentary on the sutra, I traced my way back upstream to Zizhong and followed downstream to Changshui. Their writing was substantial yet their principles were refined; their phrasing was concise yet their meanings were rich. There are those who have read them...

Regarding those who have not yet attained understanding after three or four readings: it is because they have only read them through once or twice over three or four years before finally gaining comprehension. It has always been the case from antiquity that few words contain many meanings;
there is nothing that does not accord with the Truth, and nothing that does not establish contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Now, when the Master’s commentary fills the page with its expansive waves, it is brilliantly clear as soon as one casts one's eyes over it for a moment. Yet, upon closer inspection, its flavor seems thin and insipid, like the blurred vision of one with cataracts.

They bring disorder to the Flower Garland (Avataṃsaka). There is nowhere for them to find true life. Some, perhaps, peel away the new and hunt for the exotic, counting their own treasures as precious;

yet they fail to discern how these various elements interrelate, reducing them all to withered straw dogs already cast aside. Others establish doctrines and open chapters, setting up distinct headings and sub-sections;

yet they fail to realize that each part inherently contains the whole, being originally but superfluous appendages to the enclosure. Since antiquity has long passed and the Sage Teachers no longer dwell among us, [such errors persist].
As the wisdom of scholars becomes increasingly coarse, their minds grow ever more narrow. As their learning becomes increasingly restricted, their vision grows ever less comprehensive.
Failing to grasp the fundamental source, they hastily pluck and prune [the texts] at random; failing to examine the benefits and harms, they first set up the block and hammer [of dogmatic critique].
Dao’an once said: "How could one who does not know the Dharma be so bold? I have long feared this. Having completed one round of this abridged compilation, I now offer it for impartial consideration.

I address you all with this humble request: from this day forward, regarding all Mahāyāna sūtras and the treatises composed by the various holy ones—whose fundamental tenets are profound and whose commentaries are extensive—one should follow the precedent of the *Buddhottama-sūtra* (the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*).

One should temporarily set aside the current texts and first rely upon ancient exegeses, striving to ensure that the Mind-essence of the Buddhas and the doctrinal vision of the ancient masters are brought into perfect harmony.
The channels of the blood and veins are cleared; the Great Meaning shines forth brightly, and the subtle words do not fall into ruin.
Only then may one cast a net over many schools, weighing their strengths and weaknesses, so that the four rivers may all flow together, and no single bubble be mistaken for the whole.

In this way, the life-force of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is sustained, and the lamp of the Dharma is extended. Thus, the various paths of teaching and practice need not fear being divided, nor will demons and heretics have cause for concern.

How fiercely it blazes! The True Dharma is difficult to encounter; the followers of Māra have not yet diminished. If you follow the Buddha’s words, that shall be called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
All of us, as virtuous friends, must not neglect these bitter words; together we shall cut off the torrential flow of elephants and avoid wandering through the cycles of birth and death.

If you consider the past to be right and the present to be wrong, or disparage others while exalting yourself, you will commit a great falsehood and fall into the Avīci Hell. The Buddha has given clear instructions—how could I dare to disregard them?

Regarding these words: the one who inspired, praised, consulted, and resolved [the doubts], personally adding headings and encouraging the completion of the work while vowing its circulation, was Master Chai Xueche.

The one who provided definitive guidance on the *Samādhi* (Sāmo), whose insights darkly accorded with ancient meanings, and who looked forward to the critical examination of the text before seeing its final completion, was Master Ouyi Zhixu.
The one who participated in the initial drafting and shared in the labor of its rough construction, gathering and selecting the pure [essence]... [text ends].

Liang was the assistant to those engaged in collateral discussion; he was Master Qushi Hanguang. He pointed toward the doctrinal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the *Yogācāra* teachings and examined the birth year of King Kaniṣka.
Master Songying of Chu was the one who searched out minor schools and provided extensive supporting evidence. Like a bright mirror or clear stream, he did not decline being polished;
through frosty skies and snowy nights, he was universally permitted to seek instruction. [This was done] by Xu within the Changgan community.

Master Shilin Yuan of this village, as well as my late friend Lu Xian Mengfu, have long been steeped in these teachings, having studied under Master Jieliduan, Master Xuecang Shao, and Master Jieqiu Can.
Morning and night they have struck the bell and chanted, praising them with joy and acclaim in one voice.
I venture to inform all quarters: do not withhold your instruction and guidance. All who have partaken of the milk of the Dharma shall hold this in reverence.
Awaiting the continuation of this work, on the eleventh day of the Mid-Autumn Festival in the year of *Qiángyǔ Zuò'è* (the 49th year of the sexagenary cycle),
I set down my brush once more at Bìwú Hóngdòu Zhuāng. On the day of the Longzhì (Winter Solstice) of that same year, I recorded this at the Xiūzàng Society of Chánggān Dàbào'ēn Temple.

On the winter solstice of the Dingyou year, I encountered snow while staying at Changgan Temple with Master Shao. I brought out this draft to seek his correction. Master Shao, together with Master Can of Jiqiu, braved the freezing cold to unroll the scrolls. For five days and nights, they neglected both sleep and food. Once the reading was finished, he spoke eight verses in praise and lamentation.

Jieqiu told me: "The Elder Xue has been a scholar of the Teachings for many years; he does not grant his approval of even a single word without due cause. He says that this commentary captures the full essence of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and that the countenances of the ancient sages are each present within it.

You should circulate it immediately and no longer harbor doubts or hesitations. Three years later, in the year Jihai (1659), at the end of winter in Jiangcun, I reviewed my old draft and found many errors and inconsistencies. Summoning all my remaining strength, I edited and finalized the text, transcribing it by hand. Under the dim light of a cold lamp, my aging eyes grew blurred and dim. It was only after five months that I finally set down my brush. The volumes were roughly completed. — Shao.

As the Master was returning in accordance with the sounds of the world, those who had entered his gate—such as Mao Jin, Huang Yi, and He Yun—successively passed away within a single year. As the Dharma generals were departing and his companions were thinning, he devoted himself for a time to the partial translation of scriptures.

The work has not yet been finalized, yet the feeling that "the flowing river hides the boat" has already arisen; it seems as though an immense number of kalpas have passed. Next year, I shall be eighty years old. My wife urged me to circulate this Dharma-treasure to repay the Buddha’s kindness, and so I have reluctantly yielded to her wish.

Nevertheless, I did not dare keep these commentaries hidden forever because Master Shao and those from various quarters earnestly entreated me. Furthermore, Master Shao’s entrustment of this single thought exceeds even the offering of one's body as a lamp or seat; I truly could not bear to let it remain suppressed and forgotten.

As Master Shao’s verse says: "The mind sought in seven places is empty at its root; In the eight returns, where can one find its tracks? Not realizing one’s own presence in the Han-yuan Hall, One asks again of the old man in his straw raincoat who fishes in the snow. It also says: "Neither arising nor ceasing is the causal root; The Tathāgatas of the three periods share a single gate."

If one wishes to recognize the state before the kalpas, when there was no turbidity, a single sound of the *qiang* flute causes the soul to wither in darkness. Those who read this commentary will know that Master Shao’s profound mind for the Dharma is such that each of the eight verses at the beginning of the scroll resounds like the striking of a mallet upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.

When Master Shao resided at Mount Kuang, he was consulted and requested by Xiao Boyu. Now, in this carving of the scriptures, Boyu’s younger cousin Mengfang has been the first to lead the effort; this too is a condition of the causal link.

Commentary by Dharma Master Weixiao of Chongfu Monastery, Tang Dynasty. In the early years of the Zhide era, Master Weixiao obtained a set of sutra cases with inscriptions written by Minister Fang [Xuanling]. He made a vow to compose a commentary (*śāstra*).

After eleven years, he finally began his work, completing three fascicles which he titled *Xuanzan* (Profound Praise). Its literary meaning is profound and subtle; it flourished widely in the northwest and is truly the patriarch of commentaries on this sutra. The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* states that when Master Weixiao was composing his commentary, he dreamed that Mañjuśrī, riding upon a *śarabha*, appeared before him.

When he was about to remove his ritual tablets from his mouth, he saw in a dream that they emerged from his mouth. Within the Huayan school, this is the wisdom of Mañjuśrī. In the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) by Yongming, it cites Master Daoke’s discourse on the sixty stages of holiness in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which profoundly accords with the principles of the Huayan school’s perfectly interfused dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

While people know that Changshui used the Huayan school’s tenets in his commentary on the *Śūraṅgama*, they do not realize that its origin lies with Master Daoke. In his exegesis of the opening phrase "At one time," Changshui identifies four pairs: the speaker and the teaching, and the recipient and the dharma.

The *Vajra-kanding-ji* states: "This is the purport of Master Kuò’s commentary on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. Thus we know that Changshui’s commentary drew extensively from Xuanzang’s *Xuanzan*. The *Wansong-lu* records Master Kuò’s analysis of the 'eight locations where the mind was sought,' which is particularly remarkable.
The *Chongfu-yihai* and other texts (also referred to as the *Xingfu*) likewise state this."

The Structural Analysis by the Śramaṇa Huizhen of Beiguan-tao in the Wei Dynasty (Master Zhen was the first to establish the principles of interpretation; he is the progenitor of the structural analysis of this sutra. From Zizhong onwards, all have followed his usage. Changshui says:

"Master Zhen’s eight sections and Zizhong’s seven divisions differ only in their method of opening and closing. Beifeng’s seven divisions and Wenling’s five parts differ in their headings and indications. [Note: This passage identifies the various commentators on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and their respective structural frameworks.]

The fundamental principles were not different; it was later generations who each erected their own barriers and walls, competing to establish their own topical divisions (*ko-dan*). Qingliang (Zongmi) criticized this as being like "dust already mixed with [the air] filling the paper and ink in vain. Now, I have pruned and excised these [divisions] throughout. Although I am said to follow the teacher Changshui (Zhizhou), in truth I am far more closely aligned with the tradition of Gantang (Huijing).
Following the precedent of the "River" before the "Sea," why must one innovate? Master Zhen also said: "Hui-zhen... (referring to Huijing).

The Commentary by Dharma Master Hongyuan of Zizhong, Shu (This commentary was composed following that of Chongfu; as for the principles of its interpretation, it draws upon those of Guntao. Among all commentaries ancient and modern, these three masters alone have paved the way.

Changshui’s commentary on the sutra frequently cites the old writings of Master Yuan without mentioning his name; however, by comparing the various works of *Yihai* with the present commentary, one can roughly discern them. His explanation of the three dharmas of śamatha states: ... [The text continues with the specific doctrinal analysis of the three dharmas of śamatha] ...

The general purport corresponds to the threefold contemplation within a single mind. This is the original source of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and it is the foundation upon which the masters of Mount Gu (Gushan) relied to interpret the sutras through the Tiantai system of contemplation.

*Lu Shan Fa-shi’s “General View of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra” (Pu-tai Lengyan Guanjian) from Da Xinglong Temple.* [Master Tai was a renowned monk during the Hongzheng era.

He studied the teachings and contemplations of the Xianshou school and once, while begging for alms in the nearby suburbs, encountered an elderly couple in a thatched hut who instructed him in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. He subsequently authored the *Lengyan Guanjian*, in which he vigorously refuted the *Huijie*. Master Mizang Kai remarked: "While it is not without its strengths and weaknesses regarding the intent of the scripture, there are many points therein that have not been previously articulated by others."]

*The Hanging Mirror in One Scroll and the General Commentary in Ten Scrolls* by the Great Master Deqing, Shanhai of Caoxi. [The Master] initially attended the lecture hall of Dharma Master Changqian Wujie, where he explored the teachings and contemplations of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

He bound himself at the Chan platform amidst ice and snow on Mount Tai, where he practiced with steadfast concentration and diligent investigation. Using this sūtra as his seal of verification and illumination, he dwelt in the Nārāyaṇa Cave on the East Sea, sitting in meditation for three years. As the sea became tranquil and the sky clear, one night he attained awakening.

Having fully realized the contemplative objects of the entire sūtra within his own mind and eyes, he committed his insights to brush and composed the *Hanging Mirror* in one scroll. Its language is rich and its principles are perfect, encompassing the entire web of contemplation. In his later years, he established a retreat at Mount Nanyue, where his disciples... *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary or corrupted transcription. The final sentence is incomplete, ending with "disciples" [狗門人].)*

I request that you further compose a General Commentary (*tongyi*) to explain the entire scripture. To state the essentials: it would merely be a supplement to the "Hanging Mirror. The Great Master’s spirit was like that of a king; he roamed the ocean of omniscience. He dreamed of ascending Maitreya’s Resplendent Tower, where he personally received the fundamental principles of consciousness and wisdom regarding defilement and purity.

Within his breast, a single volume of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* radiated light from the Sea-Seal (*sāgarāmudrā*), flowing forth from the inconceivable mind. He fused and expounded the threefold contemplation of the one mind. When the teachings of other masters were explained, they became the "threefold contemplation of the mouth," counting the treasures of others;

but when expounded by the Great Master, they became the "threefold contemplation of the essence itself," like observing fruit in the palm of one's hand. Since the nature of words is detached from them, there is no separate liberation. The phrase "hanging mirror" refers precisely to the meaning of the inexhaustible light of the Cool Grove (*Qingliang*) mirror. Now, [you] wish to...

"To grasp at the words of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) and attempt to measure the void—is this not the height of folly? (△ Master Zhuan Yu of Hunan, Guanheng: Initially, he relied upon Dharma Master Kongyin of Mount Wutai to study the sutras and treatises; later, he returned to the Great Master [Linji] to investigate the ultimate.)

He authored the *Commentary on the Four Reliances* in ten fascicles. In it, the Master [Zongmi] held up a mirror, dividing the scripture into four sections based on the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), which correspond to the five divisions of Wēnlíng. First is the essence of the three contemplations, which is the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Second is the aspect of the three contemplations, which is the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Third is the function of the three contemplations, which is the Path of Realization (*adhigamamārga*). Fourth is the names of the three contemplations, which is the conclusion of the scripture. Furthermore, he stated that throughout the entire *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, from beginning to end, its teachings, meanings, principle, wisdom, cause, and effect are all subsumed under the single character "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

This character "contemplation" is in its entirety the Tathāgatagarbha mind; therefore, it is called the "Ultimate Firmness of Śūraṅgama. "Ultimate" refers to the wisdom that contemplates, while "firmness" refers to the principle that is contemplated. By summarizing these essential points, one may perhaps avoid losing the fundamental tenets of the Master’s school.

*The Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra by the Great Master Zibai Daguan Zhenke*, one fascicle (extracted separately from the *Complete Works of Zibai*). (△ The Great Master attained teacherless wisdom.)

Possessing a diamond-like mind, he was like a dragon in the water or an elephant on land. In his study of the scriptural teachings (*śāstra-yāna*), he investigated with profound reflection and analyzed principles with precision; he did not use nature to negate characteristics, nor did he use the school’s tenets to abridge the teachings, nor did he use the worthy to suppress the eminent. Among the masters of recent times, none has been as public, sincere, and vast as he.

Having internalized the writings of Shimen, it is said that only after five hundred years would one finally understand the discourse on the fundamental principles of the School of the Lineage (*zongmen*) and the mechanism of illumination and function, or life and death. Regarding his discussion of Changshui, he stated: "Master Xuan, upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, gave rise to doubt;

through this doubt, he studied under Langye and suddenly awakened to the mind that is fundamentally pure and still. He thus became the patriarch of the Mind School for a hundred generations. Initially, he did not rely on Jiyin’s arguments to dismiss or brush them aside through mere intellectual interpretation. This is the Master [Fayan].

Whenever he spoke of the true teaching-essence (*dharmakāya*) of this land—namely, that its purity resides in auditory hearing—he would employ the samādhi of written characters to realize that pure auditory hearing. This is the teaching-essence of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Whenever he expounded upon it by extracting the meaning from the text, he severed all conceptual entanglements, transcending the realm of mere commentary. This present interpretation is but what happened to appear in his draft notes.
*One Scroll of the Structural Analysis of the Commentary on the *Hongen Jing* by Master Xuelang Sanhuai*. (This master and Great Master Hanshan emerged together from the gate of Wuji [the Infinite].

When the Great Master entered Mount Wutai to investigate the Great Matter amidst piles of ice and snow, Master Sanhuai inherited his former teacher’s Dharma seat. As the Buddhist Way had long been obscured in the South, he emerged as a guiding eye for humans and devas; his vow was like that of two wheels upon a single chariot.)

In the lecture halls of the north and south, scholars stubbornly cling to old hearsay; their commentaries are passed along like postal mail, becoming entangled and over-familiarized. The Master’s expositions were clear, flowing, and unobstructed, speaking in accordance with the nature of reality (dharmatā). Those who heard him felt their ears and eyes renewed, and their views were cleansed and opened.

Once the lecture ended, he would simply depart in silence. Even when people requested further teachings, he would only smile. Having cast aside all reliance on words and letters, the Master refused to compose written works. Although his lecture seats flourished after his passing, his subtle teachings were lost.

Among the texts currently circulating and studied by the world, there are often jumbled annotations that distort the original meaning. Within the bookcase of my late friend Mr. Lu, I discovered a bundle of old papers titled *Xuelang’s Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Its branch-by-branch exegesis and essential points are concise and unburdensome; its structural analysis (*kepan*) is particularly unique and profound. Observing its indications...

I believe this work captures the essentials and grasps the main principles; by pointing at the finger, one sees the moon. Regarding the lineages of classification and practice throughout the ages, they have been as turbulent as swirling dust and smoke, with everyone fearing only that they would not be swept away and eliminated. Now that the man from Ying has passed away and the art of carving wheels is no longer transmitted, I shall briefly rely upon these fragmentary manuscripts.

To preserve the profound meaning [of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*], those various spurious attributions cannot be distinguished even by a golden key. May those who possess the "single eye" of discernment be fortunate enough not to be deluded by them. (△ The high-disciple of Xuelang [Yunqi Zhuhong] specialized in lecturing and commentary;

he was known as "Nao at the mouth and Yu at the hands. This "Yu" refers to Master Tongrun of Erheng, the author of the *Lengyan Hezhe*. While this work extensively discusses the lectures and instructions of his own school, its exposition of the fundamental tenets of the sect is omitted and has not been transmitted. In his middle years, he offered incense to the Buddha and turned toward Shangdang;

furthermore, he frequently cited public cases (*gongan*) and drew upon karmic conditions, borrowing the talk of "raising the staff and shouting" from the Chan gate to supplement the oral delivery of his lecture hall. This is like a man from Lu wearing a hat from Yue while speaking with a Wu accent—how could he establish a broad school? In the end, it only served to expose his own deficiencies. As the saying goes: *(Note: The text provided ends mid-sentence regarding the proverb.)*
"Only when one's wisdom exceeds that of the teacher is one fit to transmit the Way—is this not so?
*Yunqi Lianchi Heshang Zhuhong’s One-Volume Record on Feeling the Elephant in the Śūraṃgama Sūtra*. (Master Yunqi cultivated the Pure Land path and was a great master of Buddha-recitation;

as he did not reside within the schools of Chan or Exegesis, he used the metaphor of "feeling the elephant. However, he maintained that the meaning of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) is fully present throughout the text, such that any other [contemplation] must necessarily encompass *dhyāna*, and *dhyāna* must necessarily harmonize emptiness and the provisional. At that time, the Master divided the text into sections...)

To attempt to allocate [the text] according to its literary divisions is impossible. Furthermore, it is claimed that Mañjuśrī established five titles for this sūtra, which the translators then abbreviated and established as headings; one should not, however, take these ten fascicles and force them to correspond to those titles by asserting that "Fascicle X is the Great Buddha-Crown" or "Fascicle Y is the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata," and so forth.

At that time, *Jiaoguang zhengmai* (The Correct Pulse of the Interpenetration of Light) was first transmitted to the region south of the Yangtze River. People believed it was endorsed by Yunqi [Zhuhong], and it stirred the various quarters of the Buddhist world. Yet they did not realize that this text—like the "Blind Men Touching the Elephant"—was a case of transcendent, intuitive understanding;

thus, although he had already arrived at the site of their ritual straw mats (*maojue*), he had merely pricked their vital organs (*gaohuang*). Later, Chai Zicheng took advantage of the occasion to open a lecture series at Mount Yu, where he also said: "When the World-Honored One preached the Dharma, he pointed directly to the human mind; with a single phrase or a single verse, one may enter the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama* and achieve cultivation and realization."

"O Yuantong, why must one necessarily trace every stroke and count every character, allocating the phrases of a single sutra like threading flowers with a string before one can enter the Three Contemplations? This Master’s critical selection is likewise based on 'feeling the elephant' [without seeing it];

it may serve as a teacher for those who merely recite the text, acting as medicine to address their specific ailments. (△ At that time, there were lecturers who emerged from Yunqi. Chai Zicheng produced ten volumes of lecture records; Yunqi Guangmo composed the *Zhijie* (Direct Explanation), ten volumes; and Yushan Helin Daji composed the *Wenyi* (Textual Meaning), ten volumes.)
The commentaries and sub-commentaries all contain much that is worthy of adoption.
There are ten fascicles of the *New Commentary* by Dharma Master Jie Cheng of Zhongchuan, Neijiang; and ten fascicles of the *Zhengguan Commentary* by Dharma Master Zhen Cheng of Wutai, Kongyin.

[Dharma Master] Zhongchuan thoroughly understood the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other various sūtras, extensively researched the Abhidharma Piṭaka, and probed the profound and sought out the hidden to provide a comprehensive explanation of this sūtra. He was truly what is called "one who knows much."

He expounded the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) while speaking little of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Yet, when compared to those of our own time who merely parrot what they have heard or read, he was as far apart from them as heaven is from the abyss. Kōin was one of the "Five Masters" during the Wanli era; his Dharma seats in the north were most flourishing.

He extensively cited various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras to verify the stages and positions of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and to refute the Tiantai school’s claim that they borrowed the names of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) to designate the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). The various masters of the Shanjia lineage vigorously took up their pens to criticize and challenge him, yet regarding the determination of right and wrong, no definitive conclusion has been reached.
Master Yin was profoundly versed in the Tripiṭaka and courageous in maintaining his doctrinal positions; among the worthy masters of recent times, he was truly an outstanding figure.

*One Scroll of Questions and Answers on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra by Master Qiūmíng Yīn Mài (Yìn Jiǔjìng) of Jīnlíng and Master Guān Zhìdào (Guān Gōng) of Dōngmíng, Tàicāng.* (Master Yīn also has *One Scroll of Supplementary Remarks from the Róngmù Studio*, which discusses the essential meanings of the *Śūraṅgama*;
Master Guān further has *Five Sets of Plain Discourses*. Master Yīn separately compiled the *Ten Volumes of the Wēnlíng Essential Explanations with Supplements*;

Master Guān separately has the *Record of Questions and Debates on Awakening Delusion*, among other works. (△During the Lóng and Wàn eras of our dynasty, there were two masters in the Confucian school who possessed the Way. Master Yīn practiced stillness at Niǔshǒu; he drew forth [his realization] from the "Golden Wisdom" (*Jīnhuì*) chapter of the *Śūraṅgama*, the *Vajracchedikā*, and the *Gāndhārī* [or *Qíánhùi*].)

Wu [Zhiyuan] remarked: "The *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* has circulated throughout the Five Indias; it contains many meanings not heard in other scriptures. While the commentaries of Gushan and Wuxing are extensive and provide broad exegesis, they do not necessarily accord with the original scripture. It would be better to simply explain the *Śūraṃgama* by means of the *Śūraṃgama* itself.

After his awakening, he read all the various commentaries extensively and declared that those which directly express his own realization—using the scripture to explain the scripture—none surpass those of Wenglun (Zongmi). Examining their fundamental tenets, it appears he was one who "judged the teachings through Chan. Master Dongming, a preeminent Confucian scholar of his era, attained realization within the Nature-Ocean of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

He established the learning of the *Qianyuan Tongtian* (the Great Ultimate Unifying Heaven) and maintained both Confucianism and Buddhism. In his later years, responding to inquiries from various schools, he eloquently expounded the profound meaning of the *Śūraṃgama*, discussing the primordial luminosity of the Ocean of Enlightenment and thoroughly investigating the myriad phenomena.

This treatise discusses the wondrous luminosity and clear awakening at the very point where ignorance first arises; it directly probes the primordial origin of the past universe. Its discourse traverses the three realms both horizontally and vertically, vast and unrestrained, emitting clouds and seas beyond the sands of the Ganges.

Even those of worldly wisdom and intellectual talent must all fold their tongues and retreat in awe, let alone those of middling or inferior capacity. Having been enlightened by this commentary, I have briefly set forth these introductory remarks merely to draw out the thread and open the lock [of understanding]. To raise doubts and pose challenges is not intended as a presumptuous offering of incense, nor is it an expression of mere personal preference.

Lu Ling’s Former Librarian Fengyi, *Lengyan Zongtong* (The Master of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s Penetration of the Principle). [He] visited Nanyue Tiantai Temple in Jinke, where he paid homage at the Platform of the Venerable Master Zhiyi.

He made a vow to inscribe the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* upon the stone chamber to fulfill his lifelong aspiration of venerating the scriptures. Subsequently, he extensively gathered the words of the patriarchs and harmonized them with the scriptural text, adopting the principles of "penetration of the principle" (*zongtong*) and "penetration of the teaching" (*shuotong*) to compose this work.

Yongming [Yanshou] once remarked: "When the Buddhist teachings are already clear, one must present the intent of the patriarchs. Those who attain the Buddha-vehicle all accord with the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Now, however, they borrow from the gateways of the school to arrange public cases (*kung-an*), beginning by treating the principle as the host and the teaching as the guest, and ultimately intending to use the patriarchs to command the Buddhas. [Fengyi] refers to Ānanda’s emission of light...

To grant certification (*in-ka*) is still to enter through the gate; it is not as good as a master of clear eyes who turns his head and strikes his own skull, letting go and attaining thorough enlightenment. To judge matters in such a manner constitutes a great falsehood. Not only does Ānanda fall short of a true master, but even the Tathāgata would be far surpassed by the various patriarchs.

No matter how you speak of the profound or the subtle, if you are uniformly "over-the-head" in your assessments, I fear that in judging the teachings and the school, both gates will lead to failure. Among Confucian scholars of recent times, this trend is especially rampant.

They peddle the "pointing at the moon" and dissect the "transmission of the lamp," unaware that their eyes are clouded by the five flowers; they claim to have swallowed all Buddhas with their mouths. This overflow of abuse has not yet ceased, for there are those who act as the first to initiate it. Can one not sigh three times over the golden word?
*Jiaoguang Fashi Zhenjian Lengyan Zhengmai* (Ten fascicles; Preface composed by the Prince of the Fei State in the Gengzi year of the Wanli era;
collated and carved for publication by Master Deng Miaofeng). *Tiāntái Youxi Fashi Chuandeng Xuanyi* (Two fascicles;
an exposition clarifying his teacher Baisong’s *Lengyan Baiwen*). *Huijie Yuantong Shu* (Ten fascicles). *Wuyi Suhua Fashi Zhixu Xuanyi* (Two fascicles; text by Master Zhixu).

*Jujing* (Ten Volumes). [In the preface, Jiaoguang himself recounts the circumstances of its origin: he claims to have attained awakening through the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; while ill, he beheld the Buddha, who exhorted him to compose a commentary on the scripture. He swept away the systems of Tiantai and Guanxiu, and refuted the *Huiguiji*. It was circulated as far as Youzhou and Shuofang, causing a sensation throughout Jiangzuo.]

All have said that since the scriptures first entered China, no such interpretation had existed; now, however, this deficiency has been somewhat remedied. Indeed, one who emerges from beneath a hundred generations to strip away stale expressions and bring forth his own insights cannot be called anything other than a heroic figure of the North.

Yet, because his discernment of the Dharma was not yet precise and his establishment of his school was too impetuous, he originally sought to refine the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) to honor the profound sutras, but instead dissected the entire scripture to force it into correspondence with the three dharmas. His interpretations of the *Samādhi* were confused and still followed old hearsay; the *Buddhapiṭaka* (Buddha-peak) was merely grafted onto it, failing to constitute a true meaning.

He established a separate "Initial Expedient" at the beginning, and arbitrarily discarded one of the three gradual practices (*krama-caryā*). In every case, he followed his own mind and deemed himself correct; I fear that by thus erasing the traces of the original, he only increased the errors. As for his refutation of the function of consciousness and his pointing out that the sense organs do not correspond [to their objects], these may perhaps be seen as not entirely fitting.

Regarding the doctrinal principles (*śāstra*), because they were established based on what he had heard, some have criticized his own composition of the *guanmen* (contemplation gates). Fearing that if these were not definitively edited and clarified, the path of our school would ultimately become distorted and confused, I, though ignorant, did not dare to join those who, like "those with axes in hand," sided with the Shanjia (Mount Home) faction to incite further strife.

Youxixi strove mightily to support the Tiantai school, relying exclusively on the *Huigie* (Comprehensive Explanations). While his mastery of the scriptural teachings was extensive and his exposition of the contemplation networks was detailed, the breadth of his teachings resulted in much textual prolixity, and the detail of his contemplations meant the underlying principles were not yet fully perfected. Consequently, his insights often fell into fragmentation, and his doctrinal interpretations rarely adhered to the essential core.

The *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) contains many passages that extensively clarify the Master’s teachings. These serve as the fingers and toes of a single school and provide nourishment from the stale broth of the Four Teachings; such instances are truly numerous and could well be set aside on a high shelf. However, Ouyi’s *Biaoshi Sanmo* (Explanations of Samādhi) correctly elucidates samādhi, distinguishing between the dialects of the Sanskrit sounds and verifying the general and specific characteristics of the dharmas.

The masters Changshui and Wujiang find their core intent in mutual resonance; having consulted and resolved matters at the outset, they rely on this for verification. Thus, it was adopted to guide the masses. This Master’s discipline is pure and solemn, and his insight is solitary and peerless.

[This work] is clear. Its author has been diligent in his composition, showing no sign of ceasing. As for those who establish their own altars and disregard the ancients and moderns, asserting or refuting as they please, there are not a few instances of what is right and wrong. One must await the wise masters of all quarters to publicly and impartially determine these matters; it is not something I, [the author], dare to interject my opinions upon.

(△ Regarding the commentaries and exegeses produced in recent times, they appear in great abundance. Among the Tiantai school, there are works such as those by the lecturer Cuiru; among the Chan school, there are works such as the *Yijian* (Personal Views) by Chan Master Zhanran.

Among works composed by lay officials (*zai guan*), there are those by Wang Mochi, including the *Zhizhuyue*, and Wang Jingfeng’s *Yishi*. All of these have been utilized for collection, with no intention of omitting them. However, as for those that have gathered fragments into texts that are erroneous or stubbornly biased—such as the so-called "definitive editions" (*dingben*) transmitted in recent times—they harbor the conceit of the King of Yelang and take the impoverished...)

How could the execution of those who secretly assume titles defile the void? Why use the withered and rotten remains of partisan enmity as a pretext for general eradication? (I shall not trouble you with further correspondence).

*The Ten Volumes of the Śūraṃgama Sūtra as Expounded by the Two Laymen Zhong and He* (Preface by Zhong Xing Bojing of Jingling: "Not deeming myself ignorant and stubborn, I have vainly hoped for faith and understanding. I have dwelt upon and sought through various scriptures, researching them for five years.

The middle son of the layman He of Yongxin, named Keshang, possesses a nature of wisdom and eloquence, and a profound heart for extensive study. Formerly, when we gathered at the White Gate (Nanjing), he expounded [the teachings] several times. Later, while in the official residence of Min, he spent forty days peeling away the layers [of meaning]. He distinguished cause and effect within this sutra and analyzed the similarities and differences among the various teachings. From here...)

That which is harbored within my innermost thoughts cannot be proclaimed unless through my brush; yet, fearing it might be lost, I have exerted myself to compile this commentary. I have taken the phrase "as it is taught in the sutras" (如所如說) as one of the five standard phrases used for the Buddha’s words.

Just as I had finished a preliminary abridgment, I came across this manuscript. Alas, my two friends have anticipated my own mind! Regarding the analysis of principles and the arrangement of chapters therein, Mr. He has undergone great hardship in establishing the model; regarding the elucidation of meaning through the text, Mr. Zhong contributed most significantly as the scribe.

As for what is called "harmonizing the discrepancies among the various old commentaries and weighing their repetitions and brevities," this refers to the debates between Jiaoguang and Youxi, where their arguments were like the clashing of arrows and halberds. Taking advantage of those chaotic tracks, I have offered a brief synthesis. Therefore, it cannot simply be set aside as the mere literary composition of a Confucian scholar.

To initiate something from scratch is difficult; to repair what already exists is easy. To ascend a height and gaze into a deep abyss—this is truly the moment for us. Those who have passed away could rise again; may they assist me and inspire my thoughts. It is a pity that the strings have been cut short, leaving no further way to polish the jade.
As I look up and down at these written words, my sighs are many.

(Excerpt from the *Mēngchāo* citing the *Shūsè lüèlì*: This commentary follows the tradition of Chángshuǐ. Subsequently, the main text of the sūtra is set in large characters and arranged below; following this, the full text of the citations is presented. Where only a single commentary is cited, the character "shū" (commentary) alone is used. For the *Yàoyì* of Lètán, both characters "biāo" and "zhǐ" are used.

Others, such as Xuénǚ’s *Zhèngzhēn chāo*, Gūshān’s *Gǔxiǎng*, Wúxīng’s *Xūnwén*, and Jìyīn’s *Zūndǐng lùn*, are cited by their personal names, their monastic titles, or the titles of their works, appearing interspersed throughout the text without any fixed rule.

In recent commentaries, there has been confusion regarding what has been heard and seen; thus, many list the names and titles [of previous masters] to prevent their contributions from being suppressed or lost. If one considers the *Yuántōng shū* of Yōuxī, which styles itself as "Tiān... [the title continues].)

The title "Master" (Tai) is a usurpation of the designation used by the Fourth Patriarch of our own school; I have not dared but to excise it for the sake of correction. My systematic analysis and categorization of the scriptures follows entirely that of Changshui, though I have occasionally omitted redundant elaborations. This was not done out of a desire to arbitrarily establish a definitive version, as is fully detailed in my correspondence regarding these decisions.
May those who read this examine it closely.
Preface to the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi Sūtra of the Great Buddha-Usnīsa*, Fascicle One (Part One).

Narrated by Qian Qianyi, the Elder of Meng, Disciple of Haiyin.
Question: Regarding the ten sections for resolving doubts and meanings, you have established chapter headings before composing the commentary.

While these five layers of ten sections were all previously termed "prefatory summaries" (*xuānxù*), why is it that in this present abridgment, following in the footsteps of former masters, the first ten chapters have been renamed "Resolving Doubts" (*zījué*)? Answer:
It is said that "suspended exposition" refers to outlining the purport of a single scripture, while "consultative resolution" refers to resolving one's own doubts.
Suspended exposition is discourse for the sake of definitive determination; consultative resolution is the principle of inquiry and consultation.

This is because the fundamental tenets of the Sage’s teaching must be definitively established, yet those at the initial stage of study rely on doubt to investigate and examine them thoroughly. Only when there is doubt can one consult.
There are those who can only reach a resolution after consultation; when they encounter doubt, they strike out with vigor and intensity, like fire produced by drilling wood.

When one is able to consult, the refutations and critiques are vast and manifold, comparable to wearing a *xī* (a ring for loosening knots) so that a knot may be untied. It is thus with the Bodhisattvas, and it is understandable even for ordinary people.
How much more so for the Buddha-dharma, which is profound and deep, where various doctrines are in conflict, establishing this while refuting that, and from which divergent streams proliferate?
I am troubled. To treat the master as a slave and fail to distinguish between the cardinal directions is a grave error. To set a single net for all is to promote one thing while discarding the rest;

to cast a net across all streams is to fear that many divergent paths will confuse the way. Therefore, I have extensively set forth my own views, not shying away from the simplicity of a novice, listing my many ailments to request their respective remedies.
Like one who has smeared his face and head with mud asking for directions, I rely on my own mind and make arbitrary judgments.

I know I shall be spared from error. To empty the self and seek the fundamental source, there are already many masters; yet, drawing inspiration from the "Qingliang" (Cool and Refreshing), I have briefly set forth ten intentions for composing this commentary (*śāstra*).
First, because of the general and specific aspects of the Dharma-gate; Second, because of the refutation and establishment regarding the three contemplations;

Third, to manifest the teachings and contemplations; Fourth, to specifically demonstrate the skillful means; Fifth, because of the provisional and ultimate according to the capacity of the audience; Sixth, to categorize the meanings and establish the definitive structure.

Therefore: first, because of the increase in hearing and cultivation; second, because of the stages of practice for humans and devas; third, because of gains and losses throughout antiquity and the present;

The third is the thorough contemplation of characteristics. Since it was said, "If you wish to know the path of śamatha, you must vow to transcend birth and death," from this gate of contemplation, the teaching is unfolded in successive layers:

The cultivation and realization of those of superior faculties are both based upon the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*. Unveiling the explicit texts of these two sūtras, one verifies the questions and answers of this single assembly.

The Gate of Contemplation. Herein are fully enumerated the various sages who chose their perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). This is the primary expedient through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained Bodhi;

The answer is: To cite the one is to [cite] the three; to speak of the three is to [speak of] the one. This too is but a general, inclusive discourse. It is correct to say that within the three contemplations, citing the one is to cite the three.

To single out *śamatha* (calm abiding) must necessarily imply the inclusion of the other two wondrous aspects. This is stated in the "Universal Eye" chapter of the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*, which speaks solely of relying on the practice of *śamatha*. II.

Fifteen wheels. This explains the single and the double, the sequence of before and after, and the marking and binding. It concludes by saying: "In the cultivation of *dhyāna*, first take up the method of counting.

He proceeds by other practices until he returns to the universal illumination of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Here, stillness and illumination are non-dual; it has never failed to be wondrous, and it has never failed to perfectly encompass those other practices.

This means that the three contemplations are simultaneously one and three; the gates of the beginning, middle, and end cannot be mentioned in isolation. This is correct. *Nirvāṇa*.

The Buddha said: "Vipaśyanā alone is certainly unable to destroy the afflictions. He then explained at length the characteristics of all meditative concentrations (samādhi).

That is precisely three and precisely one. Furthermore, how is this to be reconciled? When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, there is both synthesis and analysis.

In synthesis, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently so; in analysis, their manifested characteristics (*ākāra*) are distinct. As it is said: "Except for *śamatha* and the appearance of a Buddha.
To apply the principle of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-yi*), it should be stated fully: "Except for *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*, and the appearance of a Buddha."
This is either the Buddha’s speech containing subtle nuances, or it is the result of the translator’s omissions; thus we know that it certainly cannot be so.

Regarding the three types of contemplation gates, there are many instances where they are presented out of sequence according to the capacity of the audience. To necessarily condemn such cases as "losing the subtlety" (miào)—whose fault would that be?
Some say that *śamatha* is merely a single method of contemplation and that the initial expedient means is not the primary focus of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.

"The King of the Śūraṅgama [Samādhi] is not sufficient to match it. He replied: "The great Bodhisattvas who requested instruction on the practice of the *Awakening of Perfect Enlightenment* all asked:

Regarding the West Sea, when it was being constructed, there were stairways and embankments; the rivers and streams winded and curved. Tiantai said: "Expedient means (upāya) are the gates.

"Māra has obscured my mind; I weep in sorrow and lamentation. People reproach me because of the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*). Now, as I beg for alms, I have fallen into lust.

If it is still so for those who remain [in the world], how much more so for those on the stage of training (śaikṣa) who have not yet abandoned desire? Due to their past habitual tendencies toward the karma of worldly pleasure, they were always fond of singing and chanting;

Among the three poisons, sexual desire is the most poisonous; among all forms of decay, the decay caused by women is the heaviest. This sutra takes the seat of lust as its starting point and establishes its teaching by means of this warning. [Thus] the crown of the head is surrendered.
He uses light to illuminate and dispel the heat of affliction; he preaches the Dharma of the Crown to pull one from the mire of desire.

Third, it is because the karmic conditions of past lives follow one another; the Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, throughout kalpas of past lives, you and Mātaṅgī have shared causes and conditions of affectionate love."
Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) do not arise from a single lifetime or a single eon. The *Mādrī-sūtra* and other scriptures of the Hīnayāna state explicitly:
"This Mādrī was the wife of Ānanda for five hundred previous lifetimes; when husband and wife met, they regarded one another as elder and younger brothers."

Their pursuit through marriage for five hundred lifetimes is a defiled cause. Relying upon roots of goodness accumulated over many kalpas, [he] manifested in a single kṣaṇa...

Fourth, because his extensive learning over many kalpas had been without merit, the *Śāstra* states: "Ānanda listened to, upheld, and recited various sūtras with great benefit."
Because he had contemplated [the world] too much, his wisdom was great while his power to restrain the mind was slight.

Having once encountered the calamity of Dhanagā, although he had for many kalpas memorized and maintained the twelve divisions of the scriptures, they were like water poured from one jar into another, or like shadows and winds—nothing upon which he could rely.

Even if one remains for kalpas as before, it may not necessarily enable the fierce and sharp eradication [of afflictions] or the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

When medicine is administered because of an illness, even a malevolent incantation becomes an excellent remedy for the dizziness of recovery. When relying on darkness to support illumination, even a lewd woman is a guide to Prajñā.

Because he has maintained this practice with ultimate constancy, the Buddha said: "Ānanda has served me for over twenty years. Only now, while still possessing afflictions (*kleśa*), has he followed me as I traveled among the great Kṣatriya clans;

Sixth, because his great vows were ultimately perfected through universal gathering, the Buddha declared that Ānanda possessed eight kinds of [inexplicable] qualities.

though he begs for food from the lowly and humble, it is precisely to bestow universal kindness upon the four castes and to bring vast benefit to all living beings. He enters first into the five turbidities and does not take up parinirvāṇa.

Their sitting here is entirely due to this vow and this power. Within this single assembly of the Dharma, there has been an extraordinary, hidden resonance.

Ānanda, who upholds the Tripitaka through total retention (*dhāraṇī*), gained benefit by mistakenly falling [into a state of distraction]. Caṅkā attained the four fruits of the path with a mere snap of her fingers, using a brothel as the site for her great transcendence.
Brahmā devas and celestial spirits alike attended the Dharma feast; Śunyata and Nanda mutually served as the principal and the attendant. One should know that it is thus.
This sutra is not preached for the sake of minor causes or small powers of aspiration;

it should not be approached with the biased views of ordinary intellect, nor through fallacious reasoning that distorts and contradicts the reality of phenomena. Following the seven inquiries, numerous doubts and difficulties arise.

All say that [the Buddha], out of compassion for their ignorance and delusion, manifested as if he shared their confused attachments. The Buddha spoke the truthful words of the Four Noble Truths, and the Sūtras permit answering questions with a straightforward mind.

This is merely a theatrical display of scolding and abuse. Before one has attained liberation, one is like a nursing infant deprived of milk, a son fleeing from his father, a destitute orphan left exposed, or a traveler adrift in a foreign land.

Once one has attained liberation, it is like a nursing infant meeting its mother, a runaway son seeing his father, a pauper finding a jewel, or a traveler recognizing the path. Thus, [the Master] manifests as if he were still unenlightened.

Since delusion is not real, when one praises the Buddha upon awakening, that awakening must likewise be provisional. Ānanda attained the awareness of the Dharma-nature and opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
there was no root of doubt left unsearched, and no net of confusion left unpierced. He simply rested within the full extent of his own mind.
It likewise ceases according to the mental capacity of the great assembly of sentient beings. The Tathāgata, possessing great perfect wisdom, extensively expounds the characteristics of phenomena;
according to the minds of sentient beings, he accords with the measure of their knowledge, ceasing according to the mental capacity of the Tathāgata’s own mind.

Whether they stem from a thousand sources or a hundred knots, there is no ailment he does not know. Having fully understood his own illness, he also thoroughly understands the illnesses of all beings.

For this reason, he diligently knocks at the gate of the King of Physicians to extensively seek remedies. If one were to claim he is not ill yet groans, it is to manifest identity with the illnesses of all beings, sharing the same essence.

O Great Compassionate One, how could it be so? To manifest falling into error and to display delusion, while clinging to provisional means and contravening the ultimate reality—may all who possess wisdom prune away these errors and rectify them.

This has led to much contentious discourse. I shall therefore carefully summarize its major points to warn against errors and misconceptions. First is the error in judging the scriptures; second is the error in judging the stages; third is the error in judging the teachings.
What is meant by the error in judging the scriptures? The masters of antiquity held that all seven categories [of the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*] equally manifest the perfect and subtle.

Even the virtuous ones of the Southern Song dynasty still knew to receive and follow this tradition. In recent times, however, there has been much confusion, with people seizing upon isolated passages and...
It is like the blind men feeling the elephant; each sees but one corner and does not know that *śamatha* is a single gate of contemplative observation.
By judging the first three fascicles as belonging to *śamatha*, the initial gate is mistaken, and thus the subsequent gates are also erroneous.

They do not know that *samādhi* is the general gate of the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). By judging the following four fascicles as belonging to *samādhi*, one gate is mistaken, and thus the two [subsequent ones] are also... [erroneous].
Both gates fall into error. One does not realize that Chan-na (dhyāna) refers to the objective manifestations that appear within the cultivation of samādhi and śamatha;
consequently, the latter seven fascicles are judged to belong to Chan-na. The final gate arises in isolation, which means the preceding two gates have lost their illumination.
In the sutra, the Great Dharma Gate of the General Characteristics of Śūraṅgama is likened to a celestial king bestowing a magnificent mansion.
The halls and chambers once stood open and clear, with gates opening on all four sides; now they are layered with screens and shutters, partitioned in every direction.

The Great Hall of the Dharma of Goodness (Mahā-saddharma-kuṭī) has its walls intersecting one another, and the Hall of Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā-vimāna) has its watchtowers standing askew. Upon the floors of lapis lazuli, the pavilions of the seven treasures are demarcated by lines;
within the pure waters, the suns and moons of the four heavens are cut off and separated. All that was bestowed is now rendered non-existent.
Regarding the "Old Residence": how can a traveler enter its gate? This is indeed a matter for lamentation. What is meant by the error of misjudging the stages?

In the single gate of Avalokiteśvara’s perfect penetration, all five aggregates are empty; one suddenly transcends [them] through the wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
The aforementioned aligns with all Buddhas. The masters who recite the texts borrow the shrimp for eyes;

they employ the three wisdoms and the three emptinesses, and from the initial stage of the worthy to the subsequent stage of the sage, they combine these with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (the Many-Hearted Sutra) to falsely establish stages of practice. This is the error in the Tiantai school’s method of judging the stages.

When the subtle obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) are exhausted, the middle dhyāna manifests its objects; this is the sequential discernment of the signs of demons. Entering the stream and losing the object, one perfectly illumines all things.

Is it not because you have failed to eliminate them thoroughly that you must dismantle them one by one? Or is it because your application of the mind is inconsistent that these phenomena appear? A teacher said: "When you sit at the site of enlightenment..."

Since that which is entered is already tranquil—if this is so, then at that time, does the Great Being not still sit within the precincts of the aggregate of form?

To judge by conjecture when the stages of attainment are not explicitly revealed in the "Perfect Penetration" chapter, and to judge prematurely when the stages have not yet been traversed in the "Gradual Progression" chapter.

Within the ultimate exhaustion of the aggregates (*skandha*), there is originally no sequence or rank, yet they have categorized it in a piecemeal fashion; thus, the entanglements have spread like creeping vines, and profuse words have disturbed the mind.

Therefore, these must be decisively excised. What is meant by the errors of doctrinal classification? The Tiantai school’s system of doctrinal classification takes the *Lotus Sūtra* as its guiding principle.
The various classes of sutras are gathered as its retinue. Regarding the selection [of these], the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "Alas! It is not your mind; you are filled with alarm, fear, and doubt.

Unlike the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, because they dwell securely in the Buddha-way, they clearly understand the path by which their family returns home.
Unlike the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, because they have already reached the place of jewels, they resolve their minds to diligently seek unexcelled bodhi.

Unlike the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, because the treasure-store is spontaneous, those at the first and third fruits attain realization according to what they hear; it is not that there is only the One Vehicle, for there is also no second.

Believe these words: the Great Master Zhiyi has already realized that the assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly present, undispersed.
Furthermore, one should not face west and offer prostrations from afar, praying to behold the *Śūraṅgama*. Moreover, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Śūraṅgama* possess layered distinctions:
that [the former] is the king of mountains, while this [the latter] is a precious mountain; that is the king of oceans, while this is but a minor sea.
That [teaching] is like the full moon; this is like the crescent moon. That is like the day of the waxing moon; this is like the day of an eclipse.
That is like the path of the elephant, which turns away and excludes the herd of rabbits; this is like the power of an ordinary bow, which can only pierce a difficult target or a drum.

Having thus distinguished the teachings, one consequently distinguishes the Buddhas: the Buddha of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, who has attained partial realization through the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), is not the same as the Buddha of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

This refers to the Buddha of the Equal, Wondrous, and Ultimate [Dharma]. Furthermore, it distinguishes the Buddha of the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, which follows a sequential progression and retains elements of the distinct teachings, from the Buddha of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, who represents the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) of pure perfection.
To cling to the four teachings as being a mixture of the distinct and the pure is already a sign of lacking profound wisdom;

to differentiate between the three bodies (*trikāya*) in terms of superiority and inferiority is surely the height of folly. As Tiantai said: "When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he preached exclusively the Perfect and Sudden [teachings] for those who were not..."

As for the "Exposition" (the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*): because the great capacity [of sentient beings] was not yet mature, they were refined and ripened through the Tripiṭaka, Vaipulya, and Prajñāpāramitā teachings.

Only then was the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* preached to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, whereby they attained entry into the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and became equal to those of the *Avataṃsaka*. Thus, the initial and final wisdom of the Buddha are identical in their meaning of perfect and sudden realization;
therefore, following the Prajñāpāramitā, the *Avataṃsaka*’s ocean-like emptiness is taught to be equal to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. This is the view of the Great Master Zhiyi.

Such is the great tradition of doctrinal classification (*panjiao*). Now that the ocean of the *Avataṃsaka* is equal to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, what difference could there be between the perfect and sudden teachings of this sutra?

Furthermore, there are masters who insist that this present sutra is the final model left behind by the Buddha and belongs to the category of the *Lotus Sutra*, yet they allow only the "opening of the provisional" (*kaiquan*) while refusing to admit the "revealing of the real" (*xianshi*).
How rigid they are! May the followers of these two schools not fall into a dispute like those of Zheng’s people over the age of their ancestors.

Out of compassion for such people, the Tathāgata has revealed this path of practice, providing a ladder and establishing three gradual stages for cultivation.

This is the Dharma-gate for advancement. It specifically demonstrates the establishment of the *maṇḍala*, the pure cultivation and realization, and the true path toward perfect penetration through hearing-permeation and hearing-cultivation.
By not allowing the mind to flow excessively outward toward the six external sense-objects, one turns back to the source and returns to oneself because of this non-outflowing.

When the objects are no longer conditioned, the faculties have nothing with which to pair; thus, one cultivates and realizes the entry into the stream and the forgetting of the objective sphere as taught by Avalokiteśvara.

The lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure, like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli.

Thus, the cultivation and realization of Avalokiteśvara increase in this manner: hearing and that which is heard are both exhausted; with the exhaustion of hearing, one does not dwell therein. Awareness and that which is aware are empty; with the emptiness of awareness, it reaches ultimate perfection.

This person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

it takes sensory objects (*viṣaya*) as the scripture, and likewise, sound is its scripture. Now, with my shallow intelligence, I offer a speculative interpretation of this profound [meaning].
