Initially, one does not allow oneself to be separated from the five desires, using the practice of desire as a hook to draw [the mind] forward; subsequently, one arouses the fourth dhyāna, praising its purity and wondrousness while censuring [lower states].

Using the two branches of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*) as lamps and candles, one traverses the *yojana*s of the realms of desire and form, proceeding from the human and celestial worlds.
Those who have wandered into delusion are transported back to the realms of humans and devas; those submerged by the pursuit of desire and form are rescued from the great ocean of afflictions.
The jewel of awakening does not sink; amidst the filth of worldly toil, the pure flower takes root.

May they thus set out upon the path through the three realms of existence and find rest in the four formless heavens. This is the ford for sentient beings to cross over; it is truly my Buddha’s means of reception and guidance.

It is like a ladder or a beam. Among the various sūtras and śāstras, it is said that the two realms of humans and devas are places where the Path is easily attained, whereas this is not the case for other realms.
This is because, among humans, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are thin and the mind of renunciation is easily attained; among devas, wisdom is sharp.

Furthermore, among humans, there are many causes for practicing joy, while among devas, there is much joyful retribution. Wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) are the cause of the Dharma, and joy is the retribution of wholesome dharmas. As for the others...

Because the retribution received during the course of practice is relatively slight, some say that it is easier for those in the two heavens of Desire and Form to attain the Way, whereas it is not so for other heavens.
When Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages receive their karmic retribution and take birth, they frequently become kings of the heavens of Desire and Form.

The bodies of the gods in the Desire Realm possess natural radiance and do not require the sun or moon; the bodies of those in the Form Realm constantly emit wondrous light that surpasses the sun and moon. These various radiances—

This is because their inner minds are all pure. The Brahma-world subsumes all the devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The higher devas lack applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and do not delight in a distracted mind;
thus, they are born in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), where they cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma.

Some say that the devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) easily attain the Path, whereas other devas do not; however, the World-Honored One stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the seven locations that four of them are within celestial palaces.
For this reason, Śakra-devānām-indra dwells in the Śūraṃgama-samādhi and resides in the Sudharmā Hall, constantly preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens.
As for the Four World-Protecting Kings who ascend to the summit, they were originally the Four Kings of Constant Joy, Selfhood, Purity, and Permanence;
they protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma. Among the three realms, pure heavens are many; yet the disciples of the Buddha merely contemplate desire.
Heavenly Bodhisattvas are mostly born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This is because in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no body, and thus it is impossible to preach the Dharma;
and within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one becomes attached to the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and the faculty of wisdom is dull.

When those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) turn back toward the Mahāyāna and retain their bodies to generate outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), the retained birth-body is of the desire realm due to the power of their original vows. This is because the desire realm is capable of reviling and condemning sensual craving and greed.

Craving and the various coarse afflictions serve as the causes and conditions by which one can attain *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the path of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is courageous and robust because it leads toward the fruits [of the path].
Some say that the path is easily attained in the fourth heaven of the desire realm, whereas it is not so in the other five heavens;

this is because a Bodhisattva in his final birth (*caramabhavika*) constantly resides within the inner court of that heaven to preach the Dharma. This is because they all dwell together in the desire realm.
In this realm, practice is easily perfected. By focusing the mind on a single meal, one may attain rebirth within seven days.

This is because light is emitted and flowers rain down, leading one into the inner courtyard. Thus, a sutra states: "Good son, one who can practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā must have come from among human beings or from Tuṣita Heaven.
Although the five desires in Tuṣita are numerous, the Dharma is constantly heard there; thus, the power of the Dharma is superior."

Therefore, the lower heavens are dissolute, while the higher heavens are dull-witted; the lower realms have dense and turbid fetters (*saṃyojana*), whereas the higher realms have frequent and sharp fetters.
This heaven is neither dense nor sharp, for its wisdom is peaceful and secure. Furthermore, in the lower realms, life is short, and the Buddha has not yet appeared in the world.
The life-span in the higher realms is long. When the Buddha has passed away, these devas do not create karma for their own life-span, as their time and life-span are already fixed.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When a practitioner has not yet attained the Path, their mind is attached to the five desires of the human world. For the sake of such sentient beings, the Buddha taught the recollection of the heavens (*devānusmṛti*).
It is like a prince who, while in a high and perilous place, wishes to throw himself to the ground; the king then employs men to spread thick cotton [beneath him]."

The mat: had he fallen [into the hells], he would not have died; for it was better that he fell to the ground than otherwise. The Tathāgata, out of compassion for those submerged in the cycle of rebirth, entices them back to purity.

Before severing the five desires, he first delivers them from the three miserable realms (trāya). This is why he provided the various heavens as a mattress, sparing his only son from being cast to the ground.
As the Sūtra says: "These various heavens and their respective devas are all ordinary beings whose karmic fruits are being requited."

Answer: The answer is that they all enter the wheel. Furthermore, it is said that those celestial kings are themselves Bodhisattvas who, dwelling in samādhi, gradually advance and turn their merit toward the assembly of the noble ones; this refers to the path of practice.

To speak of "answering and entering the wheel" is for the purpose of uplifting those in the lower realms and awakening those in the heavenly destinies from their delusions and attachments. To speak of "gradual advancement and turning toward" is for the purpose of drawing them in.

The supreme stream propels the transport of the celestial vehicle. There are those who dwell together in the four dhyānas, possessing the four meditative absorptions (śamatha-vipaśyanā) that have reached maturity through effort;
there are the Anāgāmins who take up residence in the five [pure abodes]; they equally realize the four formless attainments (ārūpya).
Among them are Arhats whose light of wisdom is perfectly penetrating, and Arhats who exhaust emptiness and do not return. When one examines the two realms of desire and form, how could it be...

Regarding those who, without practicing the path, realize the fruit and equally sever the afflictions of views and thought, and likewise exit the triple world—those who travel three hundred *yojanas* and enter the transformation city—do they not also have cases of "great transcendence" and "small transcendence"?
When one hears the cry of "Welcome! on the level of ordinary beings and directly transcends to the four fruits of sainthood, this is such a case.

The treatise states that those who are born pure in the heavens refer to the various noble ones (*ārya*) born within the three realms—namely, the *srotāpanna*, the *kulaṃkula*, the *sakṛdāgāmin*, and the *ekavīcika*—or those who attain the path of the *anāgāmin* or *arhat* in the heavens. The *srotāpanna* is reborn at most seven times;

the *devakulaṃkula* undergoes two or three births among the gods; and the *pudgala-gāmin* (one who goes back and forth) attains parinirvāṇa after wandering between the human realm and the heavens. All of these are [included].

This is the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Judging by the classification of the Pitakas and Vehicles (*piṭaka-yāna*), the various heavens listed in this present sutra correspond to the stages and positions of the practice of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).

One should know that the noble ones of the four fruits (*catur-phala-ārya*) all reign as kings in the heavens above: those of the third fruit are born in the heavens of the Form and Formless Realms (*rūpa-arūpyadhātu*);

those of the first fruit are born among the heavens of the Desire Realm. Within these heavens of the three realms, they serve as the provisional stations for Bodhisattvas and also represent the stages of cultivation for Śrāvakas.

The same applies to those abiding in the first and second fruits within the realms of desire and form. When a practitioner within the human or celestial realms gives rise to the resolve and engenders faith, it is like the arrow of Nārāyaṇa:
once launched, it must inevitably hit the mark. Contemplating the stages and severing delusions is like ascending a multi-storied tower, gradually rising higher and higher.
Therefore, one should not casually speak of "pure birth" as being merely a general term for sinking into [the lower realms]. Nāgārjuna said: "These devas and humans..."

They all attain excellent wisdom. Upholding the precepts and guarding themselves, they do not burn sentient beings. Practicing these wholesome dharmas, their bodies and minds are peaceful and secure, free from feverish distress and affliction;
this is what is called heading toward the gate of Nirvāṇa. When their lives are about to end, they see their merit and their hearts rejoice; they have no sorrow and no regret.
If they have not yet attained Nirvāṇa, they will be born in the worlds of the Buddhas, or if born in the heavens, they will dwell in the *smṛtyupasthāna* of the True Dharma.
The Sūtra says: A son of the gods from the Kālaśodhana Heaven entered the Forest of Heavenly Play and, experiencing the retribution of celestial bliss, spoke this verse:
"Having attained the enjoyment of celestial bliss, If one does not act with negligence, One will proceed from joy to a place of further joy; Such a person shall surely reach Nirvāṇa."
All pleasures are impermanent; they must inevitably end in the exhaustion of joy. These celestial pleasures are impermanent as well; when one’s lifespan is exhausted, one must surely fall away.
Having understood this law, one should constantly seek the path to Nirvāṇa. The triple world is like smoke, and the realm of desire is like the ocean; humans and devas stand but as a drop within it.
One must truly cultivate the way and seek salvation amidst the turbulent currents—how can one not exert oneself? In the past, at the end of the Semblance Dharma age, there were many divergent paths.
Nāgārjuna realized the first bhūmi in a pure land; Asaṅga inquired about the ten bhūmis from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
While the Chan school flourished in its exposition, Tiantai propagated the teachings on contemplation within the realm of tranquil light (*sukhāvatī*). Master Xuanzang sought refuge in Tuṣita Heaven.

The ancients practiced authentic cultivation, abandoning the dharma of frivolous proliferation; they pursued what was essential for benefiting sentient beings, finding no practice superior to seeing the Buddha. Today’s "blind meditation" is no different.

Those who realize through darkness and those with wild wisdom who negate emptiness fall into the three miserable realms due to their heavy karma, while their spiritual rank remains inferior to that of the five fruits of the śrāvaka path.

Their bodies dwell within the three poisons, yet their mouths brush away the four dhyānas. Only when birth and death become vast and overwhelming will they finally realize that speaking of food does not satisfy hunger.
All you practitioners: please consider the urgent needs of the future and examine this with careful discernment.

○ Ninth, regarding the gains and losses of past and present: Thus, for the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Chongfu Monastery expanded its praise, Guantao initiated the structural divisions (*ko-duan*), and Zizhong extensively expounded the thematic gates (*yi-men*).
Among those who commissioned works from masters of antiquity, there were only these three craftsmen. As for the commentaries of the Song dynasty, they are summarized as follows:
There are three schools. Gushan established the contemplations based on the Tiantai tradition; Changshui propagated the tenets based on the Xianshou tradition;

and Wenling established the principles through the integration of Chan and doctrinal study. From that time onward, the branches and lineages have proliferated and the ritual altars have become intermingled.

I humbly desire to encompass the ancient and the modern, to rectify the similarities and differences, and to speak of their respective strengths and weaknesses. Regarding the interpretations of the ancient masters, there are diverse views.

They all return to the same destination; according to the depth or shallowness of individuals' capacities, they all proceed toward the ocean of wisdom. Yongming compiled the doctrines of the three schools—Cien, Tiantai, and Xian;
Tiantai critiqued the writings of the six masters of Hexi and Guangzhai; and Changshui annotated the sutras, encompassing ancient interpretations within his work.
The Buddha has no fixed doctrine; each person has their own teacher. It is like a multitude of branches all originating from a single root. One should not expect a single spoon to open all the doors.
Each family establishes its own school, and every individual sets up their own sect;

none fail to revise the old chapters and sweep away ancient meanings. This is what the ancients attained, yet what the people of today have lost. When the masters of antiquity investigated the Indian scriptures...

It is like the former scholars’ commentary on the *Lü Gao*, where they "transmitted without creating" and "abstained from what was doubtful despite much learning. Now that this Master’s sub-commentary has appeared, each section is titled with its own heading, and all say:

"Since the Tang and Song dynasties, there has been no such interpretation. The ancients had a wondrous realization of the two schools (*er zong*) and were renowned for their mastery of the ten sections (*shi bu*).
Their intent was to transcend the various ranks, and their wisdom surpassed the common sentiments of the masses. Now, you have instead sought to have Gu-shan [Zhiyuan]...
Like sheep following long, chaotic tracks, many today are like the River God (Hebo) who seeks to cross a river but does not consult a master mariner.
This is the attainment of the ancients and the failure of the present day. Master Qingliang’s sub-commentary on the sutras comprehensively elucidates the Tripitaka;

it captures the profound essence of the Tiantai and Sanlun schools and refines the Chan gates of both the North and South. No teaching is left uncollected, and no principle remains unaligned. Those who study today...

As for this, their wisdom was dark yet their influence spread everywhere. The masters of the five Vinaya schools vied with one another to analyze the imperial-blue bowl; the five hundred disciples contended to divide the white-wool robe.

To observe them was like comparing a single village to the vast world, or identical to picking up dregs from a puddle. Furthermore, their secular learning was shallow and crude, and the structure of their prose was disjointed.
Some were like building a house upon a bed—repeating words until the meaning became ever more obscure. Others were like gourd-vines creeping over a trellis, piling up layers upon layers.
To record [the teachings] yet fail to encompass their full meaning—this is the merit of the ancients and the failing of the present-day.
The one from Hedong (Huiyuan) spoke of the "Hermitage" (Caotang), saying: "Because he did not disparage others based on his own strengths, he had no doctrine of exclusion;

because he did not conceal people’s shortcomings with his own views, he had no argument of personal bias. He compiled and explained the *Yihai* (Ocean of Meaning), drawing extensively from many masters, providing a general framework for its essential points. All...

There were no bows or arrows [of contention]. Yet, as they drew near to virtue, they vied with one another using shields and spears; they became enemies and bitter foes, their insults as foul as the mouths of the wicked.
Furthermore, with a single word or half-explanation, they would deceive and slander the sages of old, shouting and clamoring to exalt their own virtues.

Thus they increased the disease of affliction and gave rise to disputes within their own school. This is what the ancients attained, while the people of today have lost. Now, the Master opens [the way].

Regarding the establishment of the thesis and the extensive mutual analysis, there are roughly three points that appear to be correct but are actually erroneous. The first concerns the "Investigation of the Mind and Revelation of the Vision.

Following Master Zhen’s structural divisions, Changshui established a section titled "Revealing the Tathāgatagarbha Mind," which—by means of both mind and vision—destroys the false to reveal the true.
Within the section on destroying the vision, the text is vast and the meaning profound; Jiyin indicates that it destroys and eliminates ignorance.
He extensively sweeps away doubts and attachments. Based on the eternally abiding true mind, Beifeng (Zhiyuan) follows the path to open the perfect understanding (*yuanjie*).

Throughout these various topical sections, they are spread out like stars across the heavens; their skillful exposition and subtle refutations are largely in accord. Yet people today bitterly dispute the "revealing of the mind," separately establishing ten stages for the revelation of vision.
They fail to realize that this section by the ancient masters was fundamentally intended to reveal the True as primary and refute the False as auxiliary. As for the false...

The true essence is a single entity. If it were not false, how could the true be manifested? Destruction and establishment occur simultaneously; if there were no destruction, how could establishment be achieved?
If one says that the prior destruction was not of the mind, then it should not be destroyed again. If destruction and establishment were not simultaneous, [the argument would fail].

If one says that the prior destruction was of false views, this merely manifests the true. Thus, the true and the false are manifestly two entities. Regarding the two gates of mind and vision, the Tathāgata established them as such from the very beginning.

There is no mind that perceives externally; how could there be a perception that is separate from the mind? As for the ten rounds of arduous debate to manifest the seeing, they merely distinguish between left and right as being different—this is indeed a fragmented approach.
To insist on pointing toward a single direction to manifest the mind, or to differentiate the eyes under the same designation, both result in superfluous attachments.
It would be better to point it out with an impartial mind, completely cutting away these cumbersome categories, so as not to lose the original principles. There is no... [text ends]
This contradicts the correct contemplation of principle. Second, it states that the function of consciousness is destroyed by the faculties.

The treatise says that at the stage of Arhatship, one permanently loses the name "ālayavijñāna," which is described as "abandonment. This does not mean abandoning the substance of the eighth consciousness.

The substance of the eighth consciousness is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha-citta, the pariniṣpanna-svabhāva (perfected nature). While the eighth [consciousness] may be destroyed, how could it become a ninth [consciousness]? How could it be pure?
Is it pure and stainless? The five sense-bases reside within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and the sphere of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Among the eight consciousnesses, only the sixth is taken as the "wisdom of observation. Can these two types of consciousness be completely eliminated? The Sūtra says: "The sixth is the go-between for thieves; it plunders the family treasure itself.

If the knots of the faculties are severed, the appearances of objects will naturally perish. The knots arise from the six faculties, yet that which performs the knotting is not the six faculties themselves.

Understanding arises through the six sense organs; it is not that the capacity for understanding itself is the six sense organs. For sentient beings, the Buddha has seen how the six sense organs are entangled and woven together, obscuring the truth and leading them into delusion.
Within these six sense organs, he points out the two natures of seeing and hearing, which are ever-present according to their function and clearly illuminate all things.
Therefore it is said: "The six sovereign kings are eternally pure. The faculties (*indriya*) are the gateways; consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the master.

Now you say that by using only the six faculties, there are gateways but no master. The Buddha has clearly stated that the root of the bonds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the liberation of peace and bliss both reside in your six faculties.
Now you merely calculate for peace and liberation while refusing to accept the root of the bonds of birth-and-death. The Buddha—
The phrasing should not be like this. For this reason, there is the fault of establishing the function of consciousness as the root. Thirdly, it says: "It establishes the three Tathāgatagarbhas.
Regarding these three Tathāgatagarbhas, their names do not yet appear in the sūtras. [This refers to] the *Wenling* commentary on the seven names of the fruition stage.
This is a misquotation of the *Ratnakūṭa*. To now arbitrarily divide it into three sections and arrange the scriptural text accordingly is a great error.
According to the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, Queen Śrīmālā said: "The Tathāgata’s accomplishments exceed those of the sands of the Ganges;

possessing the wisdom of liberation and inconceivable dharmas, they are called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This Dharma-body, when not separated from afflictions (*kleśa*), is called the Tathāgatagarbha. This—
The wisdom of the emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha* is further of two kinds. What are these two?

They are the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, which is devoid of all afflictions and the wisdom that is not liberated; and the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, which possesses the liberating wisdom of the Buddhas—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—and inconceivable qualities.
The *Qīngliáng shù* states: "The *dharmakāya* while enmeshed in bondage is called the 'garbha' (*kośa*). This means:

"Empty and non-empty. "Empty" refers to that which is able to conceal; it is called empty because that which conceals is non-empty. The *Commentary* cites the *Awakening of Faith*, stating: "As it truly is, it is empty; as it truly is, it is non-empty. The explanation says:

this is the simultaneous designation of the names of the two stores (*ālaya*). Next, the *Commentary* cites what is said in the *Awakening of Faith*: "That which is called empty" and "that which is called non-empty.
The explanation says: the treatise thus simultaneously explains the two stores. Furthermore, it cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
It says: "One should know that this is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha, which is the treasury of both emptiness and non-emptiness.

As explained in the citations above, this is most clearly demonstrated, extending even to the *Nanyue Zhiguan Famen* (The Dharma Gate of Stopping and Contemplation by Nanyue) and the *Zongjing Shimoheyen Lun* (The Mirror of the Principle Commentary on the Mahāyāna).
Paramārtha’s translation of the *Niyatārthadharmaparyāya-śāstra* (決定藏論) explicitly designates both [the *tathāgatagarbha* and *dharmakāya*] as "two treasuries," stating in both instances:

"The Sūtra says: 'I, by means of non-extinction and non-arising, unite with the *tathāgatagarbha*; yet the *tathāgatagarbha* is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the dharma-realm.

Guanyin also says: "Establishing the Great Perfect Mirror, it is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. This is what Qingliang refers to when he says: "The empty treasury is that which is capable of containing."
It is not empty. Since even two do not exist, how much less three? The Buddha said: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind.
Because it is neither mundane nor supramundane, we do not say that the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally empty. The Buddha said:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is the primordial luminosity of the wondrous mind. Because it is both mundane and supramundane, we do not say that it is fundamentally [not...]"

It is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. The Buddha said it is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha*, the wondrously luminous source of the mind, which is detached from both "is" and "is not," and is both "is" and "is not.
It is not called the "originally empty" or "not empty" *tathāgatagarbha*. The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says: "These two are the wisdoms of emptiness."
This has never been seen nor realized by any of the śrāvakas; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knows and sees it as it truly is.
Now, beyond the two types of emptiness, you have established yet another treasury called "emptiness-and-non-emptiness.

Is this because the Buddha’s words were incomplete and required your clarification, or because the sūtras and śāstras were not exhaustive and awaited your supplementation? As you transmit and expound these teachings one after another, do not fail to discern their origins.

The Tiantai and Xuanzang schools have each inherited and transmitted [their respective doctrines] from one another; this was an error of the ancients, yet it has become even more prevalent among people today.

Qingliang (Zongmi) once said: "If faults are not pointed out, right and wrong will be conflated. Is this not to obscure the clarity of those who transmit the teachings? It truly serves to block the path of scholars.
As for those like the "Finger-tapping Sect" (the Huayan school), they revere antiquity while disparaging the present. Ultimately...
To say that I am right and others are wrong—how could I dare?

○ Regarding the tenth section, the "Examples of the Abridged Meaning of the Commentaries": When the ancients composed their *shu* (commentaries) and *chao* (sub-commentaries), the *shu* explained the sutras, and the *chao* explained the *shu*.
It is like the existence of commentaries (*zhù*) and sub-commentaries (*shū*) for non-Buddhist classics. The term "extract" (*chāo*) carries the meaning of abridging and supplementing deficiencies.

This clarifies that [the author] does not dare to rank his work alongside formal commentaries. "Mong" means "ignorant" or "childlike. This is an extract for the ignorant; it carves and peels apart the phrasing and text, gathering fragments to provide annotations and explanations.
Thus, it possesses the way of the "childish and ignorant," and is therefore called the *Mongchao*. Within these abridged texts, there are both analytical expositions and...
Combined Explanation. There is a general explanation, yet there is also what is called a "private interpretation. Why is this? "That which is excerpted by Meng" refers to the excerpts taken by Meng;
"the one who privately interprets" refers to the person capable of excerpting for Meng. It is not that Meng requested it of me, but rather that I sought it myself.

The *Xichuan Jijie* (Collected Explanations from Xichuan) follows the precedent of Jingxi’s *Niepan Shu* (Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra) in designating its own explanations as "private remarks" (*siwei*). I have humbly borrowed its principles for this work.

Regarding the interpretation of the sūtras throughout antiquity and the present, they take Nāgārjuna as their model. As the *Śāstra* states: "A brief explanation of the distinct meanings of the five characters 'Thus have I heard at one time' is finished.
This constitutes an analytical explanation (*lieshi*). It further states: "A brief explanation of the general meaning of 'Thus have I heard. This constitutes a synthetic explanation (*zongyi*).

[The preceding section] concludes. This constitutes a combined interpretation (*he-shi*). Now, I have ventured to model my approach on Nāgārjuna’s two types of interpretation and establish them as a general principle.

Within these combined interpretations, there are further divisions into "combined interpretations" (*he-shi*) and "general interpretations" (*tong-shi*). Why is this so? A "combined interpretation" may combine and interpret a single unified passage, or it may combine and interpret the meaning of several chapters.
Therefore, one may first follow the scripture to establish a general rule (*fan*), or follow the scripture later to conclude with an illustrative example (*li*). It is not fixed.
This is a single topical heading, allocating one section. Regarding the comprehensive explanation: sometimes a single phrase is interpreted by various masters;

sometimes a single meaning is examined through the intermingling of various interpretations; sometimes they are presented together without the fault of redundancy; and sometimes they are recorded alternately without hindering their respective differences.
Thus, it serves to prune away the profuse and the superfluous, and to clear up doubts and obstructions. For instance, as in Changshui Zheng...

Apart from the [previous] explanations, one might propose establishing a separate section for each case; however, the definitive resolution herein also involves two aspects. First, while logically two positions cannot coexist, in terms of meaning they are not mutually exclusive.
The tracks of the preceding carriage and the ruts of the following one differ in their paths, yet they cannot proceed in opposition; one must strive to follow the same rails.

Second, where the crossroads run both transverse and longitudinal and the new and old contend with one another, it is precisely through critique and refutation that one may achieve decisive resolution.

I have doubts. The *Shan* (Excellence) draws upon three types of divination; the *Yao* (Medicine) should arise from many categories. I pray that you follow the guidance of the virtuous and turn to the instruction of many teachers.

As for those who depart from the [original] explanations, some merely append glosses to each phrase, some rely on etymological definitions, some provide itemized commentaries, and some harmonize and cross-reference the texts.
Regarding the divisions of sections, some are broad and others narrow; regarding the thematic gates (*yìmén*), some are specific and others are general. There are those who...
Arranged sequentially from beginning to end, the various sections are compared with one another to establish a definitive standard for what is pure and what is flawed.

Since the teachings of the "Half" and "Full" [vehicles] cannot be kept entirely separate, I have followed the model of the *Xichuan* edition in arranging the sutras alongside their commentaries; this applies to the entire work, as will become clear upon reaching each respective fascicle.

For this reason, I have omitted the section on "Explanations of Names" (*shiming*) to avoid redundancy. Regarding the "Explanation of Teachings" (*yuejiao*), I have provided analytical interpretations according to the specific passages, utilizing the fourfold classification of teachings established by the Shanjia school.

This is to be judged accordingly. One may either employ the first three [explanations] in combination or utilize the last one exclusively. The ultimate aim is the Perfect and Sudden (Yuantun), which only then encompasses both the Tripitaka (Zang) and Shared (Tong) teachings.

[Private Commentary]: Regarding the four gates above, the ancient masters provide a general explanation. However, only the first gate—the Gate of Following Characteristics—takes sound, name, phrase, and word as the essence of the teaching. In this regard, this sutra stands in stark contrast to other scriptures. This is because, at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the various methods of spiritual penetration were distinguished and selected for their perfect penetration.

It specifically selects the "ear-gate" of Avalokiteśvara; thus it says: "In this Sahā world today, the discourse on sound alone is clearly proclaimed. If one wishes to attain samādhi, it must truly enter through hearing. Within this gate, although both [sound and hearing] exist, the provisional is subsumed under the real, and only sound is taken as the essence of the teaching (*dharma-kāya*).

This is the unique significance of this sutra, which has not been found in other sūtras. In his *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, Master Xianshou states that all six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are capable of generating understanding and are therefore the essence of the teaching.

Changshui subsequently interpreted this as the "perfect penetration" of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, wherein awakening occurs in every dust mote. However, he failed to explicitly extract this point from within the text. It was Grand Master Zibo who, by means of "pure sound-hearing," brought forth Mañjuśrī’s and Avalokiteśvara’s "Sanskrit-character Samādhi"—this is precisely what is meant here.

This is the essential meaning of the sutra; therefore, I have specifically set it forth here. The *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* by Guifeng states: "Every phrase is Prajñā; this is the very substance of the sutra. The 'characters' (text) include sound, name, phrase, and sentence.

The emptiness of the nature of these characters is itself Prajñā; there is no separate substance to the characters. This is precisely what can be mutually extolled with Zibo’s discourse on the Samādhi of Characters.

In the following year, he was summoned by [Emperor Jìngǒn] regarding the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*. Those who heard of this event erroneously believed it occurred after the summons. Regarding the Indian monks he encountered:

That which has not yet obtained its name is the "Ultimate Measure" (Ji-liang). The act of recording and compiling the oral dictation constitutes the work of the "Certified Translator" (Zheng-zheng-yi). As for the discrepancies in oral traditions, one must rely on the *Tujì* (Record of Diagrams) as authoritative. Changshui [Zongze] claimed that while the translation was the same, the written versions differed; how could there not have been some variation in a single passage?

Furthermore, how can it be said that the name of the chief translator remains unknown? This already reveals the errors in the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*. One should maintain caution regarding what is missing and refrain from making definitive judgments.

I believe that since this scripture was translated only once, there is no doubt regarding the existence of two different versions. It would be appropriate to establish the correct text based on the *Tujì*.

△ Differences Regarding the Three Translations Submitted to the Interior [The Commentary states]: As soon as the translation was completed, the original manuscript was taken away by someone from his own country.
In accordance with the King’s strict decree, it was initially not permitted to leave the palace. The Tripiṭaka Master secretly departed, but was detained at the frontier.

To resolve this difficulty, he immediately returned. Fang Rong submitted a memorial on his behalf; furthermore, he encountered the initial succession of Emperor Zhongzong, during which there was no leisure for its proclamation.

[The text] was disseminated. The catalog is missing this record (according to historical accounts: in the first month of the first year of the Shénlóng era, Emperor Zhōngzōng ascended the throne. Fáng Róng, the Grand Master of Rectification, was imprisoned. In the second month, Róng was exiled to Gāozhōu. In the fifth month of that same year, the translation of the scripture was completed.

The *Tújì* states: "On the twenty-third day, the full measure of one fascicle was recited; this was precisely the time when the translation began. When the brush was set aside and the work finished, it is unknown on what date [it occurred]. Róng was exiled to Gāozhōu and died there in banishment.

How could he have encountered the early reign of Zhōngzōng to petition for the submission of this scripture? The *Shìshì Jīgǔ Lüè* says: "Róng was exiled to Gāozhōu and stayed at the translation site, whereupon he was able to serve as the scribe. The Śramaṇa Huáidí verified the translation. Such were the circumstances.)

[The translation] was completed. The court rebuked him for translating privately. Consequently, Paramārtha took the Sanskrit manuscripts back to India. Based on this, it appears that Xuánrónɡ translated the scriptures while an exiled person; having been rebuked for his private translation, he had not yet submitted a formal petition, so how could he have presented [the work] to the Emperor?

Jíliàng returned by sea to the West solely because the task of translating the scriptures was finished. That the King’s anger and rebuke are not recorded in the historical records likely stems from a transmission error. Zànníng’s *Wéimòjué zhuàn* states: "He accepted an invitation to the residence of the former Chancellor, Lord Fáng. Opening the scripture box, he said: 'Chancellor, you oversee the Southern Selection Office (Nánquān) and were involved in these translations.

I personally request that you receive the pen-recording (*bǐshòu*) for one fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which I shall keep at home for veneration. Xuánrónɡ was exiled to Gāozhōu, yet [Zànníng] says the Chancellor 'oversees the Southern Selection Office'—this suggests he was unaware of the historical precedent, or perhaps it was a fabrication by Xuánrónɡ’s family members."

These are words used to conceal [the truth]. To say that one copy was transcribed by hand and kept at home for worship implies it was never presented to the imperial court; this can be known from the facts. Master Kuo’s vow to transcribe the scripture took ten years.

He began his work in the first year of the Dali era (Bingwu), and tracing back to when he received the request to spread the scripture, it was the second year of the Zhide era (Dingyou). According to both Liangdi and the two subsequent traditions, the scripture was later sent to the capital via a southern envoy; these were all events during the Kaiyuan era.
Thus, it is certain that Prime Minister Fang had not yet submitted it for imperial review in the first year of the Shenlong era; there is no room for doubt.
△ Differences in the Circulation of the Four Texts [The Commentary states]: At that time, a Chan practitioner obtained a manuscript from within the inner quarters and transcribed it;
it subsequently spread to the northern regions. Daotong was inside the palace and personally encountered the presentation of the scripture, which he also transcribed for his own use.
Upon returning to Du Men Temple in Jingzhou, the śramaṇa Hui-zhen of Shaoguan-tao in the Northern Wei searched for the sacred text.
[The Master] Ji had long admired this sutra. At Dumen Temple, he finally encountered this manuscript. Upon first obtaining it, he established its topical divisions (*kepan*).

(According to the biography of Weimo in the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*, at the end of the account of Zanning, it says: "One tradition holds that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* was originally obtained while Shenxiu, the Chan Master of Dumen Temple in Jingzhou, was serving in the imperial court.

Later, due to the śramaṇa Huizhen of Guantao, it was transmitted from Dumen Temple. Weimo encountered it and composed a commentary to explain it. This is the text cited by Changshui [Zhixu]. According to this, the initial translation of this sutra took place in the fifth month of the first year of the Shénlóng era, while Dàtōng entered nirvana in the second month of the following year; thus, the translation hall was interrupted.)

The petition for its presentation was submitted by Jian; Daotong obtained the original text at the ritual site. How could it have been prepared so promptly within a single month? Furthermore, Daotong was summoned from Jiangling to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) in the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era;

five years passed until his parinirvāṇa at Tiangong Temple. How, then, could there have been a portable manuscript that he carried back to Dumén Temple? As for Nanshi’s attachment of the scripture to his mission to the capital and Monk Ke’s receipt of the text upon request, these events both occurred during the Kaiyuan and Zhide eras.

To claim now that a manuscript written during the initial Shénlong era was circulated is decidedly contrary to the facts. When the translators were reprimanded and Minister Fang did not return, there was originally no matter of the text being presented to the throne. To say now that Daotong was inside the palace and personally encountered the presentation of the scripture—who presented it, and who encountered it?

Indeed, there were those of the Northern School who followed the "illumination-and-quietude" (zhàojì) tradition; having attained the source within, they transmitted it through the Gate of Deliverance (Dùmén). It was subsequently discovered by Guǎntáo, who erroneously circulated it as the manuscript of Dàtōng. Master Níng’s *History of the Sangha* (*Sēngshǐ*) contains many such contradictions;
here, at the end of the biography of Wéiquè, he separately cites this account, which is not a statement worthy of reliable trust. Thus, one knows it is insufficient to rely upon.
○ General Explanation of the Title:

*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas* △ *The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization of the Ultimate Meaning, the Sūtra on the Ten Thousand Practices of All Bodhisattvas’ Śūraṅgama*
△ [Changshui Shu] The title has five names. Regarding the three titles preserved from among these:

it is because the practice, person, principle, cause, fruit, exoteric, and esoteric aspects are each fully complete therein. (Yinmai Jieti) The sutra has five names; three are preserved while two are concealed. As for the five names: the first name consists of twenty-one characters.

Of these, three characters are preserved—namely, "Mahā-buddha-uṣṇīṣa"—while the remaining eighteen characters below are concealed. The second name consists of twenty-four characters and is entirely concealed. The third name, "The Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning," consists of eight characters and is entirely revealed. The fourth...

The title consists of fifteen characters; it is entirely hidden. The fifth name consists of twelve characters, in which the four characters "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" (灌頂章句) are concealed, while the eight characters "Śūraṅgama-samādhi of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas" (諸菩薩萬行首楞嚴) are made manifest. This is what is meant by "preserving three and concealing two"—the subtle artistry of the compilation.
Although there are three names, they are fully endowed with five meanings).
△ Regarding the "brief correspondence" mentioned first: the aforementioned three characters are the general [title], which constitutes the essential body (*dharmakāya*) of this entire scripture.

It generally encompasses teaching (*śāsana*), practice (*pratipatti*), principle (*tattva*), and fruit (*phala*). While "teaching" and "practice" are explicitly indicated, "principle" and "fruit" are implicitly contained. (As for "explicit indication," the text says: "There is a samādhi named 'Great Buddha-Crown'...")

This refers to practice (*caryā*). It is also said: "Although one has received the Tathāgata’s *uṣṇīṣa* divine mantra," and it is also said: "Furthermore, this mantra is called the 'Tathāgata’s Crown' (*tathāgatoṣṇīṣa*). This refers to the teaching (*śāsana*). The teaching is twofold: exoteric and esoteric. The exoteric clearly proclaims [the truth], causing one to awaken to and cultivate non-delusion.

This refers to the ten volumes of texts. To receive and uphold them in secret, so that hindrances are exhausted and merit is realized, is precisely what constitutes the mantras. Regarding the inclusion of meaning: because tranquil illumination contains emptiness, it is called "Great" (*mahā*); because its nature is wondrously enlightened and luminous, it is called "Buddha. This reveals the principle (*li*).

The passage beginning with "I, by means of the non-extinguishing and non-arising, unite with the Tathāgata-garbha, pervading the entire Dharma-realm," etc., is why it is called "Great"; and because its luminosity is ultimate, it is "Tathāgata," etc., hence it is called "Buddha. This reveals the fruit (*guo*). As for "Crown" (*ding*), it signifies the ultimate and unsurpassed. If these three characters are explained entirely in terms of principle:

the essence of the *garbha* is all-pervasive and nothing is not contained within it—this is called "Great," which is the Greatness of Essence (*ti-da*). Its spiritual illumination is unclouded and free from all deluded thoughts—this is called "Buddha. There are two meanings to "Buddha": first, the self-...

The meaning of the nature’s manifest illumination is the "Greatness of Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇamahātman*). Second, the meaning of manifesting benefit according to conditions is the "Greatness of Function" (*karmamahātman*). This Greatness and the Buddha are most honored and supreme, unsurpassed and beyond reproach; they are the Dharma that all Buddhas take as their teacher, and are therefore called the "Crown" (*mūrdhan*).

Since the meaning of these three greatnesses is not separate from the one mind, the one mind is called the "Great Buddha-Crown. [Le Tan’s Pointer states: "Great" refers to the person’s *dharmakāya*; "Buddha" refers to the person’s *prajñā*; and "Crown" refers to the person’s *vimukti*.

This means that when a person attains this Śūraṅgama Samādhi—the courageous and powerful power of concentration—it is further this secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), which are neither vertical nor horizontal, nor parallel nor distinct. It also embodies the three greatnesses of essence, characteristics, and function, and is not separate from a single thought-moment of the person.

"From 'The Tathāgatas' downward," [the text] separately reveals superior capabilities. The first eight characters explain, by way of the self-cultivation and realization of the person who has attained the fruit, how they distinguish between teaching others and benefiting them;
that is, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, relying on this dharma-gate, cultivate the causes and realize the fruit, clearly proclaiming and teaching it to ultimately benefit others.

[It further shows that] those who have attained the fruit throughout the three periods of time rely on the essence of this Great Buddha-Crown, entering from the fruit back into the cause, not lingering in names and signs, directly revealing the mind.

The Source: practicing without practice, realizing without realization; benefiting oneself and others, establishing teachings according to capacities; pointing directly to the human mind to resolve the Great Meaning—there is no discourse here that does not lead to full understanding).
The eight characters following "All Bodhisattvas" distinguish the practices for the sake of self and others through the cultivation of the causal stage;
because these true concentrations are fully possessed, the gates of Bodhisattva conduct for self-benefit and the benefit of others are vast, manifold, and immeasurable. Thus, the text [states].

He sighed deeply and said: "This is the single path to Nirvana for countless Buddhas. [The text continues: "The people of the three periods of time, from the stage of birth-and-death, turn back from delusion to return to the Truth, cultivating the fifty-seven distinct gates of wisdom.

From cause they enter the fruit; as in the sutra below, these fifty-seven stages all proceed from the three gradual sequences. By means of the diamond-like observation of the ten profound metaphors of illusion, one purifies, cultivates, realizes, and gradually awakens to and enters [enlightenment].

This 'diamond-like observation' is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; it is also called the 'Courageous and Valiant Samādhi' and the 'Firmness of All Affairs. The people of the three periods of time, both those who have attained the fruit and those still on the path, all rely upon the Great Buddha..."

The summit is its essence; it raises the banner of the Dharma and establishes the fundamental tenet. (△ [Wenling says: Sentient beings and Tathāgatas are hidden within the storehouse-consciousness; they are not revealed except through the secret cause. Sentient beings and Bodhisattvas are hidden within the seven realms of existence; they do not cultivate [the path] except through the myriad practices.)

The Buddha, the King of Awakening, thereupon revealed the Great Dharma of constancy and pervasiveness so that beings would not be deluded by the Lesser Vehicle; he illustrated it through the Unsurpassed Buddha-Crown so that they would not be obstructed by views based on appearances; and he pointed to the secret cause of the Tathāgata to clarify the fundamentally wondrous mind.

He showed that all Buddhas of the three periods of time rely upon this as their primary cause, clarifying the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization and awakening to the ultimate Dharma. He showed that all sages rely upon this to realize the fruit, and even that the myriad pure practices of Bodhisattvas are fully contained therein.

Since all phenomena, without exception, ultimately reach the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), remaining firm and indestructible, it is therefore named *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra of the Definitive Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Crown and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*.

△ Regarding the subsequent [extensive explanation], "Great" (Mahā) refers to the Great [Buddha-Usnīṣa]. It receives its name from its essential nature (*dharmatā*). Its meaning is that of permanence and omnipresence. [Regarding "essential nature"]:

This differs from the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, which designates something as "great" by contrasting it with the "small. In that view, there must be a "small" outside of the "great" to be excluded; thus, it remains limited. How could such a thing be the ultimate Great? Here, because the essence and nature of the Treasury [of the Tathāgata] are boundless and transcend all measures, it is called "Great."

"Great" (*mahat*) is used as a designation for that which is eternal and pervasive. "Eternal" means it extends vertically through the three periods of time; "pervasive" means it encompasses horizontally the ten directions. Regarding the vertical: it has no beginning in the past and no end in the future. There is not a single dharma that precedes it; only this [Tathāgata-garbha] precedes all dharmas, and thus it is called "great.

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "That which is called 'great' is named 'eternal. Regarding the horizontal: if one searches throughout the ten directions, there are no boundaries. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* further states: "That which is called 'great' is by nature vast and expansive.

Thus, the present [text’s] description of being "eternal and pervasive" is extensively documented in the scriptures and possesses three meanings (the above is identical to the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra*).

The Buddha-Usnīṣa is ultimate awakening. Awakening has two meanings: first, the fundamental; second, the initial. (The fundamental refers to the essence of the treasury, which is spiritually discerning and never obscured.)

It cuts off all deluded thoughts because it is fully endowed with immeasurable intrinsic merits. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "The meaning of 'awakening' (jue) refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought. This state of being free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space; there is nowhere it does not pervade.

The single characteristic of the Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body. Based on this Dharma-body, it is called 'original awakening' (benjue). As for the meaning of 'initial awakening' (shijue), because of original awakening there is non-awakening, and because of non-awakening there is initial awakening.
Initial awakening is the function, while original awakening is the substance. When the initial and the original are non-dual, it is called "ultimate awakening" (jiujing jue). Ultimate awakening is...
This refers to the moment when the nature of the treasury (garbha) manifests before one. Being unsurpassed and most extreme, it is called the "Crown" (*uṣṇīṣa*).
This is designated as the "Buddha-Crown" (*buddhoṣṇīṣa*) by manifesting the essence of the Dharma from the perspective of the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*).

If considered in terms of manifest phenomena, it refers to the teachings and practices currently expounded by the emanated Buddhas who radiate light from the Buddha’s crown. Therefore, both the teaching and the practice are termed "Buddha-Crown. [The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Buddha" means "Awakened. Regarding...

Because it is the first awakening within the sleep of all ignorance, it is called "Awakening" (bodhi). [The Nirvāṇa Sūtra states: "Buddha-nature is named the 'Culminating Samādhi' (mūrdha-samādhi). By practicing the meaning of this Culminating Samādhi, one comprehensively encompasses all Buddha-dharmas."

(From the *Vajrapāṇi-guhyaka-sūtra*): After the Buddha attained enlightenment, he traveled to Vārāṇasī. To the east, there was a bodhisattva named Ādhāraṇa who, wishing to measure the Buddha’s body, traveled by the Buddha’s supernatural power to worlds as numerous as the sands of ten billion Ganges Rivers in the zenith;

yet he never saw the crown of the World-Honored One’s head. He went to question that Buddha, and that Buddha replied: "Even after the passing of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one still cannot see the crown of the World-Honored One’s head."

△ [The Definitive Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata] "Tathā" (如) refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). "Gata" (來) refers to initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*).
Because initial and original enlightenment are united, it is called "Tathāgata. This refers to a single Buddha, which subsumes all Buddhas. What follows explains the teaching and practice.
Since both [the exoteric and esoteric teachings] are established by means of the Buddhas to manifest their identity, there are two aspects to the "esoteric cause" (*mi-in*):

first, the teaching; second, the practice. Regarding the teaching: what is explained below as the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*) is the secret language of the Buddha. It can be known only by a Buddha and a Buddha; it does not admit of interpretation by others. One simply receives it through its words and maintains it through reflection, thereby extinguishing hindrances and accomplishing virtues. Regarding the practice: this true samādhi possesses emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

It is precisely the one mind, which is neither vertical nor horizontal, neither parallel nor distinct—an inconceivable state that fully encompasses the myriad practices. When the Buddhas of the three periods of time attain this dharma-gate through such practice, it is called the "Three Secret Treasuries. Therefore, it is termed "esoteric" (*mi*). (△)

[Master Rong’s commentary states: The exoteric teachings are subtle and profound; the esoteric teachings are secret. Both are capable of evoking the fruition; hence it is said that they constitute the "secret cause.

"Cultivation" refers to the cultivation of the cause; "realization" refers to the attainment of the fruit. Both the two types of conditions for the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) and those on the grounds themselves are termed "cultivation.

The first ground (*prathamabhūmi*) and wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*)—the two fruits of partial and full realization—are both termed "realization. That which is cultivated and that which is realized are both Great.

"Buddha-Usnīṣa. This refers to one's own practice, such as the Perfect Penetration of Avalokiteśvara. [Rongshi said: "In the causal stage, by means of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa, one gives rise to right faith and initiates right understanding."

Cutting off correct understanding, one achieves correct practice. Practice being perfected, one attains the stage (*bhūmi*). Entering the stage, one relinquishes practice. Abiding in the stage is called cultivation; the fulfillment of the stage is called realization. (○ [Jiyin said: Because this sutra honors the Dharma of the Crown, it takes the clear realization of Buddha-nature as its primary tenet.)

Those who clearly perceive the Buddha-nature do so because they have abandoned all views. Among the sixty-two metaphors, the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) is considered foremost. The Buddha does not see himself, for he is free from the characteristics of self-view. His *uṣṇīṣa* covers [his head], for he is free from the characteristics of other-view.

That which cannot be seen by either self or others is called "the secret" (*guhya*). It is the samādhi of immeasurable meanings and purposes; it abides in a state of *samādhi* that is profound, firm, and remote, such that no one can reach it. As the *I Ching* says: "Retreating and concealing oneself in the secret. This "secret" is like the core of a lotus root.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that what is visible and usable in a lotus is merely its base. Only that which retreats and conceals itself where there is no use is truly "secret. It is through this that the Tathāgata attains the Way; therefore, it is said: "The secret cause is cultivated and realized until completion."
...is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

As for "definitive meaning," it refers to that which explains for the purpose of teaching and transforming others, which articulates principles and meanings without any concealed aspects, which exhausts the principles and fulfills the nature [of reality], and which speaks in accordance with reality.

(The following text says: "Proclaiming the true, ultimate nature within the ultimate truth, it causes you—those śrāvakas of fixed lineage who are still in training—to all attain the ground of the quiescent extinction of the One Vehicle. It is not something remaining... )

Therefore, it is called "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*). (△ [The Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra] states: It is a teaching that definitively discerns the ultimate and is clearly manifest; it is not a discourse of concealed characteristics, hidden intent, or implicit meaning. (△ [The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Chapter on the Four Reliances] states:

Rely on sūtras of definitive meaning, and do not rely on sūtras of non-definitive meaning. Sūtras of non-definitive meaning refer to those of the Śrāvaka vehicle. Upon hearing of the profound and secret treasury of the Buddha-Tathāgata, they all give rise to doubt and wonder; they do not know this treasury emerges from the great ocean of wisdom, being like infants who have no distinct understanding.)

This is what is called the "provisional meaning" (neyārtha). For the sake of delivering sentient beings, the Tathāgata employs the power of skillful means to teach the Śrāvaka-yāna, just as an elder teaches his children the "half-syllables.

Good son, the Śrāvaka-yāna is like the first plowing; one has not yet obtained the fruit. This is called the provisional meaning. The definitive meaning (nītārtha) refers to the true wisdom of the Bodhisattva, the unimpeded great wisdom that follows their own mind, just as a great man knows all things.
This is called the definitive meaning. Furthermore, the Śrāvaka-yāna is called the provisional meaning, while the unsurpassed Mahāyāna is called the definitive meaning.
△ Regarding the ten thousand practices of all Bodhisattvas: beings of the three periods of time each cultivate their respective practices for the sake of self-benefit and benefiting others;
these have immeasurable meanings, and here we cite the general number, hence they are called "ten thousand.

This samādhi possesses such manifold meanings, and thus it is said that there is a *samāpatti* named the Great Buddha-Crown, the King of Śūraṅgama, which is fully endowed with the ten thousand practices.

[Commentary by Jiyin: The myriad practices of a Bodhisattva increase through the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). The six perfections give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Meditative concentration and wisdom are perfected through *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). *Śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* have their essence in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. Therefore, it is called the King of *Śūraṅgamas*, for it is fully endowed with the myriad practices.
Bodhisattvas study it in order to bring *bodhi* to perfection; hence it is said that it encompasses the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas.
△ [The Śūraṅgama Sūtra] "Śūraṅgama" is a term from the Sanskrit language. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Śūra" means 'the completion of all matters,' and "ṅgama" means 'firm.
This refers to the ultimate firmness regarding all matters. (Having attained this samādhi, one contemplates phenomena as being like illusions;

one attains mastery over phenomena and is able to destroy the final subtle ignorance. One is able to obtain two kinds of extraordinary power, manifesting the body to preach the Dharma with unimpeded sovereignty. Therefore, in the subsequent sections of the sutra, it is named...)

Like the illusory Vajrarāja, the Mother, the Wondrous Lotus, and so forth—this samādhi takes the quiescence and function of non-conceptual wisdom as its essence. Because all phenomena are identical to the nature of wisdom, they exhaustively pervade the dharma-realm without remainder;

thus it is called "the ultimate consummation of all things. Regarding the term "all things," there is no separation between defilement and purity. When this wisdom manifests, both defilement and purity are entirely exhausted, and not a single phenomenon is established. Furthermore, when defiled phenomena are ultimately exhausted, the pure function is ultimately revealed. As stated in the subsequent text:

I unite non-extinction and non-arising with the Tathāgatagarbha; yet the Tathāgatagarbha is solely wondrous, awakened, luminous, and perfectly illuminates the Dharma-realm. Therefore, "one becomes the immeasurable," and so forth. Furthermore, it says: "Dust and defilements vanish upon a thought;

one achieves perfect, bright, pure, and wondrous [clarity]," and since one contemplates all as illusory, one is not destroyed by external things and is able to shatter ignorance; thus it is called "firm and solid" (*śūraṃgama*). (△ [The *Huìxuán yǐnchão* states: This samādhi can contemplate all phenomena;

the three categories and seven elements, etc., are all the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore it is said so. (○ [The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, "Siṃhanāda-parivarta"]: "Good son, Buddha-nature is the Śūraṃgama-samādhi. Its nature is like clarified butter (*sarpis*); it is the mother of all Buddhas. Because of the Śūraṃgama...")

By the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, all Buddhas possess the permanence, bliss, self, and purity. All sentient beings likewise possess the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; however, because they do not practice it, they are unable to see it.

For this reason, they cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Good son, "Śūraṅgama" means the ultimate completion of all things. "Sama" (or "Yan") means firmness. That which is ultimately complete and yet attains firmness is called Śūraṅgama. For this reason, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is called Buddha-nature.

(From the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra*: The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati: "The Śūraṅgama Samādhi is not [the domain] of Bodhisattvas of the first stage, the second stage, nor even up to the ninth stage.")

It can be attained. Only those Bodhisattvas dwelling in the tenth stage are able to attain this Śūraṅgama Samādhi. This Śūraṅgama Samādhi cannot be known through a single matter, a single condition, or a single principle.

All meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and unimpeded wisdom are entirely subsumed within the Śūraṅgama. When the sūtras speak of "a single time," this refers to the time of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). First, it is not restricted to a single *kṣaṇa* (moment): among those who hear the Dharma, some may have dull faculties; thus, although the time of speaking is brief, the time for them to understand is long.

Or, the speaker may speak for a long time while the listener likewise remains for a long duration, such that even after a single *kṣaṇa*, understanding has not yet been attained. Therefore, it is not a single *kṣaṇa*. Second, it is not restricted to a single *saṃtati* (continuum): because the speaker has attained *dhāraṇī*, the meaning of a single syllable is fully understood by all.

Or, the listener has attained the purity of the ear and mind, such that upon hearing a single syllable, everything is understood. Therefore, it is not a continuum. Within a single assembly, the faculties of the listeners vary—some being sharp and others dull—and through the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, he may either extend a short thought-moment or [contract a long one].

Long kalpas may be shortened into a single thought-instant, as they are not fixed. Generally speaking, the three periods of time—preaching, listening, and completion—are established; they are not fixedly defined by four, six, eight, or twelve periods.

A single day and month illuminate the four continents, yet the lengths of days, the heat and cold, and the proximity of day and night vary across different regions. This is because the activity [of the sun] arises simultaneously in two continents at all times. Furthermore, excluding the time of the various heavens above and below, these four periods and eight periods do not exist there.

The sutras are intended for circulation in all directions throughout the higher realms; if only the four seasons were taught, their influence would not be universal. Regarding the fourth point, the indefinite nature of the years and seasons following the attainment of enlightenment: the bodies perceived by ordinary beings and sages of the Three Vehicles—the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* of the Buddha—vary in their duration.
