All the various teachings of the Tathāgatas for the sake of instructing Bodhisattvas are also like this. (The *Commentary* says: "To see the moon, one must rely on the tip of the finger; to awaken to the mind, one must depend upon the Buddha's teachings.

By means of the finger, one sees the moon; once the moon is seen, the finger is forgotten. By means of the teachings, one fathoms the mind; once the mind is awakened, the teachings are forgotten. To cling to the finger is to lose the true moon; to grasp at the teachings is to lose the fundamental mind. (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Words are used to explain meaning, but meaning is not the words themselves. It is like a person who..."

Pointing at the moon with one's finger is done to show it to those who are deluded. The deluded person looks at the finger and does not look at the moon. Someone says to them, "I am pointing at the moon with my finger; why do you look at the finger and not at the moon? This is also like that: words are the finger that points toward the meaning.
[This is] a statement that misses the meaning. (The second [point]: losing both light and darkness.
How could it be merely that the finger is lost? One also fails to recognize light and darkness. Why is this? Because one takes the substance of the finger to be the nature of the moon’s light;
thus, the two natures of light and darkness are not understood.

[Commentary on the Source Mirror: Furthermore, having lost the finger, one not only fails to understand the truth and falsity of one’s own mind, but also fails to recognize the prohibitions and indications of the teachings.
Thus, one becomes confused and inverted, unable to distinguish the cardinal directions. This is like a bird speaking of the void, or a rat claiming to be a cat;
it resembles a mere echo of form and sound—how could such things accord with the true teaching? Therefore, it is said: "How could one merely lose the finger? [Sub-commentary]
Verbal teachings belong to the conditioned and the indeterminate; therefore, they are "dark. Ultimate truth belongs to the unconditioned and is intrinsically wholesome;

therefore, it is "bright. The analogy is thus intelligible. (As Mount Gu said: "Teachings are the object of sound, and are thus like darkness; ultimate truth is the true mind, and is thus like light. (The two characters [暗] and [明] are joined).

"You are also like this. [Commentary] This applies the Dharma to the analogy, as can be discerned above. (Wuxing says: "This is the 'pointing at the moon' analogy. Although it discards the finger that points, it is primarily intended to select against the mind that perceives.

Because Ānanda said, 'I am currently using the perceiving mind,' the subsequent text refutes only the nature of discrimination. By refuting only discrimination, the nature of hearing is naturally revealed. (2) The Guest Leaves and the Host Remains, Rebuking Attachment to Perceptual Conception. (1) Regarding... [text fragment]
(3) The three points on the existence of the substance [of the mind], inferred through the analogy of the Dharma:
(1) The Dharma. If, by means of discrimination, I were to say that the sound of my Dharma-teaching is your mind, then this mind should naturally be free from the sound of discrimination.
There is the nature of conceptual discrimination.
[Gushan] As stated in the preceding text: "If there were a nature of conceptual discrimination apart from the external objects, it would be your true mind.

Since it has no substance when separated from objects, you should know for yourself that it is delusory. [Commentary] If one gives rise to conceptual discrimination because of the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma...

The mind—this discriminating mind—is originally devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, it depends upon objects as conditions. It exists or ceases according to the presence or absence of those objects and is not permanent;
it is merely like a guest.
(2. The Two Similes). It is like a guest who stays at an inn;
having halted for a time, he departs and does not remain permanently (one is called a "guest" because the conditions do not abide).
Yet the person who manages the inn goes nowhere at all and is called the "host" (one who abides is called the "master").
[Commentary: This clarifies that the conditioned mind follows objects as it comes and goes, whereas the true mind is serene and eternally abiding.
The "guest" is used as a metaphor for the deluded, and the "host" is used as a metaphor for the true. (3) [Combined].
This is also like that. If it were truly your mind, then there would be nowhere for it to go (referring to the aforementioned eternally abiding ground of the mind).
[Commentary] The subsequent scripture says: "Since sound does not exist, it cannot cease; since sound exists, it is not born. Birth and cessation are both perfectly transcended."
This is then eternally real.

(2) [This section consists of two parts: first, a refutation based on the conditions and objects of perception to demonstrate the absence of intrinsic nature; second, an illustration by analogy to establish the absence of intrinsic nature. (3) [The third part is an illustration establishing the absence of intrinsic nature.]

What is the nature of non-conceptuality apart from sound? (According to the *Zongjing*, this point should be connected to the preceding section. This, then, is not only the case for the conceptualizing mind regarding sound;
it also applies to the conceptualization of my own appearance. Apart from all forms and characteristics, there is the nature of non-conceptuality.
[Zizhong] The guest is a metaphor for the deluded mind that temporarily ceases; the host is a metaphor for the true mind that does not depart.

How can it be said that there is no nature of non-discrimination apart from sound? This places the responsibility on the deluded [mind]. [Commentary] If the mind that conditions were the true nature, it should be like its host.
How could it come or go following sounds? For when separated from sound, there is no discrimination;
how then could it be the same as the true mind, which pervades the dharma-realm and is serenely and eternally abiding? [Zizhong] uses sound as an analogy for form, speaking of them in succession:
not only does the discriminating mind of sound have no substance apart from sound, but the discriminating mind of form likewise has nothing outside the characteristics of form.
Regarding its substance: [The Commentary] states that just as it is with the mind that follows sound, so too is it with the mind that follows form;

hence it says, "How could it be only... (Wenling’s commentary notes: This section below follows Ānanda’s intention to explain the matter extensively. "The discriminating mind regarding sound" refers to the mind that takes sound as its object—that which awakens to the Buddha’s Dharma-voice.

"Discriminating my appearance" refers to the mind that takes form as its object—that which complies with what is gazed upon). [The *Zongjing* Explanation] Furthermore, if the fixedly perceived voice of the Buddha is one's own mind...
If, when the sound of speech ceases, the discriminating mind were to be extinguished, then this mind would be like a guest, for it does not abide permanently.

Therefore, if it were the true, real mind, it would not give rise to discrimination by following after other minds; it would be limpid and constantly illuminating, as its nature is inherently cognizant.
It would be like a person standing in the middle of a pavilion on the palm of their hand, who has nowhere to go. How could there be a non-discriminating nature apart from sound?

This must be understood through direct realization. Only when one personally perceives the nature (*prakṛti*) does one know that it is inherently and eternally present, independent of all conditions such as sound and form, and that it does not depend upon the cognitions and views arising from external objects.
[Master Rong’s commentary states: It was previously said that this mind should be free from all colors, fragrances, flavors, and tangibles, and that there exists a distinct self-nature.

Therefore, the mind of birth and extinction is used as a metaphor for the guest, while the non-arising, non-extinguishing discriminating nature is used as a metaphor for the host. If one were to say there is no discriminating nature, then the dharma and the metaphor would not correspond. Furthermore, the guest and the host are established in relation to one another; the guest exists because of the host, and the host...

The guest becomes the host; the same applies to the real nature and the deluded mind. However, while the guest departs and the host remains, the deluded mind ceases whereas the real nature does not cease. Therefore, the text says: "If your true mind were such, it would have nowhere to go; why then do you say that upon leaving sound, the non-discriminating nature remains?

[General Explanation] Regarding the phrase "how is it that upon leaving sound, the non-discriminating nature remains": according to the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) punctuation, this belongs to the preceding section. It definitively establishes the true mind as being distinct from sound and possessing a discriminating nature;

this is an affirmative statement. According to the punctuation of Ziqing and Changshui, this belongs to the following section. It scrutinizes the conditioned mind and asserts that apart from the mind, there is no non-discriminating nature; this is a negating statement. Although the sections differ slightly, they collectively clarify that the true mind is the host and is free from the nature of discrimination.

This returns to the point of unity. Master Xing interpreted the text according to the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), intending to clarify that apart from discriminative sounds, there exists a non-arising, non-perishing, non-discriminative true nature, which is precisely the eternally abiding true mind (*tathatā-citta*).

He held that a "non-discriminative nature" belongs to the externalist doctrine of the *amūrta-tattva* (the obscure principle), which is what is rejected in the subsequent text. While Master Xing’s distinction from Changshui also possesses its own logic, he consistently maintained that there is a substantial essence apart from sensory objects.

In the first fascicle, within the chapter on "Discrimination Apart from Objects," his commentary states: "The ear-faculty conditions objects and discriminates due to sound; one cannot say that apart from objects there is no complete nature existing elsewhere. This, however, does not accord with the *Zongjing*. Regarding the preceding meaning, I shall definitively rely upon the ancient commentaries of Yongming and Changshui.
As for the writings in the room of [Daosheng] Rong, let us set them aside for now. (The two fingers are identical to the external schools.
Thus it continues until: there is no differentiation at all; it is neither form nor emptiness. Those such as Kuśala mistake this for the *tattva* (the obscure principle).
[Gushan] It is thus. This refers to form and sound; by extension, it applies to the remaining four sense-objects (*viṣaya*). There is no discrimination whatsoever;

that is to say, the mind that discriminates the six sense-objects is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature apart from those objects. [Wenling says: This simultaneously cites the "reflected images" (*pratibimba*) conditioned by the six sense-objects, all of which lack self-nature.

[Commentary] Previously, form and sound were cited to reveal that the mind has no substance. One should likewise proceed through scent, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*) in their entirety.
Now, because this [state] transcends [all categories], it is said that even conceptual discrimination is entirely absent and cannot be perceived;

therefore, it is not form (*rūpa*). Because conditions and conjunctions exist, it is not emptiness (*śūnyatā*). (Wenling says: "Since everything is non-existent, it is not form; since things falsely exist in relation to conditions, it is not emptiness. Being neither form nor emptiness, it is dark and indistinguishable; thus the heterodox schools take this obscurity to be the 'Principle of Obscurity' (*tattva-mithyā*').

As for what is called the "Principle of Obscurity," some call it the "Nature of Obscurity" (*mithyā-svabhāva*) or the "Self-nature" (*svabhāva*). (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "By the supernormal powers of the heterodox, they reach...")

For eighty thousand kalpas, beyond which there was a profound darkness such that nothing could be known; this was termed the "Primal Darkness" (mūla-tattva). From this point, awakening and cognition first arose, and thus it is called the Primal Darkness.

In Sanskrit it is called *saṃkhya*, which here means "Enumeration" (*sāṃkhya*). [The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyā* states: "Saṃkhya is translated as 'enumeration. Enumeration refers to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā*). It is named after the fundamental enumeration of all dharmas.

Because the treatise arises from this enumeration, it is called 'Enumeration' (*sāṃkhya*). Its original source was composed by Kapila. It establishes twenty-five principles (*tattva*). The very first principle is named "Primal Nature" (*prakṛti*), which is reckoned to be eternal.

[The *Śata-śāstra* says: Kapila said: First, from the primordial darkness (*avyakta*) arises intellect (*buddhi*). Prior to eighty thousand kalpas, there was a state of profound obscurity and ignorance. At the very beginning, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) first arises; by the power of past lives, it constantly recollects and conceives [of this state], which is called the "Principle of Obscurity" (*tattva-avyakta*), also termed the "Nature of the World" (*prakṛti-loka*).

This means that the sentient beings of the world exist because of the primordial darkness; it is the fundamental nature of the world. It is also called "Spontaneity" (*svabhāva*), for it has no origin. From this, intellect arises, which is also named the "Great One" (*mahat*), namely the consciousness of the intermediate state.

The twenty-fifth is named the "Spirit-Self" (*puruṣa*), which is also reckoned as eternal. From intellect arises the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃkāra*); from the "I-consciousness" arise the five subtle atoms (*tanmātra*).

From the five subtle atoms (*tanmātra*) arise the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*). From the five gross elements arise the eleven organs (*indriya*). The *puruṣa* (Spirit/Self) is the sovereign, characterized by eternal consciousness; it dwells in the center, eternally abiding, indestructible and imperishable, and it appropriates all phenomena.

These twenty-four principles (*tattva*) constitute that which belongs to the Self; they all depend upon the *puruṣa*, and thus are called the "principles of the sovereign. When the subject and object are discussed together, there are twenty-five. The Self contemplates the supreme objects;

the Unmanifest Nature (*prakṛti*) transforms into the twenty-three principles for the Self’s enjoyment. Once the Self enjoys them, it becomes bound by these objects and fails to attain liberation. The Self...
If one does not contemplate, the obscure principle (*tattva*) remains unchanging; since there is no longer any entanglement or bondage, the self is liberated, which is called *nirvāṇa*.
As explained elsewhere, Kauśārī is not the Sāṃkhya itself, but merely of its lineage.

This was mentioned in passing (Kāpila is the master of the Sāṃkhya treatises and the original progenitor of the Six Teachers; Kauśārī and others are his branches, hence they are said to be "of that class. This was mentioned in passing). [The Zongjing says: "If it is neither form nor emptiness, then altogether..."]

Those who lack non-conceptualization and have not seen their true nature, upon reaching this state, will fall entirely into annihilationism, becoming identical to the non-Buddhists such as the Kauśikas. Their own eyes remain unopened; they mistake the obscure for the ultimate principle (*tattva*), taking that which is dark, silent, and ignorant to be the truth.

They consider this to be the ultimate. From this point, they further establish twenty-five principles (*tattva*), becoming deluded regarding the true mind and seeking the seeds of external paths (*tīrthika*). Among them, there are those in the Chan school who have not attained the essential meaning, as well as those in the Dharma-learning schools who give rise to views of emptiness; many of these sweep away both mind and objects, asserting that both are empty.

They cling to non-discrimination and, driven by madness, delusion, and blindness, take this to be the ultimate Way. However, if one seeks the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) not through causes and conditions, but instead extinguishes the deluded mind to grasp at a "true mind," such a person is one of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

Beginners must not blindly conform to such views, but should instead exercise careful discernment. [Commentary by Xuelang: To say that what is neither form nor emptiness is the obscure *pradhāna* (the primal principle) is equivalent to saying that total emptiness is the *ālayavijñāna*. This is precisely what the Kūśārī school and others mistook for the obscure *pradhāna*. If one says that they do not perceive the existence of conditions, this conversely becomes identical to the correct truth (*samyaktva*).

[Commentary by Haiyin: Because it is detached from the five external sense-objects, it is not form; because it clings to the internal as a self, it is not emptiness. This is the very essence of the eight consciousnesses in their state of obscuration. That which discriminates based on sense-objects is the seventh [consciousness].

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the root of the mind (*manas*), and thus possesses discrimination. If it were separated from external objects and lacked external conditions, it would instead take the eight consciousnesses internally as its internal self; this is why non-Buddhists reckon this to be the "spiritual self" (*ātman*) and establish it as the primary principle of primordial darkness (*avyakta*).
Since even this is not true, how much less so is that which discriminates by taking external objects as its condition? (3. Concluding Rebuttal of the Non-Self as Master)
When you are detached from the conditions of all phenomena and free from the nature of discrimination, then your mind-nature will each have its own place of return.
How then can it be considered the master? [Commentary] The true mind is like the host, while deluded thoughts are like guests. Guests come and go, but the host does not move.

If you perceive the objects of the senses (dharmas) and lack the nature of non-discrimination, this reveals that your mind-nature follows those objects and returns to them; thus, it becomes a guest. How can it be the master?

What is called the "host"? [Master Rong’s commentary states: "The auditory object exists because of sound; thus it returns to sound. ... Even so, the mental consciousness exists because of the dharma-realm; thus it returns to the dharma-object. Your mind-nature is merely like a guest; where, then, is your host? [My private reflection:

The preceding statement, "Is it not only the discriminating mind of sound that discriminates my appearance? clarifies discrimination with respect to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Therefore, it concludes by saying: "Apart from all forms and characteristics, there is no nature of discrimination.

The subsequent statement, "In this way, up to the point where discrimination is entirely non-existent," etc., clarifies discrimination with respect to the dharma-object (*dharma-viṣaya*). This is because the non-Buddhists' *tattva-smṛti* (the principle of ultimate reality) has already transcended discrimination regarding the five sensory objects; yet, what is called "discrimination" [remains].

"Entirely non-existent" and "neither form nor emptiness" specifically pertain to the discrimination of dharmas as objects; one is muddled into mistaking them for the *tattva* (the ultimate principle), yet remains unaware of this. Therefore, the conclusion states: "Apart from the conditions of all dharmas, there is no nature of discrimination.

Since it is apart from the six sense-objects that there is entirely no nature of discrimination, it is clear that what can be returned to is the guest and not the host. Thus, the concluding reprimand says, "As for your mind-nature," and so forth. These two sections of text confront each other to clarify the point; they do not merely judge heterodox schools. (△ [Combined Explanation] Section on the Mirror of the Source)

This section, together with the following passage where Ānanda speaks, forms a single chapter. Thus, the subsequent detailed analysis of the "eight returns" does not arise in isolation; students should understand this. (II. Showing that the nature of seeing has no returning. [1. Ānanda follows the preceding discussion to present his difficulty].)
Ānanda said, "If my mind-nature has various things to which it returns, then why does the Tathāgata say that the wondrous, luminous, original mind has nothing to which it returns?
I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me."
[Commentary: The term "nature of mind" (cittatā) applies to both the true and the delusive. What Ānanda clings to is the delusive; what the Tathāgata reveals is the true.
Now, because he suspects that the wondrous clarity revealed by the Tathāgata is the same as the arising and ceasing to which he clings, [the Buddha] says:

"Then why does the Tathāgata say there is nothing to return? Here, "return" (*huan*) means "extinction" (*mie*). [Supplementary Note: The eight meanings of "return" take the sense of "reverting back"; Changshui interprets it as the meaning of "extinction."]

It is extinguished. Just as the sun possesses brightness, when the sun departs the brightness vanishes; this brightness returns once more to the sun. In the place of discrimination, the capacity to grasp through conditions arises; when the discriminating mind perishes, the grasping of conditions follows in its extinction. The emptiness within a single room has the function of pervasive openness;

yet if one fills it entirely with objects, the emptiness vanishes and the pervasive openness is likewise destroyed, so that the openness returns to mere vacancy. [My private commentary: "Returns" (huan) is synonymous with "departs" (qu). Both "returning" and "departing" carry the sense of being adventitious; having paused for a time, they immediately depart, never remaining permanently.

There is the principle of returning. For example, like a person standing on a city crossroads, there is nowhere to go and no principle of returning. (△ [Wuxing says]: This question asks how the true nature has no place to return. Below, the "seeing-essence" (*jian-jing*) is specifically identified as that which does not return.

This was already stated in the preceding text: "Such a nature of seeing is the mind, not the eye. However, this seeing-essence is still a mixture of the true and the false; therefore, the text extensively examines conditions to select out the true nature. Once the sand is completely sifted away, the essence of the gold is naturally pure. (○ [Combined Explanation] [Xunwen says]:

From here below, the seeing that perceives objects is extensively examined in two parts: first, the examination through relative dependence; second, the examination through absolute transcendence. The first part clarifies what returns and what does not return; the second clarifies what is material and what is non-material; the third clarifies what is pervasive and what is not; the fourth clarifies what is correct and what is incorrect.)

This refers to the provisional [teaching] which distinguishes by means of mutual dependence. Next, the passage beginning with "I am not Mañjuśrī," etc., answers the meaning of the ultimate [teaching] which transcends dependence. (Regarding the two Tathāgatas, there are three parts based on their relative distinction. [First, distinguishing by means of the provisional designation to grant permission for the teaching].)
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, as for your seeing me—this is the luminous, pure source of seeing.
[Commentary] "Furthermore" (*qiè*) is a term of provisional expediency (*quán-yí*). It provisionally points to Ānanda’s capacity to see—the mind that sees—as the luminous source.

[Gushan says: Because Qǐngxǐ (Ānanda) had not yet realized that the wondrous mind is without anything to be returned, the Tathāgata used the nature of seeing to provide a universal analogy, causing him to turn his single faculty back from delusion and return the six realms of existence to the truth. "The luminous, pure source of seeing" is the same as in the case of King Nimi, who contemplated the river.

Although these [six] perceptions differ in their conditions and objects, they still carry with them delusion. Since delusion arises based upon the True (the Real), it is called the "Luminous Origin" (*mingyuan*). [The Wuxing Commentary states: "The wondrous mind has no trace; awakening to it is truly difficult.

Therefore, one relies upon the 'perception-essence' (*jianjing*) as a skillful means to provide instruction. [The Zhijie Commentary states: "The perception-essence is precisely the nature of the eye that reflects forms. It is luminously pure and free from dregs; hence it is named the perception-essence. The 'Luminous Origin' refers to this essential body itself. This point of radiance is originally inherent;

it is not borrowed from the light of the sun, moon, or lamps. Hence it is called the Luminous Origin. 'Luminous purity' refers to the original source. This is the seeing-division (*jiandian*) of the eighth consciousness. Although it is divided into six, it is but a single refined spirit; therefore, all six sense-bases are designated as the Luminous Origin."
Although this view is not the wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind, it is like a second moon; yet it is not a mere reflection of the moon. You should listen attentively;
I shall now show you the ground from which there is nothing to be returned.
[Commentary: This "origin of illumination" is not the fundamental true nature. It is like the moon seen when one presses on the eye;
it fundamentally does not exist. That it is "not the reflection of the moon" means it is not the reflection in water.

A reflection of the moon in water descends from the actual moon and may be used as a metaphor for wondrous response (*miao-ying*), which "responds and thereby penetrates. What is observed by pressing on the eye is entirely false and arises from a disease.

The arising of the eye may be compared to a deluded vision; fundamentally, it cannot be apprehended. It is precisely by means of this very vision that [the Buddha] provisionally demonstrates its non-returnability.

(Gushan says: "The second moon is produced by pressing on the eye; the essence of seeing arises from delusion regarding the Truth. Once subject and object are divided, how can one realize their single suchness? If one does not press the eye, the true moon remains as it is;

if one eliminates subject and object, the true mind can be understood. (Wuxing says: "Although this belongs to the deluded, it is intimately close to the True. Like a second moon, the analogy is not far-fetched. (Haiyin says: "Although this is not the Truth itself, because it originally derives from the transformation of True Suchness, it is intimately close to True Suchness.")

The second moon does not depart from the substance of the moon itself; it is not like the reflection of the moon in water, which possesses two distinct aspects. One should understand that this vision is also the vision previously described as the discrimination of objects.

However, regarding the nature of discriminating objects, it is refuted by saying "it has a place of return"; regarding the nature of the capacity to see objects, it is indicated by saying "it has no place of return. As the text below states: "Now you survey the assembly of sages here; your eyes look all around, yet it is just like looking into a mirror, without further analysis.

This is the essence of seeing (*darśana-vijñāna*); it is the second moon; it is the nature of the capacity to see that does not have a place of return. Furthermore, it says: "Your consciousness sequentially points out within [the assembly], 'This is Mañjuśrī,' and so forth; this is the discrimination of objects. (△)

[Ching-lin says: "The luminous essence of seeing" refers to the cognitive essence of the faculty of sight (*cakṣur-vijñāna*), which further receives the clarity of sensation. Because there is the faculty of sight, this faculty is taken as the "essence. Since it is the essence of seeing, it cannot be used interchangeably [with other faculties];

thus, it is not the wondrous, luminous, and pure mind. Therefore, it is like a second moon. What is called the "first moon" is the wondrous, luminous, and pure mind manifested by original enlightenment (*mūla-ajñāna*). What is called the "moon's reflection" is the natureless character of seeing and being seen—the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

If there were no true moon, there would be neither a second moon nor a moon's reflection. The second moon emerges from beside the true moon; therefore, it is like the essence of seeing. The moon's reflection is seen separately from the moon; therefore, it is like seeing and being seen. Seeing and being seen depend on conditions, just as a reflection depends on the moon; they arise and perish together with it.

Although the source of seeing is illusory, it does not depend on external conditions; simply by ceasing the toil of seeing, this illusion is extinguished. The luminous essence of seeing is like a second moon—it cannot be restored. Thus, the wondrous, luminous mind is like the true single moon; its irreversibility is clear. This luminous essence of seeing is precisely the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*).

When the nature of seeing is awakened to as luminous, its wondrous virtue is brilliantly pure. Yet, the source of seeing is likened to a second moon because if one turns away from the fundamental and gives rise to [discriminative] seeing, it is like a moon formed by pressing [the eye].

If one realizes that seeing is but the mind and does not turn away from the fundamental luminosity, this is what is called "that true essence of seeing," where seeing is not a visual defect (*timira*). [△ *Rongshi* says: Your seeing of me is able to perceive the essence of seeing. Although this seeing is illusory, it is not the wondrous, luminous mind.]

It is like a second moon: it is neither the moon nor a reflection (as the subsequent text states, "neither substance nor reflection"). Furthermore, the single moon is the true moon; that which is able to see is the true essence. Therefore, he exhorts one to observe with clarity, demonstrating the ground where there is no returning. (The sixteen characters from "this seeing" onwards should be read as a single sentence;
their meaning will then become self-evident). [Private Commentary: The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "It is like a person with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon.

Guishan’s commentary states: "In space there are originally no flowers, and in heaven there is but one moon. As for the 'second moon' here, many masters have offered interpretations. Gushan [Zhiyuan] held that the true moon symbolizes the true mind, the second moon symbolizes the seeing-essence (*darśana-vijñāna*), and the reflection in water symbolizes the discrimination of conditioned objects. Thus, according to this scripture, there is only one moon."

This [passage] states that there is only one moon. Changshui (Zunshi) claimed that the reflection of the moon in water descends from the true moon; thus, according to this scripture, there is only one true moon, which implies there are two true moons. Wuxing refuted this, arguing it is not a reflection in water, but rather the shadow of the moon itself;

thus, while the scripture says it is not a reflection, he instead asserts it is truly the moon's shadow. Furthermore, he claimed that the false cuts through to the true, like a second moon—it is empty yet not without flowers, for the heavens have another moon.

Jiefu’s formal exposition is roughly similar to Gushan’s. Haiyin Xuanjing relies entirely upon Jingjue. The scripture says: "There is only one true moon; within it, there is naturally neither 'this is the moon' nor 'this is not the moon. Since the Buddha himself has made this distinction, there should be no doubt. Master Rong’s room cites this scriptural passage.

Ānanda said: "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no place to return, how can I know that it is my true nature?

[Commentary: Ānanda’s intention in asking is this: Previously, in response to the eight objects, you provisionally pointed to deluded seeing as having the quality of returning or not returning, so that by means of this one might recognize the fundamental, original true nature—unborn and undying.

"Previously, although I had already awakened to the wondrous and perfect mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*), I still did not dare to recognize it as such. Awakening to the true nature involves soaring above doubt and entrusting oneself to discernment; it requires suppressing superficiality and searching out the essence. Yet, practitioners employ various forms of conceptual calculation, much like one in a nightmare who merely critiques the words of a person who has already awakened.

Since Ānanda himself lacked meditative power (*dhyāna-bala*) and relied on another to see, it is said that he "relied upon the Buddha’s spiritual power.

Thus we know that distance and proximity, expansion and contraction, separation and continuity, and disjunction—all are entirely products of mental discourse, established spontaneously through one's own deluded discrimination within the ground of clarity, like pointing at a second moon and debating whether it is cloudy or clear, full or crescent;

The Master said: "Only the Sage is able to take all things to complete himself. (△ [Wenling says: To be turned by things is like empty space changing according to the vessel. If one can turn things, it is like removing the vessel to perceive the emptiness.

One whose body and mind are perfectly luminous: when the body is perfectly luminous, even the tip of a hair manifests the earth; when the mind is perfectly luminous, it universally illumines the Dharma-realm.

Transformation. However, if one merely eliminates the emotional and physical apparatus, then [the reality] manifests before one, vast and open. It is brilliantly pure; its hair-pores encompass the ten directions. Why, then, entertain further doubt? By grasping at these, one becomes a sentient being—what is called "the self-mind taking up the self-mind," whereby non-illusion creates illusory phenomena. "Zhao. Only then can one fully comprehend it. Synthesis: This demonstrates that both mind and objects are all produced by one’s own delusion; there are no external dharmas with which the mind can correspond.

Thus, every dharma is suchness (*tathatā*), and every particle of dust is universally pervasive. This is clearly revealed to enable one to awaken to the original reality and become identical to the Tathāgata.

[○@║] Section Two: Extensively Resolving Doubts by Building Upon the Previous [Section], Specifically Refuting the Doubt that the Nature of Vision is Detached from the Body. [Commentary]: This doubt arises because, following the Buddha’s instruction to "turn back the objects," one fails to understand the principle of the perfect luminosity of body and mind being identical to that of the Tathāgata.

Failing to comprehend how all phenomena are unified, one concludes that the Tathāgata has caused the previously perceived objects to become one's own true vision. If the objects were indeed the vision, then this nature of vision would exist apart from the body; thus, this doubt is formed. (The text has two parts. [?∴] First, the presentation of the doubt, which has three sub-sections. [卍1. The first doubt]).

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this essence of vision is necessarily my wondrous nature, and if this wondrous nature is now present before me, then this seeing must be my true self. What, then, are my current body and mind?"
[Commentary]: If this visual essence perceived within the location of these objects were definitively my true nature, then it would be manifesting this very nature before my eyes;
yet it has already departed from my physical body. Since this presently manifest vision is the true self, then the current body and mind must not be me. What, then, are they? [Gushan says:

Previously it was said that "one deludes oneself into taking the self as an object," and so on, up to "then one is the same as the Tathāgata. This means that the mountains, rivers, and all else that are seen are all my wondrous...]

Since that which is seen is already the true nature, what then is the seeing subject? "Previously I heard the Buddha say that your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously bright mind. The preceding section, concerning the stages of faith, understanding, and practice, clarified that this true seeing does not arise following conditions nor is it produced by objects.

The true vision remains, and its own characteristic is not lost. (As the *Commentary on the Yuan* [Yuan-shu] quotes from the *Xunwen*: "The previous stage of departing from conditioned objects is the stage of semblance; it corresponds to the Three Worthies of the Separate Teaching and the Ten Faiths of the Perfect Teaching. It quotes a verse from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*:
'To manifestly posit a slight object and claim it is the nature of consciousness-only—because there is something apprehended, one does not truly abide in consciousness-only.

What is explained here concerns the period from the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) onward, up until the ultimate fruit. When the true function is manifested and the true essence is illuminated, as for that essence and...

Function and essence are both non-seeing. (Now, being free from the seeing subject, this refers to the stage of the Path of Seeing, specifically the stages of the Separate and Perfect Teachings, having already entered abiding. As the verse cites:
"When, with respect to the object of cognition, wisdom perceives nothing at all, because it is free from the characteristics of the two grasps, one truly abides in Consciousness-only.

If the higher seeing is taken as the function and the lower seeing as the essence, when the function illuminates the essence, the principle-wisdom is profoundly still; no essence can be apprehended, and the characteristics of the function also vanish. Therefore, it is said that "seeing is not seeing."

(Using the upper as the essence and the lower as the function is the first meaning. If one takes the upper vision as the essence and the lower vision as the function, when the essence gives rise to the function, there is no dharma that can be illuminated, nor is it called "vision. (Using the upper as the essence and the lower as the function is the second meaning.

If one takes the upper vision as true and the lower vision as false, when the true awakens to the false, there is no falsity to be found, nor is it called "vision. (The upper is true and the lower is false is the third meaning. Only...
The single dharma-realm, because it is devoid of dual characteristics. This means that from the object of signlessness (*animitta*), non-conditioned wisdom (*anālambana-jñāna*) arises;

by means of this non-conditioned wisdom, one takes the object of signlessness as its object. Object and wisdom merge in profound stillness, like water poured into water, such that they cannot be distinguished.

This is called "seeing. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "When, with respect to the object of cognition... [Gushan says: previously it was not the seen, and thus was apart from the four sensory objects; now it is not the seer...]

[The Buddha said: "Because it sees, it is apart from the nature of seeing. The 'seeing above' is the wondrously luminous true mind, like the real moon. The 'what is negated below' is the essence of the clarity of seeing, like a second moon. [Commentary by Xunwen:

Since the Buddha’s intention was to refute that the four conditions are all not the nature of seeing, he wished to reveal that the true nature is also not the seer. Therefore, he first restates the seer in order to separate it from the four conditions—namely, when seeing brightness, the seeing is not the brightness, and so forth.
Afterwards, he relies on the true nature to separate it from the seer—namely, when seeing the seeing, the seeing is not the seeing; the seeing cannot reach [it].
"Even seeing is detached from seeing; seeing cannot reach it. [Commentary:
The true essence of seeing is already detached from the characteristic of seeing; since no essence can be apprehended, how could the function of seeing be made to illuminate what it reaches?

(The function is above, the essence is below. Furthermore, if the essence of seeing itself has no essence, how could it reach the function of seeing? (The essence is above, the function is below. Furthermore, as for the object...
The delusion that is perceived lacks even a substantial essence; how then could the seeing that perceives it reach it? (Above is True, below is Delusion. [Commentary by Xunwen:

According to the preceding text, when one sees light, "the seeing is not the light," etc., all instances involve the perceiving subject seeing the perceived object; the subject is not the object. By analogy, when one now sees this very seeing, the principle is the same: the previous perceiving subject becomes the present perceived object.

This means that when the True Seeing perceives the essence of seeing, since the True is devoid of delusion, it is said that "seeing is not seeing. The "essence of seeing" is the nature that reflects forms, like flowers in the sky.]

Fundamentally, there is nothing at all. For one who sees truly, this is the Buddha-nature as the cause of realization (*yuan-in*), which is the wisdom of original enlightenment (*ben-ju*). Because within the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind, there was for a single moment a lack of awareness, object and wisdom were suddenly divided; what was non-dual became dual—namely, seeing and the conditions of seeing.

When ignorance is completely destroyed, true vision is revealed. This vision and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi; they are merely different names for the same thing, having no two distinct essences from the beginning. This is what is called "seeing the seeing. It is not a case of a "subtle seeing" like a second moon being seen by the eye.

One should know that at the moment of seeing the seeing, there is nothing seen; it is simply seeing the seeing within the seeing. Thus, if one has not yet realized the nature (xing), the nature resides within the seeing and is termed the "essence of seeing" (jian-jing).

If one can see the seeing, the nature is liberated from the seeing, and only then can one truly see the seeing. Therefore, the text below says: "Awakening is not within the cataract; this is truly seeing the seeing. [Private Commentary: This is Changshui’s third interpretation. "Above is truth, below is delusion"; "above" refers to the seeing.

The wondrous enlightened nature is purely true and without delusion. The subsequent passage, "seeing the cataract is not the disease; the awareness is not within the cataract," refers to this. The "seeing" mentioned below points to the essence of seeing (*jien-jing*); it is truth mixed with delusion.

The subsequent passages, such as "the cataract is precisely the fatigue of seeing" and "the shadow and the seeing are both cataracts," mean that even seeing itself is removed from seeing, such that seeing cannot reach it. This is the entry into the wondrous through the arising faith and following [the teachings], using ultimate enlightenment to contemplate the ignorance of the phase of birth (*shengxiang*). It is something that Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), within their respective degrees of awakening, cannot yet reach.

Therefore, the subsequent passage further states that because that essence of true seeing is by nature not a cataract, it is not called "seeing. This concludes the clarification of the meaning that seeing is not [ordinary] seeing. Master Wuxing, relying on Changshui’s third interpretation, provides a detailed and exhaustive commentary on the text, which is most thorough and precise. Next...

The later generations have many interpretations, each with its own new meanings; yet their lineages do not deviate from Master Yue (Huineng). [△ *Dinglin* says: "To see seeing is then to see; thus, seeing is not [ordinary] seeing.

To know that seeing is without seeing—this is the true purity and non-outflow (*anāsrava*) of *nirvāṇa*. This seeing of seeing is detached from the seeing of marks (*nimitta*); it is therefore beyond the reach of the seeing of marks. As for the seeing of marks, it is merely the seeing of marks; it cannot see the nature (*dharmatā*). [△ *Zhongfeng Huikai’s Or-wen* says:

"The Tathāgata directly pointed to the numinous mirror of the mind-body, thereby shattering the delusion of the mutual opposition between sense organs and objects (*indriya-viṣaya*), and also shattering the 'truth' that is detached from delusion and devoid of dependence. For both the paths of truth and delusion are the sickness of vision that sentient beings have possessed since beginningless time. It is the seeing of brightness..."

"At that time, 'seeing is not seeing' and so forth—this serves to shatter the false and reveal the true. When the seeing itself is seen, that seeing is no longer seeing; both the false and the true are simultaneously discarded. Thus the verse says: 'By speaking of the false, all the true is revealed; yet the false and the true are equally both false.

Since it is neither true nor not-true, how can there be a seer and what is seen? Seeing is already free from seeing; where seeing cannot reach,' meaning that once both the true and the false are discarded, one points directly to the essence of the numinous mirror. It is perfectly luminous within and without, transcending all hearing and seeing. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra also says:"

The Dharma is not something seen, heard, sensed, or known. If one seeks to see, hear, sense, or know, that is merely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is not the seeking of the Dharma. [Master Yunqi said: "Seeing-seeing" refers to the capacity to see, which is the very seeing with which we currently perceive objects.

Thus, the "seeing" mentioned below becomes the "seen. At the moment of "seeing-seeing," this seeing is not the ordinary seeing that perceives objects; therefore, it is said that "seeing is not seeing. To illustrate this by way of a Buddha’s words, a sutra asks: "If you can maintain the Buddha's teachings through hearing, why do you not [do so yourself]?"

"Listening to listening. To illustrate: "If you will see with seeing the Tathāgata, why do you not see with seeing yourself? Furthermore: "Do not contemplate with the contemplator; contemplate with the contemplation. To illustrate: "Do not see the Buddha with the seer; see with the seeing. The meaning is clear. (△ [Xuelang said:

The previous passage spoke of the 'seeing-essence' (*darśana-sāra*) as being detached from the four conditions of light, darkness, etc. This passage speaks of the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind (*prabhāsvara-citta*), wherein not even a hair's breadth is established, and there is neither a seer nor a seen.

As it says: 'When the seer sees what is seen, that which is able to see is not yet the true seeing. If even the true seeing is transcended, how much more so the seeing-essence? How much more so the various names and marks of worldly compounded causes and conditions? Although it is called 'seeing with seeing,' in reality there is neither a seer nor a seen. Generally speaking, this is an inference by analogy.)

It is said that, generally speaking, within true awakening, nothing at all can be apprehended, nor is there even this essence of seeing. One should realize its meaning through personal experience; it must not be discussed by fixating upon literal words.
Why, then, do you further speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and the characteristics of their conjunction?

[Commentary]: This concludes the critique of using worldly conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)—names and marks—to differentiate from true vision (*bhūtadarśana*). Alternatively, it may be interpreted as follows:

"From 'even seeing is still apart from seeing' downwards, it is called 'binding the true and ceasing the delusive. The meaning is this: the self-substance of true seeing is apart from its own characteristic of seeing;
it cannot even be reached by the name 'seeing,' so how much less can it be said to belong to causes and conditions, or to spontaneity (*svabhāva*), and so forth?

[Direct Explanation: Ānanda spoke of the four conditions of the nature of seeing; these are precisely the characteristics of conjunction. [This concludes the third section: Rebuking his lack of understanding and exhorting him.]
"You śrāvakas are narrow-minded, inferior, and lacking in wisdom; you are unable to penetrate the pure true reality (*dharmatā*). I shall now instruct you."
One should contemplate well and must not succumb to weariness or indolence regarding the sublime path to Bodhi.

[Commentary: The true mark is markless; it is seeing through non-seeing. For those whose consciousness is inferior and whose wisdom is dim, how can they penetrate the wisdom of the emptiness of all phenomena?

Therefore, he exhorts them to contemplate well without indolence; then the Great Practice may be within reach. (The Sub-indication: This is for the sake of those who have not yet severed the cognitive obscurations and the clinging to dharmas.)
It is entirely within the true mark (the mark free from all attachments to "is" or "is not"). △ [Zongjing] One must surely discipline oneself to accomplish the task, forgetting fatigue day and night.
If one asks about the journey but does not walk, one’s hometown grows ever more distant; it is like seeing a treasure but not taking it, remaining stuck in poverty. (Wenling says:

Free from conditions and free from marks, beyond the reach of verbal expression—this is the pure true mark, the wondrous path of Bodhi. △ [Haiyin says: This correctly shows the path of śamatha. True vision is... )

The pure true mark (*dharmatā*). (This refers to the aforementioned wondrous clarity of refined awareness. [Citation] [The *Zongjing* says: The *Tiantai Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Various sūtras employ different names to describe the true nature and true mark: some call it the Single True Truth (*ekasatyam*); some call it the intrinsically pure mind;

some call it the Tathāgatagarbha; some call it Suchness (*tathatā*); some call it the Reality Limit (*bhūtakoṭi*); some call it the Prajñā of the True Mark; some call it the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); some say it is the Śūraṅgama; some call it the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); some call it the Middle Way; some call it ultimate emptiness;

and some call it the causal Buddha-nature or the intrinsically pure nirvāṇa. These various different names are all alternative designations for the true mark. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Prajñā is a single dharma; the Buddha..."
Various names are spoken, establishing designations for them according to the various classes of sentient beings).

(Section Two: Responding to the Request with an Extensive Explanation. [Note: According to Changshui, this section follows the previous conclusion to manifest the reconciliation of the teachings and introduces the subsequent passage that extensively clarifies the two views. Beifeng Master Yin establishes the section "Establishing and Refuting Identity and Difference in Deluded Views," followed by the section "Manifesting that Vision is Neither Separate nor Combined.

Wenglun Master Huan establishes the section "Extensively Clarifying the Delusion of the Eye-Flaw and Reopening the Eye of Wisdom. The first part clarifies the discernment of delusion as an instruction; the second part clarifies the further purification of remaining dust. Thus, regarding their identity...)

The concluding passage of the separate chapter contains the words "detachment from both union and non-union. Therefore, I shall re-examine this by means of the awakened mind and its remaining objects. Now, I say that these two divisions—identity and difference—are the Tathāgata’s instruction on *śamatha*.

This subtle and profound contemplation constitutes the essential meaning of the entire sutra; it should not be linked to the section on "Natural Causes and Conditions" at the end of the "Concluding Explanation and Synthesis. Following the two masters Yin and Huan, a separate section is established here titled "The Threefold Refutation of Views:

Distinguishing Views from Non-Views and Resolving Doubts," which corresponds to the "Refutation of the Chapter on Conjunction. This should be treated as a distinct division according to the traditional classification, for the three subsequent sections below constitute the actual refutation of causes and conditions and spontaneity, while the "Seven Great Elements" constitute the actual refutation of non-conjunction.
For now, I shall follow the classification of Changshui and have not yet dared to make alterations. (1. Receiving the Prior Request).

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has for our sakes proclaimed the nature of causes and conditions, as well as spontaneity, the characteristics of conjunction and non-conjunction, our minds remain unenlightened.

Now, hearing further of 'seeing seeing' and 'not seeing,' our confusion and distress increase all the more. We prostrate ourselves, entreating Your Great Compassion to bestow upon us the eye of great wisdom and reveal to us the realization."
His mind became clear and pure. Having spoken these words, he prostrated with tears of sorrow and received the holy decree.
[Commentary] The mention of "explaining the causes and conditions" and so forth refers to what has already been heard.

One already knows that true vision is neither caused by conditions nor characterized by spontaneity (as the Buddha himself states later: "Ānanda, although you previously realized that the wondrously luminous nature of original enlightenment is neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous"). Regarding the passage beginning "All combinations," etc.:
This describes his lack of realization. Within his mind, he still harbors doubts; he has not yet attained understanding regarding this view of conjunction and non-conjunction.
(In the following text, it is stated that such an element of perception is neither produced by conjunction nor by non-conjunction)—this is one form of deluded confusion.

Since the meanings of conjunction and so forth have not yet been clarified, how can he endure hearing further that "seeing is not seeing"? This would be like drinking even more deeply from a great vessel of intoxication; who could possibly [bear it]?

Thus, one awakens. Therefore, it is said that one’s confusion and distress are further increased [as one realizes the depth of delusion]. Seeking the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena is called "bestowing the eye of great intelligence.

Perceiving the principle of the true mark is called "the awakening of the mind to clarity and purity. This clarity is true seeing; it is free from conditions and transcends all signs, beyond the reach of words and thought.

This is not the realm of the two vehicles; therefore, it increases their confusion and distress. Without receiving a definitive resolution, who could possibly comprehend it? Thus, he wept and paid obeisance with a request for instruction. (Wenling says:

"All phenomena of conjunction are those perceived through the sun, moon, and lamp; phenomena of non-conjunction are those that are neither light nor darkness, neither space nor obstruction. (Supplement says: "Conjunction refers to the marks of causes and conditions; non-conjunction refers to the mark of spontaneity.

Although they have heard of causes and conditions, they do not yet understand the mark of conjunction; although they have heard of spontaneity, they do not yet understand the mark of non-conjunction. Therefore, the preceding text asks: 'Why do you further speak of causes and conditions?')"

Regarding the characteristics of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and combination (*saṃyoga*): Ānanda’s initial question concerned the causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and spontaneity, but he did not reach the point of combination. Here, the Buddha rebukes him and speaks of his own accord because combination is itself the characteristic of causes and conditions.

The subsequent refutation of combination, which also mentions causes and conditions, carries this same meaning. [Commentary by Haiyin: When Ānanda heard that "the seeing of seeing is not seeing," his confusion and distress increased further. This is because he took the essence of seeing (*darśana-śuddhi*) to be the self-substance of the eight consciousnesses;

it is the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), namely the subtle *ālayavijñāna*. Regarding what I have "never previously expounded": now, saying "the seeing of seeing is not seeing" means that true seeing sees this essence of seeing; it is true wisdom illuminating this ignorance. It is not something that can be known by the followers of the Two Vehicles. When clarity comes, darkness departs; when wisdom arises...

Delusion is extinguished. The Sūtra says: "This ignorance has no real substance. How could there truly be an ignorance that opposes wisdom? The intent is this: one thought there was a real "essence of seeing" (*darśana-śuddhi*) and a true "object of seeing," but now, upon searching for the essence of seeing, it cannot be found; thus, one is merely bewildered and distressed.

It is only because the fundamental ignorance has not yet been understood that the five aggregates as substantial dharmas have not yet dissolved, the attachment to dharmas (*dharma-grāha*) has not yet perished, and one's own [subjective] vision still persists. Consequently, the mountains, rivers, and great earth of the world continue to obstruct the eyes.

The World-Honored One’s response does not follow the specific points of doubt, but directly explains the two kinds of false seeing to shatter the attachment to the dharmas of body, mind, and world. In the analogy, it simply says: "One who knows this is a cataract has no fault of seeing. This single phrase precisely refutes the "seeing of seeing."

Thus, all doubts regarding the various marks of the natural harmony and disharmony of causes and conditions were, for the time being, completely resolved. (This concludes the third general announcement of permission to teach.)
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly, was about to expound the great dhāraṇīs,
the various samādhis, and the sublime path of practice.

[Commentary]: *Dhāraṇī*. This is translated as "Total Retention" (*zongchi*). (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that *dhāraṇī* is translated as "that which can hold" (*nengchi*) and also as "that which can exclude" (*nengzhe*). It holds what is good and excludes what is evil; it is the root of the myriad practices.
However, there are distinctions between single-syllable, multi-syllable, and wordless [dhāraṇīs].

If one points to the divine spells (*mantra*) below, these are the multi-syllable [type]. If one reveals the wondrous principle of true reality (*tathatā*), this is the wordless [type]. (The *Vajramaṇḍala-dhāraṇī-sūtra* says: "The non-existence of all phenomena is called the 'one syllable' (*ekākṣara*).")
(Dhāraṇī Dharma-gate): This true awakening and wondrous mind elucidated here is the foundation for all samādhis and the gateway to sublime practice.
Therefore, those who practice without penetrating this are all characterized by erroneous understanding;

thus, this dharma is pointed out as the great thoroughfare. [Master Rong’s commentary states: "Wondrous vision is no-vision; it truly can eliminate the various diseases of views held by sentient beings since beginningless time. Although these diseases of view arise within the nature of wondrous vision, wondrous vision..."

Within the nature, no illness can be found. As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "All manner of illusory transformations arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment. This wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment is fundamentally devoid of the marks of illusory transformation. This wondrous mind and wondrous vision are both called the Great Dhāraṇī.
All samādhis are subsumed within the Great Dhāraṇī; thus they are both general dharma-gates. For Bodhisattvas to practice this is the correct path.

Out of compassion for the great assembly, the Buddha wished to expound this dharma-gate, thereby revealing that wondrous vision is non-vision—this is indeed the essential meaning. (△ [Private Commentary]: Following the interpretation of Master Xing of Wujiang, I designate the Gate of the Great Dhāraṇī as the general characteristic elucidated by the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*. Samādhi...)

The "Gate of the Grounds" (*bhūmi-mukha*) constitutes the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) elucidated by the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. Now, this sutra states: "I am about to expound the great dhāraṇīs, the various samādhis, and the sublime path of practice. From this, one knows that the dhāraṇī and samādhi are themselves the single Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*).

The essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate is not dualistic. What is called the "Great Dhāraṇī" does not exclude the "Small Dhāraṇī," because dhāraṇī is itself true samādhi, which universally encompasses all samādhis.

As for the phrase "all samādhis," it means that all samādhis are subsumed within this samādhi; as in the case of the twenty-five perfect penetrations (*yuan-tong*), each is said to "enter" samādhi, for it is the single path to the gate of Nirvāṇa.

According to the *Bodhisattvapraśna-viśuddhadharmamukha-sūtra*, a consecrated Bodhisattva (*abhiṣikta-bodhisattva*) is able to sport in the stage of non-exertion (*anābhoga-avasthā*), attaining immeasurable dhāraṇīs as well as the various Bodhisattva dhāraṇīs within the Śūraṅgama King Samādhi of all Bodhisattvas.

[...]. Thus one attains mastery; this is the sincere realization of having attained *dhāraṇī* and entered *samādhi*. Master Jing (Jingxiu) states that both are general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the Dharma-gate. He explains the various characters of "all *samādhis*" as being interpreted through the character "to do" (*zuo*).

This should be corrected according to the meaning of Changshui’s commentary. (○ [Citation] [Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Vol. 28]) Question: Are the gate of *dhāraṇī* and the gate of *samādhi* the same or different? Answer: *Samādhi* is exclusively a mental concomitant (*citta-samprayukta-dharma*).

*Dhāraṇī* is both a mental concomitant and a non-concomitant (*citta-viprayukta*). For example, when a person has attained the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, even if their mind is filled with anger, they do not lose it; it constantly follows the person, like a shadow following a form. This is because *samādhi* is cultivated through practice.

For a long time, one can achieve *dhāraṇī*. Just as sentient beings, through long habituation to desire, come to form its very nature, so too these various samādhis, together with the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, can produce *dhāraṇī*.

It is like an unbaked clay jar that, once fired by heat, becomes mature and is able to hold water without losing it; it can also enable a person to cross a river. Meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) without wisdom is also like an unbaked clay jar. If one attains the wisdom of the true mark, it is like a clay jar that has been fired and matured; it can maintain immeasurable merit across the three periods of time.

By means of this, a Bodhisattva also attains Buddhahood. Śrāvakas do not employ *dhāraṇī* to maintain their various merits; they are like a person who, being thirsty, is satisfied by a single handful of water and has no need for a vessel to hold it.
If one is with a great multitude of people, one must carry water in jars and pots; for the sake of all sentient beings, a Bodhisattva must maintain various merits through dhāraṇīs. (○ [Revised]:

According to Master Shenzhao of Gusu, he followed the error of Master Gushan and judged the response concerning śamatha based on this passage. (The following section answers samādhi and dhyāna; Master Jin’s doubts and errors have been successively inherited, and they are now all deleted and corrected.)
He addressed Ānanda, saying: "Although you possess a powerful memory, it merely increases your erudition;

yet regarding the subtle and secret contemplation of *śamatha*, your mind has not yet fully realized it. Listen attentively now, and I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so that all those with outflows in the future may also attain the fruit of Bodhi."
[Commentary: This wondrous mind, if one wishes for sentient beings to give rise to faith and understanding, may be explained and distinguished through various teachings.
However, if one wishes to realize it clearly and directly manifest this realm, one should employ subtle and secret contemplation.

That which is attained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) within *śamatha*, free from all conceptual discrimination, is alone called "direct realization. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Free from..."
The "Tathatā" (Suchness) spoken of here is the object of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). The "Tathatā expressed through words" is the object for generating faith.

Now, [the text] rebukes those who possess much learning and strong memory but do not cultivate meditative observation (*bhāvanā-vipaśyanā*); thus, regarding this object, their minds have not yet attained realization. Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says:

"Because there is nothing to be obtained, one obtains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. [Master Rong’s commentary states: "Ānanda increased his extensive learning but had not yet given rise to tranquil wisdom (*śamatha-prajñā*); the Tathāgata therefore directed him toward *śamatha*."

In the midst of this, at a place of ultimate stillness, one contemplates that the sickness of views since beginningless time is empty and illusory, thereby manifesting the wondrous vision. (△ [My Personal Commentary]: The Buddha said, "Regarding your subtle and secret contemplation within *śamatha*, your mind has not yet fully understood it.

Listen attentively now; I shall analyze and reveal it for you. From this day forward, I will clarify both the common and distinct karmas, repeatedly shatter the delusory thought of combination, harmonize the three categories and the seven elements to manifest the *tathāgatagarbha*, and provide a layered analysis and revelation. )

All of these are demonstrations to you of the path of *śamatha*, the extensive text on subtle and secret contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). The subsequent scripture states: "This is the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within which the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, analyzed through awakened clarity regarding subtle demonic activities," and so forth.

This serves as proof that this scripture concerns *śamatha* and subtle, secret contemplation; it is precisely the "cessation through contemplation" (*vipaśyanā-śamatha*) that subsumes *vipaśyanā*. It is exactly what is meant by "analyzing through awakened clarity.

Various masters have divided the scripture into two sections, distinguishing between the preceding and succeeding gates of contemplation; however, this does not accord with the scriptural text and openly contradicts the Buddha’s words. According to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) involve the analysis of the abandonment of delusions; this [text] concerns *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* therein.
*Commentary on the Subtle and Profound Explanation of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Fascicle Three (Part One).
Compiled by the Disciple Haiyin, Mengsǒu Qián Qiànyì.

(○ This section follows the preceding [section] to directly address the "Exposition of the Nature through the Three Categories. ● Second: Refuting the Six Entrances. (○ [Gushan says: The following three segments of the sūtra text appear to be overlapping in phrasing, yet their intended meanings have varying degrees of directness and indirectness. First, the refutation of the six faculties, although...)

By refuting [the categories] through the pairing of faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), one examines their true intent. It lies solely in the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*). Next, regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*): although the faculties and objects are both refuted, the primary focus remains on the objects, because within the preceding section, the faculties have already been refuted. Next, regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*):

They are not separate. What is called "the arising of cognition abiding in the center" and "the gathering of cognition abiding in the center" both refer to consciousness (*vijñāna*). Therefore, the subsequent text says: "Cognition arises due to objects; appearances exist because of the faculties. While the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are primarily refuted in relation to the faculties, objects and consciousness have already been fully refuted.

What follows merely elaborates upon the six present objects (*viṣaya*), which are both false and true, adding them to the preceding six sense bases to form the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). Furthermore, it elaborates upon the six consciousnesses that arise through conditions, which are both false and true, adding them to the twelve bases to form the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*).

According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is the most extensive. (2. Refuting the six [spheres] individually. (1. The eye-sphere has three [aspects]. (1. Indicating its lack of substantiality. (2. Citing an analogy to reveal its falsity.)
Ānanda, that very eyeball—when one stares fixedly until it becomes fatigued—is, together with the eye and the fatigue, likewise the appearance of fatigue produced by staring, which is itself Bodhi.

[Commentary] This borrows from the previous section on the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) the example of seeing flowers while staring fixedly; here, the eyeball is used as a metaphor for the nature of awareness (bodhātmaka).
The "staring" that causes fatigue is a metaphor for the sudden arising of deluded thoughts; this includes both the eyes and the fatigue.

This very faculty of sight—the subject that binds and the object that is bound—arises without departing from the Truth. Therefore, it is said that they are "identically Bodhi. The wording of the sutra is abbreviated;

if discussed in detail, the clear eyes are a metaphor for the nature of awakening (*bodhicitta*), while the fatigue caused by staring is a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*) failing to comprehend, thereby giving rise to discursive thought.
"Movement": because of the arousal of fatigue, one sees flowers in the sky; this is a metaphor for how, due to the movement of thought, false objects and the sense-faculties and body appear.
Furthermore, "the eyes and fatigue" below refers to the analogy and points to the dharma. The "eyes" here refer to the mind moved by ignorance (*avidyā*).
“Fatigue” refers to the manifested sense organs and objects, as well as the perceiving mind.
These mental objects and the stirring of thoughts are both manifestations of ignorance within the nature of bodhi; they have no substantial essence that can be found.

They arise falsely, like seeing flowers in the sky when one stares with fixed eyes—both are merely fatigue. (The Wuxing commentary states: This passage on the aggregate of form is like the eyeball; when one stares until fatigue arises, then within empty space...)

One perceives separate signs such as the appearance of floating flowers. Here, the eye is used as a metaphor for the True, labor (fatigue) for the delusory, and the flowers for form (*rūpa*). This refers back to what was previously explained; thus it says, "that very eyeball," etc. By including both the eye and its labor, the text takes the sense-faculties (*indriya*) from the preceding passage—which served as metaphors—to serve as the phenomena being illustrated here.

This is because that "laboring eye" is precisely the sign of the false nature of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*). However, these metaphors are stated in conjunction with the phenomena they represent. *Bodhi* is awakening; from awakening, delusion arises, just as staring causes fatigue. The intent of the Sūtra is this:

the "eye" and "labor" mentioned within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) are likewise the signs of the delusive fatigue produced by staring at the luminosity of awakening. These signs of fatigue are like empty flowers in the sky. The "empty flowers" mentioned in the preceding text serve as a pervasive metaphor for the five sense-faculties across the nine realms.

"Form. Herein, the "empty flowers" merely serve as a metaphor for the characteristics of the nine realms within the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*). The former is broad and this is narrow; they must not be conflated. One should know that from the eye-base up to the mind-base (*manas-āyatana*), all are like empty flowers.

Therefore, the text concerning the six bases states: "They are all equally the appearance of fatigue produced by staring into Bodhi. Question: Why does it not proceed by refuting the nature of seeing through the faculties and objects (*indriya-viṣaya*), but instead points to the matter of the eyes suffering from fatigue?

Answer: While the faculties and objects are universally deluded, awakening must proceed from the essential. Thus, it points to a false phenomenon easily understood by ordinary people to open the understanding of the practitioner regarding their unawakened attachments. The subsequent cases—such as stopping the ears to hear sounds or using the nose to perceive touch—are likewise to be understood in this way. This section explains the origin of the first six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*). Because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) grasps at signs, it draws in habitual tendencies and returns to the center, where they combine and form the five pure material sense organs (*pañca-viśuddha-rūpa-indriya*), which serve as the support for the physical organs (*pariccheda*).

Originally there was no entry [into these organs], but now they first come to exist. This includes the eyes; that is, the present eye-organ. The "exhaustion" regarding objective signs (*nimitta-bhāga*) is precisely the seeing-part. These two parts were originally non-existent; they are both the exhaustion-signs produced by the staring of Bodhi.

This is intended to clarify that the essence of consciousness is deluded because it relies on awakening; thus it is said that "Bodhi produces exhaustion. These two parts manifest based on consciousness and constitute its functional mode (*ākāra*); they do not depart from self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) and originally have no dual substance. Therefore, it is said they are "the same. This uses the already-formed self-substance of the six organs as a metaphor to express that they were originally non-existent.

The six sense organs arise from the initial conjunction of seeing and its object, thereby forming pure matter (*rūpa*); thus, both are mentioned together to clarify the beginning of the first formation of the six organs. (△ [Dinglin says]: *Bodhi* is the suchness of all things.
When conjoined with emptiness, it is tranquil; when conjoined with sensory objects, it is weary. (△ [2. Distinguishing Non-existence by way of Sensory Objects])
Based upon the two kinds of delusive objects—light and darkness—the faculty of vision arises in the interval between them; it draws in these objective phenomena and is called the "nature of seeing.

[Commentary: Since the movement of the mind gives rise to illusory objects (as when one stares fixedly with the eyes until they become fatigued and sees the forms of flowers in the sky), these illusory objects branch out into sense organs and their objects.

[Wu-xing says: "The 'one kind of deluded object' refers back to the 'fatigued eyes. For now, based on the condition of light, its delusive nature is demonstrated. Light must be contrasted with darkness; they exist in mutual dependence. The following text states:

"Shutting you out. [Commentary] First, the refutation of its arising from the object: within the object itself, light and darkness are mutually exclusive. Because of light, one does not see darkness;

Herein, when it is said that the organ "arises," this refers to [the organ] in relation to itself, and does not mean that consciousness is being refuted. Alternatively, it may refer to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) in relation to the conventional organ (*saṃvṛti-indriya*);

Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not maintain its own nature, when ignorance (*avidyā*) stirs for a single moment, the six faculties arise simultaneously. Based on the two kinds of false objects—movement and stillness—the faculty of hearing arises from within and absorbs these objective phenomena; this is called the nature of hearing.
Apart from those two objects of movement and stillness, this hearing ultimately has no substance.

[Commentary]: Since the sense-object (viṣaya) triggers the faculty (indriya), the faculty in turn apprehends the object. Only through the mutual dependence of faculty and object does hearing come to be established. Therefore, this ear-faculty has no essence apart from its objects. (【標指】:

It is by reason of the two objects—motion and stillness—that the nature of hearing-cognition is triggered. (△ [Gushan says]: The ear hears motion and stillness, just as the eye sees light and darkness.

What is taught in various sutras is that there is hearing in relation to sound and seeing conditioned by light. The nose's perception of permeability and obstruction, and the mind's cognition of arising and ceasing, are likewise to be understood by analogy. (II)
