Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this hearing does not come from movement or stillness; it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space.
(2. Refuting the Place of Arising). Why is this?

If it arises from stillness, then movement would cease along with it, and one should not hear movement. If it arises from movement, then stillness would cease along with it, and there should be no perception of stillness.
If it arises from the sense organ, there would necessarily be neither movement nor stillness. Such is the nature of hearing; fundamentally...

There is no intrinsic nature. If it arises from emptiness, then having the property of hearing would mean it is not empty space. Furthermore, if emptiness itself hears, what concern is that for your auditory faculty?

[Commentary] First, the arising from an object is refuted. Objects possess movement and stillness; if one were heard, the other would not be. This is because [hearing] follows that which can produce it.

Because there is arising and ceasing, [the possibility of hearing] is next refuted as being produced by the sense organ (*indriya*); since it does not depend on movement or stillness, hearing would likewise be non-existent. Finally, production from emptiness (*ākāśa*) is refuted:

if emptiness possessed hearing, it would constitute a sense organ in itself (as Wénlǐng says: "Possessing hearing constitutes its nature" means that if there is something heard, then the nature of existence is established).
Furthermore, if emptiness were to hear by itself, how could it have anything to do with the ear?
([│/○] The three [conditions] combine to form a false construct).
Therefore, one should know that the auditory sense-base is false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

Both the nose and the fatigue are equally manifestations of bodhi arising from the symptoms of strain caused by staring.

[Commentary: The nose is a metaphor for true nature (*tathatā*). External wind is a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*). "Holding" refers to the contraction of the breath; it is a metaphor for the union of the true and the delusory. "Exertion" is a metaphor for the movement of the mind.

The sensation of cold and the perception of fragrance or stench are metaphors for delusory objects. The remainder of the text is as explained previously. [Subheading and Pointer: "Perviousness and obstruction" constitute the domain of the nose.

When the breath issues forth, it is open and called "void"; when the breath enters, it is obstructed and called "solid. [Haichin says: "When it is in the ear, it is called hearing; when it is in the nose, it is called smelling. This is what is meant by 'mutually knowing within the nature' and 'mutually diverging in function. (2. Refuting [the two] to establish signlessness. 1. Indicating non-arising.)

[The text says: "Hearing exists of itself; what concern is this for your 'entry'? [Commentary:

Ānanda, it is like a person who licks their lips with their tongue; by licking repeatedly until they grow weary, if that person is ill, there will be a bitter taste, whereas for one who is healthy, there is a slight sensation of sweetness.

Ultimately, there is no essence.
(2) [This section consists of two parts: (a) Refuting [the notion of] establishment to demonstrate signlessness; (b) [The first part] indicates non-arising.

Thus it is, Ānanda; you should know it thus: when one tastes bitterness or blandness, the knowledge arises that it is not sweet or bitter, nor does it exist because of the blandness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from empty space.

If sweetness and bitterness arise, then when they are absent, one knows that [the taste] has ceased. How does one know the absence of flavor? If it were to emerge from the absence of flavor, then upon the arrival of sweetness, one would know that [the previous state] has perished.

Since the hand would likewise lack cognition if it were useless, one should not merely point to the refutation of the sensory dust (viṣaya) as the subject that touches.
The above constitutes the refutation of the locus of touch; what follows below uses two types of touch and one type of touch to refute the lack of intrinsic substance in touch.
If [touch] were present in each [part] individually, then you, Ānanda, would have two bodies.

[Commentary: This refutes the notion that two distinct substances exist [separately]. (Since [touch] is neither in the head nor in the hand, it does not constitute contact; fearing that he might further argue for its existence in both places simultaneously, [the text] refutes this. [Touch] would have to exist separately in the head and the hand.
If there were two cognitions, then two Ānandas would result. Which body would be yours? [The Lecture Record says: "If there is one cognition, it constitutes one body;
if there is another cognition, it constitutes one instance of non-cognition, which is equivalent to a single speck of dust. Therefore, you, Ānanda, ought to have two bodies."]
If the head and the hand were produced by a single contact, then the hand and the head would have to be a single entity.
If they were a single entity, then contact could not be established.
[Commentary]: This refutes [the claim] that they together constitute a single entity. The first four lines constitute the direct refutation.

If the head and the hand were to produce a single contact (*sparśa*), it would follow that these two distinct things must merge into one entity. Even if one were to concede that they are a single entity, contact itself could not be established.
This concludes the refutation. (Wenling says: Contact requires two things; with only one, it is not established.)
If they were two distinct entities, with respect to whom would contact exist? If it exists in the agent, it does not exist in the object; if it exists in the object, it does not exist in the agent.
It should not be that empty space comes into contact with you.

[Commentary: This refutes the attempted defense. The first two phrases cite the defense and pose a general challenge. If you defend yourself by saying, "Although that which is produced is one, that which produces it is twofold;
why then should my head and hands not be distinct?"—then this contact between two entities occurs where?

Does it belong to the agent of contact (the toucher), or does it belong to the object of contact (the touched)? Therefore, it asks: "Contact with whom exists? It exists in the [agent], as indicated in the following two lines.

The refutation of this point is the same as the previous one. As stated before: "If [the capacity for sensation] resided in the hand, then the head would be without cognition," and so forth. (Master Rong’s commentary says: "The hand is the agent (*kartṛ*) and the head is the object (*karman*");
whether as agent or as object, each loses one side of the equation. The subsequent section refutes the arising from emptiness (*ākāśa*).

Even dharmas with form cannot arise [from it]; how much less could empty nothingness produce tactile contact? (Since both the head and the hand have lost their respective status as agent and object, there is nothing that does not come from empty space to cause you to experience tactile contact.)
This is not reasonable. (Therefore, the three links are established as false.
Consequently, one should know that the perception of touch and the body both lack a location; thus, both the body and the touch are equally false.
This is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.

(Awakening is that which is known; contact is that which touches; the body consists of the head and hands. The refutation is divided into three parts, followed by a synthesis of two; the same applies to the remaining five passages). (The six [sense bases], the mind, and the sphere of dharmas—these three). (1. Citing an instance to pose the inquiry).
Ānanda, regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate natures that you constantly take as objects within your mind, and the laws by which they arise and are produced—
do these phenomena arise from the mind itself, or do they exist apart from the mind in some other location?
[Commentary: The phenomena of the three natures (tri-svabhāva) that serve as objects within the mental consciousness encompass everything exhaustively;

this occurs spontaneously and naturally, which is why it is said they "generate and complete. [The *Zhenji* says: The objective realm of dharmas perceived by the mental consciousness consists of the three natures, which differ from one another. They vary in being either provisional or real, and they produce understanding in beings according to their respective patterns without interfering with one another;

thus it is called the "law of generating and completing. The *Buyu* says: For example, the "evil five aggregates" are real dharmas (*dharma*), while "evil sentient beings" are provisional designations (*prajñapti*). The same applies to the wholesome and the indeterminate. The three natures that serve as objects here are the dharmas; the mental factors (*caitta*) also pertain to all three natures, but this does not refer to the mind-king (*citta*) itself.]

It penetrates all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Regarding the term "generated and formed" (*shengcheng*): these mental factors (*caitta*) arise from the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*), and are thus said to be "generated and formed. For example, in the case of wholesome mental factors, they take the wholesome sovereign as their model to establish their own norms; that which is practiced is wholesome. The cases of the unwholesome and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) are to be understood by analogy.

The *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra* states: "Model" (*gui*) refers to a paradigm that can produce understanding in sentient beings; each takes its respective norm. This is the functional activity of the dharma. [Commentary by Wang Shunging: The three dharmas of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, when considered according to their objective reality, seem to belong to external objects (*viṣaya*).

To say here that they are "objects of focus within the mind" means that they are empty objects (*śūnya-viṣaya*) manifested within the locus of emptiness. Fundamentally, they are not generated or formed; yet they appear as if generated and formed. This is merely the result of beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) becoming thoroughly familiarized. [From the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the School): Dharma]

The "abode" (*āyatana*) is the object of cognition (*ālambana*); the "wholesome abode" is the subject that cognizes. Now, regarding the dharma-abode (*dharmāyatana*), is it identical to the mind or not identical to the mind? [Commentary:
This dharma which serves as the object of cognition—whether it is identical to the mind or separate from the mind—both positions entail fallacies, which will be refuted below.

[Wenling says: "Wholesome and unwholesome" refer to the mind of discursive thought; "indeterminate" refers to the mind of dull stagnation. The mental faculty’s objects do not exceed these three. By drawing inward the internal dust (*rajas*), they constitute the dharmas that serve as objects of cognition; hence it is said, "they generate and produce the principles of dharmas. (From *Fashu*: *Lengyan San*)

Nature (*svabhāva*). First is the nature of goodness; second is the nature of evil; these refer to the nature of all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas arising from the sixth consciousness. Third is the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); this refers to the nature of all that is neither unwholesome nor wholesome which is possessed by the sixth consciousness, wherein there is initially no memory or recollection.

All are generated according to the principles of the objects perceived by the mental faculty (*manas*), and are thus called "nature. This means they are capable of functioning without being taught. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are constructed based upon these three natures, for all dharmas take the three natures as their standard.

(△ [The *Erleng* says: The mind is the locus of the faculties; wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas are the locus of the objects. The three natures taken by the five faculties are the falling away of active manifestations (*pravṛtti*), which manifest as shadows; each has its own rules, serving as the domain of the mind.)

The object of perception is called the "dharma-object" (*dharmaviṣaya*). Since this dharma-object is transformed solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), one examines it by means of both the mind itself and its separation from the mind. (2. Refuting the subsequent conceptualization by restating it.)
Ānanda, if dharmas were identical with the mind, then dharmas would not be objects; they would not be the objects of the mind's perception.

How, then, could they constitute a sense-field (*āyatana*)? [From the *Zongjing*]: If they were identical with the mind, then dharmas would be entirely the mind itself. Since the mind does not see the mind, how could they constitute a sense-field?

[Commentary] This refutes that [the dharmas] are identical to the mind. The first phrase restates [the opponent's position]; the second phrase establishes [the correct view]; "not the mind" and below refute it. Since they are identical to the mind, they certainly cannot be external objects (*viṣaya*).
If they are not external objects, then they are not the objective spheres (*ālambana*) of the mind; how, then, could they be called the "sphere of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana*)? (Wenling says:

"Since phenomena are identical to the mind, they do not belong to the category of external objects; therefore, they are not objects of perception, and the sphere of the mental faculty (*manāyatana*) is not established. (Jiaoguang says: "Not being external objects means they are identical to the mind.")

"The mind takes mental factors as its object" means that the mind does not take itself as its own object. (△ [Hōchūnan says: "When it is said that the knots are the mind itself, it means they are not objects of the mind; because they are of one substance, the mind cannot take them as an object, just as the eye cannot see itself. When it is said that the knots are separate from the mind, it means the mind is not their object;

because they lack substance, there is nothing for the mind to take as an object, just as the eye cannot see a hare's horn). (● The following three sections collectively refute the view that [the knots] are separate from the mind.)
If there were a separate location apart from the mind, then would the intrinsic nature of that phenomenon be conscious or unconscious?
[Commentary] This cites the opponent's position and poses two simultaneous inquiries. The first two phrases cite the position; "then the phenomenon" and below pose the inquiry.

Since this phenomenon is already apart from the mind, it is further investigated by asking whether it is conscious or unconscious, thereby refuting it. [Zongjing] If it were apart from the mind, then the phenomenon...

As for the intrinsic nature of these [mental objects]—that is, the intrinsic nature of *dharmas*—is it conscious or unconscious? [Wenling says: Mental objects have no form; they are manifested through the cognition of the mind. Therefore, the question is asked:
are they conscious or unconscious?]
That which knows is called the mind. It differs from you, yet it is not an external object; it is identical to the mental measure (*cittamātra*) of others. It is you, and it is the mind.
How could your mind further be divided into two distinct entities?
[Commentary: This refutes the notion that there is cognition [intrinsic to dharmas]. The first phrase negates the established view of the "Mind-Only" (cittamātra) doctrine.

If a dharma apart from the mind were to possess cognition, it should be designated as "mind. (As Gushan says: "If it knows, it is called mind": if there is a dharma apart from the mind and that dharma possesses cognition, it is likewise called mind. (△ As the *Jianglu* says:

"If one allows that the objects of dharma (*dharmālambana*) possess cognition, they should be called 'mind' and not 'dharma-objects'. The phrase "different from you," etc., further analyzes the identity and difference to refute [the opponent's position]. (Since the dharma possesses cognition, it is immediately designated as mind; thus, this...)

"Is the cognizing dharma that is separate from the mind different from you, or is it identical to you? The first two phrases refute the position of difference: if the cognizing dharma were different from your mind...

It would then be identical to others and different from your own mind; furthermore, it possesses cognition. [Gushan says: "Different from you" means that if it were different from you, it would not be your mind.]

If there is cognition, it is not your object-field (*viṣaya*). Since it is both different and not [your mind], it must be the mind of another person. (△ [Dinglin says]: The nature of dharmas is itself empty; they are not objects. If there is cognition here, it is your own mind. What, then, would constitute the dharma?)

If this were different from you, and furthermore were not an object (*viṣaya*), it would be identical to the mental measure (*citta-mātra*) of another person. By what means could it be established as a dharma? These three subsequent lines of yours refute that [the dharma] is identical to the mind.

The first half-line restates and establishes the position; the latter two lines refute it. Since a dharma that possesses cognition is already identical to your own mind, it would follow that outside of your mind there must yet exist another mind of yours.
Therefore, it says: "Furthermore, two [minds] apart from you. (If it were identical to you, then it would be identical to your mind; how then [could there be two]?)

"Your mind—furthermore, there are two [aspects] of yours. (△ [Gushan says]: "That you is the very mind," to prevent the erroneous calculation [of duality]. "How can... and so forth, is the objection. Your mind is one; how can there be two mountains? Since both the sense organ and the object are known, these would constitute two minds.

(○ [Citation of Proof]: The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "Regarding such mental objects, are they different from the mind or not different? If the mind were different from the objects, then within a single moment there should be two minds.
If the mind were identical to the objects, it should not be able to observe its own mind, just as the tip of a finger cannot touch itself)."

If it were not known by the knower, then since these objects are neither form, sound, fragrance, taste, nor touch (the five sense objects, where "separation and conjunction" and "cold and warmth" refer specifically to the object of touch), nor do they possess the characteristics of empty space (this collectively clarifies both form and emptiness), where would they exist? Now, within form and emptiness, they leave no trace whatsoever.
It should not be that there is further emptiness outside of the human realm; since the mind has no object of perception (*ālambana*), from what could its locus be established?

[Commentary] This refutes the ignorance [of those who hold such views]. The first five phrases definitively establish that it is not the emptiness of form (*rūpa-śūnyatā*). The following phrase interrogates where it actually resides.
Form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*): these two matters encompass all phenomena (*dharma*) exhaustively. Since it is neither form nor emptiness, where does it now reside? [Gushan says:

This refers to the mental object (*dharmadhātu*), not the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). The five sensory objects and empty space encompass all phenomena; they are all objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and belong to the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*). Since the mental object does not belong to the five [senses], he therefore questions: "Where should it be located? [Xunwen says: There are two kinds of phenomena:

first, mental phenomena (*cittadharma*), which refers to the various associated mental factors (*caitta-dharma*); second, non-mental phenomena, which refers to past and future forms and so forth. Thus, outside of the five sensory objects and the like, there are further mental phenomena. Herein, this is for the purpose of refuting such phenomena.

If it were not cognition (*jñāna*), it would necessarily belong to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) or to empty space (*ākāśa*); therefore, it is said that [cognition] "encompasses all phenomena" (*sarva-dharma-saṃgraha*). If it were a mental phenomenon (*caitta-dharma*), it would naturally fall under the refutations discussed in the preceding text.

The following two lines [of the verse] investigate [the object] and find nothing to represent it. If this "dharma-object" (*dharma-ālambana*) is also subsumed within form and emptiness, by what could it be represented?

If one knows it to be a dharma-object, the following two lines—which refute the existence of objects outside of emptiness—would be untenable. Since there is no representation within form and emptiness, [it cannot exist].

This would constitute a sense-object (*dharmāyatana*) existing outside of space; however, since space has no exterior, [as Mount Gu said: "There is nothing at all to indicate it, because the mental object (*dharma*) is formless and its conditions are the five past objects that have already fallen away.

Since one does not perceive the form of the mental object within the realm of form and space, how could there be a mental object existing separately outside of space? The two lines beginning with "The mind is not... conclude the meaning of having no location.
Having thus investigated and examined above, since the mental object does not exist, the mind has no objective realm upon which to depend. From...
Why is a locus established?
(The three points demonstrate that [all things] are empty and false.
Therefore, one should know that when dharmas give rise to the mind, both are without a locus; likewise, when the mind gives rise to dharmas, both are empty and false.
It is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

[Commentary on the Source Mirror: Since one knows that both the sense-sphere of mind (*manas*) and the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharma*) lack intrinsic substance, then the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—and the four types of mental factors such as the mental faculty (*manendriya*) are all of a single nature; there is no [agent] capable of [producing them].
Because the conditions and the objects of perception differ, both mind and phenomena are empty. Thus, the Treatise says: "Whatever is conceptualized is all conceptualization of one's own mind.
When the mind does not perceive the mind, no characteristics can be apprehended; then the principle of signlessness manifests, and all contrived emotions vanish."
Causes and conditions are spontaneous; both name and meaning are utterly transcended. This applies equally to the ten bases of form and mind.

Now, that which distinguishes the subject from the object and constructs the framework of maintenance—establishing both objects and the mind—is entirely within the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
If one first destroys the root of delusive discrimination, then the five preceding sense faculties and the ten bases will naturally dissolve of themselves.

(4. Refuting the eighteen *dhātus*, part 2). (1. General inquiry). (○ [Wenling says]: The three—sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses—each have six; divided into internal, external, and intermediate, they constitute the *dhātus*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the eighteen *dhātus*? They are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

[Sūtra Commentary]: In Sanskrit it is called *dhātu*, which here means "element" (*jie*). An element has the sense of being a cause. This is because the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness acts as a cause.

(The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states: "Element has the sense of being a cause. The *Bai-fa-lun-su* states: "The six intermediate consciousnesses depend upon the six faculties to arise; the six faculties draw in the six objects to produce [consciousness]. Because they serve as the cause for consciousness, they are called 'elements' [*dhātus*]. Furthermore...

The meaning of "category" (*gotra*) refers to the three—organ, object, and consciousness—each constituting a single category. Furthermore, because there are six distinct categories, such as the eye and so forth, [the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states]:

"That is to say, within a single body or a single continuum, there are eighteen types of categories; therefore, they are called the eighteen *dhātus*. Because the categories of the eye and so forth differ when compared with one another, they are termed 'elements' (*dhātu*')."

(△ [The *Zhongjing* says: "Dhātu" (*jie*) has the meaning of establishing distinct categories (*jie-fen*). This is because they are established through mutual opposition—internal, external, and intermediate. [The *Zhi guan* says: "Dhātu" means differentiation (*jie-bie*); it is also called "nature-division" (*xing-fen*). [The *Fajie cidi* says:

"If the faculties (*indriya*) are in opposition, then consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises. 'Dhātu' takes differentiation as its meaning. These eighteen dharmas each have their own distinct substance; since their meanings are not confused or intermingled, 'consciousness' takes differentiation as its meaning. Consciousness relies upon the faculties and is able to differentiate objects (*viṣaya*); therefore, they are collectively termed 'consciousness.

Thus, these three—faculties, objects, and consciousness—each have six categories, forming the eighteen dhātus. (△ [The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* says: "The meaning of the seeds (*bīja*) of all dharmas. That is to say, the seeds of all dharmas within the *ālayavijñāna* are designated as such.")

The realm (*dhātu*). Furthermore, it has the sense of maintaining its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); it has the sense of maintaining the nature of cause and effect; and it has the sense of encompassing the distinctions among all phenomena. This is because, through the body, the faculties, and so forth, it maintains the nature of the enjoyment of the six modes of activity of the past and present.

"Body" refers to the six faculties, such as the eye. "Faculties" refers to the six objects, such as form. The "enjoyment of the six modes of activity of the past and present" refers to the six consciousnesses. That which "maintains" refers to the six faculties and six objects, because they maintain the bases (*āśraya*) and objects of focus (*ālambana*) for the six consciousnesses. The six consciousnesses of the past and present... [are maintained].

Regarding the "bases that maintain and experience": because they do not abandon their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), one should know there are eighteen. They are called "elements" (*dhātu*) in the sense of being able to maintain [their respective objects]. (2. Distinct refutation of the six; 3. The first visual-consciousness element; 1. Citation of the thesis and dual interrogation).
Ānanda, as you understand it, visual consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions.
Does this consciousness arise because of the eye and take the eye as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of visible forms and take visible forms as its constituent element?
[Commentary: In the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna, the Buddha spoke of all phenomena arising through causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Now, clarifying the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), he shows that both "causes and conditions" and "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) are mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). Therefore, he restates these terms here to interrogate them. (Wuxing says: What the Hīnayāna understands as phenomena produced by causes and conditions are all taken to be substantially real;

they do not realize their immediate emptiness. This refutation is based on this point to shatter such attachments. (Wang Shungding says: Ānanda said, "The eye possesses discrimination, while the object of form (*rūpa*) is without cognition; consciousness arises between them. This clearly distinguishes the faculties (*indriya*) from the objects (*viṣaya*)).

The two realms are further divided into three realms because consciousness resides within the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*). Therefore, [the text] cites and refutes them. [From the *Zhengjìng* (Mirror of Correct Enlightenment): Question:

What are the characteristics of the eye-realm (*cakṣur-dhātu*)? Answer: It refers to the eye having previously seen, or currently seeing, forms (*rūpa*). (“Having previously seen forms” means it can maintain the meaning of the past consciousness’s experience, thereby manifesting the nature of the realm (*dhātu-svabhāva*). “Currently seeing forms” means it can maintain the meaning of the present consciousness’s experience, thereby manifesting the nature of seeing.
And it includes the seeds thereof, which are accumulated in the *ālaya-vijñāna*. (This refers to the seed of the eye, which is either merely accumulated or serves as an inducer.)

The characteristic of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is that it serves as the cause for the future arising of the eye, or that it has already matured in order to produce the present eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*). These two types are called the "eye-element" because they are the causes for the arising of the eye.

Just as this is the characteristic of the eye-element, so too are the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind elements. Question: What is the characteristic of the form-element (*rūpadhātu*)? Answer:

It is all forms that have been seen by the eye in the past or are being seen at present, and that which exercises sovereignty over the form-element (meaning that external objects arise through the sovereign power of the strength of form). This is the characteristic of the form-element. As is the characteristic of the form-element, so too are those of sound, odor, taste, and touch.
The characteristics of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are also like this. Question: What are the characteristics of the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)? Answer:

It refers to that which, depending on the eye and taking form as its object, is the discernment of what resembles form, as well as its seeds—the *ālayavijñāna* of the habituated seeds. These are the characteristics of the eye-consciousness. (As with the eye-consciousness element, so too are the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind elements.

[△ *Yuanjue shu* says: Within each sense-gate, there are distinct domains; that is, the eye-faculty and consciousness constitute a domain, and consciousness and form constitute a domain, and so forth. (2) Second, refuting [the opponent's position] by restating their calculations.

Ānanda, if [the visual consciousness] arises because of the eye, then since there is neither form nor space, there would be nothing to differentiate. Even if your consciousness were present, what would it have to function with?
Furthermore, your seeing is not blue, yellow, red, or white; having nothing to represent it, from what could a boundary be established?

[Commentary: This refutes [the view that consciousness] arises from the sense organs (*indriya*). Since the latter four propositions do not exist, what would be the use of refuting the existence of consciousness without an object?
If it arises from the sense organs, then an object is unnecessary. If that object does not exist, what is there to be discerned? The objective referent (*ālambana*) is already non-existent.
What is the use of an object of cognition? You have already seen the refutation in the following four lines: that the sense-faculties which produce consciousness lack intrinsic nature.

If you claim that consciousness arises from the faculties, yet those faculties are not blue or other colors and possess no representation, then since the faculties themselves cannot be established, from what could consciousness arise?

[Zhenji said: "You see' refers to the sense organ (*indriya*). Because it is invisible and possesses resistance (*sapratigha*), it is not blue or other such colors; therefore, it is invisible. Because it can illuminate objects and give rise to consciousness, it is 'resistant. This is the *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense organ), not the *vibhūṣaṇa-indriya* (manifested sense organ). Since it is invisible, it has no representation. [△ Wēnlíng said:

"If it were solely due to the eye, and there were neither form nor space, then consciousness would have nothing to take as its object (*ālambana*), seeing would have nothing to manifest, and the realms (*dhātu*) would have no basis for establishment. It is not [the case that] it is not due to the eye. [○ Quotation]

[Commentary on the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*]: Regarding the statement "six types of form," this refers to the objects of apprehension (*grāhya*). There are twenty-five kinds: blue, yellow, red, and white—these four are substantial (*dravya*), for even when analyzed down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), their color does not change.

Length, shortness, squareness, roundness, coarseness, fineness, high, and low—these are conventional designations of shape (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), for at the level of the ultimate atom, there is no such shape. Correctness and incorrectness, light and shadow, brightness and darkness, dust motes, clouds, mist, the color of distance, the color of manifestation, and the color of the uniform expanse of space—these are conventional designations of state (*avasthā-rūpa*), because those various phenomena transform according to location.

All these are forms manifested as spatial locations; they are colors in the sense of hue. Because they face the visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*), they are called "form" (*rūpa*) due to their resistance (*pratighāta*); this is simply the general name for form. [Below: Refutation of the Object]
If [consciousness] arises dependent on form, then when space is devoid of form, your consciousness should cease; how then could you cognize the nature of this emptiness?
If form undergoes change, you likewise perceive that form is empty and subject to transition. If your consciousness does not transition, from what basis could the realms be established?

[Commentary] This shows that while the characteristics of form shift and incline toward one another, there is no consciousness to break them apart. The first phrase restates the premise; "empty" and below comprise the four subsequent phrases.

Establishing the principle to provide a correct refutation: since [consciousness] arises from form, when emptiness appears and form perishes, consciousness should likewise perish. Who then would perceive empty space? (Wenling says: "If it arises because of form, it should perish along with form. When consciousness perishes and emptiness appears, how can consciousness know it? These five lines following "If form... constitute a refutation based on reason through interrogation. If form undergoes change and you are able to perceive that change, yet consciousness fundamentally does not migrate, then once the characteristics of form are absent, [what perceives? From... [text continues] ...the principle is established. If you say that although the nature of consciousness is originally non-migratory, it nevertheless manifests as such due to the power of conditions, then this is like a person who, though their body is originally fixed, moves about by means of the power of the wind. If so, then consciousness is not the knower; rather, it is the wind that knows. Furthermore, if consciousness is not the knower, then the wind should be the knower. If the wind is the knower, then it should be able to perceive the nature of emptiness. Why then does the wind not perceive emptiness? Moreover, if consciousness is not the knower, then the body should be the knower. If the body is the knower, then it should be able to perceive emptiness. Why then does the body not perceive emptiness? Furthermore, if consciousness is not the knower, then the mind should be the knower. If the mind is the knower, then it should be able to perceive emptiness. Why then does the mind not perceive emptiness? Moreover, if consciousness is not the knower, then the sense organs should be the knowers. If the sense organs are the knowers, then they should be able to perceive emptiness. The doctrinal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Hīnayāna explain that all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are accomplished through the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). These are further divided into internal and external; this is called the "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.

That they are quiescent and formless is still considered the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. Such [explanations] are coarse and shallow, being the Buddha-Tathāgata’s speech according to the intentions of others (*para-asaṃvidita-vāk*), established for the sake of the world. They possess names but lack reality. Although...

It is called "Great" (*mahat*). The meaning of "great" is not established [in the conventional sense]. What is taught in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is not thus: it refers to that which is all-pervasive and inclusive, whose essence is nowhere absent, and for which there is nothing that is not itself. It is not designated as "great" in dependence upon the "small"; rather, it receives this name by virtue of its own essential nature. Therefore, it is called "Great."

The seven meanings explained in this sutra are all termed "Great" because, among these seven meanings, they encompass all phenomena—namely, emptiness and existence, faculties and objects, form and mind, essence and characteristics—and there is not a single object or phenomenon that is not universally pervaded or contained within them.

This shatters provisional views and reveals the meaning as it truly is. As the text below states: "These are uniformly called the Seven Greats; their nature is truly interfused and perfectly harmonious, for all are the Tathāgata-garbha. The world is ignorant of this and deludedly regards them as having the nature of causes and conditions or as being spontaneous.

These are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating consciousness; they consist only of words and have no real substance. This is the convergence of appearances into the nature, where both nature and appearance are all-pervasive; only then can they be called the supreme greatness of ultimate reality. How could this be the same as the provisional teachings, which speak of things as having their own distinct characteristics?

Both [positions] have been rejected; I do not now understand to which category this meaning belongs. I pray that you will take pity on us and reveal to sentient beings the Middle Way, the definitive meaning, the dharma free from conceptual proliferation.

dehi) request an exposition. Through skillful means (*upāya*), [the Buddha] established that there are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and that they arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*).

They are divided into specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, they arise from deluded thoughts and are known through forced awareness. Within this, beauty and ugliness, as well as aversion and attachment, are entirely the product of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), formed through conceptualization and discrimination. Once one understands their root cause, one must maintain right wisdom (*samyagjñāna*). By simply eliminating forceful perceptions, when not a single thought arises, the mind and its objects naturally become empty together, and the boundaries of past and future are severed.

(The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All phenomena have two kinds of aspects: first, their individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). For example, earth has the characteristic of solidity, water the characteristic of moisture, fire the characteristic of heat, and wind the characteristic of motion. Thus, one discriminates all phenomena, each having its own specific characteristic.")

Second is the true nature (*dharmatā*). Within each respective characteristic, if one seeks the reality through analysis, it cannot be found; it cannot be destroyed, and it is free from all faults. As explained regarding the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*):

if earth were truly characterized by solidity, why is it that when substances such as glue or lacquer encounter fire, they abandon their own characteristics and transform into the characteristic of moisture? Why is it that gold, silver, copper, and iron, through contact with fire, likewise abandon their own characteristics and change into the characteristic of water? Just as water, upon meeting cold, becomes ice and transforms into the characteristic of earth, so too does a person possessing supernormal powers enter the earth as if it were water.

Furthermore, when wood or stone is broken apart, they lose their solid characteristic; and when earth is reduced to atoms and those atoms are further divided, they ultimately return to emptiness, thereby losing their solid characteristic. Thus one should investigate.

If one seeks the characteristics of earth, they cannot be found; in reality, all are empty. This emptiness is the true characteristic (*dharmatā*) of earth. Some say that even the names of the four great elements are, in fact, boundless and inexhaustible. The vastness of earth sustains and nurtures all things.

It is the most firm and stable. The Buddha taught that the power of the mind is great because it practices the *prajñāpāramitā*. [The mind] can scatter this great earth into subtle atoms; for the earth has color, fragrance, taste, and touch, and being heavy, it acts of its own accord.

Water has less fragrance, so its movement surpasses that of the earth. Fire has less fragrance and taste, so its heat surpasses that of water. Wind has less color, fragrance, and taste, so its movement surpasses that of fire. Because the mind lacks these four [sensory] objects, its power in what it undertakes is great.

When the master of yoga practices contemplation, he first divides a single aggregate of form into two parts. He contemplates these two portions of form and perceives that neither a self nor any phenomena exist therein. Fearing, however, that a self or phenomena might still persist within those two portions, he further employs his mind of wisdom.

It is analyzed into four distinct parts, and so on until one reaches the single characteristic of an atom (*paramāṇu*), which can no longer be further divided; this is the ultimate limit of matter. If it were further divided, it would cease to be matter. Furthermore, according to the *Record of the Western Regions*, the most minute category is defined as follows: one *yojana* is divided into eight *krośas*; one *krośa* is divided into five hundred *dhanus* (bows); one *dhanus* is divided into four *hastas* (cubits); one *hasta* is divided into twenty-four *aṅgulis* (fingers); one finger-joint is divided into seven grains of barley;

and this continues through lice, nits, the dust motes in a crevice, cow-hair, sheep-hair, rabbit-hair, and copper-water (*tong-shui*), each being divided into seven parts until reaching the "subtle dust" (*sūkṣma-rajas*).

Seven subtle dust particles constitute an "extremely subtle dust" (*paramāṇu-rajas*). Even a single atom still possesses divisions in the ten directions; if this particle is further divided into seven parts, it is termed the "ultimate atom. Thus it is said.

This refers to the fact that even a single minute particle still possesses divisions according to the ten directions (*daśa-dig-bhāga*).

If this particle is further divided into seven parts, it is called a *paramāṇu*. It also says: "If the *anu* is further analyzed, it is the nature of actual emptiness. From what does form arise? Therefore, one knows that this form originally lacks intrinsic nature. (As explained in the *She-lun* [Treatise on the Compendium]:

"If we examine the method of analyzing form to clarify emptiness according to the Hīnayāna, once the great earth is analyzed away to reveal empty space, it is evident that form has no substantial reality and is entirely produced from within empty space. That which is called the realm of contaminated atoms all arises depending upon space.

Now, if it is said that things arise through combination, then even the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal atom) must be composed of combinations, and even empty space itself must be composed of combinations. Tell me, how many spaces are used to combine and form a *paramāṇu*, and how much form is used [to compose space]?)

[The characteristics] combine to form empty space. If matter were to combine, it would only result in the formation of material characteristics; it could never result in the formation of empty space. If space were to combine, it would eternally remain as empty space and could never result in the formation of material characteristics.

Furthermore, in the world there is only the method of analyzing matter; how could there be a method of combining space? Since empty space and its subtle constituents do not exist through combination, how could various transformed phenomena possibly be produced through combination? (3. Harmonizing with the True Principle)
You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form;

it is pure and pristine by its very essence, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It accords with the minds of sentient beings and manifests according to the measure of their knowledge, appearing in accordance with their karma.

[Commentary] This clarifies true form (*rūpa*). The first two phrases point to primordial delusion. [Gushan says: "Although this principle has been primordially present from the beginning, it has also been primordially deluded since the beginning;
therefore it is said, 'You originally did not know'. The three phrases beginning with "The Tathāgata" reveal the essence of the Dharma.

The "Tathāgata-garbha" is the mind of the single Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the Middle Way, the Supreme Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). "Nature-form is true emptiness" is the truth within the conventional.
The true form of the emptiness of nature is the conventional within the ultimate; all these terms "nature" (xing) manifest the ultimate and conventional within the midst [of reality].

Because it is conventional, the ten realms are distinct and vivid—hence, it is called "the true form of the emptiness of nature. Because it is ultimate, birth and Buddhahood are quiescent—hence, it is called "the true emptiness of the form of nature. These speak of the inherent perfection of principle (*li*), not of the phenomenal creation of phenomena (*shi*);

therefore, they are termed "nature. The three truths are perfectly interfused, neither identical nor different, neither vertical nor horizontal; this is named the Tathāgatagarbha. In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is called...

It is the secret treasury (*guhyanidhi*). (From the Commentary of Mount Gu) This is the true element of earth (*pṛthivīdhātu*). The two lines following "pure and clear" describe the measure of its virtuous qualities.
It is called "pure" because it corresponds to non-delusion and is endowed with untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*).

Because it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is said to be "originally so. Because it is omnipresent, it is said to be "all-pervading. (Principle must necessarily harmonize with phenomena, and how could phenomena differ from principle? When both principle and phenomenon are simultaneously extinguished, it is called "pure and originally so. Mind and Buddha...

Sentient beings—these three are without distinction; they mutually encompass one another and each is fused with all others. Therefore, it is said that they "pervade the entire dharma-realm. This constitutes the complete fulfillment of the essence, qualities, and magnitude of the lineage (*gotra*).

If one recognizes this dharma, one accomplishes the three sublime contemplations. [The *Shiyao* says: "Inherent form is true emptiness"—this is the contemplation of emptiness. When one is empty, all are empty.

There is no provisional [phenomenon] that is not empty; the emptiness of nature is true form—this is the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*). One provisional [phenomenon] is all provisional; there is no emptiness that is not provisional. Form and emptiness are non-dual—this is the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). One middle is all middle; there is no emptiness or provisionality that is not the middle.

Only then does one know that a single atom contains all Buddha-dharmas, all mind-dharmas, and all sentient-being dharmas, none of which fail to reside within a single minute atom. This is to see Vairocana, to see oneself, and to see...
One perceives all dharmas as being like a single mote of dust; all dharmas are likewise so. The following sections are to be understood according to this principle.

"Following the sentient beings" below clarifies that the *tathāgatagarbha* follows conditions (*pratyaya*). The ten realms of sentient beings differ in being either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), and their karma is likewise not the same.

The material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) that they are deluded by also vary in being pure or defiled, and so forth (this explains how the *tathāgatagarbha* follows conditions to produce the phenomena of the ten realms; that is, it manifests differences according to whether the mind is defiled or pure).

It is merely the manifestation of the fruits of the ten realms—the environment and its inhabitants—due to individual karma. (△ [Zhenji said]: "Intrinsic form is true emptiness," meaning it is free from all marks. "Intrinsic emptiness is true form," meaning it is identical to all phenomena.
[Zongjing] "According to the minds of sentient beings and corresponding to the measure of what they know" means that it manifests precisely where the faculties of sentient beings have matured;

this refers to the differentiated objects of sentient beings. This means that within a single dharma-particle (*dharmāyatana*), one equally pervades the entire Dharma-realm, such that even a neighboring infinitesimal particle (*paramāṇu*) is no different.
Self-nature. Self-nature is itself empty space; empty space is itself true emptiness; true emptiness is itself original enlightenment.
Therefore, know that within a single pore, the Tathāgata constantly preaches the wondrous Dharma for immeasurable sentient beings.
Thus one knows that all pores and atoms do not transcend me. Yet, if one understands even the Dharma of a single atom, then—

The number [of these lands] is equal to the atoms of the entire dharma-realm. As for those that manifest according to the arising of karma, they all appear in accordance with the karmic fruits of sentient beings.
For example, when Śākyamuni appeared in the world, the land was narrow and small and the waters of the ocean rose;

when Maitreya descends to be born, the world will be vast and expansive and the four great oceans will recede. When Bodhisattvas are present in the assembly, there are no hills or ravines; as for the śrāvakas...
It dwells in the midst [of the world], filled with filth and impurity. Thus we know that it manifests in response to all sentient beings;

whether vast or narrow, pure or defiled, these are all produced by the mental capacity (*citta-mātra*) of sentient beings. The fruit of Buddhahood is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*). [Direct Explanation: The Tathāgata-garbha is primordially pure; this is the Dharma-realm of principle (*li-dharmadhātu*).

The seven elements (*mahābhūta*) are the Dharma-realm of phenomena (*shi-fajie*), wherein nature and characteristics are perfectly interfused. This is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wuai fajie*). Unity and multiplicity are non-obstructive; the large and small contain one another. The seven elements are all-pervasive—this is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wuai*).]
(Dharmadhātu). (4. Concluding Reprimand of Deluded Sentiment):

The world is ignorant, deluding itself by taking [conditions] as causes and conditions, or as a nature arising spontaneously; all of these are merely the discriminating calculations of the conscious mind.
There are only words; there is no real meaning at all. [Commentary:
Those of the common world, the heterodox, and the Hīnayāna who receive the provisional teachings are all termed "ignorant. Because they do not understand the real meaning, they are called "deluded.
Because they cling to and establish names and forms, it is said that they "act as" (or "become"). The phrase "all are" below is a general censure of their inverted consciousness-minds.
It arises from falsehood and perversion; through delusion following upon delusion, what reality can there be? (Wuxing says: "The world" generally refers to sentient beings of the nine realms.

"Causes and conditions" implies the three natures—self, other, and common. "Spontaneity" refers to the nature of causelessness. (Jiaoguang says: "The cognizing mind" refers to the six consciousnesses. "Discrimination and calculation" refers to the pervasive conceptualization and grasping.)

(2. The Nature of Fire, Part 4) [The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "This body is without self (*anātman*), being like fire. [Sengzhao says: "To act with autonomy and freedom is called 'self. Yet external fire arises and ceases depending on fuel; the fire is not independent.

Because the fire is not independent, the fire has no self. Since external fire has no self, the internal fire is likewise so. [The *Zongjing lu* says: "Fire is composed of three subtle elements (*trimaṇḍala*). It has no fixed nature, nor does it have a nature; this is precisely the absence of fire. Now, as for the name 'body'..."

It is composed of form. If the body has no fixed nature, then there is no self. The various heats within this body are fire. If external fire is without self, then internal fire is also without self. The *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* states: "The fire element—the nature of fire—arises from causes and conditions.

If it arises from conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). That which lacks reality is without self. The nature [of the other elements] and the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) may be understood by analogy with this. (1. General indication of the absence of nature.)
Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self; it relies upon various conditions. [Commentary]:
Fire born of conditions originally lacks a sovereign master. To have no master is to have no intrinsic nature. It arises through the harmony of causes and conditions.

There is only false appearance (the fire produced by conditions is not a fire of intrinsic nature). (1) [The first: citing an example to indicate and raise the issue]. (2) [The second: citing examples to extensively refute it]. (1) [The first: citing an example to indicate and raise the issue].
"Observe, Ānanda, the houses within the city that have not yet eaten. When they wish to cook their food, they hold a *sūryakānta* (sun-crystal) in their hands and seek fire from the sun.
(This is the illustration. Ānanda, that which is called 'conjunction' is like me and you, and these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus."
Now we constitute a single assembly. Although the assembly is one, when its fundamental basis is examined, each individual possesses a body and all have origins:
their clans and names, such as Śāriputra, who is of Brahmin descent, and Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, who is of the Kāśyapa clan.
"Even down to Ānanda, the Gautama clan [is cited as an example].

[Commentary: This cites the assembly to clarify harmony and union. Because the particular arises from the general, and because there must be particulars within the general, three individuals are cited to manifest their distinctions.

[Haiyan’s Note: Citing these three individuals is like the sun, the magnifying lens, and the fire—distinct yet combining to produce fire. They all trace back to the Śākya clan; thus, there is distinction within the general, just as with Śāriputra.

[This refers to] the difference in lineage (*gotra*). (△ [Xunwen says]: Question: Among the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), why is it that only the fire element is used as an analogy for conjunction? Answer: The preceding earth element has a loose sense of conjunction; its grasping is easily broken. From the fire element up to consciousness, the sense of conjunction is intimate; what is conceptualized therein is difficult to break.

For example, the nature of fire—viewed according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)—is clearly produced through the conjunction of the mirror, the sun, and the tinder. Now, by using the conjunction of the various monks, each of whom is distinct, one manifests that the conjunction of all phenomena (*dharma*) is entirely without reality.

(The phrase "each body and each lineage" is precisely an analogy for how conjunction is provisional. Wēnlíng says: "Each has its own lineage"—this is the true meaning of conjunction. Huìjiě’s interpretation is an error. The three individuals cited serve as examples identical to the mirror, the sun, and the tinder.

The three elements of water, wind, and so forth can be understood according to their respective meanings. [Supplement states: The Record Master [Yuanzhao] uses the three—water, pearl, and empty space with the moon; and the three—wind, garment, and empty space with the face—as analogies for the same principle of the conjunction of three factors.

A *yangsui* is a fire-producing lens. [Zhenzhen Chao states: Cui Bao’s *Gujin Zhu* says it is made of copper, shaped like a mirror. When reflecting an object, the image appears inverted; when facing the sun, fire emerges.

The *Huainanzi* states: "The *yángsuǐ* [sun-crystal] produces fire; the *fāngzhū* [moon-crystal] produces water. The *Lùnhéng* says: "On the day of the *bǐngwǔ* hexagram at noon on the fifth month, one smelts the stones of the five directions until they are round like mirrors with a depression in the center;

under a clear sky, facing the rising sun, one produces fire. Master Ying said: "This is the copper essence of the five stones. *Uruvilvā* is translated as "Wood-Plantain Forest" (*mùgūlín*). (In the *Fahua wénjù*, it is noted that he resided near this forest; Gushan says:)

This is called *kapittha* (mango-wood); because there was a tumor on his chest that resembled a *kapittha* fruit, he is so named. Kāśyapa is translated as "Great Tortoise Clan" (*mahā-kūrma-gotra*). Gautama is translated as "Earth-Supreme" (*bhūmi-agra*) and also as "Solar Lineage" (*sūrya-vamśa*)—formerly translated as "Sugarcane.

Nanshan says: it is the name of a star; the title was established based on this star, though later generations changed the clan name to Śākya. Cien says: it is the most eminent of the Śākya clans. In the *Wenju*, it is translated as "Pure and Virtuous."
The Dharma Master Ying translated this as "the most excellent on earth" (meaning that among humans, excluding those outside the heavens, this clan is the most excellent). Ānanda,
if this nature of fire exists because of a combination of causes, when one holds a mirror in the hand and seeks fire from the sun,
does this fire emerge from within the mirror, does it emerge from the tinder, or does it come from the sun?
(The citation and inquiry may be understood as above). (2. Refutation by logical inference):
Ānanda, if the sun were to come here, it would naturally burn the moxa in your hand; furthermore, all the forests from which it comes should likewise be consumed by fire.
[Commentary: This refutes the theory that [the heat] arises from the sun. From the sun to the hand, there are forty thousand *yojanas*.

Why is it that wherever the light shines, nothing else is scorched, yet only the mugwort in your hand is burned? [Zizhong says: "The sun and the mirror are far apart; the sun is forty thousand *yojana*s away from the human realm.
*Xunwen* says: "One *yojana* is twenty *li*."]
If it were the fire emerging from within the mirror, then as it emerges from the mirror and burns the moxa, why does the mirror not melt?
Even when you hold it in your hand, there is no sign of heat; how then could it ever be fused or dissolved?
[Commentary] This refutes the arising of a mirror. The first four lines constitute a direct refutation; the final three lines constitute a reductio ad absurdum (concessive refutation).
Fire is capable of overcoming metal; upon encountering it, the metal must melt. The exterior can burn moxa, while the interior [of the fire] would likewise dissolve the mirror.

Yet this is not the case for you; therefore, it should not be that the mirror has emerged [from the fire]. [Gushan says: *yū* means to bend, to coil, or to curve; it may also be glossed as "toiling."]
If fire were produced from the mugwort, why would it require the sun and the mirror? It is only when their radiance meets that fire is subsequently produced.
[Commentary] This refutes the view that fire is produced from the mugwort. If fire emerged from the mugwort, then even if the sun and mirror did not join, why would no fire emerge?
If it must wait for them to join before fire is produced, this demonstrates that it does not emerge from the mugwort.

You should observe this again with careful attention: the mirror is held by the hand; the sun comes from the heavens; the moxa grows from the earth. From what direction does the fire come to travel here?
The sun and the mirror are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the fire-light exists of itself without a source.

[Commentary] This summarizes that [fire] has no source. It does not emerge from any of the three locations; from where could fire arise? One should know that it must be non-existent. [Rongshi said: "The mirror, the sun, and the tinder each return to their own place;

since it does not emerge from these three locations, fire has nowhere to come from. It is like a community of bhikṣus, each returning to their respective clans. Below the section on the sun and the mirror, this refutes the causeless nature of combination.
Since the sun and the mirror are not in close proximity, there is no sense of combination. Since it is absent within the conditions, fire cannot exist apart from those conditions.

This principle is certainly untenable. [I maintain that] among the seven great elements, when the Buddha says, "You should now observe closely," or "You should further observe closely," up to "you should examine minutely and scrutinize with extreme care," all of these refer to the wisdom of subtle and secret contemplation within wondrous *śamatha*.

According to the *Zongjing Lu*, among the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings, only the sixth is taken as the faculty capable of observation. Question: Since the first five, the seventh, and the eighth consciousnesses are all capable of cognitive engagement (*ālambana*), why are they not included? Answer:

Within the state of outflow (*sāsrava*), the first five consciousnesses are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), perceiving only the actual objects of the five sense-fields. The eighth consciousness is also exclusively direct perception, as it perceives three types of objects: the seeds, the body of the faculties, and the vessel-world. Its nature is strictly indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). As for the seventh consciousness, within its state of outflow...

The eighth consciousness, when constantly taking its own seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as an object, is subsumed under non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Now, the observing mind [of the sixth consciousness] is known through inference based on the teachings; it transforms and gives rise to an image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), which is of the nature of good (*kuśala*) by means of inference (*anumāna*) and is subsumed under the category of "solitary images" (*pratibimba-gocara*). Therefore, only the sixth consciousness possesses this merit.

In this context, one should contemplate with thorough scrutiny and observe with subtle precision, taking the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) in their entirety as the substance of contemplation. By observing their perfect luminosity, they transform into what resembles the *suvicita-jñāna* (the wisdom of wondrous observation), becoming the true *suvicita-jñāna*.

This is how this contemplation is employed. The immediate teachers argue strenuously that the six consciousnesses must be entirely destroyed; please reflect upon the meaning of "thoroughly contemplating" and "thoroughly scrutinizing" in this sutra. (3. Reconciling with the True Principle)
"You still do not understand that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire.

It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm (this clarifies true fire). According to the minds of sentient beings, it responds to the measure of what they know. Ānanda, you should know that for people of the world..."

If one person holds a mirror in one place and another produces fire in another, yet they are held throughout the entire Dharma-realm and arise filling all worlds—arising so as to pervade every world—how could there be any fixed location?
They manifest according to karma.
[Commentary on the Ancient Mirror] "The nature of fire is true emptiness" means that "nature" is the nature of original enlightenment, and "fire" is the fire of original enlightenment;
both are transformations of the minds of sentient beings. For example, when the heat of the sixth consciousness arises, it is confined to the body.

However, if it arises as a transformation within the eighth consciousness, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm equally. To awaken to the nature of the Dharma-realm is to realize that all things are what is contained within the mind.
The fire of transformation is like the fires of the present world, which manifest everywhere according to the karmic power of sentient beings, appearing in greater or lesser measure as they please.

(For example, when dragons fight, fire breaks out and burns forests and thickets; even the lightning fire within the clouds is like this. When a person’s desire is intense, fire burns the celestial shrines—all these arise from the fire of the mind.

Because the mind wavers, fire arises; if the mind does not move, one is not burned. The Tathāgata has attained the fire of the nature; the fires of the three realms cannot burn him. (The Tathāgata himself gives rise to...)

The fire of wisdom burned [the body] and yielded śarīra relics. This fire was so fierce and intense that the great disciples could not extinguish it with water, nor even the Dragon King; only Śakra said, "By the power of my original vow, I have finally succeeded in extinguishing it.

Although there is the nature of fire, it does not burn itself; just as a sword can cut others but cannot cut itself, and just as the eye can see others but cannot see itself, the nature of the fire element is solely the mind.
The natures of the other seven elements are likewise thus, following the mind and pervading all phenomena.

The realm (*dhātu*). The dharma-realm is fundamentally pervasive; it is only due to the grasping mind that it cannot be pervasive. Just as within the three realms, the divine eyes of the three vehicles are all unable to see everywhere.

Only the Tathāgata is free from grasping, and his nature is conjoined with true emptiness; therefore, he is able to be omnipresent. [The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: Fire is a provisional name and has no reality.

If there were no real dharma of fire, how could one say that heat is the nature of fire? The nature of heat arises from a multitude of conditions: internally there is the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), and externally there is visible form and tangibility; through their conjunction, body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) arises.

One perceives that there is heat. If [fire] were not yet combined [with its nature], it would lack the quality of heat. If fire possesses the quality of heat, why is it that some people enter fire without being burned, and why is it that within the human body it does not burn the body? Furthermore, why can neither water nor fire extinguish the fire within the clouds?

Because fire lacks a fixed nature of burning, fire cannot burn the body. Due to the causal conditions of karma, the five viscera are not burned; due to the power of the divine dragon, water cannot extinguish it. If the nature of heat were distinct from fire, then fire would not be hot.

If heat and fire were one, how could one say that heat is the nature of fire? It is the same for the other natures as well. Because this general nature and specific nature do not exist, they are called "emptiness of nature. (4. Conclusion: Rebuking Deluded Sentiment)
The world is ignorant, deludedly taking [causes and conditions] as well as inherent nature to be real; all of these are merely the discerning and calculating of the conscious mind.
They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no actual meaning (as can be understood from the text).

(3. The Three Water-Natures, 4. (○ [The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "This body has no person (*pudgala*), being like water. [Sengzhao says: "That which is honored among the myriad things yet remains unchanged from beginning to end is called a 'person. Yet external water is good at benefiting the myriad forms;

it conforms to squareness or roundness according to the object, rising or sinking as appropriate, while its substance has no fixed nature. Since its substance has no fixed nature, water has no person. As external water has no person, the same can be known for internal water. (○ [The *Zongjing lu* says: "Water is composed of the three subtle elements (*tanmātra*). It has no fixed [nature].")

Nature. Where there is no nature, there is no water. The body is formed by the conjunction of three factors; it has no fixed nature. Where there is no nature, there is no body. Where there is no body, there is no person. Therefore, it is said that this body is without a person, which is like water. The *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-samantamukha-parivarta* states: "The nature of water does not abide.

That which abides—such as the square or round shapes of ponds—is due to obstruction, not because water possesses an abiding nature. If one examines water through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and finds it to have a nature or an attachment, this is the meaning of 'abiding.

If, regarding the four propositions, water is without nature and without attachment, this is 'non-abiding. Because it is non-abiding, it enters the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). (1. General indication of the absence of nature.)
"Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing have no constancy.

[Commentary] Because the conditions of water are impermanent, it is said to be "not fixed. It flows or stops according to external circumstances; this is the characteristic of non-fixity. (The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* asks:

What is the difference between "constant" (*heng*) and "eternal" (*chang*)? It answers: That which does not arise from causes and conditions is "eternal"; that which remains unchanging from beginning to end is "constant.")
For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, there were the great illusionists Kāpiśa Rishi, Cakravartin Rishi, Padma, Mahāsattva, and others;
these masters sought the essence of the moon to mix with their illusion-inducing drugs. On the days of the waxing moon, these masters...

Holding a *fangzhu* (concave mirror) in his hand, he receives the water from within the moon. Does this water emerge from within the bead, or does it exist of its own accord in space, or does it come from the moon?

[Commentary: Kāpiśa means yellowish-red (in the Liang language, it means blue; it is also translated as "yellow"; here it means "Yellow-Headed," meaning his head is like the color of gold). Cakravāḍa.

Cloud-wheel (some say "mandarin duck"; others translate it as Cloud-wheel Mountain, named after its mountainous form). *Padma* means red lotus (*Lankavatara Sutra*: "It is like the shape of the sun and moon;

*padma* refers to deep and perilous [depths]. Like the fire in space being extinguished, the heterodox paths lead to dhyāna. The commentary states: "The heterodox practitioners are attached to a self-soul (*ātman*). Within their meditative contemplation, they see forms like the sun and moon, or they see red lotuses beneath deep and perilous [abysses]).
*Hasada* is not yet clearly defined (some translate it as "engaging with water"). *Fangzhu* is the water-producing pearl; when the moon is at its zenith, [it sheds dew].)
He held the pearl toward it to seek water. [The Gushan commentary states: "Before the full moon, it is called 'white' (bai); at midday, it is called 'day' (zhou). According to the Huainanzi:

'When the fangzhu encounters the moon, it exudes moisture and becomes water. Gao You says: 'Fangzhu' is the 'yin-suil' (the negative lens), which is a large clam. If one polishes it until it is hot and holds it toward the moon, water will be produced. Xu Shen says: 'Zhu' means 'pearl'; 'fang' means 'stone. The translator likely adopted Xu Shen’s explanation."

The *Lunheng* states: On the night of the *renzi* day of the eleventh month, at the hour of midnight, one refines stones from the five directions in the north to create it. Its shape is like a cup or a bowl; when facing the moon, it receives its essence. It is the "Moon-Jewel" (*candrakānta*) of empty space.
The three locations have been examined.

(2. Refutation by Reasoning) Ānanda, if [the water] comes from the moon, it is already capable of causing water to emerge from the pearl from such a great distance; therefore, all the trees and forests it passes through should likewise produce water.
[The water] flows out. If it flows, why wait for what is produced by the *fangzhu* [concave mirror]? If it does not flow, it is clear that the water does not descend from the moon.

[Commentary: This refutes the theory that the moon produces [the water]. The first five phrases directly cite and refute [the opponent's view]: when the moon moves among the human realm, its size is like that of the sun.
Therefore, it is said that wherever the moonlight shines in distant places, all [the water] merges to form flowing streams; why would it be only from the pearl?

The phrase "if it were a stream" (流) refers to the final four lines, which together conclude that [the pearl] is not the source. If every place where the light shines forms a stream, what need is there for the pearl to produce one?

Furthermore, even if there were no such streams, this would demonstrate that the nature of this water does not descend from the moon. (As Gushan [Zhili] said: "Since streams do not arise from the trees and forests, this water does not descend from the moon.")
If [the water] were to emerge from the jewel, then water should flow constantly from within this jewel; why wait for midnight, or for the reception of the white moon during the day?

[Commentary: This refutes the notion that the jewel produces [the water]. If the jewel produced water, it should have a constant flow; it would not depend on the reflection of the moon—why then is there no water produced?
If [the flood] were produced from space, then since the nature of space is boundless, the water would likewise be limitless; from humans up to the heavens, all would be submerged together.
How, then, could there still be those who travel by water, land, or air?

[This is] the principle.

From the beginning of the kalpa to its end, the winds that bring about formation and destruction all arise through the karmic retribution of sentient beings. There is not a single phenomenon in the world that does not arise from conditions.

The formation of phenomena through combination is such that each individual element does not exist independently, nor does the combination itself exist. Within these conditions, there is no inherent nature (svabhāva) whatsoever;

Its substance is conjoined with empty space, and its nature is devoid of both motion and stillness. Motion is manifested due to causal characteristics;
