(II. Refutation through logical inference).
Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were produced within seeing, then in the absence of darkness, light, form, and emptiness—these four conditions—it would necessarily not exist.
Since your seeing itself would fundamentally be non-existent, from what could consciousness arise?

[Commentary: This refutes the arising from the sense organs. When there is the objective aspect (*nimitta*), there is the subjective vision (*darśana*); when the aspect is absent, vision is absent. Since the organ itself has no form, from what could consciousness arise?
If your nature of consciousness arises within the objective aspect and not from vision, then since you do not see light, you likewise would not see darkness.

When light and darkness do not strike the eyes, there is neither form nor emptiness; since even those characteristics do not exist, from what could consciousness arise? [Commentary]: Appearance and seeing are mutually dependent. When there is no seeing, there is no appearance. (If one does not perceive objects such as light and darkness, then the six sense-objects, such as form, do not exist. If even appearances cannot be established, how can seeing exist? Thus, both are empty. Consciousness arises from the conjunction of these two; if the conditions are absent, the result cannot exist. Therefore, it is known that the nature of consciousness is originally empty. Furthermore, because the nature of consciousness is empty, the nature of all dharmas is also empty. This is called the "emptiness of the nature of consciousness. Because this emptiness is itself empty, it is called the "emptiness of emptiness. It is also called the "emptiness of ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). This is the meaning of the verse. Regarding the phrase "the nature of consciousness is originally empty": the nature of consciousness refers to the essence of the eighth consciousness. Its original state is devoid of self-nature; it is not produced by causes and conditions, nor is it subject to arising or ceasing. It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither eternal nor annihilated. It is free from all conceptual proliferation and is quiescent and unconditioned. It is the true reality of all phenomena, the Tathāgata-garbha, and the Dharmakāya. It is the fundamental source of all Buddhas and the ultimate refuge for all sentient beings. It is the wondrous mind of the Mahāyāna, the pure and luminous nature of the mind. Because it is free from all delusions and afflictions, it is called "originally empty. It is also called the "Tathatā" (Suchness), the "Dharmadhātu" (Dharma-realm), the "Buddha-nature," and the "True Mind. It is the ultimate reality of all dharmas. Because it is originally empty, it is not a dharma that can be grasped or described. It transcends all words and thoughts. It is the profound and subtle realm of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. It is the ground of liberation and the source of wisdom. It is the true nature of all sentient beings, which is originally pure and eternally luminous. Because it is originally empty, it is not subject to birth or death, nor is it increased or diminished. It is the ultimate truth of the Mahāyāna. One who realizes this emptiness is called a Bodhisattva. One who abides in this emptiness is called a Buddha. This is the meaning of the verse. Regarding the phrase "the nature of emptiness is also empty": the nature of emptiness refers to the emptiness previously discussed. That emptiness is also empty; it has no fixed nature of its own. It is not a substantial entity that can be grasped. It is free from all characteristics and is beyond all conceptualization. It is the ultimate emptiness of all dharmas. Because it is empty, it can manifest all things; because it is empty, it can accommodate all things. It is the gate of liberation and the treasury of wisdom. It is the true nature of all dharmas. Because it is empty, it is not a dharma that can be grasped or described. It transcends all words and thoughts. It is the profound and subtle realm of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. It is the ground of liberation and the source of wisdom. It is the true nature of all sentient beings, which is originally pure and eternally luminous. Because it is empty, it is not subject to birth or death, nor is it increased or diminished. It is the ultimate truth of the Mahāyāna. One who realizes this emptiness is called a Bodhisattva. One who abides in this emptiness is called a Buddha. This is the meaning of the verse. Regarding the phrase "this emptiness is also empty": this emptiness refers to the emptiness of the nature of consciousness and the emptiness of the nature of emptiness. Both of these are also empty; they have no fixed nature of their own. They are free from all characteristics and are beyond all conceptualization. They are the ultimate emptiness of all dharmas. Because they are empty, they can manifest all things; because they are empty, they can accommodate all things. They are the gates of liberation and the treasuries of wisdom. They are the true nature of all dharmas. Because they are empty, they are not dharmas that can be grasped or described. They transcend all words and thoughts. They are the profound and subtle realms of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. They are the grounds of liberation and the sources of wisdom. They are the true natures of all sentient beings, which are originally pure and eternally luminous. Because they are empty, they are not subject to birth or death, nor are they increased or diminished. They are the ultimate truths of the Mahāyāna. Those who realize these emptinesses are called Bodhisattvas. Those who abide in these emptinesses are called Buddhas. This is the meaning of the verse. Regarding the phrase "it is also called the emptiness of ultimate truth": ultimate truth refers to the true reality of all dharmas. It is the Tathāgata-garbha, the Dharmakāya, and the True Mind. It is the fundamental source of all Buddhas and the ultimate refuge for all sentient beings. It is the wondrous mind of the Mahāyāna, the pure and luminous nature of the mind. Because it is free from all delusions and afflictions, it is called "ultimate truth. It is also called the "Tathatā" (Suchness), the "Dharmadhātu" (Dharma-realm), the "Buddha-nature," and the "True Mind. It is the ultimate reality of all dharmas. Because it is ultimate truth, it is not a dharma that can be grasped or described. It transcends all words and thoughts. It is the profound and subtle realm of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. It is the ground of liberation and the source of wisdom. It is the true nature of all sentient beings, which is originally pure and eternally luminous. Because it is ultimate truth, it is not subject to birth or death, nor is it increased or diminished. It is the ultimate truth of the Mahāyāna. One who realizes this ultimate truth is called a Bodhisattva. One who abides in this ultimate truth is called a Buddha. This is the meaning of the verse. Regarding the phrase "this is the meaning of the verse": this refers to the preceding discussion on the emptiness of the nature of consciousness, the emptiness of the nature of emptiness, and the emptiness of ultimate truth. These are the essential meanings of the verse. By understanding these meanings, one can penetrate the profound and subtle Dharma of the Mahāyāna. One can sever all delusions and afflictions. From what does consciousness arise? [Commentary from the *Zongjing Lu*: The above refutes arising from self and arising from other.
If it were to arise from emptiness, it would be neither form nor vision. Without vision, there is no discernment; thus, one could not know for oneself the clarity, darkness, color, or emptiness.

It is not that the conditions for its extinction are absent; rather, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have no place of establishment. Since it abides in neither of these two extremes, emptiness is the same as non-existence, and existence is not the same as a substantial entity.
Even if you were to give rise to consciousness, what would you have to differentiate?

[Commentary: From here below, the production of emptiness is refuted. The first two lines examine and determine that [consciousness] does not arise from the sense organs (*indriya*) or their objects (*viṣaya*).

"Not seeing," etc., constitutes the actual refutation. The first three lines refute the claim that the four objects are not discerned because there is no seeing; the latter three lines refute the claim that the five sense organs cannot be established because there are no marks (*nimitta*).
"Marks" are equivalent to conditions (*pratyaya*). Since the four objects do not exist, the objective conditions (*ālambana*) are extinguished. Since the objective conditions...

There is none. If there are no five sense-faculties (*indriya*), how could they exist? The preceding [passage] refutes [the opponent's view] by citing [their premises] to show that the faculties and their objects are not required.
From "Abiding herein" onwards, [the text] directly refutes the notion that consciousness arises from space.

Because it is neither form (*nimitta*) nor vision (*darśana*), it is called the "duality of non-being"; this directly points to space. As for "being equally non-existent," it is like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit—ultimately...
Because there is no cause. If one says that this emptiness possesses a substantial entity, how could it be the same as material objects, which can be formed and shaped?

(Secondly, if it were empty, it would be the same as a tortoise’s hair; secondly, if it were existent, since it is said to be neither a characteristic nor a vision, it would not be the same as material things. Furthermore, this empty space is dull and lacks discernment.
If this non-discerning emptiness were to give rise to something, that which arises should likewise lack discernment. Therefore it is said: "What is there to be distinguished? (Secondly, [it is] not).

Even if such empty space could give rise to your consciousness, what would you wish to differentiate? Would you wish to differentiate the boundlessness of a tortoise’s hair, or would you wish to differentiate the finitude of dissimilar objects? This is truly impossible to establish.

(△ [Gushan says: "If it were empty, it would be the same as non-existence," meaning there is no consciousness. One should rather say, "If it were non-existent, it would be the same as emptiness. Gushan and Wenling explain emptiness and existence as being consciousness.

In this context of interpreting the text, following Changshui is more appropriate. If [consciousness] were to arise suddenly without any cause, why would it not perceive the bright moon specifically at midday?
[Commentary: This refutes the theory of causelessness. Since there is no moon at midday, and thus no consciousness perceiving the moon, one should know that it does not exist without a cause.
[Zongjing]: The sun belongs to the rising yang; the moon contains the essence of yin. These are determined by the seasons and the divisions of time.

This has remained unchanged from antiquity to the present; each case has its own cause. That which lacks a cause does not exist. To claim that emptiness arises without a cause is to fall into the error of "causeless arising," which we refute in every instance.

You should examine this further, scrutinizing it with the utmost subtlety: you see [the visual faculty] relying upon your pupils, projecting toward external objects, and taking on a form that constitutes existence.
They do not arise from non-existence. Thus, from what source does this consciousness emerge? Consciousness moves while seeing remains still; they are neither blended nor conjoined.
Hearing, listening, sensing, and knowing are likewise so. It cannot be that consciousness emerges from non-existence without a source.

[Commentary] This is a re-examination of the place of birth. The pupils are the floating dust; the objects are light and darkness. "Becoming existent" and "becoming non-existent" refer to empty space.

This means that [the eyes] merely illuminate the object. (Your consciousness within this [process] sequentially points to and identifies [the object]; this is the movement of consciousness. When the eyes look around, they merely see clarity within the mirror.

The two subsequent lines concerning hearing and listening serve as an analogy to refute the remaining consciousnesses. "Hearing and listening" refers to the ears and nose; "awareness and cognition" refers to the tongue, body, and mental consciousness.

The two subsequent lines beginning with "should not" conclude that there is no place of origin for consciousness. Since these explain the causal conditions for the arising of consciousness, it is said: "Consciousness arises by conditions" (*Zongjing*).
To perceive clarity is the fivefold direct perception (*pañca-pratyakṣa*); conceptualization is movement. Furthermore, a sutra states: "This mind-consciousness is originally tranquil and still;

Since one cannot perceive the nature of the self, nor can one obtain the contemplation of other characteristics, and since the characteristics of others are already empty, there is no longer any synthesis.

let the student examine them carefully. (△ [Wenling says: When consciousness moves, seeing is clear; their natures are separated and distinct. If this conscious mind fundamentally has no origin, one should know that its capacity for discernment—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—is perfect and profoundly still;

its nature does not arise from any source. Together with space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are equally termed the "Seven Great Elements. Their natures are truly interfused and perfectly harmonious.

The first two phrases constitute the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). "One should know" and what follows constitute the thing being analogized (*dārṣṭāntika*). "Discriminating" refers to consciousness (specifically indicating the six consciousnesses). "Seeing and hearing" refers to the sense organs.

This refers to the faculties (the six sense organs). They are the roots from which consciousness arises; therefore, it is said that they "discriminate" seeing, hearing, and so forth. [Dinglin says: Although consciousness resides in the six faculties, its nature does not derive from them.

Even blades of grass, dust, and a single hair can all be called "great. Their nature is truly interfused and originally devoid of arising or ceasing. This has been explained in detail in the preceding text; the essential meaning is all gathered here. The five great elements—consciousness, sensation, perception, volition, and cognition—are established based on this consciousness through its division into the "seeing-part" (darśana-bhāga). (2. Refutation and Exhortation to Investigate Thoroughly)
Ānanda, your mind is coarse and restless; you have not yet awakened to the fact that what is seen and heard is the clear manifestation and perfect knowledge of the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha.

You should contemplate these six consciousnesses of the sense bases: are they the same or different? Are they empty or existent? Are they neither the same nor different? Are they neither empty nor existent?

[Commentary]: Identity and difference have been refuted in the section on the faculties (*indriya*). "Emptiness" refers to the arising of emptiness; "existence" refers to the faculties and their objects;

"neither emptiness nor existence" refers to the absence of causes. [Sub-commentary (Diaozhi)]: Your mind is coarse and superficial, exactly as the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* reproaches Gañjara: "A floating and deluded mind abounds in clever views; it cannot accomplish the skillful means of Perfect Enlightenment.

Such discrimination is not a correct inquiry. [△ Dinglin’s Note]: Regarding "emptiness," [the text says] your mind is bewildered because the nature of emptiness is awakening. Regarding "seeing," your mind is submerged because the nature of seeing manifests externally. Regarding "consciousness," your mind is coarse and superficial.

Because the consciousness-mind is latent within, when it is superficial, one merely recognizes the floating sense-roots; when it is coarse, one fails to reach the essence of consciousness. (Citation from the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "The six consciousnesses are originally one mind.

They universally emerge through the gates of the six sense-organs to form the six consciousnesses: from seeing arises eye-consciousness; from hearing arises ear-consciousness; from smelling arises nose-consciousness; from tasting arises tongue-consciousness; from touching arises body-consciousness; from discrimination arises mind-consciousness. Thus, the sense-organs, objects, and consciousnesses—these three factors in combination—constitute the eighteen realms.

If one knows according to reality that their self-nature is entirely empty, this is what is meant by being able to study the six sense-organs, the six sense-objects, and the six consciousnesses. (Citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "Consciousness with respect to the sense-organs emerges and enters momentarily, like a deer in a net, or like a bird...")

When confined in a cage, a bird pecks at one thing and leaves another, circling back again and again without a moment’s rest. Consciousness within the cage of the sense faculties is just like this: sometimes it is in the ear, sometimes in the eye; its coming and going are not fixed, and it cannot be grasped as permanent. Although it is not fixed, it continues in an uninterrupted succession.

Furthermore, Dharmapāla says: "The essential natures of the six consciousnesses are each distinct; they are merely given names based upon their respective faculties and objects. How could a single consciousness apprehend [all objects] simultaneously? If it were to arise sequentially, it would not be universal. (△ [Explanatory Text]:

According to the preceding section, following the phrase "The wondrous enlightenment is serene," there should be the eight lines beginning with "pervading the Dharma-realm" and ending with "the wondrous virtue is luminous. This may be a textual omission, or the text may have been abbreviated.

Jiaoguang’s claim that a detailed examination of the scripture shows there should be no text regarding "responding to the mind and corresponding to the measure" is also a forced interpretation. ([│/○] Fourth, concluding by rebuking deluded sentiments.)
The world is ignorant, deluded by causes and conditions as well as by the nature of spontaneity; all these are merely the discriminating calculations of the conscious mind.
They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
[Combined Explanation from the *Zhongjing heshi*]: The nature of the seven great elements is truly perfect and interfused; each and every one is omnipresent throughout the Dharma-realm.
It is like seven lumps of ice that, when melted by fire, become water; or like Indra’s net, where they are both identical and distinct.

It is like water and ice: different yet not different. Even so, the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) all completely fill the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Each and every atom (*paramāṇu*) also fills the dharma-realm; each and every pore likewise pervades the dharma-realm;
and each and every body and mind also pervades the entire Tathāgatagarbha. Thus one knows that within the realm of ordinary beings...
The faculties of seeing and hearing, the aggregates and sense bases, and the objects of name-and-form are all like the hair of a tortoise—there is nothing to which one may cling.

All objective realms arise through the transformation of consciousness and are entirely produced by following after mental conceptions (*saṃjñā*). Apart from consciousness, there are no external objects;

when consciousness is stilled, all objects are simultaneously stilled. Apart from conception, there are no phenomena; when conception is empty, all phenomena are simultaneously empty. Taking the tortoise of the world...

The emptiness of the "hair-like" misconceptions is resolved by shattering the present clinging to names and marks as real. Whether one posits them as produced by causes and conditions or as spontaneous, both result in frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Cognition, understanding, and discrimination have no origin from beginning to end; they are merely mental verbalizations and utterly devoid of reality.
Thus, the aggregates, bases, elements, the seven great natures, and so forth, do not exist inherently and spontaneously without cause from the beginning;
nor are they produced today through the conjunction of causes and conditions. They are merely established through the conceptual discrimination of the conscious mind.
Now, if this nature of consciousness is dismantled, then the natures of the seven great elements and indeed all phenomena are empty; it is like tracing a current.

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat amidst the great assembly.
He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, you have skillfully expounded for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth."
[Commentary: The Tathāgatagarbha-mind is neither empty nor existent; it is both essence and appearance, and is termed the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha).
This is what the Buddha has realized; it is definitively without delusion. Being thoroughly real, it is called "Truth" (satya).
([○@(?∴)] Second, citing a simile to describe delusion):
"The World-Honored One has always declared that among those who preach the Dharma, I am the foremost."

[The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "Among the fourfold assembly, Pūrṇa is foremost in benefiting sentient beings by employing the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) and various dharma-gates, causes, conditions, and parables. It further says:
'Within the great wisdom of Śāriputra, Pūrṇa is foremost in preaching the Dharma; he adorns it with manifold ornaments and draws in the hearts of the masses through his preaching.'"
Now that I hear the subtle and wondrous Dharma-voice of the Tathāgata, I am like a deaf person standing more than a hundred paces away, listening for the sound of a mosquito;
what I have never seen before, how much less could I have heard? Although the Buddha has proclaimed it clearly to remove my delusions, I still do not yet understand it in detail.
This meaning is ultimate; it is a ground free from doubt or confusion.

[Commentary] Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra was skilled in expounding the essentials of the Dharma, and the assembly ranked him as unsurpassed. Yet, having now heard the Buddha’s teaching, he has not yet fully understood it.
He is like one whose hearing is impaired: when facing a subtle sound at a distance of more than a hundred paces, how could he clearly discern it? This is the first point.
The ultimate truth is subtle, wondrous, and quiescent; it is a subtle sound. To hear it and yet not understand it is equivalent to not hearing it at all, like one who is deaf.
It transcends the path of speech and the sphere where mental activity ceases, as if surpassing a hundred paces. Such is the teaching of these dharmas.
"May you cause me to eliminate my delusions. Yet I am still ensnared by the net of doubt and have not yet exhausted the knots of remorse; therefore, I cite this analogy. [The Sub-commentary states:

"Not having yet attained the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, one has fundamentally not seen it, let alone heard of it. The five eyes do not behold its form, and the two ears have not heard its sound. (3. Comparing and discussing gain and loss.)
World-Honored One, how is it that these difficult-to-match individuals, though they have attained awakening, have not yet eliminated their habitual outflows?

Among those in our assembly who have ascended to the state of no-outflows and have exhausted all taints, even they still harbor lingering doubts and regrets upon hearing the Dharma-sound preached by the Tathāgata.

[Commentary] First, from the agitation of the luminous and the obscure, there arises a wind-circle. From the agitation of the wind, the luminous foundation establishes the golden jewels.
Through the mutual friction of the gold and the wind, the nature of fire is produced. As the fire steams the moisture of the gold, water is born. Fire and water...

Interacting, their forces possess degrees of superiority and inferiority. Where water is superior and fire inferior, it becomes the ocean and islands; where fire is superior and water inferior, it becomes mountains and rocks;
where earth is inferior and water superior, it becomes grasses, trees, and the like. Although external forms are thus, they all arise from the internal mind.

If the internal mind undergoes no change, how could there be external differentiation? The Sūtra speaks only in terms of the external, hence it says they "mutually serve as seeds" (Gushan says: "The mutual production of delusions").

Second, through the false conjunction of these two, all phenomena are formed. Water and fire further become the seeds of the oceans and continents. Water and earth, moreover, become the seeds of grasses and trees. They serve as the seeds for the arising of the false instruments; yet the substance of these false instruments has no reality, being nothing other than awakened clarity. Therefore, when one contemplates the false instruments, one sees only the true instruments. Furthermore, they arise individually according to different people, so that each person perceives them differently; yet when many people arise [in a state of collective perception], they all perceive them together.

They all manifest as a single appearance (or, if earth is invoked, earth manifests; if water is invoked, water manifests; or if all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm collectively invoke the appearance of emptiness, then the appearance of emptiness manifests pervading the entire dharma-realm).
This is precisely the True Suchness (*tathatā*) not adhering to its own nature, manifesting various appearances according to conditions. As stated in the preceding text:

"In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, responding to the measure of what they know, they are manifested through following their karma. In the *Awakening of Faith*, this is called the "mirror of perfuming causes" (*hetu-vāsanā-ādarśa*). It manifests...
The various objective realms are also of this same nature. [Zongjing] The four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—within and without, manifest moment by moment.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Either they manifest individually, or they manifest together. Regarding "manifesting individually":
when you perceive the perfect luminosity and your mind desires to grasp it, you lose the fundamental luminosity that is empty by nature; this is the activity of discursive thought.

When it vibrates, the wind-circle arises from the mind; when its nature craves continuity, the water-circle arises from that sensation. When the grasping mind becomes intense, the gold-circle appears.
When the seeking mind suffers its desires, the fire-circle then emerges. If both are illuminated together, a powerful awareness first arises.
The four great elements manifest together. For example, when a person harbors resentment and recollection, anger gives rise to fire;
the agitation and shifting of body and mind serve as an analogy for wind; the eyes filling with tears represent water; and the face turning crimson represents earth.

(Furthermore, citing the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, it says: "The Pure Dharma-realm is the single mind, the undifferentiated Dharma-realm. Since it takes the Dharma as its realm, how could there be boundaries? Thus, within all forms, the nature of empty space exists; how much more so do all phenomena possess peace and bliss.")

The Nature. Because this nature is concealed, it manifests various objects in accordance with the cognitive realm and its emotional capacity. If one clarifies through emptiness, then emptiness appears; if one clarifies through form, then form appears.

It merely manifests wherever it is illuminated, appearing in each respective place. All these various manifestations arise from the deluded mind; their characteristics cannot be apprehended. There is only the single-flavored true mind, serene and unmoving. [△ Jiaoguang says: There are two types of simultaneous manifestations.

First, simultaneous yet in different locations, such as when a fire-blower produces wind from his mouth and fire from the wood; the blowing and the burning occur simultaneously, yet the mouth and the wood are in different places. Second, simultaneous and in the same location, such as a single Ganges River where humans see water appear and ghosts see fire appear.]
(Also). (The double metaphor manifests both [aspects]). (1. The primary metaphor).
What is meant by "appearing together"? Pūrṇa, it is like the reflection of the sun appearing in a single body of water.
When two people look at it together, as the sun's reflection in the water moves east and west, each person perceives a sun following them—one to the east and one to the west.
Originally, there was no fixed standard.
[Commentary: The seven elements (mahābhūta) are essentially empty, like the shadow of the sun. As it moves east or west, they appear divided into seven distinct parts;

yet though they differ according to direction, they do not depart from that single shadow. Although the seven elements are divided, they do not depart from a single delusion. If the east may be taken as the standard, what then is the west?
Just as a target is one, it is illogical for it to move apart in various directions. If one knows it is a shadow, then both "one" and "many" naturally vanish.

[Guishan says: "The eye is a metaphor for true nature; the water is a metaphor for the deluded mind; the sun within the water is a metaphor for the deluded environment; the two people are metaphors for deluded karma. If they walk separately, they proceed according to their respective karma; if they move together, the deluded environment appears simultaneously.

[△ Xunwen says: "The method of the carpenter is to level objects with water. 'The mark' refers to the bullseye of an archer—the red and white center. All of these take the meaning of a fixed standard. [○ Quotation] [Qingliang says: "A single moon in a clear river; two boats, one north and one south. The southern one..."

Those facing south see the moon and follow it for a thousand *li* to the south; those facing north see the moon and follow it for a thousand *li* to the north. Those who have moored their boats see the moon as unmoving. Thus, this single moon does not leave the middle of the stream to travel to the south or north.

Even if hundreds or thousands were to behold it together, each from one of the eight directions, there would then be a thousand or ten hundred moons, each following its respective direction. (This is the second [correct] refutation.)
One should not raise the objection: "This day is one; how can they travel separately? Since each day is a pair, how can it appear as one?
This is merely a convoluted fabrication with no basis for reliance."

[Commentary]: One person is a shadow; as they move, another shadow appears following them, and that shadow again produces further shadows. What reality can there be to rely upon when one seeks to raise objections?
There is only the single "that which is clarified" (the One Mind), yet it manifests the seven great elements. These elements and the objects of delusion are but a single reflected image;

no substantial reality can be found therein. Therefore, it is said: "Winding and turning, all is empty and false. (Gushan says: When observing together, one knows the two are false. Since each travels separately, the two are established; thus, by testing this, one realizes the one is also false. (○)

[Combined Explanation] [The *Zongjing* says: The wondrously enlightened, luminous mind is profoundly still and unmoving. Due to karma, it manifests, appearing as form or emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Sentient beings turn their backs on this original enlightenment and falsely cling to the objects of emotion.

Following the place where these manifestations arise, they insistently assert right and wrong, as if defining distinctions within the very substance of empty space. In truth, this is called false and inverted; there is no rational basis upon which to rely. (This section of the *Zongjing* provides a comprehensive explanation of the preceding and following scriptural passages, and is therefore placed here. [② Second, regarding...]

The detailed explanation of the meaning (2). (1) The correct explanation based on essence and function (2). (a) The manifestation of function based on delusion and awakening (2). (b) Delusion resulting in the appearance of the mundane world (2).

Pūrṇa, you take form and emptiness to be mutually exclusive and mutually subverting; yet within the Tathāgatagarbha, the Tathāgatagarbha itself conforms to form and emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Therefore, within it, the wind moves while space remains clear, the sun shines while clouds darken.

Sentient beings are deluded and distressed, turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust of the senses; thus they give rise to worldly toil and manifest the characteristics of the mundane world.
[Commentary]: By means of a mind that discriminates between form and emptiness, you manifest an overturning and usurping within true awakening.

That nature of true awakening then conforms to and becomes form and emptiness, mutually suppressing and extinguishing one another. [Furong Shi said: "The treasury-mind does not maintain its own nature; following that overturning and usurping, it thereby becomes form and emptiness, pervading the entire dharma-realm.

Xuelang said: "Wherever you perceive form or emptiness, this is precisely the overturning and usurping of the Tathāgata-garbha. When the delusions of form and emptiness manifest, the truth of the Tathāgata-garbha is concealed. 'Overturning and usurping' refers to..."
The meaning of "obscuration" refers to the two great elements of form and space. Since these two are thus, all others follow this same principle;

hence it is said, "therefore, within this," and so forth. The preceding text states: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded regarding themselves and taken them to be external objects;
therefore, within this [delusion], they perceive the large and the small. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) also says: "The self-nature of Complete Enlightenment is not..."

The nature of nature exists; it arises following all natures. This is how sentient beings give rise to the wind of ignorance, which stirs the ocean of *tathatā* (suchness) to form the waves of the eight consciousnesses.
These transform and give rise to the various phenomena of the mundane world. Hindered by these appearances, they lose their original mind; thus it is said:

"They turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust," resulting in the appearance of the mundane world. [Gushan says: True reality follows conditions to transform and give rise to delusive objects, just as the entirety of water [transforms into ice].]

When the waves are formed, because the water is already pervasive, the waves are likewise pervasive; for these waves are identical to the water. Sentient beings are deluded and distressed, referring to the sentient beings of the nine realms who fail to realize that phenomena are transformations of principle, and instead, with their ignorant and deluded minds, grasp them as being real.

(△ [Wuxing says: The previous question concerned the fundamental nature of earth, water, fire, and wind. It was suspected that the natures of water and fire would not mutually overcome or extinguish one another, yet their characteristics would clash; and that empty space and the great earth could not possibly coexist, yet their characteristics would usurp one another).
([│/○] Second, awakening achieves supramundane function.)

By means of this wondrous clarity—which is neither extinguished nor born—I am united with the Tathāgatagarbha; and this Tathāgatagarbha is nothing other than wondrous, awakened clarity, perfectly illuminating the entire Dharma-realm.
[Commentary: "Awakening" refers to the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha; it is neither extinguished nor produced. "Wisdom of non-arising" refers to the principle of the signless Tathāgatagarbha.
Because the wisdom and the principle are in profound accord, they are called "conjoined. At that time, there is only the single wondrous mind, with no distinction between wisdom and principle.

This is the conjoining of initial awakening (śikṣā-bodhi) with the fundamental [awakening]; there is no difference between the fundamental and the initial, for there is only one awakening. Therefore, it is said: "Only the wondrous."

Awakened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm. [Wuxing says: "The Tathāgata-garbha" refers to the principle that is conjoined; "only wondrous awakened clarity" refers to the wisdom that performs the conjunction. "Perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm" demonstrates the function of reflecting objects.
The Tathāgata-garbha is like the substance of a mirror; wondrous awakened clarity is like the light of the mirror; perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm is like the mirror manifesting images.
Therefore, within this state, one becomes immeasurable and the immeasurable becomes one; the small manifests the large, and the large manifests the small.
Without moving from the site of enlightenment, they pervade the worlds of the ten directions; their bodies contain the infinite space of the ten directions within a single hair-tip.

Manifesting the Jewel-King Realm, sitting within a mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel. [Commentary] This describes the arising of wondrous function. The first five phrases indicate two kinds of mastery (*vaśitā*); the final two phrases, "without moving," explain the mastery over the one and the many. [Qingliang says: Regarding "the one and the many," because a single body manifests in its entirety, it is neither one nor many. Since a single body manifests as many, the one does not obstruct the many; and since the many manifest from a single body, the many do not obstruct the one. Thus, the one and the many are mutually unimpeded. This is called the mastery over the one and the many. Furthermore, "sitting within a mote of dust" refers to the mastery over the minute and the vast. Because the minute and the vast are mutually unimpeded, this is called the mastery over the minute and the vast. It is said that the mastery over the one and the many is the essence, while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the function. However, the essence and function are non-dual; they are merely distinguished according to their characteristics. Therefore, both are called masteries. Moreover, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *samādhi*, while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *dhāraṇī*. Because the *samādhi* and *dhāraṇī* are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *dharmakāya*, while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *nirmāṇakāya*. Because the *dharmakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *svasaṃvedana-jñāna* (self-cognizing wisdom), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *jñeya-ālambana-jñāna* (wisdom perceiving objects of knowledge). Because these two wisdoms are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *tathatā* (suchness), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm). Because *tathatā* and *dharmadhātu* are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *prajñā* (wisdom), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *upāya* (skillful means). Because *prajñā* and *upāya* are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *bodhicitta* (awakening mind), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *karuṇā* (compassion). Because *bodhicitta* and *karuṇā* are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *śrāvaka-yāna*, while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *bodhisattva-yāna*. Because the *śrāvaka-yāna* and *bodhisattva-yāna* are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *pṛthagjana* (ordinary beings), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *ārya* (noble ones). Because ordinary beings and noble ones are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *saṃsāra* (cycle of birth and death), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *nirvāṇa* (liberation). Because *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa* are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *kleśa* (afflictions), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *bodhi* (awakening). Because afflictions and awakening are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *nimitta* (signs), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *animitta* (signlessness). Because signs and signlessness are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *vikalpa* (discrimination), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *avikalpa* (non-discrimination). Because discrimination and non-discrimination are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). Because the imagined and perfected natures are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *sāsrava* (with outflows), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *anāsrava* (without outflows). Because the tainted and untainted are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *vyavahāra* (conventional truth), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *paramārtha-satya* (ultimate truth). Because conventional and ultimate truths are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *hetu* (cause), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *phala* (fruit). Because cause and fruit are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *mārga* (path), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *nirodha* (cessation). Because the path and cessation are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *vijñāna* (consciousness), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *tathatā*. Because consciousness and suchness are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *amala-vijñāna* (immaculate consciousness). Because the storehouse and immaculate consciousnesses are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *mahāmudrā*. Because mental consciousness and mahāmudrā are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *pañcavijñānakāya* (five sensory consciousnesses), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *dharmakāya*. Because the five consciousnesses and dharmakāya are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *kāmadhātu* (desire realm), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *dharmadhātu*. Because the desire realm and dharma-realm are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *rūpadhātu* (form realm), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *ākāśadhātu* (space realm). Because the form realm and space realm are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *ārūpyadhātu* (formless realm), while the mastery over the minute and the vast is the mastery of the *dharmadhātu*. Because the formless realm and dharma-realm are non-dual, they are collectively termed "mastery. Furthermore, the mastery over the one and the many is the mastery of the *triloka*

Manifesting while remaining eternally one, the many do not obstruct the one. As stated in a verse of the *Bodhicittavivaraṇa*: "A single body becomes immeasurable, and the immeasurable again becomes one;

having realized all worlds, it manifests forms pervading everything. The following six lines explain mastery over the large and the small. The first two lines describe the manifestation of the support (*āśraya*) within the central [body].

The next two lines describe the manifestation of the central [body] and its support within the one, which is also the manifestation of the central [body] and its support within the support. The final two lines, beginning with "sitting in the minute," refer to the support.

The central [phrase] manifests the correct [result]. The remaining phrases are contained within it and can be understood through the power of intention. The ten kinds of mastery (*vaśitā*) in the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra are likewise not separate from this.

[As Qingliang said: "The virtues of the fruit are twofold: first, the supporting fruit (*niśraya-phala*), which refers to the Flower Treasury World-Ocean; second, the primary fruit (*mukhya-phala*), such as the ten bodies of the Tathāgata. These two are non-obstructive, constituting the Buddha's virtue.

Furthermore, regarding the non-obstruction between the support and the supported, there are generally six phrases: 1. The support appearing within the support, such as the ocean of lands within a mote of dust (i.e., the sūtra passage on the manifestation of lands upon the tip of a hair). 2. The supported appearing within the supported, such as the manifestation of Buddhas within a pore (i.e., the sūtra passage on the hair-pore...)"

(1) The Pure Land manifests within the Treasure King; (2) the Threefold Reality manifests within the Pure Land; (3) the supporting environment manifests within the Threefold Reality; (4) the Threefold Reality manifests within the supporting environment; (5) the supporting environment manifests within the supporting environment and the Threefold Reality; (6) the Threefold Reality manifests within the supporting environment and the Threefold Reality. The above six phrases concerning the supporting environment and the Threefold Reality briefly cite the *Qingliang xuantan* (The Profound Discourse of Qingliang) to explain the present commentary.

Other numerous meanings are omitted here to avoid prolixity; those who require them should consult them elsewhere. The four phrases beginning with "A single manifestation on the reed stream is immeasurable" constitute the general and specific [explanations], while the eight phrases beginning with "Without moving" provide the detailed analysis. Furthermore, regarding "within a hair-tip or a speck of dust":
The partial interpretation that the small and medium [realms] manifest the great is unsatisfactory when applied to the explanation; therefore, it is not accepted here.
By extinguishing the dust and unifying with awareness, one gives rise to the wondrously enlightened, luminous nature of True Suchness (tathatā).
[Commentary] This concludes the reason for [the preceding]. The text below states: "Hearing further obscures the faculties; when the objects of perception vanish, awareness becomes perfectly pure.

When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere; in tranquil illumination, it encompasses empty space. This means that there is nothing to restrict it as being either large or small, nor can it be limited by being one or many.

From a speck of dust to a hair, and from a single world-system to the ocean of lands—all are simultaneously pervasive and contained within it, because this is the fundamental nature of reality; thus it is so even at the stage of fruition.
Revealing the Ear.
(2) Showing the essence by means of the three truths. (1) Showing the ultimate truth by means of non-characteristics.)
The Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind; it is neither mind nor emptiness, neither earth, nor water, nor wind, nor fire.

[Commentary: It is not the seven elements. "Mind" refers to the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), which also comprises the five aggregates (*skandhas*). [Gushan says: Mind contains four aggregates; earth, water, fire, and wind are the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).*]
It is not the eye; it is not the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. It is not form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental phenomena. It is not the element of eye-consciousness;
and so on, up to and including the element of mind-consciousness.
[Commentary]: It is not the eighteen *dhātus*. It subsumes the twelve *āyatanas* [Gushan says: it is not the mind below]. In general, it is not the realms of the six ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-gati*).
Neither ignorance nor the extinction of ignorance; and so on, up to neither old age and death nor the extinction of old age and death. [Commentary:

These are not the twelve links of dependent origination, whether in their forward progression or reverse cessation. [Gushan says: This is not the realm of the Pratyekabuddhas, because the Pratyekabuddhas contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.
It is neither suffering nor its origin; neither cessation nor the path. It is neither wisdom nor attainment. [The Commentary states:

It is not the Four Noble Truths, nor the means of realization and that which is realized. [Gushan says: It is not the realm of the Śrāvakas; it is a general negation of the principle and wisdom of the two vehicles. "Attainment" refers to the principle (*li*).
It is not dāna; it is not śīla; it is not vīrya; it is not kṣānti; it is not dhyāna;
it is not prajñā; it is not pāramitā.

[Commentary]: It is not the six pāramitās. [Gushan says]: It is not the realm of the bodhisattvas. First, it is not the practice that leads [there]; it is not the pāramitās themselves; in general, it is not the principle that is to be reached.
Thus it continues up to [the end].

[Commentary]: This refers to transcending all causal practices, namely the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment within the causal stage, as well as all resultant virtues, such as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities on the level of fruition.

It is not the Tathāgata (in the language of Qin, "Thus-Come One"), nor the Arhat ("Worthy of Offerings"), nor the Samyaksaṃbuddha ("Perfectly All-Knowing"—these are not the three titles of the Tathāgata), nor Great Nirvāṇa;
it is neither permanence, nor bliss, nor self, nor purity.

[The four virtues of non-nirvāṇa] (Gushan says: "This refers not to the Buddha-realm. First, it is not the person who realizes [it]; these are the three titles. Next, it is not the dharma realized; these are the four virtues. 'Nirvāṇa' is the general term, and the 'four virtues' are the specific ones").
Because these are neither mundane nor supramundane.
[Commentary] The wisdom that contemplates the truths as objects, as well as the paths and cessations, the six perfections and below, are all supramundane dharmas.

Suffering, origination, the twelve links of dependent origination, the three categories, and the seven elements are all mundane. This above is a general negation of all marks. (Gushan says: "Mundane...")

The six ordinary realms are bound [by afflictions], while the four noble ones transcend the world; the principle of the treasury is emptiness itself, wherein the ten realms do not exist. Therefore, neither of these is [ultimately] established. This is to clarify the meaning of the True Truth (paramārtha-satya) by means of the gate of True Suchness (tathatā).
All things are empty. Whatever marks there are are all false and illusory, because they exist in mutual dependence; they possess only names, and names are themselves empty.
(The following commentary is taken entirely from Gushan. Next, regarding the sequential negation: first, due to ignorance (*avidyā*), there arises deluded consciousness (*vijñāna*);
that which is transformed by deluded consciousness is the realm of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*). Because the realm of space manifests, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are formed.
Because the four great elements arise, there are the sense organs and their objects. Because the organs and objects combine, the various consciousnesses subsequently arise.

Since these three—organ, object, and consciousness—are of the nature of karma, they constitute the twelve links of dependent origination, which cause one to transmigrate through birth and death. This is for the purpose of providing an antidote.

There are then supramundane contemplative wisdoms regarding all phenomena. Because these supramundane [wisdoms] differ in their sharpness or dullness, they are subsequently divided into the sequence of the three vehicles.

When the three are reconciled into one, there is the fruit of Buddhahood. This fruit consists of that which realizes and that which is realized, thereby distinguishing between *bodhi* (enlightenment) and *nirvāṇa*.
Since *nirvāṇa* is endowed with virtues, it possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Therefore, these qualities arise through mutual dependence.
Names and designations are established; each lacks intrinsic nature, and all are empty.
(This second [section] clarifies the conventional truth by means of identity with characteristics.)
This is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha. Originally, it is the wondrous mind; it is mind and it is emptiness. It is earth and it is water; it is wind and it is fire.
It is the eye, and it is the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. It is form, and it is sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena. It is the sphere of visual consciousness.
In this way, up to and including the element of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*); up to and including clarity and ignorance, and the exhaustion of clarity and ignorance;

in this way, up to and including aging and death, and the exhaustion of aging and death; up to and including suffering and its origin, and cessation and the path; up to and including knowledge and attainment.
It is dāna; it is śīla; it is vīrya; it is kṣānti; it is dhyāna; it is prajñā; it is pāramitā. In this way, up to and including:
it is tathāgata; it is arhat; it is samyaksaṃbuddha; it is mahāparinirvāṇa; it is permanence;
it is bliss; it is self; it is purity. Because it is thus identical with all these, it transcends both the mundane and the supramundane.
This concerns worldly phenomena. [Commentary:

The preceding section relied upon True Suchness (*tathatā*), where it is immutable and devoid of characteristics; this section relies upon the gate of arising and ceasing through following conditions (*suiyuan*) to reveal conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

(As Gushan stated: "This relies on conventional truth to demonstrate the principle of the Tathāgatagarbha; it exists within non-existence, for the ten realms are manifest therein. This, moreover, does not depart from the single True Reality.

Following the distinctions of illusory transformations according to defilement, various characteristics are formed; yet it is not that characteristics manifest as characteristics, nor that names manifest as names.
They are established in accordance with the world, without destroying conventional designations; therefore, they are said to be "identical."
(3. Explaining the Middle Way by means of negation and illumination.

The head is fundamentally without delusion; why do you run about so wildly?

(To the right is the explanation of the single refutation of the counter-argument regarding "nature. Master Wuxing judges that this uses "causal conditions" to refute "nature," while Master Wenling judges that it generally refutes both "causal conditions" and "nature. [△ Wenling says:]

If one awakens to the original head and recognizes the deluded running, then both causes and conditions and spontaneity are equally mere conceptual proliferation.

[Commentary: The fundamental reality is immovable; delusion arises through forced effort. To speak of causes and conditions, or of a nature arising spontaneously (*svabhāva*), is to engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

One thereby knows that the originally enlightened true nature is neither caused nor conditioned; it is not spontaneous, yet not non-spontaneous; it is neither a union nor a combination, yet not a non-union or non-combination.

Within this context, I shall offer my own interpretation. I humbly consider that from the passage "Therefore I say... onwards, there are three sections of text. These collectively conclude that the aforementioned notions of "causes and conditions" and "naturalness" are both mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). The statement "Because the three conditions are severed, it is bodhicitta" is precisely the refutation of causes and conditions.

The section on "the arising of bodhicitta" clarifies that the arising of bodhicitta still belongs to the realm of dharmas characterized by the duality of arising and ceasing within causes and conditions. Only upon reaching the stage of effortless practice (*anābhoga-mārga*) on the bhūmis, where the mind of arising and ceasing is exhausted, do causes and conditions finally [cease].

[This section] is concluded. If there were a single, natural segment, its breaking would be natural; it would be like a single segment in the world that breaks while remaining in a state of conjunction. Thus, within these three fascicles, the various doctrinal gates concerning the meanings of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), spontaneity (*svabhāva*), and conjunction (*saṃyoga*) have been extensively refuted without remainder, like a chain of links.

Furthermore, the subsequent passages stating "the original is not so" and "conjunction is not conjoined" do not arise in isolation [from this context]. Therefore, I have appended here [this critique] of Changshui’s arbitrary establishment of the topical headings (*ko*) for the purpose of manifesting [the meaning], though I am unsure whether it is correct.

The text reiterates that their objects are severed; since both separation and conjunction are negated, it is shown that cognition is likewise severed. The nature (*svabhāva*) does not engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). That which is without nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) does not engage in conceptual proliferation. That which is without nature is free from nature; in that which is without nature, no further dharma can be apprehended. As for those who engage in conceptual proliferation, there are the proliferating dharmas and the locus of proliferation. The nature of form (*rūpa*) is non-existent, up to and including the nature of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is non-existent.

The *Huashou jing* says, "Having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one does not even give rise to 'non-arising. "Bodhi and Nirvana still lie far beyond you; they cannot be realized through the arduous cultivation and verification of kalpas.

It is precisely for this reason that one must practice. It is like iron that is not gold: it cannot be forged into a wondrous vessel. How profound these words are! "In the past, there were only two types of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it was not said that there was no remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*). "Wondrous samādhi" refers to the *Gandha-vyūha* (Incense Array) Samādhi, which is the contemplation of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

If one wishes to cultivate this contemplation, one must first employ skillful means (*upāya*). If these means are perfected, genuine cultivation can be expected. Therefore, the two gates of cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are designated as "awakening."

Awakening the initial mind is precisely the primary expedient (*ādikarmika-upāya*). [Wang Shungding said: "The initial mind is the primary expedient requested by Ānanda; it is the ground for the practitioner's causal stage.

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "It is like a powerful king whom the entire land looks up to and relies upon; *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are also like this. All...

First, one carefully contemplates the causal ground and the resultant mind, giving rise to practice in accordance with them; this is precisely cultivating *śamatha* (calm abiding) based on the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

this is precisely the cultivation of contemplation based on the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*).

Since the characteristics of phenomena in the state of arising and ceasing differ in terms of defilement and purity, one gives rise to wisdom to discern and apply remedies so that they may be severed. Thus, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says: "As for what is called 'contemplation' (*vipaśyanā')..."

This refers to discerning the characteristics of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions. Because it accords with the meaning of the contemplation of *vipaśyanā*, one cultivates the preliminary expedients;

There are people in the world who, due to ignorance, do not understand this; this is not the supramundane wisdom. Taking those [verses] from the latter four lines, they do not give rise to [this understanding].

It is not extinguished; it is in conjunction with birth and extinction, neither identical nor different. The conceptual clinging to the suffering of the nine realms obscures the principle, like a person of the world taking soil and throwing it into water. "Appearance" refers to the characteristics of form and mind. "Turbid."

This is "turmoil" (luan). (The following text separately elucidates the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). These are the appearances of water and soil being muddied together. [Combined Explanation] [The Five Corruptions]: [The Source Mirror states: As for the five corruptions: first is the corruption of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). One must not speak the truth; this is the characteristic of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). To be like the poor and the afflicted, yet to be called long-lived and wealthy—this is the mark of the *sattva-kaṣāya* (the turbidity of sentient beings). not remaining still for even the blink of an eye—this is the mark of the turbidity of lifespan. Dwelling in this time of turbid chaos, obstructions intensify. The objects of perception drift upon the flames of consciousness, utterly consuming the roots of goodness. The winds of karma stir the mind, blowing away the remnants of the pure Dharma (*śukla-dharma*).

One clings to the demonic realm of the *rākṣasa* spirits of anger and falls into the net of the *rākṣasa* demons of delusion. One merely grasps at the fruits of view and pride and establishes this conventional designation. The present text is not like that; rather, it defines the five turbidities based on the deluded thoughts of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Ānanda, you see empty space pervading the worlds of the ten directions; yet space and seeing are not distinguished. Space exists but has no substance; seeing exists but has no awareness.
These interweave to form a delusion. This is the first layer, called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
[Commentary] In Sanskrit it is called *kalpa*; here it is translated as "time-period" (*shifen*). The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states that days, months, years, and ages are collectively termed *kalpas*.
Even the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness do not transcend time. In this present sutra, the meaning of the "impurity of the kalpa" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) is explained:
it refers to the arising of delusion from the truth, when the world has not yet taken form and there is only empty space and deluded vision. Space...

One sees a single entity that pervades the Dharma-realm; because delusion has not yet differentiated into two distinct parts, it is said that they are "not divided. (Wenling says: Awakening is neither emptiness nor form.

Due to a single thought of non-awakening, one falsely perceives the appearance of emptiness, thereby giving rise to pervasive delusion; thus, emptiness and the seeing are not divided. (Haimin says: Because at the very beginning of delusive ignorance, there is empty space as the substance of form; this is what is first grasped by false perception.)

This stubborn emptiness muddies the true mind to produce deluded vision. This vision absorbs the characteristics of emptiness, coagulating them into form to create the "form-mind. This is the beginning of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). When one is deluded regarding wondrous clarity as stubborn emptiness, then emptiness—which is fundamentally pervasive—[is misconceived].

To mistake the wondrous clarity for deluded vision means that vision is likewise pervasive; because these two delusions are intermingled, it is said they are "undifferentiated. Therefore, the subsequent explanation states: "Space exists but has no substance; vision exists but has no sentience."
The substance consists of the four great elements forming matter; awareness consists of the six sense organs grasping objects.

Since there is no distinction between these, they become entirely dull and insentient, and are therefore called "turbidity" (*kaṣāya*). When the first thought-moment arises, it is the beginning of ignorance and the initial division of time;

therefore, it is called a *kalpa*. This is not the turbidity of the *kalpa* at the end of an aeon. [Furong’s Studio says: In correlating the five turbidities with the three subtleties and six grossnesses, the turbidity of the *kalpa* corresponds to that karma.]

"Phenomena" (lakṣaṇa): This refers to the activity of failing to perceive that the mind is in motion. When ignorance first arises—at the very moment when the luminous awareness of awakening becomes obscured and turns into emptiness—it is at this temporal juncture that phenomena arise. Because the perception of emptiness interweaves with these phenomena to form delusion, once delusion is established, it constitutes "temporal division" (kāla).

[△ *Gushan* says: This turbidity depends upon the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Why is it called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kāṣāya*)? Among the four phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, each is termed an "eon. There is empty space.

"Without substance" means that it is empty and lacks any essential nature. This is precisely the earth losing its obstructive nature and turbidifying the true nature; the fault lies herein. Because there is no weaving [of the aggregates] (the two turbidities of views).

Your body now appears as a solid mass, having the four great elements as its substance. Seeing, hearing, smelling, and knowing are congested and obstructed; water, fire, wind, and earth [are likewise so].

Consequently, the four subtle elements (*catvāri tanmātrāṇi*) manifest as formal characteristics and substantial natures. [Supplementary Note: Seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing are originally not obstructive; it is because they are interwoven by the four great elements that seeing...]

Transcending form, the ear perceives only sound; the body’s sensory awareness arises from the natures of water and fire. These weave together false perceptions, which rotate, shift, and alternate, thereby forming the six sense organs.

Although earth, water, fire, and wind are fundamentally not themselves sensory awareness, they are set in motion by the six consciousnesses and can thus give rise to cognition, much like the pure matter of the four great elements.
To be able to see, to be able to awaken, to awaken, hear, know, and see—just as warp threads interweave with woof threads, they are mutually entangled;

therefore, it is called turbidity (*kaṣāya*). Previously, it was the transformation of karma; now, it is the manifestation of signs. [My own commentary: Previously, it was said that there is emptiness and no substance; now, it speaks of seeing, hearing, awakening, and knowing. By obstructing and causing these to remain as hindrances, there is substance. Previously, it was said there is seeing but no awakening; now, it speaks of water, fire, wind, and earth, which revolve and cause awakening and knowing.

Thus, there is awareness. Therefore it is said: "Previously, karma was in motion; now, its manifestations appear. (△ [Gushan says]: This refers to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Since objects are distinguished as being disagreeable, agreeable, or neither disagreeable nor agreeable, the six sensations likewise differ as painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations. The four great elements are taken to form the body; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are originally a single entity. Due to the four elements, they become congested and obstructed. The four elements and the six sense faculties interweave to falsely form this state; thus it is called the turbidity of views (the "view" refers to the proliferation of calculations regarding permanence and impermanence). (3. The Turbidity of Afflictions)

Furthermore, within your mind, the nature of memory, cognition, recitation, and study gives rise to knowledge and vision, which allow the six sense objects to appear. Apart from the objects, there are no forms;
apart from perception, there is no nature. These forms and perceptions interweave to form delusion; this is the third layer, called the turbidity of afflictions.

[Commentary: The six consciousnesses engage in discrimination and universally take objects across the three periods of time. They recollect past objects, cognize present sensory realms, and rehearse future ones;

they engage with all such objective spheres. [The *Shiyao* states: "The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to take as its objects the realms of both the environment and the sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, and it is further capable of grasping and maintaining them.
