When consciousness takes as its object a realm that has already fallen away, it is the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness); when it perceives a present sensory object, it is the clearly manifest *manovijñāna*. When it follows what was grasped by the five [sensory consciousnesses] to take as its object a realm of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is the recitation and study of the future—that is, the pre-reflective contemplation of matters not yet manifested.

This refers to the solitary, scattered mind taking as its object a realm of inference (*anumāna*). By citing these three cases, it precisely clarifies that the mind is able to take objects of the three periods of time as its objects. Master Kuò’s commentary states: "Recalling the past, the consciousness confronts the present. The essence of this capacity for discernment is produced from the awakening and cognition of prior turbid views;
therefore, it is said that "its nature gives rise to knowledge and vision" (*xing fa zhi jian*). (The discerning nature of consciousness is produced from what is seen, heard, sensed, and known.)

Therefore, the "discriminated characteristics" (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*) are precisely the reflected images manifested by the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Hence it is said that "the appearance manifests within the six sense objects. (Regarding the "discriminated characteristics":

because they manifest from the six sense objects [as noted in the Supplement], the delusive nature of the six consciousnesses attaches to the faculties and objects to give rise to cognition and views; hence it is said "nature arises. Because one discriminates the six characteristics within the objects of the six sense fields, it is said "appearance manifests.

As for "appearance manifests," "appearance" (*rong*) refers to the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Apart from the objects and apart from cognition, there is neither characteristic nor nature. (Apart from the six sense objects, there is nothing to be recollected, cognized, or habitually cultivated.)

Because it is devoid of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is said that "being free from dust, there are no characteristics. Because it is free from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, it lacks the nature of recollection, cognition, chanting, or study; therefore, it is said that "being free from characteristics, there is no nature. These [characteristics and natures] interweave with one another and disturb each other through mutual perfuming;

this is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāluṣya*). This refers to the first four of the six coarse states (*ṣaḍ-audārika*). [Commentary by Wēnlíng: "Recollection, cognition, chanting, and study" refer to wisdom (*jñāna*) and its continuity (*saṃtati*), as well as the characteristics of grasping and calculating names.

[Commentary by Gūshān: This is based on the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). The perceived objects of the conditions that can be grasped are termed "perception," and there are six kinds. That is to say, taking the characteristics of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) that are grasped constitutes the six perceptions. From this nature, knowledge arises.

"Seeing" refers to the capacity to grasp the six perceptions, which can manifest the six sense objects; these refer to the characteristics of the six sense objects as they are grasped. When these characteristics interweave, they falsely constitute the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Once one becomes attached to what is perceived, the agitation and confusion become even greater than before, thereby clouding the true nature.

Therefore, it is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). (△ [Haiyin says]: "Thought" refers to the deluded conceptualization of the six consciousnesses. Because one has repeatedly practiced recitation within the mind, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) stir from within, and suddenly arise as objects of knowledge and views;

hence it is said, "the nature gives rise to knowledge and views. Following these deluded thoughts, the sensory objects that appear are clearly delineated within the nature of delusion. One falsely perceives the reflected shadows of the six sense-fields as the characteristics of one's own mind; hence it is said, "the appearance manifests the six sense-fields.

Thus, apart from the objects there are no mental characteristics, and apart from the faculties there is no mental nature. The triad of faculties, objects, and consciousness becomes turbid into a single phase, giving rise to greed, anger, and so forth—this is named the turbidity of afflictions). (4. The Turbidity of Sentient Beings)
Furthermore, you arise and perish morning and evening without ceasing; your perceptions and insights constantly desire to remain in this world, yet the force of karma perpetually shifts the lands.
These factors interweave to form delusion; this is the fourth layer, called the turbidity of sentient beings.
[Commentary: Arising and ceasing constitute *saṃskāra*. *Saṃskāra* is precisely karma. Sentient beings cling with craving and merely desire to remain [attached to the three realms].
The nature of karma is migratory and flows constantly; it moves and dwells, oscillating between motion and stillness, interweaving one another as all phenomena arise and cease.

[Combined Explanation: By weaving migration into flow, and weaving flow into migration, karmic views arise suddenly; the cessation of clinging and the arising of karma occur simultaneously. At the very moment of abiding in birth, there is already change.

"Cessation" (meaning that while staying correctly, one immediately departs) is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). This refers precisely to the creation of karma. [Wenling says: "Arising and ceasing morning and evening" refers to the characteristic of creating karma.

[Guishan says: "This turbidity depends upon the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). The mind of volitional activity that can move toward a fruit is called 'formation' (*saṃskāra*). There are six kinds of formations; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of them as the 'six intentions' (*ṣaḍ-cetanā*). Intention is itself karma. That is to say, following each of the six perceptions (*ṣaḍ-vijñapti*), one gives rise to wholesome, unwholesome, or imperturbable karma.

'Knowledge and vision' refers to these six intentions. 'Karmic movement' refers to shifting according to good or evil. 'Lands' also refers to the world. It is like when one's private heart, though attached to one's hometown, must go to another region due to official business."*] *Note: The original Chinese text contains parenthetical citations from Wenling and Guishan regarding the nature of this turbidity and its relation to the *saṃskāra-skandha*, the mechanism of karmic formation, and the analogy of worldly migration.*

The cycle of wandering through the six realms is likewise like this. As for their mutual entanglement: one should know that while the faculty of perception desires to remain, the movement of karma carries one away. Thus, delusion forms the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and this union of departing and remaining muddies the true nature; this is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). (5. The turbidity of life-force *āyuḥ-kaṣāya*)
What you see and hear originally possesses no distinct natures. Yet, due to the separation of various sensory objects, they appear to arise as diverse and formless variations.

They recognize one another within their essential nature, yet oppose one another in their functional application. Standards for identity and difference are lost; they interweave to falsely constitute phenomena. This is the fifth layer, called the turbidity of life-span (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).

[Commentary]: Life (*jīvita*) is a resultant phenomenon (*vipākadharmā*). It is induced by karma and consists of the seeds of the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭamavijñāna*), which possess the functional capacity to maintain the continuity of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) without interruption;

this is termed "life. [The *Shiyao* states: "Life is a resultant phenomenon" means that it is produced by the karmic laws of previous lives, and thus there are differences in its duration—whether long or short.

For one who has received a body, these three—life, warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—are inseparable. Life is the retributive wind (*vāyu*) of the breath; when it maintains continuity without interruption, matter and mind can endure for a long time. If life does not maintain continuity, matter and mind then undergo transformation. Warmth refers to the physical matter of the remains, while consciousness is the mind.

O King, the first six [consciousnesses] arise through seeing and hearing. Originally, they are a single consciousness; it is only because of the differences among the six sense organs that they become separated.

Although their functions are divided, their substance is of only one kind. (The sovereign of the collective retribution is the single fundamental consciousness; therefore, it is said to be "without difference. The six sense objects are distinct, and thus seeing and hearing are differentiated. Because the organs and objects differ, the consciousnesses are consequently separated.

Regarding the phrase "in their nature they know one another": this is because the single fundamental consciousness is their substance. Regarding the phrase "in their functions they oppose one another": the eye-consciousness only cognizes form and does not distinguish sound and so forth. This is what is meant by "being the same."
The distinct and the neutral differ; yet they appear as the same in different locations. When sameness and difference lose their standard of reference, they become interwoven with one another.

Within the substance of the collective retribution, the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*) is established; this is termed the turbidity of life. It is precisely the characteristic of suffering bound by karma. (Master Rong’s *Shi* says: "Life, nature, views, and learning constitute karma; because they are bound to suffering, [it is called the turbidity of life]. (Master Gu-shan says:

"This turbidity relies upon the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). That which cognizes and discriminates the objects of perception is called consciousness; this refers to the six consciousnesses. 'Originally there is no distinct nature' means that the mind which cognizes and discriminates is one and only. As for the various sensory objects...")

"Separated by distance" refers to the six sense objects being distinct, which draw forth the production of the six consciousnesses; hence it is said, "they arise differently without cause. "In their nature they know one another" explains that there is originally no difference in nature. "In their function they turn away from one another" explains the phrase "they arise differently without cause.

When one speaks of their sameness, their functions turn away from each other; when one speaks of their difference, their natures know one another. Thus it is said, "the standard is lost. Because these two are interwoven, they are falsely called the "consciousness aggregate" (*vijñāna-skandha*). Consciousness exists as long as life remains; when consciousness departs, life fades away. It muddies the true nature;

therefore, it is called the "turbidity of life. (△ [Wang Shunding says: This is precisely the union of arising-and-ceasing with non-arising-and-non-ceasing; it is the very life-root of sentient beings, and is thus named the turbidity of life. The five preceding layers are all...
Through the interaction of subject and object, the shadows and lights of deluded cognition mutually condition one another, progressing from the subtle to the coarse and existing in mutual dependence.

They arise sequentially, blending with the True to form turbidity; these are the five meanings [of the five turbidities]. [The Haiyin Commentary states: The five turbidities arise based on the five aggregates.

Since the mind of non-arising and non-extinction is to be shown as the fundamental cause for cultivation, the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the five turbidities are first demonstrated. This uses arising and ceasing to verify non-arising, and uses the five aggregates to verify the Dharma-body. The Buddha [teaches] that sentient beings give rise to inversion because they all rely upon the five [aggregates].

Therefore, the contemplation of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is the essential gateway for entering the Path. If one attains the essentials of this contemplation, then whether in the state of manifestation or in the state of contemplation, there will be a point of return. Thus, the gateway of the contemplation of the five aggregates is the definitive primary meaning of this sutra.
(II. Cultivating the Causes to Accord with the Fruit; A. Exhorting the Selection of the False and Relying on the True).
Ānanda, if you now wish to cause your seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to reach far back in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence,
bliss, self, and purity, you should first select the root of birth and death, and rely upon the unarisen and undying, perfectly湛 (zhan) nature to achieve it.

[Commentary: Delusion of the truth gives rise to falsehood; thus one perceives, hears, feels, and knows. To turn away from falsehood and return to the truth is to attain the permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity that do not follow the cycle of birth and death;

thereby one may reach wondrous realization. If one merely follows worldly toil, one turns further away from the true and eternal. Therefore, I urge you to discern the false and rely upon that which is non-arising and non-perishing.

[Wuxing says: "Perceiving, hearing, feeling, and knowing" refers to the mind of birth and death. "Permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity" refers to the nature of non-arising and non-perishing. Because cause and effect are different in their phenomena, they are distant; because the mind-nature and its principle are identical, they accord.]

The root of birth and death refers to the six sense organs. [Supplementary Note: In this first meaning, the teaching follows through on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, taking the conscious mind as the root of birth and death.

Since it speaks of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, which distantly accord with the four virtues (*catur-guṇa*), one should take the six consciousnesses within the six sense organs as the objects to be excluded. This is because the sixth consciousness, when associated with the eleven wholesome mental factors, can create the wholesome karma of humans and devas; and when associated with the root and secondary afflictions, it can create the evil karma of the three miserable realms. This interpretation takes the agent of the action as the mind. Master Shenxi takes the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*) to be the mind. so too it is with these thieves of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). If they enter a person’s faculties (*indriya*), they are able to plunder all wholesome dharmas, leaving one poor, destitute, and exposed, creating an icchantika.

Those six great thieves can only plunder the wealth of persons in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); they have not yet been able to plunder those in the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*). The evil thieves of the six sense objects, however, are able—whether by seeing, knowing, hearing, observing, touching, or perceiving—to plunder them all.

They plunder all the treasures of goodness within the three realms; therefore, the Bodhisattva carefully contemplates the six sense objects as being more dangerous than those six thieves. (The term "mediator" [媒] is explained as "plotting" [謀]. A plotter brings two names together, hence it is called a mediator.

The six sense organs can give rise to the six consciousnesses and cause them to become attached to the six sense objects; thus, the six organs are like mediators. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says: "It is just as when people in the world rush about in an empty village, harmed by the six thieves, yet being foolish, they do not know how to avoid them. The commentary explains: The six organs are false and provisional, like an empty village.

The six sense objects (ṣaḍ-viṣaya) defile and stain, harming the life-force of wisdom and plundering the wealth of merit; therefore, they are called the "six thieves. (2) A detailed explanation of the relative superiority and inferiority of the faculties' functions. (1) A general clarification of the merits regarding the evolution of the world.
(1) Explaining the names and discerning their characteristics.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "world of sentient beings"? "World" (*loka*) refers to the flow of time, and "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation.
You should now know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the realms;
the past, future, and present constitute the worlds. There are ten spatial directions and three temporal flows. All sentient beings are woven together by delusion.
They mutually constitute one another; within the body there is exchange, and worlds intersect with one another.

[Commentary] There are three kinds of worlds: namely, sentient beings, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). To distinguish this from the other two, "sentient beings" is specified here.

If even one of these transcends [suffering], all others are liberated. [Gushan says: The two kinds of worlds shown above are the world of sentient beings, which is the primary retribution (*vipāka*), and the vessel-world...]

The *dhātu* (realm) is the retributive environment (*niśraya-vipāka*), because one is bound by the primary retribution (*mūla-vipāka*) and thus cannot transcend the environmental realm. Here, we clarify only the primary retribution through the first four phrases: [the first two] explain the names, while "You now" and below distinguish their characteristics;

"All" and below provide a concluding demonstration. Within the body is the *dhātu*; "exchanging and shifting" refers to the *loka* (world). Because worlds and realms interweave, they are said to "interpenetrate.

("Exchanging and shifting" means trading and migrating. That worlds and realms interpenetrate is the aspect of exchange and migration; that is to say, the world interpenetrates the realm, and the realm interpenetrates the world.)

(△ [Wenling says: The world of sentient beings also has four directions; these are simply left, right, before, and behind. "World" (*loka*) refers to the successive transition of the three time-periods; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to each having its own fixed position. There are ten such realms and three periods of time. Within a single body, the principles naturally interpenetrate one another;

hence it is said that there is "exchange and transition within the body. Thus, the worlds mutually interpenetrate. (△ [Xuelang says: All the faculties and objects of sentient beings are woven together by delusion to form one another. Within the body, from moment to moment, there is exchange and transition.)

"Transformed, then the three periods of time and the four directions naturally interpenetrate. (△ [Haian] says: "The three periods and four directions are observed solely within a single body. Since the realms and the periods are already within the body, their shifting and changing is what is meant by 'the powerful one carries it and leaps across.

(○ [Cited Evidence] The *Lokadhātuparivarta* says: "There are ten ways of explaining the three periods of time. What are these ten? They are: explaining the past period as the past period; explaining the past period as the future period..."

The past world is spoken of as the present world; the future world is spoken of as the past world; the future world is spoken of as the present world; the future world is spoken of as the inexhaustible; the present world is spoken of as the past world; the present world is spoken of as the future world; the present world is spoken of as equality;

and the three periods of time within the present world are spoken of as a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). These are the ten [worlds]. [Commentary: The preceding kalpas and this world differ in length, yet all are temporal divisions and are collectively the ten worlds. They are established through the differentiation of interlocking phenomena. The preceding nine worlds are established in relation to one another;

when the fundamental is subsumed into the derivative, they do not depart from a single thought-moment. This very present thought-moment is the past and the future; it is the future and the past; it inherently possesses the three periods of time. This single thought-moment— *Note: The term "十世" (ten worlds) refers to the ten periods of time as described in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and other texts on the ten worlds, which describe the temporal dimensions of existence.*

Although [the moments] are sequential, these three time periods are entirely contained within a single moment. Within that single moment, the three periods further act as mutual conditions; thus they constitute nine periods. Since these are rooted in a single thought-moment, they are termed "ten" (i.e., the ten worlds). (2. Distinguishing and Determining the Directions)
As for the nature of this realm, even if its positions were clearly defined throughout the ten directions, the world perceives only east, west, south, and north;
there is no fixed position for above or below, and the center has no fixed direction.

[Commentary]: Regarding the essential nature of the realms (*dhātu*), they are established based on conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Although one speaks of the ten directions, if one considers them in terms of sequential position, they become clearly determinate;
east, south, and north can serve as fixed points, whereas the others are all indeterminate. [Rongshi says: "Up" and "down" are mentioned in relation to the four cardinal directions.]

Therefore, it is said that [the direction] is indeterminate. [Xue-lang says: This refers to the center of the intermediate directions. Looking eastward, it becomes west; observing south, it becomes north. Thus, there is no fixed direction. It does not refer to the center of the four corners. (The three flows transform and achieve their function.)
The four numbers must be clearly understood. (East, West, South, North) intersect with the world (past, future, present) as three times four and four times three, revolving to form twelve.
Flowing and transforming through three cycles—ten, hundred, and thousand—they encompass the beginning and the end. Within each of the six sense faculties, there are one thousand two hundred merits.

[Commentary: Regarding the meaning of the three transformations, there have been many interpretations throughout past and present; each has seen its own textual evidence, so I cannot recount them all in detail. (Master Yue also said:

"The Buddha’s intent is difficult to fathom, and human sentiments diverge into various paths. If there is no definitive authority, who can determine what is most correct? Since the Song dynasty, divergent theories have proliferated. This current abridgment takes Changshui and Wuxing as its standard.
What I am now explaining does not employ any additional methods to alter the number [of transformations]; it simply takes the present text and proceeds with the past, present, and future.
When the calculation position shifts, it constitutes one thousand two hundred merits. Just as in the first position, the three times and four directions revolve to form twelve;
this constitutes one layer. The calculation position consists of one horizontal and two vertical lines;
once the past has been established, the second [position] transforms one period of the past into the present, and the calculation position shifts forward by one vertical line.
Two horizontal lines and one hundred twenty vertical ones constitute the second layer. For the third, the present world is again transformed into the future;
advancing the counting positions with one horizontal and two vertical lines results in one thousand two hundred, forming the third layer.
Since the method of transformation concerns only the three periods of time, the numbers transformed are likewise only one thousand two hundred; therefore, there are none beyond this.

Increasing and decreasing. [Yao Huang Zongxi said: Changshui’s method of calculation uses the current instruments. What he calls "horizontal" and "vertical" refers to distinguishing the calculation positions: the fundamental position is vertical, while advancing one position is horizontal.]

The fundamental position is horizontal; advancing one position constitutes the vertical. This is what is meant in the *Qiankun Zhaodu* by "standing calculation" and "lying calculation. It is not like Xu Yue’s *Taiyi Suan*, where the calculating instruments actually have horizontal and vertical orientations.

Rather, when the three periods and four directions are multiplied together, they yield twelve. When these twelve are squared, it should result in one hundred and forty-four. That it is not so now is because the scriptural text has undergone transformation; it merely changes one to ten and ten to a hundred, no longer using the three periods and four directions as the multiplier.
Future transformations will likewise be thus. Question: Since the scriptural text states that the worlds interpenetrate across the three periods and four...
Question: Regarding the "twelve transformations," why are these numerical changes explained solely according to the worldly perspective (*loka-vāda*) rather than by way of spatial direction (*diś*)?
Answer: The substance of spatial direction is eternally fixed, whereas the meaning of time is fluid. Because it is fixed, it does not change; because it moves, it shifts.

Now, since the ten have been changed into a thousand—transforming the many from the few—it conforms to the worldly perspective, but it does not accord with the principle of spatial direction. It is not merely that they do not accord in meaning...

This is consistent. Furthermore, it is difficult for multiple layers to coincide. Since the sutra text explicitly states that there are three layers of flux and transformation, is this not solely a description of the three periods of time?
Question: Regarding the transition and change of the three periods, shouldn't [an entity] migrate from the future into the present?
Why is this passage stated in reverse, changing the present into the past? Answer:
Here, we proceed from the subtle to the manifest, transforming the small into the great. Since it has already reached twelve, it will eventually reach hundreds and thousands;
therefore, one cannot first refer to the future to correspond with the initial layer. Because the number of the future is as yet unseen, it is necessary to state it in reverse order.
This is because "change" (*biàn*) carries the meaning of "reversal. As the subsequent text states: "Birth follows from habitual conformity; death follows from the flow of change.

Since the scripture speaks of "flowing change," it is necessary to increase its numerical value through reversal. [The ancient masters explain: The first change transforms one into ten; by interchanging the three times and the four directions, this becomes twelve. The second change transforms ten into a hundred;

by interchanging the three times and the four directions, this becomes one hundred and twenty. The third change transforms a hundred into a thousand; by interchanging the three times and the four directions, this becomes one thousand two hundred. This is the numerical measure of the merit of a single faculty.

Taking the six faculties as a whole, they total seven thousand two hundred. Excluding the three faculties of eye, nose, and body—each of which lacks four hundred—the actual number obtained is six thousand; this constitutes the merit of the six faculties. One serves as the primary unit, while ten, hundred, and thousand constitute the three layers, thereby weaving together these numbers.

(The above is from Master Taijia Pan’s *Fozu Tongji*, citing the commentary of an ancient master. He follows the text to increase the numbers in order to determine the merit of the six faculties, much like Changshui’s current explanation. (○ [Wuxing says]: This is based on the twelve [links of dependent origination].)

Through the processes of transition, flow, and change, these together constitute three cycles (*tri-saṃdhi*). The enumeration of "one, ten, hundred, thousand" is merely a general method for indicating increasing numbers. Now, as we proceed through the world, let us clarify these three cycles. First, regarding the four directions, each is discussed in terms of the three periods of time.

This constitutes twelve. Second: within the three periods of time in the eastern direction, one transforms into ten, making thirty. The same applies to the south, west, and north; with thirty in each of the four directions, this totals one hundred and twenty. Third: within the three periods of time in the eastern direction, ten transforms into a hundred, making three hundred.

The other three directions are likewise; with three hundred in each of the four directions, this totals one thousand two hundred. By applying the periods of time across the directions, the principle can be understood. [Private Commentary:

Regarding the three successive transformations (*tri-vivarta*), there are differing interpretations by Changshui and Wuxing. There are two points of difference. First, Changshui restricts the transformation of the three periods to the past, present, and future [of each period], whereas Wuxing restricts the transformation to the past, present, and future [within] the current period itself. Second, Changshui exclusively clarifies that...

Regarding "the directions pervading the world": Wu-xing Jiaming interprets it as "the world pervading the directions"—this is the second point. Master Deng of Youxi, following the teachings of Jingjue, extensively cites the ten types of the three periods of time from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—specifically the single moment of a thought-instant—to explain and establish its meaning.

However, he does not realize that while those [passages] clarify the dependent origination of the three periods to prove the essential nature of a single thought-instant, this [text] clarifies the flux and transformation of the three periods to precisely define the merits of the six sense faculties. The fundamental purports of these two scriptures are thus vastly different. Chang-shui [Zong-jing] uses the past and present to distinguish the three periods, citing increased numbers in general;

his intent ultimately returns to a comprehensive summary of the six faculties, which accords with the meaning of the scripture. Since "directions" (*di*) refer to spatial positions, there are ten directions; since "periods" (*shi*) refer to temporal flux, there are three transformations. Heaven and earth constitute the four... [text ends].

Since the directions possess fixed positions, there consequently exist the temporal divisions of past, present, and future. What is extended becomes an *kalpa*, and what is contracted becomes a *kṣaṇa*. These all arise from the fixed positions of the four directions and are entirely matters of numerical calculation. The sutra-texts clearly state that the four numbers must be made manifest.

"Interpenetrating with the world" does not mean that the three numbers must necessarily be clarified; rather, it clarifies interpenetration with the spatial directions. Furthermore, it explicitly speaks of the threefold layering of flux and transformation, but does not speak of the threefold layering of spatial positions. Since the previous passage referred to the exchange and circulation within the body, it spoke of "worlds interpenetrating. If one wishes to clarify the differentiation of spatial directions, then one speaks of "interpenetrating with the world.

This is truly because the receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*) is established first, and the temporal divisions are determined next. Such is indeed the nature of the ocean-like manifestation of the world's establishment. If one were to say that the world interpenetrates the directions, [it would be incorrect].

In that case, the world would be a chaotic mixture, failing to establish a stable order; its transformations would not be formed, and its spatial orientations would also be lost. Since the sutras contain no explicit text regarding the world’s engagement with spatial directions, one should not rely on the literal text to patch together such a system.

After the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation), the various schools—including Jingjué—have existed; those in the world who possess the discerning eye should further examine this matter with care. (○ [Wùxīng further says]: Master Kuò, based on the three periods and four directions, posits the five faculties and five objects.

Each faculty and object further constitutes ten classes of sentient beings, totaling twelve hundred. Master Yùn refutes this, while Master Jié agrees with it. Master Mǐn, within each of the twelve, posits that they all possess the ten wholesome actions, totaling one hundred and twenty. Each wholesome action further possesses the "ten suchnesses," totaling twelve hundred. 至... (up to...)

Regarding Zizhong, Gushan, and Changshui, they merely combined the numbers; their methods of transformation and enumeration differ. Although I have provided separate explanations, I have not yet dared to correlate them with the specific characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of those masters. The wise do not take sides; they follow only what is good. (The passage to the right refers to what Changshui called "the many interpretations of the ancient masters":

Master Ke held that [the *āśrayaparāvṛtti*] achieves defilement but not purity; Master Min held that it achieves goodness but not evil. There are those who synthesize the interpretations of these two masters, practicing according to the conditions of defilement or purity, whether in accordance or opposition, as in Master Cao’s "perfect" exposition.

There are also those who rely on Master Ke’s principle regarding the "gate of the inherently evil nature," explaining the number based on the ten evils. These have already been examined and distinguished by the ancients, so this present commentary does not record them again. As for the distinct explanations of other learned individuals, there are...)

Those points that clarify and illuminate the ancient commentaries are appended briefly below. (△ [Wujin said: The sentient beings and the vessel-world exist within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The "world" (*loka*) cannot transcend the three; the "realm" (*dhātu*) cannot go beyond the four. As for "flowing transformation," it transforms according to the sequence of one, two, and three.

Following this transformation through three cycles—ten, hundred, and thousand—the beginning and end of its meritorious functions are exhausted. (△ [Wenling said: Because the three and four interpenetrate, they are called "winding and turning. Due to the flowing transformation across the three periods of time, there are three cycles:

from one cycle to ten, ten cycles to a hundred, and a hundred cycles to a thousand. This results in twelve hundred. All six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are fully present. However, this is merely a provisional reliance on worldly discourse to manifest the general outline of the wondrous function. If the six are liberated into one...)
There is no mutual exclusion; they are used together in perfect illumination. How could any numerical measure reach them? (△ [Yunqi said: The four realms and three periods intersect with one another.

By taking three as four and four as three, both become twelve—this is the first layer. These twelve each transform into ten, becoming one hundred and twenty—this is the second layer. These one hundred and twenty each transform into ten, becoming one thousand two hundred—this is the third layer.

The general meaning is that sentient beings dwell within the world, and their seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing arise and perish in every moment; such are the characteristics of their coarse and subtle states. As the ancient masters said: "Within a single thought-moment, there are eighty-four thousand afflictions. This is it. The above is based on Master Huan’s interpretation, as followed by Yunqi.)

(As explained by Changshui in his ancient commentary). [Haerin says: Sentient beings, from time immemorial, possess within a single thought-moment that which is naturally and inherently complete. The three periods of time are fully pervasive within a single body; thus, there are three periods for each of the four directions, making twelve in total.

When the four directions are fused and permeated within a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), each world-age possesses its own four directions; these four sets of three thus constitute twelve. Because they are interwoven by this, it is called "winding and turning" (*vartana*).

Initially, a single thought-moment constitutes one layer (*āvalī*), consisting merely of these twelve. When deluded thoughts undergo a further transformation, subtle [states] continue to arise; this single thought-moment already encompasses three directions and flows through the four, thereby forming twelve transformations and constituting three layers. The reason the initial single thought-moment does not establish a fundamental basis is that all phenomena are established from the groundless root (*anālaya-mūla*).

As for the mention of only three layers: the single thought-moment of arising and ceasing naturally migrates and flows, encompassing the three periods of time (*tryadhvan*); even if one exhausts kalpas, it is still only referred to as the "three periods. [Private Commentary: Sentient beings have no...

This clarifies non-awakening. By forcibly establishing subject and object, delusory phenomena are woven together to form the two types of retribution: the environment and the inhabitants. Where there are environment and inhabitants, there are spatial directions; where there are spatial directions, there are temporal boundaries.

These flow and shift through the three periods of time, intersecting and interpenetrating one another, whereby all numerical quantities arise. Once there are numerical quantities, there are distinctions of merit and inferiority; once there are distinctions of merit and inferiority, there is selection. The general purport of the scriptural passage is that sentient beings, dwelling within the vessel-world (the physical universe), are entangled by the six sense faculties and are unable to examine the fundamental source therein.

Therefore, it takes the differences in numerical quantities across the three times and four directions as the basis for definitively establishing merit and inferiority. The text of the seventh fascicle states: "Segmented existence arises falsely because of the establishment of these realms; the ceaseless flux occurs because of the formation of these periods. (3)

The four directions of the world intermingle in harmony, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories. The Tathāgata has provided annotations below [the text] to clarify this point. One must be able to definitively determine the superior and inferior within these categories and discern which faculties penetrate deeply;

only then will one know that in the world of sentient beings, those born of parents—such as the physical eyes and other sense organs—inherently possess such merits. The sense organs and their objects share the same source; the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual. To be deluded regarding this gives rise to the ten habitual causes and results in the sixfold retributive interactions.

To awaken to this constitutes the six kinds of purity and brings forth the six liberations. This is what is called "arousing the initial mind of enlightenment," the second meaning of definitive realization. Regarding the successive enumeration of these transformations, although there have been many interpretations in the past, they do not at all capture the essential joints and connections of the sutra. The Tiantai school...
Based on this principle, is it not far too much to establish the "Three Gates of Śūraṅgama" for the purpose of examining and distinguishing practitioners?

[Commentary] This refers to the fundamental capacity and functional operation of the six sense organs within the bodies of sentient beings as they perceive objects; thus, these are termed "meritorious functions.

This is not the same as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, where the cultivation of the sutra causes one to achieve pure functions. Nevertheless, although the defiled and the pure are distinct, [they share a common basis].

All are accomplished through the power of original perfuming; therefore, the textual accounts of these two [the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*] do not differ in their numerical quantities. (As Guishan says:

"The *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that by practicing according to the sūtra, one has already given rise to a semblance of understanding and the six sense organs are purified. Their functional application is boundless; though the eyes have eight hundred merits, they likewise possess the virtues of the other five organs, and so forth. (△ As Baiting says:

Regarding the similarities and differences between this and the *Lotus Treatise*, the latter uses virtues to adorn the six organs, and thus there are differences such as excess, deficiency, or equality. "Equality" means that by manifesting the purity of the six organs through non-dual virtue, they are the same. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* divides the six organs...)

Regarding strength and weakness: this differs slightly from the current [classification] based on the sense organs (*indriya*). There, the faculty of the eye is predominant; here, the faculty of the tongue is superior. Although the others are largely the same, they are not discussed in terms of number there. (△ [Wuxing says]: This is based on the six faculties.

Since their nature of discernment is the same, it is said that each possesses twelve hundred merits. Below, when contrasted with the six objects (*viṣaya*), the function of discernment differs; therefore, the merits are entirely lacking and unequal. Thus, while they correspond within their nature, they diverge in their functioning.)
(6) A detailed exposition of the merits categorized by the relative superiority and inferiority of the faculties (the second section). (1) The eye faculty.
Ānanda, you should further determine the relative superiority and inferiority among these. (General Summary) It is like the way the eye perceives: the rear is dark while the front is bright;

the area directly in front is entirely bright, while the area directly behind is entirely dark. When looking to the left and right, two-thirds of the field is visible. In summing up its functional efficacy, it is incomplete.
If one were to calculate its merit in three parts, it possesses merit in only one part and lacks it in the other two. You should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits.
[Zizhong] "The eyes" [refer to the following]: one side is three hundred; looking sideways is two hundred; furthermore, there is an additional half of that, totaling five hundred.
Combined with the previous three hundred, they total eight hundred. [Sūtra Commentary] The first two phrases provide a general statement, as correctly indicated below the eyes.
Regarding "looking sideways to the left and right by two-thirds," this refers to taking one side as three hundred. As for the "side":
The center has two hundred complete [squares]. The near sides have fifty-one each. Since it is thus on one side, the others follow the same pattern.
Now, looking from the left and right, each obtains two hundred complete parts and fifty-one on the near sides; together they form five hundred. [Supplementary Note to the Treatise:

As for looking from the left and right sides, the mention of "three parts missing" is a simplification of the calculation. Although each side originally possesses two hundred, when viewing the right from the left, the right gains fifty; when viewing the left from the right, the left gains fifty. Therefore, each obtains two hundred...]

One hundred and fifty. Zizhong says this is correct. Together with the full three hundred of Ming, they total eight hundred. As for the statement regarding "three divisions of merit," it refers to the three directions.

The rest can be understood accordingly. [Wuxing says: "To discuss merit in its entirety is to point to the three faculties. (△ According to Tianru’s Supplemental Notes: calculating by way of the four directions, there are two hundred each.)

Each of the four corners has two hundred [verses]. This was selected based on the interpretation within the *Zi* (資) commentary; all other quarters reject it (I shall not record them here at length). (2. The Ear Organ)
Just as the ear listens all around, leaving nothing out in the ten directions; when active, it reaches both near and far; when still, it is boundless.
You should know that the faculty of hearing is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits in full perfection.
[Commentary: When drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, they are heard at once in ten locations. Because movement has spatial limits, there is near and far;
because stillness is without boundary or measure, it is limitless. Since both are within the domain of the auditory faculty, they are here manifested together.
([○@(?∴)] The third, the nose-faculty).

Just as the nose smells, it is permeated by the inhalation and exhalation of breath; there is out-breathing and in-breathing, yet the intermediate junction is missing. This is verified by examining the nose-faculty.
Three parts are deficient by one; one should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits.

[Commentary] When inhalation and exhalation intersect within, they together form three parts. One part consists of four hundred; because the intersection in the middle is lacking, it results in eight hundred.

[Wuxing says: "The breath passing through the nose flows in and out; the front and back do not intersect with one another. (Citation: *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 27: There are two types of inhalation: first, inhalation; second, intermediate inhalation.)

Regarding the breaths: there are two types of exhalation. First, the exhalation; second, the intermediate exhalation. As for inhalation, it refers to the movement of the internal wind immediately following the exhalation, reaching as far as the navel region.

Intermediate inhalation refers to that which arises for a brief moment in a state of similarity during the interval between the cessation of inhalation and the arising of the next exhalation, while remaining in the state of stillness. This is called intermediate inhalation. As with inhalation and intermediate inhalation, so too with exhalation and intermediate exhalation.

Exhalation should be understood in the same way. The distinction here is that immediately following inhalation, the wind shifts toward the external opening, starting from the navel region up to the mouth, or reaching the tip of the nose, or even exiting externally. (4. The Tongue Faculty)
Just as the tongue proclaims all mundane and supramundane wisdom throughout the entire world— its expressions being skillful and its principles inexhaustible—
one should know that the faculty of the tongue is endowed with a full one thousand two hundred merits.
[Commentary: Regarding mundane and supramundane wisdom, as well as the objects known by them, these can only be expressed and revealed through the tongue.

While the expressive words and phrases may still be subject to limitation, the principles and patterns they express can never be fully exhausted. Thus, [the *Fahua xuanyi* states: "The tongue-faculty grasps the four unhindered eloquences;
it can, with a single wondrous sound, pervade the trichiliocosm, yet it does not grasp or know taste. To know taste is its retributive function. (5. The Body-faculty).

Just as the body perceives touch, consciousness perceives the agreeable and the disagreeable when they are in contact; it does not know them when separated. When one part is separated and two are joined, this is verified by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Since one of the three parts is missing, you should know that the body possesses only eight hundred merits.

[Commentary: When combined, both the adverse (*pratigha*) and favorable (*anugraha*) [sensations] are present; when separated, there is only neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Therefore, it is said that "there is no cognition. [Supplementary Note:

When separated, the faculty and the object are singular, hence cognition is lacking. When combined, the faculty and the object touch together, hence there is cognition of the adverse and the favorable. Since there are four types each for the adverse and the favorable, this totals eight hundred.

Because the cognition of the separated state is lacking, it is deficient by four hundred. [Gushan says: In the separated state, there is no cognition; this is the lack of one part. At the time of combination, one is able to perceive, and since there is both the adverse and the favorable, both parts are complete. [Wenling says: In the separated state, one part is lacking. In the combined state...]

It is entirely divided into two parts; therefore, it is said that "separating from one" and "uniting with both. (△ [Tongzhou says]: When uniting, both are perceived, which is called "both"; when separated, one only fails to know, which is called "one. ([○@(?∴)] The sixth, the mental faculty).
The faculty of mind silently accommodates all things: the ten directions, the three realms, all mundane and supramundane phenomena, whether sacred or profane;
it encompasses them all without exception, reaching to their very limits. One should know that this faculty of mind is complete with twelve hundred merits.

(Wuxing says: This is not so. Contemplating the marks of impurity is precisely the untainted practice of the Hīnayāna. Awakening to the nature of all forms is the śrāvaka’s awakening to the *dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*.

Nanyue says: Contemplating the rational nature of the five aggregates is the *dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*. (△ [My own view]: Upānī contemplates the marks of impurity and practices the contemplation of white bones and subtle dust. Through this contemplation, he realizes...)

To know that the sensory objects (*rūpa-dhātu*) are the *tathāgatagarbha* is to awaken to the Middle Way of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Master Yue cites the *Cidi Chanmen* (The Gate of Gradual Meditation), which states that the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*) serve as an antidote; it claims these are the untainted (*anāsrava*) practices of the Hīnayāna.

It asserts that while one may ultimately achieve the nine contemplations and develop the truth to destroy delusions, this does not permit one to be a "both-kinds" (*ubhayabhāga*) Arhat, but only a "wisdom" (*prajñā*) Arhat. This view is mired in dogma and lacks penetration. In the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), Nāgārjuna’s commentary on the first chapter explains the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the nine contemplations, and other Śrāvaka dharmas, stating:

"By analyzing with these nine contemplations, one perceives the characteristics of the body. Because the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion are thinned, all the mountains of the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are shaken. Although the nine contemplations are impurity-contemplations (*aśubhabhāvanā*), they can, by relying upon them, accomplish the Great Matter. Thus, Bodhisattvas take pity on sentient beings...

Birth. Knowing that sentient beings have the three poisons as their causal conditions, for those sentient beings who are attached to form, he teaches the contemplation of the livid corpse (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*) and so forth, thereby destroying the attachment to internal and external bodily characteristics. This is the Bodhisattva’s practice of the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*). From the "Chapter on the Noble Practice of Nirvāṇa."

The Bodhisattva is likewise. When practicing contemplation with single-minded focus, they remove the skin and flesh and contemplate only the white bones. Zhanran (Zhang’an) said: "The Bodhisattva cultivates the methods of practice with the mind of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, such as the contemplations on the floating bag, the white bones, and the eight sufferings.

Now, it is said that by contemplating the signs of impurity, one gives rise to great revulsion and detachment; this is identical to the Bodhisattva’s practice of the nine stages of contemplation (*navasaṃjñā*). It is not like the Śrāvaka, who seeks *nirvāṇa* through revulsion and detachment. Master Yue (Yuezhou) restricted his citation to the *Chanmen*, so I have corrected it here).
(2. Correctly Presenting the Realization of the Ultimate Meaning, Part Two) (1. Attaining the Way through the Completion of Contemplation)
Because [the body] proceeds from impurity, through white bones and subtle dust, it returns to empty space. When both emptiness and form are non-existent, one achieves the path of no-more-learning.

[Commentary]: First one forms the perception of impurity, and subsequently enters the contemplation of the skeleton; both are for the purpose of treating greed. Furthermore, by means of the skeleton...

One enters the analysis of form to clarify emptiness. (As stated in the *Dhyānapāramitā-sūtra*: Within the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), there are three distinct modes of manifestation for the arising of the roots of goodness. First, regarding the roots of goodness of the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*):

while in the state of "not-yet-arrived" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) within the desire realm, one suddenly sees the corpses of other men or women becoming bloated and swollen, whereby one is startled into awakening and feels self-reproach. One then develops weariness toward the five desires previously experienced in a state of dull concentration and vows never again to associate with them.

Or, one perceives such signs as the bluish discoloration (*vinīlaka*), being smeared with blood and festering with pus, being devoured and left in disarray, or the scattering and decay of white bones; these are the manifestations of the arising of the roots of goodness of the nine perceptions. Second, regarding the manifestation of the roots of goodness of the clear liberations (*vaimuktya-vimokṣa*): likewise within this state, one suddenly perceives the impurity of one's own internal body becoming bloated and swollen.)

In disarray. Or one may see one’s own white bones from head to foot, with each joint interlocking, even until it becomes a skeleton radiating brilliant light; the mind is settled and at ease, one grows weary of the five desires, and does not cling to self or person.

This is the sign of the arising of the roots of goodness for the *prātimokṣa* (liberation). As for the arising of the roots of goodness for the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and the great contemplation of impurity, [it is as follows]... Furthermore, by means of this emptiness, one perceives the true mark of form and awakens to the principle within:
that form and emptiness are of a single, true nature. Therefore, it is said that both emptiness and form are non-existent. (Wuxing says: "Cultivating the remedial dharmas, one achieves...")

Regarding the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), when one gives rise to true realization and shatters delusions, this is precisely the Arhat who destroys dharmas (*dharmabheda-arhan*). This is fully explained in the *Cidi Chanmen* (The Gate to Successive Dhyānas). (This constitutes the second layer of commentary.)
The Tathāgata certified me, naming me Niṣadha. Once the dust-like forms were exhausted, the wondrous form became subtle and perfect.
Through these marks of form, I attained arhatship.

[Commentary]: It is from awakening that this name is derived. True, wholesome, and wondrous form (*rūpa*) is precisely ultimate emptiness; when characteristics are exhausted and nature is revealed, one awakens to the *tathāgatagarbha*, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm;

hence it is called "mysterious and perfect" (*miyuan*). This constitutes the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). [Supplement states: First, the former realization is recounted, establishing the path of no-more-learning; this belongs to the Small Vehicle.

Once the dust of form has been entirely removed, the Perfect Penetration (*yuantong*) is recounted. (△ [Xunwen states]: When the nine perceptions are accomplished, one attains liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*); regarding all forms and characteristics, one manifests the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state; hence it is called "wondrous form and wondrous perfection.")

According to Master Yue, it is not permitted that what was small in the past becomes large now. He judged that the various teachings for the śrāvakas mostly involve the contemplation of the Small Vehicle, which holds the meaning of the actual existence of cessation and emptiness. The realization of the bodhisattvas should likewise involve distinctions between the sequential and the perfect-fusion.
Now, taking the revelation and manifestation as the primary principle, we have generally subjected these to revision and excision). (This concludes the third section: Responding to the Questions).
The Buddha asked about the perfection of penetration. As I have realized it, the cause of form is supreme.

[Commentary: One awakens to the Way by contemplating fragrance and attains the stage of *kumārabhūta* (the youthful), which is termed "youth" (*tóngzi*). [The *Huìxuán jì* states: "The term 'youth' signifies the initial entry into the Buddha-dharma;

(3) Second, Cultivating Contemplation Based on the Teachings. (1) First, Identifying the Object of Contemplation.
At that time, having taken leave of the Buddha, I retired for quiet seclusion in a pure chamber. There I saw various bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense; the fragrance was serene and still.
[The breath] comes and enters the nostrils.
[Commentary: During the transition toward dusk, I rested in tranquil repose within a pure chamber, a place for washing the mind.

this is precisely the object of contemplation. (II. Correct Contemplation; 1. Contemplative Practice).
I observe this fragrance: it is neither wood nor space; it is neither smoke nor fire. As it departs, there is nowhere it clings; as it comes, there is nowhere it originates. [Commentary]:
Wood, space, smoke, and fire—when investigated through reasoning, these are not the place where the fragrance arises. Since its arrival is without cause, where does it go when it departs?
By what means does it become fragrance to perfume my nose? This is the contemplation that fragrance is without arising.
[Zizhong: "Not wood, etc. means contemplating the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). [Xunwen says: When speaking of the emptiness of nature, one must necessarily investigate the four natures:

This resembles the Mahāyāna method of contemplating that illusory existence is itself emptiness. (The two contemplations and their benefits).
Thereby, the mental faculty was dissolved and the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) was manifested. The Tathāgata certified me, and I received the name "Fragrance-Veneration" (*Gandhābharaṇa*).

[Commentary: Since fragrance is ultimately without arising, how could there be further discrimination? Therefore, it is said that the mental faculty was dissolved. When discrimination does not exist, subject and object both perish.

Named Xiangyan (Jiaoguang says: "This reveals the outflow-free [anāsrava]. To penetrate the essence of the blazing fragrance is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha mind; Xiangyan adorns the Dharmakāya with wondrous fragrance"). (The three layers of explanation establish this).
The dust-like vapors suddenly vanished; a wondrous fragrance became subtle and pervasive. From this "Purity of Fragrance," I attained Arhatship. [Commentary]:

When appearances are exhausted, one returns to Suchness, and the true fragrance wonderfully manifests. If one does not discern even for a single thought-moment, one immediately ascends to the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). [Sub-commentary]:

"The wondrous fragrance is subtle and pervasive" means that the fundamental fragrance of nature is pure and clear. The Buddha asked about the perfection of penetration. According to what I have realized, the fragrance of incense is supreme.

Bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, and pungent tastes, as well as all combinations, co-nascent states, and transformations—
whether cold or hot, poisonous or non-poisonous— he is able to know them all completely.

[Commentary: Because he is capable of succeeding to the position of the Regent (Kumārabhūta) and continuing the lineage of the Buddhas so that it remains unbroken, he is called a "Dharma Prince" (*dharmaputra*).

Thereupon he attained enlightenment. [Citation: The *Bhaiṣajyarāja-sūtra* states: In the past there was a Buddha named Vaidūryaprabha. There was a bhikṣu named Gopaka who proclaimed the True Dharma.

His younger brother, named Vidyutprabha, made offerings of the most sublime medicine of *sarpis-maṇḍa* (clarified butter), and was given the name Bhaiṣajyasamudgata. "I shall rescue and protect all those in this world of suffering. Amidst the calamities of war and pestilence, I shall act as a Great King of Physicians; only then shall I become a Buddha. The Buddha Ratnagarbha said, "Today I name you 'Great Pure Medicine King' (Mahā-bhaiṣajyarāja).

In the future, you shall become a Buddha—namely, the Tathāgata Ruci. [△ *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* states: "The Mahāyāna is that which is mounted by great beings such as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī. Serving the Tathāgata, they thoroughly understand the nature of taste: it is neither empty nor existent; it is neither identical to the body and mind, nor separate from the body and mind.

[Commentary: One contemplates the cause of the flavor: from what does it arise? Whether body and mind exist or not, whether they are identical or separate, neither has a place of origin.
To understand this is precisely what is meant by "contemplation. Because there is no place of origin, the sensory object (the flavor) is tranquil and discrimination ceases.
Subject and object vanish; both are entirely without trace. There remains only this single flavor of pure, precious awakening. Thus it is said:

From this, one attains awakening and immediately realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). [Wuxing says: "Because one serves the Buddha, one will inevitably hear the True Dharma. One then understands arising and non-arising within the nature of taste.

'Emptiness' and 'existence' refer to the sense-object of taste; 'body,' 'mind,' and 'tongue-consciousness' refer to the subject. The nature of the Middle Way is thereby revealed. (△ Wēnlíng says: "Discerning the cause of taste" means understanding the nature of taste. ...as with the causes of form, water, and so forth). (The two receive the seal and obtain benefit).

He is a prince of the Dharma. Because he awakened to clarity through the taste [of medicine], he ascended to the rank of a Bodhisattva.

Following the custom, he entered the room and suddenly awakened to the cause of water. [Commentary] *Bhadrapāla* means "Worthy Protector" (*Xiánhù*).

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is translated as "Good Guardian. The *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* states: "If sentient beings hear his name, they will ultimately attain perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); therefore, he is called 'Good Guardian'. Guishan says:

"In Chinese, this is 'Worthy Guardian' (*Xiánshǒu'), meaning he himself guards virtuous qualities and further protects sentient beings; alternatively, he is called 'Worthy Head' (*Xiánshǒu'), because his rank is that of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), making him the foremost among all worthies. This person [Sadāparibhūta] was the first of these Buddhas; during the period of the Semblance Dharma, he was reviled by those who were arrogant.

Because of this, he fell into hell and remained there for a thousand kalpas. Once his retribution was exhausted, he emerged and encountered the subsequent Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja Buddha; he left the household life and attained awakening.

Neither washing away the dust nor washing the body, remaining tranquil in the interval, one attains non-existence.

[Commentary: The dust has no self-nature; it perishes as soon as it arises. Its substance is illusory existence, and its nature and characteristics are fundamentally empty.
The water has no cause and remains tranquil and unmoving. Since all three are unobtainable, what constitutes the act of bathing?

The delusive habits of beginningless time are suddenly dissolved, so that even until this present moment, one attains the state of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). [Wuxing says: "Water" refers to the cause of being touched; "dust-substance" refers to the condition of the toucher.

Since dust is already unstained, its essence is also eternally pure. Subject and object are like illusions; both extremes are empty. When the mind that perceives contact within the middle way rests in peace, it accords with its true nature. (△ [Yunqi said: This means that when water washes away dust, the dust has no inherent self-nature.)

Cold, heat, roughness, and smoothness—by which dust is washed? If you say water washes the body, the body belongs to the four great elements: earth, water, fire, and wind. Which of these elements is washed? Since external objects and the internal body both vanish, how can there be an "intermediate" [body]? Who, then, is it that is washed by the water?

From this, one awakens and enters [the truth]. Where appearances cease, the nature manifests; this is the original *tathāgatagarbha*. This is what constitutes "wondrous touch. [Commentary]: "Habitual tendencies from past lives are not delusory. "I have attained the opportunity to draw near [to the Buddha], to hear the Dharma, and to practice and study it.

It is called *Pippala* because it can outshine other objects. According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, this mother obtained [the child] through prayers at a tree; her name was Bhadrā, and her household’s wealth was a thousand times superior to that of King Bimbisāra. Throughout their lives in the human and celestial realms, their bodies were always golden in color and their minds always experienced bliss. [He was] ten cubits tall. He wore a priceless jewel-robe, which he cut into four folds to serve as a saṃghāṭī for the Buddha’s seat. Thus, in three such acts of renunciation, he was without equal in the world. This Great Man is the eldest among all those who share his name. Among the practitioners of the Buddha-dharma, Mahākāśyapa is foremost in practicing the twelve *dhūta* ascetic virtues and performing difficult and arduous austerities; therefore, he is designated as "Mahākāśyapa. These relics are that which have been perfumed and cultivated by precept, concentration, and wisdom; they are the supreme field of merit. Smearing them with oil and gilding them with gold are all causes for the golden radiance of the body.

[Commentary: The arising and ceasing of the six sense objects are the domain of the mind. Now, one contemplates these phenomena as being fundamentally unborn from the beginning and thus not subject to extinction now.

The mind does not perceive the mind, for no characteristic can be apprehended. Both subject and object are utterly tranquil, and the *dharmatā* manifests before one. Body and mind are, by nature...
Because it is immovable when approached, it enables one to traverse many kalpas as swiftly as a finger-snap. [Gushan says: To cultivate cessation is to abide within the nine successive stages.]

This is the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Even now, upon Mount Kukkuṭapāda, he still enters this absorption to await Maitreya.
