"The ingenuity of man can indeed rival that of the Creator! Zhang Zan said: "All of these are made to function by means of mechanical levers (*kāṅguān*). If the master of the levers is removed, they can no longer control one another. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:

"All the dharmas taught by the Buddha are devoid of a self (*ātman*) and devoid of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*). It is merely the conjunction of various dharmas that is conventionally designated as a 'sentient being. Like a wooden puppet operated by levers, although it can move, there is no master within; this is also the same as the analogy of Yan Shi. (○ [Private Note])

Those who interpret this verse do not fail to employ the analogy of a skilled illusionist to explain the six sense organs. By taking the extended prose as a model for this [verse], one finds that while the prose is extensive, the verse is concise; thus, it ought to belong to the category of *gāthā* (isolated verses). Having examined it repeatedly, I humbly maintain that this verse should be classified as an *udāna* (inspired utterance), which summarizes the preceding prose.

Regarding the sequence of Ānanda’s inquiry into the loosening of the knots and the Tathāgata’s taking of the flower-cloth to tie knots and then loosen them in succession—this section of question and answer, though appearing as an isolated passage, is in fact a summary verse (*anugīti*).

How is this evident? In the Western lands, various great illusionists perform all manner of illusions. The great among them can conjure cities, towers, palaces, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, music, men, women, and all kinds of objects; the lesser ones...

Tying a handkerchief to form a rabbit involves tying the cloth to create a rabbit’s head and further tying it to produce its ears; all of these are what are called illusory phenomena. The Tathāgata’s folding of a flowered handkerchief is likewise an illusory act, just like the illusionist’s conjuring of men and women. All such things are merely illusions.

This verse takes the six sense organs (ṣaḍindriya) of a conjured person created by a magician as its subject. It is like the six knots untied from the hand of the Tathāgata; it uses illusory phenomena to illustrate illusory dharmas. When six knots are tied in an illusory cloth, those six knots serve as the metaphor for the six sense organs.

When the six sense organs are attributed to a conjured person, those six sense organs serve as the metaphor for the six knots. The organs and the knots are non-dual; the dharma and the metaphor coincide, requiring no further inference. As the verse says:

"Just as a skilled worldly illusionist conjures various men and women," while the prose commentary states: "You know that this cloth originally consists of only a single strand; when I tie six knots, there are six names, yet the substance of the cloth remains the same—it is only because of the knots that differences arise. The verse continues: "Though one sees the movement of the various organs..."

"One mechanism is withdrawn. The prose commentary states: "The Buddha said it is thus. Although the six knots are different, if one traces them back to their original cause, they are all fashioned from a single cloth; if one attempts to make them chaotic, they can never be so accomplished. The verse says: "When the mechanism ceases and returns to stillness, all illusions lose their nature.

The prose commentary states: "At the very center of the knot, if one unties it, they immediately disperse. If you wish to remove the knots, you must do so at the center of the knot. It further says: "If the root-knots are removed, the appearances of the objects naturally perish. When this root is first resolved, one first attains the emptiness of the person.

The formation of the six knots arises from a single knot; the activation of the six faculties arises from a single mechanism. Between the knots and the faculties, there has never been two illusions; between the untying of the knots and the cessation of the mechanism, there are likewise no two dharmas. Because of this..."

Having explained the single gate of "untying the knots," he proceeds to state the second meaning, "determination. This involves many points of exegesis; as the text is extensive and its principles manifold, I shall summarize the essential framework and condense it into a single verse.

Taking the example of the six pairs, this is what is meant by the phrase "the dharma and the metaphor differ. Furthermore, the skillful illusionist is a metaphor for the *tathāgatagarbha* mind. The prose states that it is "pure from the beginning, wondrously enlightened, luminous, and empty"—this refers to that very point.

The illusionist’s illusory methods are a metaphor for how, due to deluded luminosity, the three subtleties and six coarsenesses arise through the subject-object duality. It is like using illusory methods to conjure men and women, wherein the six sense organs appear vividly. The prose states that the six kinds—form, scent, taste, and touch—are fully accomplished, arising from deluded vision. The mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena are likewise produced.

The faculties move when the mechanism is drawn out; the faculties rest when the illusion is stilled. This is analogous to realizing delusion and attaining emptiness, where deluded clarity is suddenly stilled, leaving behind all subject and object. Thus it is said: "When the mechanism ceases, one returns to stillness; all illusions become devoid of inherent nature. The long prose states: "This delusion has no root; its nature is ultimately empty.

When awakening realizes delusion, delusion is extinguished; once awakened, delusion does not arise again. It further says: "Then within your mind, the madness of Yajñadatta will naturally subside. This subsiding is itself Bodhi—the supremely pure and luminous mind—which is fundamentally coextensive with the Dharma-realm."

It is so. Furthermore, when a magician creates men and women, they are illusions; the six sense faculties of men and women in the world are likewise illusions. Are not Māraṅgaka and Sundarī not illusory men and women? A verse says: "Māraṅgaka is in a dream; who can retain your form?

When the mechanism is withdrawn and the motion ceases, the puppeteer holds the strings in his hand. Thus, the Tathāgata is the master artisan of skillful illusion. To proclaim this again in verse: "The non-illusory produces illusory phenomena"—this verse refers to the illusion creating all manner of men and women.

"If even the non-illusory does not arise, how can illusory phenomena be established?"—this verse refers to the fact that all illusions lack inherent nature. The Samādhi of Illusion-like [Reality], the Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening, has been transmitted from Buddha to Bodhisattva; it is identical to this state of being like an illusion.

This is the inconceivable Dharma-gate of true samādhi. A verse in the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata performs illusions; he is the sovereign among all illusions. It further states: "One should know that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the king among all illusions. If I am the World-Honored One..."

Is he not indeed the greatest master of illusion in the ten directions and ten realms, both mundane and supramundane? Both of these sutras take Mañjuśrī as their witness. (The second [section] clarifies the six functions returning to their source.)
The six sense organs are also like this: originally depending on one brilliant essence, they are divided into six harmonious unions.
When one faculty returns to its source, the functions of all six cease to exist.

[Commentary] The first phrase provides a general heading. The second phrase corresponds to the illusionist. The third phrase corresponds to the man and woman. The final two phrases correspond to the cessation of sensory activity and so forth.

If the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the ear-faculty is destroyed, the other faculties are likewise destroyed; thus, none are established. [Subheading/Pointer] "One refined spirit" corresponds to the true nature and ignorance.

This means that arising-and-ceasing arises based upon non-arising-and-non-ceasing, which is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*. It forms the six faculties. If the ear-faculty is destroyed, the other faculties become pure. (△ [Guixiang says]: "Hou" means "good. Goodness further...)

This is its nature. Furthermore, it is a state of cessation. It is the cessation of the attachment to sensory objects and the reversion to that nature. (△ [Zibo said: When the eyes are open, they harmonize with the objects of form in the waking state; when the eyes are closed, they harmonize with the objects of form in the dream state.

Thus, the six sense organs harmonize with the six sense objects. Whether awake or dreaming, every object is received by every organ. Since beginningless time, there has not been a single kṣaṇa in which they have not been in harmony. (○ [My private opinion:

The verse says, "The six organs are also like this," which corresponds to the prose section on "untying the knots. Thus, "your six organs are also like this," and "when the six are resolved, the one perishes," is also like this. Originally, based on a single brilliant essence, they are divided into six harmonious combinations. This verse summarizes the prose. One should know that these organs are not one.)

It is not six. Because of the beginningless cycle of decline and inversion, the notion of "six" and "one" has arisen within the perfectly湛 (zhàn) and profound. Even down to the mutual conditioning of light and darkness, within this wondrous perfection, the clarity is adhered to and the faculty of seeing is produced;

this passage consists of twenty lines. When one sense-organ is brought to rest and restored, all six functions cease to function as such. This verse summarizes the preceding prose: "Now, if you enter deeply through even one door, and entering that one, there is no delusion, then those six faculties of cognition will simultaneously become pure. And so it is with the Tathāgata now...

Day. If one were to completely release [the bonds], and if the knots do not arise, then there would be neither "this" nor "that. Since they could not even be called "one," how could "six" be established? (All are long and broad; the verse is abbreviated). (5. Contemplating the accomplishment of benefit, part two). (1. Briefly clarifying the stages of contemplation).

Dust and defilements vanish as soon as they are thought of; one achieves perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrous clarity. When remaining traces of dust are still perceived by the various faculties, once clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata.

[Commentary] If even a single faculty is restored, dust and defilements vanish of their own accord. As the preceding text states: "Perceptual characteristics constitute dust," and so forth, up to "should..."

At that time, [the qualities] are clear and pure; thus it is said to be "perfected, luminous, pure, and wondrous. This refers to the perfect manifestation of the three virtues (triguṇa), which are neither vertical nor horizontal, nor merely listed side by side;

therefore, they are called "wondrous" (miao). The latter two phrases establish the stage [of fruition], while the former phrase indicates that the virtue of cessation (prahāṇaguṇa) was not yet perfected.

The latter phrase indicates that the virtues of wisdom are fully perfected; this may be understood through their mutual manifestation (the bracketed commentary marks the conclusion of the stage of cause and effect). Although one at the final mind of the tenth stage is still in the state of a learner (*śaikṣa*), this is because there remains an obstacle to the Buddha-ground.

One contemplates the Dharma-body as if viewing the moon through a fine silk gauze, for the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*) is not yet complete. The following phrase refers to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), which is ultimate enlightenment. (The *He-lun* states: "A Bodhisattva of Pure Mind is called a Body of Enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*) because he has exhausted all subtle functions.

However, because there still exist the subtle marks of the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), he is said to be within the rank of a Bodhisattva. Therefore it is said: 'Other dusts remain, and he is still a learner. If one were free from the karmic consciousness, nothing would be visible; this is called the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.)

Therefore it is said: "When clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata. (△ [Wenling says: "Subtle delusions not yet exhausted are called 'remaining dust. Partial realization not yet perfected is called 'the various learners' (śaikṣas). ○ [My private opinion: When the defilements of dust vanish upon the mere thought [of them], one achieves perfect, bright, pure, and wondrousness.

This verse summarizes the prose section: "Conditioned by seeing and caused by light, darkness becomes non-seeing. If clarity arises spontaneously from within, then all appearances of darkness can never again obscure. Since the faculties and their objects have already dissolved, how could enlightened clarity fail to become perfectly wondrous? It further states: "If one abandons birth..."

Extinction. Abiding in the true and eternal, the constant light manifests before you. The faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind will, in due time, dissolve away. Conceptualization and appearances are the dust; cognitive attachment is the grime. When both are left far behind, your Dharma-eye will, in due time, become clear and bright. How could you then fail to achieve unsurpassed wisdom? "Remaining traces of dust belong to those still in training;

when clarity reaches its peak, one is a Tathāgata. This verse summarizes the preceding prose. It is like settling turbid water by placing it in a quiet vessel: if the vessel is deep and undisturbed, the sand and soil will naturally sink, and the pure water will appear before you. This is called...

This serves as the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*). Just as removing the mud results in pure water, it is called the "permanent severance of fundamental ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*). When the aspect of clarity is refined and pure, all transformations and manifestations no longer constitute afflictions; they are all in accord with *nirvāṇa* and its pure, wondrous virtues.
(Section Two: A Detailed Demonstration of the Gate of Contemplation)
O Great Assembly and Ānanda: Turn back the mechanism of your inverted hearing; by reversing this hearing to hear your own intrinsic nature, that nature will perfect the Unsurpassed Way.
Such is the true nature of Perfect Penetration.

[Commentary]: This exhorts one to turn back the inverted faculty of hearing and reflect upon the nature of hearing itself. When the nature of hearing is perfected, Bodhi may be hoped for. (Wenling says:

"To be able to revolve away from inverted delusions and return to hear one's own nature must rely upon this very nature to achieve the Unsurpassed Way. The final phrase concludes by forming the seal of realization. △ [Zongjing]:
From time immemorial, all have taken sound to be hearing and thereby given rise to inversion. Now, by means of...
Sound constitutes the text. When the mind turns away from itself to pursue external objects, is this not the mechanism of inverted hearing?

If one can reverse the flow of the sound-dust and restore the non-delusive nature of the fundamental essence, then one is returning the hearing to self-nature, attaining the root and returning to the source.

Internally, the obscured faculties are extinguished; externally, the realms of sensory objects are dissolved. When both subject and object are liberated, the path of original enlightenment is perfected.

Quiescent illumination is perfectly penetrating; such is the reality. (The "Pointer" states: Through hearing, reflecting, and cultivating, one perceives the nature. This seals the realization of Avalokiteśvara. (△ [Supplement]: "Hearing back" means not following after sensory objects. To hear one's own nature...)

"Take the very nature of hearing as that which is heard; the capacity to hear is itself contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Why not simply hear this hearing? It is the same. (○ [My Commentary]: This one verse is Mañjuśrī’s response to the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.

Having completed the discernment of the sense-faculties, he proclaims it to Ānanda and the great assembly as words of exhortation to encourage practice. The following three verses specifically indicate a single gate and extensively clarify the bestowal of grace, winding around and reinforcing the point to complete the body of the first verse.

(○ The verse says: "Reverse your inverted mechanism of hearing, and turn back the hearing to hear your own nature. This verse corresponds to the prose: "By using stillness to reverse the false, extinguishing birth and returning to original enlightenment," and "Reversing that beginningless flow of delusive karma, one attains the circulation of perfect penetration," etc. It also corresponds to the section on contemplation.)

The sounds that were spoken are known and seen to revolve and return; viewing and hearing revolve and return. Viewing and hearing return inward; the sound ceases and perfect hearing remains. Dust is eliminated and clarity revolves; form is dissolved and hearing is restored. Thus one attains the fundamental root of perfect penetration and opens the wondrous gateway of the ear.

The previous passage said, "one must use a single mechanism to extract [the essence]"; this passage says, "revolve your inverted hearing-mechanism. "Extracting the mechanism" is a metaphor; "revolving the mechanism" is the dharma. It is precisely this single mechanism that is manifested both as dharma and metaphor within the verse. "The nature accomplishes the unsurpassed Way"—this is a verse summarizing the prose section, based upon it.

It does not arise; it is the perfection of the nature of perfect stillness. When your current faculties are completely uprooted, they will become internally brilliant and emit light. Thus, these ephemeral phenomena and the vessel-world, along with all their changing appearances, will—like ice melting in hot water—be transformed by a mere thought.

"Unsurpassed Enlightenment. The various passages above are for the most part extensive and detailed, whereas the verses are concise; they are likewise explicit in prose but implicit in verse. The single phrase "Perfect Penetration is truly thus" was judged by the ancients to be the "sealing of the finger-print.

I [Mong] maintain that "sealing the fingers" refers to sealing the eighteen realms. As for the text regarding "how one attains perfect penetration," "sealing it into form" refers specifically to sealing it into the gateway of the ear. This is the meaning of the true reality of "perfection. Mañjuśrī received this mandate to select the faculties, and its essential principles are truly all gathered herein.
(The four verses command the selection and announce the completion—part three). ([卍@○] One: Concluding and Manifesting the Common Realization).
This is the path to nirvana for countless buddhas; All Tathāgatas of the past have already perfected this gate.
All Bodhisattvas of the present now each enter its perfect clarity;
All practitioners of the future shall rely upon this very dharma. I, too, have realized it through this— not only Avalokiteśvara.
[Commentary]: The first two lines generally indicate that all Buddhas attain *nirvāṇa* through this very gate. The section beginning with "The past...
specifically enumerates the three periods of time and cites Mañjuśrī, all of whom provide testimony to this same point. [Explanatory Note]:

In this Sahā world, one realizes the nature of quiescence through the three types of wisdom—listening, reflection, and cultivation. The Tathāgatas of the three periods transcend by means of this single gate; those of the future shall likewise realize it. (2. Accomplishment of the Rebirth Vow).

Truly, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has asked me about various skillful means to save those in the final age who seek to transcend the world and achieve the mind of nirvana—Avalokiteśvara is the foremost among them.
All other skillful means are the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha; they involve abandoning diligent effort through immediate realization rather than long-term cultivation and study.
[The Buddha] preaches the Dharma for both the shallow and the deep.

[Commentary: The first four lines praise the Buddha’s instruction to select [the appropriate teaching]; the latter two lines directly indicate the Perfect Gate (*yuanmen*), clearly showing it to be the most elegant and fitting.
The remaining five lines clarify that the twenty-four sages each followed the specific circumstances and characteristics of their respective causes.
The accomplishment of these contemplative practices is entirely due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which employs skillful means (*upāya*) to enable them to attain the Way;
it is not a matter of long-term cultivation and study. This is a Dharma-gate into which both those of shallow and deep capacities may enter together.

By contrast, this reveals that the [contemplation of] Avalokiteśvara is precisely a Dharma-gate for both those of shallow and deep capacities to enter together through shared teaching and shared realization, a path of long-term cultivation and study. (Wenling says: "It is the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power that bestows its grace.")

This causes one to abandon diligent effort regarding what is already one's own task; it is not a teaching that is practiced from beginning to end, nor one where the shallow and the deep are explained as the same. For example, Nārada lost his sight and then regained it; Piliṅga felt the prick of thorns and cast off his body; and Mahāsthāmaprāpta waited for the Buddha to dissolve his dust. All these were merely their own tasks. [Private Commentary]:
From this point—"These are the Nirvāṇa-gates of countless Buddhas"—there follow three verses in total. These represent Mañjuśrī receiving the mandate to discern the faculties of the assembly.

Once the selection was completed and the thematic gates established, he then proclaimed the Buddha’s decree to Ānanda and the great assembly, extending it to future generations. He responded with meticulous detail and paid reverent homage, thereby forming a clear text of taking refuge. It does not definitively belong to the *geya* (repetitive verse) category, nor does it definitively belong to the *udāna* (isolated verse) category.

This must correspond to the prose section. Previously, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions spoke with one voice to Ānanda, saying: "That which causes you to revolve in birth and death is the root of the fetters; it is solely your six faculties.

That which enables you to swiftly realize peace, liberation, tranquility, and wondrous permanence is also these six faculties. The World-Honored One spoke this verse to personally bear witness: "The Bhagavāns of the ten directions / Have but one path to the gate of Nirvāṇa. Now, Mañjuśrī concludes his exhortation by first citing this verse.

By clarifying the revolving flow of the auditory nature, this single gateway of perfect penetration is the supreme jewel-seal of all the Buddha-microdusts. In the three periods of time, those of the past and future have practiced it together; in the present, they have realized it simultaneously from within it. The Buddhas extensively expound it to deliver sentient beings.

I shall also reiterate this to repay my master’s command. The verse says: "Truly as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has inquired of me regarding various skillful means to save those of the final age, seeking those who transcend the world through long-term practice. Thus it is said: "The World-Honored One takes pity on Ānanda."

Furthermore, those among this assembly who are still in training shall also serve as the cause for transcending the world and as the eyes for all future sentient beings. Thus, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has inquired of me regarding skillful means;

such was his compassionate intent. Therefore, I did not dare fail to report with thorough and careful deliberation. As for the accomplishment of the mind of nirvana, Avalokiteśvara is supreme. This is why I now wish to cause Ānanda to attain awakening. Among the twenty-five practices, which one corresponds to his faculties?

Moreover, after my parinirvāṇa, for the sentient beings of this realm who enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle and seek the unsurpassed path, by what door of skillful means can they easily achieve success? Regarding all other skillful means, even down to the shallow and deep, I have spoken of them in the same five phrases of the Dharma. This is why I now report to you.

Observe this: the twenty-five great Bodhisattvas beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and the Arhats each spoke of their initial expedient means for attaining the Way, all declaring that they had cultivated true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). In their respective practices, there was truly no distinction of superior or inferior, nor of priority or sequence. Someone asked:

"The Buddha said there is truly no superiority or inferiority, yet the verse states that Avalokiteśvara is the most excellent. Since the stages and positions are clearly distinct, how can these two statements be reconciled? The answer is: By means of the expedient of the ear-faculty, one achieves *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, it is said that Avalokiteśvara is supreme; this does not mean he is supreme among all the sages. This is spoken in terms of his causal practice, such as the twenty-five wheels of the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Yuánjué*). When the net of contemplations is interlaced, the twenty-four other sages are designated as being arranged in single, double, or intersecting patterns.

To designate Avalokiteśvara as the "Perfect Cultivation of Wish-Fulfilling Attainment" (Ruyi Yuanshu) is because his realization of the pure *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfectly accomplished nature) is identical [to that of others]. Why then is he called the "Supreme"? If we speak in terms of the stages (*bhūmi*), Samantabhadra is the eldest son and Mañjuśrī is the youngest son;

Samantabhadra is the Chief Minister (*upasthāyaka*), and Avalokiteśvara is also the Chief Minister. Master Kumārajīva said: "The relative scale of Maitreya and Vimalakīrti cannot be definitively fixed. How, then, can one say he is supreme? Even by way of inference (*anumāna*), the various sages say:

"If I am the superior, then Avalokiteśvara is the highest among the superior. The sages say: "He is the foremost," yet Avalokiteśvara is the foremost within the foremost. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions all speak of the mutual interdependence of principal and attendant figures; there is no virtuous friend within the Dharma-realm who does not extol the excellence of another.

In this assembly of the Dharma of equality, what superiority or inferiority can there be? Mañjuśrī, I fear that many in the world will engage in mere intellectual speculation, recklessly assigning value and rank. Therefore, following the conclusion of the verses of praise, he again demonstrates the method of discernment and inclusion.

Thus it is said: "All other skillful means are the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power. This is because each of the sages achieved their own skillful means and entered the Perfect Penetration; all were taught by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power to enter samādhi through the faculty of hearing. Furthermore, it is said: "To abandon worldly toil through the very phenomena at hand is not a matter of long-term cultivation.

This is because when the sages resolved their minds and awakened to the eighteen realms as skillful means for perfect penetration, they abandoned the worldly toil of accumulated kalpas through the phenomena immediately present before them. This is unlike those of partial views and dull faculties, who exhaust themselves in strenuous effort over a long duration.

Because they practice and study, there are degrees of depth and shallowness based on the distance of their stage of cultivation; there are degrees of depth and shallowness based on the thickness or thinness of their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); there are degrees of depth and shallowness based on the loftiness or lowliness of their original nature and manifested traces.

Whether one has long been steeped in much lust or has realized emptiness as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there are degrees of depth and shallowness. Whether one was dull-witted at hearing half a verse or possessed eloquence throughout vast eons, there are degrees of depth and shallowness.

Nevertheless, they all equally awaken to the fundamental mind, equally attain samādhi, equally enter the gate of perfection, and equally proclaim the wondrous Dharma; this is what is meant by "dragons and elephants galloping together" or "oxen and sheep crossing the ford side by side. Now, the passage from "the other various skillful means" onwards is a separate selection of the twenty-four sages. First, it says: "Excluding the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, the other faculties..."

Those who entered through the Perfect Penetration (yuan-tong) did so entirely through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and skillful means (upāya), which enabled them to attain the Way. Yet, none of them said, "I thought the Tathāgata would bestow this samādhi upon me," nor did any say, "Although the Buddha has clarified it for me, I am still unable to turn back [from delusion].

Since these skillful means must be carefully distinguished, why is it called "Perfect Penetration"? Furthermore, if other faculties have already entered into Perfect Penetration, why should they be singled out again? On one hand, it is said that regarding the matters of the other faculties and sense objects, although one may abandon worldly afflictions (rajas), this is not specifically suited to the spiritual capacities of those in this land;

it is not a dharma-gate for long-term cultivation and study, nor is it a teaching spoken for both the shallow and the deep. As for the argument concerning the suitability of this land, this has been extensively refuted above. Now, as for the claim that other faculties can abandon worldly afflictions, what prevents them from being suitable for long-term cultivation and study? This is precisely the case in the Sahā world.

To follow the flow of the turning [of the Dharma wheel]—how could this not be to adapt to the capacities of beings? By using that [verse] to distinguish faculties and refute compliance with the [specific] lands, one likewise loses ground whether advancing or retreating; it is a matter where the adversary will inevitably be exhausted. This verse distinguishes and gathers [beings]; truly, it is no minor teaching. I hope that regarding this gate there shall be no delusion.

It is not that I dare to refute or disparage the ancient masters, but rather to guide the blind and open the ignorant; I respectfully require the guidance of a master of the Dharma. (3. Request for Further Proclamation and Exhortation)
I prostrate to the Tathāgatagarbha, Untainted and inconceivable. May you grant your empowerment so that those in the future May have no delusions regarding this gateway;
May it be easily accomplished through skillful means, Fit to be taught to Ānanda And to those sinking in the final age.
If one cultivates solely with this faculty, Its perfect penetration will surpass all others— Such is the true mind.
[Commentary: The Tathāgatagarbha is the Three Jewels in their essential unity; it is the principle to be entered, for it is fully endowed with untainted (anāsrava) intrinsic merits.
May he add the following five phrases as a formal conclusion of the vow. However, with the final two phrases, he exhorts [the practitioner] to study.
The very last phrase indicates that Mañjuśrī has himself selected the mind of perfect penetration (yuan-tong), which is true and without delusion, for it is not constrained by emotional attachments.

(Wenling says: "This is the essential core of the true reality; it is simply this. (Haiyin says: "Please add [the following]. It is appropriate to petition the Buddha alone. Now, prostrating to the Tathāgatagarbha refers to the Dharma.

The Tathāgatagarbha is the secret treasury of the three virtues, where the three bodies are perfectly realized and the Three Jewels are perfectly complete. It is called 'inconceivable' because its single essence is untainted. By merely prostrating to this Dharma, the three bodies and the Three Jewels are all fully present. (My own view: The end of this verse returns to the words of petitioning for the addition [of the following], embodying the Buddha's compassion.)

This is especially so in the final age, when heterodox sects arise in chaotic competition; their perverse words delude the orthodox, and demonic sophistry mimics the true. Since spurious accounts are numerous and those who follow such currents are many, if one does not discern and differentiate them, they will hinder correct cultivation. Consequently, although all ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) are able to practice meditation (*dhyāna*), they lack the virtue of the precepts. Therefore, the Buddha spoke extensively on this. If anyone says that it is permitted to keep the eight impure things, this is the teaching of Māra. External objects are not even permitted to be kept, let alone sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, lying, and the fundamental afflictions of greed and hatred. Alas! The following text extensively refutes these views, identifying them all as the works of Māra; therefore, the Buddha issued this profound warning. This is called the definitive teaching of the Mahāyāna that brings clear understanding.

Ānanda, a master of great expedient means, took pity on those of the future who would surely fall into the perils of Māra, and thus earnestly made this request as a perpetual and true admonition. [Commentary]: These sentient beings have inferior faculties; this is the deficiency of their capacity. They are gradually moving further away from the Buddha; this is the deficiency of the time. Teachers of false doctrines abound; this is the abundance of obstacles.

Wisdom is like a skilled physician who perfectly matches medicine to the disease. "By relying on these precepts, one attains various meditative concentrations and the wisdom that extinguishes suffering. By being able to protect the sense organs, meditative concentration arises; from the arising of meditative concentration, wisdom arises; and one thereby reaches the path of the Buddha. The precepts serve to check the coarse, while meditation serves to gather the subtle."

Precepts restrain the body and speech; dhyāna stills the distracted mind. It is like a person ascending a roof: without a ladder, they cannot climb up. Without the ladder of precepts, dhyāna likewise cannot be established. For one who has broken the precepts, the winds of the fetters (saṃyojana) are powerful and scatter their mind; thus, dhyāna cannot be attained.

For one who upholds the precepts, the winds of affliction are light and the mind does not scatter greatly; thus, meditative concentration (dhyāna) is easily attained. Furthermore, one who upholds the precepts contemplates the characteristics of these precepts: from what do they arise? They all arise from various transgressions. If there were no such transgressions, [the precepts would have no basis].

Thus, there is no [inherent] precept; the characteristic of the precept is such that it arises from causes and conditions. By means of this, one awakens the mind so as not to give rise to attachment—this is what constitutes upholding the precepts. It gives birth to the *prajñāpāramitā*.

For one who does not uphold the precepts, even if they possess sharp intelligence, their faculty of wisdom gradually becomes dull due to being occupied with worldly affairs. It is like a sharp blade used to cut mud; it consequently becomes a blunt instrument. If one leaves the household life to uphold the precepts and does not engage in worldly occupations, constantly contemplating that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is signless (*animitta*), then although one’s faculties were previously dull, they will gradually become sharp.
Since the two gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) have already been explained, this accords with the Vinaya and speaks of the eternal, identical to *nirvāṇa*.

[Commentary] The four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) benefit others by performing various transformations. First, one brings them onto the same path; later, one encourages them toward the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*).

All of this is for the sake of benefiting others, not out of greed for personal gain. [The *Shiyao* says: "The four means of attraction are: first, giving (*dāna*), which uses the two types of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—to cause others to attach themselves to oneself; second, kind speech (*priyavāditā*), which uses gentle and compliant words..."

To console those who receive the Way; the three types of beneficial conduct; benefiting others through the three karmas to inspire reverence; and the fourth, "common purpose," by assuming various forms to engage in their activities—such is the true sage’s benefit for beings, ultimately unfathomable.
Because one upholds the Buddha’s regulations, one must not recklessly divulge this. This is the cause of the true sage, which is realized only by the sage themselves;
therefore, it is called the "secret cause. Before one has studied it, it must not be spoken of lightly. As for those to whom it was secretly entrusted, its name is not made manifest.

This also refers to the secret indications made at the end of life, such as when Guṇabhadra used his fingers to count [the remaining years] and left instructions to his disciples (as Mount Gu Mountain said:

"It was not to publicly delude the masses, but merely to show it privately to others. This is precisely what is meant by Nanyue’s mention of the 'iron wheel,' Dushun’s indication of Mañjuśrī, Guṇavarman’s recitation of the verse, and Master Zhiguan’s counting of his fingers).
([│/○] Fourth: An Exhortation to Rely on the Teachings and Firmly Maintain Them).
You shall instruct the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, and subsequently eliminate all great false claims; this is called being a Tathāgata.
The former Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have established the fourth definitive and pure instruction:
(1) [The fifth point: Reprimanding the transgression of false speech; resulting in two losses]; (2) [The first point: Summoning the fruit of falsehood].
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever this great falsehood, it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood and hoping for its fragrance;
such a thing is impossible.

[Commentary]: This is like carving sandalwood—the essence of meditative concentration—into the excrement of a person who utters falsehoods. From afar, it may appear pleasing to the eye; yet upon close approach, its foul odor is offensive.
Those who seek the fragrance of the Way will ultimately find no means to attain it. (This second point destroys their upright cause.)
I teach the bhikṣus that the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is the straightforward mind; even within the four modes of deportment and all actions, there must be no pretense whatsoever.

(As the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra says: "The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment, because it is free from pretense. How then can you claim for yourself to have attained the dharmas of a superior person?
(3) [? (▽/○) Thus one incurs its evil retribution.
For example, it is like a destitute person who falsely claims to be an emperor and brings about his own execution; how much more so for a Dharma King—how could one falsely usurp his throne?
If the ground is not upright, the fruit will be crooked. To seek the Buddha’s Bodhi under such conditions is like a person trying to bite their own navel; who can achieve success?

[Commentary] That which is realized by the Three Vehicles constitutes the "Dharma of Superior Persons. This passage uses the shallow to illustrate the profound; it refers to other minor instances of false speech.

It is not even possible to do so; how much less so for a great falsehood? This is illustrated by the following analogies. The first metaphor concerns great falsehood, which merely establishes the root of suffering.

The subsequent metaphor concerns the seeking of the Way, which ultimately lacks the principle of attainment. It is like a person biting their own navel; they can never reach it. The *Spring and Autumn Annals* states:

"If one does not plan early on, later one will bite one's navel" (Du Yu’s commentary says: "Biting the navel" is a metaphor for that which cannot be reached). [Master Min says: This metaphor illustrates that seeking Bodhi is likewise impossible.

Regarding "and also" (及也): [My opinion is that] the *Tiantong Song* says, "Wisdom is difficult to know; it is like gnawing at a bone. The commentary states: "It does not reach it. Where wisdom does not arrive, wisdom cannot know. Interpreting the text according to this, there is indeed reason for it.

(○ [Commentary on the Text]: "The ground is not straight. Only the Changshui edition reads "not straight" (不直); other ancient editions all read "not true" (不真). [My opinion is that] the scripture above says, "I teach the bhikṣus: the straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment," and below it says, "If the minds of the bhikṣus are like a straight bowstring.

Therefore, following the character "straight" (直) is correct. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the three samādhis, saying: "In the language of Qin, it means the place where the upright mind practices. This mind has been constantly crooked and unupright since beginningless time; once one attains this place of practice for the upright mind, the mind then becomes upright.")

Straightness. For example, just as a snake’s movement is always crooked, yet it becomes straight when entering a bamboo tube, so too is the "straight mind" the site of the Way (*mārga-kṣetra*), the entry into *samādhi*, and the true Dharma-gate.

When the Tathāgata first instructed Ānanda, he taught that the Buddhas of the three periods of time all rely on a straight mind to transcend birth and death. His earnest entrustment of this matter to the bhikṣus here has a profound reason. (The sixth seal: completing the precept against stealing).
If bhikṣus have minds as straight as a bowstring, are entirely truthful, and enter samādhi, they will forever be free from demonic interference.
I certify that such persons shall achieve the unsurpassed awakening of a bodhisattva.
[Commentary: At all times, to be entirely free from falsehood is the true pursuit of the Way; how could one not arrive swiftly?
If one displays signs and assumes a form, falsely claiming to have attained the Way, harboring flattery and crookedness within while scheming for fame without—how can this be called cultivation?

Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says: "In this defiled age, there will be evil bhikṣus with perverted wisdom and crooked minds; those who have not attained [realization] claim to have attained it, their hearts filled with arrogance.
Even those who wear patched robes while dwelling in open spaces, falsely calling themselves forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka)—you should know that such as these are entirely engaged in the works of Māra."

The four stages mentioned above are called the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). They are abandoned through nine grades, each having its own degree of depth. Therefore, one shares one's body, flesh, bones, and blood with all sentient beings; this is the abandonment of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Demonstrating "one who returns once more" (*sakṛdāgāmin*), having gone and not returning again, is the abandonment of attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). It is said: Regarding the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of a *srotāpanna*, this refers to the delusion of dependent origination and the delusion of the characteristics of the body. Once the view of a self-body is severed, craving does not arise. Why, then, would one not take up the precepts?

It is because one clearly perceives the characteristics of the modes of rebirth. How is the mark of doubt severed? It is by not giving rise to the view of another as a Great Master regarding what is pure or impure; thus one knows that the four grave offenses are all suppressed and severed upon the stages (*bhūmi*).

Stating the Intent and Briefly Explaining the Four [Points]). ([○@卍] 1. A General Summary of the Previous Text).
Ānanda, as you ask about the gathering of the mind, I shall first explain the sublime gateway for training in the entry into samādhi.
One who seeks the Bodhisattva path must first maintain these four kinds of restraint, as pure as ice and frost, so that not even a single branch or leaf of transgression can arise.
The three of the mind—greed, anger, and false views—and the four of the mouth—false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech—will have no cause to arise. Ānanda, it is thus.
Regarding the four matters: if one does not lose them, the mind will not even take as its object form, sound, smell, taste, or touch; how then could any demonic activities arise?
[Commentary] Precepts are the fundamental basis for correctly conforming to liberation. Relying upon these precepts, one attains concentration and wisdom; thus it is known.
Samādhi takes precepts as its precursor. Although these grave prohibitions are formulated in terms of body and speech, each one actually governs the mind.

Since they correspond with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), form, sound, smell, taste, and touch are none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*). How, then, could there be demonic activities to disturb the practitioner? (The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states:

"Although the categories of precepts are many, they are subsumed into three groups: first, the restraint of conduct; second, the cultivation of roots of goodness; and third, the benefiting of sentient beings. As for the precept of restraining conduct, it refers to the ten inexhaustible [precepts].")

To speak in summary, although there are ten grave precepts (*śīla*), they are essentially comprised of four: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech. When these four are purified, none of the secondary branches will arise. The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "Although all ten precepts constitute paths of karma (*karmapatha*), these four increase most significantly in their obstruction of the Noble Path; therefore, they are specifically restricted within the monastic precepts.

Now, wishing to cultivate the wisdom of untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā-jñāna*), one takes morality and meditative concentration as the vanguard; for this reason, the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) specifically singles out these four precepts. Among the Śrāvaka precepts, the remaining four sections and six groups [of offenses] are likewise included.

All [the precepts] serve to protect these four; therefore, it is said that "branches and leaves do not grow. (△[Commentary on the Perfuming of Hearing] states: The four *pārājika* offenses are like the roots, while the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and other offenses are like branches and leaves. The former refers to the breaking of precepts, which destroys one's wholesome roots, and is metaphorically likened to cutting down a *tāla* tree with a sword.

The present passage refers to the upholding of precepts, which extinguishes the source of evil; hence it says that "all branches and leaves do not grow. The three mental [transgressions] and four verbal ones constitute the substance of the *saṃghāvaśeṗa* and other karmic actions, and they also encompass the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) and subsequent stages (*prstha*) of the four *pārājika* offenses.

However, as for the delusions arising simultaneously with greed, hatred, and ignorance, there is no means to subdue and sever them except through meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Here, we speak only in terms of those [offenses] common to the remaining categories, as this merely stops their coarse manifestations. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Precepts are like catching a thief; concentration..."

Wisdom is like the executioner who slays the thief. One should know that the three obstacles are all called "thieves. They are captured by the observance of precepts; they reside within karmic retribution, with afflictions as their secondary accompaniment. (2. Exhortation to Recite Divine Mantras)

If there are those whose past habitual tendencies cannot be extinguished or eliminated, you should instruct such people to single-mindedly recite my supreme divine mantra, the *Mahā-sitātapatra* (Eight Characters;
this translates as "Great White Parasol"), which is the Tathāgata himself.
The mark of the invisible crown; the Buddha of the unconditioned mind. Emanating from the crown, he sits upon a precious lotus flower. The heart-mantra he proclaims is as follows:

[Commentary] Although it was previously explained at length that one’s observance of the precepts is pure, as clear as ice and frost, such that one creates no new karma and has already distanced oneself from the heavy burden of Māra, there still remain the habitual tendencies of beginningless time—defilements and obstructions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—which follow the body like a shadow and stand as obstacles to the Path.
For a practitioner, there are obstacles at all times; these may be frequent illnesses and afflictions, excessive lust and anger, encountering false teachers, or being disturbed by demons.
When such various difficulties arise in competition, they are all due to unwholesome karmic causes from beginningless time.
The seeds of unwholesome thoughts and karma permeate the manifesting consciousness and constantly act as enemies to the Right Path.
For beginners who have newly begun their practice, the power of the Path is weak and they are unable to dispel these obstacles;

therefore, the Buddha possesses a sublime divine mantra that can extinguish the evil habits of past lives, ensuring no further affliction, so that the power of the Path may be swiftly perfected without encountering retreat or discouragement. The previously mentioned concentration and wisdom [are what] destroy...
Regarding the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it was previously clarified that the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) merely stops sinful karma.

Now, the divine mantra is taught; it can destroy past calamities and simultaneously eliminate the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). If these two obstacles are truly eliminated, what need is there to wait for realization? [The *Shiyao* says: "Holding the precepts only obstructs present karma.

If there are calamities from beginningless enmity or past transgressions, one cannot dispel them. Or if they arise within meditative concentration, even the three methods for subduing demons cannot exempt one. Only by establishing a ritual site (*maṇḍala*), holding mantras, and prostrating to the Buddha can these be remedied through other power. [The *Wenling* says: ...

Present karma is easy to restrain; one’s own current conduct can be altered. However, long-standing habits are difficult to eliminate and necessarily rely upon spiritual power (*ṛddhi*). Now, as for practitioners who prefer what is correct yet remain firmly attached to the perverse, who desire purity yet are stained by bias—acting without being taught and doing so without wishing—it is as if there is something secretly driving them that they cannot stop themselves from doing;

this is the influence of past habits. Where virtue is exalted yet blessings are meager, where one practices goodness yet suffers misfortune, and where obstacles and grievances abound, with frequent illness and distress—a state that persists as if bound by a mechanism that cannot be released of its own accord—this is summoned by past habits.

This is not a condition arising from the causes of a single lifetime or a single kalpa, but rather that which has been perfumed moment after moment since beginningless time. Therefore, were it not for spiritual power, one could not be liberated. *Mahā* and so forth; here [in Chinese] it is translated as...

The Great White Parasol is precisely the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna). (△ [Xunwen says: Regarding "past habits": in general discourse, this refers to all afflictions and karmas, such as the four grave offenses; in specific discourse, it refers to the habit of sexual misconduct. Below, it specifically points to Ānanda and Dēngqiā.

The habit of affectionate attachment is countered by placing the Fire-Head Vajra within the ritual chamber to counteract greed. (△ [Rongshi says: The emanated Buddha atop the World-Honored One’s crown is no different from the Dharmakāya;
therefore, he is called the "unconditioned mind-Buddha. Since the mind-Buddha is formless, what crown could be seen? ([○@卍] Third, pointing out the efficacy).
Moreover, your karmic conditions with Matangi over successive kalpas and the habitual tendencies of your affectionate attachment are not the result of a single lifetime or a single kalpa alone.
As soon as I proclaimed this, you were forever liberated from your love and became an Arhat—even you, who were once a courtesan.
"Practicing without conscious effort, you were secretly sustained by spiritual power and quickly realized the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).

How could it be difficult for you, Śrāvakas currently in office, to seek the Supreme Vehicle and resolve to attain Buddhahood? It would be like raising a handful of dust in a favorable wind—what difficulty or danger could there be?"
[Commentary: Tiṅga previously suffered from a chronic affliction of lust; that she has now attained freedom from desire constitutes the severing of the obstacle of karmic afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

That she was manifest as a courtesan but has now attained the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) constitutes the transformation of the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). Even one who lacks the intention to practice can still attain the fruit of sainthood upon encountering this divine mantra;
how much more so for one who aspires to the path of supreme enlightenment and practices with resolve? Through the empowerment of the mantra’s power, [this is achieved].

What hardships and perils exist that one would not go there? (According to the *Maṇḍārava-avadāna* and other sūtras concerning the causes and conditions of Gaṅgā’s past lives, these are fully detailed in the various sūtras concerning the maiden Maṇḍārava of the Hīnayāna. (4. A brief indication of the method for upholding [the practice], part two.)

(1. Showing the Ritual Practice) If there are those in the final age who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they must first observe the pure prohibitions and precepts of a *bhikṣu*.
They should specifically select one whose precepts are pure, a foremost *śramaṇa*, to serve as their teacher. If they do not encounter a truly pure monk, [they should proceed otherwise].
Your observance of the precepts will certainly not be perfected. Once the precepts have been accomplished, don new, clean robes, burn incense, and dwell in seclusion.
Recite this divine mantra spoken by the Mind-Buddha one hundred and eight times, and thereafter perform the ritual of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) and establish the site of practice (*maṇḍala*).
One should pray that the unsurpassed Tathāgatas currently dwelling in the lands throughout the ten directions will emit rays of great compassionate light and descend to anoint one’s crown.
[Commentary] If one’s observance of the precepts is incomplete, the five conditions are lacking; how much more so when acting as a teacher or model to transmit them to others?
If one’s own precepts are impure, how can the precepts of others be established? Therefore, one must select a foremost, pure, and authentic bestower of the precepts. Thus it is said.
According to the Brahmajāla Sūtra, if within a thousand li there is no preceptor to bestow the precepts, one should receive them through a self-vow before the Buddha.

First, one must repent for the seven grave offenses; thereafter, one seeks the dharma of the precepts. Only when auspicious signs are seen does one know that the offenses have been extinguished and the precepts obtained;

otherwise, they are not obtained. Once the precepts are fully accomplished, one should dwell in a quiet and secluded place, burning incense and reciting mantras until the count reaches one hundred and eight. By doing so...
The ritual tableaus eliminate the one hundred and eight afflictions. Through internal precepts and external mantras, demons are prevented from arising;

for fear they might obstruct the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), one must first thus seek the Buddhas currently residing therein. When their light shines upon and empowers [the practitioner], the mind attains valor, and progress on the Path becomes even more rapid. (Note:

If the practitioner’s past habitual tendencies have not yet been forgotten, and although they believe and understand the aforementioned methods, their obstacles remain heavy and their minds distracted, they must enter the ritual site (*maṇḍala*). They should select a preceptor to restrain themselves. When the conditions are strong and the environment superior, then the efficacy [of the practice] will manifest.)

The power of practice is great. (△ [Wuxing says: The precepts currently maintained should encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. If one is a renunciant, beyond the inherent purity of the essence of the precepts (*śīla-samvara*), one must maintain meticulous purity; furthermore, by receiving the Bodhisattva vows (*bodhisattva-śīla*), one further increases one's goodness.

If one is a layperson, whether they have previously received the Upāsaka precepts or have only received the Bodhisattva precepts, they may advance from these lower levels in their cultivation. This is because there are lay practitioners.

It is appropriate. However, according to the Hīnayāna, offenses have degrees of gravity; light ones may be repented, while heavy ones cannot. If one commits a heavy offense, one is a dead man in the Buddha-dharma.
Yet, according to the Mahāyāna, repentance is permitted, as explained in the section on the four kinds of samādhis). (2. Explaining Response and Resonance)

Ānanda, in such a Dharma-ending age, if a pure bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, or a lay donor (dānapati) extinguishes the mind of greed and lust, upholds the pure precepts of the Buddha, and within a place of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) makes the vows of a bodhisattva;

bathing and entering and exiting [the hall], they practice the Way during the six periods [of the day] and the six periods [of the night]. Thus remaining sleepless for twenty-one days, I shall manifest my own body and appear before that person.

[The Buddha] came forward, rubbed [the practitioner's] head, and comforted them, causing them to attain awakening. [Commentary: By reciting mantras and bestowing empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one gives rise to the aspiration to see the Buddha. When the Buddha manifests his body, it is called a "responsive resonance" (*saṃgati*). If one sees other objects, this deviates from one's original practice; since the event contradicts the aspiration, it is a demonic realm and not a true responsive resonance. Furthermore, *Note on terminology:* * *Adhiṣṭhāna*: Lit. "empowerment" or "blessing," referring to the transformative power bestowed by a Buddha or Bodhisattva. * *Saṃgati*: Lit. "coming together" or "resonance," here specifically denoting the harmonious response between the practitioner's sincere aspiration and the Buddha's compassionate manifestation. * *Māra*: The personification of evil or temptation, often appearing as deceptive visions to obstruct spiritual progress. * *IAST diacritics*: Used for Sanskrit terms such as *adhiṣṭhāna*, *saṃgati*, and *māra*. * *Sanskrit terms translated into English*: "Responsive resonance" translates *saṃgati*; "demonic realm" translates *māra-viṣaya*. * *Proper English translation*: "Furthermore" introduces the subsequent section of the commentary. The structure follows the pattern of defining the correct sign (*samyag-nimitta*) followed by the warning against false signs (*vitatha-nimitta*). The logic emphasizes that the authenticity of the vision depends on its alignment with the practitioner's prior resolve and spiritual discipline. The term "original practice" (*ben-xi*) refers to the specific meditative or ritual context initiated by the practitioner. The phrase "event contradicts the aspiration" (*shi yu yuan wei*) indicates a failure to achieve the intended soteriological goal. The final judgment, "not a true responsive resonance," serves as a definitive criterion for distinguishing authentic Buddhist experience from illusory or obstructive phenomena.*The following is a list If, upon seeing the True and Responsive [Buddhas], one’s mind attains awakening, afflictions become thin and subtle, and wisdom becomes bright and pure, then it is indeed the Buddhas.
However, if because of seeing the Buddhas one remains as dull-witted as before and afflictions instead increase, these are all demonic realms and not true Buddhas.

(As Gushan said: "The Buddha is fundamentally non-existent; he appears because the mind is pure. When water is clear, the moon appears; the response and stimulus are spontaneous. If you see such signs, you should contemplate emptiness and stillness. If it is the Buddha, it will manifest clearly; if it is a demon, it will vanish. (The *Commentary on the Complete Enlightenment Sutra* says: "The sutra states that after twenty-one days...")

As for this, whether the duration be long or short, there is no distinct meaning expressed [by the length itself]. Tiantai applied himself diligently for one hundred days and immediately attained the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*. For the practice of the *Lotus Sūtra* repentance rite (*lǐchàn dàochǎng*), he established the "three-week" period (*sānqī*). For the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*, he further established the hundred-day period.

Within the *Vaipulya* teachings, the minimum is seven days; more than that is not prohibited, but less than that cannot be reduced. Since the texts of various teachings describing the ritual site (*dàochǎng*) differ in the number of days and vary in their ritual procedures (*fǎshì*), how could each of these have a separate underlying significance?
(II. Responding to the Request for an Extensive Explanation) (A. Fully Elucidating the Ritual Methods of the Altar) (1. Inquiry)
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, having received the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Tathāgata, my mind has already been awakened.

I know for myself that I have cultivated and realized the path, and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is accomplished. For those practicing during the Dharma-ending age who establish a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), how should they perform the ritual of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) so as to accord with the pure regulations of the Buddha, the World-Honored One?"

[Commentary: I lived in the time of the Buddha and was personally instructed by him. Having now attained awakening, I already know the methods for cultivation and realization, and shall surely reach the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
For students of the Dharma during the Final Age (*paścimadharma*), one must certainly increase their diligent practice and establish a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

What methods are there to ensure their proper conduct? [The Haiyin commentary says: "In entering the Way and practicing cultivation, the first requirement is the equality of body and mind; the second is the oneness of mind and object. Since the objects that serve as conditions for the causes of karma act as auxiliary factors, one must inquire regarding the rules of conduct."
[This is the] principle. (Section 2: Answering and Explaining. [Section 1: Showing the Method for Establishing the Mandala. Subsection 1: The Dimensions of the Mandala Site].)

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people of the final age wish to establish a site for the Way, they should first take a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains that feeds on the rich, succulent fragrant grasses of those mountains.
This ox drinks only the pure water of the Snowy Mountains; its dung is fine and subtle."
One may take its dung and mix it with sandalwood to plaster the ground. If it is not a cow from the Snowy Mountains, its dung is foul-smelling and unfit for application to the ground;
therefore, one must dig into the soil of a plain at a depth of five feet or more and take the yellow earth from beneath.
The preceptor [prepared] sandalwood, aloeswood, *suhaka*, *kunduruka*, *turushka*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *sāra*, *agaru*, *jātī*, and *kakkola*.
Having finely ground these ten kinds into powder, he mixed them with earth to form a paste, which he used to smear upon the site.
It is sixteen feet in circumference and square, forming an eight-cornered altar.
[Commentary] The milk of the snow mountains is entirely *sarpis* (clarified butter); whatever remains after the curdling process is most fragrant and pure.
One may simply mix it with a single flavor of sandalwood and smear it upon the ground. If this is unavailable, one takes deep soil and adds various [fragrances].
Incense: Ten flavors are blended together to smear upon the ground.

○ [General Explanation of Symbolic Representations] (Wenling says: The Dharma-king’s words of Dharma accord with both phenomena and principle. Phenomena do not arise in isolation, and phenomena have no fixed location. This is like the "Single-Syllable Dharma Gate" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. )

One could write upon the ocean of ink without exhausting it. The characteristics of the five ranks (*pañca-sthāna*) are manifested through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This text is arranged so that they may consult it as a manual in their endeavors. ○ [The White Ox of the Snowy Mountains] (The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "In the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called 'Patience. If an ox eats it, it immediately obtains the *mṛdvīkā* (ghee of the cream). [My personal commentary: The *mṛdvīkā* is a metaphor for Buddha-nature."

This passage states that [the ox] "eats the fatty, fragrant herbs of the mountain," clarifying that it consumes the *kṣānti-grass* (grass of forbearance) and thereby attains the Buddha-nature. (△ [Master Jing said: Water is inferior to fire; when congealed, it forms a high mountain. A mountain is earth; earth is faith.

The Snowy Mountains are vast, and the fragrant herbs and clear water produced therein are a metaphor for great faith. The powerful white ox, pure white and without admixture, though possessing great strength, follows along with sentient beings—this is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna Buddha-nature. The fatty, fragrant herbs are a metaphor for wondrous goodness and purity.)

Water is a metaphor for pure wisdom; excrement is a metaphor for residual defilements. Sandalwood removes heat, brain-wind, and swellings; the arm can eliminate suffering and bring about purity and goodness. The Buddha-nature of the Mahāyāna relies upon vast faith and is nurtured to fulfillment by the sublime goodness of pure wisdom.

That which remains as a residue is not something coarse or foul that can be mixed with; rather, it is pure goodness that, by removing suffering and affliction, bestows [peace] upon sentient beings and solemnly completes the site of the field of nirvana. (The *He lun* states:
"The residual excrement" refers to subtle residual habits. It is mixed with sandalwood in order to cool the heat of afflictions and thereby wash away the excrement of desire.)

However, if one can give rise to the right faith of the Middle Way with a broad and impartial mind, and rely upon these various lands to cultivate pure practices as a skillful means for entering Buddha-nature, this is sufficient to adorn the site of practice.

[The Ten Incenses] (My Commentary): Regarding the ten incenses in this sutra, there are four types of incense used by the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja of the Lotus Sūtra: sandalwood (*candana*), *kunkuma* (frankincense), aloeswood (*agarū*), and resinous incense (*guggulu*).

*Turuṣka* is also used by Bhaiṣajyarāja; according to this sutra, it is boiled with water to bathe the charcoal. In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Incense Merchant has five types: white sandalwood for treating fever, *kunkuma* for treating illness, and so forth, such as aloeswood and sandalwood. There is the "Incense that Produces Joy," and the "Incense that Extinguishes Afflictions" (which is ox-head sandalwood).

As for incenses that increase afflictions, such as orchids and musk, these are not used at the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The reason one must necessarily use various incenses is that "incense" is a name for the removal of impurity, yet it also proclaims fragrance and disperses its sweet aroma.

Regarding the function of spreading fragrance: when the scent of humans reaches the heavens, it rises into the void for four hundred thousand *li*. Although the various heavens are pure, there is none that does not loathe this odor. Yet, because they have received the entrustment to protect the Dharma, even though the Buddha dwells among humans, the various devas dare not fail to come.

Thus, within the Buddha-dharma, incense serves as a means of Buddhist practice (*buddhakārya*). As for why the names of various incenses are listed first in this sutra, Qingliang says: "Knowing the various worldly incenses is to manifest the 'Dharma-incense.

This means that by perfuming and cultivating oneself with the incenses of precepts, concentration, wisdom, compassion, and so forth, one generates goodness and extinguishes evil habits; this is the practice of differentiation. Next, regarding the mention of "blended powders," Qingliang says: "Furthermore, knowing how to harmonize and blend them is the practice of integration. By means of gold...

The *vajra* crushes it; the *prajñāpāramitā* of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) harmonizes it, so that the pure and the mixed are without obstruction. Because compassion and wisdom are perfectly integrated to form the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), "smearing the ground" refers to fragrant ointment (*vilepana*).

It is mixed with water of intrinsic purity. "Adorning the Dharma-body with powder" refers to powdered incense (*cūrṇa*); it is crushed by *vajra*-wisdom to render it devoid of substantiality. "Burning incense" means tempering it with the fire of wisdom to manifest the myriad practices (*sarvacaryā*) throughout all places.

Wang Jiefu and Hong Juefan both likened the ten types of incense to the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*). These are the Dharma-incenses of the ten *pāramitās*. Now, I shall again correlate them with the tenth dedication (*daśama-pariṇāmanā*) from the fifth chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Ten Dedications. Sandalwood (*candana*) is the incense of samādhi; one *zhu* [of it] [intermingles] four...

Ten *li* away is the offering of incense. White resin (*śrīveṣṭaka*) can remove foul odors from the body and heal sores and ailments; it serves as the fragrance of precepts (*śīla-gandha*). Incense-resin (*guggulu*) can alleviate pain; it serves as the fragrance of patience (*kṣānti-gandha*). Blue sandalwood (*sīta-candana*) can awaken those suffering from nightmares; it serves as the fragrance of diligence (*vīrya-gandha*). Turmeric (*kuṅkuma*) removes toxic vapors from the heart, the harm of *gū* and *gui*, and foul odors;

it serves as the fragrance of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-gandha*). *Zerling* (*jātī-phala*) can stop seminal leakage and clarify the eyes; it serves as the fragrance of wisdom (*prajñā-gandha*). Sweet pine (*gaṇḍha-māṃsī*) can harmonize various fragrances and eliminate abdominal distension while regulating the downward-moving qi; it serves as the fragrance of the Dharma (*dharma-gandha*). ○ [The Method for the Square and Circular Altars] 【Commentary】 The eight-cornered altar should be square or circular according to the prescribed measurements.

One prepares it by clearing the ground, and it has no tiered steps; this is what is meant by a *shan* (plain). (To "clear" means to sweep. Zheng says: "An altar (*tan*) is made of piled earth; a plain (*shan*) is made by clearing the ground. The *Guoyu* states:

"The ground cleared for an altar is called a *chang* (field/site). To "raise earth" is synonymous with piling earth. (△ [Wuxing says]: The previous mention of the site refers to a plain (*shan*), which may be as it is. Since it is now called an "altar" (*tan*), one must raise the earth. First, clear the ground to make a field (*chang*); afterwards, separately take yellow earth and mix it with incense.)

On that site, apply mud to raise it up, forming the appearance of a mandala. This is to be placed within the chamber to install the ritual implements. Although the mandala has eight corners, its upper and lower sections make ten, corresponding to the number of the circle.

They manifest mutually and contain one another; this signifies the characteristic of the inconceivable realm of the *tathāgatagarbha* (the Store-Mind).

First, relying upon his teaching (that is, taking the aforementioned monks of pure precepts as one's teachers). Second, the ritual for making offerings (2): First, enumerating the offering implements (1); first, long-term offering implements.
At the center of the altar, place a lotus flower made of gold, silver, copper, or wood. Upon the flower, set a bowl.

Within the bowl, first fill it with dew collected during the eighth month, and within the water, place whatever flowers and leaves are available. Take eight circular mirrors and place each one in its respective direction.
Surrounding the flower bowl, establish sixteen lotus flowers outside the mirror and sixteen incense burners interspersed among the flowers;
these incense burners should be so adorned that the fire is not visible. Take white cow’s milk and place it in sixteen vessels.
Milk cakes, along with various granulated sugars, oil cakes, milk porridge, storax, honey, and ginger;
pure ghee and pure honey—each sixteen [units] outside the lotus, surrounding the flower—to be offered to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
[Commentary: The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not eat this food; rather, they manifest eating it in order to cause merit to increase.
This causes practitioners to become fully endowed with both merit and wisdom, swiftly attaining perfection. It is as when the Buddha accepted Cunda’s final offering.
This causes them to be fully endowed with the *dāna-pāramitā*. This case is also like this; therefore, one must make offerings.

○ [General Explanation of Symbolic Representations] ○ [Lotus at the Center of the Mandala] (〔Haimin says〕: Generally, the lotus represents the causal mind, the mirror represents the essence of wisdom, and incense represents contemplative practice, etc.

〔Wenling says〕: The lotus at the center of the mandala is the wondrous practice of the Middle Way. The lotus fruit and its stem share the same substance; defilement and purity originate from the same source; cause and effect are simultaneous. This symbolizes that the wondrous practice is of one accord. Use gold and silver.)

Regarding "copper and wood": gold and silver, even after a hundred refinements, do not change; copper’s hardness symbolizes *yi* (righteousness), while wood’s covering nature symbolizes *ren* (benevolence). These wondrous practices and deeds converge upon the Middle Way. [Commentary on the Enumeration of Dharmas]: The four flowers symbolize the blossoming flowers of the four wisdoms. [Personal Commentary]: Necklaces and the Ten Wheels symbolize the stages (*bhūmi*).

Iron represents the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), copper the stage of abiding (*sthiti*), brass the stage of practice (*pratipatti*), and gold the stage of orientation (*abhimukha*). Here, the three—gold, silver, and copper—are represented to exclude the stage of iron, or perhaps these may be used as metaphors for ascending the stages (*bhūmi*).

expedient means (*upāya*) are established so that the heterodox and the orthodox may mutually embrace one another, and through perfuming, they are transformed and dissolved. ○ [Offering to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas] ([Wenling says]: Taking milk, clarified butter (*sarpis*), and so forth as long-term offerings represents the offering to the Two Honored Ones by means of the flavor of *dhyāna*-joy and the Dharma-taste.

In the provisional teachings, the use of milk and curd is permitted; in the ultimate teachings, they are prohibited. That they are now taken up for offering represents the joy of the Dharma that fuses the provisional and the ultimate, established according to practice; thus, each is surrounded by its own [offerings]. [The Treatise says]: From milk one obtains curd; from curd, fresh butter (*navanīta*) is produced.
To speak of "milk" and then "pure butter" signifies the progression from the coarse to the sublime). (2. Offerings according to the occasion)
Every time at the hour of eating, or during the middle watch of the night, take half a *śu* of honey and three *hē* of clarified butter (*sarpis*).
In front of the altar, separately install a small fire-pit. Using *turuṣka* incense, boil it to extract scented water and bathe the charcoal with it.
Light it until it blazes fiercely, then cast this clarified butter and honey into the fire-pit, burning them until the smoke has vanished, to offer to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

[Wenling says: "The Buddha received his meals at midday; therefore, offerings are presented daily at midday. At midnight, it is modeled after midday. Because he knows the merits of the Buddha's three secrets, he is called the 'Lord. The term 'Lord' refers to the Lord of Yakṣas. In the Sanskrit original, there is no sense of 'traces' (*jì*); it is because he manifests traces as a deity that the translators established this name based on its meaning."

Descending. Once the steps have been distinguished, names and positions become distinct. If one were not deluded regarding the Truth, how could there be such positions?
