The Buddha said: "Ānanda, you should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks. Originally, there have been no worlds and no sentient beings.

[Commentary] The essence of the one true reality is profoundly still and perfectly luminous; it is neither real nor false, and all names and marks are utterly transcended. Regarding the world of birth...
This [distinction] is extinguished. Since neither world nor sentient beings are established, who can be named as the Buddha or as one who appears in the world?
It is through the deluded discrimination of sentient beings that there is a Buddha and a world. If one realizes the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is no Buddha and no world.

This is the single True Dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*), which fundamentally has no stages or positions. [The Haiyin commentary states: Because he was asked about the gradual sequence of cultivation and realization, he first established the Single True Dharma-realm as the basis for both birth-and-death and nirvana.

This is the root of the matter. The realm of birth and death is vast, yet in sum it does not exceed twelve classes of beings. The path to Nirvana is long, yet in essence it consists of no more than fifty-five stages. When one is deluded regarding the One True Reality and gives rise to the six perceptions, two kinds of inverted views become mutually dependent.
To awaken to the six characteristics and return to the direct path—this is what is termed the two kinds of *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis).

Because of delusion there is birth; because of birth there is cessation. Birth and cessation are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called truth. This is designated as the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed *bodhi* and Great *nirvāṇa*, which are the names for these two transformations of the basis. (2. Narration of the Two Characteristics) Because of delusion there is birth; because of birth there is cessation. Birth and cessation are termed delusion; the cessation of delusion is termed truth.
This is called the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed *bodhi* and Great *nirvāṇa*, the two designations for the transformation of the basis.

[Commentary: The true substance is eternally abiding; fundamentally, it is neither arising nor ceasing. Failing to know as it truly is that the dharma of *tathatā* is one, the unawakened mind moves and gives rise to thought.
Thought is precisely the phase of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*). Arising is immediately followed by cessation. Thus, thoughts flow on and change from moment to moment.
Progressing and evolving, these states gradually become coarser until they reach the fruits of karma, causing one to transmigrate through the three realms; therefore, they are called "delusions.

If one recognizes that an evil thought has arisen in the preceding moment and is able to restrain the succeeding thought so that it does not arise, one will gradually sever coarse afflictions until even the subtle afflictions are eliminated.
When ignorance is forever exhausted and one awakens to the ultimate state, that is what is called "Reality" (Zhen). It is here that Bodhi and Nirvana are established [Ziqing].

Regarding the two names for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): because one does not understand the characteristic of the single Dharma-realm, delusion suddenly arises (from the initial confusion of the True and the movement of thought, leading to the cycle of transmigration);
this is called "Non-awakening. To reverse this non-awakening and realize that, fundamentally, there is no arising, is...
It is called "Awakening" (*bodhi*). This designation of *bodhi* is established by contrast with non-awakening. From delusion arises birth; where there is birth, there must be cessation.
By overturning this cycle of birth and cessation, one reveals that which is neither born nor ceases; this is the designation of *nirvāṇa*, established in opposition to birth and cessation.

Once birth and cessation have ceased, there is nothing further upon which to rely; therefore, it is called "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). True Suchness (*tathatā*) serves as the ground for both delusion and awakening.

The basis (*āśraya*). By transforming this basis of delusion, it becomes the basis of awakening; therefore, it is called "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). It is the realm of one's own wisdom.
By transforming the storehouse (*ālayavijñāna*) which serves as the basis, it becomes nirvāṇa. Awakening and nirvāṇa are from the outset neither identical nor different.

It is merely by transforming delusion that it is named "unsurpassed bodhi," and by transforming existence that it is named "great nirvāṇa. Because of existence there is delusion; through awakening, existence is empty. The nature of existence is itself...
Emptiness is not the emptiness resulting from cessation. Therefore, there is no distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
(The above is based on the Chinese text. Thus we know that bodhi and nirvāṇa exist because of delusion; it is like how the name "awakening" exists only because of sleep. This is also like that:
it is not that the original, single True Source has two distinct fruits. Generally speaking across all stages, there are six kinds of transformations.

Relying on this, as explained elsewhere (Master Xingfu says: "The transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) has six types: first, the transformation through the weakening of power and strengthening of capacity; second, the transformation through penetration; third, the transformation through cultivation; fourth, the transformation through the perfection of the fruit; fifth, the inferior transformation; and sixth, the vast transformation [the supplement states:

judging by the four teachings, these six reside in the Perfect and Sudden; here we take the vast transformation of the basis to speak of it]). (△ Master Wenling says: Birth-and-death and true-false, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—all are what are called various names and characteristics).

The Bodhisattva arises from the previously mentioned Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Having already been able to abandon those two types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of grasping and the two types of coarse hindrances (*dausthulya-āvaraṇa*), they are then able to realize the vast transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). By transforming the afflictions (*kleśa*), they attain Great Nirvāṇa; by transforming the hindrance to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they realize Unsurpassed Enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*). How are these two kinds of transformation of the basis realized?

It is said that within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one cultivates the ten superior practices, severs the ten heavy hindrances, and realizes the ten True Suchnesses (*tathatā*); it is through this that the two kinds of transformation of the basis are attained. The fruits of these two transformations of the basis are precisely the fifth aspect of ultimate realization.

[The Mirror of the School says: "The precious, awakened true mind is perfectly complete in each and every being. Originally, it is neither called 'Buddha' nor 'sentient being. It is simply because this mind, though wondrous and sovereign, does not maintain its original nature."

According to the conditions of delusion or awakening, the affairs of the sage or the ordinary person are established. It is like gold following the artisan: when conditions form it, it is transformed into a finger-ring; like a finger-ring following the furnace fire: when conditions disintegrate it, it immediately returns to being gold. This cycle of formation and destruction is but a single gold, with no further distinction.

The Tathāgatagarbha-citta is also like this: when following defiled conditions, it is deluded and becomes the ālayavijñāna; when following pure conditions, it awakens and becomes the Tathāgatagarbha. Throughout these transformations, there is only this one mind.

Ultimately, there is no distinction between them. Therefore it is said: if one recognizes that [the mind] is beginningless, then the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is itself ignorance; if one realizes this today, then ignorance is itself the *dharmatā*. When the *dharmatā* universally produces all phenomena within ignorance, it is termed "defilement."

Ignorance, in relation to the *dharmatā*, universally responds to all conditions and is termed "purity. This is precisely the "Gate of the Mind’s Exclusive Reversion and Perfect Accomplishment" among the Ten Mysterious Gates. If it is reversed, it becomes *nirvāṇa*; if it follows [the flow], it is called *saṃsāra*.
Since both *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa* do not transcend the Tathāgatagarbha-mind. (2. Exhorting to Recognize the Cause of Delusion)

"The three kinds and the two kinds are distinguished by way of expansion and contraction. As the preceding text says: "If you merely do not follow after discrimination..."

thus, even unto the point where [delusion] ceases, it is itself Bodhi. It is not obtained by depending on others; therefore it is said:

"When inversion does not arise, this is the true samādhi. (Wenling says: One must recognize the cause of inversion before one can sever and treat it. Regarding the dependent retribution (*pariṇāmanirmita*), this refers to the arising of the four great elements and so forth. This clarifies the inversion of the world; it specifically points to the primary retribution (*mukhyopabhoga*), which consists of the twelve classes of sentient beings.

This was said in response to Ānanda, because it concerns the stages of realization entered through the cultivation of *samādhi*. Why is this? A stage is attained through awakening; awakening necessarily presupposes delusion. Delusion constitutes the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), while awakening constitutes the state of a sage (*ārya*).

These are all matters pertaining to the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*), not the characteristics of the external environment (*bhājanaloka*). [△ (Wuxing says): This is likely not the case. Regarding the passage concerning "all sentient beings," Changshui separately established a topical outline for the section on inversion (*viparyāsa*). The initial part, from "The fundamental perfect luminosity... onwards, marks the general introduction to the causes of inversion; the subsequent section, from "Deluded regarding the fundamental perfect luminosity... onwards, specifically elucidates the inversions of sentient beings. Later scholars consequently attempted to transpose the textual order of the sutra.

The phrasing has been rearranged. Yunqi said: "The world of sentient beings is fundamentally inseparable. Sentient beings must dwell in reliance upon the world, and the world, in turn, arises because of sentient beings. The world is like the great earth; sentient beings are like the grasses and trees. When speaking of sentient beings, it is not improper to first mention the world;

this is analogous to how, when speaking of grasses and trees, it is not improper to first mention the earth. In the subsequent section on the "inversion of the world," the text refers to transformed sentient beings, concluding by stating there are twelve types.

The two texts combined, their meaning becomes very clear. Now, following Yunqi’s commentary, it is most comprehensive and accessible. Following the structural outline (ke) established by Master Beifeng Yin, the initial section identifies the delusions of sentient beings; this is then divided into sub-sections through a general summary followed by specific explanations.
The sequence of the sūtra text is thus rendered clear from beginning to end, while also remaining faithful to the structural divisions of Changshui.

Ānanda, what is meant by the delusions of sentient beings? Ānanda, because the nature of the luminous mind is inherently bright and perfect, one takes that luminosity as a basis to give rise to a [false] nature, and from that nature, false perceptions arise.
Thus, from that which is ultimately non-existent, one establishes that which is ultimately existent.
[The Mirror of the Source]: True Suchness is the One Mind; it does not change from antiquity to the present. For what reason do sentient beings undergo delusion? Answer:
Within the equal and true Dharma-realm, there is neither Buddha nor sentient being. Yet, following conditions of defilement and purity, the ten dharma-realms are thereby established.
Because the true mind follows conditions and does not maintain its own nature, it is only for the sake of sentient beings that they themselves do not realize their own non-existence [of self].

Because it is the nature of the nature itself, it merely becomes an ordinary person through defiled conditions and becomes a sage through pure conditions. (Wenling says: "The nature is luminous mind," referring to the essence of True Suchness.
"The nature is perfectly luminous" means that it does not abide in its own nature. It is like an echo in an empty valley, arising according to whatever conditions prompt it;

or like clouds suddenly appearing in the great void, or dust suddenly settling on a bright mirror. Since one cannot find even a single thought's point of initial origination, it is called "Non-arising."
It begins with ignorance (*avidyā*). An ancient commentary states: "Based on clarity, the nature (*prakṛti*) is manifested; from that nature, deluded vision arises.

Relying upon the clarity of the nature, it transforms into shadows and emerges. Relying upon these shadows, it comes into being. From the void, it clings to existence; thus it is said: 'From ultimate non-existence, it becomes ultimate existence.

This is the characteristic of karma. [Supplementary Note: Unchanging True Suchness (*tathatā*) is called "nature"; following conditions is called "mind. "Arising from nature" refers to the unchanging; "clarity of mind" refers to following conditions.]

Because the luminous perfection within the nature follows conditions, sentient beings delusively give rise to illumination and cognition; thus, through false views, they manifest their nature. When delusion is added to the nature, the faculty of seeing arises. Therefore it is said: "The nature is deluded and seeing arises.

The specific inclusion of the character "perfect" (yuan) immediately reveals that this nature following conditions gives birth to deluded clarity. [Xuelang said: "Because the nature’s clarity is perfect, the perfection encompasses both the real and the delusive. This is like saying the substance of the nature’s clarity encompasses the six delusions; therefore, it can be both real and delusive."
[Commentary: The Tathāgatagarbha-mind is, by its original nature, true luminosity, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; therefore it is said, "because its nature is perfectly luminous. (Gushan says:

This means that because the True Mind inherently possesses all dharmas, it is like a bright mirror in which the nature of all images is perfectly present. From this true luminosity, movement arises from the nature, thereby forming the "characterized" (the object).
Once the characterized has been falsely established, the false "characterizer" (the subject) arises; this is precisely false seeing. These two aspects—subject and object—...

Neither is separate from the True [Nature]. Thus it is said: "Because of clarity (ming), nature (xing) is manifested; nature gives rise to deluded vision. (Because the deluded mind of clarity causes the True Nature to fluctuate, it is said that "because of clarity, nature is manifested.
Because nature is manifested, discrimination subsequently arises; hence it is said that "nature gives rise to deluded vision. Originally, this is the One True [Nature], fundamentally without marks.

Suddenly, through deluded movement, two marks (dualistic appearances) arise in an instant. From the markless True [Nature], the deluded state with marks is formed. Therefore, it is said: "It forms the ultimate."

There is. This is the distinction between their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). [Haoyin says: Previously it was said that "the cause establishes the object" (*yuan ming li suo*); there, the word "object" (*suo*) broadly encompassed such characteristics as empty space and the realm of sentient beings (*shengjie*). Now it is said that "the nature is manifested" (*faxing*).

By speaking of "nature" (*xing*) and not "characteristic," it refers exclusively to the primary retribution of sentient beings, revealing that this world of sentient beings arises through the perfuming and transformation of ignorance. Therefore, it is called "the nature arising from the cause" (*yin xing faxing*). The nature gives rise to deluded vision; the manifestation of the nature is the *karmic consciousness* (*ye shi*), and the deluded vision is the "seeing-division" (*jian fen*).

Ultimately, existence consists of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). This refers to the sense organs, the body, and the physical world, which all manifest instantaneously; it is by means of this that the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is established.

"This 'existence' has that which belongs to it" (citing the preceding to establish ultimate existence). It is not the cause of causes; it is the characteristic of the abiding and that which is abided in. It is thoroughly understood to be without root. [The Ancient Commentary on the Mirror of the Source:
"This existence has that which belongs to it" means that it is not the cause of causes; this refers to the aspect of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*).

The aspect of activity (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) constitutes the "possessor" (*śaktimat*), while the aspect of transformation constitutes the "possessed" (*śakti*). Since the possessor and the possessed are thus distinguished, these two aspects exist. Therefore, it is said that there is "that which belongs to it."

There is the aspect of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This very aspect of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*) is able to function as active manifestation. It is established based on what precedes it and arises based on what follows it;

these successive states act as causes for one another, and thus they are called "causes that are not [themselves] caused. This very aspect of manifestation is able to draw forth the objects of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).

The aspect of manifestation is the subject that abides, while the six sense-fields are the objects wherein it abides; therefore, it is said to be the "aspect of abiding and that which is abided in. [Commentary: This refers to the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

The aforementioned distinct characteristic (*visiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*) serves as the capacity (*śakti*), while the present common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) serves as that which is possessed (*svabhāva*).

(In the present sutra, the distinct characteristic corresponds to the "phase of activity" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) in the *Awakening of Faith*, and the common characteristic corresponds to the "phase of transformation" [*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*]). The distinct characteristic was originally not an existent cause by which it could arise; rather, having arisen, it becomes the cause for the common characteristic.
This is what was meant in the preceding passage: "Such is the cause of delusion; it exists because of delusion. The subsequent passage also states: "Delusion is fundamentally without cause."

Within the midst of false conceptualization, the nature of causes and conditions is established: difference arises as identity, and identity serves as that which abides while difference serves as that which is abided in;
hence it is called "the characteristic of the abider and the abode. Since this abider and abode are fundamentally without cause, what further root could there be?
Thus, these two characteristics are ultimately without abiding; hence it is said that they have no fundamental basis at all. (Wuxing says: "As for 'not having a cause,' it is as when one asks:

'Since they are called delusive, how can they have a cause? As for 'that which is caused,' it is as when one says: 'From various deluded thoughts, they successively become causes for one another. [Haiyin says: "That which 'exists' is ignorance; that which 'possesses' is the world and sentient beings; that which 'abides' is sentient beings."]

That which dwells is the world-system. (△ [Liangben says: This ignorance that is capable of existing and the sentient beings and worlds that exist have, from the beginning, no cause; yet it acts as the cause from which they are produced. It likewise has no dwelling place where they reside.
They are like flowers in the sky, like dreams during sleep; when interrogated, they have no root; when sought, they have no foundation.)
Based on this non-abiding, the worlds and all sentient beings are established. [Ancient Commentary]:
Regarding the statement "based on this non-abiding, the worlds are established": the manifested appearances are established from delusion;
fundamentally, there is nothing upon which they rely. Yet, by relying on these manifested appearances, they constitute the basis of the worlds. Therefore, it is said: "based on this non-abiding."
By means of this, the world is established. From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established. That which is "non-abiding" is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).
Ignorance has no cause; therefore, it is non-abiding. These three characteristics are all, from the beginningless past, a single moment of deluded mind.
[The text] generally designates this as ignorance (*avidyā*). [Commentary]: It is devoid of the characteristics of identity and difference.

Taking the aforementioned identity and difference as its basis, it arises as that which is neither identical nor different. These two preceding characteristics are precisely ignorance, the essence of the *ālayavijñāna*.
Although it is divided into the same and the different, in a single thought-moment it transforms into subtle arising and ceasing, which is entirely ignorance (*avidyā*).

From this, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sense organs and the body, and the seeds all arise through transformation. Therefore, it is said "to establish. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because of non-enlightenment, the mind moves; this is called..."
Karma. Because it relies on movement, one is able to see; because it relies on the ability to see, objects falsely appear.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established. This is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). Because it has no cause, it is called "non-abiding.

[Quotation] [The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: Mañjuśrī asked, "What is the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome? He replied, "The body is the root. "What is the root of the body? He replied, "Desire and greed are the root. "What is the root of desire and greed? He replied, "False conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the root. False...

"What is the root of false discrimination? He replied, "Perverted perception is its root. "What is the root of perverted perception? He replied, "Non-abiding is its root. [Sengzhao said: "The mind is like water: when still, it reflects; when moving, it lacks clarity. It is like facing a gushing spring and yet demanding that it return to its original state; such a thing has never occurred. The arising of inverted perceptions is rooted in non-abiding. The Sūtra states: "To enter into all phenomena as being of the nature of empty space is called attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). From the first stage through the third stage, one takes these three preceding stages collectively as a single practice, which is termed "nurturing wisdom and compassion" (*caryā-bhāvanā*) and is also called "conformable patience" (*anulomikī kṣānti*). This continues until the eighth stage, at which point effortful application (*prayoga*) is completed and the patience of non-arising is attained. Regarding the correlation between the treatises and the commentaries, there are differences;

From beginning to end, it is uniquely non-arising; this simultaneously encompasses the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*). As for the statement that one proceeds from here through gradual cultivation according to what is practiced, Fangshan said: "The Ten Patiences (*daśa-kṣānti*) and so forth are the culmination of the ten stages (*bhūmi*); entering into birth-and-death to benefit sentient beings is the skillful means (*upāya*).

These are also the five positions—Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), Ten Transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmana*), Ten Stages, and the Eleventh Stage—which are cultivated throughout; this is the essential principle of the Perfectly Round Gradual Cultivation and Realization. This person refers to one who previously maintained pure prohibitive precepts; when their practice reaches this stage, they finally attain the awakening of the fruit-ground of non-arising and non-ceasing, which serves as the mind of the causal ground. When a Bodhisattva first enters the stream, they immediately employ the illusion-like samādhi.

One contemplates the principle that both [subject and object] are empty and non-arising; thus, one immediately attains this principle at that very moment. While in other sutras one must enter the stages (*bhūmi*) before realizing the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), here one attains it prior to that because the names for the resolve of the causal stage and the awakening of the fruition stage correspond.

The phrase "From this, one gradually cultivates," etc., generally refers to all subsequent stages. This means that by taking this non-arising and non-ceasing as the mind of the causal stage, one subsequently perfects the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage.

Thus, the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and direction, as well as the entry into the stages and the positions of realization, all take this stage as their foundation. This directly answers the previous question regarding the sequence of gradual progress and the attainment of the perspective for cultivation. The *Tiantai Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) elucidates the stages [of practice] by means of seven categories: namely, the ten faiths (*śraddhā*), ten abidings (*vihāra*), ten practices (*caryā*), ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), and the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment.

Prior to these ten faiths, it opens up the stage of the five ranks (*pañca-varga*). These five ranks represent the merit of perfect faith at the very beginning of all dharmas; though they belong to the initial stage of the path, they surpass the state of an Arhat who has completed his training (*aśaikṣa*). This is comparable to the stage of "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-jñāna*) in the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śikṣā*), and may also be inferred from the meaning of the stage of "Patience through Subduing" (*vinaya-kṣānti*).

(From the *Qixin Lun Xuanyan Shu*: Regarding the cessation of the four marks of arising, abiding, change, and extinction, it provisionally manifests four stages. First, the mark of extinction: the treatise states, "As when an ordinary person becomes aware that a preceding thought has given rise to evil"—this stage corresponds to the ten faiths. Second, the mark of change: the treatise states, "As when those of the Two Vehicles employ contemplative wisdom. At the beginning...)

The "Bodhisattva who has resolved the mind" (*cittotpādika*) is called "partial awakening" (*sādharmya-bodhi*); it belongs to the stage of the three sages (*trividha-ārya*). Regarding the characteristics of the third dwelling, the *Śāstra* states: "As with Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), they are called 'awakening according to their portion' (*yathābhāga-bodhi*"); this belongs to the stages from the first establishment up to the ninth ground. Regarding the characteristics of the fourth birth, the *Śāstra* states:

"As when the Bodhisattva ground is exhausted, it is called 'ultimate awakening' (*atyanta-bodhi*"); this belongs to the stage where the study of the ten grounds is perfected. Guifeng’s topical outline of the "Chapter on Pure Wisdom" in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), following the demarcations in the *Śāstra*, clarifies the distinctions between the stages of realization by establishing four positions:

first, the position of faith; second, the position of the sages; third, the position of the holy ones; and fourth, the position of the fruit. These are detailed in that commentary. [The Six Identities of Tiantai: First, the Buddha as Principle (*lǐjí fó*); second, the Buddha by Name (*míngzìjí fó*); third, the Buddha by Contemplative Practice (*guānxíngjí fó*); these correspond to the five grades of practice; fourth, the Buddha by Merit-Transference (*xiāngxíngjí fó*); fifth, the Buddha by Partial Manifestation (*fēnxiànjí fó*); sixth, the Buddha by Ultimate Perfection (*jiùjìngjí fó*). (Note: The original fragment ends at the fourth identity.)

The "semblance" [Buddha] refers to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). The "partial realization" [Buddha] refers to the stages from the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) up to the stage of equal enlightenment (*samābodhi*). The "ultimate" [Buddha] refers to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), the final fruit. (○ Above, according to Qingliang, the stages were established based on the sutras and śāstras. (○ [Private Commentary]:

I have carefully examined the passage by Master Zhiyi concerning the clarification of the dharma-gates, practices, and stages, which states: "If one wishes to clarify the number of stages, one must rely on the *Necklace Sutra* (*Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*) and the *Benevolent Kings Sutra* (*Aryaratnaketudhāraṇī*). If one wishes to clarify the hierarchy of subduing and severing [afflictions], one must rely on the *Large Prajñāpāramitā Sutra* and the three contemplations (*trividha-darśana*'). )

Regarding the Abhidharma teachings, one must rely upon *nirvāṇa* and employ the intent of the various sūtras to collectively establish the two gates of the initial mind’s contemplation and instruction, so that they may be made clear. The stages of the various supreme sages cannot be fathomed by ordinary beings; how could one dare to speak of them recklessly?

Those who have a rough understanding of the general meaning do so to shatter the practitioner’s conceit (*adhimāna*) and to explain the scriptural text, leading sentient beings toward it; one must not cling to it universally or engage in disputes over right and wrong. I privately maintain that the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of Tiantai differs from the present sūtra because the Great Master had not yet seen the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-śikhara-sūtra*.

Even if the Great Master had seen this sūtra, since it is unlike the *Avataṃsaka*, its forty-one stages do not open with the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*). Furthermore, it is unlike other Mahāyāna sūtras and the preceding four periods of teaching.

Regarding the *Prajñā*, the alignment of the case and its lid fits perfectly, such that it can be known at once. Now, the various masters of the Shanjia school adhere to the doctrinal characteristics (*jiaoxiang*) of their own tradition to categorize and judge this present sutra; yet these categories were never the fundamental intent of the Great Master. Furthermore, recent virtuous ones wish to sweep away the Tiantai teachings with a broad brush, engaging in constant disputes over right and wrong.

The Great Master spoke thus: "Students of the末代 (final age) mostly cling to the methods of the sutras and treatises to engage in debates on what is severed or subdued. This is like the nature of water being cold—if one does not drink it, how can one know? This [teaching] is precisely the Buddhas' response to conditions.

Inconceivable are these words; they increase or decrease according to the capacity of the recipient, and their numerical positions differ. Since you have not yet attained realization, what is the use of empty contention? May all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm take refuge in the Saṃgha to cease their disputations and enter the great ocean of harmony.

How sublime are the words of the Sage! They hang like a mirror before the future, serving as a piercing reminder for us. Master Yue of the Bai-ting says: "While one school clarifies the stages through the differing texts of the sutras and śāstras, there is also the principle of 'borrowing' the stages; it has never been definitively established by others. As for the later followers of the Shanjia (Mount Home) school..."

To maintain such a position is vastly different from those who, like the blind, contend over the sun. (The above constitutes the complete listing of the stages. Now follows the formal exposition on the establishment of the ranks of the sages, in nine parts. [1] The Stage of Dry Wisdom.)

(○ [Combined Explanation] [The Stage of Dry Wisdom]) [The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Mahāyāna constitutes the stages (*bhūmi*). There are ten stages. From the first stage to the second stage is called 'setting out' (*prasthāna*). What are these ten stages? Answer: There are two kinds of stages.

The first is the stage exclusive to Bodhisattvas (*kevala-bodhisattva-bhūmi*); the second is the shared stage (*sādhāraṇa-bhūmi*). As for the shared stage, it refers to the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*) up to the Stage of Buddhahood (*buddha-bhūmi*). As for the stage exclusive to Bodhisattvas, it refers to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). The Buddha said:

"A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is fully endowed with the Stage of Dry Wisdom, the Stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*), the Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*), the Stage of Vision (*darśana-bhūmi*), the Stage of Thinness (*tanu-bhūmi*), the Stage of Freedom from Desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*), the Stage of Having Done What Was to Be Done (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*), the Stage of the Pratyekabuddha, the Stage of the Bodhisattva, and the Stage of the Buddha.

Commentary: There are two kinds of the Stage of Dry Wisdom: first, that of the Śrāvaka; second, that of the Bodhisattva. Because the Śrāvaka seeks only Nirvāṇa, he exerts himself with diligence, maintains pure precepts, becomes capable of receiving the Path, and discriminates and gathers all wholesome dharmas while abandoning unwholesome ones. Although he possesses wisdom, [it is limited].

If one does not obtain the water of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one cannot attain the Way; therefore, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*). For a bodhisattva, this begins from the first arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*) until one has not yet attained the conforming patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).

Regarding the Bodhisattva Stages: from the Stage of Dry Wisdom up to the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), as explained above. [The *Fahua xuanyi* states: "Now, prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), we further clarify the five grades of practice (*pañca-piṭaka*). First, the Stage of Dry Wisdom: this is the beginning of the Three Vehicles, all of which share the name 'Dry Wisdom.

It refers to the actualization of the five objects for settling the mind (*pañca-smṛty-upasthāna*), both specific and general characteristics. Abiding within these contemplations, one cultivates right effort, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path. Although one has not yet attained the water of the principle that resembles the stage of 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*), one's general characteristic wisdom is profound and sharp; therefore, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom."

[Also, Wuxing says: "The *Da-pin* [Prajñāpāramitā] has ten stages (*bhūmi*). The first is named 'Dry Wisdom' (*śuṣka-jñāna*). In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of Tiantai, five grades of practice (*wupin*) are established; it is further stated that by inference of meaning, this corresponds to the 'Stage of Dry Wisdom' in the *Da-pin*.

Master Yuan also said: 'This "Dry Wisdom" in the present sutra refers to the Five Grades of Practice in Tiantai. [Yin Mai says: "The Buddha clarifies three causes for inversion and reveals three gradual steps (*sanyanjian*) to enter the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is precisely ascending to the Stage of Dry Wisdom. Initiating practice and establishing the stages—this is Dry Wisdom, the beginning of the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*).

Yet Wuxing judges it to be outside the Five Grades of the ordinary person. The fifty-five stages are the true path to Bodhi; this is Dry Wisdom, the start of the noble path. Yet Wuxing discriminates it as not being true, [referring instead to] the 'good sons,' which correctly points to the aforementioned three [gradual steps]."

This refers to one who is progressing. Yet, Wuxing claims that this does not follow from the preceding text, asserting that the distinct stages correspond to the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena). He asks: "According to the Sūtra, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), by what means does one progress? Is this not an instance of over-reliance on other sūtras while conversely abandoning the fundamental sūtra?

Wenling’s judgment is that, based on faith, Dry Wisdom is established prior to the [ten] stages; the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*) are established prior to the [ten] grounds; and the Diamond-like Dry Wisdom is established prior to the Subtle [stage]. This constitutes the essential pivot for the transition between stages. If Dry Wisdom thus occupies two positions, how can one establish the fifty-five stages mentioned in the Sūtra?

[Haoyin says: "This clarifies the progressive advancement through the causal stages. In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is taught that there are two kinds of causes: the first three, the stages of Worthies (*śaikṣa*), are called the 'differentiated cause'; those from the first ground upward are called the 'equal cause'."

Tiantai classifies the stages prior to the Grounds and those on the Grounds as five distinct positions; this sutra does not do so in general. From the very beginning of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), the mind of dry wisdom (*ganhui xin*) is itself established as the stage of the sages (*shengwei*), without the distinction between internal and external ordinary persons (*neifan* and *waifan*). This is inferred from the authoritative words of the sages.
The meaning is clear and manifest; you may rely upon this for understanding.
Ānanda, these sons of good family have the craving for existence dried up; as the faculties and their objects no longer meet, their remaining physical forms will not continue to arise again.

[Commentary: Maintaining the precepts with purity and remaining far removed from greed and lust is therefore called the first "drying up" (*khaṇḍa*), which is the severing of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
There are two meanings of "drying up": first, because desire is exhausted, it is called "dry"; second, because there is only wisdom, it is called "dry. Here, it refers to the first meaning.

When the sense faculties and their objects do not encounter one another, through the power of *samādhi*, the flow is reversed and becomes entirely unified, thereby shattering the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This is what is manifested before one.

These two phrases signify that the obstacles of retribution are exhausted. Because desire and attachment have perished, there are no delusions of moisture; because the sense faculties do not pair, there is no nature of karma.
Even if seeds of karmic suffering exist, they will not sprout for lack of moisture. Once this retributive body is exhausted, it will never again continue.

This is precisely the stage of the true retribution (*vipākabhūmi*). Here, delusion, karma, and suffering have perished; there is no longer the principle of moistening and growth, which is the meaning of "dryness. [Xuelang said:

"This 'good son' refers to the aforementioned person who purely upholds the prohibitive precepts. The two phrases concerning 'desire for existence' correspond to the preceding text: 'the mind does not flow outward,' 'since objects are not conditioned,' and 'the faculties have nothing with which to pair.'"*] *Note: The bracketed portion represents Xuelang’s commentary on the passage.*

The remaining physical substance manifests before one, yet it no longer continues to arise; this is precisely the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas). [Haiyin said: This stage of contemplative practice for the beginner is established solely in terms of severing desire;

thus, it is not found in other sutras. When the faculties and their objects do not encounter one another, the karma that initiates rebirth does not arise. When there is no further continuation of birth, the moisture that nourishes rebirth is forever severed. These two types of non-arising are the true *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. This *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* is the mind of non-arising and non-extinction. By means of this mind of non-arising and non-extinction, these two kinds of ignorance are severed.

Therefore, taking the awakening of the fruit-stage as the fundamental causal mind, one is designated as a "sage" from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) onward. This principle of partial breaking and partial realization differs from that of other sutras.]

The mind held is empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom. The nature of this wisdom is bright and perfect, illuminating the ten directions. When this wisdom exists in a state of dryness, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (Śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi).
[Commentary: Since precept and concentration are now perfected, wisdom is generated from them. This immediately transforms the three preceding obstacles, purifying them entirely into wisdom.

The radiance of this wisdom shines forth, illuminating the ten directions with brilliant clarity; this is the meaning of "wisdom" (*prajñā*). [Xuelang said: "The mind, when held in its empty luminosity, is precisely the extinction of desire and attachment."]

"Because the faculties and their objects do not encounter one another, it is purely wisdom. These final two phrases constitute the conclusion of the name. This refers to having only that wisdom; thus, it was previously called "pure.
Since it is said that "according to what is set in motion, the noble stages are established," this refers to the desire to dry up [the stream] and turn back the flow.
It is purely composed of wisdom. Because it has not yet been moistened by the waters of the Dharma-stream of the ocean of fruition, it receives this name.

This is because it is explained here according to the meaning within the stage of *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience with the non-arising of phenomena). Truly, this means that perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential arrangement; all subsequent sections follow this pattern. (Chūka states:

"When patience is attained, wisdom becomes perfect. When desire is dried up, insight arises. Because one abides and maintains oneself through insight, it is called 'ground' (*bhūmi*). (Kachūnan states: "'The craving for desire is dried up' reiterates the preceding section on 'revolving to the source and returning to oneself. The clinging mind...")

"Vast and luminous" (*xūmíng*) refers back to the preceding section on the lands of the ten directions; thus, one should know that this is not established as a separate stage, but is rather subsumed within "contrary to present karma."

([○@●] [The Twenty Stages of Faith]) (○ [Combined Explanation] [Tiantai says]: First, through the perfect hearing, one is able to give rise to perfect faith. By means of this perfect practice, one attains entry into the perfect stage. Through skillfully cultivating the equal dharma-realm, one enters the mind of goodness (*sukha-citta*). Through skillfully cultivating compassion and pity, one enters the mind of mindfulness (*smṛti-citta*).

Through skillfully cultivating quiescent illumination, one enters the mind of progress (*vīrya-citta*). Through skillfully cultivating the breaking of dharmas, one enters the mind of wisdom (*prajñā-citta*). Through skillfully cultivating penetration and obstruction, one enters the mind of concentration (*samādhi-citta*). Through skillfully cultivating the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*), one enters the mind of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-citta*). Skillfully...)

Correcting and assisting, one enters the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*). Skillfully cultivating the categories of ordinary and saintly beings, one enters the mind of protecting the Dharma (*dharma-rakṣā-citta*). Skillfully cultivating immovability, one enters the mind of precepts (*śīla-citta*). Skillfully cultivating non-attachment, one enters the mind of vows (*praṇidhāna-citta*).

The *Ābharaṇa-sūtra* states: "One faith has ten; ten faiths have a hundred. These hundred dharmas are the root of all dharmas. Entering this mind of faith, one is able to exhaustively destroy the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the realms, as well as the dust-like ignorance (*rajas-jñāna*) beyond the realms.

One is also able to subdue the delusions of the ground of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*). The *Ratnarāja-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva of the ten good deeds gives rise to the Great Mind and dwells long within the ocean of the wheel of suffering in the triple world. This refers to this very stage. [The *Ābharaṇa-sūtra* states: "That which is within the Dharma refers to the ten minds of faith; these are the foundation of all practices. Therefore..."

Within the ten levels of the mind of faith, each single level of faith consists of ten grades of faith, forming the "Bright Door of a Hundred Dharmas. Furthermore, from within this Bright Mind of a Hundred Dharmas, each single mind contains one hundred minds, thus forming the "Bright Door of a Thousand Dharmas. The same applies to the ten thousand dharmas.

Thus progressing, one reaches immeasurable illumination. Through ever-increasing advancement and the successive higher dharmas, this becomes the gateway of illumination for the dharma of illumination. All practices and all merits numbering a million *asaṃkhyeya* enter entirely into this gateway of illumination.

(The *Xianshou pin shu* states: "Tiantai Zhiyi, based on this single chapter, established the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. He said: 'This Bodhisattva hears the perfect Dharma, gives rise to perfect faith, establishes perfect practice, and dwells in the perfect stage. Herein, the arousal of the mind encompasses both the beginning and the end.")

The perfection of virtue is the culmination of faith; yet taking this as the foundation lies in the initial aspiration. Although it may seem like a light feather, its merit is like the first basket of earth for a wall. Thus, the initial aspiration of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is itself the culmination of this [faith], and that culmination brings the initial aspiration to completion. This is the Chapter on the Initial Aspiration (*Cittotpāda-paṭala*).

This merely clarifies the merits of the initial mind of the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*). Ancient masters have explained this in brief through two gates: First, the Gate of Sequential Arrangement (*paṭala-krama-mukha*). This refers to progressing from the subtle to the manifest, and from the shallow to the deep, ascending step by step to reach the other shore.

As explained in such texts as the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, the *Arya-bhadrakalpika-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, and the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*. Second, the Gate of the Interpenetration of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-saṃgraha-mukha*). This refers to the fact that this Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused and limitless; wherever one stage is present, it inherently contains all others.

Thus, being currently within the gate of faith (*śraddhā*), there is no one who is not saved. Even if there is sequential arrangement, it is entirely encompassed within this perfect interfusion. [Furthermore, the *Sūtra Commentary* states: The *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* does not establish the ten faiths as separate stages, but subsumes them within the ten abidings. This is because the ten faiths do not constitute independent positions in themselves; they are the preparatory means for the abidings and are therefore subsumed within the abidings.

Therefore, the *Ratnarājasūtra* states: "Good son, when one first gives rise to the mind of the semblance-stage (*pratibhāsa-citta*), one believes that sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cultivate the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*). Within the Three Jewels, one generates the ten minds of the nature of the seeds of cultivation (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*):

from the mind of faith (*śraddhā-citta*) up to the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*). This is what constitutes a Bodhisattva’s ability to deliver even a small portion of sentient beings. Having already transcended all the wholesome stages (*kuśala-bhūmi*) of the two vehicles, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas nurture these ten minds as the 'wholesome embryo' (*kuśala-garbha*).

Commentary: These ten minds constitute the causes for the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) within the nature of the seeds of cultivation. Because they open the cause toward a distinct fruit, these ten are added; yet in actuality, there are only fifty-one [stages]. Furthermore, according to the forty-two ranks of worthy sages (*bhadra-ārya*) in the *Śrīgarbha-sūtra*, the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) are not established because of four reasons: faith does not enter... [the list continues].

[The reason for this is: first, because their advancement and retreat are not fixed; second, because the ten minds of mixed cultivation lack fixed stages of progression; third, because they have not yet conformed to the *dharmadhātu* while cultivating vast practices; and fourth, because they have not yet attained the *dharmakāya* to manifest the Buddha-lineage.

[Private commentary: The *Renwang yingluo jing* does not open up the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Qingliang says that the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*) opens up the ten faiths, whereas the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*) does not. Whether opening them up or not, both are instances of sequential arrangement (*paṅktibhāva*). In this sutra’s fifty-five stages, the ten faiths are separately opened up.

This means that even if there is sequential arrangement, it is nonetheless encompassed within the perfection of the *dharmadhātu*. Master Wonhyo, relying on the *Yingluo jing*, judges the ten faiths to be extracted from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*); this may be called a rigid position. (○ [Master Li says: From the ordinary person in the "Benevolent Excellence" chapter...)

The stage takes faith as its primary element. All Buddhas are born from this faith; therefore, within the Vehicle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-yāna*), fundamental faith is taken as the basis. Within this conforming faith, the principle and wisdom manifest before one. By means of the cause of faith, one accords with the fruit-dharmas of all Buddhas without the slightest error; only then is true faith established.

Through the progressive cultivation of concentration and wisdom, one passes through the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh stage.

Throughout this, the Dharma-realm remains as it was, unmoving; the Buddha-wisdom remains as it was, unchanged. Cause and effect do not shift, and time and eons do not alter—only then is faith perfected. Within this progressive cultivation, although one passes through the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten transferences, one still employs the ten fruits of wisdom from within the ten stages of faith to constitute the essence of the ten stages.

The ultimate fruit of Buddhahood does not depart from the dharma of the initial stage of faith (*śraddhā*). If there were no ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), and one could not believe that one’s own mind is the primordial fruit of Buddhahood, then even the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*) would not be established. (The *Record of the Awakening of Faith* states: "The single stage of the ten faiths has three kinds of mental states:

namely, entering (*praveśa*), abiding (*sthiti*), and completion (*niṣṭhā*). 'Entering' refers to the initial departure from divergent thoughts and the entry into the first dwelling-stage. 'Completion' refers to the full maturation of the mind of faith, which is the tenth faith. 'Abiding' refers to the eight intermediate stages of faith.

As it is with the ten faiths, so it is with the remaining stages of dwelling, practice, and direction). [The text consists of two parts; the first reiterates the preceding point to provide a general indication.]
The habitual tendencies of desire are first dried up, yet one has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma-water.

[Commentary] This follows upon the meaning of "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-jñāna) mentioned previously. Having first dried up the craving of desire, but not yet having been moistened by the fruits of the Dharma, one employs this very mind.

This serves as a skillful means for instilling faith. The designation "Tathāgata" reveals that this is the fruit-dharma (*phala-dharma*). [According to Nakagawa, in the *Renwang jing*, after one has cultivated and nurtured [the path] at the stage of Dharma-patience (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*), one subsequently gives rise to "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*);

this is identical to the present text. However, the *Huayan lun* states that it is only in the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) that one enters the "flow of the Dharma. This discrepancy arises because their pedagogical perspectives differ: contemplating the ultimate truth alone is termed "dry wisdom," whereas the simultaneous application of both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) is termed "entering the flow of the Dharma.

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "In a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva of the seventh stage practices the two modes of śamatha and vipaśyanā together, thereby entering the flow of the Dharma. [Citation: The *Ratnakaraṇḍa-avadāna* (Yingluo jing) says: "The Bodhisattvas of the Three Worthies enter..."]

The stage of the Sage: within the flow of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), mind after mind is quiescent, naturally flowing into the great ocean of wondrous enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*). The commentary explains: "The flow of the Dharma" refers to the flow of the wisdom of the Dharma-nature; therein, one proceeds spontaneously to the stage of Buddhahood.

Because the initial water and the subsequent water are of one nature—the Buddha of the cause and the Buddha of the fruit being of one nature of Buddha—there is no distinction of beginning, middle, or end therein, for there is not even a single moment’s interval. [Qingliang says: By the power of their original vows, Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage have all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear before them.

These Buddhas bestow Tathāgata-wisdom upon them, causing them to enter the gate of the Dharma-flow. This "Dharma-flow" decisively opens the still waters of non-arising (*anutpāda*) and causes the river of effortlessness (*anābhoga-caryā*) to arise, whereby they spontaneously transcend the ocean of Buddha-wisdom. Furthermore...

[This is the title]. (The ninth stage of the Dharma-Prince Abiding).
Form is produced from the womb; being a true son of the Buddha, it is called the Stage of the Dharma-Prince Abiding.

Being capable of continuing the lineage and upholding the Buddha-dharma, he is named a "Dharma Prince" (*dharmaputra*). Through these manifestations, one becomes a full person. Just as a great king of a nation delegates various state affairs to his crown prince, so too when a Kṣatriya king’s eldest son has reached maturity, he performs the rite of consecration;

One is able to attain Buddhahood and transform sentient beings. Why is it that only upon reaching the tenth stage is one called "Arrayed for Empowerment," signifying the attainment of Buddhahood? Answer: In the teaching of perfect interpenetration (*yuánróng*), the two sutras are largely in agreement. This is because the sequential progression (*xíngbù*) does not obstruct perfect interpenetration.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, one can attain Buddhahood at the very first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), because the principle of perfect interpenetration does not obstruct the sequential progression of practice. In the present sutra, however, the conferral of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) is only listed at the tenth stage. Thus, that sutra states: "The dwelling place of the Bodhisattva is vast, equal to empty space. It further says:

"At the moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), one immediately achieves perfect awakening. One thoroughly comprehends the true nature of all phenomena; whatever teachings one hears, they are realized through self-awakening rather than by depending on others. One fully cultivates the ten kinds of powers of wisdom (*daśa-jñānabala*), ultimately departing from delusion and falsehood.

Untainted like empty space, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serene and responds to all things. This is also consistent with what is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "From the moment of first generating the aspiration, one sits upon the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), turns the wheel of the Dharma, and delivers sentient beings. One should know that such a Bodhisattva is identical to a Buddha. The present sutra now states:

The ten uses interpenetrate to perfectly constitute the One Mind. It is further said that the spiritual manifestations of the ten bodies are simultaneously and fully present. These passages all clarify that a single stage encompasses all stages; this is the non-obstruction of the sequential (xingbu) within the perfect fusion (yuanrong).

Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra explains the conferral of office only upon Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, whereas this scripture clarifies the bestowal of empowerment already at the tenth abode. This is the non-obstruction of the perfect fusion within the sequential. Perfect fusion is discussed in terms of horizontal simultaneity, while the sequential is explained in terms of vertical progression; these two are without mutual obstruction.

The two sutras are largely identical; therefore, there is no doubt [regarding their meaning]. Regarding the "arrayed consecration" (*abhiṣeka*), the *Avataṃsaka* states: "When the crown prince born of a Wheel-Turning King has a mother who is the principal queen and possesses all physical marks, he sits upon a precious white elephant throne made of exquisite gold.

A great net-canopy is spread above, various musical instruments are played, and the waters of the four great oceans are taken and placed within a golden pitcher. The King holds this pitcher and pours it over the prince’s head. At that moment, he is said to have received the royal position. The Bodhisattva’s reception of office is likewise:

because the water of the Buddhas' wisdom is poured over his head, he is called a 'Bodhisattva who has received the office of Great Wisdom. That text clarifies that the reception of office occurs only at the tenth stage (*bhūmi*); yet here, in the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*), since it is termed 'consecration,' it is described as the reception of office. That [text]...

This is according to the ultimate [attainment]. This, however, refers to partial attainment. Furthermore, within the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), a single stage encompasses all stages; therefore, it may be so described. (In the *Avataṃsaka*, the first abode is the Buddha-abode. The empowerment at the tenth ground is like a crown prince of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) receiving the royal position.

In this sutra, it is only at the fourth abode that one’s practice truly becomes equal to the Buddha—comparable to a king performing the head-anointing (*abhiṣeka*) upon the crown prince and entrusting him with state affairs. Furthermore, when the crown prince of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) receives the royal consecration (*abhiṣeka*), he is at that moment said to have received the royal office and may also be called a Wheel-Turning Holy King. As the Sūtra says:

"The heir apparent who has grown up is merely the heir to a regional king, not the crown prince born of a Wheel-Turning King. "As for the mere arrangement of the consecration, there is yet no elephant-treasure, nor the exquisite golden net with webbed fingers."

It is adorned with various kinds of banners and streamers. By arranging these for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), it signifies that the person has attained maturity; yet, they have not yet actually assumed the royal position, as they still belong to the category of "Consecrated Kings" (*abhiṣikta-rāja*).

This, too, is clearly visible as the sequential unfolding of the two stages of the Grounds (*bhūmi*) and the Abodes (*vihāra*). [The *Wenling Commentary* says: "Now, the arousal of the aspiration (*cittotpāda*) must first purify the grounds; having purified the grounds, one then practices; through practice, one is subsequently born into the family of the Tathāgata, endowed with the marks of enlightenment, sharing the same mind as the Buddha, extending the essence of the Path, perfecting the ten bodies (*daśakāya*), becoming a son of the Buddha, and undertaking the Buddha's work. This is the sequence of beginning and end. (The above concludes the stage of the Ten Abidings).

[Forty Stages of Practice] (Combined Explanation: [Tiantai says] This refers to that which follows the Ten Abidings. The ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*) collectively constitute the stage of application (*prayoga*) and the stage of provisions (*sambhāra*). These ten practices and the provisions for the fruit of Buddhahood are like a cucumber: the flower and the fruit emerge together, and the flower and fruit mutually support one another, attaining mastery through effortlessness.

Regarding the fourth assembly, the teaching of the ten practices in the Yāma Heaven palace: this is to clarify that from the summit of Mount Sumeru to the limit where appearances cease, one realizes the body of Buddha-wisdom; then, descending to the Yāma Heaven, one gives rise to [realization] based on the fundamental wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*).

The myriad practices of Samantabhadra are expressed through their locations so that they may be easily understood. it does not know that this is actually a lower cause for another system. (Section Ten: [The First, the Practice of Joy]).
Ānanda, once these sons of good family have become children of the Buddha, they are endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas;
because they accord with the ten directions, this is called the Practice of Joyful Accord.
[Commentary] The first two phrases conclude what preceded; from "endowed with" (*ju-tsuk*) below, the main point is clarified. This has two meanings, therefore [the Bodhisattva] rejoices:
first, because he is endowed with immeasurable Buddha-virtues. As it says in the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*: "I have further attained this perfect penetration through cultivation and realization."
Because of the Unsurpassed Way, he is further able to skillfully attain the four inconceivable and unconditioned sublime virtues (*anabhisaṃskāra-guṇa*).
Since they are called "inconceivable," they are the immeasurable virtues of a Buddha. These sublime virtues were never previously attained, yet today they are fully perfected;
therefore, it is said that he rejoices. Second, he rejoices because sentient beings receive transformation. Regarding the "ten directions": [he manifests] ten...
The "body of realms" (dhātu-kāya) is for the benefit of sentient beings. There are two ways of conforming (*anuvartana*).

First, because the inclinations of sentient beings are unequal and their faculties and practices differ, the Bodhisattva conforms to them by means of physical form and speech; this clarifies the conformity of the one who transforms.
Second, the Bodhisattva manifests various transformations, and sentient beings conform to them, each receiving transformation and all attaining benefit; this clarifies...
This refers to the conformity of those to be transformed. Since both the subject (the capacity) and the object (the response) are in harmony, the faculty and the response both give rise to joy;

thus it is so named. [The Haiyin commentary states: "The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha possesses merits that accord with its nature, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Once ignorance is extinguished, the functional manifestations of these inherent virtues become evident; hence it is said to be 'fully endowed. Because one does not dwell in the fruition of enlightenment, one conforms to the ten directions.

When principle is fulfilled and the mind is satisfied, the benefits for self and others are complete. As both the faculty and the response are joyful, it is called the 'Joyful Practice' (*pramuditā-caryā*). This follows upon the fulfillment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), merging them into a single whole to give rise to the great Dharma-joy. (△ [My own comment: The *Avataṃsaka* establishes this.)

The Bodhisattva acts as a great donor (*mahādānapati*). The commentary explains this in terms of the three kinds of giving (*tri-dāna*). However, there is no need to specifically correlate this with that sutra; rather, this practice is judged to be the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*). The other practices should be understood accordingly. (2. Beneficial Practice).

To awaken oneself and to awaken others, thereby attaining freedom from opposition and resistance, is called the practice of non-ill-will and non-hatred.
[Commentary]: Because one awakens oneself, ignorance cannot obstruct wisdom; because one awakens others, sentient beings cannot oppose one’s transformation.

Obstacles cannot resist it; things cannot oppose it. Since both self-benefit and benefit for others are simultaneously accomplished, there is no anger or resentment. (The *Haoyin* commentary states: "By observing sentient beings in accordance with the nature of awakening, one never opposes or rejects them;

this is called 'absence of anger and resentment'."). (In the *Avataṃsaka*, this is called the "Practice of Non-opposition"; the Jin translation calls it "Absence of Resentment. The sutra says: "This bodhisattva constantly practices the dharma of patience and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.")
They cause the severing of evil such as greed, anger, and delusion, and cause one to abide in patience, compassion, and harmony.

When a Bodhisattva has accomplished the dharma of patience, even if hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of sentient beings were each to manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of mouths, and each mouth were to utter hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of words to revile and insult the Bodhisattva;

and if these sentient beings were each to have hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of hands, and each hand were to grasp hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of weapons to oppress and harm the Bodhisattva—should this continue for asaṃkhyeya kalpas without ever ceasing—the Bodhisattva would endure it all.

Experiencing extreme agony, with the hairs on his body all standing on end and life itself on the verge of being severed, he thought to himself: "If my mind is disturbed by this suffering, I shall not be self-subdued and I shall not be self-guarded; how then can I cause the minds of others to become pure? He reflected:

"Since beginningless kalpas, I have dwelt in birth and death, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction. Manifesting in various forms throughout the limits of the future, equal across the three periods of time and penetrating the ten directions—this is called "Inexhaustible Practice.

Knowledge and vision: in total, they constitute the fundamental immobility of the Chan gate. In the preceding ten abodes and ten practices, the mind of transcending the mundane was predominant while the practice of great compassion was deficient. Ānanda, when these good men have perfected their supernormal powers and completed the work of attaining Buddhahood— being pure, refined, and true,

This is called the Dedication of Saving and Protecting All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings.
[Commentary] Because function arises based on the essence, it is said that his supernatural powers are perfected; his sublime practices for self-benefit and benefiting others are unimpeded.

He is "far removed from lingering afflictions," which manifests the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

The mark of sentient beings is empty because they are fundamentally *nirvāṇa*; the conditions for transformation arise because they are fundamentally without intrinsic nature.

Therefore, it is said that one eliminates and transcends signs. This is likewise taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*. Wisdom that has lost its objective conditions is called the "unconditioned mind" (*asaṃskṛta-citta*);

Nirvāṇa is the fruit; the path is the principle (li). One treads it to establish the ground and reach the ultimate limit; therefore, it is called the "Path to Nirvāṇa. The meaning of the title is thus clear. Question:

Cause. Relying upon this true cause, one initiates the practice directed toward the fruit; it unfolds and radiates throughout the entire dharma-realm to attain the path of ultimate nirvana.
