Just as smoke is taken as the sign at the beginning of the sun, and the fire of untainted wisdom likewise takes the stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) as its preceding sign—just as the dawn-light is the sign at the beginning of the sun—it is therefore called "smoke. (The two stages of the "summit" [mūrdhan]).

Furthermore, by means of one's own mind, one attains what the Buddhas have traversed—whether relying or not relying [on external supports]—like ascending a high mountain where the body enters into empty space, yet there remains a slight obstruction below;
this is called the Stage of the Summit (mūrdhan).
[Commentary: Previously, one took the Buddha’s awakening as one’s own mind; this was using the fruit to clarify the cause. Now, one takes one’s own mind as that which the Buddha traversed;

this is the cause uniting with the fruit. (Wenling says: "The causal mind and the resultant awakening are already adjacent to the ultimate. Thus it is likened to ascending to a high place in the void: having reached the summit, one needs only a slight further push, and minor obstructions will be removed.
Although the cause and fruit are thus united, the two aspects have not yet been extinguished; therefore it is said, "If one relies [on them], it is as if one were still [in the process]."

At the mountain peak, the feet have something upon which they tread; this is intended to manifest that the *dharmadhātu* is without differentiation, and thus it is said to be "not dependent," like a body dwelling in empty space.
If there were even the slightest obstruction below, it would be a metaphor for "dependence," because two characteristics would still persist.

These two characteristics are precisely the ignorance that obstructs entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*). This is explained in terms of severing obstructions to reveal [the truth]. [The *Haoyin* says: "Contemplative wisdom seems to vanish, yet it has not yet..."]

"Perishing. Its essence is about to perish; therefore it is said: 'Whether relying or not relying,' for the Dharma-realm is like space, having nothing upon which to rely. (△ [Ōyū says: The *nirvāṇa* realized in the first stage (*bhūmi*) is like empty space, far transcending the mountain of the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) of the ten stages of practice (*prayoga*).

Within the stage of the ten practices, a portion of transformation-death is on the verge of being liberated but is not yet liberated; within the first stage, the space-like *nirvāṇa* is on the verge of being realized but is not yet realized. This is the "Summit Stage" (*mūrdha-bhūmi*). (○ [The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: All bodhi...)

[Sa]. Views and understandings constitute an obstruction. Although one has severed the obstruction of understanding, one still dwells in the awakening of views; taking the obstruction of awakening as an obstruction, one lacks mastery. This is called a Bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stages (*bhūmi*). Following the nature of awakening, the *Chao* says:

"This establishes the characteristics of realizing awakening prior to the stages. The passage from the *Buddhottama-sūtra* regarding the four roots of goodness and the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*) is likewise the characteristic of the summit prior to the stages. It says: 'It is like ascending a high mountain,' and so forth; this is also like that. Since all obstructions have been exhausted, it is as if the body were situated in space.

Yet the awakening of views still persists, like a subtle obstruction. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* verse states: "When a small object stands before one, one calls it the nature of consciousness-only. What is called a "small object" is precisely the subtle obstruction. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 41, on the patience of compliance and non-arising).

All dharmas existing between *kṣānti* (patience) and [the next stage] are called *mūrdhan* (summit). Abiding upon this summit, one truly advances toward the Buddha-way and no longer fears falling back. For example, within the Śrāvaka-dharma, that which exists between *uṣmagata* (warmth) and *kṣānti* is called the *mūrdha*-dharma. Question: If one who attains the summit does not fall, why is it now said that there is "falling from the summit"?

Answer: That which is nearly attained but lost is called "falling. One who has attained the summit possesses stable wisdom and thus does not fear falling. It is like climbing a mountain: once the summit has been reached, one does not fear falling;

however, while one has not yet reached it, one is precarious and fears falling. When the summit increases and becomes firm, it is called the stage of a Bodhisattva. Having entered this stage, all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and all Māra’s subjects cannot shake them; it is also called "the Unshakable" (*aniñjya*).

[The patience of the dharma of arising] (○ A separate explanation of the stage of the summit [according to the *Abhidharmakośa*]: The two wholesome states of "heat" and "summit" are both called "wholesome states subject to fluctuation," because they can regress and fluctuate. Among the wholesome roots subject to fluctuation, the summit is the most excellent, as it is like the crown of a person's head. The stage of patience is advancing, while the stage of heat is retreating;

this summit is the boundary between both advancing and retreating, just like the peak of a mountain. Therefore, it is named "Summit. (△ [According to the *Miaoxuan*]: The semblance-understanding increases further, like ascending the peak of a mountain and surveying the four quarters with complete clarity. Therefore, it is so named.)

The Stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*). Furthermore, it should be called the "Lower Summit" (*adho-mūrdhan*): because it is at the summit of the stage of the Soft (*mṛdu-dharma*), it is named "Summit"; because it is below the stage of Patience (*kṣānti-dharma*), it is called "Lower. Others say: it is like the path on a mountain peak where a person does not stay long;

if there are no obstacles, one will certainly pass beyond this and reach that [other side], but if one encounters obstacles, one immediately retreats. The practitioner dwells upon the summit for but a short time: if there are no obstacles, they will certainly reach Patience; if there are obstacles, they retreat to Heat (*uṣmagata*). It is thus named "Summit" because it is like a mountain peak. (The Three Stages of Patience).
Mind and Buddha are identical; one skillfully attains the Middle Way. Like a person who endures an offense, neither destroying nor escaping it, this is called the Stage of Patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
[Commentary: Initially, the characteristics of the cause have not yet been extinguished; subsequently, the characteristics of the fruit have not yet been extinguished.

Now, the two characteristics of cause and fruit are fused into a single essence; therefore, it is said that "mind and Buddha are identical. [Liu Yi says: To take the Buddha’s awakening-function as one's own mind is for the Buddha and the mind to be identical. One's own mind is that which the Buddha has traversed to achieve Buddhahood.]
This mind is identical to the Buddha. Since cause and effect have vanished, the two extremes do not stand; thus it is said that one has well attained the Middle Way.

As for the essence of this Middle Way, its realization is imminent, hence it is said "not harbored. Yet, because the conceptual mark of the Middle Way has not yet been extinguished, it is said "not emerged.

This is explained by way of manifesting the principle. (Haiyin says: Because the observing wisdom is about to dissolve, it is "not harbored"; because the conditioned shadows have not yet been severed, it is "not emerged. (△)

[Wu-xing says: "Endurance (kṣānti) carries the meaning of trustful compliance. When the mind and the Buddha are equal, that is trustful compliance. It is like when affairs are being transacted within the Saṃgha: one endures by remaining silent; neither harboring doubt nor speaking out. [Ō-i says:

"With complete clarity in one's breast, there is no further doubt; one knows it solely for oneself, without having anything to say. This uses the bodhi and nirvāṇa of the first bhūmi as a metaphor for the matter endured. [The section separately clarifies the stage of endurance. The *Abhidharmakośa* says: "From the Summit... ]

The arising of wholesome roots is called *dharmakṣānti* (receptivity to the Dharma). Because it is most preeminent in its acceptance of the Four Noble Truths, and because there is no longer any regression, it is termed the "Dharma of Receptivity" (*kṣāntidharma*). (The *Miaoxuan* states: This is also the increase of semblance-understanding; the five kinds of wholesome dharmas advance and become roots.

Within the context of the Four Truths, it signifies the capacity for receptivity and the aspiration [for realization], which is also the meaning of "acceptance"). (This is the fourth stage: the Stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharmas).

The categories of number are extinguished. Delusion and awakening are the two; the Middle Way is the one. These two have no objective referent, which is called the "World-First Ground" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
[Commentary]: Delusion and awakening are the two, which refers to the causes. The Middle Way is the one, which is the principle realized. This is what is meant by "number.
Since neither the middle nor the extremes exist, it is said that "the two have no objective referent. Because there is no objective referent, it is termed "extinguished" (*kṣaya*).

Extinction. [Wenling says: Previously, it was said that the two are identical; this already falls into the realm of numerical quantity (*saṃkhyā*). To perceive a distinction between existence and non-existence, or between delusion and awakening, is to forcibly differentiate them; now both are extinguished, and even their names no longer stand. Numerical quantity properly belongs to the mundane world.
Although it is now extinguished, if one looks toward the realization of truth at the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is still termed "semblance" because there is still something attained.
The Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the first stage is called supramundane (*lokottara*); the present state is the ultimate limit of the mundane world.

Therefore, it is called "the foremost" (surpassing the three stages of worthiness; thus it is named the Worldly Foremost. If one advances to the ten stages of the sages and reaches the ultimate state of wondrous enlightenment, this is the supramundane foremost stage).

[Haiyin says: In a general sense, regarding principle, practice, realization, and eradication, all are simultaneously extinguished; hence it is said that "measure and number are eliminated. Even the ten stages of faith still deludedly take things as existing, while the three stages of worthiness belong to awakening and take them as empty. Reaching this Middle Way, where all is extinguished and there is no place for reliance, only then is there the potential for the supramundane, which is named the Worldly Foremost.

By observing the stages of the three worthies from this perspective, one sees that they universally employ the wisdom of Middle Way contemplation to illuminate the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), which manifests according to its varying degrees of shallowness and depth. Based on this, the sequence is clarified; one knows that this is not a partial severance or a partial realization.]

(Also). (A separate explanation of the Supreme Worldly Dharma). [The *Myōgen* states: "The stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) is precisely the single moment of the highest patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*). Among ordinary persons, it is the attainment of the most excellent wholesome root; therefore, it is named the Supreme Worldly Dharma."

This mental application of the mind is the most supreme, the most excellent, the longest, the most venerable, the highest, and the most sublime among all other dharmas—or, as some say, it is preeminent above all else—not because it is superior among all worldly undertakings, but simply because it can open the gateway to the Noble Path.

The *Shiqian* states: "This is contaminated (*sāsrava*), and therefore it is called 'mundane' (*laukika*). Because it is the most excellent among them, it is called 'foremost' (*agra*). (△ [*Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*]: "The Supreme Mundane Dharma marks the beginning of the Noble Path and the end of the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).")

[Commentary] These four stages above are explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Regarding the first two stages, based on the two meditative concentrations of *ālokalabdha* (attainment of light) and *vṛddhāloka* (increase of light), one initiates the contemplations of *vitarka* (investigation) and *vicāra* (analysis) to observe the four dharmas, beginning with "name" (*nāman*).

Both subject and object are empty. (The *Śāstra*’s explanation of the characteristics of *uṣmagata* states: "Based on the concentration of *ālokalabdha*, one initiates the lower contemplation of *vitarka*; because there is no 'appropriated object' (*grāhya*), it is established as the stage of *uṣmagata*.

This means that within this stage, one first observes that the four dharmas—name and so forth—which constitute the 'appropriated object,' are all transformations of one's own mind. They are provisionally designated as existing for the sake of discourse, but in reality they cannot be found. One has for the first time obtained the precursor to the sun of wisdom.")

It is because it is a precursor (*pūrvanimitta*) that it is established as "attainment of clarity" (*ālokalabdha*). Since this is the precursor to the fire of the Path attained therein, it is also called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Regarding the "attainment of clarity," the *Saṃgrahaṇī* states: "Clarity" (*āloka*) refers to the wisdom (*jñāna*) that illuminates the absence of objective referents;

because the sought-after fruit is accomplished, it is called "attainment. Qingliang says: "Attainment of clarity is concentration (*samādhi*); thorough investigation (*vitarka*) is wisdom (*prajñā*); therefore, it is said 'to give rise to' [it]. Regarding the "contemplation of thorough investigation," the treatise speaks of the "inferior grade of the contemplation of thorough investigation," which refers to the four types of thorough investigation.

These investigate the four factors—name, object, self-nature, and distinction—as being conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent, each being empty. The text for the subsequent "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) stage is largely the same. Regarding the phrase "relying on the concentration of increased clarity" (*vṛddhāloka*), it is because the signs of clarity have become more intense. Regarding "thorough investigation," it is called the "superior grade. Regarding the "contemplation of phenomena," it is said:

"Re-observation" (chóngguān) refers to the meaning of "superiority" (zēngshàng) in all cases. Regarding the latter two stages, one relies on the two concentrations of "sealing" (yìn) and "conforming" (shùn) to give rise to the four kinds of "correct observation as it is" (rúshí guān).

These seal the two types of emptiness [of person and phenomena] discussed previously. The *Śāstra* states regarding the characteristics of "patience" (rěn): "Relying on the concentrations of sealing and conforming, one gives rise to the lower grade of 'knowledge as it is' (rúshí zhì). One definitively seals and maintains [the realization] that there is no object of apprehension (*grāhya*). Within the absence of a subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*), one likewise conforms to and delights in patience.

Since there is no real objective realm, apart from the consciousness that apprehends, how could there be a real consciousness? When one seals and conforms during the stage of patience—having abandoned the grasping consciousness because there is no grasped object—it is collectively designated as 'patience. It is called 'sealing and conforming' because it seals what precedes and conforms to what follows. Because the objects and the consciousness are empty, it is termed patience."

It is also called "patience" (*kṣānti*). Qingliang says: "There are three grades of patience. The lower grade is called 'seal-patience' (*mudrā-kṣānti*), because that which is grasped is non-existent. The middle grade is called 'joyful compliance' (*anuloma-rati*), because there is no grasper, and one complies with that cultivation. The upper grade is called 'seal-compliance' (*mudrā-anuloma*), because one seals the non-existence of the grasper and complies with the contemplation of that [object].

Therefore, it is said: 'At the time of seal-compliance patience,' the general name 'patience' is established. When both seal and compliance are fixed, it is called 'seal-compliance concentration' (*mudrā-anuloma-samādhi*). Patience is itself wisdom; it is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is. These four are free from conditions, and consciousness is not existent."

It is called "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Because one has for the first time attained the fruit of knowledge as it truly is, it is designated as "lower. Next, it says: relying on the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*), one gives rise to superior knowledge as it truly is, which seals the emptiness of both [subject and object] of grasping, thereby establishing the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

This means that while the preceding "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) only sealed the emptiness of the grasper, the present Supreme Mundane Dharma seals the emptiness of both simultaneously. Immediately following this, one necessarily enters the Path of Seeing; thus it is given the name "immediate" (*ānantarya*). Because it is the most excellent among the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
However, all of these involve "attainment" (*upalambha*) and have not yet realized the Dharmakāya; therefore, it says: "Because there is attainment, it is not a true abiding in the 'only' (*mātra*)."

Consciousness (*vijñāna*). (The *Śāstra*’s general explanation states: "In this way, from 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*) onwards, one relies on the grasping consciousness (*grāhaka-vijñāna*) to contemplate the emptiness of the grasped (*grāhya*). When 'Lower Patience' (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) arises, one confirms the empty aspect of the object. At the stage of 'Middle Patience' (*madhya-kṣānti*), one accords with and accepts that the grasping consciousness is empty just as the object is.

When 'Upper Patience' (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) arises, one confirms the emptiness of the grasper. At the stage of the 'Supreme Mundane Dharmas' (*laukikāgradharma*), one doubly confirms the empty aspect. Because all these still carry mental images (*nimitta*), they have not yet realized the truth.

Therefore, it is said that within these four stages, the Bodhisattva still establishes a slight entity before them, claiming it to be the true ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Since the two aspects of emptiness and existence have not yet been eliminated, their contemplative mind still carries images and possesses attainment; thus, they do not truly abide in the principle of true representation-only. Only when those images have ceased does one truly [abide therein]. )

[The text] reads: "Abiding in tranquility. The ancient commentary *Qīngliáng yǐn* states: "That which transforms upon the mind into a semblance is called a 'slight object' (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*). This is not without characteristics; therefore, it is termed 'possessing characteristics' (*sanimitta*). When one realizes the Truth (*tattva*), those characteristics are extinguished. These 'characteristics' are precisely the characteristics of the objects grasped by emptiness (*śūnyatā-grāhya-lakṣaṇa*)."

There is the characteristic of dependence, called the "state where emptiness and existence coexist. This refers to the characteristic of emptiness and existence, which is the true ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) of that very consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). Because this characteristic exists, as long as one has not yet realized the True Principle, one must eliminate the characteristics of emptiness and existence before one can realize *tathatā*.
These [explanations] are all discourses on distinct stages. However, the present sutra is characterized by perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) without obstructing sequential arrangement (*xingbu*);

therefore, it is possible to explain the perfect by way of the distinct. For this reason, this stage is named "the Worldly" (*laukika*). [Zhengzhen says: Sūtras such as the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Ratnavali-sūtra*) do not list the four preparatory stages (*prayoga-avasthā*). Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*...]

The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (or similar treatise) designates the forty minds prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) as the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) of the provisionary stage (*sambhāra-mārga*). The ten [four] directions (*daśacaturmukha*) and subsequent stages, specifically named "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, are designated as the stage of the internal ordinary person (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*) of the preparatory stage (*prayoga-mārga*).

This present sutra is exactly as described therein. That division of the stages prior to the *bhūmis* into internal and external ordinary persons is the doctrine of one particular path within the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*). This is because ascending to the *bhūmis* constitutes the noble stage (*āryabhūmi*) of a Bodhisattva; since the noble stage is difficult to enter, this preparatory stage is opened up. In this sutra, the terminology of the Separate Teaching is borrowed for the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), as the *Renyō-kyō* (Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra) states:

"The three worthies and ten sages abide in the fruition and retribution. This refers to the marvelous, perfect preparatory practice (*prayoga*), which distinguishes it from the partial and small vehicles. (△ [Ming-shu says: In the Perfect Teaching of Tiantai, from the initial stage of "True Entry" (*praveśasatya*) up to the "Wonderful Enlightenment" (*miao-jue*), there are forty-two positions that collectively destroy forty-two grades of delusion.)

[The *Ming* (Exposition) states: "Now, regarding the establishment of the stages of the sages (*ārya*) in this sutra, the ignorance (*avidyā*) to be destroyed is for the most part the same [as in other systems]. Although the four stages of application (*prayoga*) are divided into four, they should collectively be subsumed under a single category of the first stage (*bhūmi*), because it is precisely after the stage of ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) that one directly destroys the ignorance of the first stage.

The commentary explains: "Although previously the ten categories of ignorance regarding the characteristics of abiding and ceasing within the distinct dwelling were severed, there remain twelve categories of ignorance regarding the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*). Among these, the first category is the most difficult to sever; therefore, one further gives rise to the four kinds of wondrous and perfect application (*prayoga*) to collectively sever this single category of ignorance of arising and ascend to the first stage.

Zibo says: "The three subtleties (*sūkṣma*) serve as the root of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kāma*) and the dust-sand (*rajas*) delusions. In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, these are categorized into forty-two categories and treated accordingly. The sutra speaks of arising, abiding, change..."

This refers to the number of stages in the process of cessation. Some claim that from the stage of abiding through the stage of heading toward practice (*pratipannaka-bhūmi*), there are forty-two positions, each of which possesses its own superior progress in cultivation. They argue that the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*) are established not merely for the sake of destroying ignorance, for it is only by permanently severing ignorance that one attains the Buddha-way.

Apart from destroying ignorance, what further superior progress in cultivation could there be? In the *Avataṃsaka*’s ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), each stage involves the severance of hindrances and the realization of suchness (*tathatā*). How could it be that in the four preparatory stages one should not sever even a single grade of ignorance?
(Above were the four stages of applied practice. (The scripture states:
"It is like a precious moon suspended within lapis lazuli. The Qian Dao edition reads: "a bright moon suspended within.")

([○@●] The Seventy Stages of Practice) (○ [Combined Explanation] [Tiantai says: The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the untainted, true illumination. Entering the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*), they are like the great earth, capable of producing all Buddha-dharmas and bearing the burden of sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu*.

They universally enter the Buddha-stages of the three periods of time. Furthermore, one realizes ten successive levels of wisdom and severance, destroying ten successive layers of ignorance; therefore, they are called the "Ten Stages. (○ [Qingliang’s Commentary on the Ten Stages] says: Now, merit is never established in vain; it must ultimately have its destination.)

The preceding section has concluded the explanation of the causes for the stages of the Sages (*ārya-bhūmi*), which consist of understanding, practice, and vows. Now begins the explanation of the wisdom that realizes the true suchness (*tathatā*), wherein the fruits of the Sage-stages are established. This sequence follows the logical order of cause first and fruit later. "Understanding" refers to the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*); "practice" refers to the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*); and "vows" refers to the ten transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Therefore, this concludes the section on the Worthy Ones (*śaikṣa*). Because they have personally realized the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), the stages of the Sages (*ārya*) are clarified. The sequence from the former Worthy Ones to the latter Sages follows a logical progression. Furthermore, the preceding stage is the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*), while this is the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*);

teaching serves as the cause for realization, and realization is precisely the realization of the teachings concerning the three minds—namely, the direct, profound, and great compassionate *bodhicitta*. In the three stages of the Worthy, these are increased individually; herein, they are realized simultaneously. Regarding the term "ground" (*bhūmi*), the *Mūla-karma-siddhi-śāstra* states: "The meaning of 'ground' is 'to sustain. It sustains millions of *asaṃkhyeya* merits;

it is also called that which generates and completes all causes and effects. The *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* states: "Because it generates and sustains Buddha-wisdom, it is called a ground. This is the same meaning. Furthermore, the third [meaning] in the *Mūla-karma-siddhi-śāstra* is "abiding. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "All ten are places of abiding; therefore, they are called grounds. Fourth, regarding "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*), it is common to...

Because one anticipates the fruit, as in the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), one is able to sustain all merits of both self and others, and furthermore sustain all merits from the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*) up to the fruit of Buddhahood. If the first stage did not exist, the others would not be established. (The *Huayan lun* states:

"The Tathāgata, by means of the Wisdom of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*), establishes the essence of the stages (*bhūmi-tattva*). Although the various Bodhisattvas have ascended through the ten dwellings, the ten practices, and the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), they do not depart from this essence;

therefore, it is called the 'ten stages' (*daśabhūmi*). This dharma of the ten stages takes the ten fruits of Buddhahood taught in the Hall of Universal Radiance as the initial faith (*prathama-śraddhā*); thus, even when the five positions (*pañca-sthāna*) are fulfilled, one does not depart from the Buddha-fruit of initial faith. By means of this dharma of the ten stages, one penetrates from beginning to end, reaching a single limit.")

This is the Dharma-gate; therefore, it is called the "Ten Grounds" (daśabhūmi). When the fruits of the ten grounds are completed, merit is exhausted and practice is matured, such that there is no further advancement. Because the wisdom of the ten grounds is perfected and there is nothing further to cultivate, one constantly faces all Buddhas as they appear before one. This is the gate of the ten grounds.

However, within the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*), ten practices (*daśacaryā*), and ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), one accumulates merit until it reaches completion and becomes thoroughly matured. Thereafter, there is no further dwelling; things are accomplished spontaneously and naturally, such that all dharmas are fully perfected. The ten abidings and ten practices are metaphorically represented as being like spirits;

the stage of the ten dedications is metaphorically represented as being like a king; and these ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*) are metaphorically represented as being like devas. This clarifies that through gradual cultivation and practice, one attains increasingly superior mastery. [Master Zhang Wujin said: "In Master Li’s treatise, both the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*) and the ultimate teachings (*nītārtha*) each have three types of ten grounds.

The provisional teachings refer to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Renwang). The ultimate teachings refer to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Since Master Li had not yet seen the present sutra [the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*], Changqing judged its ten grounds to belong to the ultimate teachings. Now...

Examining this scripture in detail, it states that in the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the practice reaches its ultimate completion and its functional efficacy becomes perfected; thus, this stage is also designated as the "Stage of Cultivation" (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). Having scrutinized various sūtras and śāstras, it is found that only the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* accords with this.

From the fourth stage onward, one cultivates the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) up to the ninth stage; although there is cultivation in each successive stage, it remains incomplete until the tenth stage, when cultivation is perfected and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) becomes vast, like clouds covering everything.

"The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are the flames of wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), which can perfect the True Dharma and illuminate the wisdom of the teachings. This is here termed 'the dwelling in superior wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment' (*bodhipakṣa-saṃprayukta-adhiprajñā-vihāra*). (5. The Stage Difficult to Conquer, *Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).
Because it cannot be surpassed by any sameness or difference, it is called the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*).

[Commentary: Because true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) is unique, it is called "sameness"; because conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) possesses distinctions, it is called "difference. (Wuxing says: The wisdom attained upon reaching the grounds is called "sameness.")

The wisdom prior to the stages (bhūmi) consists of two distinct types of wisdom regarding the ultimate and the conventional; their modes of activity are mutually contradictory, yet they are brought into correspondence. (These three phrases following "ultimate and conventional" are from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*).
Because they are neither identical nor different, it is said that [this state] is "that which cannot be reached"; it is supremely excellent, and there is nothing superior to it.

Therefore, it is called "Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: Because the wisdom of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*) and worldly wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) are mutually contradictory, one must unite these two that are difficult to combine and bring them into correspondence.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* agrees with this. Vasubandhu’s commentary explains: Because within this stage, the wisdom of ultimate truth is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), while the wisdom of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is conceptual wisdom (*savikalpa-jñāna*), these two are contradictory; one should cultivate them so as to be united. Because it can unite what is difficult to unite and bring them into correspondence, it is named "Extremely Difficult to Conquer.

[The *Fǎshù* says: Prior to this stage is "Blazing Wisdom," which incinerates all marks of emotional views regarding identity and difference; it is the realm of the Buddhas, which nothing can surpass. This stage realizes the category of...
Non-differentiated *tathatā* (suchness). This means that this suchness is not like the eye and other [faculties], because it does not possess distinct categories.
It severs the obstacle to the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle. Through the cultivation of the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, it becomes preeminent. [The Commentary on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:

"Regarding the severance of the obstacle to the *parinirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle within this stage—namely, the four preceding stages where one transcends the world, grows weary of the suffering of birth and death, and seeks to enter *nirvāṇa*—this obstacle pertains to the fifth stage. Now, by entering the path of the non-differentiation between the ultimate and the conventional, one is able to sever it. This severance of longing for and aversion to [saṃsāra and nirvāṇa] constitutes two delusions (*moha*). Because...

Regarding this fifth stage (*bhūmi*), it is said that two types of delusion (*moha*) along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) are abandoned: first, the delusion of exclusively directing mental attention (*manasikāra*) away from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), which refers here to those who are weary of birth-and-death; second, the delusion of exclusively directing mental attention toward nirvāṇa, which refers here to those who delight in nirvāṇa.

By means of this, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) in which there is no differentiation of categories, because both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are equal, thereby establishing the absence of categorical distinction. Vasubandhu states: "This *tathatā* is not like the eyes and so forth, which differ individually according to the differences in the mental continuums (*saṃtati*) of various sentient beings.

[The Commentary on the Name states: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter forty-eight, speaks of the "Abiding in Superior Wisdom Corresponding to the Truths" (*satyapratisaṃyukta-adhiprajñā-vihāra*), saying: "In this present stage, it is shown how the Bodhisattva, regarding all noble..."

The Truth. It is the definitive, sublime wisdom that is extremely difficult to surpass; thus it is called the "Difficult-to-Conquer" (*Sudurjayā*) stage. The *Mūla-śāstra* states: "Because one attains supramundane wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), and is able to cross over what is difficult to cross, it is named 'Difficult-to-Conquer.

This means that because the ultimate and the conventional are non-contradictory and are extremely difficult to master, [the previous stages] could not yet transcend them. The third stage remains within the mundane world and has not yet emerged from it; the fourth stage, although it has emerged, cannot yet follow [the conventional], for it frequently stagnates in the two extremes and is difficult to transcend.

Now, having attained the supramundane while also being able to follow the conventional, and having skillfully mastered the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*) such that the ultimate and the conventional are non-contradictory, one is able to cross over all stagnation. Because this is truly difficult to conquer, and because it is first attained here, it specifically receives this name. The Sūtra says: "For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, there is no worldly art or craft that this Bodhisattva does not study," and so forth.

In jest and in conversation, he excels in all such matters. Through his skillful means and wisdom, he is able to transcend and emerge from the world. Is this not surely the case for those from the sixth bhūmi upward? Therefore, it is explained in detail: "This is because it is first attained [at this stage]. (The Sixth Bhūmi, the Stage of Presence).
Unconditioned *tathatā* (suchness), its nature pure, luminous, and manifest, is called the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
[Commentary] This means that by abiding in the wisdom of causes and conditions, one draws forth the most supreme non-conceptual *prajñā*, causing it to become manifest before one.

Because both wisdom and principle become manifest, it is said: "Unconditioned *tathatā*, its nature pure, luminous, and manifest. [Wenling says: The pure nature of *tathatā* is consistently neither identical nor different.]

When obscurations are removed and distinctions no longer arise, then clarity is revealed before one. On this stage, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that is intrinsically untainted and pure; for this *tathatā* is by nature undefiled, and it cannot be said that it becomes pure only later.
One abandons the obstacle of the active manifestation of coarse characteristics (*sthūla-nimitta-pravṛtti-āvaraṇa*) and cultivates the *prajñāpāramitā* with increasing excellence.

[The Commentary on the Stages (*Dìshù*) states: The obstacle of the active manifestation of coarse characteristics is termed "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*). This refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) aspect of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).

The coarse manifestations of defilement and purity obstruct the sixth stage. Upon entering the sixth stage, one is able to permanently sever them, as there is no longer a path of defilement or purity. For this reason, it is said that in the sixth stage one abandons two delusions along with their corresponding heavy habitual tendencies (*dauṣṭhulya*):

First, the delusion of observing the flow of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being subject to transmigration; this refers to the grasping at a "defiled agent" herein, because the transmigration of conditioned phenomena is subsumed under the category of the defiled portion. Second, the delusion of the frequent manifestation of signs; this refers to the grasping at a "pure agent" within this stage, because one apprehends pure signs. Consequently, the observation of signs frequently manifests.

One is unable to abide for long in the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*). The former delusion consists in clinging to suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*); the latter delusion consists in clinging to cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga*). What is termed "the habit-energies of subtle afflictions" (*sūkṣma-kleśa-vāsanā*) in the fundamental section refers to the clinging to subtle defilement and purity;

this is itself an affliction. Compared to the preceding stage, it is called "subtle. Because it takes consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) as its object, it is termed a "coarse characteristic. By severing this delusion, one realizes the true knowledge that is neither defiled nor pure. As the *Vyākhyāyukti* (or *Sphuṭārthā*) establishes, this is also subsumed under the text of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*; in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is called the "dharma-realm that is neither defiled nor pure" (*akliṣṭa-anāsrava-dharmadhātu*).

"Subsequently, one accomplishes the practice of Prajñā. (The *Vyākhyā* explains the name as follows: "It is called 'manifesting before one' because the wisdom of contemplation that does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa manifests before one. This refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*), for it is from the first five stages onward that one contemplates both simultaneously, and now [this wisdom] has become manifest.

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: 'After the task of subduing Māra is completed, all the dharmas of the Bodhisattva path manifest before one. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, citing the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*, says: 'One observes the flow and turning of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) manifestly, and only after extensively cultivating mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward the signless (*animitta*) does it manifest before one.

Regarding 'extensively cultivating mental attention,' this refers to the stage prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi-pūrvaka*), as one contemplates the ten kinds of equality. Regarding 'observing the flow and turning,' this refers to within the stages, for once one has entered the stream, one then contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Thus, the root treatise says:").

The practice of *prajñāpāramitā* is intermittent because the Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*) manifests before one. That is to say, skillfully penetrating dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and inducing non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*) is called the practice of *prajñā*. Because it is as if directly perceived before the eyes, it is termed "manifesting before one" (*abhimukha*).

It is called "intermittent" (*sāntara*) in contrast to what follows, for the seventh [ground] is constantly in contemplation. In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, this is also called the "Abiding in Superior Wisdom Corresponding to Dependent Origination" (*pratītyasamutpādapratisaṃyuktādhiprajñāvihāra*). (The Seventh Ground: Dūraṃgamā).
Reaching the limit of the reality-limit (*tathatā*) is called the Far-Reaching Ground (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).

[Commentary: Because in the eighth ground one attains the mind of the single *tathatā*, which is termed "signless" (*animitta*) and "effortless" (*anābhoga*), this seventh ground—from the initial generation of the bodhicitta through two incalculable eons—has involved the application of effortful practice; now, having reached the stage where signs still persist, it is termed "effortful."

It employs the latter [limit], because it transcends the worldly paths of the two vehicles. (In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the seventh is called the "Abode of the Signless with Application and Effort," and the eighth is called the "Abode of the Signless without Application or Effort.
Because one reaches the ultimate limit of the signlessness of suchness (*tathatā*) at this point, it is said that "one exhausts the limit of suchness."

Because one has practiced for many *kalpas*, it is called "Far-Going" (*dūramgamā*). [Wuxing says: "To reach the limit of *tathatā* (Suchness) is the limit of the limitless. Since the principle is already limitless, how could the practice be anything but near? (△ Wēnlíng says: "When *tathatā* manifests before one, partial realization is limited;

reaching the ultimate limit is 'far'. (△ Hǎiyìn says: "Co-nascent ignorance is termed 'Far-Going. Reaching the limit of *tathatā* and having already abandoned the *ālayavijñāna* is called the 'Far-Going Stage' (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*).
One realizes the *tathatā* that is non-differentiated among all phenomena; that is to say, although there are many teachings regarding this *tathatā*, they are established in various ways.
Established [in the seventh stage], because there is no differentiation, one eliminates the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle characteristics (*sūkṣma-nimitta-pravṛtti-āvaraṇa*).

Through the cultivation of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), practice becomes increasingly superior. [The Commentary on the Stages (*Bhūmi-vyākhyā*) states: "The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: 'The seven obstacles of the manifestation of subtle characteristics' refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Upon entering the seventh stage, they can be permanently severed.

For this reason, it is said that in the seventh stage one abandons two delusions (*moha*) along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*): first, the delusion of the manifestation of subtle characteristics; this refers to the grasping at the subtle characteristic of the flow of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in the sixth stage. Second, the pure..."*]

The delusion of seeking the signless through mental attention (*manasikāra*) arises because one still clings to the existence of subtle residual signs. Due to this clinging to cessation, one further seeks the signless. There are two kinds of signs: first, existence; second, non-existence. That which is non-existent is "subtle," because by constantly abiding in the signless, one does not cling to arising and no longer applies mental attention to diligently seek the signless.

Thus, one is able to realize the *tathatā* (suchness) that is without differentiation among phenomena. [The commentary on] the *Vyākhyāyukti* (or the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*), which is also a text on Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), states:

"It means that although all the teachings of the Dharma are established based upon suchness, because suchness is without difference... [The *Śāstra* explains the name, saying: Regarding the term "far-reaching" (*dūramgama*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "Upon reaching the stage of the Signless (*animitta-vihāra*), at the very end of effortful practice, one transcends the paths of the world and the two vehicles. This has three meanings. First, skillfully cultivating the signless.

It is called "Far-Reaching" (Dūramgamā) for three reasons: first, because it reaches the limit of the signless (*animitta*); second, because the effortful application (*prayoga*) has reached its ultimate; and third, because it surpasses what preceded it. There are two general interpretations: First, from the perspective of the preceding stages, one has reached the limit of effortful application. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Although in the previous stage one could dwell extensively in the mental attention of the signless, one was not yet able to cultivate this signless mental attention in a state that is uninterrupted and flawless. To bring this to fulfillment [this stage is established]. Second, from the perspective of the culmination of this effort, one is able to travel far toward subsequent stages. Thus the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* further states:

"One is able to realize and enter the signless mental attention—flawless and uninterrupted—which is in immediate proximity to the pure stages (*viśuddha-bhūmi*). Therefore, it is called "Far-Reaching. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "It is distant from the triple world (*tridhātu*) and near to..."
Because it is the station of the Dharma King, it is called the "Distant Ground. [The Eighth: Immovable Ground.
Because the mind of true suchness is immovable, it is called the Immovable Ground.

[Commentary]: It is neither defiled nor pure; therefore, it is called "One. It is free from all delusions and falsehoods; therefore, it is called "True" (*tathatā*). It is eternally abiding and unchanging;

therefore, it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). From this perspective, it is termed "Immovable. [Wenling says]: Having attained its limit, one then fully attains its essence. Being singular, true, concentrated, and constant, it is named "Immovable.

[Haiyin says]: Pure and singular *tathatā* does not depend on effort; it forever transcends movement and agitation. This profound stillness of the one mind is named "Immovable. [Chūkan says]: [This] refers to joy...

From the stage of Joy up to the stage of Blazing Wisdom, one gradually distances oneself from defilements. From the stage of Difficult to Conquer up to the stage of Immovability, one gradually manifests the reality. At these stages, there is pure and singular *tathatā* (suchness), for it is fundamentally immovable. Furthermore, within this stage:
Non-conceptual wisdom is called "immovable" because its spontaneous continuity cannot be disturbed by the characteristics or functions of the afflictions.

On this stage, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) of neither increase nor decrease; that is to say, this *tathatā* is free from the grasping at increase or decrease, as it does not undergo increase or decrease in accordance with defilement or purity.
One abandons the obstacle of applying effort toward the signless (*animitta*) and cultivates the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states: Among the eight types of signlessness (*animitta*), there is an obstacle consisting of the application of effort (*prayoga*). This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that prevents the contemplation of signlessness from arising spontaneously.

In the first five stages (*bhūmi*), contemplation with signs (*sanimitta*) is frequent while contemplation without signs is rare; in the sixth stage, contemplation with signs is rare while contemplation without signs is frequent; and in the seventh stage, there is exclusively continuous contemplation without signs.

Nevertheless, because this involves the application of effort within signlessness, it is not yet spontaneous. Consequently, one is unable to manifest forms and lands effortlessly. This constitutes an obstacle to the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*) in the eighth stage. Upon entering the eighth stage, this is permanently severed. For this reason, the eighth stage is said to eliminate two delusions and their corresponding gross [afflictions].

[This section concerns] two types of delusion: first, the delusion regarding the exertion of effort toward the signless; second, the delusion regarding mastery over the signless, which prevents one from attaining mastery within signs. The *tathatā* (suchness) realized therein is called the "unincreasing and undiminishing *tathatā*. It is also termed the "*tathatā* that is the basis for mastery over signs and lands.

Once a bodhisattva has attained this *tathatā*, they manifest both signs and lands with equal mastery. (As the *Sūtra on the Eighth Stage* states: "When this bodhisattva enters into all phenomena as being like the nature of space, their initial, middle, and final wisdoms are entirely equal.

Because they enter by means of non-conceptual *tathatā*-wisdom, this is called attaining the 'patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas' (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). When a bodhisattva accomplishes this patience, they enter the eighth stage, the Immovable (*Acalā*), and immediately relinquish all...

Regarding effort: having attained the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*), the activities of body, speech, and mind, as well as all mental applications, have completely ceased. Abiding in the stage of fruition and practice (*vipākacaryā*), even the Buddha-mind, the Bodhicitta, and the Nirvāṇa-mind do not manifest; how much less would worldly thoughts arise?

Due to the power of this Bodhisattva’s original vow, the Buddhas exhort him, after which he manifests the ten bodies. He attains great mastery. [The Commentary states: The first three stages correspond to the mundane world; the subsequent four stages correspond to the teachings of the Three Vehicles.

From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, [the teaching] is provisionally presented as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Commentary on the Ornament) states in its seventh chapter: "Because it is proximate to the One Vehicle. The Liang dynasty commentary also explains that from the eighth stage upward, it is regarded as the One Vehicle.

Thus, we know that one enters the One Vehicle by transcending the preceding distinctions. Regarding the term "immovable" (*acala*): the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states it refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), because it continues spontaneously and cannot be moved by the afflictions of its characteristics and functions. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "Due to signlessness (*animitta*), one attains effortlessness (*anābhoga*);

among all phenomena, one is not moved by active afflictions (*kleśa*). The root treatise states: "Retributive conduct is fully matured; because it is signless and uninterrupted, it is called 'immovable'. This also has three meanings: first, having abandoned the conduct of birth within the triple world, one receives the fruit of transformation (*pariṇāmika-śarīra*); hence it is so called.

1. Regarding "retribution-driven activity" (*vipākacaryā*): because one initiates activity based on this [state], it is accomplished spontaneously; therefore, it is unmoved by effortful application (*prayoga*). 2. Having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) and the sublime wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*), one is then unmoved by signs (*nimitta*).

3. Immediately following these two, one is unmoved by afflictions (*kleśa*). These three points constitute a single meaning: namely, that in the preceding stage, having already attained the state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), neither signs nor afflictions can cause movement. While previously one was moved by effortful application and thus lacked the name "unmoving," now, due to effortlessness, the contemplation of signlessness proceeds spontaneously and uninterruptedly;

therefore, the three cannot cause movement. (From the *Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses*: "Before the Immovable Ground, the storehouse is just abandoned. Commentary: This means that from beginningless time until the limit of the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), the *ālayavijñāna* is termed the "storehouse consciousness" (*vijñānagarbha*). Upon attaining... [text ends]

Ascending to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), afflictions are forever suppressed; they no longer receive its perfuming (*vāsanā*). Because one no longer clings to a self in the seven [consciousnesses], the name "Tripiṭaka" (*sanzang*) is abandoned from this point onward. Qingliang says: "Abiding in the practice of retribution" means abiding well within the *tathatā* (suchness) of the *ālayavijñāna*.

Since the fundamental consciousness has two divisions—the first being the deluded, defiled division where ordinary beings abide, and the second being the true, pure division where this stage abides—one abandons the name "ālaya" by virtue of abiding in *tathatā*.

The Treatise states: "It is abandoned at the stage of the Arhat," because in the Mahāyāna, the eighth stage is equivalent to the Arhat, as one abandons the coarse, segmented existence (*pariccheda-śarīra*) and emerges from the triple world (*tridhātu*). [The Ninth Stage: Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī*)]
The functioning of True Suchness (tathatā) is activated; this is called the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).

[Zizhong] states that the *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that this Bodhisattva possesses the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and acts as a Great Dharma Master, expounding the teachings for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas without the words or meanings ever being exhausted.
Therefore, it is called "the manifestation of the function of True Suchness.

[Commentary: Based on the essence of the principle of True Suchness, one gives rise to the function of unimpeded wisdom and accomplishes the four subtle and wondrous analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Because one is able to pervade the ten directions and skillfully expound the Dharma, it is called the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*). (The *Awakening of Faith* states:

"As for the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it refers to the fact that when the Buddhas and Tathāgatas were originally on the causal ground, they gave rise to great compassion to gather in and transform sentient beings. This means knowing, as they truly are, that all sentient beings and one's own body are equal in True Suchness, without any distinction.

Possessing such great wisdom of skillful means, they eliminate ignorance and perceive the original Dharma-body, whereby there spontaneously arise inconceivable karmic activities and various functions. (△ *Wenling* says: "Having already attained the true essence, one now manifests the true function. Whatever is reflected or responded to is entirely without falsehood.")

Because it is not surpassed, it is called "Excellent Wisdom" (*sādhumati*). In this stage, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) of mastery over knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā*). That is to say, once this *tathatā* has been realized, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are attained with mastery.

(In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, this is termed the Bodhisattva’s "Abode of Analytical Knowledge. These are: the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha*), the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

As the Sūtra says: "By means of immeasurable skillful wisdom, one gives rise to the four unhindered analytical knowledges. What are the four? Namely: the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of language, and [the analytical knowledge of] eloquence..."
The "unimpeded knowledge" (*pratisaṃvid*) refers to these four kinds. Having wisdom as its essence, it is called "mastery over wisdom. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"Because one has attained the supreme nature of unimpededness. As An-hui explains: "This means attaining the four supreme analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). The wisdom of analytical knowledge is the most excellent among all forms of wisdom. Since wisdom is itself insight (*prajñā*), it is called 'excellent wisdom' (*suvijñapti*).

It eliminates the obstacle of unwillingness to act within the gateway of benefiting others. It is the predominant factor in the cultivation of the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*). [The *Dìshū* states: "Therefore, the obstacles abandoned are those related to benefiting others."

The obstacle of lack of desire to act consists of four types because there are four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). The obstacle to these four analytical knowledges is divided into two. "Delusion" refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which causes one to lack the desire to apply oneself diligently to activities that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, instead delighting in cultivating one's own self-interest.

This obstacle pertains to the four analytical knowledges of the ninth stage; upon entering the ninth stage, it can be permanently severed. For this reason, it is said that the ninth stage severs two delusions along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dauṣṭhulya*).

First, the delusion regarding the subsequent analytical wisdom and mastery of *dhāraṇī* concerning immeasurable teachings, immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables. Here, "the teachings spoken" refers to the meaning (*artha*); "names, phrases, and syllables" refers to the phenomena (*dharma*); and "subsequent analytical wisdom" refers to the expression (*nirukti*). The delusion regarding mastery of *dhāraṇī* applies to all three of the aforementioned [analytical knowledges]. Second...

The absence of impediment regarding eloquence (*pratibhāna-asaṅga*) refers to the fourth absence of impediment. "Absence of impediment regarding eloquence" means the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*); it refers to being skillfully able to teach by thoroughly understanding the appropriate capacities [of listeners]. Ignorance (*avidyā*) can obstruct these four kinds of mastery (*vaśitā*).

The *tathatā* (suchness) that is realized is called the basis for mastery over knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā-adhiṣṭhāna*); this is because once one has realized this *tathatā*, one attains mastery over the analytical knowledges. (Also from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: [The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* says: "This bodhisattva falls into the *tathatā* of tranquil extinction.")

Because they do not relinquish this samādhi, the Buddhas of the ten directions preach the three bridges and nine exhortations before they arise from it. Emerging from the samādhi of True Suchness, they proceed from essence to function and immediately preach the Dharma as great Dharma masters. Even if it were the great trichiliocosm...

If one asks how deluded habitual tendencies arise in sentient beings, and what the nature of such arising is—according to the intent of the Tathāgata’s response—it is that sentient beings create karma through delusion and undergo birth through delusion; within the mind of Bodhi, these are like flowers in the sky.

The intention is for the Tathāgata to extensively clarify cause and effect; although both are illusory, the karmic conditions of good and evil and the resulting retributions of excellence or inferiority never deviate from their course.

Only when these preceding and succeeding parts complement one another is perfect realization achieved—this is precisely the meaning of the aforementioned "perfect understanding."
