Oil. Iron clubs with hazel-nut-shaped heads [strike them] until their skulls are shattered and their brains spill out, like breaking a jar of curd. They are hacked, pierced, cut, and flayed; their bodies are mangled and putrefied. Then they are led into the iron houses and towers, where black smoke billows and sears them. They push and trample one another, harboring mutual resentment and malice, each crying out, "Why are you pressing me down?

As soon as they wish to escape, the gates are already closed. Such are the various causes and conditions of this person’s past karma (*pūrvakṛta-karman*), and so forth—by these various causes and conditions, they undergo the retributions of the Raurava and Mahāraurava hells.
(III. Concluding the summary to clarify the gravity of the offense; in two parts. (I. Concluding that it is false and illusory.)
Ānanda, these are called the hells. These ten causes and six effects are all created by sentient beings through delusion and ignorance. [Commentary]:

To create karma through false delusion and to receive retribution through false delusion is all like flowers in the sky; yet, within cause and effect, there has never been any discrepancy. [The *Xunwen* says:

Among the sixfold mutual retributions, the Avīci Hell is cited as the primary example. Within it, the characteristics of the preceding seven hells and various minor hells are not absent. For instance, that which is induced by the habit-energy of greed is the eight cold hells.]

Furthermore, by consulting the Āgamas, the Abhidharmakośa, the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra, the Vibhāṣā, and other texts, one may fully understand these matters). (II. Specifically clarifying the gravity and lightness [of offenses]).
If there are sentient beings who, having collectively committed evil karma, enter the Avīci Hell and undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas.
[Commentary]: When the six sense faculties and ten causes are fully present, they collectively commit various karmas and enter the Avīci Hell, which is the Great Uninterrupted (Mahā-avīci) Hell.

It is the fulfillment of five matters (i.e., the section on "Aids"). (△ [Wenling says: Identical to the six faculties, they collectively produce ten causes; involving both objects and faculties, this is called the "collective production of evil karma.

(○ [Shiwen] states regarding "collective production of evil karma": the Qian Dao edition of the Song dynasty reads "the complete production of evil objects. Some explain that the ten causes arise together as a "complete production," meaning it is a fully perfected and most extreme evil karma.)

The six sense organs each perform their own actions, as well as those performed by others; when both the objects and the organs are involved together, such a person enters the Eight Uninterrupted Hells.

[Commentary: Just as the sixth consciousness is similar to the visual consciousness in that it only grasps its own object while simultaneously involving its organ, yet does not engage with other organs and lacks the ten causes—here, the six organs all act collectively, though at the time of acting, they do not involve the other organs.

They enter the eight hot hells; this is lighter than the preceding [retribution]. [Wuxing says: "In this case as well, all six sense organs collectively create the ten causes; however, because they occur at different times—earlier and later—it is said that they are 'separate'."

If a single sense organ encounters its object, it necessarily arises simultaneously with the mental consciousness; this is called "individual engagement" (*pratyeka-kṛta*). If two or three [organs] are added, it is called "simultaneous engagement" (*sādhāraṇa-viṣaya*), which refers to the simultaneous engagement of multiple organs.

Regarding the "Eight Uninterrupted Hells" (*aṣṭāv avīcya-narakāḥ*): they should be understood as being similar to the aforementioned hells. Since they do not require an incalculable number of *kalpas*, one knows that these offenses are slightly lighter than those preceding them. Furthermore, there is concern that the term "Eight Hells" may be used collectively to refer to all eight by taking the heavier to represent the light, thus naming them all "Uninterrupted.

In this case, those who do not possess the ten causes might fall into the first seven. (△ [Dinglin says]: If the evil committed has an objective event as its condition rather than the mind, then the object does not involve the organs. If it has the mind as its condition rather than an objective event, then the organs do not involve the objects. (△ [My own view]: Master Pan of the Tiantai school says: Since the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* already mentions *Avīci*, yet also lists [the Eight Uninterrupted Hells],...)

If that were the case, then Avīci would have to lie outside of the "Uninterrupted" (Avīci) realm. Now, examining the scriptural text: this passage states that those who "jointly commit evil karma enter the Avīci hell," which corresponds to the previous text stating that those of "pure emotion alone sink and enter the Avīci hell. As for those who "commit [evil] with each of the six sense organs,"...

They enter the Avīci Hell. This refers to the aforementioned nine types of beings with one thought of desire (*ekacittaka*), who, due to the lightness of their lives, fall into the *sāntarāya* (intermittent) hells, while those whose lives are grave fall into the *anantarāya* (uninterrupted) hells; these are the two kinds of hells. The distinction between the former and latter is precisely as Master Pan said.

According to various sūtras and śāstras, Avīci is the eighth of the five uninterrupted hells (*pañcānantarya-niraya*); there is no separate text that speaks of an Avīci outside of this. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the Avīci Hell, if a person among them commits one of the perversions (*ānantarya*), they shall possess such a single offense.

If they commit two perversions, the offense is doubled. If all five perversions are complete, the offense is fivefold. Furthermore, the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra* says: "The duration of suffering in Avīci for one day and night is equal to sixty minor kalpas of the human realm. Such is the lifespan [of its inhabitants]."

For the duration of one great kalpa, those who have committed the five heinous crimes (ānantarya) suffer their retribution for five kalpas. Furthermore, there are those who commit the four grave offenses (pārājika) and other such transgressions, whose retributions last for eighty-four thousand great kalpas and so forth.

This sutra further opens up [the discussion of] great sins such as slandering the Dharma, which lead to rebirth in the Avīci Hell throughout the ten directions. The *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* both speak in this manner. Thus, while there is a single Avīci Hell consisting of the five types of uninterrupted hells (*pañcānantarya*), the divisions of kalpas within these karmic retributions are distinct and separate from one another;

it is not that there exists a separate Avīci Hell apart from the five uninterrupted hells. "Avīci" was translated in antiquity as "without interval" (*wújiàn*). The *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states: "A" means "non-existent" (*wú*) and "vīci" means "obstructing" (*zhē*); furthermore, "A" means "non-existent" and "vīci" means "rescue" (*jiù*). Since it is translated as "without interval," it is also said to be "without... [referring to the absence of rescue].

To deny this would be to leave no room for rescue. Indeed, the single Avīci hell has many names. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* enumerates eight great *naraka*s, all of which are termed "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*). The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) enumerates eight great hells; following the seventh, the Great Heat Hell (*Mahāraurava*), is the Avīci Hell.
Thus, Master Yuan’s commentary states: "The Avīci Hell is the Great Uninterrupted Hell. This interpretation is correct, whereas Master Pan’s examination of the matter was not definitive.
If one commits the three acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through body, speech, and mind, that person shall enter the eighteen hells.
[Commentary] Body, speech, and mind are three of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are three of the ten causal transgressions (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*).

For example, if one physically commits all three offenses such as killing, while not committing them through speech or mind, it is still less grave than the former case; yet one will still enter the eighteen hells. (From *Xunwen*)

[Cloud] Regarding the three equalities of body, speech, and mind: among the evil karmas, one commits only the offenses of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Although speech and mind are mentioned, they merely assist in the completion of bodily karma. (△ [Direct Explanation] Nirvāṇa Sūtra 20: "The sinful karmas committed by all sentient beings are of two kinds:

first, light; second, heavy. If performed by mind and speech, it is called light; if performed by body and speech, it is called heavy. This means that if one conceives in the mind and speaks with the mouth but does not act with the body, the retribution received is light.

Citing this to corroborate the present sutra, the principle may be clearly understood by analogy. (△ [Supplement] This refers solely to the commission of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through the three karmas alone; since the ten causes are not complete, it does not lead to the Avīci Hell.)
If the three karmas are not performed together, and in the interim one commits either a single act of killing or a single act of stealing, such a person will enter the thirty-six hells.
[Commentary]: For example, if one alone performs a single karma such as killing without combining it with other offenses, one enters the thirty-six hells. Furthermore...
If one is light in the preceding [offense]— [the *Xunwen* commentary notes that it should also say "one instance of lust," but the text is abbreviated]—
and sees with a single faculty, committing a single transgression alone, such a person shall enter the one hundred and eight hells.
[Commentary]: This refers to a single faculty alone, involving only one instance of killing. Furthermore, it is lighter than the preceding case. One enters the one hundred and eight hells.

This includes cases such as improper thoughts within the mind, or wrong views that have not yet manifested in body or speech; or cases where one kills through the gateway of speech while the body and mind remain in a state of neutrality (*avyākṛta*).
These are all considered light. Regarding the phrase "seeing with seeing," it means seeing only with the single faculty [of the eye], without including others.

Regarding the other faculties, it is said: "seeing seeing" (jiàn jiàn). [The Wuxing commentary states: "Seeing seeing" refers to the seer and the seen; that is, a single faculty and a single object. This means one has committed only the karma pertaining to a single faculty—the eye—and a single object.

Now, according to the *Xiànyīn* (Manifest Sound), this is as follows: (△ [Yunqi says]: This section has five parts. "Delusive conceptualization arises; it does not exist from the beginning. (△ [The *Compendium* states: Maitreya says that within the desire realm there are thirty-six hells. Yet why is it that the jailers, yakṣas, and King Yama share the same prison with sentient beings suffering for their transgressions? The *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "Because there is deluded karma, one falsely perceives saṃsāra; those who weary of saṃsāra falsely perceive nirvāṇa.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata further explained the ten causes of habitual practice and the sixfold mutual retribution they receive. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The celestial drum addressed the Son of Heaven, Well-Abiding, saying: 'In the past, you were in hell. That hell did not come from the ten directions;

it arose solely from your inverted evil karma and your entanglement in ignorance, whereby you took birth in a hellish body. This has no root and no place of origin. Among these, that we now perceive cold and heat, and perceive suffering and pleasure, is entirely known by the *vijñāna* (consciousness-spirit); it is not known by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Inferring from this, death and life are no different; it is simply the consciousness-spirit that experiences suffering and pleasure. If you cannot endure hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, or the afflictions of burning, boiling, cutting, and roasting today, how could you possibly endure them later when you enter hell?

If you are unwilling to discipline the mind to do good, but instead indulge in killing sentient beings and committing various evils, you will die and enter the three miserable realms and hells: the mountains of knives and trees of swords, the cauldrons of boiling water and furnaces of charcoal, and the copper pillars and iron beds.

The agony of being sawn apart and ground to powder; the boiling excrement of the Ash River; the Avīci Hell; and the various sufferings of the Cold Ice [Hells]—how could one possibly endure these? (2. The Realm of Ghosts, 3. General Summary). (1. General Indication).

Furthermore, these sentient beings—having violated their moral discipline, transgressed the bodhisattva precepts, and subverted the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, as well as having committed various other miscellaneous karmas—are scorched by them throughout successive kalpas.
Only after their retribution for these sins is completed do they receive the forms of various hungry ghosts.
[Commentary: This does not refer to the violation of the *vinaya* precepts, nor to the slander that there are no precepts.

It refers to those who transgress the Bodhisattva precepts—failing to restrain themselves against both light and heavy offenses—and those who disparage the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*—disbelieving in cause and effect. These all sever their roots of goodness; other karmic consequences can be inferred.

Because they undergo long-term punishment in hell, it is said they are "burned for kalpas on end. Furthermore, because they receive other forms of existence, they enter the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

There are ten classes within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Due to the ten aforementioned causes—the ten causes being the primary retribution (*vipāka*) as explained in the preceding text—and because these involve extreme suffering rather than mild experience, it is said:
"Afterwards, when their transgressions are exhausted, they receive the forms of various ghosts. (The *Sutra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha* states:

"Sentient beings who violate the four grave prohibitions, consume the offerings of the faithful in vain, slander [the Dharma] with false views, fail to recognize cause and effect, sever the study of Prajñāpāramitā, revile the Buddhas of the ten directions, steal the property of the Saṃgha, and indulge in lust and lack of propriety, undergo the great sufferings of the Avīci Hell.")

After eighty-four thousand great kalpas have passed, one enters again into the eighteen compartments of the eastern direction and undergoes suffering as before; the same is true for the southern, western, and northern directions. "Avīci" means that there is no rescue. [The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: A "preta" (hungry ghost) means "fearful.

This refers to those who are timid and full of dread; thus they are called pretas. Some say: because they have committed and increased superior, firm greed through the misconduct of body, speech, and mind, they are born there; thus they experience the karma of hunger and thirst. Others say: they are called pretas because they are driven into service. They are constantly driven about everywhere by the various devas and are perpetually running to and fro.

Furthermore, they are called pretas because of their constant longing; they are always seeking food and drink from others. The *Lokadhātu-paṭala* says: "Due to a deceitful and delusive mind, one commits the minor grade of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*)."

The ten evil deeds induce this body of the [hungry ghost] path. (○ [Qingliang says]: According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, each of the three miserable realms has both primary (*maula*) and secondary (*pārśva*) categories. The primary is heavy; the secondary is light. Comparing the primary hungry ghosts to the secondary animals, the sin of the hungry ghosts is heavier;

therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* and other texts place the hungry ghosts after the hells. If one compares the primary animals to the secondary hungry ghosts, the sin of the animals is heavier; hence it is said here that the "lower" refers to the causes for hungry ghosts. ○ [Zizhong says]: Due to the ten aforementioned causes, the remaining retributions differ;
thus, the lower realm of hungry ghosts is divided into ten classes. [The first is] the habit of greedily stealing objects.

The habit of lustful desire for form; the habit of deceit through delusive greed; the habit of resentment through greed for hatred; the habit of anger through greed for recollection; the habit of arrogance through greed; the habit of fraudulence through greed for deception;
the habit of false views through greed for clarity; the habit of injustice through greed for success; and the habit of litigation through greed for factions.

(From the *Chángqìng shuōwén*) By means of these fundamental habits one creates offenses. Above and below interact and influence one another, resulting in retribution and rebirth among humans and ghosts.
These are merely cross-references within it.
(The two [sections] separately clarify this.

If, regarding the primary cause, one commits the offense of coveting material objects, when that person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter an object and take form; this is called a "strange ghost" (*guǐ*).
[Commentary]: This refers to taking the habituation of greed as the cause. One gives rise to greed for objects and takes them through improper means;

the residual retribution remains among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), who still depend upon objects—namely, the essences and spirits of gold, silver, grasses, and trees. Since their types are manifold, they are called "strange ghosts" (*guǐguǐ*).

While they undergo the retribution of suffering, they reside in the Cold Ice Hell (*śītalā-naraka*). [Supplementary Note states: Originally, because they greedily sought wealth and goods, their residual habits still cling to grasses and trees to become strange entities. As for ordinary grasses and trees...]
To act as a demon is called a "strange apparition" (*guài*).

To lust after sensual beauty is a transgression. When this person’s retribution for their sins is exhausted, they encounter the wind and take form; they are named a *pó-guǐ* (drought-demon spirit). [Commentary]:

This refers to the prior habituation to sexual misconduct acting as the cause. Sensual beauty can agitate and disorder the body and mind, just as the wind stirs objects, thereby inviting [retribution].
The *bào-guǐ* (retribution ghost) returns and again entrusts itself to the wind. The substance of the wind is fundamentally void; it arises due to habitual practice.

Cause and effect correspond to one another—how could this be in vain? [Supplement: The tradition states, "Horses and oxen have their *fēng* (wind). The commentary says: "*Fēng* means 'to let loose. The mutual incitement between male and female is called *fēng*. What remains from the habit of lewdness is said to take form upon encountering the wind.

This is like the way horses and oxen run wild (*fēngyì*); through mutual incitement and pursuit, they take form. The *pó* is a female ghost, also called a female *āo* (demon). Women are often lewd, and thus become *pó* ghosts. These ghosts likewise receive their bodies through being moved by lewdness.]**
Greed and delusion constitute transgression. When this person’s transgressions are exhausted, they encounter the form of an animal and are called a *mèiguǐ* (possessing ghost).

[Commentary] This refers to the prior habit of deceit as the cause. Having become fraudulent due to these causes, and being deluded by relying on the void, one attaches oneself to an animal and thus forms a demonic substance.
These include foxes, wildcats, pigs, and dogs; those with extraordinary spiritual qualities are of many such kinds. Therefore...

It is said that when a beast encounters [a person], it takes form; a *mei* (魅) immediately manifests a beautiful form to delude people. [Supplement]: "Beasts" refers to species such as foxes and raccoon dogs.

When these possess someone to delude them, they are called *mei*-ghosts because they seduce with charm. This is a lingering habit of deception. (△ [Personal Commentary]: As in the *Zuozhuan*, when the Marquis of Qi was hunting at Beiqiu, he saw a large boar. His attendants said, "This is Lord Pengsheng. The Marquis became angry and said:)
Peng Sheng dared to appear before him. He shot at him, and a boar stood upright like a human and cried out—this is what occurs when an animal takes form [due to karmic conditions].
Those whose transgressions consist of greed and resentment, once their retribution for these sins is exhausted, encounter insects and take their form; they are called "poisonous insect ghosts."

[Commentary]: This refers to the aforementioned habituation to resentment acting as the cause. Preceded by anger, one harbors malice without relinquishing it; the grudge remains bound within the mind, and a burning affliction dwells in the breast.

When receiving further retribution, one likewise resorts to poisonous species—namely, serpents, vipers, and venomous insects that possess a spiritual influence—which become *gudu* (poisonous spirits).

[Supplementary Note: Spirits attach themselves to serpents and vipers to poison people; this is also a habituation of resentment. (The *Zuozhuan* states that blood-worms constitute *gudu*; the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a worm within the abdomen.)
Covetous recollection constitutes a transgression. When this person’s transgressions are exhausted, they encounter a state of decay and take form, being called a *pūtana* ghost.
[Commentary] This takes the aforementioned habituation to anger as its cause. One harbors increased resentment toward suffering and the instruments of suffering, or generates anger due to jealousy;
failing to relinquish such resentment and anger is termed "covetous recollection. Consequently, upon receiving the retribution of a ghost, one encounters places of calamity and decay.

It then enters their bodies; it is called the "Leprosy Ghost" (*rākṣasa*). It is the cause of all such afflictions as toxic leprosy, contagious fevers, *chuánshī* (transmissible consumption), and *gùzhēng* (wasting fever)—all are produced by this ghost.

[Supplementary Note: To hate a person, one must first record their grievances; hence it is said, "to remember. Though one wishes to inflict an epidemic, one must find a time when misfortune can be exploited; hence it is said, "encountering decline.
The ghost attaches itself to leprous diseases to vent long-held resentment; its hateful toxicity is extreme.]
Greed and arrogance constitute offenses. When such a person’s retribution for these offenses is exhausted, they encounter the vital energies (*qi*) and take form;

this is called a hungry ghost (*preta*). [Commentary: This refers to the habitual tendencies of pride mentioned previously acting as the cause. Pride involves looking down upon others and being haughty toward things, maintaining an air of self-importance and self-assertion.
Consequently, when encountering the class of ghosts, they take the vital energies as their substance. Lacking genuine virtue within, they remain empty-bellied yet high-minded, tormented by hunger.

Therefore, they are called *preta* (hungry ghosts). [My own view: According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, the general number of hungry ghosts is thirty-six types. The *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states there are three types: those without wealth (*niḥsambhāra*), those with little wealth (*alpasambhāra*), and those with much wealth (*bahu-sambhāra*). Within each of these three, there are again three sub-types.

Among the three types with little wealth, the "torch-mouthed" (*ulkāmukha*) and "needle-throated" (*sūcīmukha*) are the most inferior; these correspond to the passage in the preceding text describing those who receive the breath of fierce fires for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. The three types with much wealth include those who obtain what they discard and those who lose what they obtain;

the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* calls them "hungry ghosts of seeking" (*paryeṣaka-preta*). These should be those born through the affliction of pride (*māna-kleśa*) mentioned in this text. Master Qingliang has the theory of "genuine ghosts" (*maula-preta*) and "peripheral ghosts" (*prānta-preta*); the former hungry ghosts are the genuine, while these hungry ghosts are the peripheral. [This is due to] past causes.
Arrogance leads to pride; the remaining retribution is the seeking [of further existence]. This is indeed the fixed principle.
Greed and delusion constitute sin. When this person’s sins are exhausted, they encounter the darkness and take on a form, which is called a *yāma-ghost* (a ghost that causes nightmares).

[Commentary]: This refers to the prior habituation to deception acting as the cause. For the sake of profit and reputation, they harbor many heterodox schemes, feigning the possession of virtue and deceiving others.

They cause others to remain in darkness, ignorant of their own affairs. When they subsequently receive the form of a ghost, they rely on the obscure and dwell in the dark, using nightmares to bewilder those who sleep;

therefore, they are called "A-yen" (Sleep-Bewildering) ghosts. [Supplement]: The cause of greedy deception consists in taking what does not exist to be existent. Ghosts likewise receive forms in the profound darkness, and through their *yān* (nightmare-spirit) power...
To be obsessed with affairs is a transgression;
to crave illumination is a sin. When such a person’s retribution for their sins is exhausted, they encounter a *jing* (essence/vitality) to form a body, and are called a *wangliang* ghost.

[Commentary] This refers to taking the habit-energy of views as the cause. Clinging to views, ordinary beings each consider themselves clearly enlightened; (the heterodox hold that their divergent views constitute clear enlightenment).
Their births are contrary [to the human state], arising from acts of defiance and rejection that invite rebirth in the realm of ghosts (*preta*).

Encountering places of refined spirit, they take on form—specifically the essence and souls of the sun and moon, or the luminous spirits of mountains and marshes; they rely upon whatever possesses brilliant radiance as their substance.

What are called *wangliang* (phantoms) are transformations of water and stone into strange apparitions. [Supplement: Through the habit of giving rise to views, and desiring to discern clearly [the truth], one falls into the realm of ghosts and becomes a *wangliang* ghost; this too is part of the destiny of ghosts.]

For those who are clever and discerning, greed becomes a transgression. When this person’s transgressions are exhausted, they encounter clarity which forms their physical shape; this is called a "ghost employed as a servant.

[Commentary] This refers to taking perverse habits as the cause. Being oppressed and stripped of integrity, one relies on emptiness to construct fabrications, exhausting the mind and laboring the thoughts.
They afflict the innocent, causing them to become guilty. When encountering manifest conditions, they rely upon them to form their bodies; they are not of the dark, obscure class.
They are those who serve as runners in battle or laborers who carry sand and shoulder stones; hence they are called "servants" (yìshǐ). [Wēn-líng says: Those who have become greedy.]
Wishing to curry favor, they follow crookedly; thus they attach themselves to the manifest spirits and serve as their minions, relying on shrines to act as their messengers.

Because they have committed the sin of forming greedy factions, when these people's retribution is exhausted, they encounter humans and take human form, being called "transmission ghosts" (shéntuōng guǐ).

[Commentary: This refers to taking the habit of litigation as the cause. Favoring oneself and concealing one's offenses leads to being litigated against by others; the retribution lies among the class of ghosts.
When manifesting in human form, they appear as worldly figures such as teachers of children or shamans and priests, all of whom serve as intermediaries for the divine.

They transmit words concerning the ominous and the auspicious, as well as calamity and fortune; these are called the "Transmitting Ghosts" (*songzhuan gui*). [Supplementary Note: Litigants must have partisans.

These ghosts possess humans to act as transmitters, much like the shamans and sorcerers of the world, wherein so-called spirits descend and take possession. These aforementioned classes of ghosts are truly numerous. One should examine their effects to verify their causes.

However, these ten—(the three fetters are indicated here)—Ānanda, all these people have fallen due to their pure delusion; their karma-fire having burned them dry, they emerge above as ghosts. These...
All of these are summoned and drawn forth by one's own deluded thoughts and karma. If one awakens to Bodhi, then the wondrous, perfect, and luminous nature is fundamentally nothing at all.
[Commentary] These ten causes and six retributions are all the products of pure emotional affliction (*qing*). Since the emotions have sunk downward, one consequently falls into the hells.

The punishment in hell lasts for a long time; when the afflictions of the mind are exhausted, one ascends. Thus it is said that "the fires of karma burn the [afflictions] dry. Rising upward, one becomes a ghost. [Gushan says:

"Those who fall due to pure affliction flow downward with the water of craving. 'The fires of karma burn them dry' means burning the water of craving dry. [Supplement says: "Burning the water of craving dry means the karmic retribution of hell has ceased. The fires of karma blaze upward; therefore, one follows the mind of thought."

Those who ascend [in rebirth] become ghosts (*preta*). Their minds are restless and agitated; they are the remnants of the fires of their own karma. These are falsely summoned by one’s own actions and cannot be obtained from others.
Within the mind of *bodhi*, they are all like flowers in the sky. (Tongzhou says: The previous question asked how the Buddha-body could be truly real while there are still realms such as the hells.
Therefore, he answers: if one awakens to *bodhi*, these originally do not exist at all. (2. The Animal Realm; 3. General Summary). (1. Initial General Statement).
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the karma of the hungry ghost is exhausted, both emotion and thought become empty.
Only then, within the world, does one encounter the person from whom one was originally indebted, meeting that karmic adversary face-to-face; taking birth as an animal, one repays that past debt.
[Zizhong] "Affection" (*qing*) refers to the pure affection of the hells; "conception" (*xiang*) refers to the deluded conception of the realm of hungry ghosts.

This conception is also affection. [Commentary]: In the hells, one is governed by affection; among the hungry ghosts, one is governed by conception. (The retribution of the hells arises from the karma of affection; the retribution of the hungry ghosts arises from the karma of conception. When affection and conception are both exhausted...

Therefore, it is said that they "accomplish emptiness. However, that which is emptied is precisely the karma generated by emotional attachments and conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*). [The Supplement states: "This refers solely to the causal karma;

once the retribution for the fruit has been fully accounted for, it is said that 'the waters of craving are burned dry,' and so forth, up to 'emotional attachments and conceptualizations are accomplished as empty. This merely means that the karmic waters produced within the mind of craving have been incinerated;

it does not mean that the emotional attachment itself has already been extinguished. The same applies to the statement below: 'All are dried up by the fire of karma. Since the karma of the two paths has thus perished, one returns to become an animal to repay past debts—such as a camel.

Donkeys, oxen, and horses—[one] repays others with one's body and life. If [the victim] belongs to another species, one receives retribution accordingly. [The *Erleng* says: "When feeling and thought are realized as empty..."]

It is only the pure emotion of the Avīci hell and the nine emotions with one thought of the Uninterrupted (Ānantarya) hells; the two emotions with eight thoughts of the Interrupted hells; and the three emotions with seven thoughts of the hungry ghosts—all of these have been dried up by the fires of karma.

Yet, six emotions and four thoughts remain as moisture for rebirth, whereby they are born among the furred and winged species to repay their past debts. [The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "Born" (*jāti*) refers to sentient beings; "beasts" (*tiryak*) refers to those raised as livestock. This means they are born horizontally; by nature they are ignorant and cannot stand upright on their own. The *Lokasthiti-śāstra* says: "In Sanskrit they are called *tiryañc*.

Because the beings of this path mostly move with their bodies covered, they are so named. The new *Vibhāṣā* asks: "Why are they called 'sideways-born' (*tiryag-yoni*)? Because their form is sideways, their movement is also sideways; because their movement is sideways, their form is also sideways."

For this reason, they are called "animals" (*tiryag-yoni*). Some say that because those sentient beings have committed evil deeds of body, speech, and mind through the predominance of delusion (*moha*), they are born into that state of dullness and thus called animals. This [category] pervades all six destinies (*ṣad-gati*).

[The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: In the animal realm, beings harm one another; for example, the weak are killed by the powerful. Lacking self-mastery, they are driven about by others and frequently subjected to whipping and flogging.
They serve as resources for humans and gods, undergoing various kinds of extremely heavy suffering and affliction. (II. Specific Manifestations)
The ghosts of those who were strange or monstrous creatures, when their retribution is exhausted and they are reborn in the world, mostly become a species of *xiāo* (owls).

[Commentary] Those of the greedy class become strange ghosts; when their retribution ends, they join the ranks of the *xiāo*. A *xiāo* is the earth-owl (*tǔ xiāo*). It builds its nest by attaching clods of earth to form its young.

"Caused by greed for objects" (*haiyin* says: because one covets the property of others as one's own; the earth-owl [the *tǔxiāo*] clings to clods of earth to form its offspring—this is due to habitual conditioning).
All strange and anomalous phenomena are subsumed under this category (*gushan* says: formerly a ghost, it clung to an object to form a substance; now a beast, it clings to a clod to form a body).

The ghosts of the *fēngbó* (wind-drought spirits): when their karmic retribution for the wind is exhausted, they are born into the human world as various ominous portents among all classes of heteromorphic beings.
[Commentary] With lewd diseases as the cause, they receive the retribution of becoming *fēngbó* spirits; subsequently, they become animals and undergo these ominous portents.

"Ominous" (*jiù*) refers to transgressions and evils; "portent" (*zhēng*) refers to a responsive manifestation. These are summoned by evil conduct and precede the occurrence of calamities and anomalies, appearing as such signs beforehand. As it says:
Flocks of sparrows and swarms of rats are omens of famine and scarcity. The *zhao* bird portends floods; the dancing of cranes indicates frequent droughts.
Such types are not limited to these alone. [Wenling says: The *ba* ghost was formerly a drought-demon (*hanba*); its residual habits now manifest again as calamitous omens.]
As for the ghosts that harbor *māyā* (sorcery): when their existence as ghosts ends and their retribution is exhausted, they are reborn in the world of humans, mostly taking the form of foxes.

[Commentary] This is the retribution for the cause of deception: having been a ghost, one becomes a *māyā*-infesting spirit. Once the basis [of that state] is exhausted, one receives the body of a fox among animals.

[Haiyin says: The fox can enchant people; this is also due to residual habits of deception. (△Guxiang says: The fox is a demonic beast ridden by ghosts. Guo Xuanzhongji states: A thousand-year-old fox becomes a wanton woman; a hundred-year-old fox becomes a beautiful maiden.)

As for the ghosts of *chóng* (insects) and *gǔ* (poisonous charms), when the insects are extinguished and the retribution exhausted, they are reborn in the world, mostly as species of venomous creatures.

[Commentary] This is the retribution for the habit-energy of resentment: the ghost manifests as a *gǔ* poison, while the animal becomes a species of venomous creature, namely such things as vipers, snakes, *fù* snakes, and scorpions.
The ghosts of decay and pestilence—those whose retributions for their exhaustion have ended—are born into this world, mostly as types of worms.
[Commentary: Due to the cause of habitual anger, these ghosts become those of decay and pestilence; they take refuge in calamity and attach themselves to misfortune, then enter within the body.

They subsequently undergo the forms of animals and again take refuge within the body as *ō* (roundworms) and *yō* (threadworms). (Wenling says: "Pestilence ghosts attack people; *ō* and *yō* worms attach themselves to people. (Liangduan says: "Formerly they relied upon humans...")
They cause epidemics; now, by relying on the treasury [of merit], they digest their solid food. Their habituation to anger subsides and fades away, transforming the violent into the most gentle.
Ghosts who subsist on vapors, once their vital energy is exhausted and their retribution ends, are born into the human world, mostly as types of food.
[Commentary]: Hungry ghosts (preta) rely on the breath [of others]. Arrogance is their causal habit; they receive hunger and emptiness, while animals satisfy the fullness of others.
Thus, they constitute the category of food—that is, those animals in the world that may be eaten.

The ghosts of those who died in the midst of fine silk (*mian*) vanish into obscurity once their retribution is exhausted; when reborn into the human world, they mostly become the category of "silk" (*fu*).
[Commentary] Due to the habitual delusions of past causes, these ghosts were accustomed to darkness.

Once that obscure and silent state has dissolved, they become the category of "silk" among animals—namely, camels, donkeys, oxen, horses, silkworm cocoons, and the like—which serve as clothing and articles of use for humans. "Silk" (*mian*) here refers to being fine and dense, not transparently exposed.

[Gu-shan says: "To serve and practice. As the *I Ching* says: 'to harness oxen and ride horses. [Wen-ling says: "'Mian' means to cling to. Because it clings to those who suffer from nightmares, it belongs to the category of 'service. It also clings persistently to people. [Jiang-lu says: "In the past, it caused people to suffer nightmares in the darkness;
now, in the light, it receives their service and riding—this too is a form of retribution."
The ghosts of harmonious essence (*jing*)—when their harmony dissolves and their retribution is exhausted—are born into the world, mostly as *ying* (responsive) species.

[Commentary] Because they were caused by the habit-energy of views, they become ghosts such as *wangliang* (sprites). Once the objects of their harmonious brilliance are exhausted, they become animals and thus constitute responsive species;
that is, they respond to the sequence of the four seasons, coming and calling out again, such as the swallow, the wild goose, and the cricket. This is what is meant.

"Harmony" (he) means "mixture. It is through the mixture of the spheres of brilliance and clarity that one becomes a ghost. [Haïin says: To foreknow subtle responses is, in essence, the habit-energy of views.]
The ghosts of the enlightened and numinous, when their illumination fades and their retribution is exhausted, are born into the world, mostly as auspicious omens among all classes of beings.

[Commentary: These are the aforementioned karmic habits of the wronged. The ghosts take birth through the power of illumination as a class of servants. When their karma in the ghost realm is exhausted, they receive the retribution of animals as auspicious omens.
"Hsiu" (休) means beautiful. When auspicious fortune is about to arrive, there are premonitory signs of it; these arise from the virtuous deeds of others.

"Zhao" refers to the class of creatures such as the qilin and the phoenix. (Wenling says: "As for all these extraordinary beings, their nature is more subtle than that of spirits and their spiritual power surpasses that of humans.
Their mysterious resonance with their kind and their auspicious harmony with the sublime are all the result of residual habits.")

"Those who were ghosts while dependent on humans, once those humans have perished and their retribution is exhausted, are born into the world of beings; for the most part, they become animals of the same kind.

[Commentary: This is due to the cause of habitual litigation. As a ghost, one is summoned and sent forth; when a person dies and becomes an animal, the retribution lies in being clever and cunning. Therefore, it is said they become 'animals of the same kind' (*xunlei*).
This refers to the types of animals that humans keep as domesticated or obedient creatures."
(III. A threefold summary indicating two points). (I. The first summary: the falsity of phenomena).
Ānanda, all these beings have their bodies withered by the fire of karma as they repay their past debts; they exist as animals on the periphery.
These, too, are all summoned and drawn forth by their own false and deluded karma. If one awakens to Bodhi, then these false conditions are fundamentally non-existent.
"All that exists.
[Commentary: Having been consumed by the fires of karma in the two realms of hell-beings and hungry ghosts, their emotional and conceptual faculties have withered away.

Now they are born as animals to repay their remaining debts; hence it is said they are "lateral" (or, "because they are animals"). They exist due to deluded thoughts, yet their fundamental nature of awakening is originally non-existent, just like...

The circular shadow. Because of the eye disease, one sees it. (Hakuchūnan says: Previously, when desire was dried up, one entered the stage of the sages; now, when the fire of karma is dried up, one emerges from hell.
If a practitioner cannot dry up their desire, there will certainly come a day when the fire of karma is dried up. How painful! (This is the second [section], citing a question to re-demonstrate.)
It is as you have said. The evil karma of those such as Ratnapadmagandhā, King Vaidūrya, and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was originally produced from within themselves;
it did not descend from heaven, nor did it emerge from the earth, nor was it bestowed by others. It was summoned by their own delusions.
Returning to receive [the results] for oneself: within the mind of Bodhi, all things are merely floating and void; they are the solidification of deluded thoughts. [Commentary:
Regarding the three conditions you asked about, these are created by those individuals themselves through their own delusions; they arise from karma and do not depend on anything external.
Therefore, it is said that "originally they do not descend from heaven," and so forth. One delusively creates and delusively receives; within the nature of awakening, all are like this.

Flowers in the Sky. (From the "Chapter on the Minor Marks of the *Avataṃsaka*": At that time, the celestial drum, through the power of the roots of goodness of the Bodhisattva’s samādhi, uttered a voice, saying:

"O sons of the gods, Bodhisattvas know that all karmas do not come from the east, nor do they come from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below; yet they gather together and abide within the mind. They arise solely from inversion and have no place of abiding.

O sons of the gods, it is as if there were a crystal mirror called 'Able to Reflect,' pure and transparent, equal in measure to the worlds of the ten directions. [Commentary]: "Excessive" (*vyatikrama*) means to go beyond one's proper measure.

It refers to acting in excess by not adhering to one's allotted portion—namely, irrational and oppressive labor regardless of its severity, or consuming food and drink without moderation, whether day or night. Such categories of behavior are what is meant.

All such matters shall be fully investigated to recover the surplus. Now there are those who, relying on their noble status, act with license; leaning upon their power and influence, they live in luxury;

When their merit is exhausted, they must repay what was taken—how fitting that this should be! As it is said of those below: "There are those who cultivate goodness and honor [the teachings]."
As for merit, it is merely within the human body that its power is repaid. Now we observe that families who have accumulated great goodness often see their wealth and goods squandered;

[He] solidifies the vital fluids without ceasing; when the virtue of moisture is perfected, he is called a "Celestial-Practice Immortal" (*devayāna-ṛṣi*). [Commentary]:

He stirs the celestial pond and swallows the vital fluids, consolidating the essence. After a long period, his merit becomes manifest, and he thus achieves the virtue of moisture. This is what is meant.

Regarding "practicing in the heavens" (*tianxing*): this does not refer to the six realms of desire (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu*). Rather, it refers to what people of the world call the abodes of numinous seers (*ṛṣi*), which they name "heavens.
This is like Zhang Qian’s journey to the source of the Yellow River, where he reached Mount Kunlun and beheld celestial palaces (*devakula*) and the like.
Alternatively, because their conduct does not involve the realm of desire, it is no different from [the heavens]; thus it is called "practicing in the heavens" (as cited in the *Zizhi*).
With firm and refined essence, they do not rest; by inhaling the pure quintessence, they achieve perfection and are called *sādhaka-ṛṣis* (accomplished practitioners).

[Commentary] By swallowing and drinking the vital energy (*tejas*) of the sun and moon, they apply their minds to effect transformations in order to prolong their physical lives. Through this practice over a long period, they attain success.

Consequently, he developed heterodox views that accorded with worldly sentiments; thus it is said, "He practiced the common way" (Zizhong says: "Practicing the common way" implies there should be five supernatural powers, namely those of the immortal). (Zhengji says:

"He inhaled the solar essence to nourish his appearance and swallowed the radiance of the dawn clouds to prolong his life beyond the mundane world. His path was profound and manifest; therefore, it is called 'practicing the common way'").
One performs firm and steadfast incantations and prohibitions without ceasing; when these ritual arts are perfected, one is called a "Daoxing-xian" (Path-Practicing Immortal).
[Commentary] Incantations and prohibitions are precisely the ritual arts and techniques of the immortals. By means of these, one sustains the body, making it long-lived and firm.

When the power of these arts is accomplished, it is termed "Daoxing. (As Wujin says: such as the Three Jia, Eight Shi, and Six Ding, or the class of sword-wielding and incantation-based practitioners.)
Maintaining firm mindfulness without ceasing, until the recollection is fully perfected, one is called an "Illuminating Practice Immortal" (Zhàoxíng Xiān).

[Commentary] Mindfulness takes the preceding object as its condition; the mind is bound to it without forgetting, focused intently without shifting. After a long time, its function is manifested, illuminating the objective realm and comprehending the source of transformation.
It is like wisdom arising from meditative concentration; therefore, it is called "Illuminating Practice. [Zhenji says: "By employing this mindfulness, one examines the object and crosses over..."]
The mind, through the perfection of recollective contemplation, is able to know those objects; this is merely the mundane supernormal power of knowing others' minds and past lives.
When [the mind] is firmly established in mutual engagement without ceasing, and the resonance and response are fully perfected, it is called a "refined-practice immortal" (siddha).
[Commentary]: In the world, there exist arts of "gathering yin" and "gathering yang," which are termed *jiaogou* (sexual union). Through long practice, success is achieved;

this triggers a resonance such that one responds to the other, inhaling their vital essence (*jingqi*) to fortify one's own body. Therefore, it is called the "practice of essence. [Gushan says: "*Jiaogou*" refers to what the *Yijing* calls "the meeting of the essences of male and female.

The *Shenxian zhuan* states that Pengzu cultivated the arts of the chamber (*fangzhong shu*). Furthermore, Zhang Ling exhorted people to practice the arts of the chamber, while the *Zhen'gao* likewise censured the red and white vapors and such defiled matters. Now, as for the immortals who practice the essence...

This is of that same category. The following passage states: "Regarding sexual misconduct, the mind does not wander or dissipate; because what he has practiced is inferior, he is thus situated below the celestial realms. [Private Commentary:

To avoid the explicit mention of sexual intercourse and impure matters, this text borrows terminology from the Buddhist teachings regarding the union of *kan* (the trigram for water) and *li* (the trigram for fire) to adorn its phrasing. How could the masters of the Xuánjuán school have failed to perceive this? It is simply because there are five conditions for cultivating the causes of the desire realm:

first, the mind does not wander or dissipate during sexual misconduct; second, one’s lustful attachment toward one’s own wife is slight; third, when encountering desire, one engages briefly and leaves without lingering recollection; fourth, [one maintains mindfulness]; and fifth, at the time of lying together, one is as oblivious as chewing wax. All such passages as these concern firm and steadfast conduct.

"Encounter" (gòu) refers to opposition and contravention. That which belongs to the Desire Realm is the cause for the Brahma-purity; the destiny of the immortals (xiánqù) is not the fruit of sovereign mastery. Within these, ascent and descent differ vastly in their gradations. The abode of the immortals is the ninth [heaven], already the highest among the ten types of immortals.

They merely achieve the arts of the bedchamber between men and women; it can be seen that their rank as immortals is high, yet they do not reach even the lowest level of those who ride the celestial vehicle. This also indirectly demonstrates that observing the precepts leads to rebirth in heaven, embodying the subtle intent of supporting the Vinaya.
Firmly established in transformation, they do not cease; awakening to perfect fulfillment, they are called *atyācāra-ṛṣis* (Transcendent Sages of Ceased Action).
[Commentary] Contemplating the world, all things are transformed. Since the objects are transformed, the mental conceptions also vanish, becoming like withered wood.

Through the application of conditioned effort, one temporarily attains such a state; hence it is called "ceasing action. [Ziqing says: "Ceased action" means that transformations continue without rest.]

Regarding the various types of "corpse-liberation" (*shijie*), those who speak of "awakening and perfect realization" mean that one severs the functions of sight and hearing, becoming like withered wood. (△ [Haiyin says: By practicing, one brings forth a yang-spirit (*yangshen*), transforming the form and changing the substance; hence it is called "transformation. After a long time, the mind attains penetration.)

Therefore, it is called "awakening," which no other immortals can surpass; thus it is named "Transcendent Practice" (*juexing*). As for the ten categories mentioned above, they are all termed "practitioners" (*xingzhe*) because, through long practice, they achieve success and attain pervasive flow.

(Regarding the "ten practices" (*shixing*): ancient commentaries all pronounce this with the level tone, whereas Wenglun reads it with the departing tone. This [latter] refers to "meritorious practice" (*gongxing*); it is not correct [to read it as ten practices]. [Private Commentary: In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, *Śūraṅgama* is explained as "ultimate firmness."

Now, when it is said that all ten kinds of *ṛṣis* are "firm" (*sāra*), this refers to those who do not rely on perfect enlightenment but instead cultivate their own self-abiding *samādhi*, maintaining mental images to solidify their forms. Because they take the coagulation of deluded thoughts as firmness, it is not ultimate firmness;

rather, they merely return to dissolution and enter the various realms of existence. That each of the ten types mentioned in the sutra is designated by the term "firm" is the profound intent behind this teaching. (Section Three: Concluding Summary)
Ānanda, these individuals all refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not cultivate Right Enlightenment.

Instead, they attain a distinct mode of existence with a lifespan of ten million years, dwelling in deep mountains or on remote ocean islands far removed from the realm of men. This, too, is saṃsāra; it is the wandering of deluded thoughts.
Failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more, scattering into the various realms of existence.
[Commentary] The principle of cultivation refers to the principle of longevity; it is precisely the aforementioned ten methods of refinement and training. Regarding the phrase "among humans":

since there is no distinct collective retribution for the realm of immortals (*ṛṣi*), one transforms into an immortal by applying these ten preceding methods of refinement upon the fruit of the human body’s collective retribution.
If one pursues delusions rather than the truth, one will ultimately fall through the power of karma.

[Pointer: "A million years for a human being does not even equal a single day and night in the Heaven of the Four Dhyānas. As the former sages said: "Even if one were to endure for a thousand million kalpas, in the end, one will surely fall into emptiness and oblivion. [Hand-mirror says:

"Those among humans who train their minds do not realize that human life does not stop, passing faster than flowing water; that youthful vigor does not stop, like a galloping horse. Consequently, they cling to this dream-like and illusory substance, regarding it as solid and long-lasting. [Wu-xing says: "Training the mind among humans must necessarily be accompanied by precepts and wholesome conduct."

It is not merely a matter of taking medicinal herbs to sustain life. That one separately attains the principle of longevity is precisely due to karma within the human realm, which separately evokes the retribution of rebirth among the immortals (*ṛṣi*). As the *Shanhai jing* says: "On Mount Kunlun, in the wilds of Guangdu, at the mound of Xuanyuan, lies the Land of the Immortals.

There is neither cold nor heat; its people all live for several thousand years. This, too, is a collective shared portion (*sāmānya-bhāga*) of many individuals, and it is not that there is no fixed location. (△ [Regarding "shared": the Sūtra says that Arhats dwell in and maintain the various sacred sites of the sages. )

The manifestations of these realms vary; they are mostly found in famous mountains and vast marshes. Now, regarding the realm of the immortals (*ṛṣi-gati*), it is also said that they dwell in deep mountains, seas, and islands, far removed from the human world. This is analogous to the twenty-five heavens, where ordinary beings and sages cohabit; though the five *anāgāmins* reside there, those in the lower four dhyānas cannot see them.

It is also like the fourth heaven (*Tuṣita*), where beyond the second enclosure, there is a separate heaven for karmic retribution; yet even when comparing this total retribution to the outer enclosure, there is already a separation between the immortals and the common folk. [Commentary by Gāngxiū]:

Zhang Wujin [moved] the fifth realm of the immortals from the *Hǎiyǎn jīng* (Ocean Eye Sutra) and appended it below the ninth section on the asura realm. Dongwu Shoushi stated: "In the original scripture’s seven realms, the realm of the immortals is superior to that of humans but inferior to that of the devas; therefore, it should follow the human realm."
"Neither after heaven nor before heaven—seeing what endlessness could one suddenly change [the text]?

Commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* Entitled *Mengchao*,
Fascicle Eight (Part Three) / Fascicle Eight (Part Four).
Compiled by the Disciple Haiyin, Mengsou Qian Qianyi.

([○@●] Sixth, specifically explaining the celestial realms. From here until the end of the ninth fascicle, the *pudgalas* are each categorized according to their respective types. (○ First, a combined explanation of the various heavens. (○ [The *Fanyi ji* states: *deva*. This means "heaven. The *Fahua shu* states:

"Heaven" means natural, spontaneous, superior in bliss, and superior in body. The treatise says: Because they are pure, radiant, most honored, and most excellent, they are called *devas*. If it were not for the cause of supreme excellence, how could one receive the retribution of supreme excellence?)

Qingliang says: "Heaven" (*deva*) has the meaning of sovereignty and the meaning of radiance. (As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 16: "Heaven" is called "day. Because days are long and nights are short in the heavens, it is named "heaven. Furthermore, "heaven" is also called "free from sorrow and vexation."

They constantly experience happiness; for this reason, they are called devas (*deva*). Furthermore, "deva" means "lamp-light"; because they can destroy darkness and act as a great illumination, they are called devas. Moreover, they can destroy the darkness of evil karma and, through wholesome karma, are born in the heavens;

for this reason, they are called devas. Furthermore, "deva" means "auspicious" (*śiva*); because they are auspicious, they receive the name deva. Furthermore, "deva" means "sun" (*sūrya*); because the sun possesses radiance, the sun is named deva. [The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: For what reason is that realm called "heaven"?

Among all realms, it is the most excellent, the most joyful, the most good, the most wondrous, and the highest; therefore, it is called the heavenly realm (*devagati*). Some say: Because one previously performed superior and sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind, one goes there.

They are born there; they are called "devas" (heavenly beings) because they cause that [existence] to continue. Some say they are called devas because their radiance increases, for they are constantly illuminated day and night by natural light. Etymologists say they are called devas because they are able to illuminate, for they manifest superior fruits and illuminate the causes cultivated in previous times.
They are called devas because of their playful enjoyment, for they constantly sport and experience superior bliss. [The *Miaoyanpin shu* (Commentary on the Chapter on Wondrous Adornment) states:

Regarding the length of the lifespan, the size of the body, the weight of the clothing, and the excellence of the palaces of the various devas, these are all extensively analyzed in the eleventh chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, as well as in treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and sūtras such as the *Lokotpatti-sūtra*. The "World Chapter" (*Lokadhātu-paṭala*) of the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "Fifty human years constitute one day and night for the lowest heaven (*Cāturmahārājika*). Based on this calculation, their lifespan is five hundred [years]."

[The life span] is one hundred [years]. Above this, it increases fivefold at each stage. In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is no distinction between day and night; the number of *kalpas* is equal to the measure of the body. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the first two [levels] have twenty thousand [great kalpas], and each subsequent level increases by two [thousand].

Regarding the "measure of the body," the verse says: In the heavens of desire, [the height is] one *krośa*, increasing by one-quarter at each [level]. In the heavens of form, [the height is] *yojanas*; in the first four, it increases by half a half. Above these, it increases twofold at each stage;

only the Cloudless (*Anabhraka*) heaven decreases [by two]. Commentary: One *krośa* is two *li*. One *yojana* is sixteen *li*, because eight *krośas* constitute one *yojana*. Thus, the bodies of the gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*) are half a *li* in height; up to the sixth heaven, the body is three *li*, as it increases by half a *li at each stage. Some cite the *Tridharmakāya-sūtra*, which states that in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven...

Regarding the statement that their height is one *yojana*, their clothing two *yojanas*, and their width one *yojana*: this is due to a mistranslation of *li* (里) as *yojana*. Not realizing this error, [the author] has falsely cited it. For the gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), it is half a *li*; for the Trāyastriṃśa gods, it is one *li*; the others may be understood by analogy.

As for what was said above regarding the kalpa-counts being equal to the body-measures: in the Brahmakāyika heaven of the Form Realm (*Rūpadhātu*), the body height is half a *yojana*, and thus the human lifespan is half a kalpa; the others may be understood by analogy. Regarding the statement that "in the first four, they increase by half a half": [this refers to the sequence of increase].

The second, the Brahmā-purohita Heaven, is one yojana; the third, the Mahābrahmā, is one and a half yojanas; the fourth, the Parīttābha, is two yojanas. From these heavens upward, the height doubles at each stage, except for the Anabhraka Heaven, which is reduced by three yojanas.
To briefly explain the reason for this reduction: the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven is four yojanas; Ābhāsvara is eight; Parīttaśubha is sixteen; Apramāṇaśubha is thirty-two; and Śubhakṛtsna is sixty-four.

Reaching the Anabhraka Heaven, the total would be one hundred twenty-eight, but after subtracting three yojanas, it becomes one hundred twenty-five. From these seven heavens upward, the height again doubles at each stage until reaching the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. Because the lifespan there is to be sixteen thousand kalpas, the body length is one [yojana].

It is sixteen thousand *yojanas*. Furthermore, it is said that for the gods from the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*) upward, a full half of a great kalpa constitutes a kalpa; that is, eighty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*) constitute one [great] kalpa.

For the various heavens below that, a full half of a great kalpa constitutes a kalpa; that is, forty intermediate kalpas constitute one [great] kalpa. An "intermediate kalpa" refers to one period of increase and one period of decrease. Regarding the weight of their garments: the clothing of the Four Heavenly Kings weighs twelve *zhu*, while that of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven weighs six *zhu*.

In the Yāma Heaven, it is three *liǎozhū* (銖); in Tuṣita, one and a half *liǎozhū*; in Nirmāṇarati, one *liǎozhū*; and in Paranirmita-vaśavartin, half a *liǎozhū*. In each higher realm, the measure is reduced by half. Regarding the distinctions among the palaces and so forth, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states concerning the city of the Moon God (*Candramas*):

its city is square, measuring one thousand nine hundred and sixty *lǐ* on each side, with a height and depth equal to that. It is divided into two parts: one part of pure gold and one part of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*). The king sits within a space of twenty *lǐ*, appearing round from a distance though it is actually square.

The Sun God (*Sūrya*) is the same, except that its dimensions are increased by half a *yojana*. Within the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is a palace named Sudarśana, ten thousand *yojanas* in circumference and five thousand in height. Its golden walls are adorned with various ornaments, and the ground is soft and supple. In its center is the Palace of Excellence (*Vaijayanta*), ten thousand *yojanas* in circumference. This...

The higher heavens all increase twofold in excellence; this can be understood through the mind. For now, I shall merely briefly explain the meaning of their names. (Next, the combined explanation of the heavens of the Desire Realm.

(According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter 4: There are six abodes in the Desire Realm: first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; second, the Heaven of the Thirty-three; third, the Yāma Heaven; fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven; fifth, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and sixth, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

Furthermore, there is the Palace of Māra, which is included within the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, though its location is loftier and more excellent. (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: One is born in the heavens due to the causal conditions of superior generosity and one’s vows.)

As it is said in the Sūtra: There are those who practice giving and maintain the precepts in small measure, yet do not understand meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Such persons, hearing of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*), constantly set their minds and aspirations upon it. The Buddha said that when such persons die, they will be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Kings. This applies likewise up to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*).

If one practices giving and maintains the precepts with a degree of purity and excellence, and feels weary of domestic life, delighting in listening to the Dharma and making offerings to virtuous people, one will be reborn in the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings. If one practices giving and maintains the precepts with complete purity...

If one makes offerings to one’s parents and those whom one reveres, and with a mind desiring excellence, is reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. If one is pure in generosity and observance of the precepts, yet delights in study, with a mind that is harmonious and gentle, one is reborn in the Yāma Heaven.

If one is pure in generosity and observance of the precepts, making these two matters even more excellent, delighting in study and extensive learning, discerning between the beautiful and the ugly, loving and delighting in Nirvāṇa, and fixing the mind upon merit, one is reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.

If one gives with a profound mind, observes the precepts, and is well-learned, delighting in study and supporting oneself through one’s own efforts, one is reborn in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven. If one is pure at the time of giving, the observance of precepts becomes deeper, one delights in study and extensive learning, possesses much self-regard, and being unable to undergo personal hardship, seeks pleasure from others, one is reborn in the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven.

[The *Fayuan zhulin* states that] according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, one merely attains rebirth in the heavens by means of the superior grade of the wholesome [roots], provided that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not dispersed. Separately, according to the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*, it is fully explained that one attains rebirth in the celestial realms through the ten wholesome actions.

[The *Ullambana-puṣpa-śūtra* states that] if one cultivates the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions alone, one reaches as far as the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven within the desire realm; if one cultivates the ten wholesome actions while seated in the *anāgamya-samādhi*, one is born from the third Yāma Heaven up to the sixth heaven.

By the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*), the gods of the four heavens all dwell in space and do not rely upon the earth. That which is called "not-yet-attained concentration" (*anāgamya-samādhi*) is also termed "not-yet-reached. Because one has not yet entered the fundamental concentrations (*maula-dhyāna*), it is also named the "desire-realm concentration" (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*); this refers to the scattered wholesome karma (*vyagra-kuśala-karma*) of the desire realm.

If one cultivates the ten types of karma or the four types of karma in association with concentration, this constitutes the wholesome karma of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu-samādhi-kuśala-karma*). (From *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter Four: The various devas experience vast [rewards]; their forms and colors are exceptionally sublime, and they possess much pleasure. Within their own palaces, they attain sovereignty.

Both the interior and exterior of their bodies are entirely pure, free from any foulness or impurity. Furthermore, within the human body there is much impurity, namely: dust, grime, sinews, bones, the spleen, kidneys, and the heart.

The liver is entirely absent in them. There are four kinds of palaces made of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli, adorned with various colorful patterns and exquisite decorations. With their terraces, pavilions, and towers in various tiers, and their windows, lattices, and nets, they are all delightful to behold.

Various mani-jewels serve as ornamental inlays, emitting light from all sides that illuminates one another. Furthermore, there are trees of food; from within these trees emerge four kinds of edible flavors called *sudhā*, namely blue, yellow, red, and white.

Furthermore, there are drink-trees from which flow sweet and delicious beverages. There are also vehicle-trees from which emerge various kinds of exquisite vehicles, namely chariots, litters, palanquins, and so forth.
There are clothing-trees from which emerge various kinds of exquisite garments; these clothes are fine and soft, with wonderful colors that are fresh and pure, adorned with variegated patterns.

There are ornament-trees from which emerge various subtle and exquisite ornaments, namely mani-jewel armlets, earrings, rings, bracelets, and various decorative items for the hands and feet, all of which are interspersed with various exquisite mani-jewels. There are also incense and garland-trees from which emerge various kinds of ointments, perfumes, and garlands.

There are various flower garlands. Furthermore, there is the Great Assembly Tree, most excellent and subtle; its roots are firm and deep, extending fifty *yojana*s, and its trunk rises straight up for one hundred *yojana*s. Its branches and leaves completely cover eighty *yojana*s.

Various flowers bloom, their fragrance wafting with the wind for one hundred *yojana*s and against the wind for fifty *yojana*s. Beneath this tree, during the four months of the rainy season, the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens enjoy themselves together with the five celestial sensual pleasures.

Furthermore, there are trees of song, laughter, and dance, from which emerge songs, laughter, dances, and various musical instruments. There are also trees of requisites, from which emerge various necessities such as food, drink, seats, and bedding.

When the gods wish to enjoy these things, according to their desires and their karma, whatever they require appears in their hands. Furthermore, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, has the Palace of Universal Victory (*Vaijayanta*), wherein there are one hundred towers;

in each tower there are one hundred pavilions; in each pavilion there are seven chambers; in each chamber there are seven celestial maidens; and for each celestial maiden there are seven handmaidens. Moreover, the ground in those realms of the gods is as level as the palm of a hand, entirely without unevenness.

When one steps upon it, it produces a sense of bliss. When the foot is set down, it sinks until it reaches the knee; when the foot is lifted, it rises back up following the foot. At all times, *mandārava* flowers naturally appear everywhere.

It is spread over the ground. At times, a gentle breeze blows away the withered flowers and brings forth new ones. Furthermore, on each of the four sides of that celestial palace, there are great streets—pure, majestic, and perfectly orderly.

On those four sides, there are four great gates, vast in scale and guarded constantly by various classes of yakṣas of wondrous appearance. Moreover, on the four sides, there are four gardens: the first is called Citra (The Painted), the second Khara (The Rough), the third Miśra (The Mixed), and the fourth Nandana (The Joyful Grove).

Outside these four gardens are four excellent grounds of exquisite beauty. In the northeastern corner of the palace is a place where the devas assemble, named Sudharmā (The Hall of Good Dharma); there the devas enter to contemplate, deliberate, and examine sublime meanings. Near this...

Beside the garden, there is a wish-fulfilling stone, yellowish-white in color and exquisite in form and substance. Furthermore, the bodies of those devas naturally radiate light; when the appearance of darkness manifests, they know that day has passed and night is now approaching. They then indulge in the five sublime sensual pleasures of the heavens.

Amidst their play, they become indolent and fall asleep; the birds of various species no longer sing in harmony. By such signs as these, day and night are indicated. Furthermore, those devas find the five exquisite sensual pleasures exceedingly delightful, giving rise only to joy and bliss.

They are constantly governed by heedlessness in their conduct. They perpetually hear the various sounds of singing, dancing, music, and clamor; the sounds of playful chatter, laughter, and jesting. They constantly see various pleasing forms and perpetually smell various subtle and exquisite fragrances.

They always taste various delicious flavors and perpetually touch the most excellent tactile sensations of the celestial maidens. Constantly indulging in these pleasures, they have their minds drawn away as they pass the time. Furthermore, those devas...

They experience many such exquisite pleasures of desire; they are constantly free from illness and never subject to aging. They lack the suffering born of the deficiency of food, drink, and so forth, as previously described regarding those born in the human realm, who suffer from various forms of deprivation.

[The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks]: "The devas of the desire realm are deeply attached to the five desires and are difficult to convert. Why does the Bodhisattva take birth there rather than among humans? Answer: "Although the attachment of the devas is great, the Bodhisattva’s power of skillful means is likewise great.

As it is said, in the Heaven of the Thirty-three there is a forest of Pārijātaka trees where holy beings of the heavens, capable of renouncing the five desires, dwell and convert the devas. In Tuṣita Heaven, there is always one who is in his final birth (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*)."

The Bodhisattva in his final birth always hears the Dharma, and the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada likewise dwells in the heavens of the Four Great Kings; such beings as these teach and transform sentient beings. (From the "Kāśyapa Chapter" of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*):

"Good son, this person contemplates that the afflictions of the desire realm have two kinds of causes and conditions: first, internal; second, external. Furthermore, within the desire realm, there are two kinds of craving: first, craving for sensual desires (*kāmatṛṣṇā*); second, craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*).

Contemplating these two cravings, he rebukes them with a sincere heart. Having thus rebuked them, he attains entry into nirvana. This desire realm enables one to rebuke coarse afflictions, namely stinginess, greed, anger, jealousy, lack of shame (*ahrīkya*), and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*). By these causes and conditions, one attains entry [into nirvana]."

Nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the path of the desire realm is courageous and vigorous by nature. Why? Because it attains the fruit of the direction toward [the goal]. For this reason, there is intermediate nirvāṇa within the desire realm, but none within the form realm. There are three types of intermediate nirvāṇa: the superior type attains nirvāṇa before having abandoned the desires of the desire realm;

the middling type attains nirvāṇa after beginning to abandon the desires of the desire realm but before reaching the form realm; the inferior type attains nirvāṇa only after having abandoned the desires of the desire realm and reached the edge of the form realm. The Ten Wholesome Deeds. (This is based on the fact that, according to the primary tenets of the sūtras, lust alone is taken as the fundamental cause for their clarity and purity. Amidst such playful enjoyment, they forget the thoughts they held at birth, yet their consciousness retains the karma of their previous lives, enabling them to be born in the heavens. (2. The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven)
Regarding their own wives, their lustful attachment is slight; yet while dwelling in the Pure Abodes, they do not obtain full flavor.
After the end of their lives, they transcend the brilliance of the sun and moon and dwell at the summit of the human realm. This class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

[Commentary]: Sensual desire gradually diminishes; even toward one's own family and household, attachment and desire are reduced, and thus there is no "complete flavor. "Flavor" (rasa) here refers to attachment.

As for the term "Pure Abodes" (śuddhāvāsa), it means they are not produced by impurity, thereby distinguishing them from those who practice deviance.
