At the time of dwelling in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, one does not remain entirely attached to sensory flavors. Master Yue’s interpretation differs slightly [from others]: because wholesome qualities increase, one transcends the sun and moon, and furthermore, affectionate attachment diminishes.
The body then ascends once more, and thus one is born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. "Trāyastriṃśa" means "Thirty-three"; it is the abode of Śakra Devendra (located on the summit of Mount Sumeru).

There are thirty-two heavens at each of the four corners, with Śakra as their ruler. These two aforementioned heavens both rely upon Mount Sumeru and are called the "Earth-dwelling Devas" (Bhūmi-vāsin), situated eighty-four thousand yojanas above the earth.

[The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Formerly, there was a Brahmin of the Kauśika clan who, together with thirty-two close friends, cultivated merit and virtue. In the groves and gardens, the various devas enjoy themselves, all giving rise to joy. To the southwest outside the city is the Sudharmā Hall, where the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven gather periodically to deliberate and adjudicate matters of what is lawful and unlawful regarding the Asuras.

Regarding their physical dimensions and lifespans: the bodies of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are one *li* tall; their garments weigh six *zhu*. Their lifespan is one thousand celestial years. Their food, drink, marriage, and courtship are like those of the Cāturmahārājika Heaven.

Their bodies are close together, and they form the Yin and Yang through their vital energy (*prāṇa*). By virtue of good conduct of body, speech, and mind, one is born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. At the time of birth, a flower blooms in the hand of a celestial maiden; she knows of herself that she has a child, and she immediately hands it to him.

Seven days after his birth, he was born with innate knowledge of celestial laws (*deva-dharma*). He was born like a three-year-old child at the place where his parents were situated—either between their two knees or two thighs—and suddenly appeared. He possessed the recollection of his previous lives (*pūrvajātismara*), as well as the practice of generosity and the observance of precepts.

When encountering desire, they engage briefly; once it has passed, they have no lingering thoughts or recollections. Regarding worldly affairs, their activity is slight while their stillness is great.

They possess their own radiance. Such a class is called the Suyāma Heaven. [Commentary]:
Having not yet abandoned the mind of desire, they encounter objects only briefly; as this [desire] gradually thins out below, it is said that they "depart without thought or recollection."

When encountering desire, one still engages with it; therefore, it is said that "movement is slight. When departing from it, there is no further recollection; therefore, it is said that "stillness is predominant. [The *Xunwen* commentary states:

"Movement" refers to the scattering of desire, while "stillness" refers to tranquility. This is spoken in reference to the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*). However, since one has not yet attained coarse abiding (*sthūla-sthiti*) or subtle abiding (*sūkṣma-sthiti*), by this we verify that the aforementioned Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) correspond to the initial cultivation of desire-realm concentration, which is perfected in Tuṣita.

As these practices increase further, the body likewise becomes superior; thus, one is born in the Heaven of the Time-Portions (*Tuṣita*). "Time-portion" (*tuṣita*) means "time"; this is the realm of space.

He dwells in the first heaven (this heaven is 160,000 yojanas above the earth; its palaces are sustained by a wind-wheel and reside in the void of space; there is ground like clouds that remains luminously suspended).

[The *Miaoyan shu* states: The fourth is the Suyāma Heaven. *Sū* means "good" or "sublime. *Yāma* means "time. In full, it is called the Heaven of the Good Time-Portion (*Suyāmā*). The *Śāstra* says: Because they experience pleasure according to the time, it is named the Heaven of the Time-Portion;

this refers to their constantly singing of joy. Alternatively, it is said: because they receive the objects of the five desires while knowing the divisions of time. Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that this heaven uses the opening and closing of lotuses to distinguish day and night; it further says that the blooming of red lotuses constitutes day, and the blooming of white lotuses constitutes night.]

"Night. Therefore, it is called a "time-period" (*kāla*). It is tranquil at all times; if sensory contacts arise, one is unable to resist them. After life ends, one ascends to a state of subtle refinement.

Because it shares the same name, Tuṣita, it is here translated as "Contentment" (Zhizu). (The three calamities do not reach this place; this refers specifically to Maitreya’s dwelling. They have made great vows and attained birth in that place; by the power of their outflow-free (*anāsrava*) merit, they are not affected by the three calamities. Seven days after their birth, Maitreya emits light and rains down flowers, leading them into the small *maṇi* palace within the inner courtyard, where he immediately preaches the Dharma for them to inspire the power of diligence. Only thereafter are they led into the inner courtyard.

Furthermore, there is another class of devas who are the result of karmic retribution; these are produced by the influence of tainted merit (*sāsrava-puṇya*) and constitute the "devas of collective retribution" (*sāmānya-vipāka-deva*). Because they are the fruit of tainted [actions], they can be destroyed by the three calamities.

By maintaining mindfulness while eating a single meal, one may attain rebirth [in the heavens] within seven days. While the workings of karma and its fruits are explained extensively throughout, it is specifically in this heaven that the subtle and profound are uniquely manifested, distinct from the mere accumulation of merit. If one speaks in terms of general retribution, although beings in this heaven have already escaped physical embracing, they have not yet transcended the desire of holding hands; how then can this be called a subtle and refined ascent? It is here that the Tathāgata, by means of this teaching, reveals the specific gate of rebirth in Tuṣita, so that people may know that without leaving the five desires, one may transcend the four dhyānas. Not only is the Inner Court within the desire heavens identical to a celestial palace, but furthermore—

I have no lustful mind; I act in accordance with your conduct. When you lie across me, the flavor is like chewing wax.

[Commentary]: The mind has no intentionality toward objects; objects simply come across it by chance. Since the objects themselves possess their own "mind" [of existence], what flavor can one find in them? Thus it is said that their flavor is like chewing wax.
This is because they enjoy and utilize the five sensory desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) which they have transformed through their own pleasure.

(Regarding the gods' requirements for food and clothing, these must still be produced through their own transformations; however, for this particular heaven, what they require arises immediately upon thought. They experience enjoyment through their own transformations. This refers to transcending the lower realms to manifest transformations; hence it is called "transcendent transformation" (*yuèhuà*). This refers to "transformation" (nirmāṇa), meaning that what was non-existent suddenly comes into being. (6. Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven)
They possess no worldly mind, yet they engage in activities identical to those of the world. Amidst the intersection of such worldly actions, they clearly transcend them.

After their lives end, they are universally able to transcend both the realms of transformation and non-transformation. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations.

[Commentary: "The activities and conduct intersect" means this is also a horizontal presentation. Although the previous state lacked flavor, the mind still gave rise to desire when encountering objects;

"Because they enjoy the five objects of desire transformed by others, and because they possess sovereign power to command others to transform [objects] for their enjoyment, it is called Paranirmita-vaśavartin.

(Whatever this heaven requires for enjoyment arrives there without being thought of. [The *Miaoyan Shu* states: "Regarding the seventh, the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the treatise says..."]

[The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*] says: *Vaśavartin*; in the language of Qin, it means "Sovereignty over Others' Transformations.

These gods seize what others have transformed and enjoy them for themselves; therefore, they are named "Sovereignty over Others' Transformations. The Sanskrit term is *dhyāna*; here it is translated as "meditative concentration" (*jing-lü*). "Meditative" (*jing*) refers to tranquility; "concentration" (*lü*) refers to discernment. Tranquility is able to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*), while discernment is able to engage in correct contemplation. In the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), there is tranquility but no discernment; although they can sever the fetters, they cannot engage in correct contemplation.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is discernment but no tranquility; although one can engage in correct contemplation, one cannot sever the fetters. Therefore, only those [states] beyond the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) receive this designation. Regarding the first four dhyānas: the first is meditative concentration with directed thought and evaluation (*savitarka-savicāra*); the second is meditative concentration without directed thought and without evaluation (*avitarka-avicāra*).

The third is the dhyāna detached from joy; the fourth is the dhyāna detached from bliss. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter on Concentration: "The first possesses vicāra, prīti, and sukha; in the subsequent stages, one gradually abandons the preceding factors. The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* says: "In the mundane [path], there are the uninterrupted and the liberated [paths].")

"Respectively taking the lower and upper [stages] as objects, they function as the aspects of coarseness, suffering, and being an obstacle, as well as purity, excellence, and detachment. The Commentary says: The mundane paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) respectively take the lower and upper stages as their objects, functioning as the aspects of coarseness, suffering, and being an obstacle, as well as purity, excellence, and detachment.

That is to say, the path of uninterrupted transition takes the various contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of its own level and the immediately lower level as its object, functioning through one of the three aspects—coarseness, suffering, or being an obstacle. As for the path of liberation, it takes the various contaminated phenomena of the immediately higher level as its object, functioning through one of the three aspects—purity, excellence, or detachment.

Because [the lower stage] is not tranquil, it is coarse; because it is not sublime, it is suffering; because it is not a means of escape, it is an obstacle. One should understand that the three aspects of purity, excellence, and detachment are the reverse of these. That is to say, if one applies diligence, one performs these six aspects.

The path for severing the fetters suppresses the afflictions of the lower stages; upon the end of life, one immediately receives birth in the two higher realms. Furthermore, regarding the six modes of practice, there are three types each of aspiration and aversion. As for the essential nature of what is aspired to or what is felt aversion toward, these differ according to each respective stage.

For example, desire, evil, and unwholesome states are what is felt aversion toward by the first dhyāna; discursive thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are what is felt aversion toward by the second dhyāna; and so on, up to the state of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), which, being tranquil, is what is felt aversion toward by the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). The aspiration for the higher stages may be inferred by analogy with this.

Furthermore, the first dhyāna is what is aspired to by the mind of the lower "unprepared" (*anāgamya*) stage as being "pure, wondrous, and secluded," yet it is what is felt aversion toward by the proximate mind of the other, the second dhyāna, as being "coarse, painful, and obstructive. Thus, the phenomena of the desire realm are exclusively objects of aversion and not of aspiration, while the phenomena of the Peak of Existence stage are exclusively... [objects of aversion].

This is what is to be delighted in, not what is to be loathed; it is a dharma of the intermediate stage that can be both loathed and delighted in. (The *Commentary on the Dhyānapāramitā* states: Regarding the sixfold contemplation, there are three aspects of loathing the lower realms for their suffering, coarseness, and obstructions—namely, contemplating the impurity, deception, and contemptibility of the desire realm.

There are three aspects of "clinging to the superior" and "emerging"—that is, "emerging" means departing—namely, contemplating the first dhyāna as honorable and precious. To speak of "loathing the lower" means to loathe the base of the desire realm because its physical and mental states are coarse and heavy. This is the first: the contemplation of loathing suffering.)

It refers to the practitioner’s reflection: "Now, I experience the retributive body of the desire realm, which is oppressed by various things such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, illness, pain, knives, and staves; this constitutes the suffering of the fruit. Regarding the mental factors arising within this body, they take craving as their object," as it is said in the Sūtra.

All sentient beings are slaves to craving; this is the cause of suffering. Both the cause of suffering and the fruit of suffering must be reviled and loathed. Second is the contemplation of revulsion regarding coarseness: it means reflecting that this body is composed of thirty-six impure substances, such as excrement and urine, which constitute its coarse fruit.

Its coarse cause is the scattering and agitation that give rise to evil by taking the five objects of the desire realm as conditions. Both the coarse cause and the coarse fruit must be reviled and loathed. Third is the contemplation of revulsion regarding obstructions:

it means reflecting that this body is obstructed by mountains, rivers, rocks, and walls, preventing it from attaining mastery; this constitutes the obstruction of the fruit. That afflictions shroud the true nature constitutes the obstruction of the cause. Both the obstruction of the cause and the obstruction of the fruit must be reviled and loathed. Fourth is the contemplation of aspiring toward excellence: it means regarding the pleasures of the desire realm as suffering, and [regarding] the form realm...

Joy is superior. Attaining the flavor of the first dhyāna is the superiority of the fruit. Craving for sensual pleasure arises from the five external sense objects and produces affliction, fever, resentment, and bondage; it is thus inferior. The superior joy of the first dhyāna arises from within; it is thus superior in its cause.

Having attained this superior joy which overcomes suffering, one must rejoice. Receiving a body in the realm of form, like a reflection in a mirror, is free from substantial obstruction; this is the excellence of the fruit. The joy of meditative concentration is a mind fixed and unmoving;

this is the excellence of the cause. Sensual craving causes the mind to move and scatter, which is called coarse. Having attained the excellent and superior state that transcends the coarse, one must rejoice. Obtaining the five supernormal powers and seeing through obstructions so that mountains and walls offer no hindrance is the emergence of the fruit. The mind attaining freedom from the hindrances and reaching the first dhyāna is the emergence of the cause.
It is also like a spring in a rock, which wells up from within; having emerged and overcome superior obstacles, one must rejoice in all of this). (2. The Brahmakāyika Heaven)
Once the habitual tendencies of desire have been eliminated, the mind free from desire manifests; one takes delight in and accords with all forms of discipline.
Such a person is able to practice the virtues of Brahma at the appropriate time. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahma (Brahmapurohita).

[Commentary: Since the afflictions of the desire realm have already been subdued, it is said that "the habitual tendencies of desire are removed. Having attained the first *dhyāna*, the concentrated mind manifests its excellence;

thus it is said that "the mind, free from desire, appears. This concludes the section on the higher [realms]. Regarding the phrase "among all the lower [realms]," this correctly clarifies this heaven (*deva*).
Within the *samādhi-sahaja-śīla* (precepts co-arising with concentration), they take delight in and accord with them, thereby perfecting the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Thus, by preventing what is non-virtuous and remaining without transgression, one simultaneously guards the discipline (*vinaya-saṃvara*), accomplishes the virtue of pure precepts, and assists the Lord of Brahmā;

therefore, they are called the "Brahmapurohitas" (Brahma-Ministers). [The translation states: *Brahmapurohita* means "Heaven of Prior Benefit. They precede the Brahmā heaven and constantly contemplate the benefit of the Brahmā heavens; they are also called the "Brahma-Ministers. (The Three Great Brahmā Heavens).

With body and mind wondrously perfect, their majestic deportment flawless, and their pure prohibitive precepts augmented by clear awakening, such persons are able, at the appropriate time, to preside over the Brahma hosts as Great Brahma Kings. This class of beings is called the Mahābrahmā devas.
[Commentary: Because his meditative contemplation has become increasingly superior and his rebirth is subtle and refined, it is said that "body and mind are wondrously perfect.

Furthermore, because he possesses the virtue of the precepts, it is said that "his majestic deportment is without deficiency. This concludes the preceding section. From "Pure" onwards, the text properly explains this heaven.

Within meditative concentration and the precepts, he gives rise to the clear awakening of wisdom; thus, his wisdom and understanding surpass those of others, enabling him to serve as the Lord of Brahmā and preside over the Brahma realm.

[The assembly: According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, [the gods] possess majestic power and radiance, travel alone, and are free from both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), as these are induced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The two lower heavens possess both vitarka and vicāra. third, without vitarka and without vicāra, referring to the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), etc. The present Heaven of Great Brahmā is precisely the intermediate dhyāna, induced by the power of meditative concentration. Furthermore...
At the end of a kalpa they depart; at the beginning of a kalpa they arrive first. Unable to fathom this, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) grasp it as being eternal.

"Permanence and the Son of Brahmā’s Impermanence. (△ [Gushan says: The three heavens above do not manifest the cultivation of dhyāna; they clarify only the observance of precepts. This scripture supports the Vinaya to encourage future generations. (○ [The Commentary on the Ten Treasuries Storehouse] says: Regarding the Brahma Heaven, the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* initially states there are three;

He immediately led the procession of attendants before Mahābrahmā. This Great Brahmā is that very Heavenly King who has attained the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). The *Abhidharma* states: "From the second dhyāna upward, there are no verbal dharmas; therefore, a king is not established. The *Yingluo* [Sūtra] states that in each dhyāna there is a Brahmā King. The Chan-men (Gate of Dhyāna) says: "In the First Dhyāna, there is internal *vitarka* and *vicāra*, and externally there are the dharmas of speech. Although they have no topknots, they appear as if wearing celestial crowns. They lack male or female characteristics, and their forms are of only one kind. (Seal No. 2).
Ānanda, these three superior classes cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction.
Although they have not yet attained the true Samādhi of correct cultivation, their minds are pure and all outflows (āsravas) remain unmoved; this is called the First Dhyāna.
[Commentary: Having already departed from the eight sufferings of the desire realm, it is said that he "cannot be oppressed" by them.

However, because this is merely the subduing of afflictions through the six practices, it is called "not the true samādhi. Generally, one who truly cultivates dhyāna does not manifest body or mind within the three realms;
even if superior and wondrous signs of concentration appear before him, he clearly knows them for what they are and remains free from attachment. Although he has now attained this...
It is pure and resembles samādhi; because it is not fully understood, one becomes attached to its flavor and is reborn [therein].

Nevertheless, because it can distance one from the coarse agitation of the desire-filled distracted mind, it is said that "the outflows (āsrava) do not move. Therefore, the conclusion states: these three superior streams are collectively termed the First Dhyāna.

(According to Gushan: There are four types of dhyāna: first, contaminated dhyāna (*sāsrava-dhyāna*), which refers to the present Four Dhyānas; second, uncontaminated dhyāna (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), referring to the nine notions, the eight liberations, and so forth; third, both contaminated and uncontaminated dhyāna, referring to the Six Sublime Methods...)

Regarding the "penetrating clarity" (*abhijñā*) and so forth—the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) that are neither with-outflows (*sāsrava*) nor without-outflows (*anāsrava*)—this refers to the Middle Way concentration (*madhyama-mārga-samādhi*) of this Śūraṅgama King Samādhi. When it is now stated, "Although it is not the true, correct *samādhi*," this uses the first [category] to distinguish it from the fourth.

"Purity of mind" specifically refers to the first dhyāna. "The various outflows (āsravas) do not move" specifically refers to the subduing of afflictions. [Commentary by Wēnlíng: There are the flow of ignorance, the flow of desire, the flow of victory, the flow of the four fruits, and the flow of nirvāṇa.

The flow of desire leads toward birth and death; although it reaches the six heavens of the desire realm, it is not yet sufficient to be called "victorious. This heaven has already emerged from the flow of desire, turns its back on birth and death, and proceeds toward supreme purity; therefore, it is called the "flow of victory. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion is free from the mixed evils of the desire realm and gives rise to the bliss of pliancy (praśrabdhi). [Commentary on the Three Stages: "Joy and bliss born of seclusion" refers to the benefits of cultivation.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Book 11) clarifies the abandonment of five factors: namely, joy and pleasure induced by desire, as well as grief and joy induced by the unwholesome, and the equanimity associated with those five feelings. Because one abandons these, joy and pleasure arise. Regarding "joy" (*prīti*), it refers to profound celebration and mental satisfaction. Regarding "pleasure" (*sukha*), it refers to physical and mental serenity. One celebrates the departure from desire, evil, and so forth; therefore, joy arises.

When body and mind are calmed and at rest, and one attains the bliss of liberation, it is therefore called "pleasure. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Book 6) states: "Lightness-and-composure (*praśrabdhi*) means that lightness is the removal of heaviness (*dausthulya*), and composure is the harmonious regulation of body and mind.

Furthermore, the merits obtained in this first dhyāna consist of five branches: first, applied thought (*vitarka*); second, [sustained thought (*vicāra*)]; third, [joy (*prīti*)]; fourth, [pleasure (*sukha*)]; and fifth, [one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*)]. First, applied thought... [text continues]
[The five factors are: first, applied thought (*vitarka*); second, sustained thought (*vicāra*); third, joy (*prīti*); fourth, bliss (*sukha*); and fifth, one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*).

Their characteristics are as described in the *Tiantai Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm). [The *Fajie Cidi* states: "Factor" (*aṅga*) means a constituent part. It is like a tree: the root and trunk are one, while the branches and twigs differ. The meaning of "factor" in dhyāna is likewise. Furthermore, it has the sense of "support. This means that when the concentrated mind is shallow and easily disturbed, it receives the support of factors such as applied and sustained thought;

thus, the concentrated mind becomes peaceful and firm. Therefore, they are called "factors. The concentration of the First Dhyāna Heaven possesses these five factors: first, the factor of applied thought. When the initial mind is directed toward its object, it is called "applied thought. A practitioner in the Desire Realm relies on this... [text continues].

Upon reaching the ground, the first dhyāna arises. The pure material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) of the form realm come into contact with the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*) of the desire realm. The mind is greatly startled and awakened, and immediately the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) arises, perceiving this color-and-touch. Second is the factor of investigation (*vicāra*). Investigation consists of subtle mental discernment.

Once the practitioner has realized the merits of the first dhyāna, they use a subtle mind to discern the material phenomena and various sublime qualities within this meditative concentration; these objects are distinct and clear, being unprecedented in the desire realm. Third is the factor of joy (*prīti*). Joy is the state of heart characterized by exultation and celebration. When the practitioner first enters dhyāna, there is the arising of joy;

the pleasure of the desire realm that was abandoned was very slight, whereas now, having attained the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the first dhyāna heaven, the benefit is immense, and their joy is immeasurable. Fourth is the factor of bliss (*sukha*). The practitioner... [enters] bliss.

At the time of the first dhyāna, once the mind of rapture (*prīti*) has ceased, one enters a state of tranquil contemplation and experiences the bliss of dhyāna. The five factors (*aṅga*) are as follows: the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*). When the mind corresponds with the dharma of concentration, it becomes unified.

When the practitioner first realizes this dhyāna, the mind relies upon the states of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture, and bliss; therefore, there is subtle distraction. However, when the mind of rapture and bliss subsides, the mind naturally becomes one with concentration. [The *Xunwen* says: "In the cultivation of the first dhyāna, one abandons the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and accomplishes the five factors. It possesses the eight touches and the ten marks of merit.

If this dhyāna is aroused, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm become pure and naturally manifest within the body of the desire realm. However, this sutra specifically clarifies how ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) take birth according to their dhyāna; therefore, it does not fully describe the characteristics of cultivation and realization. (○ [Zhi...])

The treatise says: With pure observance of the precepts, dwelling in seclusion and solitude, guarding and restraining the sense faculties, and during the first and last watches of the night, one applies oneself with focused diligence to contemplation. Abandoning external pleasures, one finds delight in dhyāna; free from all desires and unwholesome states, there is directed thought and sustained evaluation.

Detached from [sensual desires], one attains the first dhyāna through the joy and bliss born of seclusion, relying on the stage of access (anāgamya). The characteristics of the first dhyāna consist of applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), joy (prīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (citta-ekāgratā). Regarding "having applied and sustained thought": this is because one has attained the merit and qualities of wholesome dharmas never before obtained within the first dhyāna.

His mind was greatly startled and awakened. Having been constantly scorched by the fire of desire, upon attaining the first dhyāna, he felt as though he had entered a pool of cool water. A verse says: "Having already attained freedom from sensual desire, one enters the cool concentration. It is like a person in great heat and clamor who enters a cold pool and becomes cooled.

(In the Vinaya, this is illustrated by the metaphor of skillful bathing and immersion. Furthermore, it is like a poor man who suddenly finds a treasure trove. The practitioner contemplates and discriminates between the merits and faults of the desire realm; knowing that the benefits and virtues of the first dhyāna are exceedingly great, his heart is filled with immense joy.

(○ [Tiantai’s Commentary on Dhyāna states: Dhyāna is named the "grove of merit. The Samādhi of Skillful Means: When the practitioner enters meditative absorption within the stage of "Not-Yet-Arrived" (*anāgamya*), it gradually deepens. Ten kinds of wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-dharma*) arise as its retinue in succession; therefore, it is called the First Dhyāna). (2. Second Dhyāna). (3. Explanation). (1. Parīttābha Heaven).
Ānanda, next is the Brahmā Heaven, which governs the Brahmās, perfects the Brahma-conduct, and maintains a tranquil mind that is unmoving; from its profound stillness, light is produced.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābhā).

[Commentary: The King is the Lord of Brahmā; therefore, it is said he "governs and encompasses. He is fully endowed with precepts, concentration, and wisdom; therefore, it is said his "Brahma-conduct is perfected. This concludes the preceding section.

Because they are free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), they possess no speech; rather, they emit light through their concentrated minds.

Their respective ranks are distinguished by the superiority or inferiority of this light. (As it is said: "The 'light' refers to the radiance of the body's dimensions, not the illumination of wisdom. When this joyous sign first arises in these devas, their wisdom-light is still inferior;

[Regarding the distinct characteristics: The *Dīrgha Āgama*, in the *Nidāna-varga*, states: "When speaking, light issues from the mouth. (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

As for the statement in the sūtras that the physical bodies born of karmic retribution possess radiance—this is because the devas of the desire realm have practiced giving lamps, candles, and bright jewels, as well as the purity of generosity and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and thus their bodies are constantly luminous, requiring neither sun nor moon. In the form realm, through the practice of the dhyānas and the transcendence of desire, they cultivate the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-element samādhi); therefore, their bodies constantly emit wondrous radiance superior to that of the desire realm.

To summarize: all these radiances are obtained solely through the purity of the mind. The body of the first dhyāna likewise radiates light externally, yet not so internally; it is like a bright lamp that emits golden light outward while illuminating itself within. The body of the second dhyāna is also like this:
both internally and externally, it possesses radiance. (2. Apramāṇābhā devāḥ).
Light illuminates light, shining forth without end; it reflects throughout the worlds of the ten directions, universally transforming them into lapis lazuli.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Light.
[Commentary] From the preceding "Little Light" (*Parīttābha*) heaven, they further emit abundant light; as the characteristics of the light increase, it is called "Light-Light Radiance.

The characteristics of the light are perfectly bright, reflecting throughout the worlds of the ten directions. The environment becomes pure in accordance with the light, universally transforming into lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*). This occurs because meditative concentration increases further.

The light of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) radiates forth; it is necessarily boundless and is thus called Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*). [The *Zhēnjiè* says: It reflects throughout the ten directions.

This is spoken in reference to the light of concentration according to where it is utilized—east, west, and so on—and does not mean it pervades the entirety of the worlds of the ten directions. (○ [Fānyì] says: In Sanskrit it is *Ābhāsvara*; here it is translated as Immeasurable Light. Its radiance increases further and further, such that its measure is difficult to fathom. [The *Āgama* says: When speaking, many rays of light issue from the mouth. (The Third: Heaven of Utmost Light and Sound).
They inhale and sustain the circular radiance, accomplishing the essence of the teaching; they give rise to pure transformation, and their applications are inexhaustible.
This class of beings is called the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven).
[Commentary]: It absorbs and sustains immeasurable pure light, using it as the medium of verbal expression; this is termed the "essence of the teaching" (*śāsana-tattva*).
Because this light expresses and clarifies while being free from all coarseness and heaviness (*dausthulya*), it is said to be "emanated and transformed as pure.

In the realm and stage of the second dhyāna, the first five consciousnesses do not exist (for those of the outer vehicles and ordinary beings, when in meditative absorption, none of them can arise to cognize objects);

they employ only *ābhāsvara* as their medium of expression. Taking light as sound, it is called the Heaven of Light-Sound (*Ābhāsvara*). [Gushan says: "The functional application of the wisdom-light is taken as the teaching-body for conventional expression;

"Light. Furthermore, because it can accomplish the essence of teaching, it is named "Light-Sound" (Ābhāsvara). "Inhaling" means not dispersing; "retaining" means not losing. This heaven possesses the factor of internal purity. (○ [Translation states]:

Ānanda, these three superior types of practitioners cannot be oppressed by any sorrow.
Although they have not yet attained the true, correct Samādhi, because coarse outflows have been subdued within their pure minds, this is called the Second Dhyāna.

Clarity and serenity; joy and tranquility arising from the harmony of the faculties, wherein sorrow does not arise—this is called the stage of "joy and bliss born of concentration.

[The Commentary on the Third Dhyāna states: Regarding "joy and bliss born of concentration": in the first dhyāna, one rejoices in having turned away from desire and evil, and thus it is called "born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*). Now, one rejoices in the cessation of the mental activity of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), and thus it is called "born of concentration" (*samādhija*).

It is like a clear mirror or still water; therefore, body and mind are at ease and joyful. Desire and evil are like mud; the concentration of the first dhyāna is like moving water that has been stilled. Now, being free from desire and evil, and further extinguishing applied and sustained thought, it is like clear, still water. (The Dinglin commentary states: "Regarding 'the coarse outflows having already been suppressed,' because there is the factor of internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), yet the factor of joy (*prīti*) still remains, one is only able to suppress the coarse outflows of the lower stage;

[The sequence is as follows: The second dhyāna has four factors (*aṅga*). First is the factor of internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*). When the mind is free from the turbidity of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it is called internal purity. As the practitioner desires to leave the first dhyāna, they censure the various forms of applied and sustained thought; once these have ceased, the mind becomes internally pure. Second is the factor of joy (*prīti*).

When the practitioner first attains internal purity, they are freed from the affliction of applied and sustained thought and achieve superior concentration; the joy of internal realization is immeasurable. Third is bliss (*sukha*). Fourth is one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). These may be understood [as stated in the *Kunmon*]:

the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* designates this as "dhyāna accompanied by joy," because when this concentration arises, it emerges together with joy. Since the five factors of the first dhyāna already included joy, yet it was still accompanied by applied and sustained thought and carried a sense of anxiety; now that applied and sustained thought are exhausted, one experiences [bliss].

(The designation "accompanied by joy") (△ [The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says]: The practitioner knows that these vitarka and vicāra, although they are wholesome dharmas, disturb the concentrated mind. Or again, like a person exhausted from travel who, having found rest, wishes to sleep, but is disturbed and troubled by a bystander’s shouting and calling; so too it is when the mind is gathered in internal concentration—it is disturbed by vitarka and vicāra. Binding the mind to a single point, without vitarka and without vicāra, one enters the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss. Having abandoned the applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) of the first dhyāna, one attains an incomparable joy and bliss (*prīti-sukha*) within the second dhyāna that has never been attained before. Because the mind is bound to a single object, it is called "inner purity" (*adhyātma-saṃprasāda*). There are no nose-consciousness or tongue-consciousness. Thus, there is neither applied thought (*vitarka*) nor sustained thought (*vicāra*). This explains the meaning of "purity" (*śubha*): it is not the same as the First Dhyāna, because the latter possesses applied and sustained thought. [Commentary]:

Ānanda, when such devas and humans have perfected their radiant light into sound, and having unveiled the sublime through that sound, they give rise to refined practice and penetrate the bliss of cessation—
this class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parittaśubha).
[Commentary] The first two phrases refer back to what preceded. "Pī" (披) is pronounced as in the second tone. This correctly elucidates this heaven:

that is, by "peeling away" (*pī*) the substance of the teaching that expresses [the truth], one reveals the wondrous principle that is expressed, thereby accomplishing the wondrous practice that is to be performed. [Supplement states:

"By peeling away the traces of the *Ābhāsvara* (Light-Sound) teaching, one exposes this wondrous nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which then issues forth as wondrous practice. [Dinglin states: "One is able to peel away and manifest the source of sound, knowing how the teaching is formed; one is able to develop and reveal the wondrous nature, seeing from whence the light arises. This heaven possesses wisdom."

Because of these factors, once these three types of wisdom have been generated, sublime bliss (*sukha*) is thoroughly realized. Concentration and wisdom surpass what came before, as the collection of factors becomes increasingly superior.

(This refers to the factor of "one-pointedness of mind," which penetrates the bliss of cessation. Regarding the term "bliss of cessation" (*nirodha-sukha*): it is the pure bliss that arises when the preceding signs of joy (*prīti*) are extinguished.
Because the signs of joy are coarse and agitated, this resultant bliss is placid and tranquil; therefore, it is called "cessation. The characteristics of concentration remain...

Because it is inferior, it is called "pervasive" (*sāmanta*). Having first attained this bliss, but not yet having made it extensive and all-pervading, it is called "limited purity" (*parītta-śubha*).

[The *Shìjièzhì* says: "To be free from the sensation of joy and experience bliss is 'purity'; because one has not yet reached the higher stages, it is 'limited'. "Purity" (*śubha*) is also "tranquility" (*śānta*).

By abandoning the coarse and agitated characteristics of joy (*prīti*) in the second dhyāna, one observes through mindfulness and wisdom, perceives cessation (*nirodha*), and thereby gives rise to bliss (*sukha*).

Hence it is said that it "pervades the bliss of cessation. Cessation is purity (*śubha*). [Commentary: "Pure emptiness" refers to pure bliss. (Wenling says: "Pure emptiness" means being free from all movements of joy; it is the meditative state that does not take external objects as its condition.

Joy. Because its pure joy is boundless, it is called "Immeasurable Purity" (Apramāṇaśubha). (3. Śubhakṛtsna Heaven).
World, body, and mind are all perfectly pure. Having accomplished the virtues of purity, the supreme support manifests before them, and they return to the bliss of cessation.
This class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna (All-Pervading Purity) devas.
[Commentary]: Although they previously experienced the bliss of the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), it was confined to body and mind and thus not yet termed "all-pervading.

Now, however, this bliss and purity are perfectly integrated throughout both the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*). There is no place—whether in the world-system or within body and mind—that is not pervaded by this sublime and wondrous bliss.

It accomplishes pure virtue. Regarding the term "excellent reliance" (*śreṣṭha-pratiśaraṇa*): it refers precisely to this pure bliss, which is the supreme locus upon which the practitioner relies. Because one realizes this bliss, it is called "refuge. (Wenling says:

When pure virtue is accomplished, then the fundamental bliss of the nature takes refuge and relies therein. (Dinglin says: One initiates and perfects refined practice, penetrating the bliss of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).

One is merely able to penetrate; once pure emptiness manifests before one, it induces boundlessness. Body and mind become light and serene, whereupon bliss is perfected. When the excellent reliance manifests, there is a ground upon which to rely; hence it is said, "one returns to the bliss of quiescent extinction.")

(△ [Qingliang says: This deva is free from joy because body and mind are universally pure. (○ [Fanyi says: "Universally Pure" (*Abhāsvara*). In Sanskrit, it is *Abhāsvara*. Because the experience of bliss is most excellent and purity is perfected and pervasive.

(○ [Shoujian says: The calculations of outsiders do not exceed two heavens: one is Maheśvara, and one is Viṣṇu. Ānanda, these three superior classes possess great compliance; their bodies and minds are at peace, and they attain immeasurable bliss.
Although this is not the true, correct Samādhi, within a state of peace and stability, joy is fully present; this is called the Third Dhyāna.

[Zizhong] "Possessing great compliance" means that the ripening pleasure (*vipāka-sukha*) of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) complies with mastery. [Zhenzhen says: "Ripening pleasure" penetrates the mental ground;

second, being free from sorrow and joy (*daurmanasya* and *saumanasya*). Since sorrow and joy are both objects of aversion when compared to pleasure, they are merely...
It contradicts the objective realm; therefore, it is not "conducive. Now, this sublime bliss is the foremost in the world, and nothing surpasses it;

this refers to the maturation (*vipāka*) of the mental ground, which is conducive and sovereign. Bliss reaches its ultimate here; being purely singular and without admixture is called "completely possessed. By means of this...

The third dhyāna is called the stage of sublime bliss detached from joy (*prīti-viveka-sukha-bhūmi*). [The *Commentary on the Three Stages* states: "Detached from joy" refers to the obstacle that must be abandoned, namely, the factor of benefit (*anugraha-aṅga*) in the second dhyāna.

Because the mind of joy involves conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and gives rise to agitation, the third dhyāna becomes increasingly tranquil; therefore, it must be eliminated. It is like a poor man who feels joy upon finding treasure but suffers deep sorrow when losing it; it is better to sever both joy and sorrow, for only then is there true happiness. The joy and bliss of the first dhyāna are like water atop a mountain of earth and stone;

because the mind of the first dhyāna is still coarse, the water does not penetrate into the stone. The joy and bliss of the second dhyāna are like a pond atop a mountain of pure soil; in the second dhyāna, [bliss] already pervades both body and mind, just as water pervades the mountain. There is no... [further text].

Because it is obstructed by stone. Yet, it is covered by joy, just as water covered by earth only provides moisture from within. The bliss of the third dhyāna is like a mountain of pure soil situated within a great lake; the bliss extends throughout the exterior of the body while the body remains within the bliss. Therefore, this mental bliss is also called "bodily sensation.

In the third dhyāna, bodily bliss increases pervasively, just as the lake water lies outside while the water completely fills the interior of the mountain—this is self-evident. (In the Vinaya, it is likened to a lotus flower that has emerged from the ground but not yet risen above the water; its roots, stems, flowers, and leaves are all saturated with moisture.

In this stage, the factors of dhyāna consist of five kinds: first, equanimity (*upekṣā*); second, mindfulness (*smṛti*); third, wisdom (*prajñā*); fourth, bliss (*sukha*); and fifth, [one-pointedness of mind].

The Factors of Mind (*citta-aṅga*). [The *Dharmadhātu-krama* states: The meditative concentration of the third dhyāna heaven possesses five factors of merit. First, the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-aṅga*): being free from joy and without regret is equanimity.

When the practitioner wishes to leave the second dhyāna, they reprove joy through various causes and conditions; once joy has ceased and passed away, the third dhyāna immediately arises. If one realizes the bliss of the third dhyāna, one then abandons the joy of the second dhyāna, and no mind of regret arises. Second, the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-aṅga*): mindfulness is loving mindfulness.

Since the practitioner has already produced the bliss of the third dhyāna, and this bliss arises from within, one must maintain loving mindfulness so that the bliss may increase. Third, the factor of discernment (*prajñā-aṅga*): the mind that understands and knows is discernment. Once the practitioner has produced the bliss of the third dhyāna, if it were not for skillful discerning wisdom, then...]

It is capable of skillfully nurturing [the mind]. The fourth is the factor of bliss (*sukha-aṅga*). Once the practitioner has generated the bliss of the third dhyāna, if they can employ the three factors of equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) to protect this bliss, then the bliss will pervade the entire body.

Apart from the third dhyāna, no other stage possesses such all-pervading bliss. (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: The practitioner contemplates the faults of joy (*prīti*), just as they did with applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Wherever there is joy, there is much joy and much sorrow; therefore, one should abandon this joy and practice equanimity, mindfulness, and wisdom.

Experiencing physical bliss is a pleasure that the noble ones are able both to attain and to relinquish. With the mind single-pointedly focused on this bliss, one enters the third dhyāna. As for "equanimity," it means relinquishing the mind of joy so that one no longer harbors regretful thoughts. As for "wisdom," having attained the bliss within the third dhyāna, one does not allow that bliss to give rise to affliction. One experiences [this bliss].

"Physical pleasure" refers to the bliss of the third dhyāna, which is experienced throughout the entire body. "The noble ones are able to both attain and relinquish it" means that this bliss is the foremost in the world and is capable of giving rise to mental attachment;

ordinary people are rarely able to relinquish it. For this reason, the Buddha said that among the fruits of practicing wisdom, the realm of Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*) is the foremost. [△ Wuxing says: The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* designates the third dhyāna as "dhyāna accompanied by bliss," because the merit of this concentration arises together with the bliss that pervades the body.

Although the first two dhyānas possess the factor of bliss, they are obstructed by the factor of joy (*prīti*). Now, having extinguished joy, there is pure bliss; yet, when it is said that "joy is fully present," this is merely a case where the name is the same but the essence is different. [○ Dinglin says: That which is called "fully present" refers to the factor of bliss, not the agitation of joy. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*)

Question: Since there is also attachment to pleasure (*sukha*) in the first and second dhyānas, why is it said that [this is] only in the third dhyāna? Answer: Pleasure is of three grades: inferior, middling, and superior. The inferior is in the first dhyāna; the middling is in the second dhyāna; the superior is in the third dhyāna. In the first dhyāna, there are three types:

the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of pleasure associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya-samprayukta-sukhendriya*). The faculty of joy is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). In the second dhyāna, there is the faculty of joy associated with the mental consciousness.

In the third dhyāna, there is the faculty of pleasure associated with the mental consciousness. These five sensory consciousnesses are incapable of discrimination; they do not know names or characteristics. The visual consciousness arises for only as long as a finger-snap, yet by that time the mental consciousness has already arisen. Therefore, the faculty of pleasure associated with the five sensory consciousnesses cannot fulfill the experience of pleasure; it is the faculty of pleasure associated with the mental consciousness that can.

It is the bliss of satisfaction. Therefore, among the various merits within the third dhyāna, those merits are few because of the abundance of bliss. Consequently, there is no place for the liberations (vimokṣa) or the totalities (kṛtsnāyatana). Beyond this third dhyāna, there is no further bliss.

(○ Regarding the detailed explanation of the Four Dhyāna Heavens [the Commentary states]: However, the karma for the collective retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*) of this single stage consists of only three grades, which induce the three lower heavens. The five types of Non-returners (*anāgāmin*), being noble ones (*ārya*) who have cultivated the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) in a mixed manner, utilize the karma of the Heaven of Vast Fruit to make their five grades particularly sublime; they are born in those five heavens while possessing the very body of the collective retribution of the Heaven of Vast Fruit, which differs from that of ordinary beings.

For this reason, it is treated as a separate section below. This is consistent with the text of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*). "The Brahmā King, the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), and the five classes of Non-Returners (*anāgāmin*) are all collectively included within the Fourth Dhyāna. All samādhis emerge from these; therefore, they are called the "Roots. (○ [Heguanzhongnan said: In the four dhyānas, both suffering and pleasure are abandoned. This spontaneous mastery is the true worldly bliss; hence, they are named "Born of Bliss" and so forth. (○ Text, part two).
(14. Fundamental [Heavens], 2) (11. Commentary on the Four). (1. First: Tuṣita Heaven).

Ānanda, furthermore, there are gods and humans whose bodies and minds are no longer oppressed; the causes of suffering have been exhausted, yet pleasure is not permanent and will inevitably decay after a long time.
They simultaneously and suddenly relinquish both the mind of suffering and the mind of pleasure; coarse and heavy characteristics are extinguished, and the nature of pure merit arises.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava).
[Commentary] The first five phrases conclude the preceding section and introduce the following.

The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states that the fourth dhyāna is free from the eight calamities—namely, vitarka, vicāra, suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, as well as inhalation and exhalation—and is not moved by the three calamities; thus it is called the "Immovable Ground" (*āniñjya-bhūmi*).
What is here termed "not oppressed" refers precisely to being free from the suffering of the lower stages. The phrase "the cause of suffering" and below explains this lack of oppression.
This is because vitarka, vicāra, sorrow, joy, and so forth are causes of suffering; since these have now been abandoned, there is no longer any oppression.
Regarding the statement that "pleasure is not permanent," this specifically clarifies the factor of pleasure (*sukha-aṅga*) by contrasting it with the preceding suffering.

Although in the third dhyāna one attains a pleasure that thoroughly permeates the mental sphere (*manobhūmika*), it is nonetheless not permanent and must eventually perish. This perishing constitutes suffering; this explains the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). Suffering.

By extinguishing the body and returning to non-existence, he is one who, weary of form, relies upon space. Therefore, he is born by retribution in the station of cultivation. [The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "As the Buddha taught: transcending all marks of form (*rūpa-nimitta*), not attending to individual marks, and extinguishing the mark of resistance (*pratigha-nimitta*), one attains entry into the station of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). The practitioner acts thus..."

Reflect: if there were no form, then there would be no suffering of hunger, thirst, cold, or heat. This body is coarse, heavy, and wretched; it is deceptive and unreal. It is a body obtained as retribution through the conjunction of causal conditions from previous lives, and it is the dwelling place of manifold sufferings and afflictions.

"How should one escape this bodily affliction? One should contemplate this body as empty space within the body, constantly observing the body as void—like a cage or a steamer—never letting the mind abandon this practice. Thus, one attains transcendence of form and no longer perceives the body; as there is internal emptiness, so too is external form.

At that time, one is able to contemplate immeasurable and boundless emptiness. Having attained this contemplation, there is neither suffering nor pleasure, and the mind increases further. It is like a bird confined in a jar that escapes when the jar is broken. This is called the *ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi* (the concentration of the sphere of infinite space). (○)

[The *Jinglü yìxiàng* says: The gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Some call them the gods of the Wisdom of Space (*ākāśajñāna-deva*). [Next is] the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Once all obstructions have dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation; within this state, only the ālayavijñāna remains, with the entire manas and half of the subtle [vijñānas].
This single category is called the Sphere of Consciousness (vijñānāyatana).
[Commentary] The first phrase concludes the preceding stage of the sphere of infinite space. The second phrase refutes space and enters the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Since even the "non-existence" that dissolved obstructions has vanished, it is said to be "unobstructed and non-extinguished. When unobstructed and non-extinguished, one grows weary of space and rejoices in consciousness; even this 'non-existence' of the unobstructed is likewise extinguished. The section beginning with "Among these... provides the formal explanation, leaving only...

those of fixed nature who are deluded regarding the Dharma do not know it exists at all, remaining in a state of profound obscurity. (Those *śrāvakas* deluded regarding the Dharma do not know it exists, whereas those not so deluded believe it exists, as they enter cessation therein.

Regarding the division of the object-condition for consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*): because it does not retain the portion of the object-condition consisting of form and emptiness, it is called "half-portion. (Since one has already abandoned the perception of form, it is termed "half-portion.
Because this sixth [consciousness] takes both form and mind as its objects, it retains half. (〔Wenling says:〕 The eighth is Ālaya and the seventh is Manas.

Since the body-faculty has been dissolved, the six consciousnesses no longer exist; thus, only two remain. Thus, the coarse object of form is already gone, leaving only the subtle "half-portion" and "minute portion").

[△ Yunqi said: Master Huan judges that since the six consciousnesses have already ceased, then regarding the subsequent statement that "the conscious mind is entirely extinguished," which consciousness should be understood as ceasing? It does not take form or emptiness as its object like the six consciousnesses; rather, it internally takes them as objects in a manner that is half-fine [as noted by Yan Yi-xian].
