The sixth consciousness exists at all times throughout the three realms and nine stages, except during the five states where it is non-functional. Since this state of consciousness is fixed and is not subsumed under those five states, how could one say it is extinguished? Master Huan’s interpretation is erroneous.

Furthermore, to judge the "whole" and "half" subtlety based on the two delusions—the discriminative and the innate—by means of the *Erleng* (Two-Pronged) [text], is even more inconsistent. When the practitioner enters this meditative absorption, they feel weary of and distressed by...

Space is boundless. When the object of focus is manifold, the mind scatters, which can disrupt meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus, one abandons space and turns the mind to take consciousness (*vijñāna*) as its object.

Because the mind is associated with the phenomena of consciousness, it is called the "Consciousness-Sphere Concentration" (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*). [The *Chanmen* says: "Abandoning space, one takes consciousness as the object; taking consciousness as the sphere, it is named precisely after this focal sphere.

(△ The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "This space is immeasurable and boundless. If one takes consciousness as its object, when consciousness becomes excessive, it scatters and can disrupt concentration. The practitioner contemplates space as well as feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being like a disease or an abscess.)

"Like a sore, like a thorn; impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; deceptive and existing through combination, it is not real. Having reflected thus, one abandons the object of space and takes consciousness as the object. How does one take consciousness as the object? One takes past and future consciousnesses—immeasurable and boundless—as the object.

This consciousness is immeasurable and boundless, like space which is immeasurable and boundless; this is called the *vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi* (the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness). [The *He lun* (Compendium) says: "The substance of the eight consciousnesses is neither identical nor different.

The characteristics of the six consciousnesses are distinguished by their coarseness and subtlety. The mental aspect (*ākāra*) of the manas is difficult to discern; although it grasps the mark of self and is associated with pride, ignorance, craving, and views, when one investigates it thoroughly, no place of refuge is found. The ancient masters compared it to placing water at midday [which evaporates immediately]."

The vessel serves as an analogy: the water in the vessel is the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); the sun is the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*). Because the sun takes the water within the vessel as its condition, the reflection that flickers upon the wall is the *manas*. In this context, "the complete *manas*" refers to this.

This consciousness (the ālayavijñāna) only internally grasps and does not externally objectify; therefore, it is "half-subtle. The "two kinds of subtle consciousnesses" that internally objectify refer to the sixth consciousness (*ṣaḍvijñāna*) and the seventh manas. It is like a person eating an egg: having peeled away the shell and divided it, one looks at the yolk—that is the ālayavijñāna. The white part is the entirety of the manas.

The discarded shell represents the coarse aspects of all external objects, such as form and space, which are the objects of the sixth consciousness. Furthermore, there remains a thin membrane within the white part, which is the aspect of the "half-subtle."

(○ [Sūtra-vinaya-vilakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa] The Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness; alternatively called the Heaven of the Wisdom of the Sphere of Consciousness. The Loutan [Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra] calls it the Heaven of Conscious Knowledge). (The Three [Heavens of the Sphere of] Nothingness).
When both emptiness and form have vanished and the conscious mind has utterly ceased, the ten directions are silent and far removed from any destination.
This class of beings is called the Sphere of Nothingness.

[Commentary: In the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), form is absent while space remains; in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), space is lost while consciousness remains.

Both are termed "possessions. Now, in this state, both space and consciousness are extinguished; thus it is said: "Since space and form have perished, consciousness and mind are utterly ceased. These two phrases [refer to this].
First, the three dharmas are refuted. "In the ten directions" and below correctly clarifies the characteristics of practice.

"The ten directions" refers to all dharmas—the objects of perception such as form, emptiness, consciousness, mind, and so forth. Since not a single one of these exists, it is said to be "tranquil. Since the objects of perception are tranquil...
Since the object of cognition no longer exists, it is said that there is nowhere to go.

Because practitioners weary of consciousness—and given that the consciousnesses of the three periods of time are boundless—excessive objects of cognition lead to distraction and can destroy meditative concentration; therefore, they abandon the consciousness as an object and turn the mind toward the dharma of nothingness.
When the mind is associated with the dharma of nothingness, it is called the *ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*. (From the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*)

[17] This consciousness is immeasurable and boundless. By taking it as an object, the mind becomes distracted due to the multiplicity of objects, which can destroy meditative concentration. The practitioner contemplates this consciousness that takes [objects] as its condition—namely, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—as being like a disease, like an abscess, and so forth; they are not truly existent.

Having observed in this way, one then destroys the characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna*). This is the critique of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) and the praise of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). By destroying all characteristics of consciousness, one binds the mind within nothingness; this is called the sphere of nothingness. [The Commentary on the Third Stage (*Tandi shu*) states:

Previously, by abandoning the external and taking the internal as object, there were coarse thoughts. Since there is now no longer anything to be grasped (*grāhya*), the grasper (*grāhaka*) is also absent; thus, both internal and external are non-existent. The *Yukti* says: "Seeing that the previous infinite modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and agitated, one initiates this preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Therefore, this stage is called 'supreme equanimity' (*upekṣā*), because within it one no longer delights in constructing objects of focus. The mind relinquishes all that it possessed regarding the object and proceeds in tranquility. The *Yogācārabhūmi* says: When advancing from the sphere of consciousness upward, one leaves it behind.

Seeking further objects outside of consciousness, one finds nothing at all. This passage clarifies that since consciousness itself is coarse and there is nothing further existing outside of it, therefore nothing exists. Now, as for those who practice the Mahāyāna:

Many conflate this meditative absorption [with emptiness]. However, when one is entirely free from attachment, the mind has no point of reliance, and there is not a single thing at all—this is precisely the Mahāyāna.

It is no different from inert space. Yet, they do not know how to skillfully penetrate and realize the various stages of dhyāna, nor the clear process of severing and subduing afflictions, nor the sequential order of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
These are like a great round mirror that reflects myriad images without error or deviation.

This alone is the Mahāyāna; this is the true cultivation of dhyāna. (Wenling says: Although the conscious mind (*vijñāna-citta*) is here extinguished, the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) has not yet been extinguished. Practitioners whose vision of the nature is not profound often stagnate at this point.

They understand that form is empty and extinguish their mental deliberations until they reach the state of non-existence, yet they ultimately remain within the nature of consciousness. Deep and subtle, continuous and pervasive, they cannot free themselves from the cave of birth and death; they truly remain trapped herein. (Jiaoguang says: "Conscious mind" refers to half of the *manas*.

To say it is "completely extinguished" means that through deep meditative power (*samādhi-bala*), the active manifestations are all suppressed—just as, for example, the six active manifestations are suppressed in the *asaṃjñi-samāpatti* (the attainment of non-conception). [In that state, one suppresses them for five hundred kalpas; here, one suppresses them for fifty thousand kalpas. This is not like the [attainment of] Ārūpya...)

"Han" means that both the seeds and the manifestations are suppressed. It is a state of profound stillness where there is nowhere to go, the realized realm within the meditative absorption of the cessation of consciousness (*nirodha-samāpatti*). It is vast and dark, such that one cannot advance further; this is the place where non-Buddhists are deluded into regarding it as the "Principle of Obscurity" (*tattva-ambara*).

[The *Chanmen* says: This heaven is also called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). When practicing this concentration, one does not employ any internal or external objects. External objects are called "space," and internal objects are called "mind. Because one abandons these two objects at the beginning of practice, it is so named; hence it is called "Non-usage" (*apraṇihita*).

It is also called the "Sphere of the Little" (*alpa*) and the "Sphere of No-Thought" (*asaṃjñāyatana*). [The *Jinglü yixiang* says: Regarding the Heaven of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-deva*), some call it the Heaven of the Wisdom of the Sphere of Nothingness, and others call it the Heaven of Non-usage. There was one Ullambha who did not accept the Buddha’s transformation.

He then passed away. The Buddha prophesied that this person was born in the Place of Non-Use (Akiṃcanyāyatana). Furthermore, having cast off his body, he became a ruler of a borderland who harmed the people; subsequently, he was reborn in hell. His celestial lifespan was forty-two thousand kalpas (the *Loutan jing* refers to this as the Ajakhyāna Heaven). [Note:
This corresponds to the fourth level, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).]
The nature of consciousness is immovable; by extinguishing it through exhaustive investigation, one proclaims the nature of exhaustion within the inexhaustible.
It is as if existing yet not existing, as if exhausted yet not exhausted. This class of beings is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
[Commentary] The first two phrases indicate the essential nature of the basis (*āśraya*). The first phrase provides a dual designation:

"the nature of consciousness" (*vijñānatva*) indicates the presence of subtle perception (*saṃjñā*), while "immovable" (*aniñja*) indicates the absence of gross perception. (Wenling says: "The nature of consciousness" refers to the profound root of the conscious mind; "immovable" means it is quiescent and has no destination. The second phrase further explains the meaning of being immovable.
In the preceding Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one employs the mind to investigate exhaustively, causing it not to take [external objects] as its condition.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*). The mind corresponds with the state of non-existence (*akiṃcana*). Now, this single dharma thoroughly investigates the cessation of the mind, subduing it so that it does not move;

therefore, it is said: "by means of cessation, one thoroughly investigates. (Since it can remain unmoving, one further investigates it to bring about its cessation. However, although it relies on the cessation of consciousness, it is ultimately not true cessation.

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of" (*wu*) and below, this is the formal explanation of the mode of activity (*ākāra*). Because it relies on the place where this consciousness is unmoving, it says: "within the inexhaustible" (*wujin zhong*).

He distinguishes this as "not-perception" (asaṃjñā). Therefore, it is said: "To manifest and proclaim the nature of exhaustion. (Wuxing says: In the preceding station of nothingness, although it is said that consciousness is extinguished, its essential nature remains unmoving; one merely extinguishes the subtlest portion of analytical investigation.

Now, within the nature of inexhaustibility, he manifests and proclaims the nature of exhaustion—this is to emerge from exhaustion and yet establish inexhaustibility. (Haiyin says: Because the nature of consciousness is unmoving, analytical investigation is extinguished;

by relying on the state of profound stillness and non-shaking as the ultimate, it is said: "Within the inexhaustible, he manifests and proclaims the nature of exhaustion. Although exhaustion is seen, consciousness remains; therefore, it is said: "If exhausted..."

It is not exhausted; though it exists in the present, it does not arise. Therefore, it is said that "it exists as if it did not exist. For this reason, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

(That "it exists as if it did not exist" is non-perception; that "it is neither exhausted nor not exhausted" is non-non-perception. [Wenling says: This, moreover, is profound and subtle, continuous and pervasive.

This refers to the most subtle state of characteristics; it is precisely the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭhavijñāna*). While coarse perceptions do not arise, there still remain subtle divisions and the *ālayavijñāna*, which continues its flow without ceasing.
Therefore, based on this meaning, its name is established. [The *He lun* states: "Non-perception" means that the nature of consciousness is unmoving, while the coarse sixth consciousness...

Because neither [of these] arises. As for "not non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*): although coarse perceptions do not arise, the eighth consciousness continues its flow without ever ceasing. [Wang Shungding said: "The eight consciousnesses are half dependent on the arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) and half dependent on the non-arising-and-non-ceasing (*anutpāda-ananirodha*).

Neither existing nor exhausted, they reside precisely within the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, the first three formless attainments are named according to their preparatory practices (*prayoga*), whereas this Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is designated according to its essential nature.
When a practitioner enters this meditative absorption, they feel weary of and distressed by the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Perception is like delusion; the sphere of perception is like an abscess or a sore.

One then abandons the sphere of nothingness and takes as an object the dharma that is neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Because the mind is associated with this dharma, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

(The *Commentary on the Third Stage* states: The next verse says: "The three beginning with 'infinite space' are named according to their preparatory application (*prayoga*). 'Neither-perception-nor-non-perception' is so named because it is dull and inferior. That is to say, prior to the cultivation of the meditative concentration...")

In the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), because one detests and overcomes form (*rūpa*), one forms a resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) and contemplates infinite space; when this preparatory application is perfected, it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). One detests the perception of space and contemplates consciousness; detesting the perception of consciousness, one contemplates nothingness. This may be understood by analogy.

As for the fourth [sphere], because its perception is dull and inferior—meaning that the superior perception of clear wisdom does not exist in the lower stages—it receives the name "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Thus, the first three formless spheres (*ārūpya*) receive their names from their preparatory applications, while the fourth formless sphere [receives its name from its actual state].

(To be understood by experiencing it directly). (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Chapter 17): The Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). One contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being like a disease, like an abscess, and so forth;

they are not truly existent. One reflects in this way: the Sphere of Non-perception (*asaṃjñāyatana*) is like an abscess; the Sphere of Perception (*saṃjñāyatana*) is like a disease, like an abscess, like a wound, and like a thorn. The foremost sublime state is the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Question: Since there are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception, why is it called "neither with perception nor without perception"?

Answer: There is perception therein, but because it is so subtle and difficult to perceive, it is called "without perception. Because there is perception, it is not "without perception. Ordinary people think that having attained the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all Buddhas constitutes Nirvana. This is the teaching of the Buddha-dharma.

Although within this state one knows that perception exists, it is called the "Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" because of its original name. Furthermore, it is asked: "If the fault of the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is such as you have described, is there yet another attainment called 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception' (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)?

In this [attainment], all conceptual perceptions (*vikalpa*) are absent; it is not like forcibly producing the attainment of non-perception to extinguish perception. Herein, perception is absent by the power of wisdom. The answer is: "In this state, perception does exist, but because it is so subtle, it is not perceived.

If there were no perception at all, for what reason would the disciples of the Buddha seek further true wisdom? In the Buddha's Dharma, the consciousness within the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception abides supported by the three aggregates (*skandha*; *skandha* here refers to the 'groups'). These four aggregates, being subject to causes and conditions, are impermanent. Because they are impermanent..."

Suffering. Because it is impermanent and suffering, it is empty. Because it is empty, it is without self. Because it is empty and without self, it can be relinquished. You all are attached to wisdom; therefore, you do not attain nirvāṇa. It is like a measuring worm: it withdraws its hind leg and establishes it securely before advancing its front leg.

The objects of perception are exhausted; there is no further place to advance, and one returns. Non-Buddhists rely upon the first dhyāna to abandon the desires of the lower stages, continuing thus until they rely upon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) to abandon the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Since there is nothing higher to rely upon, they are unable to abandon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Because they have no further place of reliance, they fear losing their self and dread falling into a state of non-attainment. According to this text, it is clear that these non-Buddhists who exhaust the limits of emptiness have indeed come from the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).

[The *Shichan zhong* states: "Those who enter this samādhi do not perceive the characteristics of existence or non-existence. All things are obliterated, silent, and cut off; the mind is without fluctuation, tranquil and pure, like the mark of nirvāṇa. This samādhi is subtle and wondrous. Within the three realms..."

There is no fault. The non-Buddhists realize this and claim it is the Middle Way and the true mark (*dharmatā*). They become attached to this dharma and no longer practice further; they then take this very mind to be the *ātman*. (○ [The *Cánmén cìdì* says: This refers to differences in interpretation.)

Some say that this meditative absorption is called the "contemplation of one existing and one perishing. Regarding the term "neither-perception" (*naivasaṃjñā*): it is not coarse perception; thus, coarse perception has perished. Regarding "nor non-perception" (*nāsaṃjñā*): it is not the absence of subtle perception; thus, subtle perception persists. The lower character *fei* (not) may be understood as *wu* (without) for clarity; it means that it is not without subtle perception. Another interpretation states:

the previous contemplation of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) was characterized by perception, while the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) was characterized by non-perception. Now, both of these two types of perception are eliminated. "Neither-perception" dispels the perception of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, and "nor non-perception" leaves behind the non-perception of the Sphere of Nothingness.

Furthermore, when ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists attain this absorption, they claim to have realized *nirvāṇa* and severed all perception; therefore, it is called "neither-perception. However, the disciples of the Buddha [view it] according to reality...

It is known that there is a subtle perception (*sūkṣma-saṃjñā*) which abides based upon the four aggregates (*catvāraḥ skandhāḥ*); therefore, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Furthermore, ancient masters explained: within this meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one does not perceive any mental images (*nimitta*);

hence it is said to be "not having perception. A practitioner might think: "If it were entirely without perception, it would be like wood or stone, lacking sentience; how then could it know 'non-perception'? Therefore, it is called "not non-perception. [From *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, fascicle 6. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "It is not the non-perception of the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), nor is it the perception of the three emptinesses (*trīṇi śūnyatāni*).

The Master of Men (*puruṣācārya*) says: "Non-perception belongs to a different realm (*dhātu*) from the heavens of form (*rūpa-deva*); one should not derive its name from that. The name is explained according to its own realm: since all previous perceptions have already been eliminated in the preceding concentrations, and now even 'non-perception' is eliminated, it is called 'perception and non-perception. (Note: This refers to the state where both perception and non-perception are transcended.)

Because both have been abandoned, it receives this designation. (The *Commentary on the Third Stage* states: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says that one first enters the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), thereby transcending all perceptions of existence; now, one further transcends the perception of nothingness, and thus it is called "neither-perception" (*na-saṃjñā*).

Furthermore, it is called "not non-perception" (*na-asaṃjñā*) because it is not like the state of non-perception or the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), wherein all perceptions are entirely extinguished. The reason one does not escape the three realms within this state is that by taking the object of non-perception as a condition, there remains a subtle perception.

Outsiders do not understand this and mistake it for *nirvāṇa*. Since they have not yet attained the state of being without conditions, how could they be free from the mind and its objects? Moreover, they reckon this state to be a self and further give rise to craving and delusion. Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* uses the metaphor of a fire burning on the head. If one recognizes this higher affliction, one should seek further.)

One progresses upward. When seeking this upward progress, one ultimately attains nothing. Because there is nothing to be attained, [the mind] ceases and does not revolve; thus, one attains the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*). If this attainment has not yet been reached, one first develops a distaste for perception, and subsequently, as perception no longer functions, one enters the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*).

Furthermore, it is said that according to the Sarvāstivāda school, this attainment arises only from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); all lower stages are termed "possessing perception" because their mental activities are coarse and agitated, making them difficult to still. This Peak of Existence is termed "non-perception."

The modes of activity (*ākāra*) are subtle and easy to cease; therefore, only at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is there the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Non-Buddhists regard this as a worldly stūpa, because it is situated at the summit of all realms of existence. It must include both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*), as stated in the preceding text. Regarding the five *anāgāmin* heavens and the kings of the four *dhyāna* heavens, the term "only" (*du yǒu*) refers exclusively to those who have heard [the teachings].
This is spoken from the perspective of a certain class of ordinary beings; therefore, we know that it includes both categories. (Wenling says:

"This refers generally to the heavens of the desire, form, and formless realms. Their inhabitants receive retribution according to their karma and have not yet escaped saṃsāra; their kings respond through provisional manifestations according to their conduct, taking up positions to advance upward. This concludes the vertical discussion; thus, it is concluded by referring to them collectively. [My private opinion: Changshui concludes this solely with the four formless heavens.")

Wenling’s general interpretation takes this to refer to the three realms. This accords with the scriptural text which says, "These various heavens each have their respective devas. Furthermore, since the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s provisional assignment of retribution does not reach the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), [this passage] generally refers to them as such. (2. Correctly concluding the four formless attainments.)
Ānanda, in these four heavens of the formless realm, body and mind are extinguished; the nature of stability manifests before them, and there is no material form resulting from karmic fruit.
From beginning to end, this is called the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).

[Commentary: Regarding "the extinction of body and mind": the physical body (*rūpakāya*) must necessarily perish; as for the mind, whether it perishes or does not perish, it is falsely claimed to have perished. (Wenling says:

"The extinction of body and mind" refers to the absence of the form-aggregate (*rūpaskandha*) and coarse consciousness. Regarding "the manifestation of the dhyāna-nature": there is the matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhiphalavastu*).

If this matter did not exist, upon what would the four [dhyāna] minds rely? Therefore, one knows that it exists. (Gushan says: "The absence of the matter that is the fruit of karma" serves to reveal the existence of the matter that is the fruit of concentration.)
([○@●] Second, the summary showing that these are false and illusory).
All of these arise from failing to understand the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind; through the accumulation of delusions, the three realms of existence are produced.
Within them, one falsely follows along as one sinks and drifts among the seven destinies. Each *pudgala* (individual) follows according to their own kind.

[Commentary: Because one does not know as it truly is that the Dharma of true knowledge is one, one falsely identifies what is illuminated. Once discrimination has arisen, falsehood is accumulated upon falsehood;

hence the phrase "not understanding," and so forth. One should know that those who practice dhyāna-contemplation fail to penetrate this gate, and thus may remain for sixty or eighty thousand great kalpas in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Eon. Their bodies and minds are in a state of quiescent extinction, yet when their retribution is exhausted, they fall back down; these are collectively termed the "difficulty of the long-lived heavens. This was personally proclaimed by the Buddha’s own mouth. How can one not believe and understand this?

(The various sutras and śāstras describe eight difficulties [aṣṭākṣaṇa]. The eighth is the difficulty of the long-lived heavens, which refers to the Heaven of Non-conception within the Fourth Dhyāna. There, mental activity ceases, like fish in ice or hibernating insects. Many non-Buddhists who practice meditation are reborn there.

Because it obstructs seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, it is called the "difficulty of the long-lived heavens. (△ [The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: As for the long-lived heavens, they refer to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception, where the lifespan is eighty thousand great kalpas. Or alternatively...)

People say that all those in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) are collectively called "long-lived devas" (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*). Because they lack physical form and cannot be transformed, they are unable to attain the Way; they are always the abode of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Some say the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) is called "long-lived.

Others say that from the first dhyāna to the fourth dhyāna, excluding the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), all are called "long-lived," because they are obscured by and attached to false views, and thus cannot receive the Way.

*Pudgala*: This is translated as "one who undergoes repeated rebirths" (*saṃsārin*). [The translation notes: It may also be *poggala* or *putigala*, which is translated as "one who undergoes repeated rebirths. This refers to sentient beings who, having created afflictions and karma, are able to take up the five destinies (*pañcagati*) of the future; hence the name.

This is its meaning as a "destiny" (*gati*). It was translated in ancient times as "tending toward" (*quxiang*). Because sentient beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) tend toward their previous birth, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "That which has not yet reached the place it is destined to reach" refers to the six destinies. Furthermore, the treatise says: "Between the two existences of death and birth, the five aggregates are called the intermediate existence.

Therefore, it is termed a "destiny. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The intermediate existence consists of the five aggregates; it is not seen by the fleshly eye, but is seen by the divine eye. In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, among the eight types of grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*), the sixth is named *pudgala*.

This refers to the repeated taking up of various destinies; whether one is born there or born here, that which truly brings about such birth is precisely the grasping at a person. It is also translated as "sentient being" (*sattva*) or "person" (*manuṣya*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha said there are two types of *pudgalas* who are able to abide..."

Upholding the True Dharma. In the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, there are ten kinds of *pudgala*—in Chinese, "sentient beings" (*yǒuqíng*) or "persons. For these classes of sentient beings, whose karmic offenses are profound and heavy, they transmigrate through birth and death, making it difficult to obtain a human body.

Therefore, these ten kinds of distinctions are taught. (The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: A Bodhisattva, observing with the divine eye, sees sentient beings within the five destinies of the ten directions. He sees those born in the Form Realm who, having tasted the flavor of the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), fall back into the realm of birds and beasts to undergo various sufferings.
Furthermore, he sees the gods of the Desire Realm sporting amidst the fragrant flowers in ponds of the seven treasures, only to later fall into the hell of brine-boiling excrement.

Again, he sees those among humans who possess fame, worldly wisdom, and eloquence, yet because they do not attain the Way, they fall back into the wombs of pigs, sheep, birds, and beasts, knowing nothing at all. Through such actions, they lose various great pleasures and obtain great suffering; they lose great benefit and obtain great decline; they lose nobility and obtain poverty and lowliness. The Bodhisattva, by means of...)

With the divine eye, one observes the sentient beings of the three realms and five destinies. Taking the loss of pleasure as suffering, the gods of the formless realm are absorbed in the bliss of meditative concentration; their minds are so attached that they do not realize it, and when their lives end, they fall into the desire realm to receive the forms of birds and beasts.

The gods of the form realm are likewise; falling from their pure abodes, they again undergo lustful desires and remain amidst impurity. The six heavens of the desire realm are attached to the pleasures of the five desires, yet they fall back into hell, where they encounter all manner of painful afflictions.

Observing those in the human realm, who by the merit of the ten wholesome actions have traded for a human body—yet the human life is full of suffering and little joy—and when their lifespan ends, most fall into the evil destinies. The Bodhisattva, having attained the divine eye, observes sentient beings revolving through the five destinies, circling within them: dying among the gods and being born among humans.

Dying among humans, one is born among devas. Dying among devas, one is born in hell. Dying in hell, one is born in the heavens, even as far as the animal realm. Dying in the heavens, one is again born in the heavens, even as far as the animal realm. Dying within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Dying in the form realm, one is born in the desire realm, even as far as dying in the four abodes of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and being born in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, even as far as the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Dying in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, [one is born elsewhere].
They are born in the Avīci Hell. Thus, through successive cycles, they are born within the five destinies. (7. The Realm of Asuras)
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms, there are four kinds of asura classes. [Commentary]:

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also state that there are four types of asuras; they are largely identical to this account. Such are the various explanations regarding asuras.

Whether they be devas or ghosts, none of them are clearly defined [in other texts]. This sutra is explicit and may serve as a standard. [The *Miaoyan shu* states: "Asura" is also called "Asura" (*asu-ra*).

These are merely differences in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit original. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* translates it as 'Non-deva'. The fourth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: Furthermore, one should know that all non-devas are subsumed within the realm of devas; however, by their disposition, they mostly harbor deceit and illusion.]

Because they abound in flattery and deception, they are not like the gods who serve as pure vessels for the Dharma. For this reason, they are said to constitute a separate realm (*gati*). In reality, they belong to the class of gods; however, because they do not understand the dharmas of the gods, they are called "non-gods" (*asura*)—(since *asu* means "god" and they are "not-gods," they are thus called *asura*).

According to the *Abhidharma*, they are also subsumed under the realm of ghosts (*preta*), because they are characterized by crookedness and concealment. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* subsumes them under both ghosts and animals, because Rāhu-Asura is the son of a lion. The *Gāthā-sūtra* states that they are subsumed under gods, ghosts, and animals.

If one follows the eighth chapter, the *Śrutaskandha-prakaraṇa*, of the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, they are also subsumed under the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*). Some say that Asuras share the same realm as the gods; therefore, it is said: "You were formerly a god," or it is stated: [they are included among the gods].

Regarding the celestial realm (*deva-gati*): because Śacī exists there, she is able to have sexual intercourse with the various gods. Question: If that is so, why is the Lord of the Gods (*Indra*) not seen? Answer: Because he is shrouded by deceit and crookedness. Some say he is a powerful hungry ghost (*preta*), as he is not included within the celestial realm.

Question: If that is so, how is it that Śakra devendra is closely associated with the *asuras*? Answer: Because the gods crave form (*rūpa*), because their victories and defeats are frequent, and because they possess the aforementioned [qualities]. For these reasons, they are sometimes classified as a sixth realm and sometimes subsumed within the five realms. They frequently engage in strife and harbor a sense of victory and defeat.

They may dwell on Mount Viśvāmitra (Mount of All Marks) or beneath the ocean, as described in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*. However, those who possess great power and have extensively cultivated merit are born there now; many who cultivate merit while harboring a mind of rivalry, flattery, and deceit are born among them. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "When the *asuras* give birth to daughters, they are beautiful;

when they give birth to sons, they are mostly ugly. Therefore, they are called 'Ugly' (*Asura*). This name is derived from the males. Furthermore, it is translated as 'No Wine' (*Asura*), or 'Not Drinking Wine. This is as stated by Master Kumārajīva and the Dharma [Master]."

(The *Huashu* states: [The *Zhilun* says] "A long time after the Buddha’s passing, as the scriptures and Dharma were transmitted, many divergences arose after five hundred years. Some spoke of five destinies (*pañca-gati*), while others spoke of six destinies. Examining the meaning of various sutras, there should be six destinies.

Within these six destinies, there are three fortunate destinies: devas, humans, and asuras. There are three grades of worldly goodness: due to superior causes and conditions, there is the retribution of the heavenly realm; due to middling causes and conditions, there is the retribution of the human realm; and due to inferior causes and conditions... )

Regarding the retributive fruit of the asura path: when these asuras were in the causal stage, they harbored a mind of suspicion and jealousy; although they practiced the five constants (*pañca-śīla*) and the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma*), they did so with the intent to surpass others, thereby producing this inferior-grade body as a result.

Among humans, they may leave the household life and uphold the precepts, yet because their fetters (*saṃyojana*) shroud their minds, it is extremely difficult for them to attain the Way. Although the various devas also follow their fetters, their minds are straightforward and they believe in the Way; the asura hosts, however, have many crooked and perverse thoughts and cannot approach the Way, and thus they rank below humans.

Just as the dragon kings and the golden-winged birds (*garuḍa*), though possessing great power and ability to undergo transformations, are nonetheless included within the realm of animals, so too is the asura path: since their power is great and their forms resemble those of humans and devas, they are established separately as one of the six paths.

If, within the realm of ghosts, by the power of protecting the Dharma, they ride upon supernatural penetrations to enter the void, these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the destiny of ghosts.

[The *Fahua wenju* states: "Those subsumed under the realm of hungry ghosts dwell on the shores of the great ocean. Having taken refuge in the Buddha and protected the Dharma, by the power of protecting the Dharma, they ride upon their own innate supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and enter the void to go and protect the Buddha-dharma.
(○ [In the *Shiwen*, "riding upon powers" (*shengtong*) is rendered as "accomplishing powers" (*chengtong*) in the Song edition of the Tripitaka.)
If, among the gods, their merit is exhausted and they fall, the place where they dwell is adjacent to the sun and moon;
these asuras are born from a womb and are categorized within the realm of human beings.
(△ [The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states]: Within Mount Sumeru, there is a hollow space shaped like an overturned precious vessel where the asuras dwell. The *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra* states:

On the eastern side of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, at a distance of one thousand yojanas, lies the city-palace of Śambara, with sevenfold walls composed of the seven treasures. On each of the southern, western, and northern sides, there are palaces of the asura kings, exquisite and similar to one another, equal in quality to those of the gods who dwell upon the earth.

Some say they also dwell on the "waist" of Sumeru; this refers to the ones known as Dṛḍhapāṇi. (△ [The *Dīrgha Āgama* states]: The asuras possess great power and give rise to intense anger, vowing: "These devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Sun, and the Moon, pass over my head! I shall seize them! )

The sun and moon serve as his ear-ornaments (*karṇapūra*). According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, Rāhu Asura is also called "Obstructor of the Sun and Moon. He is the vanguard of Śakra’s army; when the sun first emits its rays, they strike the eyes of the Asura, causing him to lose sight of the celestial hosts.
Therefore, he obstructs them with his hands. Based on these two sūtras, it can be understood that the abode of the Asuras is situated adjacent to the sun and moon.
There are asura kings who uphold the world; their power penetrates all things and they are fearless, able to contend for authority with the Brahma King, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
These asuras arise through transformation and are categorized within the realm of the gods.

[Jingxi says: "The four types [of asuras] in the *Lotus Sūtra* all engaged in combat with Śakra; they are simply the same category as the third type in this present sūtra. [The *Dīrgha Āgama* says: "The two Asura kings, Śambara and Vemacitrin, went forth to battle the devas. The two great Nāga Kings, Nanda and Upananda, coiled their bodies seven times around Mount Sumeru;

the mountain shook and clouds spread. They struck the great ocean with their tails, causing waves to crest over Sumeru. The Trāyastriṃśa devas said, 'The Asuras wish to fight! Then the various nāgas, spirits, and deities each took up weapons and followed in succession to engage in combat.

If the devas were not victorious, they would all flee to the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, who would prepare their chariots for an offensive. First, they would inform Śakra, and Śakra would report it upward, continuing thus through the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and finally the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens."

In the heavens, he was surrounded by countless hosts of devas, nāgas, and spirits. Śakra commanded, "Bind Vimalacitra with the fivefold bonds and bring him back to the Sudharmā Hall; I wish to behold him. The asura likewise said, "Bind Śakra with the fivefold bonds and bring him back to the Saptaparṇa Hall;

I wish to behold him. They fought a great battle at once, yet neither harmed the other; they merely touched their bodies, which gave rise to pain and distress. Thereupon, Śakra manifested his body with a thousand eyes, grasping a vajra-pestle, and smoke and flames issued from his head.

The asura was defeated and retreated, and Śakra immediately captured the asura Vimalacitra. (From the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*: The asura Vimalacitra’s wife was a gandharva maiden from Mount Gandhamādana. She was pregnant for eight thousand years before giving birth to one [son].)

The woman’s name was Śacī. Kauśika sought her hand in marriage, and she was known as Manoharā. When Śakra arrived at the Nandana Grove and entered the pond for recreation with his court ladies, the woman became jealous. She dispatched five yakṣas to inform her father, the king, who immediately mobilized the fourfold army to attack Śakra.

He stationed himself upon the waters of the great ocean and sat atop the summit of Mount Sumeru; with nine hundred and ninety-nine hands acting simultaneously, he shook the city of Sudarśana and caused Mount Sumeru and the waters of the four great oceans to tremble.

At that time, the waters surged with waves. Śakra, filled with alarm and fear, sat in the Sudharmā Hall, burned various renowned incenses, made a great vow, and recited the Great Bright Mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā. Then, from the midst of the void, a wheel of blades descended spontaneously.

When the asuras ascend, their ears, noses, hands, and feet fall off all at once, causing the waters of the great ocean to turn as red as clam pearls. With no place to flee, the asuras enter the pores of lotus fibers. (The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states:

"If the people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma, serving their parents with filial piety and making offerings to śramaṇas, then the celestial hosts will prevail; if they do not follow the teachings of the Dharma, then the asuras will prevail.")
Ānanda, there is another class of inferior asuras who are born in the midst of the great ocean and dwell at the mouths of underwater caves;
they roam through the void by day and return to their watery abodes by night. These asuras exist due to moisture and are categorized within the realm of animals (tiryagyoni).

[The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "Some call them 'Inferior Devas. 'Inferior' refers to Vemacitra, which is translated here as 'High-Sounding' (*Ghoṣavat*). He is also called 'Cave-Dweller,' meaning he dwells at the bottom of the great ocean. He emits a great sound that penetrates beyond the sea;

he proclaims for himself, 'I am the Asura Vemacitra. Therefore, he is called 'High-Sounding. Because he dwells beyond the sea, he is called 'Cave-Dweller. Furthermore, it is said: there are Asuras who dwell at the bottom of the great ocean and on the slopes of Mount Sumeru, manifesting transformations within the realm of desire."

They can create forms large or small at will. They dwell in the City of Radiance. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Asura" means "my own village. They dwell in the Salt Ocean. The Asura King dwells within that mountain. [Master Youxi said: Regarding the inclusion of beings within the six destinies, each has its fixed location;

however, the Asuras are included within four of the destinies. Within each category, they may possess all four causes. One determines their specific destiny by observing which cause is predominant. If their wholesome or unwholesome karma is pure, they receive the full retribution of ghosts, animals, humans, or devas accordingly.

If their karma is fluctuating—sometimes good, sometimes evil, sometimes high, sometimes low—their retribution is experienced at the point of death, with the stronger force drawing them first. Although they belong to the realm of ghosts, they can also employ supernatural powers to enter the air; although they belong to the animal realm, [they possess such faculties].

Furthermore, they can travel through the void at dawn; is this not the shared merit of humans and devas? As for those encompassed by the two realms of humans and devas, although they dwell adjacent to the sun and moon and hold them in their hands, they still possess instruments of suffering during the three periods of day and night;

is this not the shared retribution of ghosts and animals? When the devas and asuras wage war, they always determine victory or defeat based on the relative amount of good and evil among the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa. Once the battle begins, they alternate between victory and defeat twice over.

This is truly because the thoughts of worldly people toward doing good are suddenly interrupted by evil intentions, and their desires to do evil are likewise interrupted by good intentions. It is precisely because human thoughts are not focused that the battles of the devas remain undecided. For the sake of practitioners, one must therefore establish the precepts based on this. (3. Concluding the False Causes)
(2) Admonition to Depart from the Two. (1) [The first: A summary conclusion on the falsity of causes. (4) [The first: A general summary of the illusory nature.]

Ānanda, thus it is with those in the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and seers; including the devas and asuras—(he points his fingers to encompass all realms)—when one minutely examines these seven destinies, they are all the signs of the conditioned states of delusion and torpor.
Birth is received through false imagination, and one follows along with karma through false imagination.

Within this wondrous, perfect, and luminous, unconditioned fundamental mind, all things are like flowers in the sky; they are fundamentally without attachment and possess no root or source, being nothing more than a single delusion.

[Commentary] This concludes the formation of delusion. "Thoroughly investigating" means to minutely seek out. "Birth through deluded thought" refers to the effects within the seven realms of existence;
"deluded thought following karma" refers to the causes for those seven realms. These deluded causes and effects are all ignorance—conditioned, illusory appearances from which no reality can be found.
Viewed against the perfect luminosity, they are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent. How [could they have any reality]?

Can it be obtained by tracing its root and source? [The Zongjing says: For one whose mind roams through the Dharma-realm, when observing the mutual correspondence of the faculties and their objects, they must necessarily belong to one of the ten realms. If they belong to one realm...]

Thus, the hundred realms and thousand dharmas are all fully present within a single thought-moment. This illusory master of the mind constantly creates various sentient beings, various five aggregates, and various lands throughout a single day and night—namely, the provisional and real lands of the hells, and the provisional and real lands of the Buddha-realm.
The practitioner should choose for themselves which path to follow. (2. A general demonstration of karmic causes.)
Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and undergo this cycle of rebirth for immeasurable kalpas, failing to attain true purity.

This is entirely due to their compliance with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. By reversing these three, they give rise to the state of being free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;

those who possess [these qualities] belong to the class of ghosts, while those who lack them belong to the realm of devas. As existence and non-existence contend with one another, the nature of saṃsāra arises.
[Commentary] The first five phrases demonstrate how one undergoes rebirth through deluded thoughts. The subsequent five phrases demonstrate how deluded karma follows from karma.

The phrase "there are names" and so forth concludes the discussion on cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Among the realms of ghosts and devas, four of the evil paths and two of the good paths are briefly cited.
Existence and non-existence are mutually dependent, constantly overturning and usurping one another; ascending, one falls again. Thus, the wheel of existence has no beginning.

[Wenling says: The previous question asked how the wondrous mind can be all-pervasive and perfect while there still exist realms such as hell, humans, and devas; therefore, this [passage] concludes by demonstrating that the three karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct serve as the root. [ Dinglin says: Where there is opposition, there is dependence; where there is grasping, there is an explanation.

To grasp at existence as being pleasurable is to oppose it with suffering; its explanation is that suffering takes its place. Thus, human pleasure ultimately ends in ruin. To grasp at non-existence as being pure is to oppose it with defilement; its explanation is that lust takes its place.

Therefore, when heaven is pure, it ends in falling; once fallen, that which existed is no longer there. When it is destroyed, that which was present becomes non-existent. (△ [Baiting said: The ascent and descent through the seven realms of existence result solely from the following or reversing of the karmas of killing, stealing, and lust.

Thus it is said: "All arise from following and conforming," etc. That which has name belongs to the category of ghosts; that which lacks name belongs to the realm of heaven. "Having" is conformity; "not having" is reversal. When having and not having mutually displace one another, this is nothing but saṃsāra. As for humans, they are not fixed: when they possess [these karmas], they are the same as those in the category of ghosts.)

If they do not exist, they are equal to the realm of heavenly beings; therefore, the Sūtra does not mention "human" [as a distinct category]. (○ [The Mirror of the Source says: Question: Regarding the gate of the equality of emptiness and the wondrous principle of the One Mind—since both good and evil are boundless and both ordinary beings and sages are all perfect, why is there a difference in the retribution of their experiences?)

Suffering and happiness are unequal. Answer: All things arise from causes; people create them for themselves. The single principle of "Mind-Only" (cittamātra) remains unimpaired. Good and evil arise solely from the mind; how could the retribution of happiness be obtained from another? Therefore, know that this mind is the abode of both ordinary beings and sages, and the source of the sense faculties and their objects.

It is precisely because ordinary beings cling to it as the *ālaya-vijñāna* that it becomes the cause of the suffering and affliction of birth and death. Sages realize it as the *ālaya-citta*, thereby attaining the fruit of the eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa*. If one is oblivious in every thought-moment to the nature of the Tathāgata’s *dharmadhātu*, one will step by step create the causes for the karmic fruits of sentient beings.

Bound by karma, one undergoes the four modes of birth and dwells within the nine realms of existence. Those who obtain a human body are like dust on a fingernail; those who lose a human body are like the soil of the great earth. [Those who fail to attain liberation] receive the *yǎnkǒu* (flaming-mouth) and *zhēnhóu* (needle-throat) [hunger and thirst].

This is the substance [of our condition]. Though kalpas pass, it is scorched by the fires of karma; we take on bodies with fur and horns, and at every turn, we are ensnared in nets and traps. Sometimes we fall into the Avīci Hell, embracing intense suffering as we dwell forever within the wheel of fire. Sometimes we are born in the palaces of the Asuras, where strife and contention arise and swords and blades rain down constantly.

Sometimes we briefly reside in the human realm, where in a single kṣaṇa, the eight sufferings torment us together. Or we happen to dwell in the celestial palaces, yet in an instant, the five signs of decline appear. All this is because we fail to realize the Tathāgatagarbha mind and lose the wondrous nature of Vijñaptimātratā.
