As the preceding text says: "The entire vessel-world, at the mere thought [of this], transforms into the Unsurpassed."
Regarding awareness: for one who has awakened to the truth, at the moment of attaining awakening, although they perceive only awareness, no delusion can arise; thus, there is no arising of delusion.
For one who has not yet awakened to the truth, they see this as actually possessing delusion, which gives rise to the shared transformation of the land experienced by all.

It is realized by wisdom; how could it not be shaken and rent asunder? For this reason, when the Buddhas attain the Way, they cause all worlds to tremble; this is certainly not in vain. (Changqing said:

"To be 'shaken and rent' means that when someone awakens to the Way, the palaces of the various Māras collapse and crumble. As the *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* says: 'When one son leaves home, the devas rejoice and congratulate one another; when one person awakens to the Way, the void is shaken and rent.

How can one dare not believe? (The *Commentary on the Complete Enlightenment Sutra* says: "To speak of 'the True arising' means the True arises. This refers to the unfolding of the true nature, which is identical to the boundless empty space of the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*. This awakening... )

That which is manifested is the "returning to the source," meaning that initial awakening (shijue) merges with fundamental awakening (benjue). "Perishing" means extinction. Since empty space already appears as a manifestation from the熏習 (xūnxí—perfuming habit-energies) of the mind-consciousness's discrimination, now, by destroying the characteristics of the harmonized consciousness, one manifests true, pure awakened wisdom.

Therefore, the empty forms produced by transformation perish. This is precisely the meaning of "when the mind ceases, all various phenomena cease" in the *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith). Question: If one person returns to the source and the emptiness of the ten directions perishes, why do we all still perceive the appearance of emptiness?

Answer: Did I not say above that these are transformations of one's own consciousness? Why do you not blame your own discriminative marks, instead blaming the presence of empty forms? Thus, it is said: "Fish do not see water; people do not see wind; the deluded do not see their nature; the awakened do not see emptiness. [Combined Commentary states:

"When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the voids of the ten directions are entirely dissolved and destroyed. This is naturally so for me; yet it is said that all demon kings, ghosts, spirits, and ordinary people see the collapse and destruction of their palaces."

Why is this? It is said: Generally speaking, that which was originally non-existent but now exists cannot be trusted. Why? Because it is a provisional phenomenon (*prajñapti-dharma*). Provisional phenomena depend on mental states; mental states exist through conceptualization (*vikalpa*), like the moon in water, which is not contained within the sense-base of the eye, yet is conceived as existing by the mind.

If one awakens to the fact that the triple world is but mind-only, there is only a single quiescence (*śānti*). Within this quiescence, there may still appear the forms of Māras, spirits, ordinary beings, or celestial classes—just as there might be a single thread within a blazing furnace.

Therefore it is said: "How can the void not tremble and split? [Wuxing says: The "microdust lands" refer here to the Land of Common Residence (*sahabhūmi*). Ultimately, for the void to tremble and split, all three lands must be considered. Now, according to the previous statement that these are "not without outflows," the following refers to the palaces of Māra.]

In general, whenever [a text] discards the wording of the sūtras to discuss the three lands separately—this is a common failing of the Tiantai school (as seen in Siming’s "The Awakening Caused the Arising of Demons").
"You all practice dhyāna and adorn yourselves with samādhi.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the various great Arhats free from outflows have their minds merged in profound stillness; they remain serene right where they are."

[Commentary: This reveals awakening. "Adorning" (*shì*) is also equivalent to "cultivating" (*xiū*). [The character] 泳 (yǒng) is a variant for 合 (hé), meaning "to unite. The single mind of the Dharma-realm is the same essence in both sentient beings and Buddhas.
The Buddha has realized this to its ultimate limit; Bodhisattvas and Arhats have also partially realized it. Now, as for this samādhi, one unites with that realization, fusing into a single body.

Where delusion resides, there is complete awakening; therefore, it is said that "the place itself is tranquil and still" (*zhànrán*). [Wùxīng says: "Adorning" (*shì*) is synonymous with "adorned" (*zhuāng*).*]

It means "adornment. This refers to adorning the primordially existing true samādhi through the cultivation of the merit of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). For this reason, the nature of mind realized by Bodhisattvas and Arhats is universally identical and perfectly harmonized with the nature of mind as observed by me.
All the Māra kings, as well as the ghosts, spirits, and ordinary devas, saw their palaces collapse and crack for no apparent reason;

the great earth quaked and split open, and all creatures—whether dwelling in water or on land, whether flying or soaring—were without exception struck with terror. The ordinary people, shrouded in darkness, did not perceive the calamity that had befallen them.
They have all attained the five supernormal powers, with the sole exception of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Yet they remain attached to these worldly defilements;
how can you cause them to shatter that place?
[Commentary] "All the Māra kings" and below concerns the movement of Māra. "Ordinary beings are dark and dull" and below is the discernment [of their state]. Māra and...

The various devas all cultivate meditative concentration; therefore, they attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), however, have never once subdued their afflictions (*kleśa*);
thus, they are said to be "dark and obscured. Those various Māra kings are the lords of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who govern this land as their dwelling place.

He gathers all sentient beings together as his assembly. Therefore, those who attain the Way will certainly emerge from the realm of Māra; and when they collectively experience the transformation of the land, it will surely tremble and shake.

[The *Xunwen* commentary states: "From 'ordinary people' (*pǔfán*) onwards, this explains away a latent doubt. It is feared that a doubter might ask: 'If Māra and the various devas have already perceived these signs, why is it that ordinary people do not perceive them at all?

This passage is the explanation for that. Question: The great earth is insentient, and the various species of water and land differ; why are they all equally like Māra, such that they all quiver with fear? Answer: The majestic spiritual power of samādhi is inconceivable. It is like the Great Tree Kinnara King playing the lute... ]

When a single song is performed, its sound shakes the great trichiliocosm; even Sumeru, the King of Mountains, rises and sinks because of it. How much more so the power of the Bodhisattva’s Śūraṅgama-samādhi—how could it be differentiated by the distinction between the sentient and the insentient?

[The *Zhiguan* says: When a practitioner cultivates the four samādhis, evil desires fade away and wholesome desires arise. The Māras fear that he will transcend their realm and further transform and deliver others, thereby losing their subjects and leaving their palaces empty.

They also worry that he will attain the power of great supernatural penetrations and great wisdom, which would lead to a great battle and conflict, causing them distress and potentially destroying the practitioner's roots of goodness before they have even been perfected. Thus, demonic obstacles arise. When the practitioner's path is weak, he cannot yet move Pāpīyān (Bosun). All ghosts and spirits are under the jurisdiction of the Six Heavens and serve as sentries guarding their respective domains; this is precisely what ought to happen.
Because they stir these ears,
spirits, ghosts, as well as all devas, māras, *wangliang*, and *jingling* demons will all come together to harass you during the time of samādhi.
(5. Manifesting Awakening and Subjugation). (1. First, the primary clarification of awakening).
Yet those various māras, though filled with great rage within their afflictions, are like wind blowing against light or a blade cutting through water;
they do not touch you at all. You are like boiling water, and they are like solid ice; as the warmth gradually approaches, [the ice will surely melt].
Before long, they will perish; you merely rely on your supernatural powers and act as their guest, thereby bringing about ruin and disorder.
This is because you are the master within the five aggregates (skandhas) of your own mind. If the master is deluded, the guest will take advantage of the situation.
[Commentary: The *śūraṅgama-samādhi* and the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*) are like light and water, like a host and his guests.
How could the "wind-knives" or the "water-guests" ever move them? This uses the power of the pure path to shatter the deluded and turbid minds of Māra;
being like space, unimpeded, how could any thing obstruct it? Should even a single thought waver, it is as if the host’s mind has become confused, allowing the guest to find its opportunity.

This immediately results in disruption and disorder; it will never lead to accomplishment. (Wenling says: "The master of the five aggregates is the true mind. (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 65, states: There are four kinds of Māras.

Herein, by the power of Prajñā, these four Māras cannot find an opportunity. By attaining the true mark of all dharmas, afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed, whereby the Māra of Afflictions is destroyed. Because the Māra of Heaven also cannot find an opportunity, one enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, whereby the Māras of the Five Aggregates and the Māra of Death are destroyed.

Why can they not find an opportunity? Herein the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions: this person skillfully cultivates the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and yet does not cling to emptiness. Since they do not cling to emptiness, how could [the Māras] find an opportunity? It is like, for example, [a fire in] the absence of...)

A sore does not receive poison; likewise, the signless (*animitta*) and the wishless (*apraṇihita*) are also thus. Furthermore, when all phenomena are truly contemplated, because they are characterized by emptiness, the signless, and the wishless, there is no opportunity for [afflictions] to gain access, nor is there anyone who receives such access.

Therefore, emptiness should not find an opportunity within emptiness; the signless should not find an opportunity within the signless; and the wishless should not find an opportunity within the wishless, because they share a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*). It is like fire, which cannot extinguish fire, but is extinguished upon meeting water, because their characteristics are different.

Question: Who is Māra? Why does he afflict the Bodhisattva? How does he find an opportunity? Answer: Māra is named the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa (or the Lord of the Heaven of Sovereignty). Although he is born through the causes and conditions of merit and virtue, he harbors various false views. Regarding the sentient beings of the desire realm...

These are my own subjects. Although they may pass through the cycle of birth and death, they do not leave my realm. Even if they ascend to the Form or Formless Realms, they will eventually return to belong to me. If there are those who attain the five supernatural powers of the non-Buddhists, they likewise do not escape my realm.

However, when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appear in the world, they transform and deliver my subjects, uprooting the source of birth and death so that they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and never return again, thereby emptying my domain. For this reason, he gives rise to resentment, hostility, and malice.

Furthermore, seeing that the people of the Desire Realm all go toward the Buddha and do not come to submit to him, he feels envy because he loses his offerings. Therefore, he regards the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as enemies. When a Bodhisattva enters the stage of the Dharma-position (*dharmatā-sthiti*) and attains the body born of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-janman-kāya*), even if Māra should give rise to evil intentions, [he cannot harm him].

They can cause ruin. If one has not yet attained the stage of *avaivartika*, Māra will employ various means to destroy them. However, if a bodhisattva is single-mindedly indifferent to body and life and seeks the Buddha-way through skillful means, all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great bodhisattvas will together protect and sustain them;

because of these causes and conditions, they are able to achieve the Buddha-way. If a bodhisattva is indolent, greedily attached to worldly pleasures, and unable to seek the Buddha-way with focused diligence, this is to deceive oneself and also to deceive the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions.

While claiming, "I seek the Buddha-way for the sake of all sentient beings," such a person performs mixed practices and violates the bodhisattva dharma. For this reason, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas do not provide protection, and Māra gains the opportunity. This is why...

Why is this? All noble ones (*ārya*) have already entered the stage of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and practice the Path with a single mind, deeply delighting in *nirvāṇa*. Māra, however, has entered the stage of error and is attached to the wrong path. Because the wrong and the correct are diametrically opposed, he harbors hatred and jealousy toward right practice.

Deluded and foolish, yet self-exalting, he calls the Buddha "the Śramaṇa Gautama. The Buddha calls him by his true name, "Evil Māra" (*pāpamāra*); because they are opposed to one another, he is called an "enemy" (*śatru*). (○ [The *Qixinji* states]: A verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "If one discriminates the characteristics of objects, that is the net of Māra.")

To be unmoving and non-conceptual—this is the Dharma-seal. A sūtra states that there was once a bhikṣu whom Māra sought to delude for seven thousand years, yet in the end he found no opportunity. Why? Because this bhikṣu did not give rise to the mind [of conceptualization].

"It is like a sealed chamber where wind cannot enter; that wind can enter is due to the presence of cracks and crevices. That Māra finds an opportunity is due to the arising of discursive thoughts. (From the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*:

"It is like a person who, when afraid, gives an advantage to a non-human spirit. Master Kumārajīva said: "Suppose there is a rākṣasa who transforms himself into a horse. A man mounts it without suspicion. The horse asks the man, 'Is this horse good? The man draws his sword and shows it to him. The horse asks again, 'Is this sword good?

Knowing that the man's mind is upright and he is merely afraid, the horse ultimately dares not inflict harm. If it were not so, the non-human spirit would find its opportunity). (2. Concluding Exhortation to Subdue [the Mind])
If you remain in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and awaken to the truth without delusion, then those demonic activities will be powerless against you.

As the five aggregates (*skandhas*) dissolve and you enter the light, all those malevolent spirits will be forced to absorb their dark, obscure energies. Since light can destroy darkness, they will perish from within; how then could they dare to remain?

It disturbs meditative concentration. If you do not attain clear awakening and remain deluded by the aggregates, then you, Ānanda, will surely become a son of Māra and achieve the state of a Māra-person.
[Commentary]: The first two phrases exhort reliance on the fundamental to cultivate and purify through the observation of wisdom. "Then he" and below clarify that Māra gains no advantage.
When a single person awakens to the truth, the world perishes; now, having entered samādhi, how could Māra not be moved?

If one can enter deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and contemplate only the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*), then the realm of Māras and the realm of Buddhas are identical and non-dual;
birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa, as well as the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, are all nothing but the deluded toil of false and empty flower-like appearances.

Therefore it is said: "How would they dare remain? (Léi-ān says: "The various evils dwell in reliance upon delusive thoughts; thought belongs to the yin. △ Jiāo-guāng says: "When power is gained in meditative concentration, the light pervades everywhere. Māras rely on darkness and gloom.")
It would be like an owl entering the daylight or a rākṣasa facing the sun; they could not even be seen, so how could they dare remain to cause disturbance?

If [the truth] is not revealed, one must earnestly exhort and awaken them, enabling them to recognize the delusions of Māra and the confusion caused by the five aggregates (pañca-skandha). Thus Māra gains the opportunity. Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"The five aggregates are an accumulation and concealment of all unwholesome causes, just as a band of thieves hides in the mountains and occasionally emerges among people to plunder."

They plunder one's wealth and possessions; therefore, know that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the dwelling place of Māra. If one can contemplate and destroy them, Māra will naturally vanish and cease.

(Direct Explanation: The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "When a single thought-moment moves, the five aggregates arise together. Within the arising of the five aggregates, there are fifty evils. The fifty māras of the aggregates are precisely these fifty evils. [Section 3: Proving the Delusions of Māra]
The case of Mātanga was extremely insignificant; he merely cast a spell upon you, thereby violating one precept out of the eighty thousand practices of the Buddha’s Vinaya.
Because your mind remained pure, you had not yet fallen into ruin. This [present offense], however, destroys your entire body of precious awakening.
It is like the family of a high minister who suddenly encounters confiscation of their property; they fall into ruin and dispersal, with no means for rescue or relief.

[Commentary] "Especially inferior" (*shu wei miao lüe*): *shu* means "extraordinary. This refers to an extraordinary degree of inferiority. Demons and ghosts are seen in contrast; the demons are superior while the ghosts are inferior.
Now, this Dhānakī is a human being who possesses only the power of incantations, but does not possess the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
If one considers him in relation to Māra, he is the most inferior among the inferior; he is merely lowly. This explains the characteristics of his inferiority:
based on the fact that Maṭaṅga’s resolve was extremely shallow, he merely wished to destroy your single precept against sexual misconduct;
because you were without such intent, you did not even commit an offense. This, then, is the lowest level, which reveals the superiority of Māra. This is that Māra. Māra wishes to cause you—
Samādhi will not be accomplished; one will wander and revolve in saṃsāra. The Dharma-body and the life of wisdom will be severed, extinguished, and perish.
It is like a high minister’s family that violates the supreme laws of the state: their registers are erased, and they shall have no stipends for life in this world—how truly lamentable!

(〔Gu-shan says: This cites the inferior to illustrate the superior, exhorting others to maintain profound vigilance. Because those on the path of the first fruit possess the power of the precepts inherent in the Way, they naturally commit no transgressions; hence it says, "the mind is pure," and so forth.〕 (○ Below follows the combined explanation of demonic activities. (○ 〔The Awakening of Faith says: If a person practices, gradually...〕)

Gradually, one will be able to give rise to immeasurable samādhis. However, there may be sentient beings who lack the power of roots of goodness and are thus deluded and disturbed by various Māras, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), and spirits. If, while sitting in meditation, these beings manifest forms to terrify them, or appear in the likeness of handsome men and women, the practitioner should contemplate that "this is but the mind.

Then the objective realm will vanish, and they will ultimately not cause any affliction. For this reason, the practitioner should constantly observe with wisdom so as not to allow this mind to fall into the net of error.

One should diligently maintain right mindfulness, neither grasping nor clinging; thus, one can remain far removed from all such karmic obstructions. [Xianshou said: Such spirits who harass and disturb the Buddha-dharma are certain to enter wrong paths, and for this reason they are called "non-Buddhists" (tīrthikas). These three types [of obstacles] can transform themselves into three kinds of five [senses].

Dust [defilements] destroys the wholesome mind of humans. All objective realms are merely one’s own mind; therefore, by observing that all is mind-only, the realms of Māra are eliminated. This is the method for universally dispelling them. Now, following the oral tradition of the ancient masters, we shall briefly examine this through three methods: first, refining through meditative concentration (*samādhi*); second, practicing according to the fundamental nature;

and third, observation through wisdom (*prajñā*). As the Sūtra says: "To know true gold, one tests it with three methods—namely, burning, cutting, and rubbing. Here, concentration is likened to rubbing, fundamental practice to cutting, and observation to burning. [The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"These Bodhisattvas, because they have attained the Bodhisattva path, destroy the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*). Because they have attained the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), they destroy the Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*). Because they have attained the Path and the Dharma-nature body, they destroy the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*)."

Because he is always single-minded; because his mind is unattached in all places; and because he has entered the immovable samādhi, he destroys the Māra of the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. For these reasons, it is said that he has transcended all demonic activities. Furthermore, with the exception of the true mark of all dharmas (*dharmatā*).

All remaining phenomena are entirely called *māra*. Just as the various afflictions (*kleśa*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), desires (*kāma*), bonds (*bandhana*), graspings (*parigraha*), entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), as well as the Māra King, the Māra subjects, and the Māra people—all such things are entirely called *māra*.

This is what is meant by the "affliction-māra" (*kleśa-māra*). Question: Where is it stated that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), and twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) are *māra*? Answer: On Mount Mukula, the Buddha taught his disciple Rādha: "The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is *māra*; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise *māra*."

Furthermore, if one wishes to create a form-body (*rūpakāya*) in a future state, this is a realm of movement. If one wishes to create a formless-body (*arūpakāya*), this too is a realm of movement. If one wishes to create a body of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), this is likewise a realm of movement.

This constitutes all places of movement. Movement is the bondage of Māra; non-movement is non-bondage. One attains liberation from evil herein. It is said that within this context, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are Māra. The Lord of the Gods (*Indra*), the Māras of the Māra-hosts, and human Māras are themselves Māra; there is no need to speak further. Question: Why is he called "Māra"? Answer:

Because he seizes the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*), destroys the merit and roots of goodness of the Path and the Dharma; for this reason, he is named Māra. The various followers of external paths say his name is "Lord of Desire" (*Kāmeśvara*), and he is also called "Flower-Arrowed" (*Puṣpaśara*) or "Five-Arrowed" (*Pañcaśara*). He shatters all manner of wholesome deeds. Within the Buddha-Dharma, he is named Māra.

Furthermore, as people transmigrate through the world, experiencing suffering and pleasure due to the causes and conditions of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), it is also due to the power and causes and conditions of the King of Māras. This Māra is [known] by the Buddhas.

Enemies. All noble ones destroy all such逆流 (counter-flow) human affairs. That which does not rejoice in *nirvāṇa* is called Māra. This Māra has three activities: frivolous speech and laughter; singing, dancing, and lewd glances—these and others arise from attachment (*rāga*). Beating, whipping, torturing, piercing, cutting, hacking, and severing—these and others arise from hatred (*dveṣa*).

Roasting the body, plucking out the hair, entering fire, throwing oneself into deep water, and casting oneself from cliffs—these and others arise from delusion (*moha*). Furthermore, great faults, impurity, and defiled attachment to the world are all the works of Māra.

Hatred, malice, and uselessness, as well as having no use for *nirvāṇa* or the path to *nirvāṇa*, are also the works of Māra. Sinking into the great ocean of suffering and lacking self-awareness—such instances are immeasurable, yet all are the works of Māra. [These have already been] abandoned.

"Having already abandoned them, this is called transcending all demonic activities. (The *Tiantai Zhiguan* states: "Māra acts to destroy the two kinds of goodness and increase the two kinds of evil; thus he delights in using the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) to launch strong and soft attacks to break [the practitioner].

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: 'Māra is named Flower-Arrow' and also 'Five Arrows. Each shoots at the five sense-faculties, collectively destroying the mind-faculty (*manas*). If each of the five faculties lasts for only one moment (*kṣaṇa*), and that moment shifts, it then belongs to the mind-faculty. If the mind-faculty is destroyed, how can the five faculties remain? Seeing a desirable form with the eye is called a flower-arrow;

this is a soft thief. Seeing a fearsome form is called a poison-arrow; this is a strong thief. Seeing a neutral form is neither a strong nor a soft thief. It is the same for the other four faculties. Combined, these are eighteen arrows, also known as the eighteen sensations (*vedanā*).")

For this reason, one should not accept or become attached to them. Attachment constitutes a disease; once diseased, it is difficult to cure. It will forever obstruct meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and lead to falling into the path of Māra upon death. Ānanda and Guptaka studied under Avīvara, yet both were tormented by Māra; how much more so for those with a beginner’s mind?

How can they avoid the thirty-six arrows directed at themselves and others? If one knows that both Māra and the Buddha enter the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality), then there is no fear. When the arrows of Māra first strike the five sense faculties, those who have acquired false teachings should distinguish between the false and the correct based on the ten kinds of true Dharma.

Regarding "existence": when form enters through the eye, one sees mountains, rivers, stars, and constellations, as well as the sun and moon dwelling in their palaces; one also sees various appearances within the darkness and points out specific directions. This is the error of "excessive existence" (*atiprasaṅga*). Regarding "non-existence": when form enters through the eye, [one sees nothing]. This is the error of "absolute non-existence."

It refers to all phenomena being like a void that has been severed. To say that the state of non-existence after becoming ash is utterly terrifying is not an exaggeration. For those who are enlightened, once they have entered the realm of form (*rūpāyatana*), it is suddenly and perpetually as bright as the sun and moon; for those who are ignorant, once they have entered the realm of form, it is dark, gloomy, and pitch black.

The "resolute" one, having entered the realm of form (*rūpāyatana*), remains as firm as wood or stone, dwelling in a state of total stillness. The "distracted" one, having entered the realm of form, casts about restlessly, grasping at objects of perception. The "foolish" one, having entered the realm of form, is dark, short-sighted, base, and clumsy; he is naked and shameless. The "wise" one, having entered the realm of form, is clever, sharp, and quick-witted.

The "sorrowful" one, having entered the realm of form, is filled with grief and distress, weeping tears. The "joyful" one, having entered the realm of form, constantly delights in song and dance. The "suffering" one, having entered the realm of form, experiences pain in his hundred joints, as if being burned and roasted. The "blissful" one...

As for "the intoxicated": having entered the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), one’s body becomes exhilarated and intoxicated, as if by the pleasures of the five desires. As for "the calamitous": having entered the sphere of form, one constantly invites calamity upon oneself and also brings calamity upon others, and one also recognizes the calamities of others. As for "the one who honors merit": having entered the sphere of form, one constantly invites merit for oneself and is also able to bring merit to others. As for "the evil":

having entered the sphere of form, there is nothing evil that one does not commit, and one also causes others to commit evil. As for "the virtuous": having entered the sphere of form, one personally practices giving (*dāna*) and so forth, and also causes others to practice giving. As for "the hateful": having entered the sphere of form, one does not...

"Enduring to see people" means dwelling alone far from others. "Affection" refers to being entangled by longing and attachment. "Firm" means that the mind is so rigid that one cannot move with ease when entering or exiting; it is like a piece of tile or stone, difficult to transform.

(Section Four: Explaining the Manifestations of Dhyāna; Subsection Three: Refuting the Active Skandha [saṃskāra-skandha]; Part Two: The Aspects of Exhaustion and Non-exhaustion; Part Two: Clarifying the Term "Districts"; Section One: The Aspect of the Benefit of Exhausting Thought.)
Ānanda, when that son of good family practices samādhi and the skandha of perception is exhausted, his ordinary dreams will vanish;
waking and sleeping will be ever one. His awakened clarity will be empty and still, like a cloudless sky, no longer burdened by the coarse and heavy shadows of external objects.
[Commentary]: If the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) still exists, then upon waking one immediately engages in mental imagery, and while asleep it constitutes a dream.

Now that the cause of perception has been exhausted, there are no longer any dreams, because the aggregate of perception is the very source of dreaming. Although there is still waking and sleeping, because perception is absent, waking is like sleeping and sleeping is like waking;
therefore, it is said to be "constantly one. [Wuxing says: According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, it is clarified that Arhats have sleep but no dreams. This serves as proof for the present case.]

When the marks are exhausted, the six sense faculties are likewise exhausted. The *Śāstra* states: "There are two kinds of sleep: first, sleeping with dreams; second, sleeping without dreams. An Arhat does not sleep for the sake of seeking security or attachment to pleasure; it is merely a phenomenon of the body composed of the four great elements."

There should be eating, resting, and the awareness of the eyes. A brief period of rest is called "sleep" (not the sleep of dreaming). The essence of the mind, perfectly luminous, is called "awakened clarity.
Because it is free from the floating movement of thought, it is termed "empty stillness. Emptiness is a metaphor for awakened clarity; darkness is a metaphor for being free from thought.

"Coarseness and heaviness" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*), because the aggregate of thought (*saṃjñā-skandha*) constitutes the turbidity of affliction. The "reflected images of external objects" are the realms that are perceived; the "one who perceives" is...

Once [the body] has perished, that which was conceived no longer stands; hence it is said, "there is no more. (Wuxing says: Because the two delusions—the pervasive and the specific—are destroyed by the perfect contemplation, it is like smelting iron where the coarse impurities are first removed;

hence it is said, "there is no more coarseness. (Wenling says: The five aggregates are coarse at first and subtle later; therefore, when conception is exhausted, there is no longer the shadow of coarse heaviness.)
Contemplate all worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers, as if reflected in a clear mirror; they leave no further attachment, pass away without trace, and respond to illumination in emptiness.
With habitual tendencies utterly extinguished, there remains only the single, pure reality.
[Commentary]: This refers to observing conditions. Although there are sense organs and consciousness that encounter various objects, they do not form mental images;
rather, mindfulness is bound within the mind. Thus, like a mirror, it reflects things without leaving a trace; it merely receives emptily, illuminates emptily, and responds emptily.

(The "Pointer" states: The mirror has four meanings. "Empty" means it can contain the myriad phenomena. "Receiving" means it does not reject things as they come. "Illuminating" means it manifests forms according to the objects. "Responding" means it is without grasping or rejecting. It may also be said to be like a mirror.
It illuminates with radiance; though it reflects, there is no shadow, hence it is said to "receive in emptiness. "Liao" (了) means ultimate. "Wang" (罔) means non-existence. "Chen" (陳) means ancient.
"Xi" (習) means deluded thought (*vikalpa*). Ultimately, there is no beginningless deluded habituation; there is only the single, numinous *tathatā* nature. (Wuxing says:

This refers to the fact that since perception and thought are already non-separable, they are called "habitual tendencies. (Haiyin says: Since the aggregate of thought has been shattered, the floating thoughts and habitual tendencies of the first six consciousnesses are gone.)

"Adhering": the true essence of the eight consciousnesses exists in utter isolation; this is the sign of the exhaustion of such conceptualization. Furthermore, "to understand" means to discern, which refers to the various consciousnesses. "Wang" (entangle/net).
"Entangled forms" refers to habitual tendencies; it refers to the seeds from beginningless time. "The sole pure reality" refers to the single aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
As stated in the following passage: "Then, within the profound clarity, there are no entangled forms, yet there is subtle, refined conceptualization.

This is said in contrast to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); therefore, it is called "pure reality. This reveals that the practitioner has attained the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) and possesses only the aggregate of consciousness.

As long as the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) remains, this aggregate of formations is now further revealed; therefore, the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is called the "essence of reality" (*jingzhen*).
(2. The Manifestation of the Aggregate of Formations)
The root-source of arising and ceasing is here revealed from this point. One perceives all twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category.
Although one has not yet fully understood the individual origins of their respective destinies, one sees their common basis of birth, which is like a shimmering mirage—vibrant, clear, and turbulent.
It serves as the ultimate pivot-hole for the floating sense-roots and their objects;

this is what is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). [Commentary: The *saṃskāra-skandha* is the source of arising and ceasing, because it involves constant flux and volitional activity.

Since thought (*saṃjñā*) has been exhausted and formations now manifest, it is said to be "disclosed. [The *Xunwen* says: The subsequent text states that "only arising and ceasing" is the limit of formations; now that thought is exhausted and only formations remain, it is thus called "disclosed. To exhaustively enumerate its categories:
"Exhausted" (*dan*) means "to the end. These twelve classes of beings are all produced from mental formations (*saṃskāra*), because formations constitute the substance of karma.

[Gushan says: Because formations are karma, they are able to summon retribution. Wenglun says: Formations are the root source of the birth and death of the myriad transformations; when their characteristics are revealed, there is nothing of the origin of the twelve classes of beings that is not fully seen.

As for those who have not yet attained penetration regarding their respective life-spans, although they understand that the twelve classes of beings generally emerge from formations, they do not yet know the multitude...
It gives rise to distinct species within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). This is precisely the seed of karma and suffering within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*);

it is the individual life-force of sentient beings and the primary source of their existence. (〔Gushan says〕: Although one cannot yet perceive those sentient beings through their distinct characteristics, because they cultivate causes and proceed toward fruits, one is already able to perceive that class of beings through their general characteristics;

since they all arise from formative action (*saṃskāra*), this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is called the "common basis for birth. 〔Haichen says〕: The source of each individual life is the seed of maturation (*vipāka-bīja*). Its substance is profound and subtle, and therefore cannot be known.)

Regarding "seeing the basis for co-arising": the basis for co-arising is precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It takes the aggregate of formations as its fundamental basis. [The *Zongtong* says:

"If one considers both the general and specific characteristics, one can see that the life-continuums of sentient beings differ—such that their wisdom and merit vary—due to the manifestation of seeds accumulated through habitual practice over many lifetimes; this pertains to the boundary of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)."

Therefore, it is not something that can be measured by the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). "Like a wild horse" refers to the blending of dust with the yang-energy, which stirs it into being;

its flickering is like light flashing and shimmering, serving as a metaphor for arising and ceasing momentarily. "Clear agitation" refers to this very aggregate of formations: its restless movement of arising and ceasing is subtle and never ceases.
It is called "clear" because it is free from the defilements of the aggregate of perception (*vijñāna-skandha*). (Gushan says: This means the aggregate of formations is subtle.)

Constantly shifting, arising, and ceasing, it is like the shimmering heat haze (yema). Because it is no longer coarse or heavy, it is called "clearly disturbed" (*qingrao*); this refers to the "profound clarity and restless movement" mentioned in the text below. [Quotation] Guo Xiang’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states: "The 'heat haze' (*yema*) is wandering vapor. Lu Deming cites Sima Biao as saying:

"It is the wandering vapor over marshes during the spring months. Cui [Dao] says: "It is the vapor between heaven and earth, like wild horses galloping. Shen Kuo says: "The 'wild horse' is the wandering vapor in the fields; when viewed from afar, it resembles a flock of sheep."

Furthermore, it is like ripples on water. Buddhist texts describe it as being like a mirage in the heat; [Gushan says that to take it as "the shimmering dust of a mirage" is an error]. "Yi-yi" refers to the light of fireflies (taking the meaning from the *Shijing* line:

"The fireflies flash and move through the night"). Regarding "the ultimate pivot and socket of the floating sense-bases and objects": the pivot is the door hinge, and the socket is the door mortise; these are both the essential points of movement and turning.
The arising and ceasing of the sense-bases and objects all have the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) as their mechanical fulcrum. To understand this thoroughly...

This refers to being precisely within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Hence it is said: "The Pivot and its Cavity" [Fengshi’s commentary states: "The pivot has a cavity; the gate functions through opening and closing. This refers to the various faculties of eye and ear that rush toward forms and sounds.

As for their ultimate place of return, they take the basis of co-arising with the aggregate of formations as that pivot-cavity"]. (○ [Shiwen]: "Basis of co-arising. The common edition reads "basis of life" (*shēngjī*). The "floating roots and objects" (*fú gēn chén*)—some editions read "floating dust roots" (*fúchén gēn*)—are all corruptions).
(2. Explaining the characteristic of exhaustion.
If this turbidity subsides and the radiant, fundamental nature enters its original clarity, and once clarified, the fundamental habit-energy is extinguished like the ceasing of waves.
It transforms into clear water; this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings.
Examining its source, one finds that subtle and hidden deluded thoughts constitute its foundation.

[Commentary]: "The nature enters the primordial clarity" means that when the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is exhausted, the nature of flux becomes still and returns to the single *ālaya-vijñāna*;

this is called "entering the primordial clarity. As the Sūtra says: "The ocean of the *ālaya-vijñāna* is eternally abiding. [Wuxing says: "Nature" refers to the nature of arising and ceasing; one "enters" it by means of its revolving back [to its source].

"Primordial" refers to the primordiality of the pivot-hole; it is "clear" because of its essential purity. [Haiyin says: The *saṃskāra-skandha* is the characteristic of arising and ceasing upon the substance of the eight consciousnesses; therefore, it is called "original nature. The eight consciousnesses constitute the substance of the profound abyss, being solely one pure lucidity.

Therefore it is said that by clarifying [the mind] as "one," one observes the practice until it becomes superior, thereby able to cause the root-source of the pure arising-and-ceasing and its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)—[Wuxing says:

"The root-habit" refers to the *vāsanā*, which are precisely the pervasive delusions]—to become immovable and return to the single aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), just like clarified water. [Biaozhi says:

"This is the entry into stillness merging with stillness. Because this [aggregate] is the nature of the shifting karma of sentient beings, if it is exhausted, one transcends the state of sentient beings.

This is turbidity. [Wuxing says: The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the root source of arising and ceasing. Sentient beings grasp at arising and ceasing as their essence; once that source is exhausted, this turbidity is also transcended. This refers to the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations.

Subtle and difficult to investigate, it is therefore called "profoundly hidden. [The Haiyin commentary states: When the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) returns to its original nature, the eight consciousnesses are found to be utterly devoid of arising and ceasing.

The nature enters the primordial clarity, like water without waves, becoming solely still water; this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations. [The Erleṅ commentary states: The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is like a great torrent, while the aggregate of formations is like a fine stream. The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is like a flow without waves. When the aggregate of perception is exhausted, it is like the cessation of the great torrent;

when the aggregate of formations manifests, it is like the emergence of the fine stream. If the original habit-energy becomes once clarified, then the fine stream entirely becomes clear water. This is the manifestation of pure water before one, which is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions. (△ [The Zongtong commentary states: The habitual disturbances of the aggregate of formations form...)

This is the nature. Therefore, it is said that there is both the original nature and original habituation. Habituation cannot clarify habituation; only when the nature returns to its source can it clarify habituation. When the marks of shifting and flowing are exhausted, the waves that swirl without wind transform into clear water. Reaching the state of profound stillness where there is no movement is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

(○ Synthesis of the Explanation of the Non-Buddhist Views of the Aggregate of Mental Formations) (○ [As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, Chapter 6] What are the evil views? First, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). This refers to the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self within the five aggregates. Its function is to serve as the basis for all systems of views.

There are twenty phrases of this view’s differentiation, such as the sixty-five [views], which are comprised within those arising from discrimination. Second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). This refers to the adherence to either annihilationism or eternalism regarding those same [aggregates]. Its function is to obstruct the departure via the middle way.

Regarding the differentiation of this view, among the various systems of views, there are those who grasp at the past and hold four theories of universal permanence, one theory of partial permanence, and regarding the future, sixteen theories of having perception, sixteen of having no perception, and sixteen of neither, each with eight doctrines, as well as seven theories of annihilationism, etc.; these are comprised within those arising from discrimination. Third...)

Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Among the various types of views, there are those that adhere to two theories of non-causality regarding the past; the four views concerning whether the world is finite and so forth; the equivocation of the "immortal" (*amarā-vikkhepa*); and those who reckon five kinds of present nirvana regarding the future.

Or they reckon that Īśvara, Prajāpati, Śakra, Brahmā, or other such entities are eternal and unchanging. Or they reckon that Īśvara and others are the cause of all things. Or they recklessly imagine various false liberations. Or they falsely cling to what is not the path as being the path. All such views as these are subsumed under wrong view.
(○ [Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra 87] Furthermore, among the various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) serves as the root for sixty-two types of evil views.

These are: the four theories of eternalism; the four partial theories of eternalism; the two theories of causelessness; the four theories of finite and infinite worlds; and the four theories of equivocation regarding immortality—these eighteen types of evil views are those who, calculating the past, propound a self.

Furthermore, there are sixteen theories of existence through perception, eight theories of non-perception, and eight theories of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the seven theories of annihilationism, and the five theories of nirvana in this very life—these forty-four types of evil views are those who, calculating the future, propound a self). (○ [Qingliang...])

In the *Gongdepin Chao* (Excerpts on the Chapter on Merit), the treatise arranges these views in sequence according to delusion regarding the past (*pūrvānta*) and the future (*aparānta*). Now, following the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) perspective, they are categorized according to their objects of perception. Regarding the past, there are four theories of universal permanence and four theories of partial permanence;

regarding the future, there are sixteen theories involving perception (*saṃjñin*), eight theories of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*), and eight theories of neither [perception nor non-perception]. These constitute forty varieties of eternalist views (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). There are also those who calculate the future and hold seven theories of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

These forty-seven views all arise from the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and give rise to the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). (The first forty views are eternalist, while the latter seven are annihilist; all are abandoned through insight [*darśana-heya*] and are termed "arising from discrimination"). Furthermore, there are those who calculate the past and hold two theories of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*). (As for the statement "there are those who calculate the past and hold two theories of causelessness," these all arise from...)

Because wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) arises as an incorrect perspective, it is termed "wrong. (4) There are four theories of finitude (*antavāda*). (5) There are the four types of evasive speech regarding immortality (*amarāvikṣepa*), as well as those that speculate on the future limit (*aparānta-kalpa*). (6) There are those who claim to attain *nirvāṇa* in the present life. Thus, there are sixty-two [views].

These sixty-two have wrong view and extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) as their essential nature (*svabhāva*), while the remaining two views—view-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and precept-and-vow-grasping (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—act as their attendants (*parivāra*). They rely upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their root; therefore, they are called the various divergent paths of views. [The Commentary further states:

"With the view of a self-identity as the basis, the sixty-two views arise. Regarding this, there are two explanations. First, based on the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) across the three periods of time, which will be clarified below (in the *Daśastava-vastu*). Second, based on the wrong views of non-Buddhists, as fully described in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 87. (Excerpts)

It is said: Regarding the explanation based on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the three times, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is called the "view of the body" (*kāya-dṛṣṭi*). This view of the body arises in dependence upon the five aggregates; because this serves as its basis, all views are produced. The *Abhidharma-prathama* states: "For example, one may conceive that 'form is the self,' 'the self possesses form,' 'form belongs to the self,' or 'the self is within form.

There are four [conceptions] for each aggregate, and thus there are twenty phrases across the five aggregates. Five of these constitute the view of the self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), while the remainder are all 'mine' (*ātmīya*).

This is the analytical activity that takes the aggregates as its object, without distinguishing the specific locus from which they arise. If one considers them across the three times, there are sixty; adding 'the body is the self' makes sixty-one, and adding 'the self is distinct from the body' makes sixty-two. Furthermore, by calculating [views such as] permanence, impermanence, and so forth, there are sixty-two [views]. As it is said:

The *Daśadharmaka-parivarta* (Ten-Chapter Collection). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "For instance, if one takes form (*rūpa*) as the self, there are three types of 'mine' (*ātmiya*) for each of the other four aggregates (*skandha*).

These are: 'my ornament,' 'my servant,' and 'my vessel. Thus, there are twelve [instances of 'mine']. Adding the single self of form, there are thirteen in total. Across the five aggregates, there are sixty instances of 'mine. When one views these as five selves, there are sixty-five [views]. This is the analysis of the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) that take the aggregates as their object, as well as the analysis of the basis from which they arise.

All of these are the two types of analytical view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), based on the false views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), as explained above. [My Personal Commentary]: According to Qingliang’s (Zhiyan) commentary on the sixty-two views, various treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Yogācārabhūmi* are cited. Comparing these with the text on the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) in the present sutra, this constitutes the topical outline (*mukha-dvāra*).

Regarding the "distinctive progression," there are also two explanations. The Sūtra states: "Among those who practice *śamatha*, O sons of good family, if they give rise to conceptual calculations regarding the perfect source (*pariniṣpanna*), etc. This refers to practitioners who have erred in their cultivation of the mind, as clarified by Qingliang (Fazang).

"Relying on the five aggregates throughout the three periods of time" refers to this. When the Sūtra speaks of "this person falling into the two theories of causelessness," it points to those non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who establish and maintain such false attachments;

this is precisely what Qingliang [Chengguan] clarifies when he says, "relying on the false views of non-Buddhists. The various treatises refute these as the extreme, evil, and heterodox views of non-Buddhists, which are the enemies of the Buddha. This Sūtra distinguishes that the perverse wisdom manifested by practitioners constitutes an attachment to non-Buddhist teachings outside of the Buddha-dharma;

their established positions differ, and their transgressions are likewise distinct. Therefore, there is no room for reconciling the differences between the Sūtras and the Treatises into a single unity. Furthermore, the statements regarding "passing through the five aggregates across the three periods of time" also differ from one another within these texts. As for the difference in how they describe passing through the three periods of time, it is addressed in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, Chapter on False Views (*Dṛṣṭiparyāya*).

It is said: "Whether the self existed or did not exist in past lives; views such as the eternity of the world—all depend upon the past life. Whether the self will act or not act in future lives; views such as finitude and so forth—all depend upon the future life. A verse from the *Nirvāṇa-parivarta* states:

"Existence or non-existence after death, finitude and so forth, eternity and so forth—all views depend upon nirvāṇa, the future, and the past. Now, in this current scripture, within the discussion on the four types of eternalism, it is stated that the first three [know] twenty thousand and other such eons.

The first [view] refers to the past. The fourth, which is determined by the mind, belongs to the present. Within the partial-eternalist theories (*ekaccasassatavāda*), the first—the self (*puruṣa*)—refers to the past and also includes the present. The second—the indestructibility of the eon—belongs to the future. The third and fourth—knowing the aggregates through contemplation of the mind—refer to the present and also include the future.

This differs from the [other] theories, as all views such as eternalism rely upon the past world. Within the four theories of finitude (*antavāda*), the first—calculating that there is a limit to the past and the future—refers to both the past and the future.

Calculating that the continuum is infinite belongs to the present. The second—contemplating eighty thousand eons prior—refers to the past. The third—calculating that the self is all-pervasive—belongs to the present. The fourth concerns sentient beings and the world...

The realms (*dhātu*) are half-present and half-extinguished; this refers simultaneously to the past and the future. This differs from the *Śālistamba-sūtra-ṭīkā*, which holds that views such as "extremism" (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) all rely upon the future life. Qingliang states: "This 'self' is not distinct [from the three times]; it does not transcend the three times, yet it takes *nirvāṇa* as the locus where views arise.

Regarding "this self is not distinct," it means that the self of a previous life is the very same as the self of the present life; for if one were to claim it either pre-existed or did not exist, both positions would entail logical fallacies.

Regarding "it does not transcend the three times," it is because it pervades the three worlds, primarily manifesting the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) while also clarifying the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*). This is because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) conceive of the sentient being—the conventional designation of the five aggregates—as the self. Regarding "taking *nirvāṇa* as the locus where views arise," it is because non-Buddhists reckon the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*) to be *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, this sutra correctly clarifies that the three periods of time—past, present, and future—are not separate from a single thought-moment; there is no distinction between nirvana and the mundane world. This distinguishes [the Buddha's teaching] from the non-Buddhists who cling to a self in the present life and erroneously divide it across the past and future.

Regarding the statement about "passing through the differences of the five aggregates," various treatises unanimously point out that the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises based on the five aggregates. First, it is clarified that the five aggregates have twenty phrases; passing through the three periods of time, these form sixty-two views. Second, it is clarified that the five aggregates have sixty instances of "mine" (mamakāra); based on the five views of self, these form sixty-five views. In this sutra, the four aggregates (excluding the formation aggregate) consist of four phrases each, forming sixteen phrases.

Because the formation aggregate (saṃskāraskandha) relies upon the preceding three consciousnesses, and because it is obscured by the formation aggregate, it is not mentioned here. As for the sixty-two views of the non-Buddhist masters, they are all summarized as follows: [The text continues with the detailed enumeration of the sixty-two views.]

The two views of eternalism and annihilationism serve as the root. Those who calculate [existence] as eternal say: "I see the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as eternal"—that is, they refer to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—claiming that although they perish in this life, they will arise again in the future. Those who calculate [existence] as annihilated say:

"I see the five aggregates as annihilated"—that is, they refer to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—claiming that once they have perished in this life, they will never arise again. Regarding these sixty-two views in this sutra, those established independently within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), Qingliang says: "Because the nature of all aggregates is such that their nature is constantly shifting and flowing."

Names are established according to their predominant characteristics. Although "formations" (*saṃskāra*) is a general designation for one category, it here receives a specific name. Furthermore, regarding the inclusion of dharmas, based on the *Mahāyāna-śata-dharma-śāstra*, I shall briefly clarify the extent of what is included. Within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), only the eight consciousnesses as mental sovereigns (*citta-rāja*) are included.

The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) comprises only eleven types of matter. The two aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) comprise only two of the universal mental factors (*cetasika*). The [remaining] four aggregates comprise twenty-one dharmas; excluding the six unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, all others are not included therein.

The remaining seventy-three are all subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); thus it is said that [this aggregate] is "many. This sutra extensively refutes the sixty-two views within the section on the aggregate of formations because the nature of all aggregates is fluxional (*saṃsārin*), and "formation" is their general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, because the aggregate of formations subsumes many dharmas, and because all views depend upon formations as the basis from which they arise through conceptual and non-conceptual discrimination. Therefore, according to the explanation provided by Qingliang (Chengguan), those who pass through the five aggregates do so with a principle that is pervasive yet meanings that are distinct. However, when the practitioner reaches this point, [their practice becomes] lax...

Within *samatha*, one has already dismantled the three aggregates of form, feeling, and perception; one has already transcended the two realms of desire and form; and the celestial Māras have been extinguished. This may be called supreme; yet the Tathāgata repeatedly issued admonitions, speaking of falling into the ranks of externalists (*tīrthika*). One should know that the "externalists" referred to within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) are precisely these celestial externalists.

According to various treatises, regarding the two types who hold to "no cause": one descends from the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) and is reborn in this heaven; among the four types who hold to "one part is eternal," one descends from the Brahma Heaven and is reborn in this heaven.

Regarding the four types who hold to "universal permanence," they rely on the higher and middle dhyānas to give rise to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*), and through such recollection, they give rise to the four theories of permanence, the sixteen characteristics, and the eight theories each concerning both the "non-percipient" (*asaṃjñin*) and the "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñin*); all of these [originate] from the "percipient" (*saṃjñin*).

Those who are born into the four dhyānas of the formless realm, attain the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), or are even born as far as the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), and who undergo annihilation after death—whether from the desire realm or the form realm, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—they cling to those respective stages.

Regarding those who resort to the four evasive answers regarding immortality at the summit of birth and death (*saṃsāra-śikhara-catur-amṛta-vyākaraṇa*): they reckon that the Brahmā Heaven is eternally abiding and thus name it "immortal," and they reckon that by answering without confusion, one will be born in this heaven.

Regarding the five [views] of manifest *nirvāṇa*: from the enjoyment of the five sensual pleasures up to the manifest dwelling in the fourth dhyāna, they take these to be *nirvāṇa*. These are all the practices of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) of the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*). Their modes of cultivation and the stages for attaining birth therein lie between the two pillars of the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*). This mutually corroborates the text of the sūtras that minutely investigates the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*).

In his commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Qingliang [Master Chengguan] extensively clarifies the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*) across the two limits of past and future in the "Chapter on Merits" (*Guṇaparyāya-paṭala*), and separately clarifies the views of permanence, impermanence, and so forth in the "Chapter on the Ten Treasuries" (*Daśakośa-paṭala*). There are sixty-two such views.

Regarding the characteristics of the views (*dṛṣṭi*): they do not transcend the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa*). Their faults do not go beyond [the extremes of] annihilationism and eternalism. When distinguished, they are termed the "extreme view" (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) and the "false view" (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*); when subsumed, they are termed the "self-view" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

Those who have commented on this sutra have merely provided word-for-word glosses to explain the text without extensively synthesizing its meaning, nor have they cross-referenced it with various *Āgamas* and treatises in a systematic manner; thus, their interpretations fail to accord with the true meaning of the sutra. Now, I have summarized the general outline and placed it at the beginning of this volume, awaiting those who are broadly versed in the sutras and treatises to examine it in detail.
