[Hǎiyìn says: The *saṃskāra-skandha* is the subtle arising-and-ceasing among the eight consciousnesses.

This is the characteristic of cessation. Now, by investigating through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one sees that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has, from time immemorial, been continuous yet seemingly unchanging; therefore, it is called "perfectly constant" (*paricitta-nitya*). [Direct Explanation]: Previously, "perfection" (*paricitta*) was defined as horizontal pervasiveness; now, "constancy" (*nitya*) is defined as vertical thoroughness.

By mentioning both "perfect" and "constant," the explanation encompasses both the horizontal and vertical dimensions, for constancy is also pervasive. [As Explained]: Previously, one took the causeless as the cause, which is why it was said that "reckoning arises within the perfect origin. This [present] reckoning takes the impermanent to be permanent.

Therefore it is said: "Within the Perfectly Constant (yuan-chang), conceptual calculations arise. (△ [Qingliang says]: Regarding the four types of universal permanence: this refers to the view that both the self and the world are entirely eternal, merely alternating between manifestation and concealment.

Based on the higher, middle, and lower dhyānas, one gives rise to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna), and through such recollection, four theories of permanence are produced. ([│/○] Second, the explanation of the four. ([?(▽/○)] One: Permanence for twelve thousand kalpas.)
First, this person exhaustively investigates the nature of the mind and its objects;

finding no cause for these two locations, they cultivate the practice until, within twenty thousand kalpas, they come to know that all births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions circulate in a cycle, never being lost or dispersed, and thus reckon them to be permanent.

[Commentary: Within the supreme concentration (*samādhi*), one takes the two factors of mind and objects as the locus of inquiry. [Wenling says: "The extinction of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)" means that one cultivates contemplation based on these two factors of mind and objects.

As it is said: "When perception is destroyed, mental formations (*saṃskāra*) manifest; riding upon this, the mind opens up, and one investigates the inner mind and external objects to see from what original source they arise. Therefore, it is said: "In these two loci, there is no cause.

Through this, when contemplation is perfected, one knows that for twenty thousand kalpas the birth and death of sentient beings throughout the ten directions have circulated in a cycle, never being lost or scattered, like water.
It becomes ice; the ice returns to water. Although it circulates, its essence is not lost; therefore, it is called "constant" (*nitya*). (The *Zhēnjì* says:

"In the two spheres of mind and objects, although there is no cause, for twenty thousand kalpas birth and cessation have continued without interruption; thus they are reckoned as constant. (The *Wēnlíng* says: "Because one falsely conceives of the *saṃskāra-skandha* as a perfect source of birth and cessation, one [erroneously attributes permanence] to the mind, objects, the four great elements, and so forth.")
All reckon [this] as permanent. (24,000 kalpas of permanence).
Second, these people exhaust the source of the four great elements; the four natures are eternally abiding. Through cultivation, they are able to know within 40,000 kalpas.
The arising and ceasing of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions are entirely of an eternal substance; they have never been dispersed or lost, and are reckoned as permanent.

[Commentary] In this person’s contemplation, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are taken as the object of observation. (The *Haiyin* says: "The four great elements are the objective portions (*nimittabhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses. Since the eight consciousnesses have not yet been exhausted, one employs the four great elements as the object of contemplation.
When the contemplation is perfected, one is able to know that the arising and ceasing of sentient beings throughout forty thousand kalpas are entirely of an eternal substance.
[They hold that] it is eternal. Since all sentient beings take the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as their substance, and the four great elements are eternal, sentient beings are also eternal;

therefore, there is no dispersal or loss. (Gushan says: "The birth and death of sentient beings does not depart from the four great elements. Because the nature of the great elements is not lost, they calculate this to be eternal. (Wenling says:

"Sentient beings depend on the four great elements for their birth and death, yet the nature of the four is fundamentally eternally abiding. Thus, all phenomena of birth and death are, in their essence, eternal. This is calculating eternity within birth and death. (Citation: Qingliang says: "The Lokāyata heretics calculate all form, mind, and so forth...")

All phenomena take the four great atoms (*mahābhūta-paramāṇu*) as their cause and are able to produce coarse matter (*audārika-rūpa*). Although they are atoms, their substance is substantially existent; for while worldly coarse objects are impermanent, the cause—the atom—is indestructible. (As stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, Chapter 6):

"Because of not knowing dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as it truly is, one conceives that existence precedes the arising of the fruit, and that disintegration precedes the destruction of the fruit. By reason of this, they claim that coarse material fruits arise from the nature of a multitude of subtle atoms, [and that these] gradually..."

When gross objects are analyzed down to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), they remain; therefore, gross objects are impermanent, while ultimate atoms are eternal. [Commentary: They arise from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and later return to those elements. (They remain constant for eighty-four thousand kalpas.)

Third, this person exhausts the six sense faculties; within the *manas*, the appropriating consciousness, and the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna-manovijñāna*), because the fundamental source is eternally constant in nature, through cultivation they are able to know that among all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas, the cycle of rebirth continues without loss.
Originally and eternally abiding, it exhausts its limits without losing its nature; yet one clings to it as being "constant.
[Zizhong] This refers to the six sense organs, the seventh consciousness, and the mind that grasps and maintains [the body], which are the fundamental sources and locations.

Its nature is eternally non-dispersed; it is reckoned as permanent. Regarding the "six faculties" (*ṣaḍindriya*), this refers to the supporting faculties (*āśrayendriya*) to manifest the supported consciousnesses (*āśritavijñāna*).

Since it speaks of "within mind, thought, and consciousness" (*citta-manovijñāna*), one knows that this refers to the contemplation of the eight consciousnesses. [Master Kongyin said: This is the contemplative practice based on the eight consciousnesses. Therefore, through cultivation, one is able to know the continuity of sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas.

Within "mind, thought, and consciousness," these three terms collectively designate the eight consciousnesses: "arising mind" (*citta*) refers to the eighth consciousness; "associated thought" (*manas*) refers to the seventh consciousness; and "discerning consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the [first six].

The first six [consciousnesses] are the fundamental source and locus; they collectively refer to the eight consciousnesses, which are the primordial source of beginningless continuity. [Commentary]: In Sanskrit, it is called *kḷiṣṭa-manas*.

This is called the *kliṣṭa-manas* (defiled mind). As for "appropriation" (*upādāna*), it refers to the eighth consciousness. When one exhaustively investigates the nature of these eight consciousnesses, one finds that they are fundamentally eternal.

[My private commentary: The term *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) indicates that the eight consciousnesses are constant but not discerning; the six consciousnesses are discerning but not constant; the seventh consciousness is both constant and discerning. Therefore, it says, "because its nature is eternally constant," which points to the eighth consciousness.

[Wenling’s commentary: This passage generally cites all eight consciousnesses; the fundamental source within mind, thought, and consciousness is precisely the nature of consciousness. By means of this, one can know that throughout eighty thousand kalpas, sentient beings...

It ceases, yet is neither interrupted nor dispersed. Because all sentient beings are without exception possessed of the eight consciousnesses, and since these eight consciousnesses arise and cease without being lost, sentient beings are likewise so;

therefore, it is called "constant. [The Wuxing Commentary states: The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says that the ālayavijñāna cannot be known by anyone other than Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages, including the followers of the two vehicles, non-Buddhists, and practitioners.

Since the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) has not yet been exhausted, how could one calculate this as permanent? One should know that the terms "mind," "thought," and "consciousness" collectively refer to the eight consciousnesses.

"The original source" specifically refers to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). This is because, through the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, one suddenly exhausts the eight consciousnesses and perfectly subdues the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*). Yet, at the point where the *vijñapti-skandha* (the aggregate of perception) is exhausted, one fails to discern the subtle arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, mistakenly taking it to be permanent.

This does not mean that within this samādhi one has already seen the eighth consciousness. Master Ke said: "If one had realized the eighth consciousness, how could such a divergent conception arise? These words are excellent. [Supplement: The three—mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—correspond vertically to the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses respectively.

Wherever there is arising and ceasing within these three, it is all the source of the *saṃskāra-skandha* for sentient beings. Although one may pass through the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses], one is merely observing the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha*; one does not yet know the source within the consciousnesses. This refers to those practitioners of the Perfect Teaching who have lost their way.]

If one thoroughly understands the eight consciousnesses, what room is there for divergent views? (△ [Kongyin] says: Since the eight consciousnesses are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), arising and ceasing moment by moment, they all depend on the continuity of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) to flow on.

From eighty thousand kalpas past, this continuity has not been lost. Because they do not understand this, they falsely reckon them to be permanent. That which discriminates objects is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); that which continues without being lost is due to "formations" (*saṃskāra*). Both formations and consciousness are objects of delusion; therefore, based upon them, false reckonings arise. Wuxing cites the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which states that the eight consciousnesses are the realm of Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*).

This proves that those who cannot contemplate the consciousnesses are not yet on the stages. On the stages, one transforms and extinguishes the outflows (*āsrava*) and clearly perceives their source. Although one may now contemplate the consciousnesses, to rely on them and give rise to false reckonings is precisely what constitutes delusion; it should not be so.)

This is to apply that case to the present one. According to the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation), it uniquely adopts the *Wǔxīng Tōngshì*’s (General Explanation of the Wu-xing) theory that the eight consciousnesses are specifically identified with the *xiàngyīn* (formative aggregate). Zhùān Kōngyìn has both examined and distinguished these views; here, I follow the two masters in resolving these difficulties and still adhere to the ancient interpretation.
([?(▽/○)] The fourth is non-arising, non-ceasing permanence).
Fourth, since this person has exhausted the source of ideation, the principle of their being no longer possesses the flowing, ceasing, moving, or turning of the ideating mind of arising and ceasing.

Now it has been eternally extinguished. Within the principle, it is naturally established as neither arising nor ceasing. Because of what is measured by the mind, one reckons it to be permanent. [Commentary:

The "principle of nature" is precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because one perceives that ideation (*saṃjñā*) has ceased—[Wenling says: "The source of ideation" refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*);

"the principle of nature" refers to the aggregate of formations]—and since ideation is capable of movement, and that movement has now subsided, when movement is absent, the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing naturally manifests before one. (This is falsely called...)

The cycle of transmigration and the process of arising and ceasing both belong to the realms of perception and mind. Now that these have been eternally extinguished, the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing naturally belongs to the formations (*saṃskāra*). One does not realize that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is the very source of arising and ceasing; this [state] remains within the realm of arising and ceasing.

One calculates that it is neither arising nor ceasing, and thus clings to it as permanent. (Wuxing says: Previously, one pointed to the fundamental source as permanent; this refers to calculating non-arising and non-ceasing within the midst of arising and ceasing—like seeing a thin stream and calling it still water.

Now, one takes the principle within [the mind] as permanent; this refers to calculating non-arising and non-ceasing within eternal cessation—like seeing empty space and calling it eternally abiding. This, too, is merely a false recognition of the *saṃskāra-skandha* as the ultimate principle. (Supplement says: The previous two cases involved calculating the continuity of arising and ceasing across three locations as permanence.

This case involves calculating the place where the conceptual mind (*saṃjñā-citta*) ceases; when the subtle characteristics of the mind cease, one clings to this as non-arising and non-ceasing. When the conceptual mind momentarily subsides, the root-source of the principle-nature appears; one points to this *saṃskāra*...)

The subtle characteristics of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) constitute its fundamental nature. As for the phrase "furthermore, there is no flowing or ceasing," it is because the arising and ceasing are so subtle that the characteristics of movement and stillness are not perceived. Regarding the phrase "naturally within this principle," this refers to the arising and ceasing of these subtle characteristics as being the principle;

thus, there is a characteristic of spontaneity. [△ *Haixin* says: When the practitioner is in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the coarse and floating thoughts of the *skandha* of form have already ceased. However, the subtle *skandha* of formations continues in a single stream without interruption. One falsely claims that arising and ceasing have been extinguished, yet remains unaware of the currently flowing seeds.]

[They remain] within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The root-source of arising and ceasing is precisely here. (The third knot). Based on this, they reckon [existence] as permanent;
they lose correct and universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of external paths (*tīrthika*), becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the second type of external path: those who establish the doctrine of pervasive permanence.
[Commentary] "Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (samyak-saṃbuddha) is the very nature of bodhi. Because of erroneous and inverted discrimination, one loses the "perfect" (samyak).

Because it is restricted only to within two, four, or eighty thousand kalpas and cannot be known beyond that, one loses the "complete" (saṃbuddha). Since both perfect knowledge and complete knowledge have perished, one becomes an outsider with heterodox doctrines.

Furthermore, within samādhi, O sons of good family, when one’s mind is firm, concentrated, and upright, Māra cannot find an opportunity; one thoroughly investigates the root of all living beings.
Observing that profound stillness, one constantly agitates the source of movement; among oneself and others, one gives rise to conceptual calculations.
Such a person falls into the four inverted views, the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent.

[Commentary: Some maintain that the self (*ātman*) produces others, such that the self is eternal while others are impermanent; or they maintain that the self is produced from others, such that others are eternal while the self is impermanent.

In all these cases, they calculate one part as impermanent and one part as eternal (the *Erleng* [Erudition on the Two Truths] states: "The 'self' refers to one's own person, while 'others' refers to sentient beings and the environment;

within the state of equality, one gives rise to the false conceptualizations of self and other"). (As the *Rushuo* [Discourse on Suchness] says: "Among the non-Buddhists with the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) in Yoga, some calculate everything as eternal, while some calculate one part as eternal. This corresponds to the four theories of universal permanence.")

Both schools maintain that the source of motion is true and eternal. The former calculates all things to be eternal; the latter calculates only a portion to be eternal. (This constitutes the second section, which provides two interpretations. The first interpretation is that the self is eternal while others are impermanent.)
First, this person contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the worlds of the ten directions, taking its profound stillness to be the ultimate divine self (*ātman*).
From this, they calculate: "I pervade the ten directions, remaining unmoving and solid; all sentient beings exist within my heart."
"Born of itself and dying of itself, my own mind-nature is therefore called 'constant. That which undergoes birth and extinction is truly of an impermanent nature.

[Commentary] This person, practicing meditative concentration, has not yet realized the Truth. Within his tainted contemplation, he contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the ten directions;
he perceives this through conceptualization and does not know that it is the false consciousness of ignorance manifesting shadows that appear to be real. He clings to this as being real.
The mind pervades the worlds of the ten directions and takes this as its true self. Because it is sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it remains still and luminous.
One perceives all sentient beings within one's own mind being born and dying of their own accord; this is impermanence. That which is unmoving—myself—is permanence. [Wuxing says:

"Below 'observing the subtle' (觀妙), he again raises the topic of contemplative practice (*guanxing*). Below 'serenely clear' (湛然), he correctly clarifies the arising of conceptualization. This is also due to not understanding the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (行陰), falsely claiming that the nature of the mind at this stage is serenely still.]

Nevertheless, they conceive of a "spiritual self" (*ātman*). Non-Buddhists call it the "Lord-Calculation" (*īśvara-gaṇaka*), asserting that all phenomena are "mine" and that this spiritual entity is their master. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that the non-Buddhist spiritual self is none other than the six consciousnesses;

it arises from conceptualization within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and is likewise the discriminative consciousness of objects. It is a false recognition that takes the aggregate of formations to be an immovable self. [Haoyin says: When contemplative wisdom investigates thoroughly and delusive thoughts have been eliminated, the eight consciousnesses become brilliant and pervasive throughout the ten directions.

Failing to recognize that this is the brilliance of the essence of consciousness, one clings to it as a spiritual self. This refers solely to contemplating the self. [Zongjing says: The non-Buddhists do not understand that all phenomena are formed through the combination of causes and conditions into the various aggregates (*skandhas*). Whatever they do is entirely the aggregate of consciousness; thus, they [erroneously] grasp at it.

To grasp at the aggregates as having a real self that exercises sovereign control over experience is called the "Lord" (Īśvara). To assert the existence of a divine nature within a continuum that appears to be permanent and unitary is the doctrine of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

If one understands that [the self] is produced by internal and external causes and conditions, is a transformation of consciousness-only, and appears as an object, then it is simply the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) which maintains itself without interruption and appears to have a continuity; this is the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma. (The two kalpas: the kalpa of destruction and the kalpa of non-destruction).
Second, this person does not contemplate their own mind, but surveys throughout the ten directions all the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Where they see places where kalpas are destroyed, they call that the nature of ultimate impermanence; where they see places where kalpas are not destroyed, they call that ultimate permanence.

[Commentary]: While in meditative absorption, this person employs supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to perceive the worlds of the ten directions. (The Sub-commentary states: "This is a semblance of supernormal power. Within that state, seeing a world that has not yet been destroyed, they grasp it as impermanent;
seeing a place where destruction has already occurred, they likewise grasp it as having the nature of impermanence.

Although this involves contemplating the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), it necessarily entails the primary world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*). (The *Xunwen* commentary states: "The 'sands of the Ganges' of lands refers merely to the various lands within a single great trichiliocosm. This means that from the third dhyāna downward, all are ultimately destroyed by the three calamities; this is termed 'impermanence'...")

The "constant lineage" (nitya-gotra) refers to those above the fourth dhyāna, which cannot be destroyed by calamities; it is the ultimate dhyāna. [Youxi says: Based on the stages one has personally traversed, ascending to the third and fourth *dhyānas*, one contemplates the points where the three calamities can and cannot destroy, calculating between the permanent and the impermanent.

"Permanent" refers to the place of *nirvāṇa* realized within oneself; "impermanent" refers to the place of birth and death for others. (△ [Tongzhou says: This is not contemplating the mind; rather, it is not contemplating the eternally abiding true mind. (△ [Haoyin says:

This person, within meditative concentration, does not rely on contemplation of the mind, but relies solely on contemplation of the land. This is a single contemplation of the other. (△ [The third: "The self is like a mote of dust turning"].)
Third, this person separately contemplates their own mind as being subtle, refined, and extremely dense, like a minute particle that circulates throughout the ten directions.
Its nature is immutable, yet it can cause this body to arise and perish in each instant. This indestructible nature is called the permanence of the self-nature (*ātman*).
All birth and death flow forth from this "self," which is termed the nature of impermanence.

[Commentary: "The mind of 'I' is like a mote of dust" means that because the nature of the mind is subtle and secret, it is difficult to perceive; thus it is likened to a mote of dust, not because it is small.
One clings to this subtle and minute nature of the mind and takes it to be the "self. [Jiaoguang says: The non-Buddhists reckon three types of self-characteristics.]

First, the subtle self; second, the expansive self; third, the self of both small and large [Combined Explanation: The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the self-clinging of the seven consciousnesses. Thus it is called "my mind. Because it is a hidden delusion, it is called "subtle. "Self" (*ātman*) means sovereignty and mastery.

Therefore, it is able to undergo transmigration, yet its birth remains unchanging. [Haiyin says: In meditative concentration, one observes the subtle and secret [breath] as it flows through the ten directions. Because the aggregate of formations is so subtle, one does not perceive its movement.
One calculates that there is no alteration, and thus it is termed "self. It is, however, able to cause this coarse aggregate of body and mind—

There is arising and there is ceasing. Because these coarse aggregates all flow forth from my own body, that which flows forth is called impermanent, while that which is able to flow forth is called the permanent nature.
(Wuxing says: Since the self is subtle, its arising and ceasing are likewise so; thus it is said, "arising and ceasing simultaneously.

Yet this arising and ceasing proceeds from the subtle to the coarse in uninterrupted succession; hence it is said, "all deaths and births, etc. (Wujin says: To observe the mind separately is to seek the mind with the mind. [Wenling says: ...])

Because it cannot be [realized] immediately within this very body and mind, it is said that one must "observe separately. [Direct Explanation: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to a self (*ātman*) whose essence is eternal and extremely subtle, like a single atom (*paramāṇu*), which secretly moves within the body to perform various activities.

The present text is precisely the same as that attachment; "flowing and transforming without change" means its nature of secretly moving and performing activities is eternally constant. "The ten directions" refers to the six realms (*ṣaḍgati*); it means that my mind flows through the six realms, yet its nature has never changed.

Therefore, it is said that it can cause this body to be born and perish in an instant, and so forth. [Qingliang says: Regarding "the body is different and the spirit is different," some say: the spirit is subtle and cannot be apprehended by the five senses, nor is it seen by ordinary persons. Only by purifying the mind and attaining meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) [can it be perceived].

Only a person can thus perceive it; therefore, the body and the spirit (ātman) are distinct. [The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: One who attains dhyāna possesses the power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānabala*) and can see events of eighty thousand kalpas. However, seeing only the beginning of the body—the intermediate state consciousness (*antarābhava-vijñāna*)—one reflects to oneself:

"This consciousness cannot be without cause or condition. It is merely through recollection, thought, and discrimination that there exists a principle called *Prakṛti* (World-Nature). It is not known by the five sensory faculties because it is extremely subtle. From within *Prakṛti*, the first awakening (*buddhi*) arises;

this awakening is the intermediate state consciousness (the eighth consciousness). From awakening, the self (*ahaṃkāra*) arises; from the self, the five kinds of subtle atoms (*tanmātra*) arise. From the subtle atom of sound, the great element of space (*ākāśa*) arises, and so on, until from space the ear-faculty and the others arise. In this manner, they gradually proceed from the subtle to the coarse. As for *Prakṛti*:

From *prakṛti* (the primal nature) down to the gross, and from the gross back to the subtle, it returns to *prakṛti*. It is like a lump of clay which inherently contains the nature of jars, pots, and so forth; by using the clay to make a jar, or breaking the jar to make a pot, such transformations occur without any loss whatsoever.

When transformed into the gross, *prakṛti* remains an eternal dharma that comes from nowhere. Thus the Sāṃkhya school extensively explains *prakṛti*. I [the author] say that this doctrine is identical to the first [view of] the *puruṣa* (spiritual self); it uses the contemplation of the wondrously luminous mind to separately observe the subtle.

In their treatises there is a dharma called *prakṛti*, which is not known by the five sense organs because it is extremely subtle—just as the "subtle essence" (*sūkṣma*) mentioned in the sutras is like a fine mote of dust. It is said that from *prakṛti* arises *buddhi* (intellect), and so on, down to the subtle.

Regarding "the coarsest": this refers to the subtle dust-like nature of the mind flowing through the ten directions. Yet these coarse aggregates of body and mind arise and perish in an instant; thus, it proceeds from the subtle to the coarse.

Furthermore, when it is said that "it transforms from the coarse back to the subtle, returning to the world-nature (*loka-dhātu-prakṛti*), and that such transformations lose nothing," this refers to the indestructible nature within this very process, which is called the permanence of the self-nature (*ātman*). One should know that these three [categories] all conceive of a spiritual self (*puruṣa*) and all contemplate the ten directions;

they differ only in that they employ ultimate kalpas, lands, and subtle dusts as their objects of contemplation for the sake of discrimination. (The four modes of action are permanent, while the remainder are impermanent.)

Fourth, this person knows that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) has been exhausted, yet they see the flow of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha). Because the aggregate of formations flows constantly, they reckon it to be of a permanent nature;
whereas form, sensation, perception, and so forth, having now ceased and been exhausted, they designate as impermanent.

[Commentary: Because the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is revealed as being seen to undergo constant flux, one clings to it as permanent. Within the contemplation of the other aggregates such as *saṃjñā* (perception), these formations are temporarily suppressed and do not arise;

therefore, one clings to them as impermanent. [Gushan says: "One who knows the exhaustion of the *saṃjñā-skandha* attains mastery and enters the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya*). If the beginner loses this mastery, they will give rise to views based on this;

that is, they treat what is merely suppressed as being eternally severed, rather than understanding it as the exhaustion of all [defilements]. The same applies to what precedes and follows. For this reason, this body is partially impermanent and partially permanent. [Wuxing...]

[He] said: "Previously, when I observed my own mind as it transmigrates through the ten directions, its nature was found to be without change or alteration. I did not realize that this was the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), whose essence is in constant flux. Although I now see this flow, I have still not perceived the characteristics of the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness). Therefore, I am contrasting it with form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth."

"They are neither different nor not different; this is the first view. Second, when questioned regarding the existence or non-existence of other worlds, he likewise gives this same answer.

As for calculating its modes of activity: it exists between the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), within the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*). When body and mind both cease—that is, when perceptions and thoughts are exhausted—dreams and delusions are extinguished, like a clear sky, no longer possessing the modes of activity that are coarse, heavy shadows of external objects. Within the four formless heavens, the nature of consciousness is unmoving; through the exhaustion of cessation, it is as if existing yet not existing, as if ending yet not ending. This is the moment the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is exhausted;

the generative impulse of the common lot is suspended, responses and stimuli are severed, and various classes of beings do not summon one another, revealing the modes of activity of the profound and secret. Because one does not understand that the delusions of ignorance and views arise attached to the body, the net of views is dense and thick, and one clings to them as...

The most excellent [path] abandons Māra and enters the external [realms]; the coarse and the subtle are worlds apart. The rungs of the ladder are solitary and perilous; ascent and descent are steep and treacherous. Thus, the Tathāgata, while within the realm of the gods (*deva-gati*), provides early warning and offers preventative counsel. Within the four *dhyānas*, there are two diverging paths: one leads directly to the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*), and the other leads indirectly to the Non-perception (*Āsaṃjñika*).

It is better to dwell among the third grade of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) than to go to the fourth grade of the non-Buddhist heavens. Within the Peak of Form (*Rūpāvacara-agra*), there are again two diverging paths: one goes straight out from the realm of dust (*rajas*), and the other winds through the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

It is better to be a dull-witted Arhat who does not return (*anāgāmin*) than to be a non-Buddhist of the Non-perception heaven who dwells in emptiness. The lifespan in the non-Buddhist heavens reaches a maximum of eighty thousand *kalpas* and no more; the station of the non-Buddhist heavens reaches a maximum of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and no further.

They dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; yet, because they seek transcendence with such profound intensity, their ascetic practices performed over many kalpas are never in vain. Thus, by leaving the five realms of existence, they obtain the retribution of the heavens; and by leaving the realm of desire and the realm of form, they obtain the retribution of the formless realm.

However, because they encounter false teachers and study in a manner contrary to the principles of the Truths, their deluded minds give rise to knowledge that takes arising and ceasing as its cause. Consequently, they obtain the retribution of non-perception and the retribution of not seeing the Buddha or hearing the Dharma. Once fallen into these false causes, they sink forever into birth and death.

Having labored through vast eons, they still act as demonic influences. Thus, the Tathāgata distinguished between the two demons of conduct and consciousness, establishing these exhortations. One states that one shall not encounter bypaths; the other states that one shall not encounter divergent paths.

This is precisely to certify the two heavens of the formless realm, delineate the boundaries between humans and devas, establish embankments against demons and externalists, extensively protect those who advance in cultivation, and powerfully support those drowning in the mire. Ānanda, when that son of good family practices samādhi and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is exhausted, the natures of all worlds—the subtle, pure, and restless movements of the commonality of living beings—suddenly shatter.
The deep, fine threads of connection and the profound channels through which *pudgalas* repay their karma are severed;
the resonance between cause and effect is suspended.
[Commentary] The first three phrases identify the person. From "The nature of all worlds" (*zhū shìjiān xìng*) onwards, it correctly elucidates the exhaustion of formations (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding "the nature of the world": the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is precisely the essential nature of the world. (〔Haiyin says: This means that the aggregate of formations is the substance of worldly birth-and-death.〕 (△〔Wuxing says: "The nature of all worlds" refers to the twelve classes of beings.)

This is the essential nature of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). There are three meanings of "the world" (*loka*): first, it possesses arising and ceasing; second, its nature is outflowing (*sāsrava*); third, it is subject to destruction.

Having fallen into the world, [all things] share the same nature as the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations. It is "profound" (*you*) because it is hidden; it is "pure" (*qing*) because it is free from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).

"Agitation" (*rao*) refers to movement; it is the generative impulse of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*). The former [the aggregate of formations] is the fundamental basis; the present [this term] is the pivotal essence.

[The Wuxing Commentary states: "The mechanism of birth within the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity). That is, the mechanism of arising and ceasing shares its limits with those of all categories. [The Haiyin Commentary states: "Because the birth and death of sentient beings all depend upon the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), it is called the 'mechanism of birth within homogeneity.

It suddenly breaks apart; hence it is said, "in an instant, it collapses and splits. Regarding "sinking and becoming subtle" and below, this is a re-explanation of the meaning of "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*).

(The *saṃskāra-skandha* is profound, deep, and subtle; it nets and ensnares all realms of existence, forming knots that cannot be untied. Now, by means of the power of meditative concentration, one investigates thoroughly and suddenly shatters it. The large rope on a net is called the "main cord" (*jālaka*). The place where the collar of a garment is tied...
It is said: "Toggles. These all serve as metaphors for their essential points. The twelve classes of sentient beings are like a net or a garment;

the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) runs through them, its subtle knots and essentials being like the main ropes or toggles. [The Wuxing commentary states: "Formations are the nature of karma; they can sustain the various aggregates, just as a net or a garment has main ropes and toggles.
A *pudgala* is called a "one who repeatedly takes on existence," which is a general designation for the twelve classes. The *saṃskāra-skandha* is able to sustain these classes.
Because it arises, it is called the "submerged, fine net-knot. The "net-knot" is the cause of karma; "kāra" is the retribution of karma.

When the cause of karma perishes, what can lead forth the fruit? When the retributive fruit ceases, who can provide the recompense? Since both cause and fruit have vanished, response and stimulus are cut off.

"Deep channels" also metaphorically represent the profound obscurity of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). [The Supplement states: "Channels" means a curtain. A curtain and its frame form a single entity. Karma is able to...]
He draws forth birth (like a curtain that has not yet been severed).
Regarding the heaven of Nirvana, he is about to attain great awakening, like the crowing of a rooster at dawn; looking toward the east, there is already a brilliant color.
[Commentary]: The Nirvana of the Three Virtues is called the "Ultimate Heaven. Attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) is termed "Great Enlightenment.
Because this enlightenment is imminent, it is called "imminent" (*jiang*). "Imminent" means "about to" or "desiring. It is like the "cock's subsequent crowing":

when the cock crows for the second time, the dawn is about to break. The persistence of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is like the middle of the night; their total exhaustion is like the great light of day.

The two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*) have been destroyed, like the first crowing of a rooster when the sky has not yet changed at all. [Gushan says: "The preceding aggregates of sensation and perception have ended, yet realization is still remote;
it is like the first crow of a rooster when the color of the sky is still dim. Now, perception (*saṃjñā*) is also eliminated, leaving only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna*);

clear awakening is imminent, like the rooster's later crow when the sky possesses a distinct hue. [Wenling says: "The nature-heaven of *nirvāṇa* is covered by the five aggregates and is as dark as a long night. When the first three aggregates are exhausted, it is like the first crow of a rooster; though it is a sign of dawn,"]

It is like being submerged in the two *skandhas* where essence and form (*rūpa*) have not yet been distinguished. When this *saṃskāra-skandha* is exhausted, it is like the crowing of a rooster at dawn; with only one remaining *skandha*, one is about to awaken to the Great Illumination.
If explained in terms of stages, this corresponds to the second stage of gradual progression. That text says:

"When the prohibitive precepts are perfected, then within the world there will forever be no karma of mutual procreation or mutual killing; theft and robbery will not occur, and there will be no mutual burdening of debts. Furthermore, within the world..."

"Repaying past debts" refers precisely to the profound mechanism of requiting karma found in the present text. While the response and resonance may seem remote and severed, that previous passage further states:

"This person of pure conduct cultivates *samādhi*; without needing the divine eye, their physical body naturally perceives the worlds of the ten directions," which corresponds to what this current text says:
"Looking toward the east, he already sees a refined radiance. This is it.

Thus, one correctly attains the stage of semblance (*sādṛśa-bhūmi*). This refers to the simultaneous manifestation of the semblance [of the truths]. (The *Bùyì* supplement states: "This refers to when the preceding [delusions of] the five aggregates are broken, one immediately enters the stage of semblance and is about to ascend to the stage of true reality (*bhūta-artha*).

It is like the final crowing of a rooster at the break of dawn in the heaven of Middle-Way Nirvāṇa; it is the subtle color of the eastern sky just as it is about to brighten—the semblance of the Three Truths. (△ The *Wǔxīng* commentary states: "There is a sequence in the suppression of the five aggregates, but there is no before or after in their severance.

Here, taking the imminent breaking of specific delusions as 'later' and the initial breaking of general delusions as 'first,' the sudden and gradual aspects of severance and suppression are distinguished as explained below. (○ The *Shìwén* states: "Like the final crowing of a rooster. The *Qiándào* edition reads "like the rooster awaiting its crow," while the *Shàoxīng* edition reads "like the rooster awaiting.")
(Chant). ([│/○] The manifestation of the second aggregate, consciousness):
The six sense organs are empty and still; they no longer run wild. Internally and internally, there is profound clarity; one enters that which is nowhere to enter.
[Commentary]: Because it is encompassed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are no latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Although the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) remain, consciousness does not scatter; therefore, it is called "empty and still" (*kū-śānta*), meaning there is no further wandering or flight. [Fǎróng’s Studio says: Since the aggregate of formations has been extinguished, consciousness has nothing to move upon; thus, the six faculties are empty and still, and they no longer wander to grasp the six objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*).

The reason for referring specifically to the six faculties is that they are what the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) clings to and sustains, and they are what the aggregate of formations opens and closes. It focuses exclusively on the internal realm, and the concentrated mind illuminates within; therefore, it is called "internal."

Internally, there is profound clarity. (Since the six faculties are empty and still, then within the eyes, within the ears, and so on up to within the body and within the mind, there is nothing that is not profoundly clear within and within. Thus, these six sense bases are merely empty names.)
"Then one enters, yet there is nowhere to enter. Furthermore, "entering within the inner" refers to a profound, deep, and quiescent illumination.

Reaching the ultimate limit of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate), where nothing further can be seen, is called "entering where there is nowhere to enter. [Wuxing says: Because the *vijñāna-skandha* is revealed, it is called "limpid clarity. The text below states:

"Furthermore, that which is your brilliant clarity, limpid and unmoving... (△ [Haoyin says: Illuminating the essence of consciousness within, there is only a single limpid clarity. Entering the limpid, one merges with the limpid; there is nothing further to enter. (○ [Shiwen: "Limpid clarity within the inner. Wuxing and Wenling both read this as "inner and outer. Yunqi says: Changshui’s commentary states...)
It is profoundly deep indeed. Only when the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) is exhausted can one say that one is "internally and externally clear and penetrating.

One deeply penetrates the ten directions and the twelve classes of beings to discern the fundamental source from which their lives originate. By contemplating the source through the root of grasping, one no longer summons forth any of these various classes of beings.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one has already attained their commonality; the refined essence does not sink, and what was hidden and secret is revealed.
This is called the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha*. [Commentary:

The fundamental source of receiving life is precisely the *vijñāna-skandha*. (The *Erlengqie jing* states: "The fundamental source of receiving life refers to the various threads of life, pointing to the eighth consciousness. Now...

Contemplate the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Since it is the fundamental source from which the seeds of all categories arise, if one does not give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*) and does not perform various karmas, then by means of this sustained holding, one prevents the arising of fruits and lacks the conditions for rebirth;

thus it is said that "none of the categories can summon [rebirth]. (When the sense organs and their objects have dissolved, the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) finally reveals itself. Having contemplated the fundamental source of the life-force and further maintained the root of rebirth, one can no longer be pulled among the twelve categories to summon rebirth. (△ [Wuxing says]: Consciousness, breath, and warmth—these three.)

The combination [of conditions] forms life. At the moment of receiving birth, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is primary. Furthermore, this fundamental source is the root of the two attachments to self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*). Although what is seen within current contemplation has not yet been completely dissolved, there are currently no karmic activities to attract and draw forth retributive fruits;

therefore, it is said that "the various classes do not summon one another. [Commentary by Wēnlíng]: Because activity ceases and consciousness manifests, one penetrates deeply. Because there is no pivot-hole, it can be contemplated. Because there is no shifting flow, it can be grasped. Because there is no mechanism for birth, there is no summoning. [Wáng Shùndǐng says]:

"Summoning" refers to the generative mechanism of the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*). When one moves, all move together—this is what is meant by "summoning the multitude. If there were summoning, the various classes would entangle one another and the world would fall into chaos. Without summoning, the resonance and response are suspended and severed; thus, throughout the world, there is only the single nature of consciousness.

Since one has already realized that this consciousness is the fundamental source of all living beings, throughout the ten directions, both the provisional and the ultimate are transformations of consciousness;
they share the same single substance of consciousness. This is what is meant by "the three realms are mind-only" and "all phenomena are consciousness-only.

Although one previously believed this through the teachings, now, through contemplation, it is clearly seen. [The *Haiyin* says: Body, mind, and the world are manifested as transformations of consciousness; now, through contemplation, they return to the nature of consciousness, hence it is said that "one has attained their sameness. Refinement.
"Form does not sink" means that the observed object appears. Because of the power of contemplation, the objective realm is clear and bright;

hence it is said "it does not sink. "Revealing the profound and secret" is like a general manifestation. [The Supplement states: "The refined form does not sink" refers to limpid clarity. "The profound and secret appear" means there is nothing concealed.

These two phrases describe the characteristics of the sphere of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*). Since the preceding aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations have already been subdued, and one now contemplates the consciousness-mind as luminous and limpid, the refined form does not sink and the profound and secret appear. One has not yet reached this stage.

The various faculties are dull and obscured, unable to see far; therefore, it is called "mysterious and secret. (Among consciousness, mind, and the aggregates of sensation, perception, and formations, consciousness is the most mysterious and secret.

It is like a lord staying within his chambers while his servants reside outside; thus, the essence of the consciousness-aggregate receives the name "mysterious and secret. Now, by the power of contemplation, the six sense-faculties are purified, not through the divine eye.

Because one penetrates and perceives all realms and so forth, it is said that they "manifest" (*faxian*). (The *Haoyin* [Sea-Seal] commentary states: "The substance of consciousness is profound and secret; now, clarifying the object of entry into contemplation, it is therefore said to 'manifest'. [Tongzhou says:

"Under 'refined color' (*jingse*), this restates that when gazing toward the east, there is already a refined color, meaning the sky is about to dawn. One sees a subtle and refined color that does not sink away, yet again gives rise to a hazy halo, after which there is great brightness.

Consciousness is hidden within the manifold obscurities, hence it is called 'profound and secret. This is named the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha*. (△ [Tongzhou says: ... (This second section clarifies the characteristic of exhaustion.)
If, within the collective summons, one has already attained identity with the center, the six gates are dissolved and ground away; opening and closing are perfected.

Seeing and hearing penetrate their neighbors, and the mutual functions become pure. The ten directions of the world, as well as body and mind, are like vaidūrya, transparent and clear both inside and out.
This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness. Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life.
Observing its origin, they find it to be based upon the formless and the void—the inverted deluded thoughts that constitute its root.
[Commentary] The first two phrases refer to being within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

If, within this state, one uses the power of meditative concentration and wisdom to polish away the obstructions of the sense faculties, causing them to open and merge into a single entity, then seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing will function interchangeably for one another.
This is what is meant by "clarity does not follow the roots," but rather clarity is manifested by relying upon the faculties. Therefore, it is said that their mutual functioning is pure. (Wuxing)

[It is said: "Though the various summonings differ, the substance of consciousness is the same. If, within this sameness, one grinds away the delusions of views and craving, then one can merge into a single body that unfolds as the six functions. These six functions are not separated; they all interpenetrate one another. This is the 'purity of the six sense-faculties' elucidated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. (△ [Direct Explanation says:

"Various summonings" means that while there is no summoning of individual classes, all classes respond; hence it is called "various summonings. "Interpenetrate" refers to mutual functioning. When this consciousness is fully realized, it is the third stage of gradual progression:
the realization of the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena). As the text states: "Thus pure..."
One who upholds the prohibitive precepts has no mind of greedy lust; thus, they do not flow excessively outward toward the six sense objects.

Because they do not flow outward, they revolve back to their original source. When the objects are no longer engaged, the faculties have nothing with which to pair. The flow returns and becomes entirely unified, so that the six functions cease to operate.
Since it is said that the six functions do not operate, this is precisely the wearing away of the six gates. Since it is said that the flow returns and becomes entirely unified...
First, this refers to the accomplishment through opening and closing, wherein the mutual functions are pure. That [previous] explanation was based on the precepts, and thus differs from this.

The world, body, and mind all manifest as mere consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*). Now that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, one perceives only the essence of awareness (*bodhi-tattva*).
This essence of awareness is luminous and wondrous, like pure lapis lazuli, entirely without obstruction; this is called "internal and external clarity. As the preceding text states: "The ten..."
The surrounding lands become brilliantly pure, like lapis lazuli with a precious moon suspended within. Body and mind are blissful;
wondrous, perfect, and impartial, they attain great peace and stability. Within this state, the secret, perfect, wondrous, and pure [realms] of all Tathāgatas are all manifested.

This person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). One who knows that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has been exhausted is one who has awakened according to their capacity.
Mañjuśrī also said: "In one place, rest and recovery are achieved; the six functions all cease to operate.
Dust and defilements vanish upon a thought, achieving perfect, bright, pure, and wondrousness. This refers to the essence of life, which is the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).

Because life, warmth, and consciousness function simultaneously, once consciousness has departed, life and warmth perish accordingly; thus, one transcends the turbidity of life. [Wujin said: "Life" refers to the subtle aspect of the *vijñāna-skandha*.]

It is severed, just like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Now that it is completely destroyed, the six gates open and close; body and mind are clear and penetrating, and thus one transcends the turbidity of life. This is not the teaching that "life and warmth perish together" [Direct Explanation says: Consciousness, warmth, and breath—these three rely on one another as the support for life;

if one is lacking, death occurs; hence it is called the turbidity of life. Changshui’s interpretation follows ancient exegesis, but Wujin rejects it; to take the life-faculty as a metaphor for the consciousness-aggregate is coarse and lacks scriptural basis].
As for "formless and void," this is the appearance of reflected images when the initial awakening-clarity first arises. Grasping this deluded thought, it is a void reflection.

"Xiang" (罔象). This is taken as the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna*), which consists of the two aspects of karma and transformation. (〔孤山云〕 "Wangxiang" is also modeled after "xiang. (△〔溫陵云〕 Consciousness is the reflected light of deluded awakening; it originally has no self-substance.

It arises from inversion, and is therefore called "wangxiang," "xuwu," and "inverted delusive thought. (△〔海印云〕 "Wangxiang xuwu" is the reflected light of the Dharma-body, referring to the ignorance of the initial phase of arising, which is taken as the substance of consciousness.

(○〔釋文〕〔翻譯云〕 "Liu-li" (琉璃). In full, it is *vaiḍūrya*. This means "blue-colored jewel. It is also translated as "not far away. In the Western Regions there is a mountain not far from the domain of Vārāṇasī.)
The mountain produces this jewel, and it is named after it. Master Ying (Yìng) says that some add the character *ve* (吠), or some add the character *bi* (毗), or it is called *Vaidūrya*;

it is named after the mountain. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Abiding in the *dānapāramitā*, or manifesting worlds like *vaidūrya*. (2. Correctly clarifying the manifestation of the objective realm, in ten parts. (1. Grasping at causes and what is caused, in two parts. (A. Regarding what is understood.)
Ānanda, you should know that this good man has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations and returned to the source within consciousness;
he has already extinguished arising and ceasing, yet regarding quiescent extinction, his subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected.

[Commentary: Although the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted and the cycle of arising and ceasing has already ceased, consciousness has returned to its source but has not yet attained quiescent extinction;

therefore, it is said that "the subtle essence is not yet perfect. (Wenling says: Consciousness flows from formations; thus, when formations are empty, one returns to the source. Since the aggregate of consciousness is now empty, arising and ceasing have already ceased. Yet, because one still relies upon the source of consciousness, quiescent extinction is not yet perfect.
This is because consciousness has not yet been shattered, as one is currently in the midst of subtle arising and ceasing. "Subtle essence" refers to the truly subtle, wondrous, and luminous nature.

[Wu Xing says: "The state where the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) is limpid and unmoving is precisely the return to the source. This is designated as such in contrast to the previously extinguished formation-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*). However, with respect to its own essence, it has not yet realized quiescent extinction. [Supplement says: "Regarding 'returning to the source within consciousness': the substance of the mind is but one;

fundamentally, there is no distinction between the sovereign [mind] and its mental factors (*caitta*). Because of grasping at objects, sensation (*vedanā*) and the other factors arise latently. Now, through the power of contemplation, sensation and the rest are momentarily suppressed, and one turns back to see the source of the mind. This refers directly to the sovereign mind itself as the source. [This begins the first of the ten demons below.]

It further states: "Regarding 'that to which one returns,' this refers to returning to the fundamental source (the *pratyāgama*). Departing from those [perceptions] such as suffering and so forth, one returns to the essence of the mind (*cittatattva*) to serve as the basis for observation; it is from this that conceptual calculations arise. [Commentary by Gushan: The preceding and subsequent arousal of objects both occur within the mind of contemplative practice (*bhāvanā-citta*).

Here, in order to reveal the basis upon which these objects depend, they are explained through their mutual relationship by way of the sequence of the exhaustion of the aggregates (*skandha-kṣaya*). One should know that even if the aggregates are exhausted and [objects] are aroused, it only serves to further increase correct understanding.

If these [objects] are activated while within the mind of contemplative practice, following them leads to error, whereas restraining them leads to correctness. One should comprehend the text according to this principle, and thus one will not be confused regarding the directions of the stages of practice (*pratipatti-bhūmi*).

It enables one's own faculties to alternate between closing and opening, and it allows for universal awareness with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions, as well as universal penetration and comprehension.
"One is able to enter the perfect and fundamental.

[Commentary] This refers to a temporary state within meditative observation. For a brief moment during observation, it appears as though the barriers between the sense faculties have opened, yet they have not yet attained full mutual interchangeability.
[The Wuxing commentary states: "This demonstrates the signs that arise within meditative observation. Regarding those who have attained universal awareness:

within this contemplation, they have already perceived that the sentient beings of the ten directions and their own bodies share the same enlightened nature (*jue-xing*), merging with one another such that there is no distinction between cognition and awareness.

This is precisely the ability to enter the perfect source (*yuan-yuan*). [The Wenling commentary states: "The perfect source refers to the fusion of the sensory faculties and the penetration of the fundamental consciousness (*shi-yuan*) of all categories of beings. (△ [The Supplementary Note states: "Within the fundamental source of the conscious mind, employ dhyāna...")

For this reason, one is able to understand and penetrate their perfect fusion; the six sense organs are no longer obstructed, and thus it is called "perfectly fundamental" (*yuán-yuán*). This refers to the cause of the "true permanence" previously conceptualized. Regarding the universal awareness of all categories of beings, it means realizing that the nature of their awakening is not different from what was already attained as "sameness" in the preceding text.

"This is mere consciousness" (△ [Haiyin says]: "Contemplating the various classes of beings in the ten directions, one realizes they are all manifested by consciousness. One’s awakening and cognition become pervasive and flowing, entering the perfect, primordial nature of enlightenment").

This realm is entirely a shadow of consciousness; it is not yet quiescent extinction. Therefore, it is said: "Yet regarding quiescent extinction, its subtle and wondrous essence is not yet perfected" ([Jiaoguang says]:

"Being able to enter the perfect and primordial, the four aggregates are swept away. Returning to abide here is like all waves having ceased and dissolving back into the sea. This is precisely the domain of the aggregate of consciousness").
If one establishes a cause that is true and eternal regarding that which is taken as refuge, and gives rise to resolute conviction therein—[Commentary]:

This refers to the formation of a conceptual attachment. Regarding this realm of universal awareness into which one enters, one regards it as true and eternal, establishes it as the cause capable of producing all things, and takes it to be the ultimate place of refuge that is definitively unerring; therefore—

This is called "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*). [The *Erlang* says: "That to which one returns; it is the perfect source (*yuan-yuan*). That is, within the perfect source, one recognizes it as the place of rest and repose. Within this state, one gives rise to attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) and falls into the ranks of the heterodox. ([1/○] Second, judging this as belonging to the faction of the heterodox.)
Such a person falls into the attachment to causes and their underlying conditions. They become companions to Śvikaṛa and those who take refuge in the obscure *tattva* (principle).

They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s *bodhi* and lose their wisdom and insight. This is called the first: establishing a mind that seeks attainment and forming a fruit toward which one takes refuge.
They deviate from and distance themselves from perfect penetration; they turn their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa and give rise to the seeds of external paths.
[Commentary] Regarding the causal consciousness-aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*), they cling to it as being truly eternal and as the cause of all phenomena;

hence it is said, "clinging to the cause of causes. [Zhenji says: "Clinging to the cause of causes" means recognizing the perfectly luminous as truly eternal, and calculating that true eternity as the root of delusion. Wuxing says: The former "cause" points to the essence, which is the perfect origin; the latter "cause" refers to...]

Function: Since the "True" serves as the basis for the "delusory" and is able to give rise to the myriad dharmas, the name "that which is caused" is established in contrast to the function of these various dharmas. [Otherwise,] the myriad dharmas would be without cause, being merely empty, delusory, and subject to arising and ceasing.

Now, to calculate that which possesses causes is the nature of true permanence; this is no different from the "Primal Darkness" (Ālaya-tattva) clung to by non-Buddhists as being eternal and capable of producing all things.

[The Haiyin commentary states: "The myriad things of the world arise due to delusion; since delusion itself has no cause, they are said to be 'unborn. Now, to cling to this consciousness as being able to produce the myriad things is no different from the Primal Darkness.
This is precisely calculating that the Ālayavijñāna, prior to the emergence of any signs or manifestations, is a state of profound obscurity.

"First" refers to the True Principle (*tattva*). [Wenling says: The Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists identify the obscure initial phase prior to the manifestation of the *ālayavijñāna* as the true cause to which all returns. [Zizhong says:

Those who cling to the "cause of causes" are deluded regarding the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) as the Obscure Principle (*tattva*), and they cling to this Obscure Principle as the generative cause.
[Wuxing says: The two explanations by Yuan and Jie seem similar; the correct interpretation follows Jie’s meaning.]
[Commentary: Regarding "deluded about Buddha-enlightenment" (*buddhabodhi*): *bodhi* means awakening. The essence of awakening is free from thought.

That which is free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception; it is the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) of the dharma-realm (from the *Awakening of Faith*).

Now, [the deluded] cling to the existence of dharmas as being produced from a single cause, with distinctions between subject and object; therefore, it is called "delusion. Because they do not know according to reality, it is called "losing knowledge."

That which is seen—that mind which is attained—is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). In the causal stage, it is that which is attained; in the resultant stage, it is that to which one returns. (The Supplement states:

"From this cause of true permanence, the fruit of permanence is accomplished; this is what I take as my refuge. Furthermore, it is said that "all are perfectly penetrating" (*sarva-samantābheda*); thus, one knows for certain that those who are far removed from this perfect penetration have not yet entered the stage of faith.

One must understand that the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*) corresponds to the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The root of the bonds of birth and death remains vividly intact; how can such a person be said to have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)? What is here called the "aggregate of consciousness" does not refer to its ultimate exhaustion, but rather to its partial exhaustion. Why is it called partial exhaustion? The *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "It arises based on the perfuming of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*)."

Regarding "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): from the time a Bodhisattva first gives rise to right faith and begins their contemplation, if they were to realize the *dharmakāya*, they would be able to know it only partially. Furthermore, applying the principle of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), those with the initial resolve experience joy, yet they still manifest latent afflictions (*anuśaya*). Only prior to the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) is one said to have merely abandoned the storehouse (*ālaya*). Based on this, even on the stages (*bhūmi*), knowledge remains partial; how could it be fully exhausted all at once at the initial position?

Therefore, it is said that this constitutes "partial exhaustion," which refers to the ability to realize a small portion of the *dharmakāya*. However, while the Sūtra speaks of the "exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness" (*vijñānaskandha-kṣaya*), it does not say "partial exhaustion. This is because individuals who attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through the three gradual stages enter the diamond-like wisdom (*vajropama-prajñā*), purify their practice, and achieve perfect realization, proceeding directly toward the fruit.

The ocean is the ultimate emptiness of maturation (*vipāka*); the *ālayavijñāna* is ultimately relinquished. [The sixth and seventh consciousnesses] arise together with their perfuming.
