"Is it like descending from a lofty tree and entering a deep valley? The Master said, "He relies on the attainment of 'having something gained,' guarding what is before him and obstructing what lies behind.

I rely on the learning of 'no-more-learning' (aśaikṣa), where the myriad rivers flow toward the central sea. (The *Lingyuan Shiyi* states: When Master Xinti of Heitang went to visit Yuegong Hai at Baofeng, Yuegong was profoundly enlightened in the deep principles of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and was peerless in the land of the Eastern Sea.

Whenever Heitang heard a single phrase or a single word from him, he felt as though he had obtained the most precious treasure, his joy beyond measure. Among the monks, some raised private criticisms [of this]. Heitang said: "I shall strike at his strengths to sharpen my own weaknesses. I—"
"What is there to regret? The Master showed this to Xie Jingwen, saying: "Since the true nature is manifested through words and letters, the essential point lies in seeing it for oneself directly.
If one can see it directly, one will then be able to fully understand whether what is currently before one is true or false, and what constitutes birth or death."

Once one is able to fully comprehend both the true and the false, as well as birth and death, one looks back upon all language and written words and realizes they are merely expressions used for manifestation, devoid of any ultimate reality.
If one does not understand this now, the illness lies in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is because one does not know, as they truly are, the destination of the True Limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
One mistakenly identifies these faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as one's own perceptions, failing to realize that this is not so.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing all arise from the presence of external objects;

if there were no external realms, then these very faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare—utterly without basis. This instruction on the Dharma is intimate and its expedient means are wondrous and subtle;

it is found in the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*. (According to my current research, Changshui attained enlightenment under Langye, who was a dragon-elephant of the Chan school. Once he received the entrustment to uphold the school, he did not hesitate to open his breast.)

He styled himself the "Seat-Master" (Zhuangzhu). Master Yue and Changshui were fellow disciples of Langye; they were brothers from the same school. [The author] has annotated the meaning of the *Lengyan jing shu*, received its structural divisions and practices, and expounded the Dharma to lead the fourfold assembly. Having already sought instruction from Old Nan and shared the seat at Huangbo, Huìtáng subsequently visited Master Yue to inquire about the essential meanings of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

For every single word and phrase, he felt as though he had obtained rare treasures. Once Master Qiàn attained realization at Donglin and entered the world to benefit others, he provided guidance to the Chan forests, following the explanations of his teacher and humbly compiling these records.

As for these four gentlemen who call themselves students of the Way: they have emptied their own selves to embrace all with open hearts and have forgotten themselves for the sake of the Dharma. Truly, they can serve as models for the Dharma-gate and extensively encourage the customs of later generations.
The Sixth Awakening (Middle):

The Venerable Master Chen of Muzhou during the Tang dynasty asked a lecture master who was expounding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "Is it true that there are the 'eight returns' and the 'four meanings' within the sutra?
The master replied, "Yes. The Master struck the head of a young attendant with his staff once and asked, "What meaning is this? The lecture master was speechless.
The Master said: "This passage is lengthy; we shall address it on the following day.
The Great Master Chan Yue, Guan Xiu, in response to the poem sent by Wei Zhuang, wrote: "The Qin guest has long since cast aside his chessboard."

Regarding the *Lengyan Chanmei*, there is nothing that surpasses it (Zhao Wenyuan said: "Guanyou’s poetry takes the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as the marrow of Chan; Bo Juyi’s poetry takes the *Platform Sūtra* as the Buddha-mind.
In all such cases, I praise them both equally").

Master Xuan Sha Shibei served Master Xuefeng Yicun as his elder brother before eventually taking him as his teacher. Once, carrying his bag, he set out from the ridge intending to travel through various regions.
Upon crossing the pass, he injured his foot and sighed, saying: "This body is not something that exists; from where does this pain arise?
This body is suffering, yet ultimately it is unborn. Enough, enough! Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land, and the Second Patriarch did not dwell in the Western Heaven."
He returned to the peaks of Qiongling and entered the room to seek final instructions. Thereupon, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he realized the nature of his own mind.

From then on, his responses to circumstances were swift and nimble, and they accorded perfectly with the *Sūtras*. Whenever he engaged in cross-examination with Xuefeng, he never shied away from taking the lead in the practice of benevolence.
Xuefeng remarked, "Bai is a man who has come back for a second incarnation."
Nanyue Weijin studied under Xuefeng and befriended Xuansha. Hearing that the Venerable Jian had written a commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he asked, "How do the two Mañjuśrīs comment upon it?
Jian replied, "I request you, Master, to examine Weijin. Thereupon, Weijin raised his sleeves and departed.
While at Xianyan, Master An encountered [the Master] while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Upon reaching the passage, "When cognition and vision establish cognition, that is the root of ignorance;
when cognition and vision are without seeing, this is nirvāṇa," he read it by breaking the phrasing as follows:

"Cognition and vision establish (phrase) / Cognition is (phrase) the root of ignorance / When cognition and vision are without (phrase) / Seeing, this is (phrase) nirvāṇa. (Note: All other records take "Cognition and vision establish cognition" as a single phrase and "is the root of ignorance" as the subsequent phrase.)

Now, based on the Critical Commentary by Wansong and supplemented by the Combined Treatise by Leian, the punctuation has been corrected for accuracy. Upon attaining realization herein, he received the seal of his mind from National Teacher Shao. Someone said to the Master, "You have read this with broken syntax.
The Master replied, "This is my place of awakening; it will not be easy to read it this way for the rest of my life.

At that time, he was called "An Lengyan" (An of the Śūraṅgama). (Wansong says: This too is using the heterodox to strike the orthodox; like a strand of pearls passing through nine curves. (○ When the Master was about to pass away, he bathed his body, changed his robes, and had his coffin carried forth.)

After remaining in his chamber for a long while, he entered the coffin himself. When three days had passed, people opened the coffin and were struck with grief and lamentation; the Master then rose once more, ascended the hall, and preached the Dharma. He rebuked them, saying, "Those who open my coffin for a second time are not my disciples. Having finished speaking, he entered the coffin again and departed forever.

Only such a person as this could read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* by breaking the phrasing (it is truly terrifying that nowadays false teachers frequently use "breaking the phrasing" as a pretext for their own errors).
The Great Master Wuyan was twenty years old when he shaved his head to become a monk after reciting the scriptures. He received the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* from Jishu;

after Jishu passed away, he completed his studies under Xingfeng Wenzhao. When Lord Zhao Qingxian invited him to ascend the Dharma seat, the Master engaged in impassioned discussions on the definitive meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Among those in the assembly, both monastics and laypeople, were like those drinking fine wine—there was none whose heart was not intoxicated.
Like meat on a spit, its meaning and flavor are identical throughout; indeed, regarding this single sutra, his mind was harmonized with it and his body was its commentary.
He moved freely through both internal and external classics, swift as the wind and striking like lightning, achieving everything according to his will (Epitaph for Huang Shan-gu).

Baoci Wensui was a guiding teacher who thoroughly investigated the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. He discerned and synthesized the arising of reality and delusion; his work was both profound and extensive in its treatment of the fundamental and the derivative.

His topical outline and commentary interwove the textual phrases with intricate detail. Upon visiting Fayan, he described his own scholarly achievements. Fayan asked, "Does the *Śūraṅgama* not contain the principle of the 'eight returns'?
Wensui replied, "It does. Fayan then asked, "To what place does clarity return? Wensui said, "Clarity returns to the sun. Fayan said: [The remainder of the dialogue follows.]
When asked, "What do you return to the sun? he was dazed and had no reply. [The Master] sternly commanded that his annotated writings be burned (from the *Zongmen Tongyao*).
Zen Master Jingduan of Xiyu in Huzhou, whose courtesy name was Piaoming, first received the monastic robes at the age of twenty-six.

Subsequently, upon observing the play of a lion, he suddenly attained realization of the mind-dharma. He then followed Dharma Master Renshuo to receive the essential principles of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
One day, Yue presented ten or so difficult passages from the sutras and had his disciples answer them. Only Xuedou presented two verses, saying:
"The mind was sought in seven locations, yet it was not found; Poor Ānanda did not perceive its ground.

Even if one were to seek until seeing the mindless state, It would still be like washing clods of earth in the mud. He further said: "The teaching of the eight returns has been handed down for a long time; since antiquity..."

The various masters each analyzed and dissected [the teachings]. Even if one were to attain the state of "returning" or "not returning," it would still be like a shrimp leaping out of a measuring bucket.
Master Yue looked on with awe and remarked, "Your insight is lofty and subtle; you will surely propagate the Sudden School.

Following this, after Duan Shizi had awakened to the mind-ground, he received the essential tenets of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* from Master Yue. Master Yue was able to [transmit] the *Śūraṃgama* school...
This was done to examine and verify Master Duan Shizi, granting him formal certification; how could he have been an ordinary lecturer?
Those who today claim the title of "Patriarchal Master" should reflect deeply upon this (from the *Luohu Yalu*).
When Chan Master Tiantong Jue visited the residence of Wei Shichen Jinke at the end of the year, there was a hall named Liuzhan (Sixfold Tranquility).

This was derived from the meaning of the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* regarding the six sense bases returning to stillness and abiding in a single state of profound clarity (*zhanran*). Jue composed a verse, which says:

"When the wind and waves have not yet arisen, one beholds the spiritual source; When the six sense bases have vanished, the essence remains profoundly tranquil. Only when the nature of all phenomena is realized as empty does one truly take their seat. One.
In the snap of a finger, the gate suddenly opened. Cold plum blossoms on the hedge herald an early spring; wild snow before the lattice window does not darken the night.
The myriad phenomena of the universe are sealed by the seal of the mind; all sensory dusts are transcended and cleared away, wondrously without a trace. The Elder Miaoxi arrived next.
The Master said: "Neither still nor wavering—this is the source of the Dharma. When the opportunity arises, do not weary of the persistence of provisional names.
Only those of extraordinary spirit can enter the boundless and vast gate. Myriad phenomena interlace yet are fundamentally non-dual; the six windows are never dark by day or night.
Reflecting upon the deeds of the Elder Pang, there is nothing else: casting a sword into the void, how could there be any trace? Director of the Temple.

This is called the "Hall. Desiring to assist those who would advance in this Way, both elders pointed to it as the swift path for entering the Way, not sparing even a single hair on their eyebrows (from the *Luohu Yalu*).
Chan Master Huazang Min was renowned for his lectures on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. He went to visit Yuanwu, who asked, "Preceptor, what sūtra do you lecture upon?
He replied, "The *Śūraṅgama*. Yuanwu said, "In the *Śūraṅgama*, there are seven locations where the mind is sought;

ultimately, where does the mind reside? The Master offered many explanations, but Yuanwu rejected them all. One day, he said to Yuanwu, "When you ordinarily brandish the mallet or raise the whisk, is that not..."
"This sutra is the Middle Way. All phenomena existing throughout all worlds are none other than the wondrously luminous true mind of Bodhi.
Wuzu laughed and said, "You have been living right here all along. He added, "When you shout or strike the meditation seat, is this not 'hearing back' to hear one's own nature?
When that nature is perfected, it becomes the Unsurpassed Way. Wuzu said, "Have you not heard that the wondrous nature is perfectly round?"
"Clearly, one must be free from all names and signs; fundamentally, there have never been worlds or sentient beings. At these words, Min was relieved and at ease.

Zen Master Fozhao of the Song dynasty addressed Emperor Xiaozong, saying: "If you wish to attain the direct and swift path, you must depart from language and written characters and engage in genuine investigation.
Therefore, as the ancient masters said: 'Even if you can recite the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, it is still...'"
It is like the clear, ringing sound of mountain stream water. When someone asks about the meaning of the Westward Journey, it is just like a mosquito or a gnat biting an iron nail.
The Master said, "It is truly difficult to enter. The Teacher said, "This is precisely when one must apply effort."
Emperor Xiaozong asked Chan Master Xiatang Yuan of Lingyin: "The other day, while asleep in a dream, I suddenly heard the sound of a bell and woke up.
I do not yet know whether the dreaming and the waking are one and the same. The Master replied, "Your Majesty asks about that which is within the dream."

Regarding that which is realized upon awakening: if one asks about what is realized upon awakening, this is precisely the talk of one still asleep. If one asks about what was within the dream, there is no difference between the dream and the awakening;
who then could make a distinction? The dream is itself an illusion. To know it as an illusion is to depart from it; to depart from the illusion is to awaken.

When the awakened mind is unmoving, it is said: "If one can transform things, one is identical to the Tathāgata. The Emperor said: "Since both awakening and illusion are non-existent," [what is there to transform?]
"Furthermore, from where does the sound of the bell arise? The Master said, "It arises from the place where Your Majesty asks. The Emperor was greatly pleased (*Zongmen tongyao xují*).
Chan Master Qianguang Huansheng had thoroughly investigated the Vinaya-piṭaka and settled his mind in the Perfect and Sudden *Zhiguan* of Tiantai. Because he was reading...
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is profound and vast in its literary principles; I had not yet fully understood it. One night, after reciting the sutra for a long time, I leaned over my desk as if dozing off.
In a dream, I saw a solar disc descend from the sky and opened my mouth to swallow it. From that moment on, I suddenly attained awakening.

The gates of the various distinctions opened wide and flowed without obstruction. Later, he attended upon Master Yongming Quan. Yongming merely confirmed his prior understanding and offered no further instructions or metaphors.

Subsequently, Chan Master Shigui of Longxiang in Wenzhou devoted himself heart and soul to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* for over five autumns; he then traveled south to pay respects to various venerable masters.
One night, as he was about to ascend Longmen (succeeding Longmen Yuan), he presented the understanding he had attained during his ordinary life to Baizhang Huaiyan.

Huaiyan said, "Your realization of the mind is already ultimate; you simply lack the exertion to open your eyes. He then appointed him to serve in the Hall Office. While standing in attendance, Huaiyan asked, "What is it like when all dualities are transcended?
Huaiyan replied, "It is just like your striking the wooden mallet in the Sangha Hall. The Master was at a loss. Huaiyan—
He arrived at the Hall Office late in the evening. The Master (Zhaozhou) brought up their previous conversation, and Xuedou said, "Idle talk. At this, the Master attained great enlightenment.
The Hermit Zongyuan of Jianning once gave a teaching in his room, saying: "In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are fifty kinds of demonic realms."
"Nowadays, all the people throughout the great earth practice Chan. Even those who are most eminent cannot escape his realm of Māra.
The monk asked, "In which realm do you, Master, fall? The Master said, "I am right here with you.
The monk said, "I will not enter this community. The Master said, "You beast! Where do you intend to go?"
The Chief Seat Fashang of Bao’en Monastery in Jiaxing had deeply penetrated the ocean of meaning in the Śūraṅgama Sūtra.

Having met Xuechao and attained karmic resonance, he was appointed to oversee the monastery's correspondence. He led the assembly at Bao’en; in his quarters there was only a single low couch, and no other possessions besides.
In the ninth month of the Gengzi year of the Xuanhua era, he told the monks of the temple, "I shall not remain here after one month.

On the twenty-first day of the tenth month, he went to the abbot’s quarters for a meal. As dawn approached, he wrote a *yúfǔ* (fisherman) lyric on the door of his room, then lay upon his mat, drew up his legs, and passed away.
The lyric reads: "This matter was already revealed in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Where the plum blossoms, snow, and moon intermingle their radiance. One..."
A laugh echoes through the vast void of all ages. The wind-chimes speak; far off, the Milky Way spans the heavens. The dream of the butterfly in the *Nanhua* [Zhuangzi] is still in full flight;
who is it that treads upon the brindled tiger of Fenggan? Now, the path by which one came has been forgotten. The rivers and mountains grow dark at eve.

Watching the wild geese fly away toward the horizon, Master Duan Ya sat at the Chan hermitage on Mount Jing Shan and vowed that if he did not attain realization within seven days, he would surely depart.
Before the period had even concluded, he attained a sudden and great awakening. He rushed to Siguan and cried out, "Old Monk, today you have deceived me!"

"It is not permitted. The next day, Gao Feng ascended the hall and brought up the matter. The Master then seized Feng’s whisk and, for the sake of the assembly, proclaimed it, rebuking his fellow students.
He further said, "If there is one person in the entire world who awakens to the true source and returns to the origin, from that moment on everyone knows it.
Gao Feng sighed at his brilliance and quickness (as recorded in the *Epitaph* composed by Yu Daoyuan).

The monk Jing of the Qitang [Hall] at Miaojue [Monastery] in Huzhou was a son of a farming family from Wujiang. Having received ordination, he went to visit Miaofeng Xuan, who was the son of Zhongfeng.
Xuan instructed him to investigate: "Before the birth of one's parents, what is that which is my original face?
He investigated this for thirty years without attaining entry. When the monk Master Zhao of Huayan Monastery in Mingzhou arrived in the region of Lake [Huzhou], he exhorted him...

While he was reciting the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, one day, upon reaching the passage, "When birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests," he suddenly attained a profound realization. His entire body was filled with joy;
he could not speak, but could only dance with his hands and feet. Someone asked him, "Are you mad? He replied, "Quiescent extinction has manifested. (Hongwu)
On the twenty-fifth day of the first month of the tenth year, he addressed Zhao Gong, saying: "The first day of the eleventh month is my birthday;
on this day, I shall pass away. When the appointed time arrived, he bathed, changed his clothes, and instructed them: "Three days after my death, perform the cremation."
The bones were calcined for seven days; it was only feared that they would not withstand the heat. When the bones were placed in the forge, they melted and overflowed into liquid.
Once the fire cooled, they solidified into a single branch of a divine fungus (*lingzhi*), its radiance brilliant and shimmering, with five colors intermingled. Striking it produced a resonant sound.

Even with the finest carvings, engravings, and paintings, they could not compare to it. It remains to this day in the Miaojue Period Hall (from *Shuyun’s Miscellaneous Records of Zhongshan Hermitage*).

Chan Master Qi Chushi, while reading the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, reached the passage: "When conditions are dark, consciousness relies on light; when darkness becomes non-seeing, clarity arises spontaneously of itself.
Thus, the various appearances of darkness can never again obscure it. He was suddenly enlightened. Thereafter, he perused a multitude of books...
"Relying on the teacher’s instruction, the words and phrases were naturally understood" (Epitaph for the Pagoda at Qianxi, Song).
The Great Master Hanshan’s own account says: "In the *bingxu* year of the Wanli era, I was dwelling in the Nayana Cave by the East Sea.

My meditation hall had just been completed, and I had set aside both body and mind. One night, while sitting in stillness, I rose; I saw the sea as profound and the sky as clear, all luminously transparent."
Within this great treasury of radiant light, there is not a single thing to be found. He then spoke a verse: "The ocean is still and the sky is clear; the moonlight shines upon the snow.
Within this, both ordinary beings and sages transcend action and concealment. The adamantine eye suddenly pierces through, and the flowers in the sky fall away;

The entire earth returns to the field of quiescent extinction. He returned to his room. At his desk, he saw the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Upon unrolling it, he immediately beheld your body and mind, as well as the external world.
Mountains, rivers, space, and the great earth are all objects within the wondrously luminous true mind.

With the entire contemplative scope of the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* clearly manifest before my eyes and mind, I took up my brush to compose the *Lengyan Xuanying* (The Suspended Mirror of the Śūraṃgama) in a single volume. My hand did not rest from its wrist until the candle was but half-burnt.
Having finished drafting the composition, an attendant entered to check on me and was surprised to see the remaining candle still upon the desk.

At that time, the meditation hall had just begun its period of silence. I immediately summoned the *vinaya-dhara* (the rector) into my room to read it for me; even as I listened, it was as if I were hearing the words of a dream. (The Master’s Separate Record states:

"One night, while sitting in meditation, body and world both became empty. The Sea-Seal manifested light, and there arose a state in which mountains and rivers shook. I attained the wisdom of correspondence. After a short while, I awakened to the crucial points of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and they appeared vividly before my eyes. I hurriedly dipped my pen and wrote them down.")
Awakening and Understanding, Part Six (Lower).
Fang Rong visited the quarters of Master Guo at Guangsheng Temple in Shixing and composed a poem which says: "I lament my failing life, now fallen and decayed."
In this desolate state, I entrust myself to the supreme cause. Just as the fires of the three realms are about to burn, I suddenly wash away the dust of the six sense-faculties.
Beyond the ridges, celestial flowers bloom; soaring into the void, the moon palace is renewed. Who will pity my thoughts for my native land? From now on, I shall learn to manifest multiple bodies.

(*Yijue liao zaji* states: Fang Rong was in power during the time of Empress Wei. Exiled to Nanhai, he passed through Guangguo Temple in Shaozhou—present-day Lingjiu. He composed a poem [as cited above]. Rong’s literary works are seen in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. This poem consists of a single piece and is considered the progenitor of regulated verse (*lüshi*). According to Fang...)

The Duke, serving as a high-ranking minister, composed these verses with a serene detachment; they lack any trace of sorrowful lamentation. Is this not because, following his initial mastery under Pen-shou and Leng, he has attained a state of transcendence through his own self-realization?
Du Qigong and Zhang Wending both retired from office and resided in Suizhou. They frequented one another’s quarters in the neighborhood.
There was a man named Zhu Chengshi who traveled between these two elders as a physician. Du Qigong was upright and strict;

he never indulged in miscellaneous studies and would often laugh at An Dao’s devotion to Buddhism, mocking him in the presence of his guests. Zhang Wending, however, would merely smile. Taking advantage of a private moment, Zhu spoke to Wending.
"Ding! Lord Du is a great man of the world; it is a pity he does not yet know of this matter. He possesses great power—why not urge him to awaken to it?
Wending said, "Your connection with this old man is more mature than mine; I can do no more than assist you. Zhu bowed in assent and departed.
One day, Lord Qi called for Zhu and felt his pulse with great urgency. Zhu said to the messenger, "Go ahead and inform the Chancellor first."
The Duke merely said, "I have not yet finished reading the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. The messenger reported these words as they were spoken. Lord Qi remained silent for a long while before arriving.
He leaned on his armrest, bowed to him, and motioned for him to sit. Then he spoke slowly: "I took you to be a man of broad learning and capable understanding;

I did not expect that lately you too would fall into the category of the mediocre and muddled. As for this so-called *Śūraṅgama*, what kind of talk is it that you are so addicted to? The subtle [teachings] of the Sage..."
[The Master] said, "There is nothing that surpasses Confucius and Mencius. To abandon this and take up that is a great delusion.
Zhu said, "If Your Excellency has not yet read this scripture, how can you know it does not equal Confucius and Mencius? From my perspective, it seems to surpass them.
He produced the first volume from his sleeve and said, "Your Excellency, please examine it for yourself. Lord Qi gazed intently at Zhu; having no other recourse, he took it and read silently.
He looked at it and, before he realized it, the scroll had reached its end. He suddenly rose, greatly startled, and said, "How could such a book exist in this world?
He dispatched messengers to fetch all copies and read them through thoroughly. Taking Zhu's hand, he said, "You are truly my spiritual friend; An Dao has known you for a long time."
"And yet you did not inform me. Why was that? He immediately ordered his carriage to visit Wending. Wending said, "It is like a person who has lost an object and suddenly finds it again;
one should simply rejoice in having found it. One must not regret whether it was found early or late.
It was not that I did not wish to inform you; rather, because your karmic connection with Master Zhu was mature, I sent him instead. Even the Buddha—
The Patriarchs instructed people by necessarily relying on shared practice. Lord Qi was greatly pleased (*from the Linjian Lu*).

Zhu Yan, the Judicial Commissioner, asked Chan Master Yijiang, "I do not yet understand: after this body dies, where does this mind go? The Master said, "Before this body has died, where does this mind go?
Zhu realized the essential meaning and composed a verse, saying: "There is no need to first [examine] the four elements..."
Later Awakening: When the six sense-faculties return to their state of functioning, it is difficult to present this to the Master through speech or silence;
it exists only within ordinary speech and silence. The Master said, "You must further spit it out" (*Chánlín lèijù*).

During the True Zong era, Zhu Yan, the Administrative Assistant of the Regional Commander, suddenly attained realization regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and composed a verse (*etc.*). Later, he eventually passed away while sitting in meditation (*Fófǎ jīntāng*). (○)

Yan was the person mentioned in the *Lengyan jing* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra) who, according to the *Duke Du’s Exhortation*, was known as Zhu Chengshi. Shen Kuo’s *Bishitan* records that when Yin Shilu was on his deathbed, he wrote a final letter of parting to Fan Wenzheng;

Zhu Yan, the Secretary to the Councilor, was present in the assembly. This elderly Yan was a lover of Buddhist studies. When Wenzheng ordered him to go and provide exhortation, Shilu sat and conversed with him before passing away while leaning against a couch—it was this very man. Tao Gong of Dianshan said: "The great matter of birth and death is something our Confucian scholars avoid speaking of.
Yet, do we not know whether the four elements and six sense bases can truly be realized as empty? It is through this that one knows the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* must indeed be read."
When Lord Wang Wen retired from the相位 (prime ministership) and returned to live in seclusion at Mount Zhong, he would invariably inquire into the Way and learning of the monastics he encountered.
He was particularly well-versed in the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* and once composed his own commentary on its meaning. His prose was concise yet unrestrained;

he expanded upon what previous masters had omitted and condensed what they had elaborated. None but those who perceive the subtle could fathom it. He would often say: "Nowadays, whenever one reads this scripture, one sees..."

That which you have pointed out as the nature of awakened wondrous clarity and original awakened wondrous clarity—knowing the faculties, the body, and the world of vessels—arises without departing from my own mind.
I privately suspect that these mountains and rivers of Mount Zhong are but a single common environment, yet within them, there are no fewer than a thousand people who move about.
How could it be that a thousand people share one and the same external object? Suppose, for instance, that among those thousand people, one person...

If one dies suddenly, how could these mountains and rivers ever perish along with them? When a person departs but the environment remains, the principle of the arising of the "mountains, rivers, and great earth" as spoken of in the sutras would otherwise be untenable;
how then could this be reconciled to accord with the Buddha’s original intent? (From the *Línjiān lù*). [○ Hánguāng’s supplementary commentary states:

The Dharmalakṣaṇa school clarifies the transformation of common seeds (*sādhāraṇa-bīja*) and uncommon seeds (*asādhāraṇa-bīja*). For instance, the mountains, rivers, and great earth are transformations produced by the seeds of the common characteristics of all sentient beings. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says: "It is like the light of many lamps; each is pervasive and appears as one. This means...

When one person dies, their eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) has never ceased. Only when this principle—that the person departs while the objective realm remains, as pointed out by Master Jing—is examined through the lens of the Dharma-characteristics school (*lakṣaṇa-yāna*) can its meaning be truly understood.

(Pengxian County Lady, wife of Wu Anchih and daughter of Prince Shu, was skilled in poetry. She sent a poem to Prince Shu which read: "The western wind does not enter the small window-curtain; the autumn air surely makes me long for my home. My gaze reaches the mountains and rivers—a thousand miles of resentment;

as before, I gaze at the chrysanthemums through tears. Prince Shu gave her his new commentary on the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* and she composed a poem in response: "A single point of blue lamp reflects upon the window-curtain; one should read the *Śūraṃgama* rather than longing for home.
If one can realize that all conditions are like illusions and dreams, then in this world there is only the wondrous lotus flower. —From Hong Juefan’s *Cold Studio Night Talks*.)

The Great Wisdom Dharma Discourse states: "The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra and beheld the World-Honored One on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa preaching this scripture, majestically present and undispersed. The Layman Zhang, known as Wujin, read the Śūraṅgama Sūtra..."
At this point, the person first attains the state within the Vajra-heart. Suddenly, they reflect upon what the Great Master (Zhizhe) realized at that time:
it was not a mere symbolic teaching. He once said to me, "When one truly enters into realization, the entire body dwells within the Vajra-heart."
Master Li said: "The realms of boundless lands are not separated from one another by even a hair's breadth;
the ten eons of past and present do not depart from this very moment of thought. When the wise behold the single assembly on Vulture Peak, it appears as if they are already dispersing.

Only those who have realized this samādhi will nod their heads in silent agreement without waiting for further illustration. (When Yaoshan first visited Shitou, he heard [the teaching] but did not grasp it. Later, upon reaching Jiangxi, he saw...)

Mazu said, "Sometimes I teach them to raise their eyebrows and blink; sometimes I do not teach them to raise their eyebrows and blink. Sometimes that which I teach them to raise their eyebrows and blink is correct; sometimes that which I teach them to raise their eyebrows and blink is incorrect.

Upon hearing these words, Shanzhao attained the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*). There was nothing more extraordinary, mysterious, or subtle through which he could communicate his realization; he simply paid his respects. Mazu, knowing that he had already entered into realization, asked, "What have you seen lately?

Shanzhao replied, "The skin and flesh have fallen away entirely; there remains only the single reality. Mazu said, "Since it is so, take three strands of rattan and bind your belly, then go dwell in the mountains wherever you please. This, too, is an instance of attaining the efficacy of the adamantine mind.
In the postscript to his transcription of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Dongpo wrote:

"I have often heard from Zhang Wending that there is no distinction of great or small within the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), nor is its teaching either false or real; it depends entirely upon how one perceives it. All phenomena (*dharmas*) are of one principle.
If I possess true insight, then parables are themselves the actual truth; if I lack such insight, then even what is real is but a metaphor. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*..."
The Sūtra says: "If even a single sentient being has not yet attained Buddhahood, I shall never enter Nirvāṇa here.

If Bodhisattvas are urgent in delivering others and not urgent in attaining Buddhahood for themselves, only when all sentient beings throughout the triple world have attained the Way of the Buddha will I then enter Nirvāṇa.
If Bodhisattvas realize that this body, from time immemorial, has been nothing but the mark of a sentient being—whether enemy or kin—"

Refusing to accept [what is offered], being shielded by internal and external obstacles—this is the characteristic of egg-birth (*aṇḍaja*). Destroying that to bring this into being, harming others to benefit oneself—this is the characteristic of womb-birth (*jarāyuja*).
Being stained by craving and lingering on, attaching itself to existence or non-existence—this is the characteristic of moisture-birth (*saṃsvedaja*).

All things undergoing transformation, yet taking them as one's own master—this is the characteristic of transformation-birth (*upapāduka*). These four types of sentient beings' characteristics have been revolving with me; I was neither aware nor conscious of it.

To claim that through diligent and arduous practice and the accomplishment of illusory powers, these four marks subdue one's faculties and constitute the mark of nirvana, thereby attaining Buddhahood—such a thing is impossible.
These two bodhisattvas both possess right view; thus they understand the Buddha’s words.
Neither provisional nor real. ○ *Record of the Hall of Great Compassion*. Now, "Great Compassion" is a manifestation of Avalokiteśvara.
Avalokiteśvara attains awakening through hearing. Beginning with hearing, he is able to hear nothing; beginning with hearing nothing, he is able to hear everything.
Being able to hear nothing, it would be permissible for him to have no body; being able to hear everything, although...
It is possible for there to be thousands of millions of bodies; how much more so for hands and eyes?

Nevertheless, were it not for the body, there would be no means to raise up the multitude of thousands of millions; and were it not for those thousands of millions of bodies, there would be no way to demonstrate the ultimate state of being bodiless.
Thus, they disperse to become thousands of millions of bodies, and gather to become eighty-four thousand *śākalas* (adamantine) heads. Eighty-four...
A thousand *mudrā*-like arms and eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes; their principle is one and the same. In the past, I once observed this:
my hair is beyond counting, and the pores of my body are likewise beyond counting.
If one pulls a single strand of hair, the head moves with it; if one plucks a single hair, the body shifts with it. Thus, all hair is mine.
The head. Yet every pore is my body; they are all my heads, yet they cannot perform the functions of a head;

they are all my bodies, yet they do not possess the intelligence of a body. This is because things have confused them. I shall cause the people of the world to wield an axe with their left hand while holding a chisel with their right;
to count flying geese with their eyes while keeping time with a drum with their ears; and as for their heads—
If one relies on others to recognize the rungs of the ladder, even a person of wisdom will find themselves lacking the leisure for such discernment;

how much more so when a thousand hands grasp different objects and a thousand eyes look in various directions? I sit in quiet meditation, my mind concentrated and still, as serene as a great bright mirror.
Humans, ghosts, birds, and beasts are arrayed before me in confusion, while forms, sounds, scents, and flavors pass back and forth.

The body is unified; though the mind does not arise [as discrete thoughts], there is nothing it does not engage. Engagement necessarily possesses a Way, which is the manifestation of a thousand hands and the operation of a thousand eyes.
Although these may not yet be visible, the principle is fully present. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise so.
Although a single body does not become two Buddhas, yet one Buddha can manifest as Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

this is not due to anything else. They touch [objects] without being disturbed; they arrive and are able to respond. Since the principle necessarily leads to this, why do you alone harbor doubts regarding Great Compassion?

(This passage is quoted in full from Juefan’s *Zuntong lun* [Discourse on the Honored Crown], in the chapter "Explaining Avalokiteśvara’s Perfect Penetration. [Zipeng said: "The fish is alive while the trap is dead; the meaning is alive while the words are dead. Therefore it is said: 'Those who rely on words perish; those who cling to phrases are deluded. Having read the *Mahā..."* (text truncated).

The *Beigeji* (Record of the Hall of Compassion). From this we know that Dongpo attained life by employing death; thus, all who have died shall live. Dongpo once praised the subtlety of literary composition, stating that nothing excels the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* in its winding elegance, its exquisite thoroughness, and its peerless excellence. Judging from these two records, this is indeed so.

The Master did not merely attain the subtlety of the "Lengyan" of the deceased; had he not attained the "Lengyan" of the living, how could he have transcended words through words, and having transcended words, manifest hands and eyes?
Su Ziyou’s postscript to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "I read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and learned that the six sense-bases originate from a single source.
When they encounter the six external objects, they flow outward and become six; following after things and sinking away, they are unable to return of their own accord.

Out of compassion for sentient beings, the Tathāgata established skillful means to enable them to know that the very door one exits through is the path of return. Therefore, in this sūtra, he points to nirvāṇa..."

The Gate of Liberation. From the beginning, there has been no concealment. If sentient beings can cleanse their minds and practice the Dharma, such that the sense objects do not engage with one another and the sense faculties have nothing to pair with, they will reverse the flow and become entirely unified.
When the six functions cease to operate and they enter the state of "middle-of-the-middle" day and night, they will connect with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma-flow.
Then, from within their very physical bodies, they may attain Buddhahood. The Tathāgata still fears that sentient beings, regarding...
Among the six sense faculties, [the Buddha] did not know from which one [to choose], so he had twenty-five disciples each explain what they had realized.
Among them, Avalokiteśvara was ranked first for his perfect penetration through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation. He said:

"First, within the faculty of hearing, one enters the stream and loses the objects of perception," continuing until "quiescent extinction manifests before one. If one can thus perfectly uproot a single faculty, then all the other faculties will likewise be liberated.
He was liberated. In the space of a single finger-snap, he traversed the three realms of emptiness and became no different from all the Buddhas.

Later, while reading the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he encountered the passage concerning those who have attained the four fruits: "The srotāpanna is called 'one who has entered the stream' yet there is nowhere they enter;
because they do not enter into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomena, they are called a srotāpanna. Thereupon, he set aside the scripture and sighed, saying: "The srotāpanna..."
Is this what is realized—that which Avalokiteśvara referred to as "first entering the stream within hearing and losing the objects"?
Entering the stream is not a substantial dharma; it is simply not entering the six sense-objects and abiding peacefully and eternally—this is what it means to enter the stream.
As for the *sakṛdāgāmin*, they are called "once-returners," yet in reality there is no coming or going. The *anāgāmin* is called "non-returner," yet in reality...

There is no "not coming. For when one goes, one enters the dust [of the world]; when one comes, one returns to the source. Although a Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner) is able to come, he has not yet attained the state of no-going.
Anāgāmin (Non-returner) does not merely not go, but is also without coming.
Upon reaching Arhatship, the intention of going and coming is exhausted; there is no dharma to be obtained. Thus, what are called the four fruits are in reality but a single dharma.
It is merely that one passes through the three emptinesses, with differences of depth and shallowness. Observing the words of these two sutras, they are fundamentally like matching seals;
yet the world may not understand this, so I have explained it clearly. Ziyou’s Inscription after the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"For over ten years, I have gradually attained some realization within the Buddha-dharma. The trials and tribulations I have undergone are all rare in this world."

Yet his true mind remained undisturbed, and he constantly attained peace and joy. In the *Guimǐn* year (1093), while preparing to move from Xǔ to Cǎi, he shut himself away in seclusion and sat in quietude.
Taking up the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he read it repeatedly and thoroughly, whereupon he realized that the direct path to the nirvāṇa of all Buddhas enters through the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

Whenever he sat in meditation in tranquil ease, he perceived how external objects provoke the six faculties; if the faculties follow after them, one immediately falls into the cycle of birth and death.
On the path toward death, if the faculties do not follow outward, they may instead flow back to become entirely unified; flowing into the center of the center is the true limit of Nirvana.
Like clear lapis lazuli containing a precious moon within, I prostrate to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and the Sangha of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Out of compassion and pity, grant me the patience of non-arising and the supreme fruit of outflowlessness. This is my vow.
Guard the mind; do not let it decline or be lost. Recorded on the twenty-fifth day of the third month. Ziyou was exiled to Jinyang to manage the salt monopoly.
There, Chan Master Shun of Jingde Temple in Hongzhou, who shared a spiritual affinity with his father, Mr.

Wen’an, went to visit him. Ziyou consulted him regarding the essentials of the mind. Shun cited the karmic occasion from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* concerning the pinching of the nose, and Ziyou attained realization. He presented this verse:
He said: "In middle age I studied the Way and realized my former errors. By chance I met Master Lǎoshùn; pinching the nose, I finally encountered his true countenance.
Shaking my head, I refused further tongs and hammers. 'Withered cane and tattered robes—what business have you, Master? White wine and green salt—who am I?
Ashamed under the waning moon at the eastern window, a cup of nectar as smooth as syrup. (From *Zōngmén Tǒngyào*) (○ East)

The *Sūnzhai jí* (Collected Works of Su Shi) states: When Ziyou was in Junzhou, he composed the "Record of the Eastern Studio" (*Dōngxuān jì*). Someone jokingly called him the "Elder of the Eastern Studio. His son-in-law, Cao Huan, traveled to Junzhou, and I wrote a quatrain to see him off, joking with Ziyou as follows:

"I present you with a basket, take it well; Fill it with the Elder of the Eastern Studio. Cao passed through Mount Lu and showed the poem to the Elder Yuan Tong Shen. Shen was delighted and also composed a quatrain. As the guest was leaving, Shen returned to his seat, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away. (*Shīhuà zǒngguī* [Compendium of Poetic Anecdotes] states:

Ziyou recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and realized the meaning of "one awakening and six extinctions. He said of himself that he had no further obstacles on the Way. Yet, in his poem on wind-paralysis, he wrote: 'When my number is exhausted, I shall go; I should not fall into the dark void. This indicates—)

This still leaves a logical difficulty. Yet Dongpo (Su Shi) claimed that Ziyou had realized the Way before himself; why was this so? In his "Parting from Ziyou at Fengxin," Dongpo wrote: "How can I dispel my sorrow? It lies in having roughly settled one great matter. He also laughed at Dun'er’s poem, saying: [text follows].

In my middle years, I have had the honor of hearing the Way; its nature as a dream or an illusion has been explained in detail. To the Monk Qian, he said: "Since the head has already been severed, there can be no one who severs it. When ice melts, how could there still be 'ice' that knows?

The host insists that I must recognize him, but when I try to recognize the host, who exactly is it? He also said: "If there is a host, there must also be a guest; it is better to have no mirror so that there is no dust. "From the moment I attained peace of mind at midnight, I lost the person of former times who felt pain upon awakening.

Presented to Elder Donglin Zong, he said: "The sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue; the color of the mountains is surely the pure body. Last night, eighty-four thousand gāthās were spoken; how shall I present them to others on another day? Such excellent verses would humble even veteran monks.
Ziyou’s commentary on the Laozi chapter "That Which Cannot Be Seen" states: "That which is seen when one looks at it is color; that by which color is seen cannot itself be seen.
That which is heard when one listens to it is sound; that by which sound is heard cannot itself be heard.
That which is grasped when one touches it is tangibility; that by which tangibility is grasped cannot itself be grasped. This...
Third, even though there are those who possess wisdom, none are able to interrogate [this matter]. It must necessarily be blended and returned to the One before it can be so.
What is called "the One" is nature (*xing*). These three are the functions of nature. At the beginning, humans possess only nature;
only when they engage with external things does it subsequently split and radiate outward, becoming seeing, hearing, and touching. Thus, it is used daily without [one's realizing it].

To know how to return to the source is not to merge back into a single unity; otherwise, one would be increasingly distant from it. If one extends this principle further, then all that the Buddha taught regarding the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is likewise so.
As the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* says: "When the flow is reversed and the One is restored in its entirety, the six functions cease to operate. This is precisely what is meant.

(Ziyou attained enlightenment through the passage in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* concerning the reversal of the flow and the restoration of the One; thus his interpretation of Laozi is as such. Zizhan marveled at this, saying: "I did not expect that in my old age I would see such a thing.")
How extraordinary!
Zheng Yifu of Wu was a man of refined talent who passed the imperial examinations in his youth. During the Jiayou era, he served as the supervisor of the customs and tax office in Gaoyou Commandery.
He once encountered a master of arts who could calculate the time of one’s death with unerring accuracy. [The master] was asked to calculate his own destiny, but...

After he passed the age of thirty-five, he was overcome with grief and lamentation to such an extent that it was almost unbearable. People encouraged him to read the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi to broaden his mind.
After some time, a monk from Jìnshān in Rùnzhōu sat upright while conversing and laughing with others, and then suddenly passed away.
When Yi-fu heard this, he sighed deeply and said, "Since I cannot attain longevity, what more could I regret about having such a monk as this? (The *Xu deng lu* states:
Upon hearing that Yuan had passed away with a smile and in conversation, he said, "If I can obtain one like Master Yuan, what more could I regret?

He then received the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* from the follower of the Buddha and traveled back and forth through the Wu region for over a year. Suddenly, he attained realization and said, "As for the principle of birth and death, I now understand it."

Thus, his mind was set at ease; he cast off all worldly concerns, and no further resentment remained within him. Later, while serving as the Administrative Assistant (Panguan) of Fengzhou, he foreknew the date of his own death.

Within ten days, he wrote letters to his friends and relatives to bid them farewell, and he provided detailed instructions for the management of his household affairs. When the appointed time arrived—
He bathed and changed his clothes. Outside the official residence was a small garden facing a stream, containing a pavilion that had been freshly decorated.
When Hui-fu arrived there, he personally supervised the servants in sweeping and burning incense. While he was gesturing with his hand as if sketching, he suddenly stood up and passed away.
His family rushed out and called to him, but he was already stiff; he stood upright like a planted tree, one hand still in the posture of sketching.

The district magistrate and his subordinates all arrived shortly thereafter. The scholars and commoners who came to witness the event stood like a wall. On the following day, the body was enshrouded for burial.
Cui Bo’yi of Gaoyou composed the tomb inscription, briefly recounting these events. I am a distant relative of Yi-fu and know the details very well;
among the scholar-officials, such a thing has likely never occurred before. (From Shen Kuo’s *Mengxi Bitan*)
During the Yuanyou era, Liu Jingchen (style name Xingchao), who served as a Commissioned Administrative Assistant, had never previously placed his faith in Buddhism.

Upon meeting the Elder Donglin Zong, he conversed with him for seven days and only then gave rise to the mind of faith. He subsequently visited various Chan assemblies until he reached the Master Yipeng of Zhikai.

He was summoned into the inner chamber for interrogation. Baohai recounted the circumstances regarding the Venerable Prajñātāra’s response to the Incense King, as if drawing out an old object from his breast.

Upon reaching this point, at the seventh day and night, he rose from his seat at the fifth watch; his two eyes opened immediately, like the light of hundreds of thousands of suns illuminating the universe.
All past causes and conditions converged within his heart-mind; his six sense organs shook, and heaven and earth trembled.
As he circled about, hundreds of thousands of spirits gathered together, with the ocean itself serving as witness. He said, "You must still be able to put this to use before it is truly attained.
He recorded its beginning and end, saying: "When I first attained the illumination of this matter, I only felt that the state was extraordinary."

I did not yet know which gateways [to enlightenment] they were. More than ten months later, while looking at the desk of the attendant Zhikai, I saw the *Wuzong ji* (Anthology on the Realization of the School).

Thereupon, I came to know that the skillful means of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, in uplifting and receiving beginners so as to enable them to attain awakening and entry, possess their own distinct gateways.
If one enters through the gate of Mañjuśrī, the eyes are opened first; the great are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, and the small are the soil and wood.

The rubble all assists you in triggering the mechanism [of awakening] (assisting in the manifestation of one's own nature of seeing; it does not pursue those external forms). If one enters through the gate of Avalokiteśvara:
(The Ear-Gate opens first: From the massive sounds of thunder, bells, and drums down to the minute cries of frogs and earthworms, all assist you in triggering the mechanism [of awakening].
(This assists in manifesting one’s own nature of hearing; it is not chasing after those external sounds. For those who enter through the Gate of Samantabhadra, (the Mind-Ground opens first:

without needing to move a single step or stir a speck of dust, one is able to penetrate mountains, rivers, rocks, and walls. (The mind pierces through the ten directions, requiring no further kalpas. This is what I attained upon my initial realization and entry.
There are three gates. Thus, I have composed a song for entering these three gates to show it universally to many people.

How marvelous! Every person possesses this, yet it is difficult to open and penetrate. If one can open and penetrate it, then every single thing is the realm of Mañjuśrī; every step is the practice hall of Avalokiteśvara;
and every place is the seat of Samantabhadra—is this not a source of great joy? The gate of Mañjuśrī enters through the faculty of the eye.
The gate of Avalokiteśvara enters through the faculty of hearing; the gate of Samantabhadra enters through the faculty of mind.
Among the twenty-five gates of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, the six faculties serve as the foundation, and among these six, these three faculties are the primary ones.

Although there are eighty-four thousand gates in total, if one attains awakening and entry through a single gate, then all six faculties become permeated. This is what is meant by: "Once one faculty returns to its source..."
"The six sense organs achieve liberation. It is also said: "When one faculty achieves rest and recovery, the functions of all six cease.
This is precisely it. When I first attained awakening, I obtained these three gates; as they opened up in succession, all the faculties suddenly came to rest. Yet now, they function once more.
The ear alone is the most discerning. If a student of the Way does not attain this, it is impossible for Prajñā to manifest before them.

(Master Liu had a collection of his own accounts on the realization of the Way, in which he said: "Of the three gates and six sense organs, if one organ returns to its source, one knows that [enlightenment] enters through the *Śūraṅgama* [Samādhi]. It was from this that he attained entry.)
The scholar-official Zeng Hui was a lay devotee who had lived in the same quarters as Mingjue during his youth; however, they took different paths upon reaching adulthood.

During the Tianxi era, while the official was serving as the governor of Chizhou, he met with him at Jingde Temple. The official then took the *Zhongyong* and *Daxue*, cross-referencing them with the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and used these to verify the sayings of the Chan school with Mingjue.
Mingjue said, "This [the *Śūraṅgama*] does not even accord with the Three Vehicles, let alone the *Zhongyong*."
"Great indeed is the University! A scholar must understand this matter through a direct and swift path. Then, snapping his fingers once, he said, "Just realize it in this way!
Under these words, the official attained realization of the ultimate meaning.
The layman Minister Li Hao, whose courtesy name was Deyuan, read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in his youth; it was as if he were visiting an old home, and he cherished its meaning without forgetting it.
He entered the room of Mingguo, where Ying’an struck him in the chest and asked, "After you die, Minister, where will you go?
Startled, he broke into a cold sweat. Within ten days of withdrawing to reflect on this, he had finally ascended to the inner sanctum.

Wu Keci, whose courtesy name was Fuzhi and pen-name Kaian, was a candidate for the imperial examination who had achieved the rank of "Fourth Rank" (Sikuai) during the Chunxi era. He retired to live in seclusion at Zuoxi.

Suddenly afflicted with an eye ailment, he recited the name of the Bodhisattva (Avalokiteśvara), after which his condition was fully cured. Thereupon, he developed deep faith and read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Upon reaching the passage, "Empty space arises within your mind, like a single cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky," his understanding opened up as if the veil of ignorance were suddenly lifted. He subsequently composed the *Lengyan ji* (Collection on the Śūraṅgama).
Jie was a dharma successor of Beifeng Yin of the Tiantai school (as recorded in the *Fozu tongji*).

Song Wuyi was a native of Yuyao; his courtesy name was Yong’an. He was erudite in the Confucian classics and cultivated in learning, yet in his later years he took a profound interest in Chan studies.
He was summoned to the capital by the Imperial Court and participated in the compilation of the *Yuanshi* (History of Yuan).

Having obtained leave to return home, Wuyi visited me at Ding Peak to inquire about the essentials of entering the Way. I presented him with the *Lengyan jing* annotated by Master Huan as well as the correspondence between Dahui and his disciples.
From then on, Wuyi constantly sat upright with eyes closed, repeatedly investigating the purport of these two works. There was...
He entered into realization. In the sixth month of the ninth year of the Hongwu era, due to illness, he instructed his disciple Wang Zhi and others to write out a poem for his son;
he spoke and laughed with composure. Suddenly, waving a fan, he told his family members, "I am sitting in meditation;
do not disturb me. He then closed his eyes and passed away with the fan covering his face. At that time, the weather was intensely hot; by the time the body was enshrouded...
His countenance bore a joyful smile and was increasingly fresh and radiant (*Shuzhong Yunshan’an zá lù*).
Minister Yin Mai of Jinling, styled Qiuting, cultivated the practices of a *dhūta* while holding the rank of a high official.

He bound himself in meditation at Changgan Temple, purifying his mind through tranquil illumination. Having attained awakening through the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, his conduct was austere and detached. [This was also true of] Lu Wending of Huating.
Yang Cigong compared [the poem] to that of Chao Wen-yuan. It contains a poem titled "Reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* at Night on Mount Niushou," which says:
A single scroll of the *Śūraṅgama* not yet finished, The four mountains are silent, the evening woods empty. Suddenly encountering a magnificent hall, my body enters it;
Having attained the divine pearl, the Way is inexhaustible. Tree shadows seem to join where the clouds pass; The sound of the sutra is heard from afar amidst the moon.
In the Ming dynasty, it is commonly transmitted that after the spring had deepened, a deer and a bird still went toward the misty vines to pay their respects to Fǎróng.

(The Master also composed a poem of self-description which says: "In the desolate Chánggān Temple, for ten years I have grown weary of minced meat and gruel. Vastly free from thoughts of worldly ties, my mind of the Way is clear at midnight. At dawn, I solemnly simplify my practice of the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*. Donning my robes beneath the lamp, I read; through hearing, I awaken to non-arising. The mind becomes empty and the spirit returns of its own accord.

The Master himself recorded that when he was twenty-one, first beginning his study of the Way, he passed by the city south and saw the Buddhist temples and the dwellings of the people as if they were within a crystal void, cool and luminous. Returning to lie in the monk’s quarters, a reflected light happened to shine upon him, and he remembered being a child of seven or eight years old.)

My mind suddenly felt as though twenty years of mental cultivation had been forged into a single, seamless whole. During the period of mourning in the year Wushen, while practicing stillness in Mount Niushou, I read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
