When the masters of old commented upon the sutras, they invariably first provided a comprehensive exegesis. They relied on these "fish-traps" to measure the "bird's tracks.

The recent master [Zongmi] followed the path of Zao Bo and looked up to the Moon Canopy (the Buddha). His realization of the principle and his mastery of the teaching were both free and unimpeded in their horizontal and vertical dimensions; thus, he compiled this as the *Tonglu*.
To don the robe and grasp the collar, one must not follow the "Spiritual Source" (Lingyuan) while brushing against the "Venerable Summit" (Zuoding).
In the *Preface to the Zongjing Lu* by Chan Master Yongming Yanshou, it is said: "I humbly observe that the True Source is profoundly still and the Ocean of Awakening is clear and pure.
It is beyond the beginnings of names and forms, and devoid of traces of subject and object. At the very beginning, there was non-awakening, and suddenly the stirring mind arose."
The origin of karmic consciousness lies in the fault of awakened clarity. Because of this clarity, illumination arises; suddenly, the "seeing-part" (darśana-bhāga) is joined with it.
Following this illumination, the "object-part" (nimitta-bhāga) is established and arrayed. Like images appearing in a mirror, the sense-faculties and the physical body arise all at once.

Next, according to conceptualization, the world-systems come to differ. Finally, due to discernment, likes and dislikes become unequal. From this point on, one abandons the Truth and loses one's true nature, clinging to appearances and pursuing them.
It is called the accumulation of the emotional dust of attachment, the binding of the successive waves of consciousness, and the locking of true awakening within the night of dreams.
One becomes immersed within the three realms, blinding the eye of wisdom on the dark path, and crawling about within the nine abodes.
Thus, one is bound by the suffering of karmic fetters and loses the gate of liberation; taking form within that which has no body, one stands amidst that which has no destination.

Regarding the realms of rebirth (*gati*), there are twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*) when categorized by their physical bases (*āśraya*). When discussing the primary retribution (*vipāka*), there are twelve classes of sentient beings.

All these arise from the roots of emotion and perception, resulting in the distinctions between the physical basis and the primary retribution. Thus, within a realm that never actually shifts, one undergoes samsara in vain.

Within the state of dharmas that are inherently unliberated, one spontaneously creates bondage for oneself—like a silkworm in spring spinning its cocoon, or like a moth in autumn rushing toward a lamp.

With the threads of delusive thoughts born of the two views, one entangles the karmic substance of this mass of suffering; with the wings of ignorance and craving, one flutters into the fire-wheel of birth and death.
Using the resonant sounds of an echo, one debates the beauty and ugliness of the four modes of birth; with the mirror of the delusive mind, one...
Manifesting the three forms of physical appearance, the winds of thought—both contrary and compliant—then stir the ocean of awareness.

The waters of craving, delusion, and attachment nourish the sprouts of suffering. One pursues sensory objects exclusively, utterly unaware of returning to the source. Mad and chaotic cognitions arise, obscuring one’s own mind;
illusory forms and sounds are established and perceived as external phenomena. From this, a single atom engages with objects, gradually becoming a grating obstruction.
At the high peak of the Han [tradition], a single drop of water raises waves that eventually give rise to a massive surge capable of swallowing a ship.

Hereafter, as one seeks to return to the origin and restore the fundamental, there are differences in the faculties—whether sharp or dull—within the single realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, the three vehicles and five natures are opened:

some perceive emptiness and realize the fruit; some understand conditions and enter the truth; and some undergo refinement through the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, gradually becoming fully endowed [with the qualities].

Regarding the gate of practice: one may, through a single thought-moment of perfect cultivation, suddenly attain the Buddha-way. Thus, while there are differences in the realization of the fruit, the single nature is not distinct.

This gives rise to the names of ordinary beings and sages, appearing to differentiate between the aspects of the conventional and the ultimate. However, if one wishes to exhaustively investigate the subtle and penetrate the root, or to thoroughly examine the purport and master the source, then the fundamental nature is detached from all attributes;
it is ultimately quiescent and extinguished, transcending the distinctions of rising and sinking, and free from both bondage and liberation.
Regarding these distinctions: since there is no person remaining in the world, nor is there anyone who has entered extinction, the two limits are equal and the single Way is pure and void.
Consciousness and wisdom are both empty; names and essences are all quiescent. Transcending all that exists, there is only the single True Mind.

To realize this is called one who has "seen the Way"; to be ignorant of it is termed the beginning of birth and death. Furthermore, there are those of heterodox faculties and externalist lineages, and the small...
Lacking the wisdom of skillful means, they fail to understand the root cause of birth and death and remain ignorant of the fundamental nature of the views of self and other.

They merely seek to loathe clamor and reject movement, destroying appearances and analyzing sensory objects. Though they claim to savor stillness and merge with emptiness, they do not realize that they are burying the truth and obstructing awakening.

It is like failing to recognize that the visual impairment lies within one's own eyes, yet instead extinguishing the layered light upon the lamp; thus, they fail to exhaust the illusions within consciousness.

The body vainly avoids the empty shadow in the midst of the sun; this is but to exhaust the form and enslave the mind, losing strength and wasting effort—no different from treading on water to resist ice, or throwing wood to increase a fire.
How could one know that the double radiance resides within the cataract, and the empty shadow follows the body?
Once the diseased eye is removed, the double radiance vanishes of itself; when the illusory substance ceases, the empty shadow shall be extinguished. If one can turn the light back upon oneself...
Turning back from external objects to contemplate the mind, the Buddha-eye becomes clear and the shadows of karma vanish; the Dharma-body manifests and the traces of defilement are severed.
One strikes open the lock of doubt at the gateway of right wisdom and weeds out the grass of delusion from the field of true awakening.

Thus, the deep-seated chronic ailments that have penetrated to the very marrow are healed, and the stubborn attachments with roots as firm as a tree trunk are cut away. Then, when subject and object encounter the flames of wisdom, they are melted in the crucible of "Mind-Only."
Names and forms encounter the light of the Wisdom-Sun; it explains the ocean of the Single Reality. This is a dharma realized within; how could it reside in verbal expression?
Knowledge and understanding cannot exhaust it; seeing and hearing do not reach it. Now, for those who have not yet seen, I shall expound the wondrous vision that is beyond seeing;

for those who have not yet heard, I shall lead them into the perfect hearing that is beyond hearing; for those who have not yet known, I shall speak of the true knowledge that is beyond knowing. Not yet...

The one who understands achieves the Great Liberation that is itself liberation-free. It is hoped that by following the finger one may see the moon, and having caught the hare, one will forget the snare.

Embracing the One to clarify the source, one discards the provisional explanations to simplify the principle. Although this marks the general gateway to the Dharma-realm, one must discern the specific purport of the One Vehicle.
The meanings of the various natures and characteristics are perfectly integrated within the Great Awakening; as for the gates of the successive mutual entries, they exist only...
One may possess the various wisdoms and be subtly proficient, yet if one’s faculties are weak, one lacks discernment; if one’s learning is meager, it is difficult to be comprehensive.

Thus, one fails to realize that the two gates of *dharmatā* (nature) and *lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) are the essence and function of one’s own mind. If one possesses the function while losing the eternally constant essence, it is like having waves without water.
If one attains the essence while lacking the gate of wondrous function, it is as if there were water without waves. Yet, there has never been water without waves.

In water, there is never a wave that is not moist. Because the waves penetrate to the source of the water, and the water reaches to the end of the waves, it is like when one exhausts the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) to reach the essence (*svabhāva*), or when one attains the essence to reach the source of the characteristics.
One must know that essence and function mutually complete one another, and essence and characteristics manifest each other.
Having fully understood the origin of achieving Buddhahood, one is suddenly perfected without obstruction; clearly recognizing the path home, one proceeds directly—what doubt could there be? Or...
To depart from this and practice otherwise is to follow the deluded interpretations of others; it is like trying to extract milk from a cow’s horn or seeking fish from wood.

One may labor through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* in vain, ultimately achieving nothing. If, however, one relies on this essential principle, receiving it with faith and upholding it widely, one will be like a swift ship following the current, free from all obstructions.
Furthermore, if one encounters the force of a favorable wind while adding the effort of oars and rudders, one will swiftly reach the City of Jewels. Suddenly—
To ascend the shore of enlightenment, one may say that the provisions are easily gathered and the fruits of the Path are first realized.

It enables even a lowly laborer to fully inherit the estate of a great householder; it suddenly causes those of the Lesser Vehicle who have sunk into emptiness to instantly receive the prediction of Buddhahood from the Tathāgata.
Through this, past Buddhas-Kings attained Buddhahood, and future Great Beings rely upon this to realize the Truth. Thus, what single Dharma-gate could surpass this?
Yet they do not open. What single principle does not manifest? There is not a single form that is not *samāpatti*; there is not a single sound that is not a *dhāraṇī*-gate.
Tasting a single flavor, it is entirely transformed into *amṛta* (clarified butter); smelling a single fragrance, one enters the *dharmadhātu*.
Radiantly, the eyes that observe phenomena are opened, fully restoring the self-nature; serenely, the mind that seeks the jewel is guided.
Return together to the fundamental Dharma (The entire preface to the *Zongjing* [Record of the Source Mirror] fully elucidates the wondrous essence of the Śūraṅgama school;
therefore, I have excerpted and recorded it). *Zongjing* III: Question—Taking the Mind as the School’s Principle requires ultimate penetration.

Within the realm of sentient beings, the true and the false appear to be distinct and must not be treated as identical, lest they be confused with Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*). It is like heating gold and brass together: their authenticity and falsity are instantly distinguished, just as sand and rice are separated.

They cook together, yet there are differences between what is raw and what is cooked. I do not know with what mind one should take as the primary principle. Answer: It is exactly as you have asked. One must clearly discern the mind;
this subtlety is difficult to know, and only a Buddha can distinguish it. It is precisely because those of the Three Vehicles aspire to the Way that their perceptions differ.
They mistakenly point to the deluded mind and take it to be real; they recognize a false thief as their true son, plundering all the family treasures.
They collect fish eyes to pass off as dragon pearls, causing their eye of wisdom to go utterly astray.

Consequently, these ignorant children fall through the heavy gates of the prison of existence, and these perverted people drown in the terrifying waves of the river of views. The flames of play burn within the decaying house, and they forget their suffering.

Forgetting weariness, they lie in a great dream throughout the long night. Their minds and natures are deluded, for all have taken these conditioned thoughts as their own bodies and abandoned this true mind, recognizing instead external sounds and forms.
This is the error of both world-transcending non-Buddhists and worldly ordinary people.
Even those of the Three Vehicles who aspire to the Way—whether studying the Dharma or the Chan school—are likewise deluded regarding this mind, clinging to the Buddha.

Through skillful means, the teaching opens eight nets to correspond to four types of capacity. Yet, by leaping over a single thought-moment, one rushes far toward the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; thus, one's merit is wasted over great eons.
Departing from the place of treasure, one remains long submerged in the fortress of transformation; one's traces are exhausted upon the long road.

This is precisely the failure of those with provisional capacities who attain only minor fruits, and even of those within the Chan school who have not grasped the essential meaning. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: [The passage continues: "If one does not understand the true nature of the mind... and so forth.

The text says: The Buddha told Ānanda, "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have undergone various inversions, even to the point of failing to realize their own errors and thus entering the various realms of existence.
The commentary explains: These two kinds of roots are precisely the two minds of reality and delusion.
The first is the root of beginningless birth and death; this is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). This is the deluded mind.
The second is the primordially pure essence of beginningless bodhi and nirvāṇa; this is the true mind. It is also called the intrinsically pure mind (*svabhāva-viśuddha-citta*).

It is also called the "pure fundamental awakening" (*viśuddha-mūla-bodhi*). Because sentient beings have lost this fundamental nature and pursued only its superficial manifestations, they have been perpetually submerged in saṃsāra.
Knowing only how to transform the mind into objects, they mistake awakening for delusion; accumulating delusion upon delusion, they have passed through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Like dreams arising from dreams, they remain forever enshrouded in the midst of the long night of ignorance. Thus, a sutra says: "One should know that all sentient beings, from the beginningless..."
Come! The continuous succession of birth and death arises entirely from not knowing the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of nature that is pure and luminous.

By employing various false thoughts, and because these thoughts are not real, there is cyclic wandering. Because one does not understand the unmoving true mind, one follows the deluded consciousness of saṃsāra.
This consciousness has no substance of its own; it does not depart from the true mind, but originally, from the signless true source, it has transformed into a sentient being.
Delusory thoughts are like waves stirred upon a clear, still pool by the wind; though the waves move, they always abide within the source that is unmoving.

They are like flowers produced in the empty realm by the presence of cataracts; though the flowers appear, they do not depart from the nature of space. When the cataracts are cleared away, the sky is pure.
When the waves subside and the pool becomes clear, there is only the single true mind, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, this mind is not born from the past limit, does not abide in the present limit, and does not perish at the future limit. It neither ascends nor descends; it is unmoving, its nature and characteristics being one and the same.

Thus, receiving the transmission from the ancestors above, one takes this true mind as the fundamental principle. To practice apart from this is to be entirely ensnared by the nets of Māra; to seek elsewhere is to stray.
They have all fallen into the forest of heterodoxy. For this reason, his profound compassion is stirred and his pity increases manifold.

Thus, when the Second Patriarch sought this deluded mind and could not find it, the First Patriarch then transmitted the robe to him. Ānanda clung to this deluded mind, which is why the Tathāgata rebuked him.
As the sutra says: The Buddha told Ānanda, "If you now wish to know the path of śamatha," and so forth.

"Who has cultivated and realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)? The ancient commentary states: "That which is capable of deliberation is precisely the deluded mind.
It possesses the function of objective consideration and can also be called 'mind,' yet it is not the true mind. The deluded mind is a reflection upon the true mind; therefore it is said:
'Your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously luminous, essential, and wondrous true mind. (From *Sengbao zhuan*)

The tradition records that a monk asked Changsha, citing a verse: "Those who study the Way do not recognize the True; it is only because they have always recognized the consciousness-spirit (vijñāna). Since time without beginning, this has been the root of birth and death; yet deluded people call it the 'Original Person.

Is there not a true mind (citta) that exists apart from the nature of consciousness? Zhijue said: "The Tathāgata, during the assembly at the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, distinguished this matter for Ānanda in great detail. Yet you still do not believe it. Ānanda took that which investigates and pursues as the mind, and was rebuked by the Buddha. That which investigates and pursues is consciousness (vijñāna).

If one follows the functioning of consciousness according to phenomena, then affliction is called 'consciousness' and not 'mind. 'Mind' (manas) means recollection; when recollective thoughts arise toward external objects, they give rise to delusion—all of these are merely false consciousness and have nothing to do with the true mind."

It is neither existent nor non-existent. It is not defiled by existence or non-existence; the mind is neither stained nor pure, and it is not sullied by stain or purity. Even from delusion and awakening, or the ordinary and the sage, through walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—all these are but deluded consciousness, not the mind.

The mind is fundamentally unarisen and now likewise does not perish. If one knows that one’s own mind is thus, it is the same for all Buddhas. If one grasps at these images as real, then when the images perish, this mind will be severed.

Therefore it is said: If one clings to the perception of objects, this is identical to annihilationism. For the deluded mind grasps at objects to form its own substance, like an image in a mirror or a bubble on water.
To be deluded about water and cling to waves—when the waves cease, the mind perishes. To be deluded about a mirror and cling to images—when the images vanish, the mind is lost.

If the mind were to perish, one would fall into the view of nihilism. However, if one knows that the nature of moisture is indestructible and the substance of the mirror is ever-luminous, [the mind does not perish].

Then waves are fundamentally empty and reflections are originally quiescent. Thus one knows that the realm and wisdom of all Buddhas pervade the world and pervade space, while the body and mind of ordinary beings are like shadows and like images.
If one grasps at the derivative as the fundamental and takes the delusive for the real, then birth and death will manifest.
This proves that [the former] is not real. Thus, the ancient sages said: "One sees the ore but does not recognize the gold; only upon entering the furnace does one realize the error. Question:
Regarding the two minds—true and false—by what definitions are they each called "mind"? What is their essence (*tattva*), and what is their characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)?

Answer: The true mind takes spiritual awareness and tranquil illumination as its mind. It takes non-emptiness and non-abiding as its essence, and the true mark (*dharmatā*) as its characteristic. The false mind takes...
The shadows of the six sense-objects taken as the mind have no intrinsic nature as their substance; they take the act of grasping at objects and conceptualizing as their characteristic.

This deluded mind of discerning awareness and knowing has no self-substance from the beginning; it exists only in accordance with the preceding sense-objects. It arises when an object appears and ceases when the object departs.
Arising because of objects, the objects themselves are entirely the mind. Furthermore, because the mind illuminates objects, the objects themselves are entirely...
The mind takes objects as its domain; each lacks intrinsic nature and exists solely through causes and conditions. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* (or *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*) states:
"One falsely identifies the reflected images of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one's own mind.

Therefore, we know that this discerning mind does not arise in the absence of causes and conditions, but arises only from conditions. All phenomena born of conditions are impermanent, like forms in a mirror, having no substantial body.
Yet it depends entirely upon external objects; like the moon in water, it is unreal yet appears as a void-form.
To mistake this for reality is the height of folly. Thus, Ānanda clung to it but found no basis, becoming bewildered in the seven locations;

while the Second Patriarch realized its nature and did not give rise to it, attaining the Way in a single word. Consequently, the Second Patriarch could not find that mind of restless conceptualization he sought.
He immediately realized that the true mind pervades all places; taking this awakening as his fundamental principle, he subsequently succeeded to the position of the Patriarch for the first time.

Because Ānanda had been led by the Tathāgata to dismantle his deluded mind—probing minutely through each of the five aggregates, six sense bases, twelve sense fields, eighteen elements, and seven great natures—he reached the bottom of the matter: they were all merely empty and entirely devoid of self-nature. Since...
It does not exist through the conjunction of causes, conditions, self, or others; nor does it arise spontaneously without cause.

It is entirely the conceptualization of mental discourse and the consciousness of perceptions. Through this, one suddenly awakens to the wondrously luminous true mind, which is vast, all-encompassing, and pervades all places.
Thereupon, together with the great assembly, they realized this mind and praised the Buddha with one voice. Thus the Sūtra says: "At that time, Ānanda..."
Together with the great assembly, they received the subtle and wondrous instructions of the Buddha-Tathāgata, whereby they attained the Dharma-body without passing through the kalpas of the *saṃghī*.
This is identical to the First Patriarch’s direct pointing to the human mind and seeing one's nature to become a Buddha. (Mirror of the Source, Section 36)

Question: If objects fundamentally do not arise and the mind is constantly non-abiding, why trouble yourself by establishing contemplation? Is it not to turn one’s back on one’s own innate spontaneity? Answer:
It is for those who have not yet realized that objects fundamentally do not arise, yet desire to practice falsely by looking outward.

To cause them to contemplate within themselves and merge in darkness with true nature—just as one must first board a boat before crossing the sea; without a boat, how could one cross? To cultivate the mind, one must enter into contemplation. Without...

One contemplates how to clarify the mind; yet the mind is not yet clarified. When will there be correspondence? Regarding the various gates of contemplation explained above, the principle of the single mind is clearly manifest.
Although the understanding is distinct, practice must be in dark harmony with it. Through understanding, one brings about practice.

When practice achieves completion, conceptual understanding ceases. One must not cling one-sidedly to intellectual understanding, for to do so is to turn one's back on the Way and lose sight of the fundamental principle.

Only when practice and understanding correspond does one clearly manifest the Mirror of the Fundamental Principle (*zongjing*). As clarified in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, this is entirely for the purpose of practicing to see one's nature;

it does not rely on extensive learning or intellectual comprehension. Therefore, the Tathāgata rebuked Ānanda, saying: "This is not something you have achieved through diligent cultivation and realization over kalpas, nor is it something you have attained merely by recollection."
"Even if one upholds the twelve divisions of the sūtras of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions (and so forth), one cannot escape the calamity of Mātanga. ...
Up to where Ānanda said to the Buddha (and so forth): "By subduing former objects of attachment, one attains dhāraṇī and enters the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision," etc.
(Volume Four). Therefore, the Buddha told Ānanda: "You have often heard me, within the Vinaya, proclaim..."
This explains the meaning of the three determinations in practice. It continues: "If one does not cease from great falsehood, it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood;
to seek its fragrance is impossible. (Volume Six) It further states that one creates the ten causes of habituation.

They undergo the sixfold retributions of their interactions (Volume Eight). Thus, Ānanda, having already awakened to the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind and knowing that the fundamental source is not obscured, now again addresses the Sugata to secretly request instructions on practice.
Therefore, one should know that awakening comes first and cultivation follows; principle and practice must be in profound accord.
If one merely grasps a temporary intellectual understanding and does not aspire to progressive cultivation, yet wishes to realize ultimate Bodhi, it is impossible.
Such a possibility exists. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Even if one attains wondrous enlightenment, it is all rooted in lust, because the root of birth and death has not been severed.

One must directly protect the life-preserving bag [of the precepts] before crossing the ocean of karma. Once the ten habitual causes have been created, how could the sixfold intersecting retributions be avoided?
All arise from the mind of evil discernment and the emergence of inverted thoughts; they are caused by confronting external objects."
This is provisional. Driven by the deluded mind that pursues its own attachments, one fails to observe with the eye of wisdom and consequently falls into the karmic paths of ordinary beings.
Though one may indulge one’s whims for a single lifetime, one fails to consider how one’s body will sink for ten thousand kalpas. For this reason, all Tathāgatas proclaim it in unison.

One must truly engrave this upon one's bones; the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions all stand in awe. It is indeed enough to cause the heart to tremble. (The two preceding chapters encompass the primary meaning of the entire Śūraṅgama Sūtra.)
The *Biographies of the Sangha Jewel* (*Sengbao zhuan*) cites two passages from the *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Source). A monk asked:

"Regarding the principle of the single mind as the Mirror of the Source, as discussed by the Master, it is able to encompass immeasurable dharma-gates. Does this mind contain all dharmas, or does it give rise to all dharmas?"
If it arises, does it arise of itself, from another, from both, or without a cause? The answer is: this mind does not arise from these;
it is not accidental, nor from another, nor from itself. How is this known? If one says it contains all phenomena, that is "accidental" (horizontal);
if one says it gives rise to all phenomena, that is "from another"; if one says it arises of itself, then how could the mind...
Does it arise again? If you say it arises from another, then it cannot be self-originated; how much less could there be an "other"?
If you say it arises from both self and other together, then since neither self nor other exists, with what could they be combined?

If you say it arises without cause, you should consider that even when a cause is present, arising is not permitted—how much more so when there is no cause? The monk said: "Truly, it is not produced by any of these four natures."

[The interlocutor asks: "If [consciousness] is produced, why does the World-Honored One say that the mental faculty gives rise to mental consciousness? He says, 'The mind is like a master painter; there is nothing not created by the mind.
Is this not, then, [an admission that consciousness] arises from itself? Furthermore, he says that the mind does not arise in isolation, but necessarily arises in dependence upon conditions."
If volition arises when there is a condition and does not arise when there is no condition, is this not "arising from another"?
Furthermore, it is said that the six feelings arise with the six contacts as their conditions, whereby all dharmas are obtained; is this not then "arising together"?
Moreover, it is said that the twelve links of dependent origination are not created by Buddhas, devas, humans, or asuras, for their nature is such of itself; is this not then "causeless"?
[The monk asked: "How is it that [birth] arises? The Master smiled and said: "The Buddhas respond to conditions with various distinctions, stooping to accord with the capacities of all beings.
To generate goodness and destroy evil, they cause them to enter the First Noble Truth (paramārtha-satya). These are the expedient words of the four kinds of *siddhānta*.
It is like using an empty fist to show a small child; how could there be any real dharma therein? The monk said: "In that case, are all dharmas the mind? [The Master] said: "If it were so..."

This immediately constitutes two. The monk said, "If this is truly so, then is it that nothing at all is established, being 'neither"? He replied, "Even 'neither' constitutes two. Have you not heard what the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says:

'I am truly Mañjuśrī, yet there is no such Mañjuśrī. If there were such a thing, then there would be two Mañjuśrīs. Yet today I am not without Mañjuśrī; within this, there are truly no dual characteristics of 'is' and 'is not.'"* *Note:

This passage reflects the non-dual, middle-way perspective of Chan/Zen, where even the negation of extremes remains a duality, and true reality is beyond the conceptual constructs of affirmation and negation.*
Furthermore, he once said to his disciples: "The true orthodox lineage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is True Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).

As soon as one has a place of faith, one is fit to be a teacher of others. Regarding the gate of cultivation and realization, all quarters say that one's merit is not yet equal to that of the various sages;

however, according to what is permitted within the teachings, even Bodhisattvas at the initial stage can attain comparative knowledge, and it is also permitted to speak in terms of the provisional teachings, first by means of..."

One enters through hearing, understanding, and faith; subsequently, one achieves realization through contemplation that accords with this. If one enters the gate of faith, one immediately ascends to the rank of the Patriarch.
To speak briefly in terms of worldly matters, within the realm of sentient beings, there are three ways of knowing: first, inferential knowledge; second, direct perception;
and third, knowledge derived from the teachings. Regarding the first, inferential knowledge: for instance, consider this present body of outflows (*āsrava*), which every night...
A dream: the good and evil realms seen within a dream, with their sorrows and joys appearing so vividly, vanish when one awakens to find oneself sleeping peacefully upon the bed;
how could they have ever been real? All are merely produced by the mental consciousness and thoughts within the dream.

By this analogy, one can understand that events occurring during the waking state are all as unreal as those in a dream. Indeed, the objective realms of the three periods—past, future, and present—are fundamentally...
The direct objective aspect (*sākṣāt-bhāga*) of the eighth ālayavijñāna is transformed solely by the fundamental consciousness itself.

If it is an object of the present, it is the discernment of the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness); if it is an object of the past or future, it is the reflection of the independent, scattered *manovijñāna*.
Although the objects of dreaming and waking differ, both do not transcend the *manovijñāna*. Thus, this serves as an analogy for the principle of "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*).
It is manifest. Second, regarding "present cognition," this refers to clarity with respect to an object without depending on the establishment of an analogy.
For instance, when one presently perceives a blue or white object, the object is fundamentally empty of self-nature; it does not say, "I am blue" or "I am white.

These are all the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*), which spontaneously discriminates by its own nature, together with the simultaneous, clear mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which performs conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) and determines it as blue.

To take white as an example: the mind discriminates it as "color," and through verbal expression, it is designated as "blue. All of these are merely false constructions established by the mind’s own conceptualization (*manojalpa*).

Because the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are insentient, their substance does not establish itself, nor do their names call themselves forth. If this is true for a single color, it is so for all phenomena;

Yet, when these medicinal dharmas are bestowed, the ordinary and ignorant do not realize they originate from the sages themselves. These are all instances where the sages manifest traces among the common folk, appearing as if there were no Buddha."

The World. To guide and instruct the ignorant, the Great Sūtra states: "All the sūtras and books of the world’s non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are all spoken by the Buddha; they are not spoken by non-Buddhists. The *Prabhāsa-sūtra* states: "All the virtuous treatises existing in the world derive from this sūtra.

If one deeply understands worldly dharmas, these are themselves the Buddha-dharma. Why is this? That which is bound within the ten wholesome actions is identical to the five precepts. A profound understanding of the meaning of the Five Constants and the Five Elements is also similar to the five precepts. Zhou and Kong established these Five Constants as the medicine for worldly dharmas to treat and save humanity."

Regarding illness: Bodhisattvas who have emerged from provisional [expedient] states should, within the context of the universal clear-observation (sāmānyābhijñā-vipaśyanā), diligently cultivate it with a devoted mind. Through the power of great compassion and vows, and by practicing with tireless diligence, they receive the majestic empowerment of all Buddhas and attain sudden, luminous understanding. Thus, regarding the medicinal remedies for worldly dharmas, they shall forever be free from doubt or stagnation.

However, these worldly medicinal remedies are not an ultimate cure; they are like shifting one’s steps when limping. Although one may nearly exhaust the three realms of existence, one must eventually regress. This is like a painted robe whose colors fade and peel away; though a worldly physician may effect a recovery, once recovered, the illness returns. It is said to be "according to the illness. Furthermore, one should [treat] according to the illness...

As for the one who administers medicine: having understood the diseases of suffering and its origin, and recognizing the bliss of the path and its cessation, if sentient beings lack the capacity for transcendence and their faculties are so weak that they cannot endure profound transformation, one merely administers worldly medicine—just as Confucius and the Duke of Zhou established the roles of ruler and minister.

Establishing the certainty of father and son, and the rites, laws, and regulations—these support *śīla* (morality). Music harmonizes the mind and transforms customs and traditions—this supports *samādhi* (concentration). The supreme virtue and essential way of the ancient kings—this supports *prajñā* (wisdom). In the primordial antiquity of chaotic unity, it was not yet appropriate for the world-transcending [teachings] to appear.

The nature of the faculties at the frontiers does not call for the appearance of a Buddha; therefore, I dispatched the Three Sages to transform that land of Zhendan (China). Once the rites and righteousness had been established there, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras could then be trusted. As it was with Zhendan, so it is with the ten directions. Thus, worldly teachings were first employed to instruct them.

In *Dahong’s Reply to Wujin*, it says: "The ancients have said: 'In the past, before the True Doctrine had arrived, Confucius provisionally used [worldly teachings] to bind the mind. Now that we know where the Principle ultimately resides, we should no longer cling to these provisional teachings.

This is precisely the original intent behind the establishment of the teachings and the formulation of words by the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi; it is the beginning and the end of the Great Matter of Cause and Condition. Regarding the *Renlun* (Treatise on Humanity), which seeks to harmonize the beginning and the end in a single gate: that the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism both return to the true source is precisely this meaning. As for the "Inexhaustible Treatise" (*Wujin lun*), what place do these two [teachings] occupy? As for its judgment that Vimalakīrti (*Xūhuáng*) is the Great Brahmā Heaven (*Mahābrahman*), it is likely a partial reflection of the Tiantai school’s theory identifying Laozi as one who has emerged from the First Dhyāna.

One does not realize that the *Yùjīng* (Jade Capital) and *Xūhuáng* (Vimalakīrti) of the Daoist scriptures were merely excerpted from the Buddhist sūtras’ descriptions of Mount Sumeru and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, then compiled and assembled; they cannot be taken as authoritative principles.

To calculate the three tiers of Mount Sumeru using the three hexagrams of the *Zhouyī*, or the sequence of Xin, Ren, Gui, and Jia in the *Yushu*, or to measure the distance from the North Pole to the South Pole by the steps of Shùhài—who could possibly correct such errors? Having failed to investigate the source and flow of ancient meanings, [the author] has merely fabricated a system.

Furthermore, they do not rely on the great harmony of the vast flow [of the teachings], but instead selectively cite mere shadows and echoes based on their own limited measurements. To employ such views to unify the gates of the Dharma and bring an end to contentious debate—I know not whether this is possible.

Since the time of Yongming and Guifeng, the lecture halls of both Chan and the Exegetical schools have all sought to incorporate external doctrines to clarify their own breadth and magnanimity. Yet up to the present day, these blind masters and their students merely gather up fragments of the "Three Mysteries," plucking at the dregs and leftovers of those great sages to boast of their own achievements. It is as the ancients said: by adding water, one loses the *amṛta* (clarified butter).

Now, to criticize the milk of a donkey results only in excrement and urine. Qingliang had a saying: "Seeking a momentary minor reputation, one muddles the ultimate unity of the Three Teachings; practicing the poisonous seeds of false views becomes a profound cause for rebirth in hell. Is this not something to be cautioned against? Is this not something to be feared?

I have therefore briefly initiated the discussion on the *Haiyan* (Ocean Eye) treatise on the cessation of disputes, and respectfully recorded the fundamental teachings of the *Haiyin* (Ocean Seal). I have elucidated the profound meaning of how worlds are successively formed and sustained by the four wheels of wind and gold, citing analogous examples to follow upon these principles.

It was not my intention, with the narrow vision of a provincial scholar, to recklessly judge the tenets of the various schools or to lightly critique the sages of the past. Master Hanshan’s General Commentary states: "The world..."

This is the realm (*dhātu*). As for the statement that a wind-wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) sustains the world:

Furthermore, he takes the nature of emptiness to be the Great Way of Non-being and identifies this aspect of wind as the "pneuma of the void" (*ch'ung-ch'i*). Thus he says, "Concentrate the pneuma to achieve suppleness," and again, "Between heaven and earth..."
"It is like a bellows. This is the source of the Way of the Old Master (Laozi). The Confucians take the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*) to be the nature of the mandate of Heaven;

they point to the element of space (*ākāśa*) as the Supreme Ultimate (*taiji*), and they point to this element of wind (*vāyu*) as the primordial pneuma of chaos (*hun-yuan yi qi*). They claim that from this single pneuma all things are generated.
All of these fail to understand that [the world] is a transformation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). In the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (*Taiji tu*), black and white are intermingled...

"Clear" is the nature of awakening; "dark" is ignorance (*avidyā*). When the non-arising and non-ceasing [nature] unites with arising and ceasing, it forms the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which serves as the beginning of the production of all phenomena.
This consciousness has three divisions, and the world of empty space is its *nimitta-bhāga* (objective division).
As for the statement that there is a golden wheel that sustains the land, this refers to the "One Yin" spoken of in Confucianism.
The single Yang is called the Dao. It is regarded as the foundation from which heaven and earth are born. Within this, emptiness and stillness are dark and profound;
therefore, they are Yin. Movement and vibration are awakening and luminosity; therefore, they are Yang. Thus it is said: "Movement and stillness have their constant laws."

The hard and the soft are distinguished. Through movement and stillness, the Golden Wheel is formed, serving as the great element of earth; this is precisely the beginning of the initial formation of heaven and earth.
Movement constitutes the essence of Qian (Heaven), while stillness constitutes the essence of Kun (Earth). Thus, that which is above form is Heaven, and that which is below form is Earth.
This is what is meant by "Qian and Kun are arrayed in order, and the Yi (Change) resides within them. This, then, is Yin...
Before the Yang has taken form, movement and stillness, as well as hardness and softness, are already present. Therefore it is said: "When thought clarifies, the land is formed.
This refers to the *Yi* (Change) of the Pre-Celestial. As for the statement that "there is a fire-light which constitutes the nature of transformation," this refers to what the *Yi* describes:
the interaction of hardness and softness produces transformation. That which is above form becomes an image in heaven; it is the sun, the fire of the Great Yang.

It is the essence (*jing*). That which is below form takes shape in the earth; it becomes fire, which is the nature of transformation and change—meaning the transformation of the raw into the cooked and the transformation of existence into non-existence.
Furthermore, among the five elements of the post-heaven (*houtian*) system, *Xun* represents wind and wood; therefore, one drills wood to obtain fire.
This is because one has attained the nature of the primordial heaven. These four symbols (xiàng) are the sun within the day.
As for the statement that "there is a water-wheel containing the realms of the ten directions," this refers to what the *I Ching* calls that which is "above form":

It is complete. From the mutual interaction of the two delusions—the clarity of awakening and the darkness of emptiness—there arise the two great elements of wind and gold.

From the friction between wind and gold, there arises the great element of fire. From the vaporization of the moisture within the treasure by fire, there arises the great element of water. Thus, by reason of these four great elements, [the world is formed].

Thus, the four images (*xiàng*) of heaven and earth, yin and yang, the sun and moon, and the stars and constellations were formed. Therefore, the *Yī* says: "The Great Ultimate (*tài jí*) gives birth to the two polarities (*liǎng yí*);

the two polarities give birth to the four images, which constitute the substance of the eight trigrams (*bā guā*). It further states: "Heaven is honored and Earth is humble; thus Qian and Kun are established. The low and high are displayed;
thus the noble and the mean find their positions. Movement and stillness have their constants; thus the firm and the yielding are determined. This applies to that which is in Heaven.

Forms are completed; on earth, shapes are formed, and transformations become manifest. The four great continents, rivers, streams, lakes, and seas, mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees—all flow from the single vital breath (*qi*).
Yin and yang interweave, the five elements generate one another, and the eight trigrams (*bagua*) undergo transformations until they reach sixty-four.
Thus, the hexagrams of the *Yi* begin with Qian and Kun and conclude with Ji-ji and Wei-ji. The Scripture says: "When delusions intersect and erupt..."
Beings arise, taking one another as seeds; by these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession. This is the transformation of heaven.
Inferring from this, the world arises from awakened clarity and is manifested solely by consciousness—this is evident and beyond doubt.

The Confucian school follows the theory of the transformation of Yang into Yin to explain the five elements;

thus, they take the truth of the "two fives" and unite it with the truth of the "Ultimateless" (*wuji*), saying: "The five elements are one with Yin and Yang; Yin and Yang are one with the Great Ultimate (*taiji*); the Great Ultimate is fundamentally the Ultimateless. Furthermore, there is the theory of the "confusing movement of wandering qi. What is this confusion if not false conceptualization (*vikalpa*)? The Buddhist school follows the theory of beginningless false conceptualization to explain the four great elements; thus, they take the unarisen and undying *tathatā* to encompass the arising and ceasing of ignorance (*avidyā*), and say: "From the moisture of false conceptualization..."

When one recalls the water element and the others, in reality, all four great elements (mahābhūta) originate from the One True Reality. If they were not true, how could they share the title of "Great" with the Awakened Sovereign? Furthermore, there is the teaching that their essential nature is indestructible; if it were not indestructible, what else could it be but the True Constant?

Ultimately, the Confucian Five Elements are discussed at the level of ultimate refinement and subtlety, pertaining to the period after heaven and earth were established. The Buddhist explanation of the four great elements traces back to the very beginning of the creation of heaven and earth, asserting that the world is established upon emptiness (*ākāśa*), and that above the wheel of emptiness lies the wheel of wind (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), and so forth.

Moreover, it investigates the reason why this is so, stating: "Awakened clarity and empty dullness interact to produce agitation; even down to the mutual occurrence of delusions, which serve as seeds for one another. This is the account of the initial dependent origination of the world.

Furthermore, why did the sages of the Confucian school not extend their principles to this? It is because they remained within the framework of the social constants (gāngcháng); they merely sought to regulate and harmonize within the realm of yīnyáng and the five elements (wǔxíng), rather than seeking the Ultimate (wújí) outside of yīnyáng and the five elements.

This is what is meant by "the real being hidden and the provisional being manifest. In contrast, the Buddhists manifest both the provisional and the real simultaneously.
