It refers to the act of identifying the substance [of reality] as the self, and clinging to it through conceptual discrimination. What is meant by "wisdom" (*jñāna*)?

It refers to the realization that the substance is not the self, and being free from all conceptual discrimination. Someone may ask: "For one who has attained awakening, upon seeing a mountain they do not say 'water'; upon seeing a monk..."

[The questioner] says: "It is called 'conventional' (sāṃvṛta). Is it appropriate to call this 'non-discriminative'? [The answer: Within the essence of true quiescence, there is inherently present a spiritual mirror-like discernment.

What distinguishes this from the discrimination of consciousness (vijñāna) is that consciousness involves the arousal of the mind to discriminate, whereas wisdom (jñāna) is discrimination without thought-conception (nirvikalpa).
Someone asked: "If it is said that there is no-thought (*amanasikāra*), by what means is discrimination performed? I replied: "Do you not see the bright mirror? A mirror is insentient;

it does not possess the various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). How could it have a substance of thought? When confronted with the beautiful, it reflects the beautiful; when confronted with the ugly, it reflects the ugly.

Although it appears to have discrimination, in reality it has no thought capable of discriminating. How is this different from the substance of our own numinous mirror? Ten thousand apertures [resound] because..."
The wind whistles; what intention does the wind have in whistling through the myriad apertures? The various hidden depths are illuminated by the sun;

what thought does the sun have regarding illuminating the hidden depths? In all cases, the substance is fundamentally thus: it appears as if there is action, yet in reality, there is no mind that can act.
If you understand this, then even if you eat your fill all day long, it does not hinder you from saying you are full; for when has a single grain of rice ever been chewed to pieces? All day long...

When putting on clothes, they do not hinder one’s speech of "warmth," for how could they ever have hung even a single thread? They cultivate the Brahma-conduct of empty flowers and sit in meditation within a Dharma-hall of water-moons.
Truly knowing the numinous awareness, the single path is level and uniform; how could one distinguish between the body within and the body without?
You asked: "Outside the body, there is entirely no sensation. Now I ask you again: Apart from this body composed of the four great elements, do you perceive anything?
Or do you perceive nothing? If you say you do not perceive anything, you should be the same as earth or wood.

Since you say there is perception, are you able to discern it, or are you unable to discern it? Even if you were to lose your mind and were unable to discern it, [the fact of perception would remain].
To identify darkness as light and to point to form as emptiness, though called a mistaken presentation, is not without awareness and perception.

Moreover, when one points with an extended hand, there is nothing—whether space, objects, large or small, beautiful or ugly—that is not clearly known. If there were no awareness and perception, how could such things be reached?
In a sudden moment, when delusive confusion is instantly emptied and clinging emotions dissolve, one then knows that the empty space of the ten directions [is likewise].
This is the Great Perfect Mirror; without being polished, it reflects both the past and the present. The ocean of three thousand worlds is itself the King of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
how could it require the cultivation of realization to harmonize the ordinary and the sacred? Reaching this state, so-called false and deluded cognition will find no place to lodge.
Master Yongxi said: "If one uses cognition to cognize stillness, this is not cognition without an object."
This [delusion] is known through the breaking down of the subject and object based on words; it is the substance of this numinous awareness (*lingzhi*).

This is precisely what the Sūtra refers to as "establishing knowledge" and "establishing views," which is the very root of ignorance. Why is this so? It is because one wishes to wondrously accord with the substance of the numinous mirror, which inherently possesses non-conceptual knowing (*wunian zhi*).
This non-conceptual knowing does not tolerate any other object of knowledge. Furthermore, it says: "If by means of oneself..."

To know stillness is also not a knowing that lacks an object; it means that without relying on the causal conditions of words and letters, one’s innate faculties are not obscured, and one is able to know from birth.
To say it is not without an object is merely to preserve the trace of the "knower. Therefore, it is said: "The mind takes hold of the mind;
through what is not illusion, illusory dharmas are formed. Why is this? Because the awareness within the body of true stillness fundamentally does not depend upon any single dharma.

And yet, they are complete. If one does not realize [the truth] by relying on the essence, and if even a hair’s breadth of words regarding knowledge and vision remains, all such things fall into frivolous discourse (*prapañca*).
Your talk of "inside" and "outside" the body is not merely frivolous discourse; it is truly the ravings of a madman. Someone asked:
"Are the cognition and awareness of sentient beings the same as or different from the cognition and awareness of the Tathāgata? The answer was: "Sentient beings eat salt."
The Buddhas speak of salt as "not bland"; the Buddhas point to fire and call it "cooked," while sentient beings call it "not cold.

Although the expressions used for concealment and revelation differ in their paths, the nature of cognition follows the same track. If truth and falsehood were not separated, how could there be any difference between a sentient being and a Buddha?
Nevertheless, cognition is generally categorized into two types: first, true knowledge and true awareness; second, false [knowledge and awareness].

Knowledge of delusion and awakening—these two appear similar yet are different; though different, they are the same. Thus, by means of this, the ordinary and the sage are distinguished, and delusion and awakening are separated.
The *Preface to the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states: "That which belongs to the realm of blood and breath must possess knowledge;
all that possesses knowledge must share the same essence. This precisely refers to the essence of true knowledge, which sentient beings have inherently possessed from the beginning. And...

The Dharma-body of all Buddhas is eternally abiding; its essence is manifest and not distinct [from ours]. This essence is profoundly still and ever-quiescent, a vast and luminous awareness, which is called "mind.
It pervades the entire Dharma-realm and all worldly phenomena, undergoing birth, abiding, change, and extinction moment by moment.
Yet this essence is unmoving. That which the Tathāgata interrogates is intended solely to reveal this mind.

This mind is free from all names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), as well as from the distinctions of sage and ordinary person, defilement and purity, causal conditions and spontaneity, and the union of the real and the false—extending even to such phenomena as seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing.
As for what is called "the false," it refers to the present body composed of the four great elements, wherein the sense organs and their objects correspond, forming the aggregates (*skandha*).

The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) conceals the shadows [of the seeds] and, according to circumstances, grasps and sustains them, giving rise to discrimination. It involves taking and rejecting, love and hatred, flowing and shifting from moment to moment.
This deluded substance arises from the false conjunction of the sense organs and their objects; it appears to have a substantial body, yet when the organs and objects suddenly dissolve, so does it.
This delusion is also extinguished; this is precisely the "mind" that Ānanda pointed to. Why, then, would the Tathāgata not have rejected it? Therefore, he said:
"This delusory mind, apart from the external objects, ultimately has no substance. He further said: "Cognition arises because of objects; appearances exist because of the sense faculties.
Both appearance and seeing lack inherent nature, being like two reeds leaning against each other. This is what is meant by "appearing the same yet being different."
...as well. Someone asked: "Regarding this illusory substance, does it exist in dependence upon the Real, or does it exist separately apart from the Real?
If one says it exists in dependence upon the Real, then the false is identical to the Real. If one says it exists separately apart from the Real, then two distinct entities are clearly established.
Answer: "The false is established in dependence upon the Real, like ice being formed by freezing water. The Real is revealed through the false, just as fire is perceived through smoke."
And yet one knows fire. Indeed, solid ice is nothing but water; how can it be otherwise? Ice lacks the form of movement.
Though it is said that fierce fire is nothing but smoke, fire likewise lacks the appearance of billowing vapors. If one clings to them, a thousand divergent paths arise;
if one realizes them, the single Way is level and uniform. Since this is the principle of the Dharma-realm, the Tathāgata could not remain silent. Truly.
Because sentient beings do not comprehend the noble ones' skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), they give rise to attachments and fetters according to their respective words.

Within that which is neither identical nor different, they passionately construct distinctions. This is why the Tathāgata establishes difference in contrast to identity, so that truth and falsehood may be revealed;

he then refutes difference to establish identity, whereby both truth and falsehood are extinguished. In the sutra, the analogy of a single cloth with six knots is raised to explain this in detail. First.

The headcloth is a metaphor for the True; the six knots are metaphors for the delusory. Without the single headcloth, the six knots could not be formed; thus, the True is that upon which the delusory depends.

Without the six knots, the single headcloth could not be manifested; thus, the delusory is that by which the True is made manifest. Therefore, the Tathāgata said that the sequence of the knots being tied and untied is such that when the six are untied, the one also vanishes.
Thus we know that once the multitude of delusions has been eliminated, what "one True" could there be? From the perspective of the delusory...
True. Though they differ, they are the same. Someone asked: "The True encompasses the deluded derivative; the deluded reaches the source of the True.

If the True and the deluded are thus identical, why is it that the paths of sentient beings and Buddhas are always distinct? Answer: "Arising yet without birth"—the Buddhas enter nirvana within the ocean of consciousness of sentient beings.
"Quiescent yet constantly moving"—sentient beings fall into birth and death within the mind-source of the Buddhas. This is sought through principle."
If one examines their essence, they are identical; yet if one traces their actualization, they are worlds apart.

Although it is said that they equally possess the substance of sentience, since the empty kalpa, the Buddhas have understood according to reality, acted according to their understanding, and realized according to their practice;
whereas sentient beings remain deluded and have not yet understood, or have understood but have not yet practiced, or have practiced but have not yet realized. For this reason:
They are indeed different. However, as for those who are deluded and have not yet attained understanding, it is certainly impossible to discuss them;

how much more so for those whose mouths profess the true reality (*dharmatā*) while their minds chase after conditioned objects (*ālambana*), whose tracks tread upon empty space while their emotions sink into the ocean of existence. They vainly assume the hollow title of "one who understands," yet in truth they fall into the inferior conduct of the ordinary and ignorant.
Nevertheless, since the true and the false share the same source, when speaking of the inherent nature (*prakṛti-prakṛta*), there is no one who does not sever the false.

Yet one returns to the truth. To accord with principle without discarding the truth involves only the distinctions between the sudden and the gradual; this is spoken of in terms of phenomenal practice.
If, however, we speak in terms of principle, then the ten dharma realms are equally endowed with the one mind. As the sutra says: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings..."
Third, there is no difference. How could the fruit of the mind and the Buddha be distinct?

That which differs and cannot be made identical is simply that delusion has not been dispelled and reality has not been extinguished. In sum, it is only because the nature of Mind has not yet been clarified.
Someone asked: "Apart from the true and the false, is there a separate mind? Or is there no separate mind? The answer is: A house is a general name;
by means of the house, one manifests its formation and destruction. The mind is the primary substance; by means of the mind, one gives rise to its falsity and truth.

To provide a detailed illustration through metaphorical text, I shall again add these annotations: "One Mind" is a metaphor for empty space. "True" is a metaphor for light. "False" is a metaphor for darkness.
When it is bright, space is bright along with it; when it is dark, space is dark along with it. Thus, the true and the false seem to share the same nature as the mind.
Yet, were it not for empty space, there would be no way to manifest this brightness and darkness; therefore, the true and the false do not depart from the mind.
When one investigates to the ultimate limit, however, the substance of empty space remains vast and open throughout past and present, never being shifted by brightness or darkness. It is thus...
When one realizes that the single mind and its true or false aspects are utterly distinct, the myriad peaks arrayed among the Five Marchmounts all lose their forms of high and low;
the ten thousand streams drawn into the four oceans together forfeit their traces of shallow and deep. How could there be any further talk of "true" and "false"?
Question: Someone asked, "I have long been entangled by delusion (*moha*). I wish to sever it, yet I have no method for doing so. What should I do? Answer:

If you do not recognize from where delusion arises while wishing to sever it, how can you succeed? If delusion were to arise from the mind, then delusion could indeed be severed, but the mind itself would also have to be severed.
If the mind were to be severed, then the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the Buddhas, the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) of the Bodhisattvas, and the [path of the] Pratyekabuddhas... [would all be lost].
The twelve links of dependent origination, the four truths of the śrāvakas, and the ten wholesome actions of devas and humans can all be severed.

If their fruits could be severed, then that which is seen by the eye, heard by the ear, and even that which is tasted by the tongue or conditioned by the mind—as well as the moisture of water, the heat of fire, the movement of wind, and the solidity of earth—both mundane and supramundane phenomena—could all be severed. As for the various conditions mentioned above, they cannot [be severed].
Because it is severed, that which you call "delusion" likewise lacks any principle by which it could be severed. [The opponent] says:

"If it cannot be severed, then it will inevitably continue on. [The Master] exclaims: "What kind of talk is this? If even the very arising of the mind to sever delusion is not permitted, how could its continuity be tolerated?
According to what you say, then the substance of your delusion must actually possess the quality of being severed and extinguished."
It is at such a time. If it has never been severed or extinguished, what could there be to continue?

You fundamentally do not realize that from before the beginningless kalpas, due to the initial lack of awakening, a fleeting thought suddenly arose, which contravened the true mind and gave rise to shifting flux.

This has continued until now, with every moment of renewal failing to abide; even the appearance of the Buddhas in the world and the arrival of the Patriarchs from the West were all [manifestations] of your deluded sentiments.
Regarding that which is grasped and clung to: if one wishes to sever this delusion, one must clarify one’s own mind.

Once the self-mind is clarified, the boundless delusive conditions will, upon direct encounter, merge into a single essence. It is said: Delusion is not the mind; though it is not the mind, it does not cease. The mind is not delusion;

though it is not delusion, it is not luminous. When the mind is luminous, delusion ceases and clarity arises. When delusion ceases, the mind is clarified and delusion is severed. Because delusion is severed, form is empty.
Brightness and darkness do not obstruct the eye’s light; how then can what is seen be distinguished? Because the mind is luminous, there arise seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

If these are withdrawn back into the tip of a single hair, how can the mind be verified? Truly, it is because the patriarchs and ancestors did not understand that the calamity has reached later generations.
Should there still be doubts, I request those who have attained realization to provide an answer.
The Seven Articles on Master Zibo Ke’s Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: Regarding the Clarification of the Mind, what mind is being clarified?

Is it the true mind that is being clarified, or is it the deluded mind? If it is the true mind being clarified, since there is no delusion apart from the truth, whom else would one teach to clarify the true mind?
If it is the deluded mind being clarified, does the deluded mind possess something that can be clarified such that it is thereby clarified, or is it without such a thing?
"Can it be clarified by means of clarity? If there were a mind that could be clarified, Ānanda would have identified that which is capable of investigation as the mind;

however, the World-Honored One directly rebuked him and did not grant his request. The World-Honored One’s intention was to hope that Ānanda would turn his faculty back toward self-illumination and examine this investigating mind:
does it reside within the seven locations, or does it not reside within the seven locations? If it were within the seven locations, then [it would be] in those locations..."
When one investigates where the mind resides, it is found to have no location whatsoever. If it is not in these seven locations, then neither the sense faculties nor their objects exist;
where, then, does the mind rest? When Ānanda investigated the mind through these seven locations, his inquiry was not thorough and his response remained incomplete.

As for that which is thought to be capable of investigating and exhausting [the object]: one investigates it across the seven locations and finds it to be nowhere. Yet, what is this very mind that knows it is nowhere?

If one first considers the mind that was initially reckoned to be in those seven locations and investigates each one until it is found to be nowhere, then what is this present entity that is capable of knowing it is nowhere?
The former is the mind that exists in dependence upon the sense organs and their objects; the latter is...
As for this mind that exists apart from the sense organs and their objects, although it cannot be found when sought directly, the fact that it cannot be found must itself be my mind.
Thus Ānanda said, "I take that which is capable of such investigation as my mind.
However, since you have already investigated it through the seven locations, you have long understood that the mind which has a location does not exist. Yet, this mind that has a location...
Relying upon objects of perception, there arises cognition. This is a mind that has no fixed location; it is to rely upon that which has no location while yet having a point of reliance.
As for the mind that has a fixed location, Ānanda has already forgotten it. Yet, as for this mind that relies upon that which has no location, he still regards it as his "mind.
Therefore, although the Buddha rebuked him, Ānanda’s mind did not ultimately die. This persists even when seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing are all...
"Departing from [external objects], one maintains internal stillness in a secluded state; yet this is still but a matter of the shadows of mental discriminations regarding dharmas.

Ānanda, though his mind has found some degree of acceptance, he is ultimately unable to accept it fully because he has not yet realized that these dharmas and these shadows are merely different names for that which has no location.
If he truly knew that these dharmas and these shadows are fundamentally a realm of non-existence, [he would be liberated]."

It is drawn forth and arises; yet from the beginning, it possesses no inherent nature. Thus, one who discriminates this reflection further transforms into the wisdom that realizes there are no external objects (*an-artha-jñāna*).
Now, as for this wisdom that realizes there are no external objects, it leads from the ordinary person to the sage, and from delusion to awakening.

If one were to lack even this wisdom, then all sentient beings would ultimately be unable to attain Buddhahood. Is it not therefore fitting that the title of this chapter be "Clarifying the Mind" (*Mingxin*)?
The numinous light shines in silent stillness, pervading all with purity such that nothing else can enter it. It is impossible for there to be any phenomenon existing apart from this.

When ordinary sentient beings perceive phenomena as existing outside the mind, a fleeting thought arises; once a thought arises, there is a self. Once there is a self, there are limitations. There is "internal" and "external":
the internal refers to the sense organs and consciousnesses, while the external refers to the environment and its conditions. Because of this...
This is so. There is "self" and "what belongs to self. The three subtleties and six coarsenesses arise in succession. Originally, this is but a single, perfect, and eternal Buddha-nature.
After sentient beings give rise to thoughts, they become stuck in the sense organs and their objects; consciousness takes its lodging therein, becoming attached to both the subject and the object.

The "subjective" (neng) refers to the six sense organs; the "objective" (suo) refers to the six sense objects. These subjective and objective factors—the organs and their objects—have distinct and firm boundaries.

At the very beginning of the organs and objects, the fundamental radiance was inherently complete. This radiance originally lacks any nature of permanence; yet, in a fleeting moment of non-awakening, it transformed and gave rise to the organs and objects.
The light that becomes immersed within it is what is termed consciousness (*vijñāna*). Therefore it is said: "Having lost that essential clarity, the attachment to delusion gives rise to light.

The faculties and objects are that which is adhered to; consciousness is that which adheres. Just as visual consciousness cannot arise of itself but must be triggered by the two objects of light and darkness, if there were no external objects, consciousness would ultimately not exist.
Thus, for one who perceives phenomena as being outside the mind, there must be external objects.
Where there are external objects, there is deluded consciousness. Once there is deluded consciousness, there are boundaries.
The six sense organs then function in succession, unable to achieve a single point of unification; this is entirely because they are shrouded by emotional consciousness.

If one can, in this very moment, illuminate this single thought, then that thought is fundamentally non-existent. If even the thought itself does not exist, how could there be external objects? Whenever there are external objects that create obstructions, [delusion persists].

It is simply that one cannot, right here within oneself, directly penetrate and shatter this thought. Thus Zao Bo said: "The ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from the present moment;
the boundless ocean of lands, self and other, are not separated by even a hair’s breadth.

Tiantai Zhiyi said: "A single thought-moment possesses the three thousand [realms]. This means that when there is thought, the three thousand exist; when thought ceases, the three thousand vanish—this is called non-thought.
At that time, when the practitioner gives rise to a thought, it is realized to be ungraspable. When the thought ceases, one clearly illuminates the ten directions.

As the true mind gives rise to illumination, its arising does not rely on sensory objects; it perfects its original radiance, standing far removed and utterly detached. Outside the mind there are no phenomena—what, then, can be called "roots" and "objects"?
As the Sūtra says: "Vision depends on light; in darkness, vision becomes non-existent. This is what is meant by "falling into the roots."
The appearance of the sense-object (*viṣaya*). If it does not arise spontaneously from within, then all dark appearances can never obscure it.
This is the manner of uprooting the sense-objects. Yunmen said, "The entire great earth is the single eye of a śramaṇa. This is identical to what the Sūtra says:

Now, if your faculties have been completely uprooted, and you have even transformed yourself into supreme enlightenment, [you will realize that] the vessel-world is insentient while sentient beings are conscious.
How then do sentient beings awaken to the fact that the entire insentient vessel-world is [identical to themselves]?
It is also transformed into unsurpassed awakening. As for this "aperture," one does not know where it is located. Yunmen’s "head-word" has a place of illumination, and therein lies its function.
Even if you were to grasp the essential meaning of the sutras, it would still be nothing more than a single instance of illumination and function.

The mutual functioning of the six sense organs is not particularly extraordinary. If you can realize it through conditions and attain the phrase of swift resonance, you will immediately be able to take it up and put it into use.
Seeing while relying on light is what is called the way of ordinary people. Seeing without relying on light is what is called the way of the sages.
Yet, while owls and hawks can pluck fleas and lice at night and see the finest autumn hair, they close their eyes during the day.
One sees hills and mountains; thus, there is seeing due to darkness, and when light appears, seeing becomes non-existent. Furthermore, tigers, wolves, cats, and dogs see both by day and by night;

how do they differ from seeing that does not depend on light? When the faculties of cats and dogs are complete, they see; when the faculties of sages are complete, they also see. Even when the faculties are incomplete, they still see.
This extends to the crown of the head, where they see; to the feet, where they also see; and to the back and belly, where they also see—throughout the entire body.
There are eighty-four thousand pores, none of which are not seen. The Great Compassionate Bodhisattva has eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms;
each arm has hands, and each hand has eyes. At the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi* assembly, the Great Awakened Sage briefly cited the faculty of the eye among the six faculties.
Linji said: "Upon the lump of red flesh of you all, there is a 'positionless' [state]."
The True Person dwells within the six sense faculties of humans and emits a great radiance. Does this light wait for the attainment of Buddhahood to exist?

It is because the attachment to the false discrimination between light and darkness has not yet been eliminated that one perceives it only when relying on the sensory dust of light; without such reliance, one remains in darkness.

If the attachment to light and darkness were to cease, one would perceive [this light] even in the midst of the great night no differently than in broad daylight. Yet, within the daylight itself, the light does not increase.
Only when the faculties and their objects are utterly detached do both faculties and objects return to their original luminosity.

During the Jiajing era, there was a monk who transcribed the Avataṃsaka Sūtra with such profound sincerity and steadfastness that he was able to write the scripture in a dark room as if it were broad daylight. I did not dare keep this secret.
"I wish to share this with all under heaven. When Chan Master Qi Chushi was reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the passage: "Seeing depends on conditions, while clarity constitutes the cause;
when darkness becomes non-seeing, if clarity arises spontaneously, then the various appearances of darkness can never again obscure it. He then attained great enlightenment.

He realized that the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) do not initially reach one another; yet because sentient beings' arbitrary conceptualizations have not been eliminated, they wander within the darkness of ignorance.

One merely perceives light and darkness. In the teachings, this is termed *apramāṇa* (non-valid cognition). Because the sixth consciousness cannot examine names or verify reality, it follows the principle to subdue the emotions;
yet, arising from the objects (*viṣaya*) as the cognition of knowing, that knowing rushes toward external objects and is thus turned by the beautiful and the ugly.
If the sixth consciousness has not yet arisen, the five sense organs reflect like the light of a mirror, being entirely devoid of discrimination. This is what is meant.

This is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If, regarding the vision that perceives conditions, one is able to investigate through mutual negation how cognition arises from objects and how appearances exist because of the sense organs—observing until there is entry [into the essence]—then that which is not dependent on external things will not be forgotten, and that which has never before afflicted the visual essence will remain so.
This is the wisdom of no-objects through mental observation; it is called inference (*anumāna*). This is the contemplation.
It is not yet matured. One cannot use principle to subdue emotion, and because the faith that penetrates wisdom has not opened, one is unable to transcend the faith in supernatural powers.
All phenomena of light and darkness are neither light nor darkness; what connection do they have with my essence of seeing? The same applies to the sounds of movement and stillness.
At the Śūraṅgama Assembly, Ānanda reckoned that the present capacity for investigation and discrimination was [the self].
The Mind. The Buddha commanded Rāhula to strike the bell, wishing to cause him to realize the place where the sensory object of sound arises and ceases through its movement and stillness.

This was like Xiangyan, who repeatedly visited Muzhou without attaining realization; having departed, he heard the striking of bamboo and attained great enlightenment, whereupon he returned to Muzhou to pay his respects.
It was fortunate that [Xiangyan] did not reveal it to me at that time. There is a verse that says: "A single blow causes all that is known to be forgotten;
No further cultivation or maintenance is required. Every movement reveals the ancient path; One does not fall into the trap of silent stillness.

Xiangyan’s "that which is known" refers to the mind with which Nanda (Qingxi) was able to investigate and pursue [the source]. This mind is precisely the cognition that arises from sensory objects. If this cognition is not forgotten, then...

The faith based on intellectual penetration can never enter [the ultimate truth]. Even if you discourse extensively on the profound and the subtle, and your eloquence rivals that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it will not exceed the faith based on intellectual penetration.
Furthermore, the knowledge that arises from sensory objects is precisely the mind of subject and object that Xiangyan possessed before he had seen Master Muzhou.
Even a great spiritual friend like Muzhou could not cause this mind of subject and object to cease.
It must be forgotten all at once; one can only achieve this forgetting when one hears the sound of the bamboo being struck. Thus, we know that this matter can by no means be sought through emotion.
Seeking it through emotion does not transcend the deluded thoughts of the sense bases (*āyatana*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

If one thoroughly realizes that the sense bases and their objects have no inherent nature, then the cognition arising from those objects will also naturally be forgotten. To be able to perform such an observation is what is called "inference" (*anumāna*). ○ *Pǎn* (General)
If there are three kinds, they are what are called *prajñā* of letters (*akṣara-prajñā*), *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), and *prajñā* of true reality (*dharmatā-prajñā*).

Furthermore, these three *prajñās* are named the three Buddha-natures (*buddhadhātu*): the Buddha-nature as the condition-cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), the Buddha-nature as the cause of realization (*jñāna-hetu*), and the Buddha-nature as the direct cause (*svabhāva-hetu*).
The essence of the teaching in this Sahā world truly resides in hearing sounds; only after there is sound does there arise writing, and only after there is writing [does there arise the teaching].

Thereafter, there is the conditional cause (pratyaya-hetu) of Buddha-nature. By means of this conditional cause of Buddha-nature, one is then able to permeate and awaken the light that is inherently possessed.
Once this inherent light is opened, one can finally come to understand the direct cause (hetu-hetu) of Buddha-nature.

Since the direct cause of Buddha-nature has already transformed into emotional affliction (*kleśa*), if it is not brought into accord with the conditional cause through realization, then the direct cause will ultimately never be realized. This is the conditional cause.

Although one may accord with the direct cause (*zhengyin*), if it is not stimulated by the subtle perfuming of the contributing cause (*yuan-yin*), then the revealing cause (*liao-yin*) can ultimately never manifest of itself.
"Contributing cause" is an alternative name for the *samādhi* of words and letters; "revealing cause" is an alternative name for the faculty of hearing sounds.
If a student can apply this principle to other categories and expand upon it, then the *samādhi* of Mañjuśrī’s words and letters and—
The Samādhi of Avalokiteśvara’s Hearing of Sounds does not reside in Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, or Śākyamuni Buddha;

In the following passage from the Second Patriarch’s *Treatise on the Dharma-Gate of Settling the Mind*, it is said: "When deluded, the person pursues phenomena; when awakened, phenomena pursue the person.

All these are but dreams. If one realizes that the mind is quiescent and there is not a single place where a thought stirs, this is called perfect awakening (*samyaksambodhi*). Question: What is the manifestation of one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*)?
Answer: One perceives all phenomena as existing; yet their existence is not inherent. It is the mind itself that calculates and conceives them to be existent.
One perceives all phenomena as non-existent; yet they are not non-existent by their own nature. It is one's own mind that conceives them as non-existent. This applies even to all phenomena:
they are all conceived as existent or non-existent by one's own mind.

Furthermore, if a person has committed all manner of transgressions, upon seeing the Dharma-King within themselves, they immediately attain liberation. If one attains liberation through the activity [of practice], it is by means of the power of the breath.

The Patriarch said, "If it is not samādhi, how can it be named? Since you have not realized anything, what is there to be realized in 'non-realization'?

When he reached the third question at the monastery of Dinghui Zong, he asked, "In your practice of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*), are they one or two? A man named Póluántu replied, "This concentration and wisdom of mine are not one."
"It is neither two. The Patriarch said, "Since it is neither one nor two, why do you call it 'concentration' (samādhi) and 'wisdom' (prajñā)? He replied, "In concentration, there is no concentration;
in wisdom, there is no wisdom. One is not one, and two is not two. The Patriarch said, "When it is one, it is not one; when it is two, it is not two."
"Since it is neither concentration nor wisdom, by means of what concentration and wisdom could it be known? He replied, "Neither one nor two; concentration and wisdom can know this.
That it is neither concentration nor wisdom is likewise so. The Patriarch said, "If wisdom is not concentration, then how can it be known? 'Neither one nor two'—[how can that be known]?"
"Who possesses concentration and who possesses wisdom? When they reached the fourth section on the "Principle of Preceptual Practice," a question was asked:

"What is called 'precept' (śīla)? What is called 'practice' (caryā)? Regarding this preceptual practice, are they one or two? A certain worthy one replied: "One is two, and two are one; both are born from that.
Relying on the teaching without defilement—this is called preceptual practice. The Patriarch said: "Your statement that one 'relies on the teaching' is precisely [the presence of] existence."
If both [inner and outer] are simultaneously destroyed by defilement, how can one say they rely on the teachings? These two are contradictory; they do not reach the practice.
When inner and outer are not clear, how can it be called precept? He said: "I have inner and outer. Once he has fully known this, he immediately attains thorough penetration;

this is precisely the practice of the precepts. If one speaks of contradiction, then both are right and both are wrong. When speech reaches purity, it is the precept and it is the practice. The Patriarch.
He said: "If it is both 'is' and 'is not,' why speak of purity? Since one has attained penetration, why compete over internal and external?

When asked by the proponent of the fifth school, the School of Non-Attainment (Wude-zong): "You say there is non-attainment; what is attained through non-attainment? Since there is nothing to be attained, there is likewise no attainment of attainment.
The venerable Baojing replied: "I speak of non-attainment, but this is not the attainment of non-attainment. I shall now explain the attainment of attainment."

"Non-attainment is attainment. The Patriarch said: "If attainment is already non-attainment, then attainment is also non-attainment. Since you speak of 'attaining attainment,' what is there to attain in attaining attainment?
He replied: "To see attainment as non-attainment—this non-attainment is itself attainment. If one sees non-attainment, this is called attaining attainment."
The Patriarch said: "To attain is not to attain; to attain attainment is to have no attainment. Since there is nothing to be attained, how can one attain attainment?
Upon reaching the sixth school, the School of Quiescence (Jijing Zong), he asked: "What is called 'quiescence'? Within this Dharma, what is still and what is quiescent?
A venerable master replied: "This mind is unmoving; this is called quiescence. To be unstained by phenomena is called stillness."
The Patriarch said, "If the fundamental mind were not inherently quiescent, it would require the support of stillness. Since it is originally quiescent, what need is there for stillness?

The other replied, "All phenomena are fundamentally empty. Because they are empty of emptiness, they are called 'quiescent' with respect to that emptiness of emptiness. The Patriarch said, "When even the emptiness of emptiness is empty, all phenomena are likewise so.
Quiescence is without mark; what is there to be stilled, and what is there to be quiescent?"
King Yijian questioned Master Poluotiduo: "What is the Buddha? Poluotiduo replied: "To see one's nature is to see the Buddha. The King asked: "Does the Master see your own nature?
Poluotiduo replied: "I see the Buddha-nature. The King asked: "Where does this nature reside? Poluotiduo replied:
"The nature resides in its functioning. The King asked: "What is this functioning? I do not perceive it now. Poluotiduo replied: "It is functioning right now. The King—

[The King] himself did not recognize [him]. The King said, "Since you, Master, have seen [this], you speak of its functioning. Does it exist within my own person? Deyi replied, "If Your Majesty functions, it is manifest everywhere before you. If Your Majesty does not function, its essence is difficult to perceive. The King asked, "When it is being used, in how many places does it appear? The Master said, "When it emerges in use, there are eight instances. He continued: 1. When the King issues an edict, it is the functioning of the Way. 2. When the King sits upon the throne, it is the functioning of the Way. 3. When the King bestows wealth and honors, it is the functioning of the Way. 4. When the King governs the people, it is the functioning of the Way. 5. When the King hears sounds, it is the functioning of the Way. 6. When the King sees forms, it is the functioning of the Way. 7. When the King smells fragrances, it is the functioning of the Way. 8. When the King tastes flavors, it is the functioning of the Way. Thus, when the King acts, he is the Buddha; when he speaks, he is the Dharma; and when he moves, he is the Sangha. There is no place where the Way is not present. It is like the moon reflected in water—wherever the water is, the moon appears. Therefore, it is said: "The ten thousand phenomena are all the Buddha-nature; the six sense objects are all the true source. This is what is meant by "the functioning of the Way. It is not something that can be grasped by the mind or sought through words. It is only when one is free from conceptualization and thought that one can see it for oneself. This is the ultimate teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. One must realize it within one's own mind; it cannot be attained through external seeking. If one seeks it outside, one will wander in birth and death for countless eons. Therefore, the Master said: "If you wish to see the Buddha, look at your own mind. If you wish to see the Dharma, look at your own nature. This is the essential point. Do not seek elsewhere. If you seek elsewhere, you will lose your own true self. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is the Buddha; the Buddha is the mind. There is nothing else. This is the great matter of life and death. One must resolve it decisively. Do not let it pass in vain. If you understand this, you will know that from the very beginning, you have been the Buddha. There is no need for further cultivation or practice. Just as the sun shines in the sky, it illuminates everything without discrimination. Thus, the functioning of the Way is vast and boundless. It is not confined to any single place. It manifests in all things and all activities. This is the true meaning of "the functioning of the Way. One must realize this for oneself. Do not rely on others' words. If you rely on others' words, you will fall into delusion. Therefore, the Master said: "Do not seek the Way from others; seek it within your own mind. This is the final instruction. Practice this diligently, and you will attain liberation. This is the path to enlightenment. May all beings realize this and attain Buddhahood. Namu Amida Butsu. Namu Amida Butsu. Namu Amida Butsu. The verse declares: In the womb it is called the body; dwelling in the world it is called a person. In the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing. In the nose it discerns odors;
in the mouth it engages in discourse. In the hands it grasps; in the feet it moves with speed. It manifests everywhere, encompassing the entire Dharma-realm;
yet when withdrawn, it does not exceed the size of a minute speck of dust. Those who recognize it know it as Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*jinghun*).

Master Jinshan Puning raised this case, saying: "Though it be so, you see only the sharpness of the chisel’s tip, yet you do not see the squareness of the chisel’s head. If it were I, Jinshan, it would not be thus: having eyes, one does not see; having ears, one does not hear; having a nose, one does not know fragrance; having a tongue, one does not engage in discourse;

having a body, one does not perceive touch; having a mind, one does not grasp at objects. When a single thought accords with reality, the six sense-faculties are liberated. I dare ask the various Zen communities: is this the same as what came before, or is it different?

[Seal] Official Liu Jingchen, Minister of the Imperial Secretariat, composed this verse to clarify the Mind-Ground: In the womb, it is the body; following conditions, it assumes form to manifest true nature. If one clearly perceives the events of that time, day and night it radiates light and turns the Wheel of Dharma. Dwelling in the world, it is called a person; I now know this to be the Buddha.

The body of Kāśyapa is capable of enduring the turmoil and the dark confusion; each and every one buries a priceless treasure. That which is in the eye is called seeing: last night at the third watch, a flash of lightning struck, shattering the sense-bases and objects until not a single thing remained;

only then did he realize his own body sat within the Palace of the Empty King. That which is in the ear is called hearing: how could it be that the darkness and obscurity fill the entire universe? Who knows that after the beating of drums and the ringing of bells, all the wondrous gates were opened together throughout the night? That which is in the nose discerns fragrance: within the sandalwood forest, one hears it directly; its scent pervades the earth and heavens, known only to oneself—when meeting face-to-face, it is difficult to recognize.

That which is in the tongue engages in discourse: the ocean of skillful means opens the gate of Dharma-giving. If two who know the sound meet, what need is there for silence or many words? That which is in the hand grasps and releases...

Opening and closing, gathering and grasping, all depend on "I. He laughed at Pang Jushi’s words from years past: "Carrying water and hauling firewood is not yet extraordinary; when the feet move and run, the straw sandals are worn through, yet there is no news.

I now clearly inform you: it is simply that by not returning, one returns as soon as one arrives. (○ Master Mingdao, discussing the *Zhongyong*, on the passage concerning the soaring hawk and the leaping fish, said: "If you recognize it, it is lively and vibrant; if you do not recognize it, you are merely playing with your own spirit.")
The Second Patriarch, Master Ke, said, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to bring it to rest. The First Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will bring it to rest for you.
He replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unattainable. The Patriarch said, "I have finished bringing your mind to rest. The Patriarch then said:

Ordinary people claim that the past is different from the present, and that the present is different from the past; they further maintain that apart from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there exists a separate Dharma-body.

When understood correctly, however, the very mind of the present five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is perfect and pure *nirvāṇa*. This mind is fully endowed with the myriad practices. As the Fourth Patriarch, Daizong, pointed out to Master Rong:
"The hundreds of thousands of wondrous gates all return to the single square inch [of the heart]; the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all..."
Within the source of the mind, all gates of concentration, all gates of wisdom, and all gates of practice are fully complete.
The wondrous functions of supernormal powers reside entirely within your own mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are fundamentally empty and still.
All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world to escape, and there is no bodhi to seek. As for humans and non-humans, their nature...
The marks are equal; the Great Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation. You have now attained such a gateway;
it lacks nothing further. How does this differ from that of a Buddha?
The Fifth Patriarch said: "If you wish to know the essentials of the Dharma, the mind is the root of the twelve divisions of the scriptures. There is only the Single Vehicle Dharma;
that which is the Single Vehicle is the one mind. Simply maintain this one mind, and it is the gate of the true suchness of the mind."
The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, said: "You all, people of this world, your own minds are the Buddha; do not harbor further doubt.
Outside of the mind, there is not a single dharma that can be established; it is all from the mind that the myriad kinds of dharmas arise.
As the Sūtra says: 'When the mind arises, the myriad dharmas arise. These dharmas are non-dual, and the mind is likewise so. Its Way is pure and free from all [defilements]."
"Disciples, do not contemplate purity, nor empty your minds. This mind is non-dual; there is nothing to be grasped or rejected.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, if the mind is always straightforward, that itself is the Pure Land. Those who rely on my words will certainly attain Bodhi. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"The wondrous nature of worldly people is fundamentally empty; there is not a single dharma to be obtained. The true emptiness of one's own nature is likewise so."

It is so. Do not hear my teaching of emptiness and then immediately become attached to emptiness. Above all, do not be attached to emptiness. If you sit in meditation with a mind of emptiness, you will instead become attached to the indeterminate.
Emptiness is like the world of space, which can contain the forms and images of all things: the sun, moon, and stars; mountains, rivers, and the great earth;
springs, streams, and brooks; grasses, trees, and forests; evil people and good people; evil dharmas and wholesome dharmas; and the heavens.
The halls and grounds of hell, all the great oceans, and the Mount Sumerus—all these exist within space. The emptiness of human nature is likewise so.
O Good Friends, ordinary beings are themselves Buddhas; afflictions are themselves Bodhi. When the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary being;
when the succeeding thought is awakened, one is a Buddha. When the preceding thought clings to objects, it is affliction; when the succeeding thought leaves objects, it is Bodhi.
"Disciples, good spiritual friends, you should use great wisdom to shatter the afflictions and defilements of the five aggregates.
By practicing in this way, you will certainly attain the Buddha-way and transform the three poisons into precept, concentration, and wisdom.
This dharma-gate of mine arises from one prajñā and gives birth to eighty-four thousand forms of wisdom. Why is this? Because sentient beings in the world possess eighty-four thousand afflictions."
If there is no affliction, wisdom shall manifest. What is called "non-thought"? To see all phenomena with a mind that is unstained by attachment—this is non-thought.
Its function pervades all places, yet it does not cling to any place.

It merely purifies the fundamental mind so that the six consciousnesses emerge from the six gates; amidst the six sense objects, they are neither stained nor confused, coming and going with freedom and penetration.
To act without obstruction is precisely the samādhi of prajñā. This sovereign liberation is called the practice of non-thought. The Master said:
"O Great Assembly, for worldly people, the physical body is the city; the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are the gates. Outwardly there are five gates, and inwardly there is the gate of the mind.
The mind is the ground, and the nature is the king. The king dwells upon the ground of the mind; where the nature is, the king is. Where the nature departs..."
The King has none. Nature resides within body and mind; when nature departs, body and mind perish. The Buddha acts from within nature; do not seek him outside the body.
When self-nature is deluded, one is a sentient being; when self-nature is awakened, one is the Buddha. Compassion is Avalokiteśvara.
Joyful relinquishment is named Śrīkṣetra; the ability to bring tranquility is Śākyamuni; impartiality and rectitude are Amitābha. The self and others are Mount Sumeru;
a deviant mind is the ocean water; afflictions are the waves; harmful poison is the evil dragons; falsehood is the ghosts and spirits;
worldly toil is the fish and turtles; greed and anger are the hells; ignorance is the realm of animals. A virtuous friend is always...

If one practices the ten wholesome deeds, the heavenly realms will be reached. If one eliminates the notions of self and other, Mount Sumeru will topple. If one is free from deviant thoughts, the ocean waters will dry up.

If afflictions cease to exist, the waves will subside. If harm and poison are removed, the fish and dragons will vanish. Within the ground of one’s own mind, the Tathāgata of awakened nature emits a great radiance that shines outward;
the six sense gates become pure, and it is able to shatter the heavens of the six classes of desire. When this intrinsic nature shines inwardly, the three... [text fragment ends]
Poison is immediately removed; the offenses of hell and other realms are extinguished all at once. Internally and externally, one becomes transparently clear, no different from the Western Land.

If one does not practice this cultivation, how can one reach that place? Regarding the three categories of the Dharma-gate, they are the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas).

The "elements" refer to the eighteen elements, which consist of the six objects, the six sense organs, and the six consciousnesses. Because the self-nature is capable of containing all phenomena, it is called the ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness).
If thought arises, it is the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*). It gives rise to the six consciousnesses, emerges through the six gates, and perceives the six sense objects.
Thus, the eighteen realms all arise as functions from self-nature. Fahai asked about "mind itself is Buddha. The Patriarch said:
"The non-arising of the preceding thought is mind; the non-extinguishing of the succeeding thought is Buddha. To manifest all phenomena is mind; to be free from all phenomena is Buddha."
This is precisely the Buddha. [He] answered Attendant Bye: "Luminosity and ignorance—these two natures are non-dual.

This non-dual nature is the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As for this true nature: it does not diminish when among the foolish and ordinary; it does not increase when among the worthy and sages. It is not disturbed by afflictions (*kleśa*);
it is not quiescent while abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). It is neither annihilated nor eternal; it neither comes nor goes."
In the midst, as well as within and without, its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*); it is eternally abiding and unchanging, and is therefore called the Way (*mārga*). Question:

If it is neither extinguished nor born, how does this differ from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)? Answer: The non-Buddhists speak of non-extinction and non-birth by intending to stop birth through extinction.
By means of arising, extinction is revealed; yet even extinction is not extinguished. Arising is said to be non-arising; I speak of neither arising nor extinction.
It was originally without arising, and now it is likewise without extinction. This is why it differs from the heterodox paths.

Chan Master Zhītōng had read the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* more than a thousand times, yet he did not understand the three bodies or the four wisdoms. The Patriarch said: "As for the three bodies: first is the pure Dharma-body."
The Dharmakāya is your nature; the Sambhogakāya is your wisdom; and the thousands of billions of Nirmāṇakāyas are your practice.
If one were to speak of the three bodies apart from the fundamental nature, they would be called "having bodies but lacking wisdom.

If one were to discard the three bodies and lack self-nature, they would be called the "four wisdoms of Bodhi. [The questioner asked: "May I hear the meaning of these four wisdoms? [He] replied: "Since..."

When one realizes the three bodies (*trikāya*), the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) are naturally clarified. If one were to speak of the four wisdoms apart from the three bodies, this would be called "having wisdom but no body.

As the verse says: "The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure; The Wisdom of Equality has a mind free from affliction. In the sphere of Wondrous Observation, seeing is not a result of effort;
The Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks is identical to the Perfect Mirror. The five, eight, six, and seven [consciousnesses] transform as fruit and cause; however—
Using names and words, there is no real nature. If one leaves no lingering attachment toward the place of transformation, then amidst all profuse activity, one forever dwells in the *nāga-samādhi*.

A monk asked Changsha Chengyan: "The sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses have been shown to have no substance once they are brought forth; how then can the eighth consciousness be transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom? Chengyan showed him this verse: "The seven arise depending on the one's cessation; The one ceases while sustaining the seven's arising."

"First, cessation ceases; the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] never again undergo transition. (Jiyin said: Because the five consciousnesses and the eighth [consciousness] take the direct objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) as their objects, it is said that the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is To Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is identical to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

These all transform only at the stage of fruition (*phala*). Since the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] have no separate substance, they merely function to cognize; thus, their nature is equal. These all transform within the causal stage (*hetu*). (Zibai said: The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* takes the eight consciousnesses, the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*), the five dharmas (*pañcadharma*), and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)—the transformation of consciousness into wisdom—as its primary tenet.

Those who do not understand this meaning think that after attaining the mind, there is nothing more to do. They do not know that while the Way can be realized suddenly (*tunwu*), emotions must be eliminated gradually. This is the path of the mind transmitted by the Patriarchal Founder. The method of transforming consciousness into wisdom in the *Laṅkāvatāra* is for the purpose of treating these emotions.)

[This is] complete. If one hears the Way yet does not cultivate purity, this must be the work of demons or externalists; within my Tathāgata’s Dharma, such a thing simply cannot exist. The Master showed [this principle] to the monk Zhiche, saying:

"If Buddha-nature were permanent, what would be the need to speak further of the various dharmas of good and evil? Even until the end of kalpas, there would not be a single person who could give rise to the bodhicitta.
Therefore, when I speak of impermanence, it is precisely the True Permanence taught by the Buddha. Furthermore—

If all phenomena were merely impermanent, then every individual thing would possess its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) that undergoes birth and death, and the truly eternal nature would have places where it does not pervade.
Therefore, when I speak of "eternity," this is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the true meaning of impermanence.
This is because ordinary people and non-Buddhists cling to a false eternity, while those of the two vehicles conceive of eternity as being non-existent.

Together with these, they constitute the eight inversions. Therefore, within the definitive teachings on *nirvāṇa*, he refutes those biased views and clearly proclaims the true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true purity. You now rely on the words while turning your back on the meaning;

by taking what is annihilated as impermanent and what is fixedly mortal as permanent, you have misinterpreted the Buddha’s perfect, wondrous, and final subtle words. Even if you were to read them a thousand times, what would it avail?
[On] Benefits. The monk Zhidao, having read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, requested instruction, saying:
"All sentient beings possess two bodies, namely the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The form-body is impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing;

the dharma-body is permanent, devoid of cognition and awareness. The sūtra states: 'When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss. I wonder which body it is that attains this quiescent extinction?"

"You experience pleasure with the body. The Patriarch said, "You are a son of the Śākya; why do you practice the heterodox views of annihilationism and eternalism, and discuss the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle?
According to what you say, you claim that apart from form and sound there exists a separate Dharmakāya, and that one seeks quiescence by departing from birth and extinction.
Furthermore, you infer the permanence and bliss of Nirvāṇa, asserting that it possesses physical enjoyment. The Buddha [taught this] for the sake of all deluded people who cling to..."
The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in combination constitute the characteristic of the self-body; the differentiation of all phenomena constitutes the characteristic of external objects.

One takes birth as good and death as evil, thus suffering in vain through saṃsāra. Taking the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa as the characteristic of suffering—out of compassion for this, the Buddha reveals the true bliss of nirvāṇa:
in each moment there is no characteristic of arising, in each moment there is no characteristic of ceasing, and furthermore, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
It can be extinguished; this is the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*śānti*). At the moment of its manifestation, there is no measure of that which manifests;
this is what is called "eternal bliss. Listen to my verse: "The unsurpassed Great Nirvāṇa is perfectly luminous, eternally quiescent, and illuminating.
The ignorant call it death; non-Buddhists cling to it as annihilation. Those seeking the Two Vehicles regard it as non-action. All these belong to the realm of emotional conceptualization."
Consider this: the sixty-two views are fundamentally based on false and provisional designations; what therein could be called the true meaning?

Only those of transcendent capacity penetrate this without grasping or rejecting. By knowing that the phenomena of the five aggregates, as well as the "self" within the aggregates, and all external manifestations of forms and individual sounds, are equal to dreams and illusions, they do not give rise to views of ordinary or holy beings, nor do they construct the notion of nirvana.

Understood. The two extremes and the three periods of time are severed; one should always employ the functions of the sense faculties without giving rise to the thought of "functioning. One discerns all phenomena without giving rise to the thought of "discernment.
Even when the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and winds blow mountains together until they clash, the bliss of true permanence and quiescent extinction—the mark of nirvāṇa—is like this.
I now speak these words by force, so that you may abandon false views; do not follow after the words.

[The Master] replied: "I grant you that you understand a small portion. ○ Heze [Shenhui] read through the Great Tripitaka and had doubts regarding the six sense bases. First Question: (What is the substance of the precepts one employs?

From where does concentration (*samādhi*) arise? By what cause does wisdom (*prajñā*) emerge? Why is what is seen not flowing freely? The Patriarch said: 'Concentration is precisely the settling of the mind; with the precepts, one restrains the mind.

Within the nature, there is constant luminous wisdom; thus, one sees for oneself and knows deeply. Third Question: (One takes arising and extinguishes it; taking..."*] *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly at the third question.*

To extinguish extinction so as to extinguish birth—this is not understanding the meaning of birth and extinction; what one perceives is like being deaf and blind. The Patriarch said: "Using birth to extinguish extinction causes people not to cling to their nature;

using extinction to extinguish birth causes the mind to detach from its objects. Yet, without immediately leaving the two extremes, one falls of one's own accord into the sickness of birth and extinction.

The Fourth Question: "First sudden and then gradual, first gradual and then sudden; those who do not awaken to the sudden and the gradual are constantly confused and distressed within their minds. The Patriarch said: "Listening to the Dharma is gradual within the sudden; awakening..."
The Dharma is gradual within the sudden; practice is sudden within the gradual; and realization is sudden within the gradual. Suddenness and gradualness are the constant causes.
Within this nature, there is no delusion or confusion.
The Fourth Patriarch of India, the Venerable Upagupta, left the household life, realized the fruit, and traveled to Mathurā to propagate the teachings.

In the kingdom of Rājagṛha, the various devas rained down flowers and the terrestrial deities all manifested themselves. Consequently, Māra’s palace shook violently, and Pāpīyān was filled with grief and fear.

Using his demonic powers, he repeatedly conjured flowers and celestial maidens (*apsaras*) in an attempt to disturb those listening to the Dharma. The Venerable One immediately entered *samādhi* to examine the cause.
While Māra was caught within his meditative concentration, the Venerable One took a necklace and fastened it around his neck. When the Venerable One emerged from *samādhi*, he [took it].
The three corpses—the human, the dog, and the snake—transformed into flower garlands. Māra spoke with gentle words and had them fastened upon him;

though they were worms and filth, Māra, by the full power of his own supernatural faculties, was unable to remove them. He then ascended through the six heavens of desire up to the Brahmā heaven, seeking release from them.
The Brahmā King said, "You must turn your heart toward the Venerable One; only then will you be able to have them removed. He then spoke this verse for him: "If [one relies] on..."

A fall from the ground arises because of the ground itself; to seek to rise apart from the ground is ultimately impossible. Pāpīyān immediately descended from his celestial palace, prostrated at the Venerable One’s feet, and offered a sorrowful confession.
The Venerable One said: "From this day forward, you shall reform your ways. Will you no longer harass or harm the Buddha’s True Dharma?"
Pāpīyān said, "I vow to turn toward the Buddha-way. The Venerable One said, "You may chant for yourself: 'I take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Pāpīyān joined his palms and chanted this three times; the three corpses were all eliminated. He prostrated, offered praise, and departed. (The Sūtra says:
All the Māra kings and their ghosts and spirits saw their palaces collapse and split without cause, and the great earth tremble and crack—truly such things occurred.)

The Fifth Patriarch transmitted [the Dharma] to Venerable Tāka. He traveled and taught until he reached Central India. In that country, there were eight thousand great sages, with Micchaka at their head;
they led their assembly to pay him homage and said to the Venerable One: "We recall that we were once born together in the Brahma Heaven.
I encountered the sage Asita and was granted the methods of the sages, while you, Master, met a disciple of the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha) and practiced *dhyāna*. (One version says:)

The Venerable One realized the fruit and attained arhatship; from that point on, our karmic destinies diverged, and six kalpas have already passed. It is said: "Separated and fragmented for many kalpas."
"It is indeed true and not false. You may now abandon heterodoxy and enter the Buddha-vehicle. Kāśyapa said, "In the past, the seer Asita gave me this prediction:
'Six kalpas hence, you shall, through a fellow student, attain the fruit of out-flowlessness. Our meeting today [is the fulfillment of that prophecy]."

Is this not so? He was immediately ordained and left the household life. The rest of the assembly of seers all subsequently submitted to him; having received the precepts, they attained the four fruits of arhatship.

(The tenth scripture, the *Vijñāna-māra*, states: "Such persons fall into the attachment to greed and non-greed; those Āsitas who seek long life become their companions. They lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision. Now it says they were born together in the Brahma Heaven.)

He transmitted the dharma to the seer Asita; their karmic destinies diverged along different paths, remaining separated for many kalpas—how painful it is to speak of this! When Maitreya had succeeded to his ancestral position, the rest of the assembly all realized the fourth fruit; thus, the stage attained by the non-Buddhist practitioners of the *vijñāna-skandha* [is now revealed].
This can be known by comparison; therefore, it cannot be discussed as being on the same level as the ten classes of *ṛṣis*.
When the tenth patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was resting beneath a tree, the son of an elder, Pūrṇayaśas, stood before him.
The patriarch asked, "From where have you come? Yaśas replied, "My mind does not go anywhere. The patriarch asked, "Where do you dwell? Yaśas—

[The Master] said: "My mind does not cease. [Ananda said: "The Buddha’s hand does not abide, yet my seeing-nature has no stillness; what, then, could be non-abiding? My head moves of its own accord, yet my seeing-nature has no cessation;
what, then, could be shaking? [The Master] said: "Are you not unsettled? Shanxiao said:

"All Buddhas are likewise so. [The Master] said: "You are not the Buddhas. Shanxiao said: "The Buddhas are also not [the Buddhas]. Shanxiao spoke a verse in praise, saying: "The Master sits upon the golden ground, Ever preaching the Truth."
The true meaning turned its light back to illuminate me, causing me to enter samādhi.
The Twelfth Patriarch, the Great Master Aśvaghoṣa, was turning the wondrous Wheel of Dharma in the city of Pāṭaliputra. A small insect, like a gnat, had hidden beneath his seat.
Taking it up, he showed it to the assembly, saying, "This is a māra who has transformed himself to eavesdrop on my Dharma. He then released it and let it go.
The Māra could not move him. The Patriarch commanded him to take refuge in the Triple Gem; immediately, he returned to his original form and prostrated, saying, "My name is Kapiṃjala.
I have three thousand followers. The Patriarch asked, "Exerting all your supernatural powers, what can you transform? He replied, "I can transform a vast ocean; that would be a very minor feat.
The Patriarch asked, "Can you transform the Sea of Nature (dharmatā-samudra)? He asked, "What is meant by the 'Sea of Nature'? [The Patriarch replied: "It is not..."
I know this. My ancestor explained it to me, saying: "This ocean of nature is that upon which the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all depend for their establishment;
the three samādhis and the six supernormal powers are manifested from it. Upon hearing the Dharma, Māra gave rise to great faith and, together with his followers, sought to leave the household life.
Later, [the ancestor] entrusted him with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
The sixteenth patriarch, the Great Master Rāhulabhadra, arrived at the city of Śrāvastī and followed the source of the Golden Water River.
There he saw Saṃghanandin in meditative concentration within a stone cave. After twenty-one days had passed, Saṃghanandin emerged from his samādhi, whereupon the Master questioned him, saying:
"Is your body settled? Is your mind settled? Daiten replied, "Both my body and my mind are settled. The Patriarch said, "If both body and mind are settled, how can there be coming and going?
Daiten replied, "Though there is coming and going, it does not lose the characteristic of stillness. It is like gold in a well: the essence of the gold remains eternally tranquil.
The Patriarch said, "Whether the gold is in the well or the gold has come out of the well, the gold itself has neither motion nor stillness. What, then, comes and goes? Daiten [remained silent].
[Daowu] said, "When you speak of gold moving and being still, what substance is entering and exiting? If you allow that gold enters and exits, then gold itself is not moving or still.
The Master [Nanyue Huairang] said, "If the gold is in the well, what is the gold that comes out? If the gold has come out of the well, what is the thing remaining inside?

Daiten said, "If the gold has come out of the well, then what remains is not gold. If the gold is in the well, then what is it that comes out? The Master said, "This interpretation is not correct. Daiten...
Tianyi said, "That meaning is not attached. The Patriarch said, "This meaning shall fall. Tianyi said, "That meaning is not established.
The Patriarch said, "That meaning is not established; my meaning is established. Tianyi said, "Although my meaning is established, the Dharma is not mine.
The Patriarch said, "My meaning is already established, for I have no self. Tianyi said, "Since I have no self, what further meaning is established? The Patriarch said, "I..."
"Because there is no self, your proposition is established. Bodhidharma said, "Virtuous one, whom do you take as your teacher to have attained this non-self?
The Master replied, "My teacher is Kanadeva; through him I realized this non-self. Bodhidharma praised him with a verse: "I bow my head to Teacher Deva, From whom you, O Virtuous One, emerged.
Since you, Virtuous One, are without self, I wish to take you as my teacher. The Master answered, "I am already without self..."
"Because you take me as your teacher, you must see my 'I' as 'I. If you take me as your teacher, you will know that my 'I' is not truly an 'I.
At these words, Nandi’s mind was suddenly enlightened; he immediately sought ordination and liberation. The Patriarch said, "Your mind is already free and is not bound to me.
Why do you need to rely on me to seek liberation?"

The seventeenth patriarch, the Venerable Saṃghanandin, was traveling to convert sentient beings at an ancient temple accompanied by the youth Gayāśata. A bronze bell atop the hall was ringing as it was stirred by the wind. The Patriarch asked, "Is it the wind that sounds? Is it the bell that sounds? Or is it the bronze that sounds? The youth replied, "It is my mind that sounds; it is not the wind, the bronze, or the bell. The Patriarch said, "If it is neither the wind, the bronze, nor the bell, then who is it that hears? The youth remained silent. The Patriarch said, "You have now attained my Dharma. He then transmitted the Dharma-garment and the bowl to him and passed away. The youth subsequently traveled to Mount Malaya in South India, where he resided for thirty years. He then returned to the country of Kalinga, where he converted the King and his ministers. He later descended to the human realm and propagated the teachings for fifty years. He then returned to Mount Malaya, where he sat in meditation beneath a tree and entered *parinirvāṇa*.
