The nineteenth patriarch, Kumāralata, had previously been born in the Brahma Heaven.

Out of craving for the bodhisattva’s jeweled necklace, he fell and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he preached the Dharma to the devas and humans there. Those devas subsequently realized the first fruit of the path;
for this reason, the celestial hosts honored him as their teacher. At that time, a celestial jade maiden came to pay homage at the assembly, which numbered one thousand two hundred people. Suddenly—

Affection arose, and thus they were bound together by mutual entanglement. When the karmic destiny of his ancestors had reached its appointed time, he descended to be born in the country of Mo-ti (Yuezhi).

(A celestial maiden also fell into this land, becoming a member of the Brahmin caste. After transmitting the Dharma, he went to convert those in Central India. There was a wise man named Jayata who asked:
"My parents have long revered the Triple Gem, yet they are constantly afflicted by chronic illness. A neighbor has long practiced the deeds of a Caṇḍāla, yet remains robust and healthy."
"It is as you wish. How could the retribution for good and evil be a hollow teaching? The Patriarch said, "The Buddha taught that karma extends through the three periods of time.

There are those who do good in this life yet do not receive blessings; this is because the retribution for past evil is still predominant. There are those who commit evil in this life yet do not suffer calamity;"

The former is the excellence of past karmic retribution. If the karma of good and evil performed in this life increases further according to its meritorious reward, then the realms of good and evil in future lives will become increasingly deep.
However, if the causes of good and evil from previous lives are shifted and altered by following the movements of the mind, [the future course may change].

In that case, the arising of the fruits of sin and merit would be indeterminate. When ordinary people see the benevolent die young and the violent live long, or the rebellious meet with good fortune and the righteous suffer misfortune, they immediately claim that cause and effect do not exist and that sin and merit are empty.
They fail to realize that form and shadow follow one another, differing not even by a hair's breadth;
through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, these never perish. How can one seek [the truth] in a single lifetime alone? You have already gained faith in the three periods of time.

[He spoke of] karma, yet had not yet clarified that karma arises from delusion (*kleśa*), that delusion exists because of consciousness (*vijñāna*), that consciousness depends on non-awakening (*avidyā*), and that non-awakening depends on the mind (*citta*).
The mind is fundamentally pure; it is without birth or death, without good or evil, and both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are like dreams and illusions.

On this night, Daye was deeply moved and his innate wisdom (*pūrvajñāna*) was awakened; he subsequently sought to leave the household life. (Hao Yue, a court attendant, asked Changsha: "If one has realized it, then the debts of karma are originally empty; if one has not yet realized it, one must repay past debts. But as for [this matter]... )

The Venerable Siṃha asked, "Why was the Second Patriarch able to settle his karmic debts? Zhaozhou said, "Great Virtue, you do not recognize that all is originally empty. Yue asked, "What is 'originally empty'? Zhaozhou said, "Karmic debt is it. Yue asked, "What is karmic debt?"

He said: "It is originally emptiness. Then he indicated this with a verse: "Provisionally existent, it is fundamentally not existent; Provisionally extinguished, it is also not non-existent. The meaning of Nirvana as the settling of debts— In its single nature, there is no further distinction."
In the Five Indias, there was a monk named Dharmadatta who possessed eloquence and wisdom. He served as a disciple to the twenty-fourth patriarch, Venerable Siṃha.

The Venerable One, recognizing his realization and understanding, praised him before the assembly. However, when it came to the transmission of the Dharma and the succession to the patriarchate, the position fell to Vasubandhu (Vasubhadra).
Dharmadatta harbored resentment in his heart and said, "The Venerable One knew me so deeply, yet regarding the position of the patriarchal successor—"

"Since he has granted it to me, how could there be any further teaching? A long time after the Venerable had passed away, one day Dharmada was walking alone across a river when he saw a woman washing her feet.
He thought to himself, "How white and fair these shanks are!
Suddenly, the Venerable Siṃha appeared at his side and said, "Every day you think to yourself, 'He did not grant the patriarchal seat to me. Today—"
“Xin, may you be granted the position of Patriarch? Thereupon, Bodhidharma composed his mind, prostrated at [Xin’s] feet, and entreated him with grief, saying:

“Is such a minor transgression as this so difficult to overcome? (Jiyin says: The World-Honored One’s four definitive exhortations place the impulse toward sexual misconduct before those of killing, stealing, and lying.

This Great Compassionate Father did not forget this even in moments of haste, providing instruction through every detail. It is that which a novice Bodhisattva ought to recognize as a debt of gratitude.)
In this land, the Sage Xian, Master Zhigong, questioned a foreign monk:
"I have heard that you, Venerable Sir, call me a butcher. Have you ever seen me kill a living being? The monk replied, "I have.
The Master said, "Is it a seeing with a seer? A seeing without a seer? A seeing that is neither existent nor non-existent? If there is such a seeing..."
"To see" is the view of ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*). "The seeing of non-seeing" is the view of the *śrāvakas*. "Neither existence nor non-existence" is the view of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
I do not yet know how you, Venerable One, see. The Master said: "Do you have such views as these?"
Master Fu said to his disciples: "The Great Way of non-action is beyond words and speech. For the speaker there is nothing shown; for the listener there is nothing heard;
for the student there is nothing attained. Because the speaker has no fixed method, there is nothing shown. Because the listener has no reception, there is nothing heard.
Because the student has no grasping, there is nothing attained. Why is this so? Because the Dharma is formless, being free from physical characteristics."
The Dharma is without reception, for it is free from grasping and abandoning. The Dharma is without activity, for it is free from footprints.

The Dharma is without names, for it is free from conceptual discrimination. Such a path is precisely the unconditioned, true, singular, and untainted path that severs all攀缘 (pāraṇa, objective clinging).
It is ultimately undefiled. Above, it is not dragged down by the fetters and afflictions to fall into the three realms and transmigrate through birth and death;

below, it is not dragged down by the fetters and afflictions to fall into the three miserable states and the hells to undergo various sufferings and vexations. Therefore, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
This is precisely quiescent concentration and the unconditioned; it stands majestic and eternally abiding.
Master Xuanzang of Qin asked Dharma Master Sheng, "How do you explain the meaning of the emptiness of form?

He replied, "The aggregation of many atoms is called form; that these many atoms lack intrinsic nature is called emptiness. The Master said, "Before the many atoms have manifested, what would you call them? Sheng was speechless.
He was at a loss for words. His disciples followed him up, asking, "We do not understand how you explain the meaning of form and emptiness.
The Master said, "I am not saying that your teacher’s explanation is incorrect. Your teacher only knows how to speak of the form and emptiness of the fruition;

he does not know how to speak of the form and emptiness within the cause. They asked, "What is the form and emptiness within the cause? He replied, "Because a single atom is empty, all atoms are empty. Because all atoms are empty..."

Therefore, a single atom is empty; within the emptiness of a single atom there are no manifold atoms, and within the emptiness of manifold atoms there is no single atom. (Tianyi Huai’s verse says: Form is emptiness, emptiness is form;

form is emptiness, emptiness is form. The road of Tongguan is blocked and impassable. When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and even the finest hairs are consumed, the green mountains remain as before amidst the white clouds.)

Kumārajīva replied to Yao Xing, the ruler of Later Qin: "The Buddha taught that the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is the totality of the convergence of the three times, which is collectively termed 'form.
This is true for all five aggregates. Furthermore, it is said that from mind arises mind, just as from grain arises grain.

For this reason, we know that the past must necessarily exist; thus, there is no fault of attributing things to causelessness. Moreover, it is said that among the six consciousnesses, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) relies upon [the preceding one]..."
The essence of cessation gives rise to the mental consciousness. Furthermore, right view is termed the past karma that constitutes the resultant phenomena in the future.

Moreover, among the ten powers, the second power is the knowledge of all karmas across the three periods of time. It is also said: "If there were no past karma, there would be no retribution in the three miserable realms.
And it is further said: "If a practitioner is within a mind characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*), they should not be so named [as one who has transcended them]."
Thus, one becomes a sage. By these various analogies, it is firmly known that the past must not be non-existent.

If the past and future were non-existent, it would not accord with reason and would be disallowed by the teachings of the Sūtras. Furthermore, the twelve links of dependent origination are the most profound aspect of the Buddha-dharma.
If the past and future were definitively existent, they would contradict the nature of this dharma. Why is this?

For example, when there are seeds of grain, earth, water, and the proper season, the sprout and root can arise. If these were already definitively existent beforehand, they would have nothing further to depend upon.
If they existed beforehand, they could not be said to arise from conditions. Furthermore, if they existed beforehand, this would constitute the inversion of permanence. Therefore, [it is not so].
One can certainly say that [the past] exists; one cannot definitively say it does not exist. The discourse on existence and non-existence is merely appropriate to the occasion.
Because past dharmas give rise to karma and its effects, one cannot say they do not exist. Furthermore, because it is said that the present does not confront the past, one cannot say they exist.

Moreover, as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the suchness of the past is not separate from the suchness of the future and present, and the suchness of the future and present is likewise not [separate from the past].
Being separated from the suchness of the past does not mean that it is non-existent.

The Great Master Zhiyi wrote in a letter to Emperor Xuan of the Chen Dynasty: "In the method of studying the Way, one must first recognize the fundamental source.

When the deluded mind perishes, form becomes vast and the mind becomes expansive; when form is small, the mind becomes subtle. Eventually, by knowing that the mind is empty and quiescent, one enters the Dharma-gate of Emptiness and Quiescence.

One immediately enters the Dharma-gate of wisdom.

Furthermore, by means of the mind, one realizes the Buddha within the objective realm; by means of the objective realm, one perceives the Tathāgata who is nothing but mind.

Though mind and Buddha are layered and manifold, their fundamental enlightened nature is one. Since they cannot be grasped, both mind and object vanish; since they cannot be exhausted through illumination, wisdom and principle penetrate each other completely.
Since the state of mind is thus, when objects are compared with one another and minds are mutually examined, the myriad transformations, though manifold, are all of one essence.

Only through realization in accord with this can it be called the *Avataṃsaka* of the Buddha. (The commentary states: People today understand only that "mind is Buddha" and that "this mind makes Buddha," but they do not know that "objects are Buddha" and that "these objects make Buddha.

Now it is clarified that taking suchness (*tathatā*) as the Buddha—since both mind and objects are suchness—if the suchness of the mind is the Buddha, how could the suchness of objects not be? Furthermore, the mind possesses the nature of mind and can become a Buddha; since objects also possess the nature of mind, why should they not become Buddhas? To subsume objects within the mind...)
To see the Buddha within the mind is the Buddha of the objective realm; by using the realm to gather the mind, one sees the Buddha within that realm (this is the Tathāgata who is Mind-only).

National Teacher Qingliang, in his response to the Prince’s inquiry on the Essentials of Mind, stated: "If one is deluded regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then afflictions and suffering will arise in confusion."
When one awakens to the true nature, it is empty, luminous, vast, and penetrating. When there is proof and cognition, the sun of wisdom sinks into the realm of existence (*bhava*).

If there is neither illumination nor awakening, then the clouds of delusion shroud the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Delusion and awakening depend upon each other; the real and the false attend one another.
If you seek the real while abandoning the false, it is like discarding your shadow while wearying your body. If you realize that the false is itself the real, it is like remaining within the shade.
Extinction. If one is without mind and forgets illumination, then all anxieties are cast aside. If one allows spontaneous, tranquil awareness to prevail, then all practices arise.
To speak of cessation is to forget both awareness and tranquility; to discuss contemplation is to illuminate both tranquility and awareness.

Regarding realization, it cannot be shown to others; regarding principle, it is not understood except through realization. Therefore, awakening to tranquility means there is no tranquility; true knowledge means there is no knowledge. By means of this—
One knows the single mind of non-dual quiescence and accords with the Middle Way in which emptiness and existence are mutually fused. Prajñā does not newly arise outside of the mind;
the nature of wisdom is inherently complete from the beginning. Yet, this primordial quiescence cannot manifest of itself; it truly arises through the power of prajñā.
Prajñā and the nature of wisdom are mutually constitutive in their reciprocal relationship. There is, in truth, no distinction between original wisdom and that which is cultivated at the outset.

When both bodies are forgotten and one enters into realization, then wondrous enlightenment is perfectly luminous. When beginning and end are encompassed and fused, then cause and effect mutually penetrate.
Below, the *Zongjing* quotes the testimony of the eminent monk Lingrun, who said:
"Abandoning external objects and false attachments, one attains the conceptualization of mental discourse; abandoning the notion of *vijñapti-mātra*, one attains..."
The true dharma-realm: first he contemplates signlessness and abandons the marks of external objects; later he contemplates non-arising and abandons the notion of mere-consciousness.

He frequently ascended mountains with his dharma-companions to wander and observe. Once, when wild fires broke out on all four sides, the multitude fled in all directions, yet he alone proceeded calmly, looking back as he climbed.
The saying goes: "Outside the mind there is no fire; fire is truly from within the mind itself. One may think that fire can be escaped, yet there is no way to avoid it.
When the fire reaches the moisture, it is suddenly extinguished. ○ Master Fuli said: "In observing karma, one sees that karma arises because of the mind."
The mind functions as karma; karma draws forth the mind to receive a physical form, and the mind follows karma to create its objects.
Thus, one receives a body because of karma, and that body in turn creates karma; from the mind one creates objects, and those objects in turn give rise to the mind.

It is like a shadow following a form, bending or straightening according to it, or an echo following a sound, being large or small according to it. (The *Chizengchuan* states: The *Śataśāstra-kārikā* says: "In the eye there is no form or consciousness; in consciousness there is no form or eye. Within form, both [are absent]...")
[Both are] non-existent. How could they cause one to see form? (The eminent monk Lingrun once practiced this contemplation. Chan Master Fazhao said:
"The Sūtra states that the hundreds of thousands of names throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas are all alternative names for the Tathāgata;
they are distinct designations for the true mind. Now, bondage arises from the mind’s bondage, and liberation arises from the mind’s liberation. Bondage and liberation [originate] from..."

The mind does not concern itself with other matters; the essential method for liberation is solely the contemplation of the mind. Even if one raises the gate of the single mind, all things are nothing but this single mind.
If there were even a single dharma that were not mind, it would exist outside of the mind; but who could exist outside of the mind?
Regarding the formulation of a separate article: Master Fanzhen said, "If one knows that all dharmas are themselves dharma, one immediately attains liberation.
The eye is dharma; form is dharma. The Sūtra says: 'Not seeing dharma, one is not bound by dharma;
not seeing dharma, one is not liberated by dharma. Master Zang said, "In all dharmas, there is nothing..."
As for "attaining," it is simply that the mind is the Way. The eye does not grasp at any forms; the ear does not grasp at any sounds. Master Yuan said:
"Suppose there is a large rock in one's house. One usually sits or lies upon it, or perhaps carves it into a Buddha image.

If the mind interprets it as a Buddha, one fears transgression and dares not sit on it. All of this is merely the functioning of the conscious mind. It is like drawing with a brush-tip; one is busy with oneself and afraid of oneself—the rock remains as it is."
Within this, there is in reality neither sin nor merit. Master An said: "The direct mind is the Way. Why is this? Because the direct mind acts directly;
it does not further contemplate emptiness, nor does it seek expedient means. As the Sūtra says: "Direct vision sees nothing; direct mindfulness thinks of nothing."

Directly receive it and do not practice; directly explain it and do not complicate it. Master Jue said: "If one realizes that the mind has no point of attachment, one immediately attains the traces of the Way.
When the eyes see all forms, the eyes do not belong to those forms; this is liberation through self-nature. As the Sūtra says:
'Because all dharmas are mutually unattached, the mind and all dharmas do not know one another. Yuanji.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "All phenomena are mind-only and have no counterpart; this is itself sovereign liberation. A sūtra states:
"All phenomena do not confront the eye. Why? Because phenomena do not see phenomena, and phenomena do not know phenomena."

An ancient sage asked: "If you say that both self and other are manifestations of one's own mind, and that apart from the mind there is no real self or person, then since the Buddhas also perceive the existence of sentient beings, could it be that their deluded minds have not yet been exhausted? The answer was:

"When the Buddhas perceive the existence of sentient beings, they see them all as illusory existences arising through conditions. Sentient beings do not know this, and thus they claim there is a real self; for this reason, they create karma."
They undergo retribution and wander aimlessly in saṃsāra. This arises because there is no real self, which moves the compassion of the Buddhas.
If there were a real self that was not falsely existent, why would the Buddhas deludedly save sentient beings?

Since a real self cannot be saved, the fact that they now act as saviors proves that there is no self; it is merely a false conceptualization of its existence. Thus, one knows that sentient beings are not separate from the Buddhas.
Regarding the realms: being deluded, one lacks awakening and awareness (from the *Zongjing*).
A student asked Master An-guo: "If one has not yet attained enlightenment, do the karmic conditions of good and evil exist? He replied: "They do not exist.
It is like a dream at night when one is pursued by an evil person, or when one becomes a Brahmā King or Śakra; one takes these to be real, but upon waking..."
Yet upon waking, all is silent and still; one comes to know with certainty that the three realms are fundamentally empty and are but this single mind.
The student asked again: "What is meant by 'recognizing the mind and seeing its nature'? He replied: "It is like a dream at night where one sees both good and evil.

If one realizes that the body is on the bed sleeping peacefully and there is no longer any sorrow or joy, that is precisely recognizing the mind and seeing its nature. Nowadays, there are people who hear...

To become a Buddha brings joy; to hear that one has entered hell brings sorrow. Failing to realize that the Buddha of the mind is sleeping peacefully upon the bed of Bodhi, you falsely give rise to grief and delight.
The following are the Dharma heirs of the various patriarchs of this land.

He said to the layman: "Shadows arise from forms; echoes follow sounds. To toy with shadows is to weary the form; yet one does not realize that form is the root of the shadow. To raise a sound is to produce an echo;
yet one does not recognize that sound is the source of the echo. Thus, to seek nirvana while eliminating the mind of affliction is a futile effort."
It is like seeking a shadow by removing the form; it is like seeking the Buddha-way apart from the minds of sentient beings. It is like searching for an echo while remaining silent.
Thus we know that delusion and awakening are one path, and folly and wisdom are not distinct. Where there is no name, names are created; because of these names, right and wrong arise.
Where there is no principle, principles are created; because of these principles, disputes and arguments arise. These are illusions and not reality. Who is it that is not [deluded]?
Who is it? It is false and not real. What is there to possess? What is there to be empty? One should know that what is gained is nothing gained, and what is lost is nothing lost.
The First Patriarch of Niutou said: "As for the Buddhas who attain Bodhi herein, they attain Bodhi at this very place of the mind."
The wheel of Dharma turns within the sense-field of form; one enters nirvāṇa within the sense-field of the eye.
If this is so, then with ultimate liberation within the body, the Dharma-body is eternally present and the pure land is fully perfected. What further thing is lacking? What more remains to be sought?

At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening. Master Rong said: "From all ordinary beings and sages above the three miserable realms, down to the stage of the knowledge of all modes."

All these are false imaginings that one believes to exist; they are all like dreams. It is as if a person in a dream sees themselves in hell and, employing various means, strives to escape, laboring in vain.
One need only shake oneself awake, and then all such matters will vanish entirely.
Everything now is but what is done within a dream, and thus one returns to receive the retribution of a dream. ○ It is further said: "There is no Buddha apart from the five aggregates. ○
A mirror-image originally has no mind; one says that a mirror-image has no mind. From that which has no mind, one speaks of no-mind.

When people say there is a mind, one says that the person has no mind. From that which has a mind, one speaks of no-mind; to speak of no-mind within that which has a mind is the derivative contemplation (*mūla-vipaśyanā*).

To speak of no-mind within that which has no mind is the fundamental contemplation (*mūla-vipaśyanā*). Sentient beings reckon that body and mind exist; one speaks of the mirror-image to shatter this reckoning.
Sentient beings are attached to reflections in a mirror; ultimate emptiness is taught to shatter these reflections.
If one knows that reflections are ultimately empty, then body and mind are ultimately empty, provisional names are ultimately empty, and even "ultimate emptiness" itself does not exist.
The Buddha-way is not born of heaven, nor does it emerge from the earth; it is simply the nature of the empty mind, illuminating the world like the sun. ○ Boling.

The King asked: "When an object arises, it has no location; through conditions, awakening perceives its birth. When the object passes away, awakening turns back; awakening then transforms into the object.
If one uses the mind to pull the mind, it is again what is perceived by awakening. Following it, following it as it goes, one does not leave the boundary of arising and ceasing. The Master said:
"In the beginning, middle, and end of form and mind, there is in reality no realm of dependent origination. In a single thought-moment, one forgets self-doubt."

Who can calculate movement and stillness? This knowing is itself without knowing. Knowing and the objects of knowledge do not meet; one should examine one's own fundamental form. Why seek it beyond the realm?
The preceding object does not change or pass away; the subsequent thought does not come into the present. It is like grasping at the moon to seek its dark reflection.
To track footprints and pursue flying birds, while wishing to know the nature of the mind’s essence, is like looking into a dream; it is comparable to ice in the sixth month—alike in every respect.
One cannot escape emptiness by avoiding it, nor can one achieve it by seeking it. Ask, then, of the image within a mirror.

From where does the mind arise? (Master Zhi said: "The Great Being’s physical eyes possess perfect penetration; the divine eyes of the Two Vehicles are merely medicinal. Master Rong said: "Do not grasp at the five supernatural powers, such as the divine eye, for they are the practices of externalists who create phenomena.")
[This refers to] only those ordinary people who have entered into principle).
The Master of the Lower Stone Cave at Niutou asked: "The Buddha-body is untainted; its five aggregates are perfumed by precepts and meditative concentration, neither bound nor liberated.
For instance, as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: 'The unwholesome body of the five aggregates of sentient beings is likewise neither bound nor [liberated].'"

This causes people to be startled and filled with doubt. He replied: "If one were to claim that there are the liberation and deliverance of the Buddhas existing separately outside the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of sentient beings, such a thing is impossible.
It is because sentient beings do not realize the purity of form and mind, and are deluded by false imaginings and inversions, that they fail to attain liberation.
If one knows that persons and phenomena are eternally empty, then within them there is truly neither bondage nor liberation."
Below the section on "The Buddha’s Cave," Master Yunju said: "Both the mundane and the supramundane do not transcend the deluded mind of a single thought-moment.
As soon as a single thought arises, the myriad phenomena are differentiated; as thoughts arise in succession, they immediately constitute subject and object.
If it were not for subject and object, how could there be thought? It is evident that once there is the thought of that which is seen, there must also be the mind that sees."

One should know that the object of thought is precisely the objective realm (*viṣaya*), and the seeing is precisely the mind (*citta*). The thought that is seen becomes the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), while the mind that sees becomes the four [mental] aggregates.
As the Sūtra says: "The five aggregates are the world. A single thought-moment possesses all five aggregates, and within each individual aggregate, all five aggregates are present.
Therefore, the one does not obstruct the many, and the many do not obstruct the one. Thus, as for the mind and the objective realm...
Interpenetration: they act as guests and hosts to one another. As the Sūtra says: "Object and wisdom interpenetrate one another, layer upon layer without end;

thus, a single atom contains the Dharma-realm, and every single phenomenon is omnipresent. When one contemplates the movement of a single thought-moment of one's own, the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges tremble all at once.
When one contemplates the constant stillness of a single thought-moment of one's own, all sentient beings of the six realms are likewise in constant stillness.
If one truly realizes the essence of a single thought-moment, then the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will constantly manifest as one's own mind.
Due to delusion regarding this single thought-moment, however, object and wisdom become as far apart as Hu and Yue.
Empress Dowager Wu asked National Teacher Huian, "How many years have you lived? The Master replied, "I do not record it. The Empress asked, "Why do you not record it?
The Master said, "The body of birth and death is like a cycle; as a cycle, it has neither beginning nor end. What need is there to record it?
Furthermore, this stream of mind flows on without interruption. To perceive the rising and ceasing of bubbles is merely deluded thought. From the very first consciousness..."

When the signs of movement finally cease, it is likewise just like this; how could years or months be recorded? Later, [Emperor Wu] prostrated himself with his forehead to the ground and accepted the teaching with faith.

During the Liang dynasty, he invited one hundred great virtuous ones to the palace gate and prepared armor and weapons in full array to test whether they would feel fear. Ninety-nine men all fled in terror, but only one man felt no fear. The King asked the Master, "For what reason do you not fear?"
He replied: "Of what am I afraid? From the moment I was first born as a child, I have died moment by moment and thought after thought; how could I now, on the contrary, fear death?"
Du Hongjian went to Baiya Wuzhu to inquire about the Dharma. At that time, he heard a crow cawing.

Du asked the Master, "Did you hear it? He replied, "I heard it. When the crow had gone, Du asked again. He replied, "I heard it. Du said, "The crow has gone and there is no sound; why do you say you heard it? The Master said, "Hearing and not hearing have nothing to do with the nature of hearing.
When there is sound, it is simply the auditory object arising of itself; when there is no sound," [the nature of hearing remains].
This auditory object (śabda-viṣaya) perishes of its own accord, yet this nature of hearing does not arise with the sound, nor does it perish with the sound.

To awaken to this nature of hearing is to escape the transmigration of auditory objects. It is the same for visible forms, odors, tastes, and tactile objects. One should know that hearing is without arising or ceasing;

hearing is without coming or going. (Master Shennian remarked: "To preach the Dharma without abiding perfectly accords with the principle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* that 'hearing is without arising or ceasing'.").
Chan Master Daoshu of Shouzhou received the Dharma from Xiu of the Northern School. He selected Sanmao Mountain in Shouzhou to settle in a thatched hut.

There was often a wild man there, whose dress was simple and plain, and whose speech was strange and unconventional. At times he would suddenly transform into the forms of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, arhats, celestial immortals, and the like;
sometimes he emitted divine light, or manifested sounds and voices. When the disciples witnessed this, they were struck with awe.
None were able to fathom him. After ten years had passed, he became silent, leaving no trace or form. The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"The rustic fellow employs many-colored wiles to dazzle and delude people; it requires only that this old monk neither see nor hear them, for his wiles will eventually reach their end."

I have neither seen nor heard of anything that is inexhaustible (*akṣaya*). (In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, a celestial Māra possessed a person; his form would momentarily become that of Śakra, or a bhikṣuṇī. The *Qixin lun* also says:

"Or he manifests the image of a deva, the image of a bodhisattva, or even the image of a Tathāgata, complete with all the marks and signs. One should know that such a 'rustic' is not a mountain ghost, but a celestial Māra.)
Chan Master Benjing of Sengong Mountain said: "If one interprets this through the lens of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, one is worlds apart from the Way;
such a person is seeking seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, rather than being a seeker of the Way. As the sutra says: 'There are no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

Since even the six sense faculties do not exist, upon what could seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing be established? When one exhaustively investigates their source, they are fundamentally non-existent."

Wherein does the mind abide? Because there is delusion, one takes the true to confront the delusory; yet when one investigates the nature of delusion, it is fundamentally empty, and as for the true, how could it ever have existed?
Thus, know that both the true and the delusory are merely provisional names; these two things exist only as mutual remedies and possess no substantial reality whatsoever.
It is asked: "If you say that all is delusory, then delusion is the same as the true. Since there is no distinction between the true and the delusory, what, then, is this thing?"
The Master said: "If one asks what thing it is, even 'what thing' is illusory. As the Sūtra says: 'There is nothing similar; there is no analogy.
The path of language is cut off, like a bird flying through the sky. A verse says: 'When you examine the Real, the Real has no marks; When you exhaust the illusory, the illusory has no form.
Turn back and examine the mind that examines and exhausts; Know that this mind, too, is a provisional name. Realizing the Way is also like this: In the end, there is only peace. [Seal] Good."

The two unwholesome faculties both exist because of the mind. If, upon investigating the mind, it is found to exist, then the faculties are likewise not empty. Since the mind, when scrutinized, is ultimately non-existent, on what basis could the faculties be established?
A sutra says: "Wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are born through transformation from the mind; the karmic conditions of good and evil have no inherent substance. A verse states:
"Since the wholesome arises from the mind, how could the unwholesome be separate from the mind? Good and evil are external conditions; [they do not exist] within the mind."
In reality, nothing exists. From where could one abandon evil? To whom could one entrust the grasping of good? Alas for those caught in dualistic views;
they cling to objects and run back and forth between two extremes. If one awakens to the fact that the mind is fundamentally non-existent, only then will one repent of former faults.
Question: From where does this body come? After a hundred years, where does it return? The Master said: It is like a person in a dream—from where does it come?

"When one sleeps, where does it go? He replied, "In a dream, it cannot be said that it is non-existent; once awakened, it cannot be said that it exists. Although there is existence and non-existence, its coming and going have no location.

The Master said, "This body of mine is also like a dream. He spoke in verse: When dreaming, it is not non-existent; Upon awakening, it is not existent. Though existence and non-existence occur, Its coming and going have no place. My body, too, is just like this dream.
Viewing life as being like a dream: within the dream, there is indeed clamor; when suddenly awakened, all affairs cease. This is identical to awakening while still asleep.
The wise understand the awakening within the dream; the deluded take the dream’s clamor to be real. To understand the dream is to be as one; once awakened, there is no separate awakening.
National Teacher Zhong asked a Zen practitioner, "How do the masters of the South instruct people? He replied, "The masters of that region [teach] directly."
The following demonstrates to people that mind itself is Buddha. "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening. You now fully possess the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

This nature is well able to raise the eyebrows, blink the eyes, and engage in coming and going; it pervades the entire body. When the head is touched, the head knows; when the foot is touched, the foot knows.
Therefore, it is called the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (Samyak-saṃbuddha). Apart from this, there is no other Buddha. This very body...
Therein, there is arising and ceasing. Yet the nature of the mind has never arisen or ceased since beginningless time.

As for the arising and ceasing of the body, it is like a dragon shedding its bones, a snake sloughing its skin, or a person leaving an old dwelling; thus, while the body is impermanent, its nature is eternal. The Master said:
If this were so, there would be no distinction between you and the non-Buddhist outsider Śreṇika. He said: "Within this body of mine, there exists a spiritual nature (*ātman*).
This nature is capable of knowing pain and pleasure. When the body perishes, the spirit departs, just as when a house is burning, the owner of the house goes out;
the house is impermanent, but the owner is eternal. If it were truly thus, how could one distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox?

[Daosheng] argued: "How tragic! Our school is lost. If seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing were the Buddha-nature, then Vimalakīrti should not have said, 'The Dharma is apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing;
if one practices seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, that is merely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.'"
"This is not seeking the Dharma. He asked again, "The *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of the definitive meaning that opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
How is this to be understood? The Master said, "He says it 'opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,' yet he does not even mention Bodhisattvas or those of the Two Vehicles.

How could the deluded and inverted perceptions of sentient beings be the same as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? He asked again, "Which one is the Buddha-mind? The Master said, "Walls, tiles, and pebbles."
The assembly said, "This greatly contradicts the sutras. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that because it is apart from insentient things such as walls and partitions, it is called 'Buddha-nature.
Now you say it is the 'Buddha-mind. We do not know whether this mind and this nature are distinct or not. The Master said:

In delusion, there is differentiation; in awakening, there is no differentiation. It is like the cold months when water freezes into ice, and upon the arrival of warmth, the ice melts back into water.
When sentient beings are deluded, they congeal their nature into mind; when they awaken, they dissolve mind back into nature. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
One should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm: all things are created solely by the mind. Now, let me ask you:
do insentient objects exist within the triple world, or do they exist outside the triple world? Or are they the mind, or are they not the mind?

If they are not the mind, then the sutras should not state that "the triple world is mind-only. If they are the mind, then one should not say they lack intrinsic nature. You are contradicting yourself.
“Sutra: I do not contradict this. [The monk] asked, “If insentient things possess Buddha-nature, do they also understand how to preach the Dharma?
The Master said, “They preach it incessantly and without interruption. [The monk] asked, “Why is it that I do not hear it? The Master said, “It is you yourself who do not hear it.
[The monk] asked, “Who is able to hear it? The Master said, “All the sages are able to hear it. [The monk] asked, “Would that mean that sentient beings have no share in it?”
The Master said, "I speak for the sake of sentient beings; I do not speak for the sake of the sages. [The monk] said, "I am deaf and blind; I have not heard the insentient preaching the Dharma.

You, Master, ought to have heard it. The Master said, "I, too, have not heard it. [The monk] said, "Since you, Master, have not heard it, how can you know that the insentient are able to preach the Dharma?
The Master said, "It is fortunate that I have not heard it. Had I been able to hear it, I would have been equal to the sages."
“You would not hear me preaching the Dharma. He asked, “Do sentient beings ultimately hear it? The Master said, “If sentient beings were to hear it, they would no longer be sentient beings.
He asked, “What scriptural authority is there for ‘insentient things preaching the Dharma’? The Master said, “Have you not seen that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
‘The lands preach, sentient beings preach; all things of the three periods of time preach’? Are sentient beings not sentient beings? He replied, “Master, you merely—”

[The student] asked: "It is said that insentient things possess Buddha-nature; what then is the case for sentient beings? The Master said: "If even insentient things are thus, how much more so sentient beings? [The student] asked again:
"If that is so, the South says that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are Buddha-nature. It would not be right to judge this as being the same as the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
The Master said: "I do not say that they lack Buddha-nature. Do the non-Buddhists perhaps lack Buddha-nature? It is simply because of their views..."
[The student] said: "This is an error. To give rise to two views regarding a single dharma is mistaken. [One might argue:

'If the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is identical, then by a single Buddha practicing cultivation, all sentient beings should attain liberation simultaneously. Since this is not the case now, where does the meaning of identity reside?

The Master said: 'The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*’s doctrine of the six characteristics states: within identity there is difference, and within difference there is identity; there are completion and destruction, as well as the general and the particular.'"

All such examples are like this. Although sentient beings and Buddhas share the same nature, it does not hinder each individual from practicing for themselves and attaining realization for themselves;
one has never seen another’s food satisfy one’s own hunger. A person of knowledge said to a student: "Simply recognize your own nature.

When the time of impermanence arrives, cast off this shell-like body, and the numinous wisdom-nature will depart in transcendent clarity—this is called liberation. The Master said: "This is still [merely conceptual]."
The measure of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists is as follows: the followers of the two vehicles loathe birth and death and rejoice in nirvana;

the non-Buddhists likewise say, "I have a great affliction because I possess a body," and thus they proceed toward the obscure principle (tattva). For those at the stage of Srotāpanna, eighty thousand kalpas remain.

Those who have attained the third fruit [of the *śrāvaka*] remain for sixty-four thousand *kalpas*; *pratyekabuddhas* abide in the emptiness-concentration (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) for ten thousand *kalpas*;

and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) abide in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) for eighty thousand *kalpas*. Even when their *kalpas* are exhausted, those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) are still able to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), whereas non-Buddhists return immediately to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
It is said that the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is of one kind; the Master said: "It cannot be said to be of one kind, for there are some who are complete [in it]."
"Non-arising and non-ceasing; or half-arising, half-ceasing, and half-non-arising-non-ceasing.

My Buddha-nature here is entirely non-arising and non-ceasing, whereas your Buddha-nature in the South is half-arising, half-ceasing, and half-non-arising-non-ceasing. He asked, "How are these distinguished?

The Master said, "This [nature] is such that body and mind are one and the same, with nothing remaining outside the body; therefore, it is entirely non-arising and non-ceasing. As for the Southern [nature], the body..."
"This [body] is impermanent, while the nature of the spirit (*ātman*) is permanent; therefore, half is subject to birth and extinction, while half is neither born nor extinguished.

The Master said, "The Master also says that 'this very mind is Buddha. How can there be difference or agreement between this and the teachings of the masters of the South? The Master replied, "In some cases, the names differ but the substance is the same."
Some names refer to the same essence while differing in form; for instance, *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, *tathatā*, and *buddhadhātu* differ in name but are identical in essence.
Conversely, the true mind and the deluded mind, or Buddha-wisdom and worldly wisdom, are identical in name but differ in essence.

Those in the South have mistakenly taken the deluded mind to be the true mind—mistaking a thief for their own son—and they have identified worldly wisdom as Buddha-wisdom, like confusing fish eyes with pearls. These must not be treated as equivalent; the matter requires [careful discernment].

[The student] asked for clarification. [He said: "If one were to depart from this, would one not incur this fault? The Master said, "You need only carefully look back at the aggregates (*skandha*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), investigating each one thoroughly.
Is there even a hair’s breadth that can be apprehended? [The student] said, "I have looked carefully; I do not see a single thing that can be apprehended.
[The Master] asked, "Have you destroyed the characteristics of body and mind? [The student] said, "The nature of body and mind is detached; what is there to be destroyed? [The Master] said, "Body..."
"Is there anything further outside the mind? He replied, "Body and mind have nothing external; how could there be any thing? He asked, "Do you destroy the characteristics of the world?

He replied, "The characteristics of the world are themselves without characteristics (*animitta*); why use effort to destroy them further? The Master said, "If this is so, then you have departed from error. Question:
"Regarding 'the mind itself is the Buddha,' may one still cultivate the myriad practices? The Master said, "All the sages were fully endowed with them."

Regarding the two adornments (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*), how could one possibly negate cause and effect? A student asked National Teacher Zhong: "When one does not apply mental effort (*amanasikāra*), can one attain stillness?

He replied: "If you perceive stillness, that itself is mental effort. (The *Zongjing lu* says: This is why the faculty of mind is so difficult to transcend; both movement and stillness fall into the dust of dharmas.

Not only does one fall into false thinking by failing to understand non-attachment and letting conditions be as they are, but even if one gives rise to a mind that seeks a dark union with stillness, one still retains a standpoint of views. Thus we know that all such instances are taking intellectual opinions for Chan and mistaking illness for the Dharma—like steaming sand in hopes of making rice. 緣 (Condition).

To seek fish by means of wood is to expend effort and labor in vain for countless kalpas. If the mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are unborn; as soon as the mind arises, one immediately forms attachments.
The *Śamatha Verses* of Yongjia say: "If one uses knowledge to know stillness, this is not a knowledge devoid of an object;
it is like a hand grasping a wish-fulfilling gem—it is not a hand that lacks the gem. If one uses self-knowledge to know, this too is not a knowledge devoid of an object;

it is like a hand forming a fist—it is not a hand that is not a fist. Yet, one neither knows by means of knowledge to know stillness, nor does one know by means of self-knowledge to know. It cannot be said [that there is no knowing].
It is "without cognition," because its self-nature is luminously clear; thus it is not the same as wood or stone.

The hand does not grasp a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), nor does it clench into a fist; yet one cannot say it is "handless," for the hand remains at ease. It is not the same as a rabbit's horn. (The *Qingliang Shu* says: "How does it transcend words?

If one grasps at cognition as being able to know the quiescent, one has not escaped words, for there is an object of perception. If cognition knows itself, this is also not without an object. Therefore, subject and object must be equal; in this equality, the illumination is never lost. This 'knowledge without cognition' is not like wood.")

Stone. Therefore it is said that one is able to see; this constitutes the subtlety of the Chan school. Regarding the three types of concentration (*samādhi*), they must be distinguished: first, the concentration of abiding, which means that the wondrous nature is natural and fundamentally unmoving;
second, the concentration of arousal, which means that with a mind clarified and tranquil, brilliance is manifested and increased;

third, the concentration of accomplishing tasks, which means that when the water of concentration is stilled and clear, all phenomena are reflected therein. Regarding the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), they must also be distinguished: first, the emptiness of persons...

Wisdom (*prajñā*). This refers to the realization that the aggregates (*skandha*) are not the self; that within the aggregates there is no self, just like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.

Second is the wisdom of the emptiness of both [subject and object] (*ubhaya-śūnyatā-prajñā*), which means realizing that all phenomena such as the aggregates are conventionally designated based on conditions and lack substantial reality, like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water.

Third is the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-prajñā*), which means realizing that both the object and the cognition are empty, and that even this emptiness is itself empty. Among these, one must recognize three types of views: first, the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*), which refers to the view...
1. Seeing emptiness as non-empty. 2. Seeing non-emptiness: this refers to seeing that which is not empty as being non-empty.

3. Seeing the emptiness of intrinsic nature: this refers to seeing intrinsic nature as being non-nature. ○ Regarding the method of analytical discernment, one must clearly recognize the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within a single thought-moment.
That is to say, when there is vivid discrimination and clear recognition of mental correspondence, this is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). As for the reception [of objects]...

The mind is the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha). The mind taking this principle as its object is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha). The mental formations operating upon this principle are the aggregate of volitional formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
That which defiles the true nature is the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha). These five aggregates, in their entirety, are a single thought-moment;
this single thought-moment, in its entirety, is completely the five aggregates. When one clearly perceives within this single thought-moment, there is no master.

The "master" (the subject) is the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which perceives [all things] as being like illusions and transformations; this is the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

The *Vipaśyanā-gāthā* states: "The object is not understood apart from wisdom, and wisdom does not arise apart from the object. When wisdom arises, it understands the object, and when the object arises, wisdom is produced."

When the object is apprehended, wisdom arises and apprehends; when wisdom arises, it apprehends. This apprehension has nothing to apprehend. It apprehends the object and thus arises; its arising has no power to produce. Though it is wisdom, it is not existent;
though it apprehends, there is nothing to be apprehended. Though it is an object, it is not non-existent. Non-existence is not non-being; existence is not being.
When existence and non-existence are both illuminated, wondrous realization is serene and vast, like fire finding fuel that grows ever more intense.
"Abundant. The firewood is a metaphor for the many objects of arising cognition; the fire is compared to the wondrous wisdom that cognizes those objects. The verse says:
"If wisdom cognizes an object, that is the emptiness of the object within wisdom, just as when the eye perceives the emptiness of a flower, it is the eye that perceives the emptiness of the flower.

If wisdom cognizes wisdom, that is the emptiness of wisdom within wisdom, just as when the eye perceives the emptiness of the eye, it is the eye that perceives the emptiness of the eye. Although wisdom..."

One realizes that the object is empty, and one realizes that the wisdom is empty; yet it is not that there is no wisdom that realizes the object. Although the object is empty, the wisdom still exists.

When the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of the object-realizing wisdom is present, there is no lack of realization regarding the object and the wisdom. It is like the eye realizing that the flower is empty and realizing that the eye itself is empty:

it is not that there is no eye realizing the flower; although the flower is empty, the eye still exists. When the eye realizing the emptiness of the flower-realizing eye is present, there is no lack of realization regarding the flower and the eye. [The character] "You" (優) [is used here].

The *Bichasong* (Verses on the Completion) states: Regarding the third point, that which corresponds to it—when the mind corresponds with emptiness, then whether there is slander or praise, what is there to fear or rejoice in?
When the body corresponds with emptiness, then whether there is cutting with a blade or anointing with fragrance, what is there to suffer or delight in?

When the conditioned environment corresponds with emptiness, then whether there is giving or plundering, what is there to gain or lose? When the mind corresponds with the non-empty aspect of emptiness...
When one responds [to conditions], then craving and views are entirely forgotten, and compassion universally rescues others.

When the body corresponds with both emptiness and non-emptiness, it is internally like withered wood while externally manifesting dignified deportment. When the environment and its resources correspond with both emptiness and non-emptiness, all greedy seeking is forever severed, yet wealth and provisions are used to provide relief.
When the mind corresponds with that which is neither empty nor non-empty, the true mark (dharmatā) first becomes manifest.

To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision: when the body corresponds to emptiness, non-emptiness, neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, then a single mote of dust enters right concentration, while all motes arise in samādhi.
When the environment and its retributions correspond to emptiness, non-emptiness, neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, [the same occurs].

Thus, the fragrant terraces and jeweled pavilions adorn the land for those born through transformation. (The *Zongjing lu* says: "Therefore, if one does not sever the four kinds of deep delusions, yet seeks the wondrous fruit of the One Vehicle, it is like covering one's ears while shouting loudly;
one cannot avoid others hearing it. It is like pouring water into a leaking cup; in the end, there will never be a day when it is full. Seventh, clarifying right and wrong:

the mind is not existent, nor is the mind non-existent. The mind is not non-existent, nor is the mind not non-existent. To say it is existent or non-existent is to fall into the extreme of existence; to say it is neither existent nor non-existent...

If there is no [affirmation], one immediately falls into negation. Thus, this is merely the negation of affirmation and negation; it has not yet reached the affirmation that is neither affirmation nor negation.

Now, by means of the double negation, both affirmations are refuted. When affirmation is refuted, non-affirmation remains as a form of negation. Furthermore, by means of the double negation, both negations are refuted.
When negation is refuted, non-negation becomes affirmation—this is precisely the affirmation that is neither affirmation nor negation. It has not yet reached the state of non-non-affirmation.

Neither "is" nor "is not," yet it is not that it is not "not. This delusion of "is" and "is not" is subtle and difficult to perceive; only when the spirit is clear and the mind is tranquil can one examine it minutely.
Regarding the gradual progression of the Three Vehicles: although the Three Vehicles differ, they all lead back to the essential means of escaping suffering.
Although the śrāvaka’s attainment is minor, the delusions of views and craving have already been dispelled; thus, he has no sorrow within the three realms.

The form of fragmented existence has ceased, the three knowledges shine with brilliant clarity, eighty thousand kalpas manifest before him, and the six supernormal powers are exercised with ease in the unconditioned.
He traversed mountain cliffs directly; at times he walked or stood in mid-air, or sat and lay down with complete ease. Upon swimming across a deep pool, he was as light as a goose feather;

when treading upon the ground, it was as if he were walking on water. Having perfected the power of the nine meditative concentrations (*navasamādhi*), he exercised the eighteen transformations according to his will.

Nevertheless, compared to the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriyaviśuddhi*) attained by a Buddha of the Tripiṭaka, his own [attainment] was both equal to and inferior to theirs. Thus they were the same.

The removal of the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*) constitutes the limit of this stage. If one suppresses ignorance (*avidyā*), the Tripitaka [teaching] is considered inferior (as stated in the Tiantai texts).

Since even the Buddha is regarded as inferior here, it goes without saying for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Although there is a distinction between suppressing and severing [afflictions] when compared to the higher [stages], there remains a gap regarding awakening and delusion at the lower levels.

If this is so, what fault is there in the two vehicles that they would wish not to cultivate? It is only because the Tathāgata, for the sake of those with great faculties, leads them back to the place of treasure.

It causes one to cultivate the wisdom of the seeds (*bīja-jñāna*) and to harmonize with the perfect *E* (the *I* of the *Siddham* syllable). Whether disparaged or praised, these are merely matters of suppression or exaltation according to the occasion.

Regarding the non-duality of phenomena and principle (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), it is said: Since nature is empty, although conditions assemble, they are not existent. Since conditions have assembled, although nature is empty, they are not non-existent.
Therefore, the existence of the assembly of conditions is an existence that is not existence; the non-existence of the emptiness of nature is a non-existence that is not non-existence.

There is no [inherent existence]. Since that which assembles is itself empty of intrinsic nature, it is said to be "not existent. Since emptiness itself is the assembly of conditions, it is said to be "not non-existent.

What is now called "neither existent nor non-existent" does not mean that there is a separate non-existence apart from existence, nor does it mean that there is a separate existence apart from non-existence.

In this way, it clarifies that phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, they are designated by the name "neither existent nor non-existent. It is not a negation [of something else].
It is not existent, yet it is not non-existent. Since it is neither existent nor non-existent, it is also neither "not existent" nor "not non-existent.
Why should it be said only that the path of language is cut off? It is also that the pathways of mental activity have ceased.
The *Record of the Manifestation of the School by Heze* states: "Nirvāṇa and Prajñā differ in name but are identical in essence; names are established according to their respective meanings.
Therefore, it is said that dharmas have no fixed characteristics. Nirvāṇa can give birth to Prajñā, which is thus called the True Buddha-Dharmakāya.

Prajñā can establish Nirvāṇa, and is therefore termed the Tathāgata’s Knowledge and Vision. 'Knowledge' refers to knowing that the mind is empty and quiescent; 'Vision' likewise refers to seeing that the nature is unborn."
The functions of knowing and seeing are neither one nor different; thus, they can be both active and quiescent, eternally wondrous. Principle and phenomena are both suchness (*tathatā*);

the six sense organs remain unstained—this is the merit of concentration and wisdom. The six consciousnesses do not arise—this is the power of suchness-as-it-is. When the mind is as it is, objects subside.
When objects cease, the mind is empty; when both object and mind are extinguished, essence and function are not different.

The nature of True Suchness is pure, and its wisdom-reflection is inexhaustible, like the moon divided into a thousand reflections upon the water. That which is able to see, hear, perceive, and know—this seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing—is eternally empty and quiescent.
Emptiness is formlessness; quiescence is non-arising. A monk asked Master Heze Shenhui: "When seeing and hearing illumine sounds and forms, [what is it that]..."
"Furthermore, do you practice 'resistance' (kàngxíng)? Is there only 'priority and sequence' (xiānhòu)?

Huì said, "Setting aside for a moment 'resistance,' 'priority,' and 'sequence,' what exactly do you take to be sound and form (shēngsè)? The monk said, "According to what the Master has discussed, then no sound or form can be obtained.
Thereupon, he prostrated twice and departed that very day. Later, he lived in seclusion on Mount Méng.

Master Caotang said: "When the celestial net has not yet been spread, how can one see its thousand tassels? Once the great framework is suddenly raised, the ten thousand meshes open of their own accord.
When mind and Buddha are both illuminated, that is contemplation (*guan*). When mind and Buddha are both absent, that is cessation (*zhi*).

When concentration and wisdom are balanced, what mind is not Buddha, and what Buddha is not mind? Since this is so for mind and Buddha, then the myriad realms and myriad conditions are nothing other than [the Buddha-mind]."
This is samādhi. ○ Guifeng showed this to the Minister Wen Zao, saying: "Since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have never attained awakening.
They falsely cling to the body as the mark of self; they create karma according to their emotions and receive retribution according to that karma, undergoing birth, old age, sickness, and death."

One wanders through saṃsāra for long kalpas; yet the awakened nature within the body has never been born or died. It is like being driven and enslaved in a dream, while the body is originally at ease.
It is like water turning to ice—the moist nature does not change. If one can awaken to this nature, it is the Dharmakāya.
It is fundamentally unborn; how could there be any dependence? It is vividly lucid and never obscured, clearly and eternally cognizant. It comes from nowhere, nor...

There is nowhere to go; yet, one frequently gives rise to deluded attachments, which become ingrained through habit until they form one's very nature. Joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure flow subtly and continuously;
one must constantly observe them, diminishing them again and again, until they cease like wind suddenly stopping and waves gradually subsiding.

How could the practice cultivated in a single lifetime be equal to the power and function of the Buddhas? (Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty asked Chan Master Hongbian: "What is sudden seeing? What is gradual cultivation? He replied: "Suddenly clarifying one's own nature is to be the same as the Buddha.")

[This is] a category. However, because there is defiled habituation from beginningless time, one must rely on gradual cultivation as an antidote to cause the function [of the mind] to arise in accordance with its nature—just as when a person eats rice, they are not satiated by a single mouthful.

The verse says: To perform meaningful actions is the awakened mind; To perform meaningless actions is the deluded, distracted mind. The deluded follow emotional thoughts, and at the moment of death, they are dragged away by karma.
The awakened does not depend on emotions, and at the moment of death, it can transform karma. The commentary says: Since one follows delusive thoughts, if one desires...
To act while acting is to fail to use the wisdom that realizes the principle to discern right from wrong; one is thus like a madman.

Consequently, at the time of death, one is dragged along by the path of karma and led away by it to undergo retribution in the future. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Ignorance is the lord, and craving is the Māra king;
they employ the body and mind as servants, driving them like slaves. Thus, while one desires to act according to one's emotions, one fails to examine the underlying principle.
One should not do it; one must stop immediately. If, within the heart, there is no desire to act, yet the action accords with principle, then one must act immediately.
This depends solely on the principle of right and wrong, not on feelings of love or hatred.

Thus, at the time of death, karma cannot bind one, and one will be free to roam as one wishes between the heavens and the human realm. Generally speaking, this applies to whatever occurs during the morning and evening.
If one’s actions are led by the dust of the passions (*kleśa*), then at the moment of death one will be led by karma and undergo rebirth.

If one’s deeds are performed through awakened wisdom rather than the dust of the passions, then at the moment of death one will undergo rebirth through the sovereignty of the self (*ātman*) and not through karma.
One should know that to verify whether or not one possesses such sovereignty over rebirth at the time of death, it is sufficient to examine one’s ordinary conduct.
When the mind acts upon sensory objects, it may be free or not free.
Regarding this, the Five Lamps (Wudeng Huiyuan) and other masters of the various schools have said:
"All phenomena arise from the mind; the myriad forms and ten thousand images are but a single dharma."
Seal. Whatever forms are perceived are all one's own mind. Mind is not mind in itself; it is because of form that there is mind.
That which arises from the mind is called form. Because one knows that form is empty, arising is non-arising (from the *Zongjing*).
Master Si of Jizhou said: "The speech and language of this very moment are your own mind. This mind is the Buddha; it is the Dharma-body of true reality (*dharmakāya*).
A Buddhist sutra states that there are three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names and titles, established according to the circumstances of each world.
It is like a mani jewel that reflects color: when it touches blue, it becomes blue; when it touches yellow, it becomes yellow. Yet the jewel’s own original nature remains as it is."
A finger does not touch itself; a blade does not cut itself; a mirror does not reflect itself.
According to where an image appears, each instance is distinct. This mind shares the same lifespan as empty space. If one enters the gate of samādhi, there is nothing that is not samādhi.
If one enters the gate of signlessness, everything is signless. Wherever it is established, one fully attains the essence of the school. Whether in speech, weeping, or laughter—this is it.

Bending, extending, bowing, and raising each proceed from what is issued forth by the ocean of nature; thus they receive the name "Essence" (zong). Buddhas of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are Buddhas of cause and effect;
they are the functioning of the Buddha-house of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As a sutra says: "The thirty-two marks and eighty minor signs all arise from the mind’s thoughts.
It is also said they are the flames of the Dharma-nature, and again, the meritorious achievements of the Dharma-nature. According to the purity of the mind, [they manifest].
The Buddha-land is pure. Whenever any thoughts arise, one attains the fruit in accordance with those thoughts, manifesting in response to beings;
this is called the Tathāgata. Departing in accordance with what is appropriate, there is thus nothing to be sought. At all times, there is not a single dharma that can be practiced;

it is from this that the Dharma is attained, yet by means of attainment one does not further attain. Therefore, the Dharma does not know the Dharma, and the Dharma does not hear the Dharma. Equality itself is the Buddha.
The Buddha is itself equanimity; one does not employ equanimity to further practice equanimity (Zongjing).

Mazu addressed the assembly, saying: "The self-nature is inherently complete. It is only when the mental constructs of the triple world are exhausted that a single moment of delusion arises—this is the very root of birth and death within the triple world.
If one simply lacks that single moment of thought, the root of birth and death is eliminated. There is none.
For immeasurable kalpas, the deluded thoughts of ordinary beings—characterized by flattery, crookedness, deceit, falsehood, self-conceit, and arrogance—have coalesced into a single entity.
Therefore, a sutra says: "This body is merely composed of various dharmas; when it arises, only dharmas arise; when it ceases, only dharmas cease."

When this dharma arises, it does not say, "I arise. When it ceases, it does not say, "I cease. The preceding thought, the middle thought, and the succeeding thought—thought after thought do not depend upon one another;
each thought is quiescent and extinguished. This is called the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*), which encompasses all dharmas.
It is like hundreds of thousands of diverse streams that all return to the great ocean and are collectively termed "ocean water. It is as if a person were bathing in the great ocean...
Using all water: thus it is that Śrāvakas awaken from delusion while ordinary people are deluded regarding awakening.

They do not know that the Sage’s mind is fundamentally devoid of stages, positions, causes, or fruits, nor of the gradations of mental capacity. They cultivate causes and realize fruits through false conceptualization, dwelling in empty samādhis for eighty thousand kalpas or twenty thousand kalpas;
though they have attained awakening, once awakened they fall back into delusion. To the contemplation of the Bodhisattvas, this is like the suffering of hell.
To sink into emptiness and stagnate in stillness is to fail to see the Buddha-nature. All sentient beings, since immeasurable kalpas past, have not emerged from the samādhi of dharmatā;

they have long remained within this samādhi of dharmatā. Whether putting on clothes or eating food, speaking or responding to others, employing the six sense faculties, or performing any activity whatsoever—all are entirely dharmatā.
If one can, for even a single thought-moment, reflect back upon oneself, the whole body and mind will be the enlightened heart.
Each of you must realize your own mind; do not merely rely on my words.

Even if you could explain as many principles as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, or even if you were to manifest the eighteen transformations by dividing your bodies and emitting light, it would not equal bringing me back my dead ashes.

Dead ashes that have already been watered are powerless—this is a metaphor for the Śrāvakas who falsely cultivate causes and seek to realize the fruit. Dead ashes that have not yet been watered possess power—this is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva path and its practice.

Mastery. One is untainted by any evils. If one were to speak of the Tathāgata’s provisional teachings of the Tripiṭaka, even speaking for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges would not exhaust them;
they are like a chain of hooks, never severed. Yet, if one awakens to the sacred mind, there is nothing remaining at all. The Way does not require cultivation;
it simply requires that one not be defiled. What is meant by "defilement"? All instances of birth and death, and all purposeful activity or directed striving, are defilements.

[To] dye. If you wish to directly realize the Way, the ordinary mind is the Way. Right now, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, responding to stimuli and engaging with things—all of these are the Way.
The Way is the Dharma-realm; even the wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges do not transcend the Dharma-realm.
If it were otherwise, how could one speak of the "Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground"? How could one speak of the "Inexhaustible Lamp"? If [one does not understand this], then...

Within the gates of the teachings, one attains mastery according to the occasion. If one establishes the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), all is the dharma-realm; if one establishes true suchness (*tathatā*), all is true suchness;
if one establishes principle (*li*), all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely principle; if one establishes phenomena (*shi*), all phenomena are entirely phenomena.
Taking one as the primary and the thousand as following, there is no distinction between principle and phenomena; it is all due to the turning of the mind, like the reflection of the moon.
There may be many things; yet the true moon has no multiplicity. There may be many waters from various sources; yet the nature of water has no multiplicity.
There may be many phenomena in the myriad forms of the universe; yet empty space has no multiplicity. There may be many ways of explaining principles;
yet unimpeded wisdom has no multiplicity. All these various establishments arise from the one mind. One may establish them, and one may also sweep them away.
All of this is the wondrous function. It does not exist apart from the Truth; where it stands is itself the Truth. All of this is one's own essence.
All phenomena are the Buddha-dharma. All dharmas are liberation. Liberation is itself suchness (*tathatā*).

The Sūtra says: "In every place, there is a Buddha. When both person and phenomena are empty, and the conceptualizations of ordinary beings and sages are exhausted, one turns the peerless wheel that transcends all calculation and measure.
Like clouds arising in the sky, like patterns formed by writing upon water, it is neither born nor extinguished;

this is Great Quiescence. When entangled in afflictions, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha; when free from entanglements, it is called the Pure Dharmakāya. It manifests forms in response to things, just as...

It is like the moon in water: it does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), nor does it abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The conditioned is the function of the unconditioned; the unconditioned is the support of the conditioned.
Because it does not abide in its support, it is said to be "like space, having no support. This is the meaning of the arising and ceasing of the mind.

The meaning of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind. Regarding the *tathatā* of the mind: it is like a bright mirror reflecting images. The mirror is a metaphor for the mind; the images are metaphors for phenomena (*dharma*).
If the mind grasps at phenomena, it immediately engages with external causes and conditions, which is the meaning of arising and ceasing.

If it does not grasp at phenomena, that is the meaning of *tathatā*. In delusion, it is consciousness (*vijñāna*); in awakening, it is wisdom (*jñāna*). To accord with principle is awakening; to accord with phenomena is delusion. Delusion...

Thus, delusion is the failure to realize one's own fundamental mind; awakening is the realization of one's own original nature. Once awakened, one is forever awakened and shall never again fall into delusion.
It is like the rising of the sun, which cannot coexist with darkness; when the sun of wisdom rises, it does not remain together with the darkness of afflictions (*kleśa*).

When the realm of the mind is fully understood, delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) are immediately eliminated. Once delusive thoughts are eliminated, this is precisely the *dharmatā* of non-arising—originally present and eternally present. It is not...
If one practices the cultivation of the Way through seated meditation, yet does not cultivate it nor sit [in that manner], this is the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna.

If one perceives this principle truly and correctly, one will not create various karmas; according to one's lot, one passes through a lifetime with but a single robe and a single *nāṃsa* (patchwork cloak), sitting and rising in their company.
As the fragrance of preceptual conduct increases and pure karma accumulates, if one can simply act in this way, why worry about not attaining penetration? If, during this life...

Regarding places where one walks for meditation, as well as one’s own fields, houses, and dwellings, or one’s parents, brothers, and so forth—whenever the mind raises itself to perceive these, this mind fundamentally does not go.
Do not say that when perceiving those objects, the mind goes [to them]. (The *Zongjing* says: "The nature of the mind is fundamentally without coming or going, nor is there arising or ceasing.

Those places where one has walked, as well as one's parents, kinsmen, and others now perceived, are due to having seen them in the past; they are all retained within the heart in the eighth *ālayavijñāna*. It is not that the present mind goes [there]; it is also called a 'seed' (*bīja*).")

Consciousness is also called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness). It stores and accumulates what was previously perceived.
