Thus, one succeeds to the ancestral seat. Do you not see how Ānanda asked Kāśyapa, "Aside from the transmission of the golden robe, what else did the World-Honored One transmit?
Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said, "Turn around! (The meaning is that he transmitted nothing other than this.)
"Set down the banner-pole at the front gate. This is the hallmark of the Patriarchs.

Ānanda served as an attendant for thirty years, yet because he relied solely on his erudition and wisdom, the Buddha rebuked him, saying: "Your three hundred days of studying wisdom are not equal to one day of studying the Way."
Master Dà'ān said: "Within each of your own bodies, there is a priceless great treasure.

From the gate of the eyes, it emits light that shines through and pierces the mountains, rivers, and the great earth. From the gate of the ears, it emits light that perceives and hears all sounds, whether good or evil.
These six gates constantly emit radiance day and night; this is also called the Samādhi of Emitting Light. You simply do not recognize it within this body composed of the four elements."
In the center, supported from both within and without, it is not allowed to lean or tilt. Its two legs are large and can carry two loads of stone;
even when crossing a bridge of single logs, it does not allow itself to fall to the ground. What is this? If you seek it even by a hair’s breadth—
Thus, it is invisible. Therefore, Master Zhigong said: "Searching within and without, one finds nothing at all; yet the functioning upon the objective realm is entirely present.
Zhaozhou, in ascending to the hall, said: "The golden Buddha does not pass through the furnace; the wooden teacher does not pass through the fire; the clay Buddha does not pass through the water."
The True Buddha sits within; bodhi, nirvana, suchness, and buddha-nature are all but clothes clinging to the body—they are also called afflictions.
Upon the ground of ultimate reality, where would they be placed? When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
Among thousands upon thousands of people, they are all men seeking the Buddha; yet among them, can you find a single true practitioner? If one were to accord with emptiness...
The King was his disciple. [The Master said: "Do not teach that the disease of the mind is the most difficult to cure.
Before the world existed, this nature already existed; when the world perishes, this nature does not perish. From the moment you first saw me, an old monk, you have never been anyone else;
you are simply this very host. Why do you seek this elsewhere? At such a time, do not turn your head or change your countenance."
[The Master] looked at him and immediately dismissed him. A monk asked: "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? The Master said, "No. The monk asked:
"From the Buddhas above down to the ants below, all possess Buddha-nature. Why does a dog have none? The Master said:
"It is because it possesses the nature of karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*). Later, another monk asked: "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? The Master said, "Yes."
[The monk] said, "Since it exists, why does it enter the skin bag? Zhaozhou said, "Knowing it yet deliberately committing the offense.
Zhaozhou ascended the hall and said: "It is like a bright pearl in the palm: when a barbarian comes, it appears as a barbarian; when a Han Chinese comes, it appears as a Han Chinese.
(Yuanzhao Fajie) This old monk takes a blade of grass and uses it as a sixteen-foot golden body; he takes a sixteen-foot golden body and uses it as a blade of grass. (Small within..."

The Buddha appears within the great as the small; the Buddha is affliction, and affliction is the Buddha. (Do not seek to extinguish dust to unite with awakening. A monk asked, "Whose affliction is the Buddha?
Zhaozhou said, "He is the affliction for all people. The monk asked, "How can one avoid this? Zhaozhou said, "Why try to avoid it?"
Master Chen of Changsha addressed the assembly: "The entire ten directions of the world is the single eye of the śramaṇa.
The entire ten directions of the world is the whole body of the śramaṇa. The entire ten directions of the world is one's own radiance.
The entire ten directions of the world is within one's own radiance. Throughout the entire ten directions of the world, there is not a single person who is not oneself."
I have always told you all: the Buddhas of the three periods of time, together with all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm, are this light of the *mahāprajñā*.
Before this light has been emitted, where could you all have found certainty?
Before the light was emitted, there was not even a trace of Buddha or sentient beings; from where could mountains, rivers, and lands have come? Question:
"What is Mañjuśrī? The Master said, "Walls, tiles, and rubble. "What is Avalokiteśvara? He said, "Sounds and speech. "What is Samantabhadra?
He said, "The minds of sentient beings. "What is the Buddha? He said, "The physical bodies of sentient beings. A question was asked:
"The essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical to Suchness (tathatā). For what reason are there various names? The Master [replied].
It is said: "Returning to the source from the eye-faculty is named Mañjuśrī; returning to the source from the ear-faculty is named Avalokiteśvara;
returning to the source from the mind is named Samantabhadra. Mañjuśrī is the Buddha’s wondrous wisdom of observation; Avalokiteśvara is the Buddha’s unconditioned great compassion;
Samantabhadra is the Buddha’s wondrous non-active practice. These three sages are the Buddha’s wondrous functions; the Buddha is the true essence of these three sages."

As for its essence (*tǐ*), when functioning (*yòng*), there are as many provisional names (*jiámíng*) as there are sands in the Ganges; yet when considered in its essence, it is collectively named the One Bhagavān.

The Master of the Avataṃsaka asked: "Is space definitively existent, or is it definitively non-existent? The Master said: "To say it exists is permissible; to say it does not exist is also permissible.
When space exists, it exists only as a provisional existence; when space does not exist, it is simply the absence of provisional non-existence. [The Master] said: "Venerable Monk..."
"What scriptural passages support what you have said? The Master replied: "The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

'The empty space of the ten directions arises within your mind, like a single fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the sky. Is this not to say that when empty space arises, it merely gives rise to a provisional name?
Furthermore, it says: 'When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions is entirely extinguished. Is this not [the case] regarding empty space?"

When they cease, it is only the provisional name that ceases. Therefore, it is said that existence is provisional existence, and non-existence is provisional non-existence. [The Master] addressed the assembly:
"If the mind were subject to arising, then dreams, illusions, and empty flowers would also be subject to arising.

If the body were subject to arising, then the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the myriad phenomena of the universe would also be subject to arising. (Juefan Chenggu’s *Praise of Master Cen the Tiger* says: "The Tathāgata said to Ānanda: 'You fundamentally do not know that all floating dust...')"

All illusory manifestations arise where they are and perish where they are; though illusory and false, they are designated as "phenomena. Their nature, however, is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity. As Nāgārjuna said: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both together, nor without a cause."

Therefore, it is said that there is no arising. Using the discernment of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to discourse on the subtlety of the mind-dharma, its purity and clarity are as evident as seeing an object in the palm of one’s hand; there is nothing about which doubt can arise. Yet, sentient beings of the末代 (final age) ultimately do not understand this. This is because their deluded nature is not accustomed to what they have heard.

The Chan Master took pity on them and, regarding the realm of the known, illustrated it by saying: "If the mind were to arise... and so forth. How magnificent these words are! They correspond from beginning to end with the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and the *Vigrahavyāvartanī-śāstra*.
Question: The Sūtra says, "Like within pure lapis lazuli, the image of true gold appears within. What does this mean? The Master said: By means of...
Pure lapis lazuli constitutes the essence of the *dharmadhātu*. A statue of pure gold constitutes the essence of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Since the essence can give rise to wisdom, and wisdom can penetrate the essence, it is said: "As within pure lapis lazuli, a statue of pure gold appears within."
Zihu Zong addressed the assembly: "As for the two words 'sound' and 'form,' how can they be sought? If you realize their source, they are ultimately nothing other than yourself.
It is like a round mirror: when a man approaches, a man appears; when a woman approaches, a woman appears—even so with monks and laypeople, or blue and yellow."
Mountains, rivers, and the myriad things follow their respective forms and appearances, yet within a single mirror they transmit their brilliance; it cannot be that this mirror has many varieties.
It simply reflects objects so that they are revealed. O benevolent one, do you recognize the mirror?

If you do not recognize the mirror, you will be entirely obstructed by men and women, blue and yellow, mountains and rivers, and the like, which will hinder your radiance. What outlet for your vital energy will there be? If you recognize the mirror, however—

From blue and yellow, men and women, the great earth, mountains, and rivers, to those with perception and those without, four-footed and many-footed beings, those born from wombs, eggs, or moisture, and the heavens and hells—all find their respective proportions within a single mirror.
Whether long or short kalpas, whether form or emptiness, all are fully understood therein; it is nothing other than this. Question: What is the Great Perfect Mirror? Answer: One.
"One cannot be attached to any thing. Question: "Why can one not be attached to any thing? The Master said: "You are all things;
can you, in turn, be attached to yourself? "Originally complete in itself, originally fully equipped;

it must be such that not even a speck of dharma obstructs your eye-sight before it is attained. If there is even a trace of something remaining unexhausted, it will not be so for one or two lifetimes."

For kalpas, you have been deceived by this skin-sack. Within the roots of your life, the sense objects, and the dharmas, you have conjured all manner of monsters; mountain spirits and ghostly charms have attached themselves to your practice.
Mistaking a trifle for enough, you ply your meager skin like a drum, yet instead bring harm to the Buddha-dharma.
You mock the veneration of stupas and temples, and you disparage those who uphold the sutras. You are like a worm within a lion’s body, devouring the very flesh of that lion.
When the Patriarch came from the West, it was simply this: winter is cold and summer is hot; the night is dark and the day is bright.

It is only because you conceive intentions where there is no intention and create affairs where there is no affair, that you forcibly construct an inner and outer where none exists, and falsely speak of east and west where none exist.
For this reason, *śamatha* cannot be clearly realized; it reaches the point where the faculties and their objects cannot be brought under one's own control.

A monk asked, "How can one avoid being deluded by various objects? The Master said, "Try to point out the object that deludes you and show it to me. The monk stepped forward and said, "I do not see it.
The Master said, "Since you do not see it, from where could a delusive object arise? The monk bowed. The Master said, "Now you have seen the delusion."
"I wish to go.
Master Qianqing said, "All sentient beings—donkeys, mules, elephants, horses, centipedes, and millipedes; those in the ten evil paths and five realms of existence;
ignorance, deluded thoughts, and the unextinguished dharmas of greed and anger—all manifest from within the *tathāgatagarbha*. Fundamentally..."
This coming [mind] is the Buddha. Since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have allowed a single thought to arise in a flash, from which they have rushed headlong until this very day.

Now that a Buddha has appeared in the world, he instructs them to extinguish the faculty of the mind and sever all discrimination. If one attains resonance with this single thought, one immediately transcends to perfect enlightenment.
Why then use much knowledge and many interpretations to disturb the body and mind? Thus, the radiance of Bodhi cannot manifest.
A student asked, "When there is no lamp after midnight, Master, what then? The Master said, "For one who has realized the Way, the constant light is ever-present;
what day or night could there be? The student asked, "Why do we not see the Master’s light? The Master said, "With what kind of eyes would you attempt to see it?
The student said, "Ordinary people all see with their present eyes. The Master snapped his fingers and said, "How bitter! All sentient beings!"

Birth occurs when the sense organs and their objects interact. Since beginningless time, you have mistaken the thief for your own son; thus, until this very day, you have been constantly bound by shackles and chains.

You take the consciousness that discriminates what the eyes see and attempt to seek the Buddha-way with it; this is precisely to turn your back on your original mind and to wander in pursuit of every thought.
Such a person is separated from the truth even while facing it directly.
Master Zhao of the Great Sui ascended the hall and said: "The three thousandfold world-system is contained within a single mote of dust; the waters of the four great oceans return to a single drop.
Mount Sumeru is subsumed within a mustard seed. If you seek your own self, it lies in nothing more than a single hair.
If you can perceive the entire trichiliocosm as a single scripture within that single hair, you will see that it is simply this very movement of your own."
When the objective realm cannot be attained, the true state does not manifest. Why speak of "noticing even a hair's breadth"?
All such efforts are merely leaning against a sword or dodging an arrow, fearing a mirror and hiding one’s form. Brothers, would you call this "nature"? It is like pressing down grass with a stone;
even if you were to pull the stone away, the habitual tendencies would remain as before. You must bring things to a conclusion in every situation before it will begin.
To attain mastery over objects and escape being summoned by the dust of sensory realms—this is truly a great difficulty, a great difficulty! A thousand difficulties, ten thousand difficulties!
It is only after one has shed the shell that they must bear the iron bit and carry the saddle; who then suffers?
Master Lingyun Qin said: "O virtuous ones, all that is long or short is entirely impermanent. Observe the vegetation of the four seasons: leaves fall and flowers bloom.
How much more so for the cycles of formation and destruction throughout kalpas of dust, wherein devas and humans, and the seven realms of existence, revolve through earth, water, fire, and wind.
As causes and effects reach their end, the suffering of the three evil paths has never increased or decreased by so much as a hair’s breadth; it remains only as a latent tendency."

The divine consciousness is eternally present. Those of superior capacity, upon encountering a virtuous friend who provides clarification, attain liberation in that very place; this is itself the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

Those of middling or inferior capacity, being deluded and ignorant, are unable to awaken to this illumination; they remain immersed in the triple world, wandering through the cycle of birth and death. For their sake, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni—
Whether in heaven or among men, he established teachings to provide proof and reveal the ultimate Way. Do you understand?

If you say that one attains [enlightenment] by entering meditative absorption and concentrating the spirit in tranquil contemplation, then even the non-Buddhist teachers such as the Nirgranthas can enter and attain the great samādhi of eighty thousand kalpas—would they not then be Buddhas?
From birth until death, this old man has been but an old bhikṣu. Though born within the three realms, he remains undefiled;
yet, if he seeks liberation, where can he go? Even if there were a place to go, it would still be a cage where Māra finds his opportunity.
Since neither body nor mind can be grasped, one need only ensure that at all times one does not employ external sounds or forms, remaining without thought and without recollection.

There is but one dharma that accords with the true nature of reality. Even for those who have left the household life, up to Bodhisattvas at the stage of the tenth bhūmi who have perfected their minds, they cannot find its traces or grasp it.
For this reason, the devas rejoice, the earth spirits cradle their feet, the Buddhas of the ten directions offer praise, and the Māra kings weep.
Why is this? Because this dharma is as lively and agile as empty space; it has no root and no place of abiding. If...
"Where would one arrive? As soon as the eye-sockets stir, there is no connection. Deshan ascended the hall and said:

"If you have nothing to do within yourself, then do not seek falsely. Even if you were to obtain something by seeking falsely, it would still not be attainment. You need only be free from affairs within the mind."
When the mind is free from concern for phenomena, it is void yet spiritual, empty yet wondrous. To speak of its beginning or end in terms as small as a hair-tip is entirely self-deception. Why?
A single thought tied to even a hair’s breadth is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting stir of emotion results in being shackled for ten thousand kalpas.
The names "saint" and "ordinary person" are all empty sounds; their extraordinary features and inferior forms are all illusory colors. You who desire...
One seeks it; does this not lead to entanglement? When one eventually grows weary of it, it becomes a great affliction.
In the end, it provides no benefit. Master Dongshan said to Caoshan: "In the age of the Final Dharma, many people possess only dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

If you wish to distinguish between the true and the false, there are three kinds of leakage (*sāndrāva*): the first is the leakage of views (*dṛṣṭi-sāndrāva*), wherein the faculty of discernment does not leave its station and falls into a sea of poison."

The second is the leakage of sentiment (*qing-shen-lou*): it stagnates in preferences and aversions, and one's perspective becomes lopsided and withered. The third is the leakage of speech (*yu-shen-lou*): in investigating the subtle, one loses the fundamental source;

the capacity for discernment is clouded regarding the beginning and the end, and turbid wisdom continues to circulate. Regarding these three types, you should be aware of them. (Ruilu previously said:)
"Intelligence cannot rival birth and death; how can dry wisdom escape the wheel of suffering?
Jiufeng Qian said, "Brothers, do you recognize life? Flowing water is life; profound stillness is the body.
A thousand waves surging together is the realm of Mañjuśrī; a single expanse of clear sky is the couch of Samantabhadra. Next, he borrowed...
A single phrase points to the moon; within it, the matter is the speaking of the moon. Brothers, by what standard do you deliberate?
Reaching this point, one cannot rely on the "three inches" [of the mouth]; try to speak and understand! One cannot rely on the ears; try to listen and discern!
Do not rely on the eyes; try to discern this clearly. Therefore it is said: "Before the sound, it cannot be cast out; after the phrase, its form is not hidden.
The entire universe and the great earth are all, in their entirety, your own true person's very body. Where, then, can you place your eyes, ears, nose, and tongue?
Do not merely attempt to calculate or construct an intellectual understanding through the faculty of thought; even until the end of the future, there will be no rest.
[The Master] paused. Question: "The entire universe is, after all, this very eye. What is the 'eye of the universe'? The Master said: "The universe is within it. [The questioner] asked:
"Where is the eye of the universe? The Master said: "It is precisely the eye of the universe. [The questioner] asked: "Does it still illuminate? The Master said:
"It does not borrow the power of the three luminaries. [The questioner] asked: "If it does not borrow the power of the three luminaries, by what means does it function?"
"It is called the 'Eye of Heaven and Earth. The Master said, "If it were not so, one would see countless ghosts and spirits before one's own skull.
Chan Master Jiufeng Qian received the seal of transmission from Shishuang. A monk asked, "In the teachings it is said that the three luminaries arise through conditions."

"When the visual faculty is first formed, the three luminaries have not yet appeared; does it still constitute 'seeing' or not? Huiming said, "Because conditions differ, seeing itself is neither diminished nor impaired.
The monk asked, "If there is no impairment, why can one not see objects in the dark? Huiming said, "Though you do not see objects, how could you possibly not see the darkness?
The monk asked, "Setting aside the three luminaries, what is the locus of true seeing? Huiming said:

"The sun overhead covers the earth, black as lacquer. (As the *Stonehead Cansong Qi* says: "When there is light within, do not meet it with darkness; when there is darkness within, do not gaze upon it with light.
Yongquan said with joy, "Those who possess intellectual understanding are many, but among ten thousand people, there is not one who possesses both realization and practice.
I dare say they are still subject to the cycle of rebirth. Why is this? It is because their outflows of consciousness have not been exhausted."
Master Yuan’an of Luopu said: "The profound gate is firmly closed; the lock of consciousness is difficult to open. Ensnared within the net of doubt, the blade of wisdom is too dull to cut through it.
If one does not provide a clear revelation from the vantage point of the present, how can the deluded child know where to return? If you wish for the Great Function to manifest before you,"
One can only suddenly forget all views. When all views are exhausted, the murky mist does not arise; the illumination of wisdom is penetratingly clear, and there is nothing else remaining.
Now, students of the Way form understandings based on external quantities and are encompassed by those very quantities; thus their minds cannot be shifted or transformed.
This is like hearing that does not transcend sound, or seeing that does not surpass form—even if they were to sweep the gateway of their own doors clean.
Pure. His own Dharma-eye was not yet clear; this man possessed only one eye. He could not penetrate the continuity of right and wrong, yet he was free to break them apart at will.
Xuefeng Cun composed his own epitaph, which says: "That which exists by virtue of conditions undergoes formation and decay from beginning to end. It does not [arise] from..."
Regarding "attaining through conditions": it becomes ever more firm throughout successive kalpas. (Fayan said: "Right now, as for what is formed and what is destroyed, no one can answer.
Nanchan Qi-fan ascended the hall and said: "As for famous names and wondrous phrases, everyone everywhere says they have already been exhausted.
Today, is there anyone among this assembly who can transcend the primary principle? Bring forth a question. A monk asked: "What is the primary principle?"
"One meaning. The Master said, "Why do you not ask about the primary meaning? He replied, "I have already asked. The Master said, "That has already fallen into the secondary meaning.
Caoshan Wenheshang said, "The walls, tiles, and rubble are the mind of all Buddhas; this is also called the 'ground-nature' (xingdi). It is also...
It is called the "total realization of the essence," and is also termed "insentient beings preaching the Dharma.

If one knows that here one attains a state beyond verbal expression, then the lands of the ten directions, the mountains, rivers, and great earth, stone walls, tiles, and pebbles, space and non-space, sentient and insentient beings, grasses, trees, and forests—all are universally one body.
This is called "attaining the prediction of enlightenment" (vyākaraṇa), and it is also called the "Dharma-gate of the Single Syllable. It is also...
It is called the Dharma-gate of Total Retention (*dhāraṇī*); it is also called a single mote of dust or a single thought-moment; it is also termed "simultaneous penetration.
If this is the ground of nature (*prakṛti-bhūmi*), one does not know its existence. No Buddha can illustrate it through a thousand metaphors, nor can any analogy succeed among ten thousand kinds.

All sages—thousands and tens of thousands—emerge from within this very place, which has never changed since time immemorial. Thus it is said: "The Bhagavans of the ten directions all follow the single path to Nirvana."

The Gate (The Mirror of the School). ○ Addressing the Assembly: Those in the monastic community who dwell within these "threads of the robe" must investigate and penetrate the matter that transcends [the mundane].
If you are clear in your capacity to assume this responsibility, you will turn all the sages behind yourself;
only then do you attain freedom. If you cannot turn them, then even if you have mastered the teachings to the full extent, you will merely be standing behind them with palms joined in salutation.
What great talk! If you can turn yourself around, then even when all manner of coarse and heavy circumstances arise, you will be able to exercise mastery over them.

Even if you were to fall prostrate in the mud, you would still exercise mastery. Whether in heaven or hell, as a hungry ghost or an animal—no matter where you are—you do not shift from your original state;
you are fundamentally the same person as before, it is simply that you no longer act as you did before.
The Path. If there is a mind of longing, it becomes an attachment once again. If you can break free from this, what is there to choose? Each person has their own sitting mat;
even if a Buddha appears in the world, he cannot encroach upon it. If you wish to know this matter, even if you were to become a Buddha or a Patriarch right now, it would still remain so.
"This very thing" causes one to fall into the three paths and six realms; "this very thing" must be brought under one's own mastery before it can be so.
If one cannot master it, it will simply undergo transformation and change.

A monk asked Master Yunju Zhi, "The Master says that seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood. Since the pure nature does not belong to existence or non-existence, for what reason is there 'seeing'?
The Master said, "Seeing is seeing nothing. The monk said, "If there is nothing seen, how can there still be seeing?"
The Master said, "Even the place of seeing does not exist. [The student] asked, "When one sees in this way, who is it that sees?

The Master said, "There is no one who can see. [The student] asked, "What is the ultimate principle of this? The Master said, "To falsely reckon things as existing is to have subject and object; this is what is called delusion.
To give rise to conceptual understanding following such [deluded] seeing is to fall into birth and death. It is not so for one who sees clearly. All day long..."

[The student] said, "I see. Yet I have never truly seen it. When seeking the locus of this seeing, its substance and characteristics cannot be found; when both subject and object are utterly transcended, this is called 'seeing the nature' (*xing*). The Master asked, "Does this nature not pervade all places? He replied, "There is nowhere it does not pervade. The Master asked, "Do ordinary beings (*pǔfán*) possess it? He replied, "There is nowhere it does not pervade. How could ordinary beings not possess it? The Master asked, "Are Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not subject to birth [and death]? He replied, "No. The Master said, "If so, how can you say they do not possess it? The student said, "It is because they have already realized it. The Master said, "If that is so, then even an ant possesses it. The student said, "How can an ant possess it? The Master said, "Because there is nowhere it does not pervade. How could an ant not possess it? The student said, "If this is so, then why do ordinary beings not realize it? The Master said, "Because they are attached to their bodies and minds. If they were to cast away body and mind, they would immediately realize it. The student said, "What is meant by 'casting away body and mind'? The Master said, "When you see forms, do not grasp at them as forms; when you hear sounds, do not grasp at them as sounds. When you no longer grasp at forms and sounds, you will naturally cast away body and mind. The student said, "If one casts away body and mind, what then? The Master said, "At that moment, you will see your own original face. The student said, "What is the original face? The Master said, "It is that which you see right now. The student said, "I have never seen it. The Master said, "If you have never seen it, then where is it? Seek the locus of this seeing, and you will find that its substance and characteristics are unobtainable. When both the perceiver and the perceived are completely severed, this is called 'seeing the nature. The student said, "Does this nature pervade all places? The Master said, "There is nowhere it does not pervade. The student said, "Do ordinary beings possess it? The Master said, "There is nowhere it does not pervade. The Master said, "Because they are attached to their bodies and minds. If they were to cast away body and mind, they would immediately realize it. The student said, "What is meant by 'casting away body and mind'? The Master said,
"Bound by death, the ordinary person alone is entangled in this suffering; how could it ever be universal?

The Master said, "Within the nature of purity, the ordinary person calculates the existence of subject and object, and thus falls into birth and death. The Buddhas and Great Beings know that within the nature of purity, one does not belong to existence or non-existence;
thus, subject and object do not arise. [The student] asked, "If it is explained in this way, then there must be people who possess understanding and those who lack it."
The Master said: "If even 'realization' cannot be apprehended, how could there be a person who realizes?

You should immediately understand that within the nature of purity, there are neither ordinary beings nor sages, nor anyone who realizes or fails to realize. Both 'ordinary' and 'sage' are merely names.
If you give rise to understanding based on these names, you will fall into birth and death. If you know that provisional names are not real, then there is no one who corresponds to those names."
This is the ultimate point of culmination. To say, "I can understand this, but they cannot," is a great illness.

To perceive distinctions between the pure and the defiled, or the ordinary and the sage, is likewise a great illness. To form the understanding that there are neither ordinary beings nor sages belongs to the denial of cause and effect.
To perceive a pure nature as something in which one may dwell is a great delusion; likewise, to interpret it as something in which one does not dwell is also a great delusion.
However, within this pure nature, there is the application of indestructible skillful means and the arousal of compassion.
Where such things are aroused is precisely the entirety of the pure nature; this may be called "seeing the nature and attaining Buddhahood. It is like a person [in whom] head after head...
It has been attained. It penetrates through every single thing; one may simply call such a person "one who has accomplished the task," but one never calls them "the Noble One.
From this we know that the path of the Noble One is distinct by itself. Even the most weighty and most precious things in the world cannot be brought into the presence of the Noble One;
you must know that it is inconceivable and does not admit of ordinary concern. Therefore, the ancients said: "It is just like..."
Two mirrors: their radiance faces radiance, their light reflects light; there is no waxing or waning. Is this not the same as it is?
Yet you still call it a matter of images and reflections. When the sun rises and its light illuminates the world, this clarity is one half;
what do you call that other half? At present, you have not yet recognized the light and shadow at the gates and thresholds—this is merely the coarse and shallow level.
As for the matter of doing household chores, how could one possibly compete with them? To descend from heaven is poverty; to spring up from the earth is wealth.
It is easy to emerge from within the gate, but difficult to exit from within the body. To move is to bury oneself ten feet deep;
to remain still is to sprout right where one stands. With a single word, one may leap free and stand alone in that moment. Words do not...

It must be much. If it is too much, it is of no use. (Yongming’s commentary says: "If the treasure of wisdom wells up from the ground of the mind, how could it ever be exhausted? Therefore, it is called the inexhaustible treasury.

However, if you can truly attain the mind, and if you can be thoroughly grounded in its reality, then naturally the words that emerge will correspond with the true mark (*dharmatā*). Under such speech, one rescues beings from birth and death, transforms the ordinary into the sacred, and turns pebbles into gold. If the mind is not yet grounded and perfect faith is not established, then to merely indulge in empty and superficiality only increases wild wisdom.

Even if one could speak so that celestial flowers fall and stones nod their heads, if the matter is not real, it all becomes mere sorcery and illusion. Thus, when Master Zhigong saw Dharma Master Yun Guang lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra* and being moved by the falling of celestial flowers, he said:"
This is the meaning of "biting the flea. Baishui Benren said:
"An old monk like me generally does not wish to play with people's sons and daughters before sound or after form.
Furthermore, sound is not sound; form is not form. [A monk] asked: "What is 'sound is not sound'? He replied: [The following dialogue ensues].
"Can it be called 'form'? [The Master asked. "How is it that form is not form? [The monk replied: "Can it be called 'sound'? The monk bowed.
The Master said, "Tell me, did I speak for you, or did I answer your question? If you can understand it here, there will be a point of entry."
Master Longya said: "Dharma" is a name for that which provides a standard and sustains; "the Way" is the essential nature of sentient beings.
This nature existed long before the world came into being, and it does not perish when the world is destroyed. It is called the nature that follows the flow.
It is eternally without change; its movement and stillness are equal to empty space.

It is called the "Eternal Abiding of Worldly Phenomena," and it is also named the "Emptiness of Ultimate Meaning" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the "Original Limit" (*koṭi*), the "Mind-King" (*citta-rāja*), "True Suchness and Liberation" (*tathatā-vimukti*), and "Bodhi and Nirvāṇa.
These hundreds of thousands of diverse names are all merely provisional designations. Although there are many names, there is no multiplicity of essences.
One integrates many names into a single essence; one unifies myriad meanings and returns to the One Mind.
If you recognize your own original mind, it is called "returning to the root and attaining the essential meaning. If you wish to obtain all flowing waters, seek them only within the great ocean;
if you wish to know the characteristics of the myriad dharmas, simply realize their accord within the mind (the Mirror of the Source).
Master Ying said: "Mañjuśrī asked the Golden Woman, 'Does your body possess the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements?
The woman replied, 'Just as my body possesses the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements [so do yours]. The Brahmajāla Sūtra says:"
All earth and water were my previous bodies; all fire and wind are my original substance.

Furthermore, the two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—stand in mutual dependence upon one another. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The fact that all phenomena are without marks is the true essence of the Buddha.
The sutra clarifies that if one reckons the spirit of enlightened wisdom (*citta*) to be permanent while form (*rūpa*) is decaying and impermanent, then one is a non-Buddhist nihilist.
The view of permanence. The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that the realm of sentient beings is itself the realm of the Buddha; the realm of the Buddha is itself the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Beyond the Dharma-realm, there is no other separate phenomenon. Even though the myriad phenomena differ, their essence is eternally identical.

If one is not deluded regarding this identity, then essence and function are eternally non-dual. This principle of non-duality is, indeed, the essential discipline for transcending the world. A single thought-moment...
It should be so; one must not be separated from the ordinary in order to become a sage (from the *Zongjing*).
Master Xiansha Shibei of Fuzhou addressed the assembly, saying: "If the mind retains the measure of the sacred, one still falls into the dust of dharmas (*dharmaraja*);

if one's own views have not yet been forgotten, it still results in leakage. The non-Buddhists of the Western Heavens can enter the samādhi of eighty thousand kalpas, yet they close their eyes and hide [themselves away]."
The eyes [are closed]; the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom extinguished. Even after the kalpas have passed, one cannot escape saṃsāra.
This is because the eye of the Way is not clear and the root-source of birth and death has not been severed. A renunciant must not be the same as those non-Buddhists.
Which of these is the place where you have gained strength throughout your life? You must, in moments of urgency, regard it as if losing your own life; settle your mind to save yourself. Let go...
Abandon idle conditions and bring the mind-consciousness to rest; only then will there be a slight degree of resonance.

If you do not do so, then tomorrow or the day after, everything will be carried away by the emotions of the discriminating consciousness. What freedom will you have? Now, these insentient things are actually superior to you;
they proclaim clearly and distinctly. Earth, wood, stone, and rock preach the Dharma with a truth that is most extraordinary. It is simply...
Few people are able to listen. Only upon hearing this teaching can one begin to deliberate.

Generally speaking, beneath the three rafters, those who possess this true realization and illumination will find that within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, they are identical to the pure lands of all Buddhas;
what more need they fear regarding birth and death? Furthermore, who among them knows that all dharmas are entirely devoid of substantial reality—even at Vulture Peak?

This was once presented [to the assembly]. Kāśyapa heard it directly from the Buddha himself, as if they were conversing about the moon. An ancient worthy said: "Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all;

this is like pointing at the moon. Even the stages and positions of practice, liberation, the bodhisattva’s nirvāṇa, and the holy virtues and fruits of the Three Vehicles are all like flowers in the sky or the horns of a rabbit.
It is not that the Way does not see them, but rather when one returns to observe the world, it is like the affairs of a dream—all conditioned phenomena.

Mental dharmas cannot rely upon one another; it is simply because you have violated the Truth and abandoned the Source, loathing the mundane while delighting in the sacred, that you produce such views and cognitions that do not transcend the limitations of others.
You cast off the five aggregates yet fail to leave them behind. "You all, for your part, what matter can you truly take up?
In what world do you establish yourselves and sustain your lives? If you cannot discern this, it is just like pressing on the eyes and seeing flowers where there are none."
To perceive things as they appear is already a mistake. What currently exists before one’s eyes—the mountains, rivers, and great earth; form and emptiness, light and darkness;
all these various phenomena—are all but the illusory signs of a weary delusion. To call them such is termed "inverted perception.

For those who have left the household life and realized the fundamental source of mind and consciousness, when they look upon these things now, they see them all as a vast, pitch-black expanse, like ink. As for the ancestral school from of old—
This is the lineage of the crowns of all Buddhas. Since you are unable to uphold it, I have used expedient means to urge you to enter through the gate of Kāśyapa;

thus, you may continue on and transcend directly. This single gate transcends the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages, transcends the world-ocean of Vairocana’s wondrous adornments, and transcends the expedient gates of Śākyamuni.
From this very moment, for eternal kalpas, I shall not teach you [otherwise].
There is but one thing; I shall let you see it with your own eyes. Why do you not investigate it with all haste?

Even though Śākyamuni preached the twelve divisions of the teachings and performed a great display of Buddha-activity, within this gate, not a single point can be used, nor can even a hair’s breadth of clever artifice be employed.
It is like a dream, and like the prattle of one asleep. To recognize this is to emerge greatly.

One who has attained great penetration and liberation transcends both the ordinary and the holy; they give birth to life and depart from death; they leave behind cause and effect; they surpass Vairocana and transcend Śākyamuni.
Do not remain long attached to the net of love for birth and death, for you will be bound and carried away by the karma of good and evil, leaving you no share of freedom.
Even if you refine your body and mind until they are as empty as space, even if you reach a state of brilliant clarity and profound stillness that does not waver—
These abodes do not transcend the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The ancients called this "like a rushing torrent";
because the flow is so rapid, one is unaware of it and falsely perceives it as stillness. Practicing in such a manner, one cannot escape the bounds of saṃsāra.

Furthermore, there is another class who speak of "luminous clarity" and the "numinous spirit," claiming that the numinous faculty of intelligence can see and hear, acting as the sovereign within the field of the five aggregates. I now...
I ask you: if you take this "bright and alert" state to be your true reality, why is it not bright and alert when you are drowsy?
If it is not your true self during drowsiness, why do you still call that which is bright and alert "yourself"?
This is called "mistaking a thief for one's own son"; it is the root of birth and death, the conditioned breath of deluded thought. Do you wish to know its origin? I—
I have told you: that which is luminous and intelligent exists only because of the dharmas of external objects, such as form, sound, fragrance, and so forth;

it is on this basis that one says, "This is the luminous and intelligent. If these external objects were absent, this luminous and intelligent nature would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Where, then, would its true reality reside? If you wish to attain mastery over the field of the five aggregates, simply...
Recognize your secret vajra-body. Do you still see the sun in Jambudvīpa?
All the activities, endeavors, and various mental states of worldly people that sustain their bodies and livelihoods—do they not all depend upon the light of the sun to come into being?
As for the essence of the sun itself, does it possess such manifold mental states? Does it have any place where it is not all-pervasive? Vajra.
The substance is likewise so. Just as the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the lands of the ten directions; form, emptiness, light, and darkness;
and your own body and mind—all these without exception are manifested by the majestic radiance of your perfected nature.

Whether it be gods, humans, or the various classes of living beings, their karmic activities, the succession of births, and the retributive fruits they receive—whether sentient or insentient—all without exception rely upon your majestic radiance, even unto the Buddhas.
The attainment of the fruit of enlightenment and the benefiting of beings by guiding others—all these are entirely sustained by your majestic radiance.

As for the adamantine essence itself, does it contain ordinary people or Buddhas? Does it possess your mental activity? One cannot say it is non-existent; yet, one must not grasp at it as something that can be attained.

You possess such a wondrous place of manifesting yourself in the presence of reality; why do you not bring this forth? Instead, you follow along with the five aggregates as a field for the body and make your living within the realm of ghosts.
To move is to give rise to the root of birth and death; to be still is to become intoxicated in the land of dullness and stupor.
When both movement and stillness are extinguished, one falls into a void of nothingness; when both movement and stillness are grasped together, one is muddled regarding Buddha-nature. Directly!
One must face the dust and confront the objects of perception, like withered wood or cold ashes, applying oneself as the occasion demands without failing to act appropriately.

A mirror reflects all forms without its radiance becoming confused; a bird flies through the sky without being mixed with the color of space. Therefore, throughout the ten directions there are no reflected images, and within the three realms there are no traces of movement.
One does not fall into the mechanism of coming and going, nor does one dwell in the mind of the middle way. Within the bell there is no drum.

An echo. Within the drum there is no sound of a bell; the drum and the bell do not intersect. In every phrase there is neither before nor after. (Jiyin said: The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "Nothing arises from conditions; nothing ceases because of conditions.

Arising is merely the arising of conditions; ceasing is merely the ceasing of conditions. By this one knows that when form arises, it is only emptiness that arises; when form ceases, it is only emptiness that ceases. It is like drawing patterns upon water.)

It has never undergone birth or cessation. Xuansha said: "In the bell there is no sound of the drum; in the drum there is no sound of the bell. The bell and the drum do not intersect; every phrase is without before or after. This is the true principle of unarisen dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Like a strong man extending his arm, he does not rely on the power of another; like a lion roaming, how could he seek a companion? When the nine heavens are free from obscuration, what need is there for piercing through?
This single segment of luminosity has never been darkened. Within this, even a hair’s breadth cannot be fully expressed; to do so would be a demon.

The preceding and succeeding phrases regarding the King’s retinue are difficult points for students. Thus, a single phrase can encompass the whole; through eighty thousand gates, birth and death are forever severed.

Even if one attains a state like the moon’s reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a still night—unimpaired by being struck and undispersed by touching the waves—this remains merely a matter on the shore of birth and death. This is the path of practice for those who walk the Way.
It is like fire melting ice; once melted, it never returns to being ice again. Once an arrow has left the bowstring, it has no power to return.
Therefore, it will not stay when confined and will not turn its head when called. The ancient sages made no arrangements for it, and thus to this day it has no fixed location.
If you arrive here, you ascend the profound at every step; it belongs neither to the heterodox nor the orthodox. Consciousness cannot perceive it, and wisdom cannot know it.

To move is to lose the source; to awaken is to become confused about the intent. If you do not now realize this underlying principle, you will remain entangled in worldly affairs and the dust of mundane existence.
Every single thing is a fetter. Even if you achieve some degree of awakening, the sensory realms will remain in chaotic confusion, and names and forms will prove to be unreal.

If you then intend to settle the mind and withdraw thoughts, or to subsume phenomena into emptiness—suppressing them the moment subtle conceptions arise—you will simply fall into the ranks of the externalists who pursue a void, a walking corpse whose soul has not yet dispersed.
Here, in our discernment, it is not so; nor is it a matter of seeking refuge in concealment.
The gates flank the doors; every phrase manifests before one. It cannot be deliberated upon; it does not involve literary ink. Fundamentally, it is severed from the realm of dust;
fundamentally, it has no stages or positions. True Suchness, ordinary beings, and sages; the hells, humans, and devas—these are merely prescriptions for curing the madness of children.
Even empty space undergoes no change; how could the Great Way have rising or sinking? To realize this is to be free and unimpeded, never departing from the original limit. If you reach this point...
In this place, there is no standing ground for either ordinary beings or sages. If you direct your intention toward the words, you will be drowned and destroyed.
If you run outward in pursuit, you fall again into the realm of Māra. As for that which is above suchness, there is nothing to be contrived; it is exactly like a furnace of flames.
"Not harboring even a mosquito or a gnat"—even if a thousand sages were to emerge, not a single character could be placed there.
Jingqing Daofu ascended the hall and said: "Now, having no other choice, I shall tell you: each of you must examine for yourselves with intimacy.

When it reaches your own station, why is it that you have suddenly become so distant? It is simply because you have been away from home for too long and have wandered through the world for many years."
Turning toward objects, one comes to see things in this way; this is called "turning one's back on awakening and joining with the dust," and it is also termed "abandoning one’s father and fleeing.
The Master of Taiyuan said: "If you wish to resolve to enter the Way, you must first recognize your own original mind.
If you do not recognize your own original mind, you are like a dog chasing a clod of earth; you are not a lion king. Your speech at this very moment is your mind; your movements—
Who else could it be that performs this act of giving? If one says there is someone else, it is like Yañjadatta searching for his own head (Master Ganquan said: "The mind of faith is the Buddha.

Beginningless ignorance causes one to transmigrate through birth and death within the four modes of birth and the six realms. This is solely because one does not dare to recognize one's own mind as the Buddha. If one can recognize one's own mind, there is no Buddha apart from the mind, and no mind apart from the Buddha.
Aside from this mind, there is no other mind. If you say there is something else, you are like Yañjadatta taking his own head to search for his head").
Master Yunmen picked up his staff and said, "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the Buddhas of the three periods of time—all are entirely upon the tip of this staff.
What obstruction could there be? Now that it is bright, where has the darkness gone? This very brightness is itself the darkness.
All sentient beings are merely obstructed by form, emptiness, light, and darkness; thus they perceive birth and extinction."

The Dharma of this. To come and go during the day, to discern people during the day—suddenly at midnight, when there is no light from the sun, moon, or lamp—is it truly so for those who have reached this state?
But as for those who have not yet reached it: could they still retrieve a single object? (Yuánwù Qín said: "...")

The *Cantong qi* says: "When there is brightness within darkness, do not perceive it through the aspect of darkness; when there is darkness within brightness, do not encounter it through the aspect of brightness. If you can cut off both brightness and darkness, tell me: what is this? Therefore it is said: 'The flower of the mind shines forth.'"
Illuminating the lands of the ten directions). ○ Throughout the entire earth, what object exists that could serve as a condition or an opponent for you?
If there were even so much as the point of an awl to separate you or obstruct you, bring it here to me! What would you call the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
What would you call the mountains, rivers, and the great earth? What would you call the sun, moon, and stars? What would you take to be the four elements and the five aggregates? ○ If...

This is attained through learning, understanding, and spiritual ingenuity. Consider, for instance, the sages of the Ten Grounds: though their preaching of the Dharma was like clouds and rain, they were still rebuked;
their vision of the nature remained as if separated by fine gauze. Thus we know that all who possess a mind remain worlds apart from the ultimate state.
For one who has truly attained it, the fire of the Way has never burned their mouth. If light does not penetrate through, there are two kinds of illnesses. All...
"In all places there is no clarity; that there is something before one's face is one [aspect].

Furthermore, even if one penetrates the emptiness of all phenomena, there is still a lingering sense that something exists—this too is light not having been fully penetrated and released. (Wansong says: Yunmen’s statement, "In all places there is no clarity;

that there is something before one's face is one," is not telling you to eliminate illusory objects or extinguish the illusory mind to seek a separate place of penetration and release. The Third Patriarch said: "The six dusts are not evil; they are identical to true enlightenment. This is the same as the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* which states: "To know illusion is to be free from it; no expedient means are required. To be free from illusion is to be enlightened.")

There is no gradual progression; one immediately perceives the stages of making, ceasing, settling, and extinguishing, which is like a diamond rubbing the back of a clay figure. It is also said: "There is something vaguely present, as if there were a thing; this is precisely the *pūrṇajñāna* (perfect enlightenment) preserving the self and awakening to the self, continuing secretly like life itself—the subtle illness of the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: 'The Great Compassionate World-Honored One has skillfully explained the illnesses of meditation. Guishan said: 'Not a single dharma can be taken as an object of sentiment. Sentiment still implies being within an objective realm. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: 'Even if you eliminate all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness...'"

This is still merely a conceptualized reflection of the dharma-dust. Nan-yuan Rong said, "At that time, I was like walking within the shadow of a lamp; therefore it is said, 'The light also does not penetrate through. (O Daie:

Some say that stillness is the root and awakening is the branches, claiming that if one remains still for a long time, awakening will naturally occur. I, this mountain monk, dare to say they are speaking nonsense. Furthermore, they cite the passage "When purity reaches its limit, light penetrates through" as proof. Do not misunderstand this! The former sages had no other choice but to speak of "purity reaching its limit and light penetrating through.")

"Thoroughly penetrating, silent illumination encompasses empty space. It is like a skilled physician who prescribes medicine according to the illness. If one today does not believe in wondrous enlightenment, but instead claims that 'enlightenment' is a conceptual construction, is this not taking the medicine for the illness? (Master Yunqi Hong said: [The circle symbol indicates a pause or a separate commentary. Master Yunqi Hong said: "..."

The people of the world already know that seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing constitute the "consciousness-spirit" (*vijñāna*). Once they have extinguished these functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, they assume they have escaped the realm of the consciousness-spirit; yet how could they know that this is still merely the nest of the consciousness-spirit, the very root of birth and death?

Among a thousand or ten hundred people, not even one or two reach this point. And even if they do reach it, five out of ten remain unable to shake themselves free or let go. Alas! How many heroes of antiquity and today have been buried in this secluded place! The secret essentials of Chan meditation are almost entirely revealed herein. Furthermore, there are two kinds of illnesses regarding the *dharmakāya*:
reaching the *dharmakāya* and becoming attached to the Dharma, or failing to forget one's own views, which still persist.
To sit beside the Dharma-body is one [kind of sickness]. Even if you manage to penetrate through to the Dharma-body, it is still not permissible to let it pass unexamined.

If you scrutinize it closely, what breath of life is there? This too is a sickness. (Wansong says: Of the two previous sicknesses, there are few; as for this latter one, the Master administers medicine according to the ailment, employing various skillful means.

Regarding the two kinds of "light and light not penetrating through," there are two types, yet the sickness is no different. In the tradition of the Dongshan school, when still, one sinks into stagnant water; when moving, one falls into the present moment—these are called the two kinds of sickness. You need only emerge from them without following along.)

One should enter without dwelling in emptiness; externally, do not seek out branches; internally, do not abide in meditative concentration. Then, the three illnesses and two lights will naturally and simultaneously be transcended. After that transcendence—whether there is further transcendence or not—one should set it aside and examine it minutely:

what scent or trace remains? That too is an illness. Yunmen merely pointed out the illness; he did not speak of how to treat it. Do you understand? When one has many illnesses, one becomes well-versed in the nature of medicines; once efficacy is achieved, one dares to transmit the prescription.
Chan Master Dizang Chen asked a monk from Baofu, "How do they instruct people regarding the Buddha-dharma there?

The monk replied, "Sometimes they address the assembly by blocking your eyes so that you cannot see, blocking your ears so that you cannot hear, and sitting upon your faculty of thought so that you cannot engage in discrimination.
The Master said, "I ask you: what about when they do not block you?"
The Eye—what do you see? It does not block your ears; what do you hear? It does not sit upon your faculty of thought. How do you make distinctions?
A monk attained realization. Ascending the hall, he said: "What do you call 'the level and real'?

What do you take to be 'the perfect and eternal'? Do not bury yourselves [in delusion]. Having obtained a mere fragment of sound, form, name, or concept, you store it in your hearts and merely memorize it."
That which you have attained is merely a name. That which you have discerned is sound and form. If it were not for these sounds and forms and names, how could you possibly remember or discern them?
The wind blowing through the pine trees is sound; the croaking of frogs and the cawing of old crows are also sound.
Why do you not listen there and discern from that very place? Right now, sounds and forms are resounding all around. For...
It must either reach you or not reach you. If it reaches you, then your numinous nature, the adamantine secret, would necessarily undergo destruction and departure.
Why is this so? Because sound pierces through your ears and form penetrates your eyes;

thus, causes and conditions immediately block you up, and illusory falsehoods run about to slaughter you. Such is the very substance of sound and form—they allow no room for you. If they do not reach you...
Furthermore, from where do form and sound come? Are they in contact with one another, or are they not? Try to discern this.
Chan Master An-guo Qiu addressed the assembly, saying: "I shall use the circumstances of our daily meals here to provide instruction for you, my brothers."
In the end, it is not permanent. If you now wish to seek the essential afterlife, it is actually the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.

To bring this matter clearly to light, even the permanent can lead to ultimate realization. If you enter through the gate of Mañjuśrī, all unconditioned things—grass, trees, tiles, and pebbles—will assist you in triggering your awakening.
If you enter through the gate of Avalokiteśvara, all sounds and voices—even those of frogs and earthworms—will do so as well.
I assist you in awakening the fundamental pivot. If you enter through the gate of Samantabhadra, you will arrive without taking a single step.
I have shown you these three gates as skillful means, like using a single broken chopstick to stir the great ocean, so that its fish and dragons may know that water is their life.
Were they to be separated from even a fraction of that water, the fish and dragons would not preserve their lives. If you lack the eye of wisdom, examine this with careful scrutiny.
"No matter how many hundreds of clever and skillful means you employ, they do not constitute the ultimate.
The senior monk Jing of Guoqing asked Xuansha, "The scriptures state that one must not use the mind of discursive knowledge to fathom the unsurpassed wisdom and vision of the Tathāgata.
How then should one proceed? Xuansha said, "If you say you have thoroughly investigated it to the very bottom..."
"Do you know whether the mind can still be measured and reached? Because of this, the Master gained faith and entered [the Way]. Someone asked:
"Disciple, whenever I sit in meditation at night, my thoughts fly about in confusion. I do not yet understand the method for subduing them; I pray that you will deign to instruct me. The Master said:
"If, while sitting peacefully at night, your thoughts fly about in confusion, then take that very mind which is flying about and investigate the place where it flies about."

When one investigates until there is no place [for it to be found], where then do these fluttering thoughts exist? When one turns back to investigate the investigating mind itself, where is that very mind capable of investigation?
Furthermore, the wisdom that is able to illuminate is fundamentally empty, and the objects perceived are likewise quiescent. This is "quiescence that is not merely quiescent."
This is because there is no person capable of achieving stillness. That which illuminates yet is not illumination is because there is no objective realm to be illuminated.
When both realm and wisdom are stilled, the mind and its deliberations are at peace. One does not seek out branches externally, nor does one dwell in meditative concentration internally.
Both paths are extinguished, and the single nature is serene. This is the essential path for returning to the source.
When Dongshan first addressed the assembly, he proclaimed the ancestral style and stirred up the Great Vehicle. It was not that they were entirely absent; rather, it was that they were still lacking.

This was simply because they had not yet reached the source and remained within the eighth realm of the maras (as the eighth *vedanā-skandha* states: "one has already spoken of realizing sainthood and attained great mastery").

If one recognizes that which is neither named nor materialized, where there is neither right nor wrong, then in every instance and every thing, there is nothing that does not fully possess [this reality].
It is sufficient. I have attained the field of peace and happiness; I seek nothing more. Whenever there is a challenge or a difficult question, I simply strike the bench and raise the whisk.
Without further deliberation, I bestow, I provide, I act, and I employ [the teaching] right into the pit of foul water.
Emerging from the head and submerging back into it, he plays with a tailless monkey. By the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, the drum has been shattered and the monkey has run away;
with hands flailing and feet stumbling, what regret can avail?
If one is a true monk, it would be better to freeze to death or starve to death than ever to don that "hawk-stink" robe.
Master Fayan addressed the monks: "You say that the six sense bases do not perceive sound. The eye-base does not perceive sound; the ear-base does not perceive sound.
If their fundamental nature were existent, how could they be non-existent? An ancient said: 'To leave behind sound and form yet cling to sound and form;
to leave behind names and words yet cling to names and words. This is why those who cultivate the realm of non-conceptualization remain there for eighty thousand great kalpas."

If one falls back even for a single day, all previous accomplishments will remain as they were; this is because one does not know that the fundamental reality is to practice through successive stages.
Thus, it takes sixty kalpas for three births and one hundred kalpas for four births, until the fruit is fulfilled after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Yet it is said that this is not equal to a single thought-moment of the non-arising of dependent origination, which transcends the provisional views of those who study the Three Vehicles. It is further said that by a mere snap of the fingers, one achieves perfect completion.
"Eighty thousand gates. In a single *kṣaṇa*, they are extinguished throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Master Baogong said, "If you are willing to refrain from seeking for even a moment, how could there ever have been anything different from today throughout kalpas? Do you understand? Today is nothing other than the dust-motes of kalpas.
A monk asked, "In the midst of the twelve periods of the day, how can one suddenly bring all conditions to rest? The Master said, "Is emptiness your condition, or is it form?"
Is it form that serves as the condition for you? To say that emptiness is the condition implies that emptiness fundamentally has no conditions.
To say that form is the condition implies that form and mind are not two. In your daily life, what thing could possibly serve as the condition for you?
National Teacher Shao of Tiantai said: "In the eye there is no form-consciousness; in form there is no eye-consciousness.
Both the eye and consciousness are empty—how can they cause one to see form? This eye cannot see its own substance. If it cannot see itself, how can it see other things?
The expedient means of the ancient sages were all intended to break through this [delusion]. If you can realize stillness within this clarity..."
The dharmas of stillness encompass all non-still dharmas; the dharmas of clear detachment encompass all non-detached dharmas.
With nothing remaining from the future or the present, this is called the single dharma-realm. How could there be any obstruction? Let each person take it up with confidence.
Lingyin said, "To see form is to see the mind. But what do you call "mind"?
Are the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the myriad phenomena, and the appearances of blue, yellow, red, white, male, female, and so forth, the mind or not?
If they are the mind, why do they instead become material objects? If they are not the mind, yet it is said that "to see form is to see the mind"—it is simply because...
Deluded by this, one falls into perversion; within that which is neither identical nor different, one forcibly generates identity and difference.
If you now directly accept and take responsibility for this, your fundamental mind will suddenly open up, and it will be luminously clear that not a single thing exists to be seen or heard.

If you seek liberation apart from the mind, you are mistaking the waves for the source; it will be difficult indeed to attain awakening. As the Sūtra says: "If the tree is not the seeing, how can one see the tree? If the tree is the seeing, then how can there be a tree?"
Chongshou Zhi said: "The primary truth is manifest and perfected; the Buddha-nature constantly illumines; all dharmas are eternally abiding.
Yet, if one perceives that there are dharmas that abide eternally, this is still not the true source of dharmas. The Buddha said:

'When one person gives rise to the true realization and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions is entirely dissolved. Is there then even a single dharma to be grasped by intellectual understanding?"
The Dharma-eye’s son, the practitioner Huiming, asked a Chan practitioner, "Where have you recently departed from? He replied, "Chengdu.
[Huiming] said, "Venerable sir, since you left Chengdu to come to this mountain, Chengdu is deficient by your presence, while this mountain is in surplus by your presence.

If there is a surplus, then phenomena exist outside the mind; if there is a deficiency, then the mind and its phenomena are incomplete. [Huiming] continued, "If you can explain this, you may remain here. The monk was speechless. (Foyan, ascending the hall, said: "This mountain monk... )

At one time, there were no mountain monks in the Dharma Hall while they were in the sleeping hall; when they went down to the Dharma Hall, there were mountain monks in the Dharma Hall and no mountain monks in the sleeping hall. If they exist, then there is a dharma outside the mind; if they do not exist, then the dharma of the mind is incomplete.

When the elder monks are beneath their robes and bowls, upon hearing the drum, they immediately ascend to the Dharma Hall. Thus, the Dharma Hall gains the elder monks while those beneath the robes and bowls lose them. To gain is to increase; to lose is to diminish. Because of diminution, one falls into nihilism; because of increase, one falls into eternalism.

"Constantly. How can a wandering monk (yōjō-jin) attain liberation from existence and non-existence, and transcend permanence and annihilation? The doubts regarding birth and death are extremely difficult to penetrate and escape. This is the essential core of the Tathāgata’s pure mind; it must be decisively discerned and not treated with indifference.

(△*The Record of the Forest* [Rinkanroku] states: "Hui-ming was the son of Fa-yen; his insight and realization were exceedingly high, looking down upon all quarters. The Chan school values great capacity and great function, rather than mere intellectual understanding.
Yun-an often said: 'You all know that there is something, yet you simply cannot put it to use. A man like the practitioner Hui-ming may truly be called one who makes skillful use of it.")
Chan Master Junian stayed at Dongshan for ten years, where he studied Fazang’s *Huayan lun*.

Upon reaching the third assembly, which describes the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) atop Mount Sumeru, [he realized that] this represents entering the principle and relinquishing intellectual knowledge, as it cannot be attained by a mind subject to arising and ceasing.
It is like Mount Sumeru in the great ocean, eighty-four thousand *yojanas* high, which cannot be reached by hands or feet.
It can be grasped and reached. This clarifies that the eighty-four thousand mountains of affliction (*kleśa*) dwell within the great ocean of delusion.

If sentient beings are able to remain in all phenomena without thought or conditioned action, then the ocean of affliction will naturally dry up, and the mountains of affliction will become the mountain of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
The ocean of affliction will then become the ocean of omniscience. If one should again give rise to a [discursive] mind...

To engage in discursive thought is to have objects of attachment; thus, the mountain of defilements becomes ever higher and the ocean of afflictions ever deeper, making it impossible to reach the summit of the Buddhas' wisdom.
Reflecting on this three times, he sighed and said:

"Shigong said there was no place to begin, yet Mazu said that the ignorance of kalpas has today been entirely extinguished—this is no empty talk. (Jiyin said: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "You... [text continues])

"Simply discard that which arises and perishes, and maintain the true and eternal. When the light of the eternal manifests before you, the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind will dissolve in accordance with the moment.
Jiyin’s *Biography of Chan Master Yongming Zhijue* states: "In using the Dharma as a standard, he took the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as his criterion.
He said: 'When Kāśyapa first heard the verse: "All phenomena arise from conditions; all phenomena cease due to conditions," I...'"
The Great Master, the Great Śramaṇa, once spoke thus: "This is the very marrow of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Nāgārjuna said: "Nothing arises from conditions;
nothing ceases because of conditions. Arising is merely the arising of conditions; ceasing is merely the ceasing of conditions.
Thus one knows that when form arises, it is only emptiness that arises; when form ceases, it is only emptiness that ceases. For example, the nature of wind is fundamentally..."
It moves because it arises through conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*). If the nature of wind were inherently moving, how could there ever be a time of stillness?

If there were wind within a sealed room, why would the wind not move? If there is no wind, it arises as soon as it encounters conditions. It is not only wind that is thus; all phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise so.
Vimalakīrti said: "Welcome, Mañjuśrī! You have come with the characteristic of non-coming; you have seen with the characteristic of non-seeing."
[Mañjuśrī] said, "It is so. If it has already come, it does not come again; if it has already gone, it does not go again. Why is this? That which comes has nowhere from which it comes;
that which goes has nowhere to which it goes. That which can be seen cannot be seen again.

This is the principle of dependent origination as non-arising. (The *Línjiān Lù* states: *The Awakening of Faith* says, "If the mind has seeing, then there is the mark of non-seeing. When the nature of the mind is free from seeing, [it is thus].")

This is because it signifies the universal illumination of the Dharma-realm; thus one knows that there is no phenomenon outside of the mind, and the meaning of universal illumination is established. If there were any signs of coming or going, or of being seen, then the true principle would be abandoned.

It is like a person saying, "The nature of wind is fundamentally motion. This is most certainly not so. Wind is fundamentally non-moving; it is able to move all things. If it were already in motion beforehand, it would lose its own essence and could not move again. Thus we know that what is called "motion" is precisely used to clarify that it has never actually moved. The same applies to the signs of coming and going. *Zongjing* asks:
Are the ignorance of the myriad objects and the Dharma-nature of the One Mind one, or are they two? If they are one...
There is no distinction between the two names, "defiled" and "pure. If they were indeed two, why would the teachings state that ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)?

Answer: Their essence is one, while the two names are provisional. The names are established based on emotional affliction (*kleśa*), whereas the truth is clarified by wisdom (*jñāna*). Affliction and wisdom are distinct from one another.
The true source is immovable; it cannot be definitively said to be the same, for it does not destroy conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
It cannot be definitively said to be different, for it does not lose ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "For the foolish, clarity and ignorance are two.

The wise understand that their nature is non-dual. This non-dual nature is itself the true nature. An ancient master, explaining this in terms of the ten dharma-realms, said: "As for 'the foolish'..."
The nine realms are the realm of delusion. Deluded people grasp at signs and perceive all phenomena as having two natures; according to their grasping at signs, their minds are entirely in ignorance.
It is like a valley of cold where, for a thousand years, solid ice has never turned into water. The wise possess the wisdom of the Buddha-realm.
Those practitioners who observe with perfect completeness and have opened the Buddha-eye see things as the ancient Buddhas did. The perfect eye does not see [duality].
Ignorance (*avidyā*) has as its root the fundamentally pure *dharmatā*. It is like the sun that shines constantly;
the seawater has never become ice. Ice and the nature of water are one; they appear as two according to conditions (*pratyaya*). One does not maintain its own nature but always follows conditions.

Even while following conditions, it does not destroy the *dharmatā*; how much more so for the *dharmas* and ignorance—how could they be fixed as one, and how could they be fixed as different? Thus, they are not...
Following after phenomena, it loses its essence; it is neither common nor divisible. Not guarding its nature, it accords with conditions; it is both identical and distinct. Question:
If bodhi is one’s own body and mind, why do the teachings say it cannot be attained through body or mind? Answer:
That which is called the "bodhicitta-mind" is precisely the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*).

It is profoundly still and unmoving; it is the true wisdom of correct awakening that is devoid of marks (*animitta*). Its Way is empty and profound, wondrously transcending all ordinary realms. Those who are clever have no means to accommodate its hearing;
those who are wise have no means to exercise their knowledge; those who are eloquent have no means to deploy their speech; and those who seek images have no means to...
