I have described these manifestations because deluded people do not understand; they cling to the aggregate of form as their own body and identify the faculty of cognition as their own mind.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The body is like grass and wood, possessing no awareness or knowledge; the mind is like an illusion or a transformation, empty, false, and unreal.
To eliminate this mind of grasping, it is said: "Bodhi cannot be attained through body or mind. Bodhi...
It is not the sense-object of touch, for it cannot be apprehended by the body. Bodhi is not the sense-object of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), for it cannot be apprehended by the mind.

If one realizes this personhood, one immediately penetrates that the aggregates (*skandha*) and realms (*dhātu*) are fundamentally empty and that the deluded mind is without marks. Because they are fundamentally empty, the Dharma-body is ever-present;
because it is without marks, the true mind is never diminished. To clarify it in this way: the five aggregates are themselves bodhi; they are not separate from it.
This is non-enlightenment (*abodhi*). One cannot seek enlightenment by means of enlightenment, nor can one attain enlightenment by means of enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī said: "I do not seek enlightenment. Why? Because enlightenment is myself, and I am enlightenment.
Vimalakīrti said: "Enlightenment is not an object of observation; therefore, there is no perceiving mind. As for the object of observation..."

The emptiness of objects is the *bodhi* of true reality (*dharmatā*). The emptiness of the perceiving mind is the *bodhi* of self-nature. (As the Sūtra says: "Perfect *bodhi* returns to non-attainment. Question:
Regarding what was said about the functions of the five faculties, they are all called the "Luminous Jewel Maṇi King" and are all able to rain down jewels.
Is it the same for the faculties of ordinary beings? Answer: The Sūtra says: "The six sovereign kings are eternally pure. Regarding what is...
It is called "King" (*rāja*). "King" carries the meaning of sovereignty. Thus, when the eye-faculty contemplates objects spontaneously, it is sovereign and unimpeded.
Furthermore, it is always within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and its fundamental nature is immutable; is this not like a king who constantly attains sovereignty?

As it is said: "When the eye functions, it is like a thousand suns; the myriad forms cannot escape their physical reality. Is this not the meaning of "raining jewels"? From the gateway of the eye, [it radiates...]

Light shines through and pierces the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; is this not the meaning of emitting light? Thus, profound discernment leaves nothing behind, and the subtle and minute are thoroughly understood.
The five sense faculties function accordingly in the same way, even up to the mental faculty (*manas*), which reaches a thousand *li* in a single thought-moment without obstruction.
As it is said: "When responding to the mind, all discrimination ceases; the illumination of the myriad phenomena never stops, penetrating through mountains and rivers."
Within the stone walls, it is essential that illumination remains eternally quiescent. Thus we know that the six sense-faculties are not evil; they are identical to perfect enlightenment.
The wise remain non-active, while the foolish bind themselves. This may truly be called the treasure-trove of the body and the luminous pearl of the mind;
if one does not speak of it, one will not know it, and will sink in vain into the sea of suffering.
Chan Master Yongming Jue issued these instructions: "In the gateway of studying the Way, there is nothing particularly extraordinary;

it simply requires washing away the defilements of the sense bases and the seeds of karmic consciousness accumulated over immeasurable kalpas. I deeply lament that in this degenerate age, people falsely claim to practice Chan while only learning empty gestures.
They possess no real understanding at all; in every step they walk according to existence, yet in every word they speak of emptiness. They do not hold themselves accountable for their karma."

Dragged by the power [of karma], they further teach others to negate cause and effect, claiming that drinking alcohol and eating meat do not obstruct bodhi, and that committing theft and sexual misconduct does not hinder prajñā.
In life they encounter royal law; in death they fall into Avīci.

Once they have received the retribution for their hellish karma, it is exhausted, yet they enter again as animals or hungry ghosts for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, with no time of escape, unless in a single thought-moment...
Turn the light back upon yourself. Immediately transform the heterodox into the orthodox. If you regard cutting out your own heart and liver as being like wood or stone, then you may eat meat.
If you drink wine as if it were excrement or urine, then you may drink wine. If you see handsome men and women as if they were corpses, then you may engage in sexual conduct.
If you view your own wealth and the wealth of others as if they were dung or soil, [then you may possess property].
Then you may indeed commit such transgressions. Even if you were to refine yourself to this stage, it would still not be permissible to follow your own whims.
Only when you have realized the body of an immeasurable sage can you then engage in worldly matters of both adversity and favor. This is the provision established by the ancient sages;
it is extensively protected by thousands of sutras and presented in ten thousand treatises. If one does not abandon lust, one cuts off all seeds of purity.
If you do not remove the sprinkling [of blood], you sever the seeds of all wisdom. If you do not remove the theft, you sever the seeds of all merit.

If you do not remove the meat, you sever the seeds of all compassion. Thus have the Buddhas of the three periods proclaimed with one voice, and the Chan school of the world has expounded this in a single resonance.
How can later students fail to heed this even slightly? To thus destroy the true cause and instead act contrary to it—how can this be?

The Māra said: "It is solely because of the seeds of karma perfumed in past lives that one encounters false teachers in this life. The power of goodness is easily dissipated, while the roots of evil are difficult to uproot.

Have you not seen the path of the ancient sages? To see a single demonic deed is like ten thousand arrows piercing the heart; to hear a single demonic sound is like a thousand awls boring into the ears.

You must distance yourselves from them with all haste and each investigate your own minds. (Yongming’s admonition truly accords with the four kinds of pure and clear instructions of the former Buddhas; engrave them into your very bones.)

[The passage] "Dripping blood" is spoken with true concern for others. Yet Leian criticized it, saying: "This too is a skillful means (upāya). Viewed through the words of the Tathāgata, this person has actually been possessed by a demon of emptiness. Alas! How regrettable!

In the Dharma-ending age (mofa), demonic beings may borrow the words of Yongming to further increase their deluded interpretations, leading to reckless behavior that invites calamity. Thus, what Leian said can serve as a "single blow to the head" for Yongming himself.
Duanlu first ascended the hall: "All phenomena that arise are manifested solely by the mind. Such words are a fine gateway for entry.

You all see all forms with your eyes, hear all sounds with your ears, smell all fragrances with your noses, experience all tastes with your tongues, feel all textures of softness and smoothness with your bodies, and discern all phenomena with your minds."
Consider, for instance, the objects encountered by the six sense organs, such as the eyes and ears: are they your own minds, or are they not?
If you say they are your own minds, why do they not become one with your bodies?
Why, instead, do the objects encountered remain outside your six sense organs? If, on the other hand, they are not your own minds, then what can be done about it?
These words, manifested solely from the mind, have remained in the world; who would not cite them? It is further said:
"At night, when one sleeps soundly, one knows nothing at all. Since one knows nothing at all, let us ask: does the original nature exist at that time, or does it not?
If you say it exists, yet one knows nothing at all, it is no different from death. If you say it does not exist..."
Suddenly awakening from sleep, one realizes that everything is as it was before.
At such times as these, what is this? Master Yunju Daoci said to his disciples: "I read a verse from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* which says:
'All phenomena have no inherent substance; they are said to be nothing but mind. Failing to see one's own mind, one gives rise to conceptual discrimination. This may indeed be called..."
The Great Compassionate Father has spoken with ultimate truth as it is. Yet we do not personally receive this;
we turn our backs on his grace, which is as vast as the sands of the Ganges. Someone asks: "In that case, does one sever conceptual discrimination simply by seeing one's own mind?
He replies: "It is not so. It is like taming a horse. When a horse sees its own reflection, it is not startled. Why? Because it knows that the reflection originates from itself."
Because it emerges from the body, I know by this that one does not sever discernment (*vikalpa*), nor does one abandon the characteristics of the mind.
Observe right now before you as it truly is; not even a hair’s breadth is to be seen. The Patriarch said: "If you see the present, you should also see the past and future.
If you do not see the past and future, you should not see the present either. These words are clear and distinct. People—
"Self-delusion and obscurity. Yunju Qi assembled the community to show his illness, saying: "This old monk, being pressed by the fires of wind, has come specifically to meet you all.
But where do you see me? Do you see me within the four elements and five aggregates? Or do you see me within the six entrances and twelve bases?
Since these various locations cannot be seen, who is it that is questioning me right now?"
Someone asked Longji, "All bells and drums are fundamentally without sound. How can one believe they are soundless? The Master said, "The Patriarch said:
'Just as the sound of a drum has no maker and no place of abiding, because it is ultimately empty; it merely deceives ordinary people.
If the sound of a drum were truly existent, then when the bell and drum are struck together, their sounds should not intermingle. Therefore, it is profound."
Sha said: "In the bell there is no sound of the drum; in the drum there is no sound of the bell. Bell and drum do not intersect or mingle; every phrase is without before or after.
If one does not realize the quiescent extinction within the very substance [of these sounds], how could one attain this state where every phrase is without before or after?"

Chengtian said: "The Buddha-nature of all sentient beings is perfectly complete; it is a state of profound stillness, nirvana. The three periods of time are expansive and level, and the ten directions are never extinguished.

It is only because sentient beings do not understand this that they are deluded by themselves and recognize others as real. Thus, they are disturbed by the dust of worldly toil and their false thoughts grasp at conditions.

They depart from the true by clinging to appearances, becoming deluded by themselves and pursuing external objects—all because of a single moment of non-awakening. Then, one perceives only emptiness."
A flower blooms, yet one does not realize there is a film over the eye. This delusion has no fundamental basis; its nature is ultimately empty.

To awaken to the fact that there was originally no delusion is like having a perception of delusion where none exists. When awakening perceives delusion, the delusion is extinguished; when awakening arises, it does not give rise to delusion.
Therefore, a sutra says: "All dharmas arise in this way; all dharmas cease in this way. If one can understand them thus, the Buddhas will always manifest before one."
Tianyi Huai addressed the assembly, saying: "Two thousand years ago, the Great Awakened World-Honored One took the assembly of sages to the sixth heaven to preach the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra.
He commanded all the fierce and evil ghosts and spirits from other regions, this land, the human realm, and the heavens to assemble and receive the Buddha’s entrustment.
For those who did not attend, the Four Heavenly Kings of the Gates flew forth glowing red-hot iron [to punish them]."
The wheel pursued him. Only one Māra King said to the World-Honored One:

"Gautama, I shall wait until all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood, until the world of sentient beings is empty and the very name 'sentient being' no longer exists; only then will I resolve to attain Bodhicitta."
"To remain unchanging in the face of peril—this is the mark of a true Great Man. How, O virtuous ones, will you provide a turning word to give vent to the indignation of the Yellow-Faced Gautama?
At such a time, one's ordinary supernatural powers, wondrous functions, wisdom, and eloquence are all rendered useless.
Throughout the entire land of Jambudvīpa, there is no one who does not love the Buddha; yet when it comes to this point, what is the Buddha, and what is [not the Buddha]?"
"This is Māra. "Is there anyone who can discern this? After a long silence, he said:

"If you wish to recognize Māra, it is seeing light with eyes open. If you wish to recognize the Buddha, it is seeing darkness with eyes closed. As for Māra and the Buddha, I pass a staff through their nostrils at once!

(Miaoxi said: "The old fellow Tianyi’s such a critique is truly extraordinary. Nevertheless, he cannot avoid splitting the discourse into two separate parts. If one could simply rest right where it asks, 'What is the Buddha? What is Māra?', it would be quite sufficient to make use of it.)

People are suspicious and attached to this. Yet he further says, "Opening the eyes and closing the eyes—how much of a clumsy affair! He also says, "As for demons and Buddhas, I shall at once pierce their nostrils with my staff"—this is like adding frost to snow. Miaoxi, however, speaks on behalf of the Yellow-Faced Gautama with a substitute phrase:

when that Mara King says, "The realm of sentient beings is empty, and thus I have resolved upon Bodhicitta," [Miaoxi] simply says to him, "I nearly mistook you for the Mara King. This statement contains two points of defeat; if anyone can discern them, they have truly understood.

"I grant you the eye of a monk. (Nantang Jing said: "I would have said to him: 'O assembly, the Mara has already awakened his mind. Mara always abides thus. Otherwise, I would have asked: 'What do you call a sentient being?
and as soon as he opened his mouth, I would have struck him with an iron wheel)."
The Regional Commander Li Duanyuan asked Daguan, "Ultimately, do heaven and hell exist or not? Daguan replied, "The Buddhas speak of existence within non-existence;
it is like seeing flowers in the sky with one's own eyes. Your Excellency seeks non-existence within existence; it is like grasping at the moon reflected in water with your hands—truly laughable!
You see the prison before your eyes yet do not avoid it, while hearing of heaven beyond your mind you desire to be born there. This is quite extraordinary.
One does not realize that joy and fear reside within the mind; rather, good and evil are perceived as external objects. If one simply understands one's own mind, delusion will naturally vanish.
Yunfeng Yue ascended the hall and cited the teaching: "These views and conditions are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi."
Furthermore, it is said that the trees, forests, ponds, and marshes all proclaim the sound of the Dharma; their interlacing lights entwine like a jeweled net.
When the sages of old spoke thus, they were calling for one to turn back from worldly toil, skillfully opening up expedient means. Therefore it is said: "If I press my finger..."
The Ocean Seal emits light. As soon as you raise your mind, the dust of affliction first arises. Do you understand? For now, let the whisk sweep across the world;
let the staff serve as the one who answers the question. Before realizing that objects are but mind, all manner of discriminations arise.
Once one realizes that objects are but mind, discrimination no longer arises. Knowing that all phenomena are but mind, one then abandons the appearances of external objects. Only—
Like the great earth, mountains, and rivers, or light, darkness, form, and space—when all phenomena manifest before you, how can you speak of "letting go"?
Even if you attain clarity regarding this, you are still only halfway there; you must know that above this, there is yet another aperture.
Chan Master Da Hongbaoen replied to Zhang Wujin: "The non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Regions do not transcend the four views of existence and non-existence.
If they do not take the One Mind as the Way, then the Way is not their own possession; thus they are called 'outsiders' (waidao).

If they do not recognize that all phenomena are the Mind, then phenomena will vary according to their views; thus they are called 'erroneous views' (xiejian). For example, if one says 'it exists,' then with existence comes non-existence."
To say "it is non-existent" means that if it is non-existent, then there is nothing. When existence and non-existence are present, views arise in competition;

when there is no existence, the view of non-existence arises. The views of both existence and non-existence, and the view of neither existence nor non-existence, are likewise the same. One cannot escape these various views.
Thus, there is no means to clarify one’s own mind. Without clarifying one’s own mind, one cannot know the Right Path.
As the Sūtra says: "To have a view is itself defilement; this is not yet seeing. To be far removed from all views—in this way, one sees the Buddha.
The divergence between the heterodox and the orthodox arises precisely because their insights and realizations differ. Indeed, the three realms are but mind; the myriad conditions are of one essence.
It encompasses all phenomena yet is not existence; it reaches ultimate quiescence yet is not non-existence. It is neither non-existence nor the negation of non-existence;
it is neither existence nor the negation of existence. When these four attachments have vanished, the hundred negations are thereby dispelled.
Thus, "natural causality" is merely idle discourse, and both "emptiness" and "reality" are but provisional designations. All the great masters of the Western Heavens [India] have likewise...
To hold that phenomena exist apart from the mind is the way of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); that all phenomena are but mind alone is the True Teaching.

Yet the non-Buddhists of the Western Heavens are all Great Power Bodhisattvas manifesting through transformation; their various actions are intended to give rise to diverse views and exhaustively display heterodox paths, thereby clarifying that the Buddha-dharma is the True Path.
Whether in accord with or contrary to these views, all take it as their ultimate source—a truth that cannot be known through ordinary thought or deliberation.
Huanglong Huítáng was conversing with Xià Yì Gōnglì when they reached the *Zhào Lùn* passage on "taking all things as oneself" and "sentient and insentient beings being of one body.
At that moment, a dog was lying beneath the incense table; the Master struck the dog with his ruler.
Again, he struck the incense table and said, "The dog has sentience and thus departs; the incense table lacks sentience and remains here.
How can sentience and insentience become one body? Guo Li was unable to answer. The Master said, "As soon as one engages in discursive thought, it becomes a superfluous dharma.
When have you ever realized that all things are oneself? Later, the layman Wu Dunfu happened to read about Deng Yinpeng.
The Biography relates: He saw [the monk] stand on his head and vanish, yet his robe remained aligned with his body without slipping off.
He privately wondered, "The marvel of his transformation is indeed unfathomable; but why does his robe also conform to him? He questioned Huitang about this.
Huitang said, "Now your own robe hangs down to the ground; do you still find that strange? He replied, "I have no such doubt. Huitang laughed.
He said: "Since this is beyond doubt, then that inverted transformation is resolved; even clothing conforms to the body—what room is there for doubt?

Master Dun understood this immediately upon hearing these words" (this can serve as a remote resolution to the meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* regarding the hanging down of the hand to correct the inversion).
Master Zhenjing ascended the hall and said: "The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa take sound as their Buddha-work.

That which is called 'the true essence of the teaching in this land'—its purity resides in hearing sounds. The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the canon are each produced from sound;
even the various paths of Chan and the Dharma of the ancestral patriarchs are all produced from sound. [He paused at] "In front of the courtyard..."
The cypress tree, the Northern Dipper concealing its body, Deshan’s shout, and Linji’s staff—all of these are produced from sound.

How much more so for all the phenomena and affairs of the mundane world; their sounds are inexhaustible, their expositions are inexhaustible, their being seen and heard are inexhaustible, and their benefit and joy are inexhaustible.
If one enters this Dharma-gate, one will attain the Samādhi of the Ocean of Sovereignty of the Dhāraṇī of Revolving.
If you wish to ensure that birth and death do not continue in succession, you need only directly recognize the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of nature-purity and luminosity;
then, birth and death will naturally have no connection. If you lack faith and refuse to listen and accept this, you will sink into the ocean of ignorance within the consciousness of karma.
During the summer retreat, Zhenjing Wen addressed the assembly, striking the meditation seat with his whisk and saying: "Heaven and Earth..."

In the process of creation, there are yin and yang, life and death; the sun and moon shine upon all, with their brightness and darkness, concealment and manifestation; rivers flow and pour forth, with their heights and depths, embankments and breaches;
when an enlightened ruler governs the world, there are sovereign and minister, ritual and music, reward and punishment; and so it is when the Buddha-dharma exists in the world.
There are the sudden and the gradual, the provisional and the real; there is binding and there is unbinding—this is binding.

On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, throughout the ten directions of the Dharma-realm, whether saint or ordinary person, grass or wood—from this point, he strikes once with the whisk on the left side and says: "All are bound at once."
He raises his whisk and says, "Is it all upon the tip of this whisk? Do you see it? He then shouts, "Understood!
This is the same as on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, except that he strikes with the whisk on the right side and says, "Understand it all at once here! Do you see it?
He then shouts, "As for before the fifteenth day of the fourth month and after the fifteenth day of the seventh month—tell me, what do you say?"
"This is bondage; this is liberation. Holding up his whisk, he said, "It is all upon the tip of this whisk—do you see it?
Letang Ying, while reading the *Huayan Shiming Lun*, reached the passage: "Because true wisdom has no essence or nature, it cannot know itself as being without nature;
therefore, it is called the nature of no-nature. Because it cannot know itself as being without nature, it is named ignorance (*avidyā*)."
The sixth stage of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Because one does not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is termed 'ignorance' (*avidyā*).

Since one knows that true wisdom is fundamentally without intrinsic nature, one cannot understand it by oneself. If one encounters conditions for understanding and thereby understands, then ignorance is extinguished."
This is the essential gateway to attaining Buddhahood.
Huanglong Xin addressed the assembly, saying: "An echo transmits through an empty valley; from moment to moment, one hears what has never been heard before. Within form, the true is revealed."
Seeing everywhere yet seeing nothing; since there is no seeing in this seeing, one hears what has never been heard before.
This is called the gate of the Samādhi of the Inexhaustible Treasury, the gate of supernatural powers, the gate of wisdom, and the gate of liberation.

If one can thus know, see, believe, and understand, practicing, realizing, awakening to, and entering [this state], I say that such a person has reached the heart-essence of the Buddha and entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Since they have already entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision...
Is this seeing the act of seeing? Or is it the seen that is the seeing? If it is the seen that is the seeing, then what serves as the agent?
If it is the agent that is the seeing, then what serves as the object? To posit both an agent and an object constitutes a dualistic view;
neither belongs to the Buddha-vehicle (Buddhayāna). What, then, is the Buddha-vehicle? It is because the Tathāgata does not employ clever artifice; the wise must rely upon the Tathāgata.

This constitutes the fundamental tenet. It is not that the Patriarchs did not possess wondrous realization; rather, those who possess wondrous realization must take the Patriarchs as their ultimate aim.
Doushuai Yue said to Zhang Wujin: "The sole purpose of practicing Chan is to sever the life-root and to avoid generating intellectual interpretations based on words."

"You have already deeply understood such teachings as these. However, when it comes to the most subtle point, it causes people to be unaware and unknowing, causing them to fall into the realm of conditioned existence.
Therefore, I shall compose a verse to certify this: In the midst of ordinary activity, every step is as it should be.

Though dwelling amidst sound and form, how could one be stuck in being or non-being? The One Mind is without difference; the myriad dharmas are not distinct. Cease distinguishing between essence and function; do not..."

Discerning the refined from the coarse, one encounters circumstances without obstruction and responds to things without constraint. When notions of right and wrong are exhausted, both the ordinary and the sage are eliminated.
Who gains and who loses? What is near and what is distant? To take the head as the tail, and to point to reality as being empty;

to turn one’s body within the realm of Māra and shift one’s feet upon the path of heterodoxy—realizing that these are neither contrary nor compliant, one does not violate the essential practice. (As the Sūtra says: "Such inversions cause the beginning and the end to be exchanged.")
A monk asked the Ancient Tower Master, "How is it that within a single word, one must possess the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials?

The Ancient replied, "The world of emptiness is fundamentally unconditioned; responding to conditions as they arise, there is nothing it does not do. Therefore, within the void world, the myriad phenomena are arrayed:
the four seasons and the yin-yang, the eight nodes of prosperity and adversity, the flourishing and withering of plants and trees, and the seven [realms] of humans and devas."
The realms of existence, the noble sages and Buddhas, the five teachings and three vehicles, the crooked scriptures of external paths, and all that is mundane and supramundane—all emerge from this.
Therefore it is said: "There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm; in the end, all returns to this Dharma-realm. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Within the tip of a single hair, one manifests jeweled royal lands; sitting within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel. Thus, we know that the myriad dharmas...
Fundamentally non-existent, it is established by grasping the True. The nature of Truth is immeasurable; its principle cannot be divided.

For one who reaches this realm, every single dharma, every single speck of dust, every color, and every sound all possess the four meanings of pervasiveness and containment. The rational nature is boundless, and phenomenal appearances are boundless;
they interpenetrate without being confused, and they blend without becoming one. Why, then, should one doubt that within a single word, the Three Mysteries are not fully present?
Third, regarding the essential point:

Hong Juefan, while residing at Qingliang, cited the meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* concerning the nose smelling sandalwood, stating: "Entering this contemplation of the nose, one personally realizes non-arising.

Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "How does the hearer hear? Is it by means of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) that hears, or by means of the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*)?"

Is it heard by the ear-faculty? Is it heard by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)? If it were the ear-faculty that hears, it could not hear because the ear-faculty lacks awareness and cognition.
If it were the ear-consciousness that hears, it could not hear because the ear-consciousness lasts for only a single moment and is incapable of discrimination.

If it were the mental consciousness that hears, the mental consciousness likewise cannot hear. Why? Because the five consciousnesses first cognize the five sense-objects, and only thereafter does the mental consciousness [arise].
"Consciousness is that which can cognize the five sense-objects of the present. Even a blind or deaf person should be able to cognize sound. Why?

Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has not been destroyed. The Master said: "If one investigates this object of hearing (*śrotra-viṣaya*) to its ultimate limit, it merges with the original wondrousness. Once one realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*), it again merges with the original wondrousness.
Ultimately, what kind of realm is this? After a long silence, he said: "The white monkey has already called out as evening falls over a thousand crags; the green threads..."

At first, one horizontally encompasses the furnace of the myriad phenomena. ○ The *Zongjing* says: "Although mind is itself karma and karma is itself mind, since [karma] arises from the mind, it is returned to the mind for its retribution.
How, then, can one now eliminate the retribution of these deluded karmas? Answer: "Simply by realizing non-action (*wu zuo*), karma naturally becomes empty. Therefore it is said:

It is as restless as a monkey; it delights in impure places like a flying rope; it is insatiable like wind or fire;

Hair acts as an obstruction for me. Thus it is said: "Observe the sequence of phenomena; distinguish right from wrong through wisdom;

The Earth. This is why it is said that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only. Here, they are forged into a single mass and refined into one solid block, pervading the entire dharma-realm without interior or exterior.

When one awakens and is called by another, one finally realizes that within the dream there were originally no marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span, nor any such things as earth, water, fire, or wind;
they are ultimately empty space, existing solely with the sixth consciousness as their fundamental basis.

Thus, when one awakens to the mountains, rivers, and great earth that people perceive, as well as the twelve classes of living beings and their own physical forms, one realizes they depend solely upon the eighth consciousness, the karmic consciousness.
When those of Great Awakening explain the True Emptiness, one finally understands that this long night has been like a grand dream.
They are equal and without difference.
Master Zhongfeng said: "The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that as long as the deluded mind has not ceased, once it ceases, it is bodhi.

How intimate this is! If someone, upon hearing these words below, understands them with thorough penetration and, in a sudden flash, turns back their wild mind to reflect upon their own nature, they will immediately come to rest.

[Another time,] he asked Caoshan, "Is it not the case that a śramaṇa is a person of great compassion? The Master said, "Yes. [The monk] asked, "What if you suddenly encounter the six thieves? The Master—

"A whole brood of six thieves, life after life deceiving and killing people. Now I know you; I will not be your neighbor. If you do not submit to me, I shall go everywhere to speak of you, so that everyone knows you and your path is cut off.

If you are willing to submit to me, I shall make no distinction and dwell with you in one place, together realizing the non-arising and non-ceasing. Chan Master En of Zhongyi, because Yangshan asked him, "How can one attain..."
"Go and see the nature. The Master said, "It is like a room with six windows. Inside there is a monkey, and outside there is a monkey.
From the eastern window someone calls out, 'Singing-sing! and the monkey responds immediately. In this way, if called from all six windows, it responds to each.
Yangshan bowed in thanks and rose, saying, "I have now understood everything through the Master’s analogy. However, there is one further matter—"
"Suppose there is an inner monkey who is dozing off, while an outer monkey wishes to see him. How can they meet?
The Master descended from his rope-corded seat, took Yangshan’s hand, and danced with him, saying: "Singing-monkey! We have met.
It is like a tiny gnat building a nest upon the eyelashes of a mosquito, yet shouting at the crossroads: 'The ground is vast and people are few; those who encounter me...'"
[The Master] said, "Few. A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a newborn infant possess the six consciousnesses?
Zhaozhou replied, "It is like hitting a ball on a swift current. The monk then asked Touzi, "What is the meaning of 'hitting a ball on a swift current'?

Touzi said, "Every thought-moment leaves no trace. Xuedou Xian’s verse says: "The six consciousnesses are of no use—here he poses a question. The masters of old have together discerned the source. Vast and boundless, hitting a ball on a swift current; Where does it land?"

"Who can perceive it when it does not stop? (△ The Sūtra says: "It is like a rapid stream that appears tranquil from afar; the flow is so swift that it cannot be seen, yet it is not that there is no flow. When the profound enters and merges with the profound, one returns to the limit of consciousness. The *Avataṃsaka* says:

"It is like the water in a river, where the turbulent currents rush past one another, each unaware of the others; all phenomena are likewise. (△ Caoshan asked a monk: "When a Bodhisattva is in meditative absorption, he hears the fragrance of an elephant crossing a river. From which sūtra does this passage come? The monk said: "The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Caoshan said: "Did you hear it before the concentration or after the concentration?
The monk said: "You are just following the current, Master. Caoshan said: "Catch it downstream at the rapids.")
There is no pain that is not felt. ○ When Baofu saw a monk approaching, he struck a pillar with his staff and then struck the monk on the head.
The monk made a sound of wincing in pain. Baofu said, "Why does that one [the pillar] not feel pain? The monk was speechless.
He immediately smelled the incense given to him; both instances were false. A monk asked Master Haiyan, "What is the single burner of incense in an ancient temple?
The Master said, "Throughout successive dynasties, no one has smelled it. The monk asked, "What of those who do smell it? The Master said, "It does not reach any of the six sense organs."
These various heavens each have their own devas, who are all ordinary beings. They receive the retribution of their karma; when that retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth.
Yunmen asked Minister Chen: "Do you read the *Lotus Sutra*? In the sutra it says:
'All livelihoods and productive enterprises are not at variance with the true mark (*dharmatā*). Now tell me, how many people from the Heaven of Neither Thought nor Non-Thought fall back?"
[Seat. ○ Xuedou Xian ascends the hall. A monk asks, "What is the causal condition of the time? The Master says, "A sleepyhead. The monk then shouts.
The Master says, "A deceitful orangutan. He continues, "It is like when the world is about to perish and the great waters surge forth;
within them, immeasurable sentient beings—some submerged, some not—are wailing piteously to one another, looking up at the vast blue heavens."
"Let us rescue one another! Upon seeing this, a deva from the fourth dhyāna heaven raised his voice and shouted: "Alas, sentient beings!
I warned you repeatedly to come up here, yet you would not listen. Now, what means of salvation remains for you?
He then clapped his hands and said, "Return to the hall."
If one forms a conception of "sainthood," one immediately succumbs to various heterodoxies. ○ Wansong said: "Setting aside the primary meaning for a moment, what do you want with the Noble Truths?

Tiantai said: "Simply exhaust all mundane sentiments; there is no separate conception of sainthood. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If one forms a conception of sainthood, one immediately succumbs to various heterodoxies.
This is precisely what Bodhidharma meant when he said: "Vast and empty, there is no saint. Within the flash of a spark or a bolt of lightning—no [time to linger].
It was a matter for the Master’s own eyes to discern.
One part [of the teaching] is the doctrine of impermanence; one part is the doctrine of permanence. ○ Once, when a certain heterodox teacher asked the World-Honored One, "Are all phenomena permanent?
the World-Honored One did not answer. When he asked again, "Are all phenomena impermanent? he likewise did not answer. The heterodox teacher said: "World-Honored One..."
"World-Honored One, you possess all-encompassing wisdom; why do you not respond to me? The World-Honored One said: "All that you have asked is mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
[End of] Section Five of the Records at the End of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* (Volume Seven).
[End of] Section Five of the Records at the End of the *Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Illuminating Extracts* (Volume Eight).
Compiled by the Disciple Haiyin, the Elder Qian Qianyi:
*The Record of the Zong of the Buddha’s Crown*, Part Five.

Third: Selections of Verses on the Gāthās (This section further contains three parts: first, a general clarification of the fundamental source, as the causes and conditions of the teachings of the One Vehicle throughout the ages constitute the source; second, the specific selection of phrases and sentences, such as the seven [cases]...).
Section on the Eight Returns and Other Passages: This section generally clarifies the meaning of the sutra’s principles (rather than allocating them according to the literal sequence of the text).

It provides a comprehensive explanation of the fundamental source based on a verse spoken by a Buddha of the past in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing. Arising and ceasing...
Having ceased, extinction is bliss. (The Buddha said: "Such verses were spoken by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; they open the path to the Dharma of emptiness. [△] Zhan’an said:

"As for the 'half-verse,' it speaks only of one side—impermanence—and does not speak of the side of permanence; therefore it is called a half-verse. Regarding the three characteristics of conditioned phenomena, why is only arising and ceasing explained while 'abiding' is not mentioned? Because the four-line verse is restrictive, it is omitted here.

Since the characteristic of abiding is not manifest, and arising and ceasing involve transition and change, it suffices to clarify the beginning and end; the middle is appropriately abbreviated. The text says: 'The meaning of emptiness that has been taught. This verse clarifies impermanence, so how can it be emptiness? Impermanence itself is simply another name for emptiness. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: 'Impermanence is movement.'"

Regarding characteristics: movement is the characteristic of emptiness. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Neither arising nor ceasing is the meaning of impermanence. Now, that which is impermanent is likewise the meaning of neither arising nor ceasing.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Aśvajit (the first of the five bhikṣus) spoke this verse to Śāriputra:

"All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; These phenomena are explained by causes and conditions; When these phenomena reach the end of causes and conditions, The Great Teacher has thus spoken.

[Note: After hearing this verse, Śāriputra immediately attained the First Path (*srota-āpanna*). He returned and informed Maudgalyāyana, who also attained the First Path. According to the original sutra, both Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana stated that this was spoken by the three Kāśyapas, whereas Ānanda stated that it was spoken by an old brahmin. Thus, the accounts of the origin differ.]
The Verse Response of Aśvajit (also known as Aśvaśirī; here translated as "Horse-Winner") from the *Fahua Wenzu*:

"All phenomena arise from conditions; therefore they are called 'dependent origination. These phenomena, their conditions, and their cessation—thus my Teacher has taught. [Some say: "All phenomena arise from conditions; all phenomena cease from conditions.

My Teacher, the Great Śramaṇa, always speaks thus. [Another says: "Such is cessation and such is arising; my Teacher has taught it thus. (*Chizengtuan* states: The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-Legged Beings knows that phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature. The Buddha-seed arises from...")

Regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): for this reason, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is taught. Yongming said: "The Buddha-seed of dependent origination refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha, not the *dharmakāya* Buddha. Since the Sūtra speaks in terms of the One Vehicle, how could one possibly differentiate between the *dharma-kāya* and the *saṃbhoga-kāya*?

As for what is called 'this Dharma abiding in the station of Dharma,' it is as Aśvaghoṣa stated: because one accords with the various cognitions of the world. Since the characteristics of the world are said to be 'various,' they do not arise solely from their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but rather all proceed from dependent origination.

Why is this so? Knowing that dependent origination is non-arising (*anutpāda*) is itself the Buddha-seed. Zao Bo said: "A single thought-moment of non-arising dependent origination transcends the provisional views of those in the three vehicles. Thus, one suddenly realizes the intent of the verse spoken by Kāśyapa."
Verses from the "Examination of Causal Conditions" (*Pratyaya-parīkṣā*) chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*: All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another;

They do not arise from both, nor without a cause; Therefore, it is known (or stated) that there is no arising. Commentary: Regarding "not arising from themselves," among all things, nothing arises from its own essence;
it must necessarily depend upon various causes and conditions. Furthermore, if something were to arise from its own essence, then a single phenomenon...
There are two entities: first, arising; second, that which arises. If [arising] were to arise from its own essence independently of other causes, then it would be without cause and without condition.

Furthermore, if there were an arising of arising, then arising would be infinite. Since the self does not exist, the other also does not exist. Why? Because it is through the existence of the self that the other exists.
If it does not arise from itself, nor does it arise from another, then as for arising from both— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "共生則" (arising from both then...).*
There are two faults: [the faults of] arising from self and arising from another. If the myriad things existed without a cause, they would be eternal;
this principle is not tenable. If there were no cause, there would be no effect. If there were an effect without a cause, then [virtues such as] giving and observing the precepts [would be useless].
One should fall into hell for the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes; yet one should be born in heaven because there is no cause. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"It is like an image in a mirror; it is not made by the mirror, not made by the face, not made by the one holding the mirror, nor is it produced spontaneously."

Nor does it arise without causes and conditions. Why is it not produced by the mirror? If the face has not yet reached the mirror, there is no reflection; for this reason, it is not produced by the mirror.
Why is it not produced by the face? Without the mirror, there is no reflection. Why is it not produced by the one holding the mirror?
Without the mirror and without the face, there is no reflection. Why is it not present spontaneously? If the mirror has not yet existed...

The face, however, has no image. The image exists only by depending on the mirror and depending on the face; for this reason, it is not produced spontaneously. Why is it not without causes and conditions?
If it were without causes and conditions, it should exist at all times. If it existed at all times, then even when the mirror and the face were removed, [the image] would remain.
They must also arise from themselves; for this reason, they do not lack causes and conditions. All phenomena are likewise:
they are not self-made, not made by another, not made by both, and not without causes and conditions. Why are they not self-made?

Because a "self" cannot be apprehended, because all things produced by causes lack autonomy, and because all phenomena are dependent upon causes and conditions. Nor are they made by another, for [the other] lacks...
Therefore, there is no other [agent]. If it were created by another, then the power of one's demerit and merit would be lost. If it were created by both, there would be two faults:
the fault of self and the fault of another. All phenomena necessarily have causes and conditions; these are the causes and conditions for the conjunction of suffering and pleasure.
When sought through reality, there is no person who acts and no person who receives. It is the empty five aggregates that act, and the empty five aggregates that receive.

The *Tiantai Zhiguan* states: When the sense faculties and their objects encounter one another, a single thought-moment arises. Both that which gives rise [to the thought] and that which is given rise to are without exception immediately empty.
To falsely claim that the mind arises is to overlook that this arising has no self-nature, no other-nature, no common nature, and no causeless nature.
When it arises, it does not come from self, other, both, or from neither; when it ceases, it does not go toward the east, west, south, or north.
This mind is not found within, without, or in between the two; nor does it exist eternally of its own accord. It exists only as a name, which we call "mind."
This term does not abide, nor does it not abide, because it is unattainable. Arising is non-arising, and there is also no non-arising. All phenomena do not arise from themselves;

how then could there be objective and subjective cognition arising from itself? They do not arise from another; how then could there be objective and subjective cognition arising through mutual dependence? They do not arise from both;

how then could there be objective and subjective cognition arising from causes and conditions? They do not arise without cause; how then could there be objective and subjective cognition arising spontaneously? You should know this.
The four graspings are the root of birth and death; therefore, Nāgārjuna cuts them down. Where there are four graspings, there is dependence; where there is dependence, there is right and wrong;
where there is right and wrong, there is attachment and aversion. From attachment and aversion, all afflictions arise. Because afflictions arise, conceptual proliferation and contention arise.
Because contention arises, the karma of body, speech, and mind is produced. Because karma is produced, one wanders in the ocean of suffering of saṃsāra.

There is no time for liberation. Now, by means of non-arising and so forth, the four natures are refuted. Because the natures are refuted, there is nothing to rely upon; thus, even karma, suffering, and the like do not exist.
When the pure mind is constantly one-pointed, one is able to see Prajñā. (One should contemplate this single thought: does the mind arise from itself?

Does the mind arise in response to an object? Does the mind arise from the sense organ and the object together? Does the mind arise apart from the sense organ and the object? (If the mind arises from itself: the preceding thought would be the sense organ (*indriya*) and the succeeding thought would be consciousness (*vijñāna*). [Does the mind] arise from the sense organ? Or does it arise from consciousness? If [it arises] from the sense organ...)

It is said that the sense organ (*indriya*) produces consciousness (*vijñāna*). Is it because the sense organ possesses consciousness that it produces consciousness? Or is it because the sense organ is devoid of consciousness that it produces consciousness? If the sense organ possessed consciousness, then the organ and the consciousness would be coextensive; furthermore, there would be no distinction between the producer and the produced. If the sense organ were devoid of consciousness yet could produce consciousness, then one must consider that an object devoid of consciousness cannot produce consciousness. Since the sense organ is itself devoid of consciousness, how can it produce consciousness?

If you argue that although the sense organ lacks consciousness, it possesses the *nature* (*dhātu*) of consciousness and therefore can produce consciousness, then we must ask: does this nature of consciousness exist or not? If it already exists, then it is already consciousness; and if it resides within the sense organ, then the organ itself would be consciousness.

What is meant by "the absence of nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*)? It means that the sense-faculties lack the nature of consciousness and are thus unable to produce consciousness. Furthermore, is the nature of consciousness identical to consciousness itself, or are they different? If they are one, then nature is itself consciousness; in that case, there would be neither a subject that acts nor an object upon which it acts.

If they are different, then consciousness would still be produced by something else, rather than arising from the mind itself. By investigating in this manner, one concludes that the mind does not arise from itself. [Objection: If it arises from another, then if you say the mind does not arise from itself, you must admit that the mind arises because external objects come to stimulate it. As a scripture states: "Thought arises when there is an object-condition; thought does not arise when there is no object-condition."

If that were so, since external objects exist outside [the mind] and come forth to trigger internal consciousness, the mind would arise from something other than itself. Now, let us investigate these objects: does the mind arise because they are of the nature of mind, or does it arise because they are not of the nature of mind? If the object were of the nature of mind, it could no longer be called an "object," nor would it be external to the mind;

thus, it would be identical to self-arising. Furthermore, if two minds were simultaneous, there would be neither subject nor object. If the object were not of the nature of mind, how could it produce a mind? This has already been refuted above. If you argue that the object possesses a generative nature and therefore produces the mind, is this nature existent or non-existent? If the nature...

If it exists, then the nature and the object likewise lack the distinction of subject and object. If it does not exist, then non-existence cannot produce anything. Thus, through such investigation, one knows that the mind ultimately does not arise from objects. (△ If they were produced together: If the mind arises because the sense organ and the object have conjoined, then since each of the organ and the object has its own [potential] mind, the mind must be produced by their conjunction.

Yet, since each individually lacks a mind, the mind must be produced by their conjunction. If each possessed a mind upon conjunction, then two minds would arise, falling into the error of self-nature and other-nature. If each individually lacks a mind, then there is no mind even at the time of conjunction; it is like the surface of a mirror.)

If each possesses a form, their union should produce a form; if each lacks a form, their union cannot produce a form. If the mirror surface were to unite as one and produce a form, it would not actually be uniting; for when there is union, there is no form.

If the mirror surface were to produce a form because it is separated [from the object], then since they would each occupy a different location, there should be a form; yet this is not actually the case. The same applies to the union and separation of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). By investigating in this way, one knows that the mind ultimately does not arise from union.

Furthermore, if it is claimed that the sense organs and objects each possess the nature of the mind and that the mind arises when they unite, one must examine whether this nature exists or does not exist (as was refuted previously regarding "arising from itself"). [△] If it arises from separation: if the sense organs and objects each exist separately, [the mind should arise].

Regarding the arising of the mind: this arises without causes or conditions. Is there such a thing as "separation" (detachment), or is there not? If there is such separation, it must still arise from conditions; what, then, would constitute "separation"? If there is no such separation, how could anything arise? If one says that this separation possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), is that nature existent or non-existent?

If the nature is existent, it still arises from conditions and cannot be called "separation. If the nature is non-existent, how could anything arise from nothing? By investigating in this manner, one knows that the mind ultimately does not arise from separation. (From the *Chizengtuan*)

It is said: The Tathāgata investigated the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), finding each and every one to be empty. That which is not produced by causes does not arise from itself; that which is not produced by conditions does not arise from another. Since there is neither self nor other, how could there be a combination? This is non-arising through co-production. Since it is not of a spontaneous nature, it is not produced without cause.

When the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) reveal no arising, from where could the elements (dhātus) possibly exist? [Commentary] Xunwen says: The Venerable Nāgārjuna, because the faculties of people in later ages had become dull, extensively composed methods of contemplation. In reality, he used these to investigate the four [propositions].

Nature is the fundamental basis. This is to correctly follow the final instructions bequeathed by the Tathāgata. (The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* states: "The 'cause' is the conceptualization of self-nature; the 'condition' is the conceptualization of other-nature; the combination of cause and condition is the conceptualization of common nature;

and spontaneity is the conceptualization of causelessness. These constitute the investigation through the contemplation of the four natures, which leads one to perceive non-arising. If all phenomena were to arise from self-nature, how could they arise without conditions? It would be like water without wind—how could it spontaneously form waves? If one says they arise from other conditions, how could another entity itself produce a phenomenon? It is as follows...")

If there is no water, how can the wind give rise to waves? If you say they arise together, this is not tenable, for if each lacks [the capacity] individually, how could it exist when combined? Furthermore, since "togetherness" involves both sides, to which entity does the essence belong? Since even "arising together" is not possible, how could there be "causelessness"? When these four are empty, names are also extinguished;

once the attachments to nature and characteristics are removed, the three emptinesses manifest of themselves. Qingliang says: Non-Buddhists claim that the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the self and Brahmā is the other.
The combination of atoms constitutes the "common" [cause]; spontaneity is thus without cause.
Furthermore, these four views also belong to the Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Ajita Keśakambalin, and Lokāyata schools.

Verses from the "Examination of the Four Noble Truths" chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*: "Of those phenomena produced by various causes and conditions (in the *Zhi guan* and other editions, this is rendered as 'phenomena produced by causes and conditions'), I say they are emptiness;
they are also provisional designations, and they are also the meaning of the Middle Way. Commentary:

Regarding the statement, "Of those phenomena produced by various causes and conditions, I say they are emptiness," why is this so? Because when a multitude of conditions are fully assembled, a thing arises. This is...

All phenomena depend upon a multitude of causes and conditions; therefore, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty. This emptiness is itself empty as well.
It is spoken of through provisional names merely to guide sentient beings. By departing from the two extremes of existence and non-existence, it is called the Middle Way.
The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "Now, we shall combine the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* with these fourfold Four Noble Truths. The treatise says: "That which is produced by causes and conditions..."
"Dharma" refers to the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing; what I call "emptiness" refers to the Four Noble Truths of non-arising.
It is also called "provisional names," which refers to the immeasurable Four Noble Truths. It is also called the meaning of the "Middle Way," which refers to the unconditioned Four Noble Truths.

(When the Northern Qi Chan Master Huiwen read this verse, he attained a sudden and profound awakening, realizing at once that all dharmas are nothing other than those produced by causes and conditions. Furthermore, these causes and conditions are not fixed as existing, and emptiness is not fixed as empty. The non-duality of emptiness and existence is called...)

It constitutes the Middle Way. Having obtained the textual basis for the "one mind and three wisdoms," the Master Zhiyi established his contemplation based on these treatises. Having received the transmission from Nanyue, he established the Four Teachings based on the Three Contemplations.

○ Qingliang said: "The term 'causes and conditions' applies universally to the Four Teachings. Because of causes and conditions there is arising and ceasing; because of causes and conditions there is emptiness; because of causes and conditions there are provisional names;
and because of causes and conditions there is the Middle Way. Since causes and conditions are primary, all four teachings are permeated by them. Furthermore, regarding these four teachings:"

It arises through three types of contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). From the conventional entering into emptiness, because the substance is analyzed as distinct, there are the first two teachings (the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings).

From emptiness entering into the conventional, and from the conventional entering into the Middle Way, there is the arising of the Distinct Teaching. When the three contemplations are attained within a single moment of mind, there is the arising of the Perfect Teaching. (△孤山云 [Gushan says])

These three forms of stillness (*śamatha*) are precisely the Three Contemplations of Tiantai: *śamatha* is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); *samādhi* is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*); and *dhyāna* is the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*). This is what is meant by Nāgārjuna’s Fourfold Verse.

When Ānanda first requested instruction on the three dharmas and received this revelation, his realization culminated in him praising the Buddha with these very same three: "The Wondrously Profound, the Universal Retainer, the Immovable Honored One. Here, "Wondrously Profound" refers to the wisdom of emptiness; "Universal Retainer" refers to the wisdom of the provisional; and "Immovable" refers to the wisdom of the Middle.

Furthermore, when the Buddha expounded the Tathāgatagarbha to Pūrṇa as the fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind—neither mind nor empty, yet both mind and empty; transcending both affirmation and negation—the Three Truths shone forth as clearly as pointing at one's own palm. And when he explained the six deliverances to Ānanda...

Upon his passing, he sighed in lamentation, saying: "This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Vajra-King’s Precious Enlightenment, and the Illusion-like Samādhi. The metaphor of 'the flower opening and the lotus appearing' represents the Middle Way (the Provisional). The metaphor of the 'Vajra's hardness and sharpness' represents Emptiness. The metaphor of 'illusion having form' represents the Provisional.

Furthermore, when Mañjuśrī selected and demonstrated the Perfect Penetration, he likewise used this as a metaphor, saying: "I, relying on the Buddha’s majestic power, proclaim the Vajra-King, the Illusion-like, the Inconceivable, the Mother of Buddhas, the True Samādhi. Thus, it is merely the "Mother of Buddhas" that serves as the metaphor.

The Middle Way is merely different [in its expression]. Throughout various texts, it is expounded layer upon layer, refuting delusion point by point. Sometimes it employs emptiness (*śūnyatā*), sometimes it discusses the provisional (*prajñapti*), and sometimes it reveals the Middle; though the words may seem partial, the intent is always complete, for they all fully possess the three natures (the three dharmas). [Longshui says:

"The seeing, the objects of seeing, and the perceived characteristics" refer to the phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*). "Like flowers in the sky, originally non-existent"—this I call emptiness. "This seeing and its objects are also called provisional names.
"Originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi"—this is also called the meaning of the Middle Way.]
The Verses of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Pal-zhen-lun): "The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty, For they arise dependently like illusions. Unconditioned phenomena have no reality;
Their non-arising is like flowers in the sky. Qingliang states: "The verses of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* were composed by the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka."

The *Ekavyavahārika* (or *Ekalakṣaṇa*) treatise explains only this verse. According to the current text, this is the opening verse of the gāthās further proclaimed by the World-Honored One in the fifth fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
Qingliang states that Bhāviveka composed a treatise that explains only this verse;
it is precisely an exegesis of the verse spoken by the Tathāgata. Within this, there are two layers of inference (*anumāna*), as fully detailed in the *Mengchao*.
A separate phrase: "Seven Places Examining the Mind.
Master Duan’s verse says: "Seven places examined, yet the mind was not found; Dull-witted Ānanda did not perceive it.
Even if one were to examine until seeing the mindless, It would still be like washing clods of earth in the mud. [East]...
Linyan said: "The interrogation regarding the seven locations of the mind has already reached its conclusion; the investigation and pursuit have yielded clear evidence.

The tip of the nose (as the verse by Meihua Ni says: "All day long seeking spring, one finds no spring; straw sandals tread across the clouds atop the ridge. "How can there be hells, hungry ghosts, and animals? Wan’an Yan’s verse says: Before the Double Sword Peak lies the ruins of an ancient temple;

Greed, hatred, and delusion. Dongshan’s verse says: Greed, hatred, and delusion—how utterly ignorant they are!

The manifestation of spiritual penetration: all that is done constantly contains wondrous enlightenment. When *śrāvakas* cling to dharmas and practice seated meditation, they are like silkworms spinning silk to bind themselves.

To fully realize the equality of all phenomena is to dwell in a state of carefree, pure, and joyful emptiness. When deluded, one takes emptiness to be form; when awakened, one takes form to be emptiness. Thus it is with delusion and awakening.
Fundamentally there is no distinction; form and emptiness are ultimately identical. The fool calls south north; the wise person realizes there is neither west nor east.
If you wish to seek the wondrous principle of the Tathāgata, it is always present within a single thought-moment. A mirage is fundamentally not water.
The thirsty deer chases in frantic haste; its own body is empty, false, and unreal, yet it seeks emptiness within emptiness.
How extreme is the delusion of worldly people! They are like dogs barking at thunder, their howling echoing loudly.
Master Fu’s "The Difficulty of Traveling the Road. Do you not see? Within the dharma of certainty, there is no certainty;
delusion and inversion are themselves bodhi. If the mind discriminates the dharmas of bodhi, such discrimination regarding bodhi leads back to confusion.
If one realizes this confusion is without discrimination, then confusion and discrimination are themselves bodhi. Discriminating bodhi is neither identical nor different; it is ever...
Of the same essence, they do not exclude one another; they abide securely in the true nature of emptiness. In emptiness, there is no emptiness, nor is anything carried away.
This same essence contains all through great compassion; thus, know that true nature does not conflict with delusion.

This very confusion is itself without self-nature, and it cannot be discussed in terms of being equal or unequal. If one abandons worldly toil, there is no other dharma; it is like a pure flower growing from filth.
The mire. The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata has no separate location; it pervades the mire of suffering throughout the three realms. Yet, the mire of the three realms is fundamentally non-existent.
Who, then, can perceive its subtle path? Difficult is the journey. This difficulty is itself, from the very beginning, Nirvāṇa.
The internal and external, body and mind, are all together empty and still. Where can inverted greed and anger find rest? Do you not see?
The wise person seeks the mind, not the Buddha. When all phenomena are extinguished, that is itself free from lust.

Lust neither arises nor ceases; its inversions are neither shallow nor deep. Furthermore, one cannot find that which is not lustful;
this wondrous state, beyond both attainment and non-attainment, is difficult to seek. Within the nature of the three poisons, it is always thus: fully present, ever the same as a firm forest.
Taking other matters of lust as the Buddha-work, the three poisons can no longer intrude crosswise. If one seeks liberation...

They sink back down again; though they distinguish between emerging and submerging, they sink once more. The Buddhas have skillfully mastered the three poisons, yet sentient beings, through their delusions, cannot bear them.

The path is difficult; though the path is difficult, within the mind there is fundamentally nothing. This absence of anything is itself pure bodhi; within this mind of non-seeing, it is ever thus.

Behold the Buddha! Do you not see? Mañjuśrī’s wondrous virtue is not far away. The three obstacles and the three poisons are themselves the three emptinesses. The fivefold Dharma-body envelops the five aggregates;

the ignorance within the six sense-bases constitutes the six supernormal powers. How could the four inversions ever differ from the four fruits? The essence of the eight heterodoxies and the eight orthodoxies is identical.
The nature of the seven factors of enlightenment and bodhi is without distinction; the seven consciousnesses that wander in flux shall eventually meet [in realization].
In the True Sect, all afflictions are empty and quiescent; the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas resides within the heart and breast.

One constantly follows along with the patience of the Dharma, yet due to one's own errors, one does not encounter it. Where do the Buddhas and Tathāgatas dwell? They are found entirely amidst greed, lust, and desire.

Primordially, Bodhi has been my craftsman; now it makes me the master craftsman for the multitude. In the past, I sought the Buddha in a thousand external directions; only now do I realize the Buddha was within my own robes.

In former days, through arduous toil, one studied knowledge and views, yet did not know that wisdom and vision are themselves non-knowing.

The four realms of existence and the three evil paths do not exist at all; the three obstructions and the three liberations are not separate. The path is difficult; the difficulty of the path has no duality.

Do you not see? Unsurpassed Bodhi is most near; the four elements and five aggregates are all profoundly deep. (The Dharma-nature is without knowledge and cannot be described; the out-flowing and non-out-flowing are both empty and pervasive.

Sudden and violent; within the nature of harmony there is no reality. Therefore, it is called the essential core of all phenomena (*dharmas*). Within it, there is neither falsehood nor truth;

The Verse on the Dharma-Eye: "The Three Realms are Mind-Only. It says: The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Consciousness-only is mind-only:

Place a flat stone upon your heart (the eyes have no object before them). Master Rong’s verse says: "A blind dog barks at a thicket of reeds;

If one allows that delusion arises from the true, then this delusion... Master Mi (Mazu Daoyi) explained: "The meaning is that the fundamental purity is like space; since it is the very root of delusion, how could it ever arise? [He] permits that delusion arises from the true. This delusion...

How could it possibly cease? (If the real were truly able to give rise to the delusory, then only by removing the real would the delusory be removed. (Regarding the beginning and end, there are four analytical propositions: first, having a beginning but no end, which is *samyagbodhi* (perfect enlightenment); second, having an end but no beginning, which is *avidyā* (ignorance);

third, having neither end nor beginning, which refers to the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality); fourth, having both beginning and end, which is the cycle of birth and death over a single period. I pray that you will reveal the secret and analyze this so that I may transcend birth and death. Master Chengguan replied: "When one is deluded regarding the Real, deluded thoughts arise; when one awakens to the Real..."

When delusion ceases, that which can cause confusion is no longer what is confused; how could they be entirely identical? (Because they are neither one nor different, as in the analogy of the ocean and its waves found in the Treatise.

when one is deluded, it is termed beginningless. Causes and conditions are like illusions and dreams—what end could there be, and what beginning? This is the original source of sentient beings.
Exhausting [the root of] delusion brings one out of birth and death. Furthermore, many people claim that the Real truly gives rise to the false;

thus, they doubt whether the false can ever be exhausted. To resolve this principle, he again answers the previous verse: It is not that the Real gives rise to the false; rather, the false arises from the delusion regarding Suchness.

Knowing that the false is fundamentally Real, and knowing the Real, the false immediately ceases. When the false ceases, it seems like an end; when awakening comes, it seems like a beginning. This is the nature of delusion and awakening.

All are empty. Their nature is emptiness, having neither beginning nor end. Birth and death arise from delusion regarding this; to penetrate it is to transcend birth and death (*The Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states:

"Delusion falsely relies upon the True to arise, and thus the True is spoken of as the source. At present, one is deluded regarding the True, yet the True is fundamentally without delusion. Since that which serves as the basis has no arising at all, what could there be to cease? This first chapter can precisely clarify this point; it also accords with the citations from the "Universal Worthy Chapter" found in Guifeng’s *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra*.
The verse by Changqing Lǐng says: "Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. Only when a person consents of their own accord do they become intimate with it.
In the past, I mistakenly sought it along the road; Today, looking at it, it is ice within fire. (Fayan asked Head Seat Zhāo:

"As for the saying, 'Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed,' does this negate the myriad phenomena, or does it not negate them? Zhāo said, "It does not negate them.
