Zuo said, "What do you call the myriad phenomena? Fang said, "The ancients did not negate the myriad phenomena. Yan said, "'Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. What do you mean by 'negating' or 'not negating'? (Wansong said:

"This shows that Fayen received the words and realized the source, thereby developing the subtlety of the two masters. Zhaofang investigated the subtlety but lost the source; this is the fault of his turbid intellect wandering in transmigration. (Neijiang Jicheng said: "The Tathāgata said, 'It is present before you,' yet this meaning is not ultimate. Within the myriad phenomena, it is not...")

It can be peeled away; it must be that which is manifested by the object itself. A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou replied, "The cypress tree in the courtyard.

This means that there is not a single thing that does not proclaim the name of the Tathāgata; the principle that "insentient things preach the Dharma" lies herein. He further said, "Among all these things, which one is not seeing? Previously, through the mutual negation of subject and object, the tree was excluded and no seeing remained. Now, through the mutual differentiation of subject and object, the tree is able to possess seeing. Changqing said, "Within the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed.

Fayan raised this question to test whether [Zhaozhou] was negating the myriad phenomena or not negating them; this is the intent of such an examination. Furthermore, he said, "If there were seeing, there should be something pointed out"—this is not negating the myriad phenomena. If it were not seeing...
[If it were] such, there would be nothing to point toward (it would be a denial of the myriad phenomena).
Nanquan’s verse says: "Empty space asks the myriad phenomena; the myriad phenomena answer empty space. Who has personally heard this? The novice monk Mokṣa.
Where there is obstruction, it is not a wall; where there is penetration, do not call it empty space. If a person understands in this way, [they will see that]...
"Mind and form are fundamentally the same.
The following passage is a general verse from a sutra.
Yun’an Zhenjing’s *Lengyan Ge* (Verses on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) sent to Xu Chaosan says: "The ten-volume *Śūraṅgama* is a forest of myriad dharmas. Dharma...
The gates are opened wide as the capacity of beings is profound; eight returns and four approaches first remove the ore. Three gradual stages and seven inquiries still refine the gold.
When seeing sees, one should see the nature; where hearing hears, one must hear the mind. May you, O Governor, for the sake of all beings, extend invitations to the Sangha;
entrust this to them so that the Buddha’s true voice shall not be forgotten. Written by Qi Chushih for the Dharma Master Dezhan of Zhaoti Temple.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* speaks in eighteen verses: "To attain the Way, one must extensively deliver sentient beings;
to deliver sentient beings, one must cause their fundamental nature and mind to be clear. In Jambudvīpa there is the Brahma-mantra; in Naraka there is no lustful passion.
When Ānanda emerged, he encountered the net of Māra; when Mañjuśrī arrived, he protected the sinking boat of the Dharma. Extensive learning alone cannot be considered extraordinary."
Cultivation through vast eons lies in diligent practice. Whether externally reaching to empty space or internally within the physical body, nothing at all exists apart from the truth of this mind.

A floating bubble is insufficient to exhaust the vastness of the ocean; one must cast aside the finger and recognize the lunar orb. The mind that conditions hearing the Dharma is not the fundamental nature;
the true master of the pavilion is surely not a passing traveler. Free from sound and form, there is no discrimination. To plant upon a stone—
Flowers bloom at the bottom of the well; with hands opening and closing, jewel-lights fly forth. Looking back and forth to the left and right, who is this?
One must believe that where this head moves, it does not hinder the state of total stillness. When the mind is clarified and nature is seen, there is neither expansion nor contraction.
To recognize objects and follow after the flow of deluded perception—this is the true speech of the Unsurpassed Dharma King.
How could it compare to the falsehoods of Maskari Gośālī? The nature of King Prasenajit has never shifted; seeing the Ganges as he did in his youth, he perceives it now as it was when old.

There is no need for sorrow over aging or white hair; floating clouds will surely disperse into the blue sky. From whence they came, those people of antiquity are gone; having departed, they have become the wilderness.
The bones of the mound have already been discarded; when the kalpa-fire blazes forth, not a single thing remains. This is clearly the state before one’s parents were born.

When the mind is interrogated at the seven locations, the mind is not found; when the seeing is analyzed through the eight returns, the seeing is fundamentally non-existent. Thus, the thousandfold secret locks are rent asunder.

A single, luminous pearl bursts forth; from this point on, the conceptual understandings of sages and ordinary beings are severed. What birth and death, or the constraints of temperament and nature, can there be?
When the *huatou* (critical phrase) is raised, those who truly know it are few; it is left for the world as a model.

Earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—pervading the entire Dharma-realm, they are originally perfect. One should know that the true meaning is not found in words; it arises from false conceptualization.
Conditions and nature arise and cease without source; the essence is eternally abiding. Those who are coarse and superficial do not realize what this sutra explains:
which sentient being does not become a Buddha? This serves as a condition for their deliverance in the future. The faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are the Tathāgatagarbha.
Within a single hair-tip, one penetrates the ten directions. The great earth never fails to assist in its manifestation; empty space, having a mouth, proclaims it of itself.
Sentient beings do not maintain their true *tathatā* nature, yet all Buddhas dwell in the light of eternal quiescence. What can obstruct birth, death, departure, or arrival?
A bird flies across the vast blue sky, which knows no end. Awakened clarity is distinct from the clarity of awakening, yet they are ultimately the same as the mountain.
The great earth and the void are like a river; the madness of Yanjadha’s mind subsides of its own accord. The spell of the Mātanga girl cannot ensnare him;

it directly causes fundamental ignorance to be severed, thereby bringing one into communion with the wondrous principle of the Tathāgata. All conditioned phenomena of the three periods of time possess extinction;

the ten directions of space are beginningless and certainly have no end. Within the perfect and profound stillness, the meanings of "one" and "six" arise; once "one" is lost, the "six" are entirely dissolved.
Melted away, detached from clinging, the mind is inwardly stilled and is not something that exists; the labor of manifesting the external objects is revealed as being fundamentally empty by nature.

Free and at ease, rising and sinking like a fish released from a net, there is no hindrance to going or staying, like a crane leaving its cage. How can one describe the mutual functioning of each faculty? It is precisely the same as untangling the knots on the flowered silk scarf.
How excellent are these twenty-five perfect means of penetration (*āveśa*); each has practiced them so as not to dwell in emptiness. Thus they have realized entry.
Though the Dharma gates differ, the awakening to the original nature of the mind-ground is the same. Contemplating the words of Samantabhadra is most discerning;
choosing the ear of Avalokiteśvara is most acute. By the embankment, green willows freshen after the rain; several times the yellow birds warble in the spring breeze.
Abandon lust, eliminate killing, and further distance yourself from theft; it is difficult to attain Buddhahood by seeking it through false speech.

If one maintains these four precepts without defilement, those demonic obstacles will have no cause to arise. Once the site of practice is established and the mind and body are pure, the divine mantras are proclaimed throughout the oceans of lands.
Immeasurable Vajra-holders come to protect the Dharma; may they take their vajras and shatter the heads of the evil Māras. Eighty thousand...

The four thousand inverted perceptions serve as the causes for the twelve classes of beings. When the wondrous, luminous nature of awareness is awakened, the false and floating mind is itself the fundamental reality.
Whether dragons, ghosts, celestial immortals, or those with red flesh-topskirts, with feathers, scales, or shells, they all possess bodies of purple-gold.
Who can sit in stillness and contemplate this? Within, without, and in between, it is utterly free from a speck of dust. All sentient beings in the three realms dwell by means of food;
forever abandon wine and meat, and sever the mind of lust. When mutual birth and mutual killing no longer exist as karma, external objects and external demons will never invade.
Carve the precepts into the bone and engrave them upon the skin; wherever you are, draw near to the Buddha and receive his profound voice. Amidst the lapis lazuli...
Furthermore, it hangs like the bright moon; a single radiance illuminates both past and present. When wisdom first clarifies, the tendencies of desire dry up;
the stage proceeds from the forty-fourth mind to rest in peace. Believing in the original Middle Way as the pure, true nature, one receives empowerment like a king handing over his kingdom.

The mind that benefits others and delivers sentient beings grows ever more vast; turning toward the truth yet facing the mundane world, how broad is the path! To ascend the Ten Stages, one must apply diligent practice;

the workings of awakening are layered upon layered, both manifold and singular. I have heard that hell originally does not exist; as soon as the ten habitual tendencies are formed, the six retributions arrive.
If one turns evil thoughts to teach others, they become the blessings of a Buddha; by a single shout, the mountain of blades becomes a golden terrace. One who is not greedy for heaven...
Regarding the matters of celestial joy and pleasure, he was willing to receive a human womb of love and desire. His original nature as Amitābha is ever-manifest;

a single lotus flower awaits the time to bloom. The ten classes of beings originally stem from the division of the ten ghosts; when their lives end and their retribution is exhausted, they are reborn as humans once more.
The ten classes of immortals rely on this short or long life; within the three realms, they do not escape the body of birth and death.

Though the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha) dwells at the summit of existence, and great Arhats have emerged from the mundane dust, even those who exhaust the Great Way of Emptiness find no place of return. They cannot avoid entering the cycle once more from the beginning.
They must successively dissolve the five aggregates and the ten dhyānas, and through fifteen stages, repeatedly destroy the evil Māras. Only when one’s own [nature] is enlightened...
Sorrow is separated by deep darkness; how can solid ice withstand boiling water? When one’s own mind is awakened, it is no different from attaining sainthood;
like water flowing level, how could there be any difference between waves? Reaching even unto Bodhi, there is not the slightest lack—everyone praises Ānanda.
The five aggregates have always been empty in essence; these five layers of delusive thought await eradication. They do not depart from the wondrously luminous nature of original enlightenment;

one must recognize the root source from which they first arise. For countless kalpas, they have been perfumed by habits beyond calculation; yet when the six faculties function interchangeably, they are extinguished without remainder.

Even if one were to fill the void with precious offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, such merit would not equal that of one who extensively propagates this sutra. —Zibo Ke *Note: This is a verse from the *Sūtra of the Lotus Flower of the Wonderful Dharma*, specifically the "Expedient Means" chapter, translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva.*

In the *Verses on Reading the Śūraṅgama Sūtra* (Lengyan ge), Shishi (Shishuang Qingzhu) says: "The ten-fascicle *Śūraṅgama* is a single-edged blade; The golden ox does not see the hair before its eyes.
If you test-drive the sword of wisdom upon the horse of the mind, The ignorance of accumulated kalpas will vanish in an instant."

Written by the junior scholar of Dagu in Luoyang, the śrāmaṇera Zhikong, who resides at Guanglong Temple.
